messages.content: I have Alesha, Who Smiles at Death and Sakashima of a Thousand Faces. Can I use them together with Medomai the Ageless to gain extra turns?

Yes, this combination creates an infinite loop. The combo works by using Alesha, Who Smiles at Death to return Sakashima of a Thousand Faces from your graveyard to the battlefield tapped and attacking as a copy of Medomai the Ageless. You must pay {W/B}{W/B} (not {U/B}{U/B}) to activate Alesha's ability. Because Sakashima enters as a copy of Medomai, it gains Medomai's triggered ability: 'Whenever Medomai deals combat damage to a player, take an extra turn after this one.' By dealing combat damage with this copied Sakashima, you trigger that ability and gain an extra turn. To repeat the loop, sacrifice Sakashima using Umbral Collar Zealot's ability ('Sacrifice another creature or artifact: Surveil 1') to put it back into your graveyard, allowing you to reanimate it again on subsequent turns.
Is there a way to generate infinite sacrifice triggers by manipulating my graveyard with cards like Circling Vultures and Ashnod's Altar?

Yes, you can achieve infinite sacrifice triggers using a combination of Disa the Restless, Enduring Renewal, Circling Vultures, Ashes of the Fallen, and Ashnod's Altar. The loop works as follows: 1. Use Ashes of the Fallen to give all creature cards in your graveyard the type 'Lhurgoyf'. 2. Discard Circling Vultures from your hand using its static ability. 3. Disa the Restless triggers because a Lhurgoyf card was put into your graveyard, putting Circling Vultures onto the battlefield. 4. Activate Ashnod's Altar by sacrificing Circling Vultures to add {C}{C}. 5. Enduring Renewal triggers when Circling Vultures is put into the graveyard from the battlefield, returning it to your hand. 6. Repeat by discarding Circling Vultures again.

I have an artifact that creates Food tokens and turns sacrificed Food into Treasure, plus a creature that lets me sacrifice artifacts to look at the top of my library. Can I use these together for something bigger than just mana or card selection?

Yes, you can generate infinite resources using this combination. By pairing the Nuka-Cola Vending Machine with the Umbral Collar Zealot, you can trigger a loop that produces infinite tapped Treasure tokens. The Vending Machine's triggered ability creates a Food token whenever you sacrifice one, and if you also have Academy Manufactor on the battlefield, it converts that single creation into a Clue, Food, and Treasure simultaneously. Since the Umbral Collar Zealot allows you to sacrifice an artifact (like the newly created Food) as a cost to activate its ability, you can keep sacrificing the Food tokens generated by the Vending Machine's trigger. This cycle repeats indefinitely, resulting in infinite tapped Treasure tokens.
I have Krark-Clan Ironworks and want infinite cards. Is there a creature combo that generates mana from artifact sacrifices?

Yes, this is possible using Krark-Clan Ironworks, Eldrazi Displacer, and Wavesifter. The combo works by using Eldrazi Displacer ({2}{C}) to exile Wavesifter and return it to the battlefield tapped. Because Wavesifter has the text 'When this creature enters, investigate twice,' its ETB trigger fires upon returning, creating two Clue tokens. You then sacrifice these Clues using Krark-Clan Ironworks ('Sacrifice an artifact: Add {C}{C}') to generate four colorless mana. Since you can now pay the activation cost for Eldrazi Displacer again, you repeat the process infinitely. The concrete outcome of this combo is infinite card draw.
I have Yomiji, Who Bars the Way and Altar of Dementia in my deck. Is there a way to loop them for infinite value?

Yes, but you need one more specific piece: The First Sliver. By combining Yomiji, Who Bars the Way, Altar of Dementia, and The First Sliver, you can generate infinite death triggers. The process works as follows: First, activate Altar of Dementia by sacrificing The First Sliver. This causes a legendary permanent (The First Sliver) to go from the battlefield to the graveyard, which triggers Yomiji, Who Bars the Way's ability: "Whenever a legendary permanent other than Yomiji is put into a graveyard from the battlefield, return that card to its owner's hand." Yomiji returns The First Sliver to your hand. Then, resolve the Altar of Dementia trigger. Next, cast The First Sliver again (it costs {W}{U}{B}{R}{G}, but since you just sacrificed it, you can recast it). When The First Sliver enters the battlefield, its Cascade ability triggers, but more importantly for this specific loop context in the provided data, you simply repeat the sacrifice. However, based strictly on the authoritative combo steps provided: Step 1 is sacrificing The First Sliver to Altar of Dementia. Step 2 is Yomiji returning it. Step 4 allows you to cast it again. This cycle repeats indefinitely, resulting in infinite death triggers.
I have a way to cast historic spells from the top of my library for free. Can I use Sensei's Divining Top with Displacer Kitten to generate value?

Yes, this is a highly efficient engine. By using The Fourth Doctor's ability 'Would You Like A...?' to play a historic land or cast a historic spell from the top of your library for {0}, you can cast Sensei's Divining Top (which is an Artifact and thus Historic) without paying its mana cost. This triggers Displacer Kitten's ability, 'Whenever you cast a noncreature spell, exile up to one target nonland permanent you control...'. You target Sensei's Divining Top itself. When it blinks (exiles and returns), The Fourth Doctor also sees you have played/cast a historic spell from the top of your library, triggering its ETB-like text 'When you do, create a Food token.' This creates one Food token per cycle. After blinking, the Sensei's Divining Top is back on the battlefield with summoning sickness, but you can activate its second ability '{T}: Draw a card, then put this artifact on top of its owner's library' to return it to the top of your library untapped. In subsequent turns, you repeat the process: play the Top from the library for {0}, blink it with Displacer Kitten, get a Food token, draw a card, and place it back on top. This loop generates near-infinite Life Tokens (Food) and card advantage.
How does the Sarkhan and Deadeye Navigator infinite combo work with Kaya?

This combo creates an infinite loop generating Treasure tokens using three key pieces: Sarkhan, Dragon Ascendant; Deadeye Navigator; and Kaya, Geist Hunter. Here is the step-by-step chain: 1. Activate Kaya's [-2] ability to double tokens created this turn. 2. Pay {1}{U} to activate Deadeye Navigator's blink ability on Sarkhan (they must be soulbonded). 3. Sarkhan enters the battlefield, triggering its ETB ability. You behold a Dragon and create a Treasure token. Kaya doubles this, creating two Treasures. 4. Activate the two Treasures ({1}{U} each) to pay for the next blink. 5. Repeat step 2. The concrete outcome is an infinite number of Treasure tokens created per loop.
I have Jegantha, the Wellspring in my command zone and Horde of Notions in play. Is there a way to generate infinite value with these two cards?

Yes, this combination generates Infinite LTB (Legends To Battlefield). The process begins by activating Jegantha's ability: '{T}: Add {W}{U}{B}{R}{G}. This mana can't be spent to pay generic mana costs.' You tap Jegantha to produce these five colored mana. Next, you activate Horde of Notions's ability: '{W}{U}{B}{R}{G}: You may play target Elemental card from your graveyard without paying its mana cost.' Assuming Ashling's Command is in your graveyard (or cast previously), you use the mana from Jegantha to return it to your hand and cast it. When resolving Ashling's Command, you choose the mode 'Create a token that's a copy of target Elemental you control,' targeting Jegantha. This creates a copy of Jegantha on the battlefield. Because you now control two legendary permanents with the same name (the original tapped Jegantha and the new token Jegantha), the legend rule forces you to put one of them into the graveyard. You choose the original, tapped Jegantha. This leaves you with an untapped copy of Jegantha and Ashling's Command in the graveyard. By repeating this process—tapping the copy of Jegantha, returning Ashling's Command, copying the new Jegantha, and sacrificing the old one via the legend rule—you achieve Infinite LTB.
I have a big elemental elk and a vampire knight. How do I loop them to get infinite life total changes?

To achieve an infinite Life Total change (LTB), you need four specific pieces: Jegantha, the Wellspring; Horde of Notions; Bartolomé del Presidio; and Fervor. The combo works by cycling mana and creatures. First, activate Jegantha, the Wellspring's ability ({T}: Add {W}{U}{B}{R}{G}) to generate five colored mana symbols. Next, sacrifice Jegantha as a cost for Bartolomé del Presidio's ability (Sacrifice another creature or artifact: Put a +1/+1 counter on Bartolomé del Presidio). You now have five colored mana and Jegantha in your graveyard. Then, pay {W}{U}{B}{R}{G} to activate Horde of Notions' ability ({W}{U}{B}{R}{G}: You may play target Elemental card from your graveyard without paying its mana cost) to cast Jegantha again for free. Finally, use Fervor to give her haste, allowing you to tap her immediately in the same turn to repeat the cycle. The concrete outcome of this combo is Infinite LTB.
I have Cauldron of Souls and Altar of Dementia. Is there a way to use them together to mill an opponent's entire library quickly?

No, you cannot achieve this with just Cauldron of Souls and Altar of Dementia. To make the combo work infinitely, you also need Corridor Monitor and Cathars' Crusade. The sequence is: 1) Tap Cauldron of Souls to give Corridor Monitor Persist. 2) Sacrifice Corridor Monitor to Altar of Dementia to mill cards equal to its power. 3) Corridor Monitor returns to the battlefield with a -1/-1 counter due to Persist. 4) As it enters, Corridor Monitor's ETB untaps Cauldron of Souls, and Cathars' Crusade puts a +1/+1 counter on every creature you control (including the returned Corridor Monitor). 5) The +1/+1 counter cancels out the -1/-1 counter, leaving Corridor Monitor with no counters. 6) Repeat. Without Cathars' Crusade, the monitor will retain the -1/-1 counter and fail to persist on subsequent deaths.
I have Dimir Aqueduct, Voyaging Satyr, and Pemmin's Aura. How can I use these together to generate resources?

This combination creates an infinite resource loop. Here is the step-by-step mechanism: 1. Activate Dimir Aqueduct by tapping it ({T}), which adds {U}{B} to your mana pool. Note that Dimir Aqueduct enters tapped, but you can tap it immediately upon playing it or if it was previously untapped. 2. Activate Voyaging Satyr by tapping it ({T}) and choosing Dimir Aqueduct as the target. This untaps Dimir Aqueduct. 3. Now that Dimir Aqueduct is untapped, you have {U}{B} available. Pay {U} to activate Pemmin's Aura's first ability ("{U}: Untap enchanted creature"). Assuming Voyaging Satyr is the enchanted creature, this untaps Voyaging Satyr. 4. With both Dimir Aqueduct and Voyaging Satyr untapped, you can repeat steps 1 through 3 indefinitely. The concrete outcome of this combo is: Infinite {U}{B} mana.
Can I build an infinite loop with Furyborn Hellkite and Atog?

Yes, by adding Cauldron of Souls and Dross Scorpion to the deck, you can achieve a specific loop. You start by activating Cauldron of Souls ({T}) to give your Furyborn Hellkite Persist until end of turn. Then, you sacrifice the Hellkite using Atog's ability (Sacrifice an artifact: This creature gets +2/+2 until end of turn). When the Hellkite dies, its Persist trigger returns it to the battlefield from the graveyard (as it had no -1/-1 counters), and Dross Scorpion triggers to untap Cauldron of Souls. The Hellkite enters with +1/+1 counters due to Bloodthirst 6. This sequence allows you to repeat the process indefinitely. The concrete outcome is infinite death triggers.
How does the interaction between Sakashima the Impostor and Candelabra of Tawnos work in this specific combo to enable the loop?

The interaction works as follows: 1) Cyberdrive Awakener animates Candelabra of Tawnos. 2) Sakashima the Impostor enters copying Candelabra, gaining '{X}, {T}: Untap X target lands'. 3) Uthros generates mana ({U}{U}{U}+). 4) Activate Sakashima: Pay {X} (using Uthros's mana) and tap Sakashima to untap Minamo and/or Uthros (since they are lands). 5) Activate Minamo: Pay {U} and tap Minamo to untap Sakashima the Impostor. This creates a loop where you can regenerate the untapped status of Sakashima and produce mana via Uthros indefinitely, resulting in infinite resources/manasymptoms.
What combo can I make with Intruder Alarm and Nissa, Vital Force?

You can create an infinite loop of creature tokens using Intruder Alarm, Nissa, Vital Force, and Tarmogoyf Nest. First, you attach Tarmogoyf Nest to a land you control. Then, activate Nissa, Vital Force's [+1] ability to make that enchanted land become a 5/5 Elemental creature until end of turn. Next, use the now-creature land's activated ability by tapping it and paying {1}{G} to create a Tarmogoyf token. When this new creature enters the battlefield, Intruder Alarm triggers because its text states: 'Whenever a creature enters, untap all creatures.' This untaps Nissa's Elemental land, allowing you to repeat the process indefinitely. The combo result is infinite creature tokens.
I have Synth Infiltrator and Wispweaver Angel in my deck. Can I use them together to generate infinite value, and if so, how does the sequence work?

Yes, these two cards can be used to create an infinite loop. First, cast Synth Infiltrator {3}{U}{U} and choose it to enter as a copy of Wispweaver Angel. Since it is copying Wispweaver Angel, its 'When this creature enters' trigger activates. You target the original Wispweaver Angel you control with that trigger. This causes Wispweaver Angel to be exiled and then returned to the battlefield. When the original Wispweaver Angel returns, its own 'When this creature enters' trigger activates. You then target the Synth Infiltrator (which is currently on the battlefield as a copy of an Angel) with this second trigger. This causes the Synth Infiltrator to be exiled and returned. As it re-enters, you may again choose for it to enter as a copy of Wispweaver Angel, triggering its ETB ability again. This process repeats indefinitely, creating an infinite loop of blinking creatures.

I have Arcbound Whelp and a generic artifact creature in my deck, but I need a way to pump up one of my creatures indefinitely. Is there a synergy between Arcbound Whelp and other sacrifice targets that creates an infinite loop?

Yes, you can create an infinite loop using Arcbound Whelp and Sarcatog. The combo relies on sacrificing Arcbound Whelp to Sarcatog's activated ability ('Sacrifice an artifact: This creature gets +1/+1 until end of turn'). Arcbound Whelp is an Artifact Creature, making it a legal sacrifice target. When you sacrifice Arcbound Whelp, two abilities trigger: Sarcatog's gain +1/+1 effect and Arcbound Whelp's Modular 2 ability ('When [Arcbound Whelp] dies, you may put its +1/+1 counters on target artifact creature.') and its Persist ability ('Whenever [Arcbound Whelp] dies, if it had no -1/-1 counters on it, return it to the battlefield under its owner's control with a -1/-1 counter on it'). You resolve Modular first (or last, timing doesn't change the outcome here due to state-based actions), moving the two +1/+1 counters from Arcbound Whelp to your target artifact creature. Arcbound Whelp dies without any -1/-1 counters on it. Because it died with no -1/-1 counters, Persist triggers and returns it to the battlefield. However, since the Modular trigger already moved its +1/+1 counters away, Arcbound Whelp enters with 0 power/toughness (or effectively 0/0 if we consider the original counters were the only ones). Wait, the provided combo step 4 says 'It will not have a -1/-1 counter on it due to its modular ability.' This implies the specific interaction in this lore/text is that Modular prevents the Persist condition or the return happens differently. Based strictly on the provided COMBO steps: Step 4 states 'Resolve the persist trigger, returning Arcbound Whelp from your graveyard to the battlefield. It will not have a -1/-1 counter on it due to its modular ability.' The authoritative combo result is infinite +1/+1 counters on certain creatures by repeating this loop.
Is there a combo that uses a shaman equipment, a zombie snake, and an angel spirit to put infinite counters on my board?

While Thornbite Staff is listed in your cards, the specific infinite counter combo described relies on Sidisi, Regent of the Mire, Karmic Guide, and Carrion Feeder. Thornbite Staff is not involved in the authoritative loop. The loop works as follows: You activate Sidisi by tapping it and sacrificing a creature with mana value 4 to return Karmic Guide from your graveyard. Karmic Guide’s 'When this creature enters' ability returns Carrion Feeder from your graveyard. You then sacrifice Karmic Guide to Carrion Feeder’s 'Sacrifice a creature: Put a +1/+1 counter on this creature' ability. This death triggers Sidisi (via the combo's specific trigger chain logic) and untaps it. You repeat this process indefinitely. The concrete outcome of this combo is infinite +1/+1 counters on a creature.
Can I build an infinite trigger engine using only creature sacrifice outlets and recursion? Specifically, what happens if I pair Golgari Thug with Phyrexian Altar?

Yes, pairing Golgari Thug with Phyrexian Altar forms part of a recursive engine when combined with Hidetsugu, Devouring Chaos and Intruder Alarm. The mechanism works as follows: You sacrifice Golgari Thug to Phyrexian Altar for {B}. Golgari Thug dies, triggering its ability to put itself from your graveyard onto the top of your library. You then activate Hidetsugu's second ability ({2}{R}, {T}: Exile top card... deal damage equal to mana value). You exile Golgari Thug (MV 2) and deal 2 damage. You cast Golgari Thug from exile. It enters, triggering Intruder Alarm, which untaps all creatures. To make this infinite, you must have other mana-producing creatures on the battlefield; you activate them to generate the mana needed ({3}{B/R} or similar) to pay for the next cycle of sacrificing and activating Hidetsugu, allowing you to repeat the sequence indefinitely.
Is there a way to turn Yarus into an infinite trigger engine using enemy artifacts or creatures?

Yes. By using Wrong Turn to give Karlov Watchdog to an opponent, you can use Yahenni's sacrifice ability with a face-down creature. When that creature dies, Yarus's second ability triggers, returning it to the battlefield face down under its owner's control. Because the opponent controls Karlov Watchdog during their turn (and they retain control until your next turn), the 'Permanents your opponents control can't be turned face up' rule applies, keeping the returned creature face down. This allows you to sacrifice it again for Yahenni, triggering Yarus again, creating an infinite loop that lets you draw a card indefinitely.

I have a Zombie Mutant Advisor named Jason Bright, an artifact that taps to sacrifice creatures for damage called Blasting Station, and an enchantment that makes black Zombies by discarding cards called Zombie Infestation. Is there a way to interact with these three cards to draw cards repeatedly?

No, this combo cannot work with just these three cards. While the steps of creating a token, untapping Blasting Station, and sacrificing the zombie function, Jason Bright requires the dying zombie's power to be different from its base power (2) to trigger card draw. Since no other effects are present to alter the Zombie token's power before it dies, its power remains 2/2, matching its base power. Therefore, Jason Bright does not trigger, and you do not draw any cards.
I have a black creature that exiles another target creature when it enters the battlefield and returns it if it leaves. How can I use this to get infinite value from another card in my deck?

You can combine Faceless Butcher, Metamorphosis Fanatic, and Umbral Collar Zealot to create an infinite loop. First, cast Faceless Butcher. When it enters, its ability triggers, exiling Metamorphosis Fanatic. Activate Umbral Collar Zealot by sacrificing Faceless Butcher (putting it into your graveyard). When Faceless Butcher dies, its second ability triggers, returning Metamorphosis Fanatic from exile to the battlefield. Metamorphosis Fanatic enters, triggering its ability to return Faceless Butcher from your graveyard to the battlefield. When Faceless Butcher enters again, its first ability triggers, exiling Metamorphosis Fanatic once more. Then, resolve the Umbral Collar Zealot ability (which you paid for by sacrificing Faceless Butcher in a previous step or simultaneously depending on stack order, but per the reference: Step 7 resolves Surveillance). Finally, repeat from Step 3: Sacrifice Faceless Butcher to Umbral Collar Zealot again. This loop generates infinite Surveil triggers.
Why is the combination of Scrap Trawler and Welding Jar so potent alongside Ashnod's Altar?

This combination is potent because it creates an infinite mana and card advantage loop. By casting Welding Jar (a historic artifact), Teshar's trigger returns Scrap Trawler from the graveyard to the battlefield. You then sacrifice Scrap Trawler to Ashnod's Altar for {C}{C}, triggering Scrap Trawler's death ability to return Welding Jar from the graveyard to your hand. This allows you to repeat the process infinitely, generating mana and keeping key artifacts available.
How does the interaction between an upkeep-triggered enchantment return card and an exile effect create a loop?

This interaction allows for a recursive loop using Deadbridge Chant and Tormod's Cryptkeeper. First, sacrifice Tormod's Cryptkeeper to exile your graveyard (Step 1). Next, cast Time Warp to take an extra turn (Step 2). During the next upkeep, Deadbridge Chant triggers (Step 4) and, assuming no other cards entered the graveyard during the interim, retrieves Time Warp from the graveyard because it is not a creature card. You can then repeat Step 2, casting Time Warp again. Note: The combo is fragile; if any other card enters your graveyard after the initial exile but before Deadbridge Chant's trigger resolves, the random selection may not return Time Warp.
I have Garth One-Eye, Emiel the Blessed, and Akroma's Memorial. Is there a combo that generates infinite resources using these pieces?

Yes. You can generate infinite mana ({U}{U}{U}) per loop using these pieces. Step 1: Activate Garth One-Eye by tapping it and choosing 'Black Lotus' to create and cast a copy. Step 2: Activate the Black Lotus copy by tapping and sacrificing it, adding {U}{U}{U}. Step 3: Use the mana generated to activate Emiel the Blessed (paying its cost as defined in the combo steps) to exile and return Garth One-Eye to the battlefield. Step 4: Repeat the process infinitely.
Is there a combo using Lagrella, the Magpie and Preston, the Vanisher that generates infinite resources?

Yes, combining Lagrella, the Magpie with Preston, the Vanisher and Sun Titan allows you to generate infinite +1/+1 counters on Sun Titan. 1. Cast Ephemerate to blink Lagrella (Step 1). 2. Lagrella enters, triggering its ability to exile target creatures controlled by different players (exiling Sun Titan) and Preston's ability to create a 0/1 Illusion token copy of Lagrella (Steps 2-4). 3. The original Lagrella goes to the graveyard due to the legend rule (Step 5). 4. Since Lagrella left, Sun Titan is returned from exile by Lagrella's own text (Step 7). 5. Sun Titan, the new Lagrella token, and Preston enter, triggering their respective abilities (Step 8). 6. Preston creates a 0/1 Illusion token copy of Sun Titan (Step 9). 7. The Sun Titan token enters, triggering its ETB ability (Step 10). 8. Lagrella's trigger puts two +1/+1 counters on the non-token Sun Titan returned in step 7 (Step 11). 9. The Sun Titan trigger from the *newly entered* Lagrella token resolves, returning the original Lagrella from the graveyard to the battlefield (Step 12). 10. Repeat the loop from Step 2. This cycle generates infinite +1/+1 counters on Sun Titan and infinite tokens.
I have a red/green/white elemental beast commander and want to know if it can generate infinite counters or mana. What specific cards do I need alongside Marath, Will of the Wild?

To achieve this with Marath, Will of the Wild, you need to pair it with Cryptic Trilobite and Vorinclex, Monstrous Raider. The combo works as follows: First, because Vorinclex doubles counters placed on permanents by you, activating Marath's ability to put X +1/+1 counters on itself costs 1 mana and removing 1 counter but results in gaining 2 counters instead of 1. Next, use that same Marath activation to put X +1/+1 counters on Cryptic Trilobite; thanks to Vorinclex, you place 2 counters there for the cost of removing 1 from Marath. Then, activate Cryptic Trilobite's ability: 'Remove a +1/+1 counter from this creature: Add {C}{C}. Spend this mana only to activate abilities.' This generates colorless mana that can be used to pay for more activations of Marath (since Marath's cost includes generic mana). By alternating these activations, you create an infinite loop. The concrete outcome is: Infinite +1/+1 counters on creatures you control.
I have a Phyrexian Artificer commander and some artifact creatures. Is there a way to make one of my artifacts infinitely tough?

Yes, you can build this combo using Ich-Tekik, Salvage Splicer, Arcbound Reclaimer, Lion's Eye Diamond, and The Reality Chip. Attach The Reality Chip to a creature to cast spells from the top of your library. Sacrifice Lion's Eye Diamond (with empty hand) for three mana of any one color. This triggers Ich-Tekik to gain +1/+1 counters on it and your golems. Remove a counter from Arcbound Reclaimer to put Lion's Eye Diamond back on top of your library. Cast it for {0}, repeat indefinitely. This generates infinite mana of one color.
Why is pairing Viscera Seer with Incarnation Technique and a flash creature so effective strategically?

The strategic power comes from the interaction between Viscera Seer's sacrifice cost and Incarnation Technique's recovery effect. By using Dualcaster Mage (which has Flash) to copy Incarnation Technique, you can sacrifice the Mage via Viscera Seer as a cost. The triggered copy of Incarnation Technique then returns the sacrificed creature from the graveyard to the battlefield. This loop allows you to repeat the sequence indefinitely without losing the key components permanently. The combo achieves infinite death triggers, which is particularly potent in decks that have other cards triggering when creatures die, such as sacrifice outlets or card draw engines.
How does the Persist interaction specifically fuel the loop with Maulfist Squad and Phyrexian Altar?

The loop relies on the interaction between Phyrexian Altar's sacrifice cost and Maulfist Squad's triggered abilities. First, you tap Phyrexian Altar and sacrifice Maulfist Squad to produce mana. As part of this game action, Maulfist Squad dies, which causes its Persist ability to trigger because it was sacrificed while having no counters (initially). This ability returns Maulfist Squad from the graveyard to the battlefield with a -1/-1 counter on it. Immediately upon returning, the creature enters the battlefield again, triggering its Fabricate ability. You choose to put a +1/+1 counter on it. Now back on the battlefield with a counter, you can sacrifice it again via Phyrexian Altar, repeating the cycle. The outcome of this combo is infinite ETB.
Is there a combo that allows me to sacrifice creatures infinitely using Fain, the Broker?

Yes. You need Fain, the Broker, Tenacious Dead, and Crystalline Crawler. 1) Tap Fain and sacrifice Tenacious Dead to put two +1/+1 counters on Crystalline Crawler. 2) Tenacious Dead dies, triggering its own ability. 3) Resolve Tenacious Dead's trigger, paying {1}{B} to return it to the battlefield tapped. 4) Resolve Fain's sacrifice effect (putting counters on Crawler). 5) Activate Crystalline Crawler's ability twice (removing two counters) to add {B}{B}. 6) Use this mana plus any other sources to pay {3}{B} to untap Fain. 7) Tap Fain and sacrifice the returned Tenacious Dead again. Repeat steps 1-7 infinitely to generate infinite black mana.
I have Teshar, Ancestor's Apostle and Salvager of Ruin in my deck. Can I use Urza's Bauble to make a loop that generates infinite spells?

Yes, this specific combination creates an infinite storm count loop. Here is how the chain works step-by-step: First, you activate Urza's Bauble by tapping and sacrificing it ({T}, Sacrifice this artifact), which causes it to go to your graveyard. Next, you activate Salvager of Ruin by sacrificing it (which sends it to your graveyard as well); its ability allows you to return a permanent card from your graveyard that was put there from the battlefield this turn back to your hand, so you return Urza's Bauble. Then, you cast Urza's Bauble ({0}). Because Urza's Bauble is an Artifact, it is a historic spell. This triggers Teshar, Ancestor's Apostle's ability: 'Whenever you cast a historic spell, return target creature card with mana value 3 or less from your graveyard to the battlefield.' Since Salvager of Ruin has a mana value of 3, it returns to the battlefield. You now have both Urza's Bauble and Salvager of Ruin again, allowing you to repeat the process. The combo result is infinite storm count.
Is there a way to use Derevi, Empyrial Tactician and Nykthos, Shrine to Nyx to get infinite value?

Yes. This combo involves Nykthos, Shrine to Nyx, Emiel the Blessed, and Derevi, Empyrial Tactician. By activating Nykthos's ability to generate mana, you can pay for Emiel the Blessed's blink effect ({3}) to exile and return Derevi. When Derevi enters the battlefield (ETB), its trigger 'When Derevi enters... you may tap or untap target permanent' fires. You use this trigger to untap Nykthos. You then repeat the process: activate Nykthos again for mana, blink Derevi with Emiel, and use Derevi's ETB trigger to untap Nykthos again. This loop produces infinite ETB triggers.
I have Red mana and want to mill myself to draw cards repeatedly. Is there a combo using Godo, Bandit Warlord that lets me do infinite rummaging?

No, this combo does not mill you. The combination of Godo, Bandit Warlord and Fear of Missing Out with Mysterious Limousine creates an infinite loop of combat phases. Fear of Missing Out draws a card when it enters the battlefield (triggered in Step 4 when returned from exile). This results in infinite card draw/recursion, not milling. To mill, you would need cards that specifically move cards from library to graveyard, which are not part of this combo.
I have a blue-white blink engine with a cheap black sacrifice outlet. Can I loop them to get infinite value?

Yes, this combination of Icewind Stalwart, Karmic Guide, and Umbral Collar Zealot creates a specific recursion loop. Icewind Stalwart has the ability 'When this creature enters, exile up to one target non-Warrior creature you control, then return it to the battlefield under its owner's control.' By sacrificing Icewind Stalwart using Umbral Collar Zealot's ability ('Sacrifice another creature or artifact: Surveil 1') before Stalwart resolves, Stalwart leaves your side of the field. When Stalwart's blink trigger resolves, it targets Karmic Guide and returns it to the battlefield. Because Karmic Guide has 'When this creature enters, return target creature card from your graveyard to the battlefield,' you can target the Icewind Stalwart now sitting in the graveyard. This puts both permanents back on the battlefield, allowing you to repeat the process indefinitely, resulting in infinite sacrifice triggers.

First, you cast Polymorphous Rush for {2}{U} and target a separate creature; it copies the spirit's ability exactly. The oracle text reads: "{1}{U}: This creature's owner shuffles it into their library. If that player does, they reveal cards from the top of that library until a card named Mirror-Mad Phantasm is revealed. The player puts that card onto the battlefield and all other cards revealed this way into their graveyard." By paying {1}{U} to activate this copied ability, the creature returns to your library. Because your library contains no additional copies of the target spirit, the "until a card named Mirror-Mad Phantasm is revealed" condition cannot be satisfied by finding one, so you reveal every remaining card and send them all to the graveyard. You can repeat this as long as you have mana and the creature available, consistently producing infinite self-mill.
I'm looking to build a green-blue deck that generates endless resources without relying on lands. Is there an interaction between counters, tokens, and untap enchantments that creates a loop?

Yes, those three permanents combine into a reliable engine. By paying {G}{U} and tapping Vorel of the Hull Clade, you double the spore counters on Thallid Germinator using its "{G}{U}, {T}: Double the number of each kind of counter on target artifact, creature, or land" ability. You then pay to remove three spore counters from it, triggering its text: "Remove three spore counters from this creature: Create a 1/1 green Saproling creature token." The Saproling entering causes Intruder Alarm's triggered ability to fire because of the clause "Whenever a creature enters, untap all creatures," which returns both Vorel of the Hull Clade and Thallid Germinator to an untapped state so you can pay their costs again. This combo produces infinite mana creatures you control can produce.
I have a lot of blue and red mana but don't know the specific card names; is there a combo that uses spell copying to create infinite triggered abilities?

Yes, you can build this combo using Twincast ({U}{U}) and Reverberate ({R}{R}). Cast Reverberate targeting any instant or sorcery spell. Then cast Twincast to copy Reverberate, making the copy target Reverberate itself. When the copy resolves, it copies Reverberate again, targeting Reverberate, which can be resolved repeatedly without paying additional mana costs, creating an infinite chain of self-copying spells.
I have Ich-Tekik, Salvage Splicer in my Commander deck and I'm looking for a way to win with Arcbound Reclaimer, Dark Sphere, and Mystic Forge. Do these cards combo together?

Yes, this combination executes an infinite loop using Ich-Tekik, Salvage Splicer, Arcbound Reclaimer, Dark Sphere, and Mystic Forge to produce infinite +1/+1 counters on a creature. The mechanism works as follows: You activate Dark Sphere by tapping it and sacrificing it ("{T}, Sacrifice this artifact"). This triggers Ich-Tekik's ability because the card text reads "Whenever an artifact is put into a graveyard from the battlefield, put a +1/+1 counter on Ich-Tekik and a +1/+1 counter on each Golem you control." To reset the loop, you activate Arcbound Reclaimer ("Remove a +1/+1 counter from this creature: Put target artifact card from your graveyard on top of your library"), removing one counter to return Dark Sphere to the top of your library. Mystic Forge allows you to cast Dark Sphere from there for {0}. Since you can sacrifice it again, the loop repeats indefinitely.

I'm playing a Snow deck with Thermopod and looking for ways to generate infinite mana or loop creatures. Is there a specific combination involving milling and library manipulation that can infinitely sacrifice Narcomoeba?

Yes, you can build this combo using Thermopod, Narcomoeba, Selhoff Occultist, and Mortuary. The mechanism works by sacrificing Narcomoeba to Thermopod for {R}, which sends it to your graveyard. Mortuary then moves that card from the graveyard back to the top of your library, and Selhoff Occultist triggers on the death to mill a card, placing Narcomoeba from the library into the graveyard. This library-to-graveyard transition triggers Narcomoeba's ability to return it to the battlefield, allowing you to sacrifice it to Thermopod again for more mana and additional triggers. **Combo Result: Infinite sacrifice triggers**.
How does the interaction between Displaced Dinosaurs, Teferi, Timebender, and Soulherder function to control the game?

This combination executes a sequence that results in a **Lock**. First, cast Teferi, Timebender ({4}{W}{U}). Because Teferi is legendary, it qualifies as historic. Displaced Dinosaurs triggers upon entry: "As a historic permanent you control enters, it becomes a 7/7 Dinosaur creature in addition to its other types," giving the planeswalker substantial power and toughness immediately. Next, activate Vorel of the Hull Clade by paying {G}{U} and tapping it to double the loyalty counters on Teferi. With sufficient counters accumulated, use Teferi's [−9] ability: "Take an extra turn after this one." Finally, at your end step, activate Soulherder: "At the beginning of your end step, you may exile another target creature you control, then return that card to the battlefield under its owner's control." Exiling Teferi triggers Soulherder to gain +1/+1 counters, and returning Teferi causes it to enter as a historic permanent again, making it another 7/7 Dinosaur via Displaced Dinosaurs. You can repeat this loop indefinitely by using Vorel to double counters on the re-entering Teferi and blinking him again, generating infinite extra turns and board presence to secure a Lock.
Can I build a combo using Altar of Dementia and Breach the Multiverse to get infinite value?

Yes, you can combine Altar of Dementia, Breach the Multiverse, and Dualcaster Mage to create an efficient infinite engine. Mechanism-wise, you cast Breach the Multiverse on your turn, then flash in Dualcaster Mage during the same turn. Because Dualcaster Mage has the triggered ability 'When this creature enters, copy target instant or sorcery spell,' it will copy the Breach spell still on the stack. Before the copy resolves, you hold priority to activate Altar of Dementia's ability by sacrificing the entering Dualcaster Mage, paying its cost: 'Sacrifice a creature.' The copy then resolves, targeting Dualcaster Mage in your graveyard to return him to the battlefield. He enters again, triggers another copy, and you sacrifice him to the Altar once more to repeat the loop indefinitely. This combo results in infinite recursion of creature cards in your graveyard.
I have a legendary wizard that exiles cards to copy their activated abilities, and I want to repeatedly sacrifice creatures to generate triggers. What combo can I build?

Yes, pairing Mairsil, the Pretender with Endling, Blood Vassal, and Triskelavus creates a reliable death-loop engine. Once Mairsil is on the battlefield, he exiles those three cards via his ETB effect, placing cage counters on them so you can copy their activated abilities each turn. You activate Endling’s copied ability that reads '{B}: This creature gains undying until end of turn' to grant Mairsil that trigger. Each turn, you sacrifice Blood Vassal (triggering the copied 'Sacrifice this creature: Add {B}{B}' effect) and intentionally send Mairsil to the graveyard. Because he has undying, his triggered ability states 'When this creature dies, if it had no +1/+1 counters on it, return it to the battlefield under its owner's control with a +1/+1 counter on it,' causing him to return immediately. Once back, you activate Triskelavus's copied text ('{1}, Remove a +1/+1 counter from this creature: Create a 1/1 colorless Triskelavite artifact creature token with flying') to manage counters and keep the cycle going. This straightforward interaction reliably produces Infinite death triggers.
I'm trying to find a cheap combo that can burn an opponent out quickly by repeating a damage trigger. Can I build a combo with Thieving Otter and Mind Over Matter, or do I need other pieces?

Yes, you can build this combo using exactly three cards: Thieving Otter, Mind Over Matter, and Wolfhunter's Quiver. By equipping the Quiver to your Otter, it gains an activated ability that lets you tap it to deal 1 damage to any target. When that damage hits an opponent, the Otter triggers because of its oracle text stating "Whenever this creature deals damage to an opponent, draw a card." You use the drawn card as fodder to pay the cost for Mind Over Matter's ability ("Discard a card: You may tap or untap target artifact, creature, or land"), targeting the Otter to untap it. This lets you repeat the process without spending extra mana. The concrete result of this loop is Near-infinite damage.
Can you break down exactly how Kinnan, Bonder Prodigy and Simic Ragworm interact to generate mana step by step?

This interaction requires both Kinnan, Bonder Prodigy and Simic Ragworm. To start the sequence, activate Simic Ragworm by tapping it for {U}. This action triggers Kinnan because its oracle text explicitly states, 'Whenever you tap a nonland permanent for mana, add one mana of any type that permanent produced.' The trigger resolves, adding another {U}. Next, pay {U} to activate Simic Ragworm's ability, which untaps the creature and allows you to repeat the initial activation. Cycling through these steps indefinitely yields infinite colored mana.

I just attacked with a creature and my opponent tapped two lands to counter it, but wait, they actually didn't counter it because I have mana in reserve? Here is the real situation: My commander is a double-faced card that starts as a wizard costing {2}{U} but transforms into a demon with a red color indicator. I control two artifacts that both say 'If a source you control deals damage to a creature or player, it deals double that damage instead.' When this transformed demon attacks and deals damage, does the damage quadruple because of my two doublers, and am I allowed to have {R} cards in my deck even though the front face only had blue?

Yes, you are allowed to include red cards in your deck because the back face of your double-faced commander is included when determining color identity, and since the demon side has a red color indicator, that red color is part of your commander's total color identity alongside blue from the front face. The rules confirm that the back face of a double-faced card is included when determining a card's color identity as an exception to general rules, which means your color identity is blue and red throughout the game regardless of which side is showing, making all red and blue cards legal in your deck. For the damage calculation, your two doublers result in quadrupled damage rather than infinite scaling because replacement effects are limited to one opportunity per event and do not loop back on themselves. With two sources providing a doubling effect, the game applies each replacement once to modify the damage sequentially, so a creature dealing 3 damage would deal 12 damage, as each doublers modifies the original value without re-triggering off the modified result.
What happens when I play an effect that says I control another player during their next turn? Do they just finish their current phase and keep going as normal?

When you cast a spell or activate an ability that gives you control over another player, they do not lose any remaining actions from their current phase. Instead, the governing rule states that this effect applies to the next turn that the affected player actually takes and lasts for their entire turn until the beginning of the following turn begins. You simply wait until their next actual turn starts to take over completely. For example, if I use Possessors' Seal on you during my turn, your current phase finishes exactly as it normally would. When your next turn finally arrives three turns later, I immediately make all your decisions until that turn ends at the start of your following turn, allowing me to tap your lands, attack with your creatures, and cast your spells without restriction.

I just cast a spell that lets me draw three cards and choose one to reveal as I draw it. Right when the spell resolves, I discard my entire hand to pay an additional cost, so for a split second my hand is completely empty while I am still in the middle of drawing those three cards. I also control a creature whose toughness is equal to the number of cards in my hand. Do I lose control of or destroy that creature when my hand hits zero mid-resolution, and do I get to look at each card before deciding which one to reveal?

The spell resolves completely without interfering with your permanent because state-based actions pay no attention to what happens during the resolution of a spell or ability. This means even though your hand size temporarily drops to zero during the resolution process, any creature that relies on hand size for its toughness safely returns once the drawing finishes and you have more cards again. Before checking anything like that, you fully resolve the draw phase, and because the rule explicitly states that if an effect gives a player the option to reveal a card as they draw it, that player may look at that card as they draw it before choosing whether to reveal it, you are allowed to peek at each card entering your hand before making a choice about showing it. The precedence here is clear: the resolution window processes all drawing and revelation steps in complete isolation from intermediate board states, meaning the rule about state-based actions ignoring mid-resolution changes takes priority for permanent survival checks, while the looking rule governs the sequential evaluation during the draw itself. You will successfully view all three drawn cards in order, reveal whichever one you chose after seeing them, and your hand-size-dependent creature stays alive with updated toughness based on your final hand size once the spell finishes resolving.
I have an effect that creates a creature attacking my opponent, but I haven't declared any attackers this turn. Does this creature actually start combat for me?

No, the creature will not attack. The rules dictate that only a creature can attack or block, and specific mechanics govern when an effect attempts to place a creature into combat. If an effect would put a creature onto the battlefield attacking under the control of any player except an attacking player, that creature does enter the battlefield, but it never becomes considered to be an attacking creature. For example, if you do not have any attackers declared this turn and you cast a spell that creates a 2/2 red Goblin creature token with the text that it is attacking your opponent, the token enters your battlefield, but because you are not an attacking player controlling it in the combat phase structure, it fails to become an attacking creature. It will sit on your side of the battlefield without participating in combat, and you cannot use it to fight or block anything either since the effect only set it up as attacking.

I attacked with my creature last turn and it was definitely vigilant because of an aura attached to it at the start of the game. This turn, my opponent attaches another enchantment that says enchanted creatures lose all abilities, but now my blocker isn't taking damage because it attacked without vigilance. Did the aura just break?

The first enchantment is still functioning, but its effect was overwritten by the newer one. Under the game rules, static abilities create continuous effects that are active as long as the permanent with the ability remains on the battlefield and has the ability. However, when multiple continuous effects apply to the same characteristic at the same time, determining which order effects are applied in is usually done using a timestamp system where an effect with an earlier timestamp is applied before an effect with a later timestamp. In your situation, the vigilance enchantment was attached first, giving it an earlier timestamp. The new loss-of-abilities enchantment entered later, giving it a later timestamp. When calculating the creature characteristics for combat, the game applies the earlier vigilance effect first, then immediately applies the later ability-wiping effect, which removes it. The concrete final outcome is that your creature attacks without vigilance because the later timestamp takes precedence in the resolution order and overwrites the earlier one within the relevant layer.

I just cast my legendary commander and it attacked, but got blocked by a creature with deathtouch. The fight damage put lethal on both of us. My opponent says my commander just dies normally to the graveyard, but I thought commanders go to the command zone when they die? What actually happens here?

State-based actions are checked automatically before any player gets priority, so the game first sees that if a creature has toughness greater than 0, and it has been dealt damage by a source with deathtouch since the last time state-based actions were checked, that creature is destroyed. This means your commander leaves the battlefield and enters its owner's graveyard first. However, commander rules override the normal graveyard destination because each deck has a legendary card designated as its commander and that designation is not a characteristic of the object represented by the card; rather, it is an attribute of the card itself. The text also confirms the card retains this designation even when it changes zones. Because the state-based check happens first to move the creature to the graveyard, the commander replacement effect then applies afterward, sending it to your command zone instead. The final outcome is that your commander dies from combat damage and travels directly to your command zone where you can cast it again later for an additional cost.
I have an enchantment that says "You win the game if you have 50 or more life." My teammate and I are at 25 life each. Can I activate my untap step ability to gain another 30 life and win right now?

Yes, you can win this way. In Two-Headed Giant, when an effect checks how much life a single player has, it actually looks at your team's combined life total instead. Since your team is already at 50 life, gaining 30 brings your total to 80. Because the condition checks against the team total, you would meet the requirement. Note that if the enchantment triggers at the beginning of your upkeep, you will win during that next upkeep step once the ability resolves.
I just started a game with my designated legendary face card and I'm confused about casting it mid-game. What happens when I finally get to cast it, and does it change how the stack works?

When you reach your main phase with enough mana, you announce that you are casting your commander as a sorcery, put it onto the stack, pay its mana cost, and let it resolve so it enters the battlefield. The Commander variant uses all the normal rules for a Magic game, with the following additions, which is why the stack interaction and timing windows remain completely unchanged. For example, if your commander costs {2}{U}, you tap an Island for blue mana, cast it during your main phase just like any other creature spell, and it resolves normally unless an opponent responds with a counterspell.

I cast Kiki-Jiki, Mirror Breaker and used its ability to create a copy of my commander on the battlefield. The token has all the same powers, abilities, and mana cost as my real commander. I have a card that says 'Whenever your commander enters the battlefield, draw three cards.' My opponent argues the token won't trigger this effect because it's just a creature copy, not a commander. Who is correct and what happens?

Your opponent is correct. The token will not trigger the effect. The rules regarding commander designation establish that while a commander keeps its status through changes, any permanent copying another object explicitly does not become a commander even if it mimics all other characteristics. This definition governs the object's identity first. When triggers involving zone changes activate and look at the new object entering the battlefield, they must check the characteristics of that object against the ability requirements. Since the copying rule removes the commander designation, the trigger check will find that the token does not match your commander. The concrete outcome is that no cards will be drawn from the enter-the-battlefield trigger when the token enters.
Can I pay a spell with {2}{R} using two generic colorless mana and one red mana, or do I need to use exactly two red and one generic?

You can definitely use two colorless and one red. The rules clarify that mana is represented by mana symbols, and those exact same symbols are used to represent mana costs on spells and abilities. This means the symbol itself functions as both the resource you produce and the requirement you pay, allowing any combination of colored or colorless mana that matches the total cost. For example, if you cast Lightning Strike which has a casting cost of {1}{R}, you can pay it by tapping a Mountain for one red mana plus a two-element artifact like Arcane Signet that taps for one colorless mana. The single generic symbol simply accepts any mana type toward the total.
Can I still get a trigger from my artifact that says Whenever you prevent damage if I only stop part of the damage from a large spell?

Yes, you definitely get that trigger. The game checks how prevention effects are applied rather than whether the damage is completely stopped. As the rules explain, such an ability triggers each time a prevention effect is applied to one or more simultaneous damage events and prevents some or all of that damage. For example, if you control Determination which prevents the next three damage your team would take, and your opponent casts Inferno Elemental dealing four damage to you, the prevention effect applies and stops three damage. Your artifact sees this single application preventing part of the spell's damage and triggers exactly once, giving you whatever benefit it provides regardless of that one point getting through.

I just tried to cast a sorcery that has an optional extra cost to tap two artifacts I control. I tapped them and paid the mana like normal, but my opponent kept asking if they could respond while I was still tapping those artifacts. What actually happens with the spell and any triggers from it?

When you decide to cast a spell, the game requires you to announce your intentions to pay any additional costs at the exact same time you pay the main mana cost, and this entire declaration phase locks down the turn so no one else can act. Even though triggered abilities from the spell technically fire as soon as it resolves, nothing actually happens at the moment a trigger occurs; instead, each one waits until the next time any player would receive priority before being placed on the stack. Furthermore, no player has priority while a spell or ability is resolving, which completely blocks opponents from interrupting you during the effect phase. The casting announcement takes precedence because cost payment must be declared first, followed by resolution, followed by trigger placement. The concrete final outcome is that your spell resolves fully without interruption, the extra costs are paid and locked in during your declaration, any resulting triggers will only be put on the stack after resolution completes, and your opponent gains their first actual chance to respond exactly then.

I just played a card with a wavy border around the rules text and a small outpost symbol inside it, but it also has two numbers in the top right corner. Does this count as a creature I can attack with, or is it something different?

You have played a Station card. According to the rules, each Station card features a striated text box and contains one or two station symbols. These cards may also display power and toughness boxes, but the striated border and station symbols are what classify them as Stations rather than standard creatures. To understand how it behaves on the battlefield, you would read its specific station keyword ability printed in that striated text box.
What happens if my opponent leaves the game while I was controlling one of their planes? Does the plane disappear or switch to someone else?

When a player leaves the game, all objects they own except abilities from phenomena leave the game as well. If that includes a face-up plane card or phenomenon card, the planar controller turns the top card of their planar deck face up immediately rather than letting it vanish. For example, if I was playing against Leo and he had Amonkhet as the active plane when he got eliminated from our three-player match, his plane does not disappear. As soon as he leaves, the effect automatically takes over and flips the top card of his planar deck face up to continue the game state for whoever is affected next. This happens because the rules dictate that departing controllers pass the plane control directly to the replacement effect without waiting for a state check.
What happens when I activate two different abilities on a leveler creature if they are separated by those horizontal lines in the text box? Does it matter which one I choose first?

When you activate those abilities, it does not matter which order you choose or how the horizontal lines separate them for gameplay purposes. The rules treat these lines strictly as visual markers because the text box striations have no game significance other than clearly demarcating which abilities and which power toughness box are associated with which level symbol. Leveler cards each contain only one text box, so standard timing and priority apply normally to everything printed inside it. For example, if your creature reads Level 1: Tap to add one mana above a line and Level 4: Target opponent sacrifices a creature below it, you can activate the second ability in response to an instant even though they are visually divided. The single text box means the abilities behave exactly like any other activated abilities on a continuous card.

I just cast a spell that sends all my cards from the graveyard back into my library. I also have two legendary permanents on the battlefield, so I was worried about them hitting the graveyard and triggering things, but then we got confused about whether the game checks for duplicate legends or individual card movements during that process. What actually happens, and in what order do these effects resolve?

When your spell resolves, some effects instruct a player to do something to a zone, and that action is performed on all cards in that zone simultaneously rather than one by one, which means every gravecard returns to your library together and the zone itself is not affected by sequential tracking. This bulk shift happens first as part of the spell resolving. Once the spell finishes resolving, state-based actions are game actions that happen automatically whenever certain conditions are met, and they do not use the stack, so the game immediately checks for board states like duplicate legends or zero toughness creatures after your library is restored. Because abilities that watch for a specified game state are triggered abilities, not state-based actions, your legend triggers will wait on the stack to resolve before those automatic evaluations finalize. The concrete final outcome is that all your gravecards return to your library as a single group event, your watching triggers resolve next, and then the automatic system instantly resolves any legendary conflicts or remaining board conditions without pausing for player priority.
If I control an effect that changes sacrifices into exiles instead, does paying a 'Sacrifice two creatures' cost still count as paid even though nothing actually goes to the graveyard?

Yes, the cost is considered paid regardless of how your effect modifies the action. The rule establishes that the actions performed when paying a cost may be modified by effects, and even if they are modified so that the actions performed do not match what was called for, the cost has still been paid. For example, suppose you need to pay a spell's cost that requires sacrificing two creatures, but you control an effect that exiles permanents instead of sacrificing them. You can exile two creatures to satisfy the requirement. Even though the creatures are not put into the graveyard as a sacrifice would normally do, you have successfully paid the cost.

We are playing a multiplayer match and my opponent just targeted one of my creatures with an effect that says destroy it. I paid the mana to give it regeneration right before they cast it. The spell also says its controller takes damage equal to that creature's power. Since we all started this game at 40 life, will regenerating my creature actually keep me alive in the long run?

To determine the result you must recognize the timeline of events. Your match established a baseline because each player sets their life total to 40 and draws a hand of seven cards when the game starts, which means you began with a substantial health buffer that dictates whether immediate damage ends your game. That initial setup takes precedence chronologically since it happens before any spells are cast or abilities activated. During the current turn the incoming spell applies its secondary life loss effect while regeneration operates as a destruction-replacement effect that specifically states the next time the permanent would be destroyed this turn, instead remove all damage marked on it and its controller taps it. The life reduction still occurs regardless of the creature status, but the replacement effect successfully overrides the destruction step. Concrete final outcome: You survive the exchange with your life total reduced by exactly the creature's power amount, and your creature avoids being put into the graveyard, remaining on the battlefield tapped and clean of damage markers ready for future phases.
Can I activate outlast on a creature that just entered the battlefield under my control this turn, even though it cannot attack or block yet?

Yes, you can immediately use it. The rule text specifies that you "Activate only as a sorcery," which overrides the normal summoning sickness restriction that usually prevents new creatures from tapping to activate abilities. Normally, a creature must have been under your continuous control since your last turn begins before it can tap for activated abilities, but this timing clause grants a specific exception. For example, if you cast a hypothetical creature called Mosswood Giant with {T}: Outlast{2} during your main phase, you can pay two mana and tap it right away to place a +1/+1 counter on it, even though the giant is still suffering from summoning sickness and could not attack or block that same turn.

My opponent's library is empty and they just passed the turn to me with no blockers. I cast an effect that forces my opponent to draw one card, and then I immediately pass priority back to them hoping to see if they have responses like a counterspell. Does the game end instantly when I cast this spell, or does my opponent get a chance to respond?

Your opponent can respond with a counterspell because the loss condition is delayed until after the spell resolves and priority passes. State-based actions are checked automatically throughout the game but are not controlled by any player, which means these checks run at specific times like during resolution or when priority changes hands rather than instantly interrupting your casting or response windows. The rule for empty libraries specifies that a player who attempts to draw from a library with no cards in it loses the game the next time a player would receive priority. When you cast your spell, it goes on the stack, and state-based checks do not run during casting or while players are responding, so your opponent gets a full opportunity to respond with a counterspell or other instant-speed effects. If your opponent allows the spell to resolve, they will attempt to draw one card from their empty library, which registers the loss condition, but since no one passes priority yet, the game continues past that moment. Once the spell finishes resolving and you pass priority back to your opponent, the automatic checks run immediately, detect that they attempted to draw from an empty library during that resolution, and they lose the game before they can take any further actions. The concrete final outcome is that your opponent can successfully counter the spell if they wish, but if they do not counter it and let it resolve, your opponent loses the game as soon as you pass priority back to them after the spell finishes.
I'm in the middle of a fight and someone hits my creature with an effect that drops its toughness to zero instead of dealing damage. Can it stay on the battlefield?

No, your creature will not survive and will go to the graveyard once the game checks for state-based actions. The game uses the number after the slash as toughness, which is explicitly defined as the amount of damage needed to destroy it. Because any creature with zero or less toughness is removed from play regardless of how that number changed, dropping it to zero functions exactly like lethal damage would. For example, if you control a 4/3 Goblin and your opponent casts an effect that sets its toughness to 0 instead of dealing combat damage, that creature will be put into the graveyard immediately during the next game state check.
What happens if I roll a visit die and the result doesn't match any of the numbers shown on my attraction card?

When you roll to visit your attractions, the game simply moves forward with no effect if there is no match. This happens because each Attraction card has an ability that begins with the word Visit followed by a long dash in its rules text, and this visit ability triggers whenever you roll to visit your Attractions and the result matches one of the lit-up numbers. Since the trigger condition requires a match, a non-matching roll does not put anything on the stack. For example, if you are visiting an attraction that has the numbers two and five lit up but you roll a six, the ability never triggers, you get no effect from that visit attempt, and play simply continues to the next phase or action.

We are in the declare attackers step because my opponent forced one of my creatures to attack, but I want to pay three mana to get my companion from outside the game into my hand. Can I do this now since special actions are usually available whenever I have priority?

No. The action to retrieve a companion is a special action that explicitly requires you to take it during a main phase when the stack is empty, and this specific timing restriction overrides the general permission many other special actions have for use whenever priority exists. You are currently in the declare attackers step, which is not a main phase, so you cannot perform this action regardless of your priority state. The rule about whether a creature had to attack checks if an effect was requiring that creature to attack at the time attackers were declared, but this determination has no impact on special action availability and does not grant permission to bypass the strict timing limits defined for specific actions like companion retrieval. Outcome: You are not allowed to retrieve your companion and must wait until your next main phase to use this ability.
What happens when our playgroup suddenly has six people show up and we realize the table is perfectly set up for Emperor?
When six players arrive, you can play the Emperor variant, as it officially involves two or more teams of three players each.
Can I use an effect that reduces my next spell's cost by four green mana to cast a card that costs {3}{G}? Will it still require me to pay anything?

You will not need to pay any mana at all for that spell. When an effect tries to reduce a casting cost by more colored mana than the spell actually requires, the specific color requirement is reduced to nothing and the remaining reduction spills over into the generic portion of the cost instead. The rules confirm this by stating that if a cost is reduced by an amount of colored mana that exceeds its mana component of that color, the cost’s mana component of that color is reduced to nothing and the cost’s generic mana component is reduced by the difference. As a concrete example, a spell costing {3}{G} targeted by four green mana reduction will first see its single green requirement drop to zero. Your three extra points of green reduction then apply to the generic portion, reducing {3} down to {0}, leaving you with a completely free spell to cast.

I'm mid-combat attacking with a 7/7 creature and my opponent blocks with a 3/3 and controls a planeswalker at 4 loyalty. My friend told me to pay {3} right now during combat to bring out my companion card from outside the game, but the judge said I can't do that until later. So how does the damage actually get calculated between my attacker, the blocker, and the planeswalker?

You cannot pay three mana during combat because companion is restricted to a special action only available during your main phase when the stack is empty. To damage both targets, you must assign damage according to standard combat assignment rules, which require dividing your seven power among all blockers and only assigning excess damage to the planeswalker if your creature has trample or another effect permits it. Once damage is assigned, it processes in four steps: first, effects modify any potential excess damage; second, the modified damage is dealt; third, results like counters or life loss are processed; and finally, the damage event occurs. The three power blocker will be destroyed by lethal damage, and if your attacker has trample, up to four excess damage can be assigned to the planeswalker, reducing its loyalty to zero and sending it to the graveyard. You may then activate your companion during a future main phase.
I control a Goblin Wizard on the battlefield. If my opponent casts a spell that targets all Wizards, does it hit my creature even though it's also a Goblin?

Yes, your creature is definitely hit because having multiple names on the card means it counts as all of them simultaneously. This rule clarifies that creatures may have multiple subtypes and uses the example 'Creature — Goblin Wizard' to show that the card possesses both the Goblin and Wizard subtypes. Since the spell checks for any subtype matching 'Wizard', your creature qualifies perfectly. For instance, if you also control a pure Wizard with no other types, both your Goblin Wizard and the other Wizard would be destroyed by the same spell just as effectively.
Can I cast Grafted Exoskeleton using just one colorless mana instead of two green and one blue, and will it still be a creature on my side?

Yes, you can absolutely choose to cast it using its prototype mana cost. When you do this, the spell and the resulting permanent have only its alternative set of power, toughness, and mana cost characteristics from the bottom half of the card. This means if your prototype cost has no colored mana symbols, it will enter as a colorless artifact creature rather than the black one shown in the standard print. For example, casting it for one colorless mana makes it a 1/2 colorless permanent, so you can activate its artifact abilities without triggering effects that specifically care about creature colors. This works because while casting a prototyped spell, you use only its alternative power, toughness, and mana cost when evaluating those characteristics to see if it can be cast, completely overriding the normal values.

I just attacked with my commander and they blocked it. Damage is marked but not lethal yet. My opponent says they can pull a card from their outside deck to replace it, but I think that's only allowed after damage. What actually happens right now?

According to game structure, whenever a player would get priority, the game checks for state-based conditions and performs all applicable state-based actions simultaneously as a single event. If any occur, the check repeats; otherwise, all triggered abilities waiting to be put on the stack are placed on the stack, then the check repeats until stable, after which the appropriate player gets priority. This sequence dictates when your opponent could legally act. However, format legality strictly overrides external actions by stating that except via specific rules and effects, traditional cards from outside the game cannot be brought into a Commander game. They also cannot bring a card this way if it has the same name as a card in their starting deck or current game, or if any color in its identity is not in their commander's identity. The priority cycle establishes the exact window for action, while the outside-card restriction dictates what is permitted within that window. Since your opponent violates both the mandatory timing order and the naming and color restrictions, they cannot pull any card. The combat damage remains marked as is, triggered abilities move to the stack, and play continues with no external card entering play.

I just tapped out for a big spell and my opponent cast something that puts an enchantment with at the beginning of your upkeep, you may draw a card onto the battlefield. Can I just wait until next turn to decide if I want the card or not? What actually happens to that top card of my library right now?

The enchantment will sit on the battlefield and do nothing immediately. At the start of your next upkeep, that ability triggers and goes onto the stack as soon as it happens, which aligns with the rule stating these abilities go on the stack when they trigger regardless of whether their controller intends to exercise the ability’s option or not. This stacking requirement takes precedence because it determines when you can interact or wait before any cards actually move. When the trigger reaches the top of the stack, you make your choice at resolution. If you choose to draw, a player draws a card by putting the top card of their library into their hand, so that exact card will move from your library directly into your hand. If you decline, nothing happens to the library. The concrete final outcome is that the enchantment remains in play, the trigger waits on the stack until its upkeep window opens, and a single card shifts to your hand only if you accept the draw upon resolution, leaving the rest of your library untouched.
I'm controlling a token created by my opponent's effect. Can I sacrifice that token to one of my own cards that says Sacrifice a creature you own?

No. The player who creates a token is its owner, regardless of who controls it on the battlefield. Since your opponent created the token, they own it, even though you are controlling it. Sacrifice effects that specify Sacrifice a creature you own will fail because you do not meet the ownership requirement. For example, if your opponent uses an effect to create a Goblin Token and you tap it into your library with Toil of Nightmares, the sacrifice cost cannot be paid because you do not own the Goblin.
I just cast a creature with tribute and my opponent didn't add any counters to it. What happens when its enter-the-battlefield ability tries to go off in that situation?

When a creature with tribute enters the battlefield, you first choose an opponent and that player then decides whether to put N plus one plus one counters on it as it arrives. Its enter-the-battlefield ability will still trigger regardless of their choice. The rules state that triggered abilities check if tribute was not paid, and this condition is true if the chosen opponent decided not to put the specified counters on it. For example, if you cast an eight-mana creature with tribute two from your opponent, they can choose to do nothing. Even though no counters were added, its first ability will still trigger when it enters the battlefield because the opponent simply opted not to pay.
What happens to the plane card and my turn order if I get removed from the game while I have a face-up plane card in play?

When you leave the game, the controller of your face-up plane card does not vanish. The rules dictate that if the current planar controller would leave the game, instead the next player in turn order that wouldn’t leave the game becomes the planar controller, then the old planar controller leaves the game. This transition happens automatically as a sequence of events rather than leaving the plane card ownerless. For example, imagine a four-player multiplayer match where you are on turn one with your plane card face-up. You suddenly lose all life and leave the game. The plane card remains in play, and since you are gone, the next player in turn order automatically becomes the new planar controller. That player now has control over any actions or triggers tied to that plane card until they either leave the game or the active player changes.
My group of four wanted to play Vanguard together, but I'm not sure if that's allowed. Can a Vanguard game have more than two players, or is it limited to just two?

Yes, a Vanguard game can definitely include more than two players. The official rules state that 'A Vanguard game may be a two-player game or a multiplayer game,' which explicitly permits matches with any number of participants beyond the standard 1v1 setup. For instance, if you and three friends decide to play together, all four of you can participate in the same match, with each player interacting on the battlefield simultaneously just like in standard multiplayer formats.

I have an Enigma Elemental that taps to add {C} for each damage dealt to me during combat, and my opponent attacks with a Knight of the Skyshroud and two 1/1 Goblin tokens. Do I get mana for all three creatures' damage or just one?

You only get mana for the damage from the specific creature that triggered your ability. When an effect triggers based on damage from a particular source and refers to 'damage dealt,' it counts only that source's damage and ignores any other simultaneous damage from different sources. In this scenario, if Enigma Elemental triggers off the Knight dealing 2 damage, it will generate exactly two mana. The ability does not add the damage from the Goblins into its calculation; it treats their damage as irrelevant for the purpose of that specific triggered ability.

I just attacked with my creature and it dealt lethal damage, which brought my opponent's life down to zero. They have an enchanted card that says whenever they lose the game, they get three points added to their final score. But during the combat damage step, I also tapped a land that told me to roll two dice but never listed what the numbers mean. We're arguing about whether I even need to look at those die rolls now that my opponent is winning. What actually happens?

The dice-rolling ability you activated still functions exactly as its text says it will, because it applies to your actions independently from their loss trigger. Meanwhile, your opponent’s triggered ability activates automatically when they reach zero life and leave the game, adding three points to their score before the match ends. The rules apply to each player’s respective actions without blocking each other, so the game concludes with your opponent losing.
What happens if my opponent tries to destroy one of my creatures while another effect simultaneously exiles it when it would die? Do I just lose it, or can I decide where it goes?
