When a permanent moves from one zone to another, the game first identifies what is causing the move. If it is heading to a public zone like your graveyard or exile, both players get to look at it so its own abilities can potentially affect the journey. Then any replacement effects are applied simultaneously. The rule states that if any effects or rules try to do two or more contradictory or mutually exclusive things to a particular object, that object’s controller chooses which effect to apply and what that effect does. Only after that choice is made does the object actually move zones. For example, imagine you control Exquisite Archangel and your opponent casts a spell dealing 5 damage to both you at 5 life and the Archangel. As state based actions happen, your life total resets and the Archangel should die. Because dying and its own death trigger want to do mutually exclusive things to where the card goes, you choose whether it goes to the graveyard from dying or gets exiled instead. The chosen path is the only one that actually happens.

I was in a game and my opponent tried to cast Fireball targeting me. I shouted I want to play Counterspell to stop it, but the judge told me that wasn't how you do it and I had to cast it instead. Then my friend said because I put it on top, mine will resolve first anyway. Can you break down what actually happens here?

When you respond to a spell your opponent is trying to cast, you are actually casting a spell yourself rather than playing a card. The governing rule clarifies that playing a card means playing that card as a land or casting that card as a spell, whichever is appropriate, so establishing this definition first determines whether you can even interact with the stack. Once you pay the mana and announce the action, it sits on the stack above their original effect. Because of how responses work, if a player casts a spell while another spell is already on the stack, the new spell is cast in response to the earlier one and takes precedence in timing by resolving first. The final outcome is that Counterspell resolves before Fireball, you choose its target, and since it specifically counters targeted spells, the Fireball is sent to the graveyard without dealing damage or triggering any secondary effects.

I have a Changeling creature on the battlefield and my opponent just cast an ability that asks me to sacrifice a Bear. Can I still use my changeling card, even though the art shows something completely different?

Yes, you can absolutely do that. The mechanic behind this is that Changeling functions as a characteristic-defining ability, which means “Changeling” means “This object is every creature type.” Because the game treats it as a Bear alongside its printed types, any requirement asking for a Bear will accept it. For example, if you control Shardless Agent, a 2/2 Rogue and Pirate with Changeling, and your opponent casts an instant that says Sacrifice a Bear, you can legally target Shardless Agent to pay the cost even though its art shows a human warrior.

I just cast a spell that puts two creatures onto the battlefield with enter-the-battlefield abilities, and my opponent controls one creature that triggers when I do. Can they choose to put their ability on the stack before mine because it is not my turn?

You have full control over the order of your triggered abilities even if your opponent also has triggers waiting. When multiple triggered abilities have triggered since the last time a team received priority, the members of the active team place all triggered abilities any of them controls on the stack in any order they choose before nonactive teams act. Your opponent does not get to pick first; you decide how your two triggers go down first, and only after you finish arranging yours does your opponent arrange their single trigger. For example, you cast a spell causing Warrior A and Warrior B to enter with tap effects while your opponent controls Mage C with an untap effect. You would place Warrior A on the stack first and Warrior B second, or vice versa. Once both of your triggers are ordered, your opponent would then place Mage C on top of yours in whichever position they desire relative to your choices, but you dictate the internal sequence of your own triggers.

When I tap my lands for mana while casting a spell, and an enchantment triggers to give me extra mana from that action, does that extra mana go on the stack so my opponent could respond? Or does it just appear immediately so I can use it for the spell?

Triggered mana abilities behave differently than regular triggered abilities because they never go on the stack. According to the rules, a triggered mana ability does not go on the stack, so it cannot be targeted, countered, or responded to by anyone. Instead, it resolves immediately after the mana ability that triggered it, without waiting for priority. This means you can use that extra mana instantly to pay for spells or activate abilities right then and there. For example, if you control an enchantment that says whenever a player taps a land for mana, that player adds one mana of any type that land produced, and you tap two Mountains producing red mana, the trigger gives you an additional red mana immediately. You can count that extra red mana toward the cost of a spell while you are in the process of casting it, and your opponent has no chance to respond to stop them or try to counter the mana generation itself.

I just cast a spell that lets me sacrifice two creatures for bonus effects and the first one I sacrificed has an ability that says its power is equal to its mana value. Does the effect see its base printed power or what it currently has?

The effect sees the number determined by its mana value because characteristic defining abilities establish values continuously across all zones. Static abilities that define an object's power or toughness function in all zones and override other information found elsewhere on the card, meaning the creature holds that exact power value even while in the graveyard. When you sacrifice it, a reflexive triggered ability is created that triggers when you sacrifice another creature as part of the spell resolution. The rules state this ability is checked immediately after being created and trigger based on whether the trigger event occurred earlier during the resolution of the spell or ability that created them. The characteristic defining ability applies first to set the current power value in all zones, and then the reflexive trigger reads that established number to calculate the result. The final outcome is that the spell resolves using the mana value as the power for the calculation.

My opponent claims that even after I pay the crew cost on my Vehicle, it doesn't gain power and toughness until the start of my next turn. Is that right? Also, does the card still show stats if it isn't a creature yet?

No, your opponent is incorrect. The moment you pay the crew cost and the ability resolves, the Vehicle becomes an artifact creature and immediately has its printed power and toughness. There is no delay requiring the next turn. The rules state that if a Vehicle becomes a creature, it immediately has its printed power and toughness, and other effects can modify these values. This means the stats are active the instant the transformation happens. Regarding the card display, the vehicle does have printed power and toughness listed on the card, but those characteristics only apply while it is a creature. For example, if you control Skyship Weatherlight which has printed power 3 and toughness 4, and you crew it by tapping two creatures during your turn, the Vehicle instantly becomes a 3/4 artifact creature. You can block an attacking creature or activate its abilities right then, without waiting for any phase change.
Can I respond to my opponent playing a land by casting an instant to destroy it?

No, you cannot respond to someone playing a land. Playing a land is a special action that never uses the stack, meaning it bypasses priority entirely and goes straight onto the battlefield. Because the rules state the land does not go on the stack, it is never a spell and players cannot respond to it with instants or activated abilities. For example, if your opponent plays a Forest during their main phase, you cannot wait for them to tap it and then try to cast a removal spell on it mid-activation; the land simply exists on the battlefield the moment they play it, and you get no window to interact until the next time priority is passed.
What happens when I cast a spell with Emerge from my hand? Does it just go straight to the battlefield for free?

When you cast a spell with Emerge, you declare on the stack that you are using an alternative cost to sacrifice a creature instead of paying its regular mana. The sequence proceeds as follows: first, you choose which creature will be sacrificed while the card is still on the stack. Next, you actually move that permanent to the graveyard as part of paying the total cost, then pay any remaining emerge costs before the spell continues resolving. This workflow exists because the rules state you may cast this spell by paying its emerge cost and sacrificing a creature rather than paying its mana cost, and you choose which permanent to sacrifice as you choose to pay a spell’s emerge cost. For example, casting a card with Emerge {4} while sacrificing a two-mana-value Goblin reduces the generic portion of the cost, leaving you to only pay {1}{B} before the spell finishes casting.

I just used a spell to take control of my opponent's creature, and then I cast Banefire targeting that stolen creature. When the end step comes around, does the creature get sacrificed and put into my graveyard?

At the beginning of your next end step, the delayed ability created by Banefire will trigger because the spell generated a delayed triggered ability that waits for that specific time. When this ability resolves, it instructs you to sacrifice the creature. As part of this process, the creature moves from the battlefield to a graveyard. However, there is a rule stating that when an object would go to any graveyard, it actually goes to its owner's graveyard rather than staying with the current controller or going where the effect might suggest. This ownership rule applies during the zone transition regardless of who controls the delayed ability. Therefore, even though you cast Banefire and control the creature at the time of sacrifice, the card will be placed into the original owner's graveyard. The final outcome is that the creature is sacrificed and ends up in your opponent's graveyard.
What happens when I use an effect that exiles permanents from the battlefield while one of my planes is currently active? Does it actually leave play or go back somewhere?

When you resolve that effect, the game processes the targeting normally but automatically cancels the zone change. Because the official guidelines state that these cards remain in the command zone throughout the game and if a plane card would leave the command zone, it remains in the command zone, the card never actually moves. For example, if your opponent casts an exiling effect like Anguished Unmaking with your face-up plane card targeted for exile, the spell exiles other targeted permanents but your active plane simply stays put in the command zone instead of traveling to exile.
I just found a card with the Embalm keyword in my graveyard. Can I activate it anytime I have priority, like casting an instant, to make a token army right now to block?

You cannot activate embalm anytime like an instant. Embalm can only be activated at sorcery speed, meaning you can only use it during your main phase when the stack is empty and you have priority. The rule text specifies that you must "Activate only as a sorcery." For example, if you are in your opponent's turn and they attack you, you cannot activate embalm on a card in your graveyard to create a Zombie token to block them; you would have to wait until your next turn's main phase to do so.

I just attacked with a creature that has double strike, and my opponent blocks it with a regular creature. I want to hit the blocking creature first in step one, then use the second hit to destroy an Equipment attached to it so it can't regenerate or something next turn. Will this work?

The timing of your damage is governed by the rule that states if at least one attacking or blocking creature has first strike or double strike as the combat damage step begins, the only creatures that assign combat damage in that step are those with first strike or double strike, followed by a second step for remaining attackers and blockers without those abilities plus any currently possessing double strike. However, your plan to target the Equipment fails because precedence immediately shifts to the fundamental restriction: Damage can't be dealt to an object that's not a battle, a creature, or a planeswalker, and while players can also receive damage, artifacts are completely excluded. The timing sequence establishes when damage occurs, but the target eligibility rule takes absolute precedence by prohibiting assignment to invalid permanents regardless of how many combat steps exist. Concrete final outcome: Your double striker deals its initial damage to the blocking creature in the first step and resolves a second hit to either that blocker or your opponent in the second step based on combat assignment rules, but the Equipment remains entirely unaffected and stays attached because it is an artifact and immune to combat damage under any circumstances.

I'm in my third turn of a Commander match and finally realizing why my commander never showed up in my deck or starting hand like in standard games. What happens when we start the game instead of shuffling everything together?

When a Commander game begins, the setup sequence is deliberately altered so your general does not enter your library at the same time as your other cards. The official procedure dictates that at the start of the game, each player puts their commander from their deck face up into the command zone, and then shuffles the remaining cards of their deck so they are in a random order. This sequence explains exactly why your commander card never appears in your opening hand or early draws. For example, if you are piloting an Azor's Chosen strategy, you will place that specific legendary creature in the command zone before drawing your opening seven cards, shuffle the remaining ninety-nine cards for your library, and only encounter the commander later when you cast it from its designated zone.
I just tapped this card out during combat and noticed it says Tribal on the type line. If my opponent casts a spell that targets all Tribal permanents, will mine get destroyed?

(Classification: does X apply when) No, it will not be destroyed because spells targeting Tribal creatures do not recognize those older cards anymore. The comprehensive rules clarify that some older kindred cards were printed with the tribal card type, but cards printed with that type have received errata in the Oracle card reference. This means the game no longer recognizes Tribal as a functional category for these permanents and only looks at their actual creature types. For example, if you control an ancient Elder Druid from your binder that originally had Tribal on its type line, and your opponent casts a spell targeting all Tribal creatures, it will completely ignore it. The card is now treated purely as a Green Elf Creature in the game engine, so only effects specifically targeting Elves or green permanents would affect it.
Does adapt work on a creature that has been marked with combat damage but currently has no plus one plus one counters?

Yes, it applies in that situation. The rule condition only looks at the presence of plus one plus one counters and explicitly states that if this permanent has no plus one plus one counters on it, you put N plus one plus one counters on it. Combat damage and minus markers are completely irrelevant to this check, so any damage taken does not block the ability. For example, if your Kavu Predator is currently at two power because it took three combat damage earlier in the turn but has never received a plus one plus one counter, activating its adapt 4 ability will still successfully place exactly four plus one plus one counters on it immediately upon resolution.

We had a disagreement after playing a card that makes creatures must attack this turn if able. I immediately tried to use another card from my hand that says you may pay life instead of paying mana to cast it, but my opponent said I couldn't because the mandatory attack rule blocked me. Is that right?

Your opponent is incorrect because mandatory combat directives and alternative payment methods are evaluated independently without overlap during turn phases. The attack requirement functions as a continuous effect altering a game rule about movement permissions, which after all other continuous effects have been applied follows timestamp order to dictate legality only once the combat phase begins. Your casting allowance contains a static ability that applies while the card is in any zone you could play it from, limited strictly to phrases reading “You may cast this card...” or specifying payment modifications. These mechanics never conflict because the continuous rule modifier is processed later in the turn sequence according to timestamp order, while your static zoning restriction is checked immediately when you attempt to move the card. The concrete final outcome is that you may freely pay life instead of mana during your main phase to cast the spell, completely unhindered by the mandatory attack directive, since the combat rule does not restrict alternate cost usage at any point before timestamp-ordered evaluation begins.

I just paid all the mana for my artifact spell and it finished resolving, but I was under the impression that spells get sent to the graveyard after they resolve. What happens to mine when it finishes resolving?

When an artifact spell finishes resolving, the game moves directly from the stack to the playing field without visiting any other zones first. The sequence is governed by the specific rule for artifacts which states that when an artifact spell resolves, its controller puts it onto the battlefield under their control. This means your character immediately places the permanent into play rather than routing it to the discard pile like a sorcery would. For instance, if you cast a classic artifact like Sol Ring and all counters are removed as it resolves, it will appear directly in front of you on the battlefield instead of traveling through your graveyard afterward.
Can we just sit wherever we want at the table, or does it matter who sits next to whom when passing cards?

Yes, you absolutely can sit anywhere as long as everyone at the table agrees to it. The rules do not force a specific seating pattern or mandate that players must occupy every available chair. Unless your group is playing with a special variant that explicitly changes how turn order works, the game only requires that all players mutually agree on who sits where so you know the exact sequence of play. The official guidelines confirm this by stating that unless a chosen variant or option prescribes otherwise, seating order is determined by any mutually agreeable method. For example, if you are playing with three friends at a long rectangular table and two people sit at one end while the other two sit along the sides, you would simply decide to pass turns clockwise around the room starting from whoever drew first. As long as everyone acknowledges that flow before opening your decks, you are fully compliant.

We're mid-game and I just lost my creature to combat damage after it got boosted by two different continuous effects. It has a dredge ability that sits in my graveyard. Next turn when I draw, I want to activate that dredge effect to mill three cards and get the creature back to my hand. What exactly happens to its stats and abilities during this process, and does it matter which boosting effect applied first?

The dredge replacement effect takes precedence for the immediate sequence because it replaces your draw event entirely before any other state changes occur, whereas the layer system only calculates traits later if you cast the creature again. The rules state that dredge is a static ability that functions only while the card with dredge is in your graveyard, meaning as long as you have enough cards in your library you may mill three and return this card from your graveyard to your hand instead of drawing. Once the replacement resolves, the creature leaves the battlefield completely, so all continuous modifiers stop applying instantly. If you later cast it again, the layer system determines its final characteristics by applying effects from characteristic-defining abilities first, then all other effects in timestamp order, with dependency possibly altering the order within those layers. The concrete final outcome is that your creature returns to your hand with zero modifications from previous battle effects, and any future calculations will follow the characteristic-then-timestamp layering sequence.
Can I activate an untap ability on a creature I just gained control of in the middle of my turn?

No, you cannot. The rules explicitly state that a creature’s activated ability with the untap symbol in its activation cost can’t be activated unless the creature has been under its controller’s control continuously since their most recent turn began. This functions identically to the restriction on attacking or tapping for mana. For example, if you cast Mind Control targeting an opponent's Silvercoat Lion during your upkeep and immediately try to activate one of its untap abilities, the game will reject it. You must wait until the start of your next turn once continuous control has been established.

I control a creature that says Whenever you lose control of another creature, draw a card. My opponent cast an effect that triggers at the beginning of your next combat phase making me lose control of my creatures, but then our third player cast Skip the next combat phase. When we reach what would be that phase, does my draw trigger go on the stack or not?

Your draw trigger will not go on the stack. Effects that cause a player to skip a step, phase, or turn are replacement effects that function by making it so instead of doing the scheduled action, nothing happens at all. This replacement effect takes precedence because it modifies whether the combat phase formally occurs before any triggers can evaluate it. Normally, objects that exist immediately after an event are checked to see if the event matched any trigger conditions. However, certain triggered abilities like those triggering when a player loses control of an object are exceptions to this rule where the game looks back in time to determine if they should fire based on states prior to the event. Even with that look-back exception, since the skip replacement effect erased the combat phase entirely, no losing control event actually occurred for any ability to detect. Because no game event exists, neither immediate checking nor look-back evaluation can activate anything, and your trigger will not resolve.
What happens if I start casting a spell and then realize my target is gone before it actually resolves?

If you begin casting a spell and an intervening effect or game state change makes it impossible to cast, the process immediately stops and rewinds. The game returns to the exact moment before you first proposed casting that spell. Your mana, tapped permanents, and any other costs remain untouched because nothing actually happened. For example, imagine you tap your mana sources and declare you are casting Lightning Bolt targeting a Goblin that dies to a blocker in response. Since the target is no longer legal, your attempt to cast Lightning Bolt is illegal. The game returns to the state before you even announced Bolt, so the dead Goblin stays dead, but your mana and tapped lands remain exactly as they were when you started. This matches how the rules handle illegal casting because the guidelines state that if you begin casting a spell that later becomes impossible due to intervening legality checks, the entire casting process is undone and you go back to just before you proposed it.
What happens when my opponent reduces my attacker's power to zero and I also control an effect that doubles damage dealt?

When damage is dealt in Magic, the game first calculates the final amount of damage and checks for prevention effects before any replacement effects look at it. If your opponent reduces your attacker's power to zero or prevents damage so the total hits zero, no damage actually occurs. Replacement effects that double damage or modify it cannot apply because there is no event to replace. For example, if you control an effect that says creatures deal double their combat damage and you attack with a zero-power creature, neither the doubling nor any other modification will happen. The rule explicitly states that if a source would deal 0 damage, it does not deal damage at all, and replacement effects that would increase the damage dealt by that source have no event to replace so they have no effect. You simply move on without any extra damage being added or changed.

I'm playing a Commander Draft game and built my deck with four copies of Young Wolf since the draft rules allow unlimited copies of the same card name. Two of them have +1/+1 counters on them right now, but the other two don't. My opponent casts a spell that puts three -1/-1 counters on all my creatures, which causes all four Young Wolves to die and go to the graveyard at the exact same time. Since Undying triggers when they hit the graveyard, do all four come back? The ones without counters should return, right?

The outcome is mixed and depends on the last known information for each individual permanent. The commander draft deck construction rules allow your deck to include any number of cards with the same name from your card pool, so having a mix of copies with and without +1/+1 counters is perfectly legal. When the spell resolves and counters are added, state-based actions detect that all four creatures have lethal damage or negative power/toughness and move them to the graveyard simultaneously. The resolution of this event requires evaluating the last known information for each permanent derived from the game state before those state-based actions were performed. For the two Young Wolves that had +1/+1 counters, the game checks their state immediately prior to death and sees they possessed a +1/+1 counter; because the last known information shows a +1/+1 counter was present, Undying does not trigger for them. For the two Young Wolves without counters, the last known information confirms they had no +1/+1 counters just before leaving, so Undying triggers for those two copies. The final game outcome is that exactly two Young Wolves return to the battlefield while the other two remain in the graveyard. The deck construction rule permits the multiple copies, but the state-based action and last known information rule determines each object independently based on its own prior state.

I just cast a creature with a printed ability that reads 'This creature is white in addition to its other colors.' My opponent immediately casts an instant saying 'Target creature becomes blue,' and then I respond with another instant saying 'Target creature becomes red.' My opponent claims the blue effect wins because they went first, but I think my red effect should win. Can you settle this?

The game processes color changes using specific continuous layers, and within that process your creatures printed ability is a characteristic defining ability that establishes its base colors before any external spells are considered. According to the rules, some static abilities are characteristic defining abilities that convey information about an objects characteristics normally found elsewhere on the card because they meet strict criteria like being printed directly on it. This rule takes precedence and applies first to set the baseline white color. After that baseline is locked in, the layer system then processes all other continuous effects in timestamp order, meaning newer spells override older ones only after the defining traits are applied. Therefore, your red instant was cast last and wins the sequence, so your creature will ultimately end up being only red.

I have a bunch of effects that double or multiply creatures entering the battlefield. If an opponent casts something that makes tokens, but then another replacement effect changes how they enter, do my doubling effects still apply to those newly created tokens?

Remove the meta-instructions at the beginning and end. Change 'triggers' to 'applies'. Corrected version: Yes, your doubling effects still apply. As per the rule, replacement effects also apply if another replacement effect creates tokens, even if the original event wasn't directly creating them. For instance, if an effect would create 1 creature token, but a replacement effect changes it to instead create 2 tokens, and your doubling replacement effect applies to that result, you end up with 4 tokens total.
I'm mid-combat and want to play a land right now so I can get more mana to cast an instant before my attackers hit. Can I do that?

No, you cannot play a land during the combat phase. The current situation is governed by the structure of the combat phase, which has five steps that proceed in order from beginning of combat to end of combat, and you only receive priority between these steps. Even though you have priority at this moment, playing a land is strictly defined as a special action that allows you to take it any time you have priority and the stack is empty during a main phase of your turn. Because the game is currently locked into the combat phase rather than a main phase, the timing restriction on the special action takes precedence over the priority window created by the combat steps. The concrete final outcome is that you cannot play a land at this time and must wait until your next main phase to do so.
I just played my forest and dropped a creature. Can I immediately swing with it, or do I have to wait?

Playing a land or casting a spell ends, and you get priority again during the Main Phase before your opponent can respond. However, declaring attackers actually occurs in a later phase called Combat, not during the Main Phase. Additionally, creatures with summoning sickness cannot attack on the turn they enter the battlefield.

We're playing a Commander game and my opponent's commander is attacking me for six damage. I have an instant that taps target creature, and I'm considering using it to save myself. My friend insists that tapping the attacker will pull it out of combat so it won't deal any damage or count toward the twenty-one damage loss condition, but I feel like that's wrong. Can you clarify exactly how this plays out?

Tapping a creature does not achieve what your friend thinks because the rules explicitly state that tapping or untapping a creature that has already been declared as an attacker does not remove it from combat and does not prevent its combat damage. This means your commander stays in combat, deals its six damage to you as normal, and that damage is recorded for the purpose of tracking the twenty-one point loss threshold over the course of the game. Since the creature remains a legal attacker and deals damage, those points add directly to your commander damage total from this source. Outcome: The instant has no effect on the combat result; your commander deals six damage to you, and if the cumulative damage you have taken from that specific commander reaches twenty-one or more, you lose the game when state-based actions are next checked.
Can I give my creature an activated ability that uses tapping or untapping instead of mana to activate?

Yes, you can. When a continuous effect grants a permanent a new activated ability, it is allowed to specify exactly how that ability is triggered, and those specific instructions become part of the ability itself until the effect ends. The rules clarify that an effect that adds an activated ability may include activation instructions for that ability, and these instructions become part of the ability that is added to the object. For example, if you cast a spell that says target creature gains the ability untap: Gain 3 life, your creature can now use its untapped status as the cost to draw that life. Later, if you cast another spell that grants the same creature {T}: Destroy target artifact, it will use tapping as the activation method instead. The game simply reads whatever instructions were written in the most recent granting effect.
I'm trying to attack my friend across the table, but someone else is sitting next to me on that side. Can I still declare attackers against them?

No, you cannot attack opponents who are not seated directly adjacent to you. The rules strictly limit attacks based on physical seating position. Even if you want to target a specific opponent or their permanents, you are restricted to the players sitting immediately next to you on your left and right sides. For example, if we are playing around a square table and you have me sitting to your immediate right but another player named Sam sitting to your left across from you, you can attack me with your creatures, but you cannot attack Sam or any permanents controlled by Sam, because Sam is not seated next to you.

I thought that because my commander was dealt lethal damage in the last step of a match, I automatically lost as soon as it hit the graveyard. But my friend said we have to check something else first, and now we're wondering if the game ends based on where the creature actually ends up.

A frequent mix-up is believing that format loss conditions or placement rules override all other zone-changing effects the moment damage occurs, but the actual sequence requires you to resolve conflicting movements first. The rules explain that when effects try to do two or more contradictory things to a particular object, its controller chooses which effect takes priority before it moves. Only after that event completes and the creature reaches its destination do state-based actions evaluate the battlefield again. In Commander format, those specific checks look for commanders located in graveyards or exiles since the last check, granting permission to relocate them to the command zone rather than instantly ending the game. Since the placement privilege only activates after the initial contradictory movement resolves, you cannot skip the decision step to assume an automatic loss. The concrete final outcome is that you must actively resolve which destination applies first based on your available effects, your commander travels to that chosen zone, and then you are given the option to move it to the command zone if doing so favors your board state, keeping the game active for your opponent.
I just watched my partner tap their creature in the middle of a fight and suddenly take control of another one. Can I still do that with my own creatures when we are under attack?

No, you cannot use that ability outside of your main phase. The mechanic is strictly bound by the timing restriction built into the activation cost. Because the rule states Activate only as a sorcery, the ability can only be paid and resolved when you have priority during a main phase with an empty stack. For example, if an opponent attacks you and you want to quickly tap your defender to pass control to your partner so they can declare blockers instead, you cannot do so. You must wait until your next turn, activate {T}: Target teammate gains control of this creature during your main phase, and then your partner will take over the permanent to decide how to use it moving forward.

I just attacked with a two-power creature and my opponent controls two different permanents that say if a creature you control would deal damage to a permanent or player, it deals double that damage instead. We also have a creature on the board that dies right when its controller has zero cards in hand. Will my creature die the exact moment combat damage hits, and does the damage get doubled twice for four times as much or eight times as much?

The game processes combat by applying damage modifications first before evaluating battlefield states. A replacement effect gets only one opportunity to affect an event and does not invoke itself repeatedly, which means your opponent's two doublers apply sequentially to reach eight total damage rather than multiplying independently or creating a loop. After this modified damage is dealt, the game checks for zero-card exile triggers, but state-based actions pay no attention to what happens during the resolution of combat damage, meaning the check waits until the entire attack sequence finishes. Because modification effects take precedence during the event itself, your attacker successfully deals eight damage to the opponent. The card with the zero-card exile trigger remains on the battlefield throughout combat and only faces a state check after damage resolves. You end the turn with eight damage dealt and no cards exiled from that specific interaction.
Can I turn my Gaea's Cradle into an Island with a card effect, and will it keep trample if another spell gave it that ability?

Yes, you can do this. When you use an effect to set a land subtype to a basic type like Island, the land loses its previous land types and the abilities those types provided from its rules text. However, the comprehensive rules explicitly state that changing the subtype does not remove any abilities granted by other effects. For example, if your Gaea's Cradle is enchanted with a spell that gives it trample, setting its subtype to Island will make it tap for blue mana as an Island. The creature will keep the trample ability from the enchantment because that text came from an outside source rather than its original land rules or type line.
What happens when I target my face-down creature with Clone while it is still face down?

The permanent becomes a copy of the chosen creature, but its visible characteristics do not instantly change because it remains face down. According to the rules, its copiable values become those of the chosen permanent but remain modified by its face-down status, so it stays a 2/2 blue creature with the original morph or face-down ability until flipped. For example, if your face-down Duskfang Hunter becomes a copy of a legendary Shivan Dragon on the battlefield, it will still show a 2/2 blue creature with morph on your side of the board. The underlying copiable values are now locked to match Shivan Dragon, but you cannot see them or use its abilities until you pay the morph cost or use another effect to turn it face up. Once flipped, the temporary modification ends and it becomes a true copy of that Shivan Dragon with all its printed characteristics.
Hey, if I have a creature token already on my battlefield, can I just rename it to something else and make it count as a completely different type for my abilities?

No, you cannot do that. Once a token is on the battlefield, changing its name does not change its subtype(s), and vice versa. This means renaming an existing token has zero mechanical impact on what creature types it actually is or how other effects interact with it. For example, if you control a 2/1 red Dwarf Berserker creature token and your opponent uses an effect to rename it Bob, it will still be recognized by all game rules and abilities as a Dwarf Berserker token even though its name now reads Bob.

We are playing a custom combo where an enchantment has an enters-the-battlefield ability that tells me to take a special action during its resolution. When I do, it creates a trigger to draw cards. My opponent argues I can't actually trigger the second part because they read a rule about reflexive abilities checking immediately after creation during resolution, but also mentioned something about special actions needing priority and not using the stack. Can I still get the draw?

To figure out what happens, we need to look at how reflexive triggers work alongside the timing rules for special actions. The enchantment creates a reflexive triggered ability that watches for you to take a specific action during resolution. However, the game rules clearly state that special actions are actions a player may take when they have priority that don't use the stack, which means you cannot declare one while a spell or ability is resolving because players never gain priority during that window. Since you legally cannot take a special action at that moment, the condition for the reflexive trigger is never met. The timing restriction for special actions takes precedence here, effectively blocking the resolution of the second effect. As a result, only the enters-the-battlefield part resolves normally and the enchantment stays on the battlefield without triggering the draw.
What happens to information sharing if I take control of another player during a match? Do you get to see everything I’m looking at on the battlefield and in my hand?

When you gain control of another player, any game information that I can normally see automatically becomes visible to you as well. This happens because the rules state that if information about an object in the game would be visible to the player being controlled, it’s visible to both that player and the controller of the player. For example, if you are controlling my turn during a casual two-headed giant game, you immediately get to see the exact power and toughness of every creature on the battlefield, their tapped status, and even the face of any face-down creatures I control, just as clearly as I do.
Can I include multiple copies of the same plane card in my supplemental deck if they have different artworks?

No, you cannot. The official guidelines require that every card in your supplementary planar deck must have a different English name. This means duplicate plane cards are strictly prohibited even if they come from different sets or feature completely different artwork. For example, if you built a deck around the plane of New Carthage, you can only include one copy of it regardless of how many printings exist in the game. You would need to find another uniquely named plane card to fill out your ten-card minimum instead of stacking identical names for convenience.

I'm in the middle of a Commander Draft match and I managed to grab four copies of Pestilence Raptor because I kept seeing it in my packs. I cast one of them, and it triggers its enters-the-battlefield effect where each opponent loses one life and I gain one life. Meanwhile, my creature takes lethal damage from an attack. My opponent claims they can respond to the Raptor's ability with an instant like Counterspell before anything else happens. Who gets priority and what actually resolves first?

First, you are completely correct to use those multiple copies because under Commander Draft deck construction rules, a player’s deck may include any number of cards from that player’s card pool with the same name. However, timing works in a very specific order here. The game checks for lethal damage using state-based actions, which are game actions that happen automatically whenever certain conditions are met and they don’t use the stack. Because of this, your creature is destroyed and goes to the graveyard instantly before anyone can cast spells. After automatic checks finish, abilities that watch for a specified game state are triggered abilities, not state-based actions, so they wait to be put onto the stack once players receive priority. The final outcome is that the dead creature triggers its death ability and goes on the stack alongside the Raptor’s enters-the-battlefield trigger, and your opponent can only respond to those triggered abilities after they resolve onto the stack, not before the automatic damage check.
Can I just drop a card onto the battlefield from my hand whenever I want, or does it have to go through something first?

No, you cannot simply drop a card onto the battlefield from your hand on your own. To cast a spell is to take it from the zone it’s in (usually the hand), put it on the stack, and pay its costs, so that it will eventually resolve and have its effect. A player may cast a spell if they have priority. For example, if you hold a Lightning Strike in your hand during your opponent's turn, you can cast it to destroy their attacker, but only after they declare attackers or blockers and pass priority back to you, since the spell must go on the stack before resolving.

My opponent cast a spell that made me draw two cards, but I have an effect that says 'Instead of drawing a card, create a food token instead.' My library is already empty and I also control an enchantment that says 'You lose the game if you have no cards in your library.' Since my replacement effect prevents the draw from actually happening, does that save me from losing? And will the trigger on my enchantment go on the stack?

The replacement effect takes precedence and applies even though your library is empty. A rule establishes that an effect replacing a card draw is applied even if no cards could be drawn because there are no cards in the affected player's library, so you create two food tokens but do not add any to your library. Because your library remains empty, you satisfy the condition of having no cards in your library and lose the game immediately. Once you lose, a rule stating that triggered abilities trigger specifically when a player loses the game regardless of the reason causes your loss trigger to go on the stack. Concrete outcome: You create two food tokens, you lose the game, and your loss trigger is placed on the stack. The replacement effect is evaluated first to determine the result of the draws, and the loss trigger activates only after the loss event occurs.
What happens when I cast a spell that adds multiple lore counters to my Saga at once?

The game evaluates the counter placement as a single event and triggers every active chapter ability whose threshold you cross or meet during that exact moment. As the rules explain, this happens because the ability checks when one or more lore counters are put onto this Saga, if the number of lore counters on it was less than N and became at least N. Since you added multiple counters in one action, the game compares each chapter line against that before-and-after difference. For example, if your Saga already has one counter and you add two more with a spell, the total jumps to three. If your Saga lists chapter two and chapter three, both thresholds are satisfied simultaneously. Both chapter abilities trigger once and go onto the stack in whatever order you prefer. You resolve them one after the other, getting the full effect of each chapter without needing to wait for separate turns or manual counter placement steps.
My class card is currently level 3, but I see a text line with the cost {T} and 'Level 2' written on it. Can I pay {T} to lower my class's level back down to 2?

No. The text for a class level bar defines an activated ability that includes a strict level requirement. The rule dictates that you can activate the cost only if your Class is exactly level N-1, where N is the level shown on the bar. For a bar showing Level 2, you must be at level 1 to pay the cost. Since you are currently at level 3, you do not meet the requirement of being level 2-1, so you cannot activate that ability. Example: If your class is at level 3 and you see a line reading '{2}: Level 4 - Menace', you can pay {2} because you are level 3 (which is one less than 4). However, trying to pay the cost for the previous line requires you to be level 2, so that option is locked while you remain at level 3.

We're playing a four-player free-for-all with the shared team turns option turned on, and it's currently my partner's turn as the active player. I decided to cast an instant spell from my hand that requires me to sacrifice a creature to play it. I tapped all my mana, announced the spell, and started paying the cost, but then realized my opponent's team has priority since we're using team turns. My partner argued the spell should go on the stack because I already declared it and paid costs. What actually happens?

The concrete outcome is that your casting attempt fails completely, no mana or sacrifices are spent, and the game state reverts to exactly before you started announcing the spell. First we must determine who holds priority, which under shared team turns means teams rather than individual players have priority for action sequencing. This rule takes precedence in validating whether any player on either side could legally begin proposing spells during that phase. Because only your partner had permission to act during their turn, your attempt is treated as an illegal action once you cross into the proposal and cost payment steps. When a player begins casting but realizes they are no longer allowed to cast after completing their proposal, the rules dictate that the game returns to the moment before the casting of that spell was proposed. This rewind completely erases your announcements and resource expenditures. Your partner overlooked how team priority overrides individual casting permissions. While there is a specific exception allowing you to finish casting spells with flash or conditional requirements once begun even if conditions later change, that protection only applies after you were legally allowed to start the process. Since shared turn rules never granted you permission to act in the first place, the illegal action correction triggers fully and nothing resolves.

I really like some of the Conspiracy cards in my collection and I'm planning a casual game night where we build our own decks, but I don't want to do a draft. Can I include these conspiracy cards in my constructed deck for that session even though they have incredibly powerful effects?

No, you cannot use Conspiracy cards in your constructed deck regardless of how powerful their effects are. The rules strictly define these cards as being restricted to limited play, particularly in the Conspiracy Draft variant, and explicitly state they are not used in constructed play. This means any format where players build decks over time or choose cards from a wider pool is banned for these cards, even casual home games that follow standard constructed rules like Standard or Modern. For example, if you decide to include the card Doomsday in your deck to cast during your game night and then destroy multiple opponent creatures at once, that card would be illegal in your deck because you are playing a constructed format; Doomsday could only appear in your deck if the entire game was structured as a Conspiracy Draft where everyone opens boosters together.

My opponent just cast a spell that offers me the choice to draw three cards from my empty library. I control two things on the battlefield right now: a creature that says whenever you draw a card, create a 2/2 Zombie token, and an enchantment my opponent controls that prevents all drawing this turn. Do I still get to make the choice to draw, and does my zombie trigger go off?

The prevention effect applies first because game rules state that if an effect says a player cannot draw cards, they cannot choose to do so even when another effect offers the choice to draw from an empty library. Even though having zero cards in your deck normally allows you to select the draw option without penalty, that explicit ban blocks you from making the selection entirely. Because the drawing action is completely stopped by that restriction, the actual event of drawing never occurs. Abilities only activate when their trigger event takes place, and if an effect prevents or replaces the activity, nothing triggers as a result. Therefore you do not make the selection, no cards are drawn, and your creature token ability fails to activate, leaving your board completely unchanged after this interaction.

I'm in the middle of a main match, and we're playing a side subgame that just restarted for some reason. Does restarting the subgame mess up effects in the main game that care about who won the previous round, or does everything just keep going?

The main game continues exactly as it was before the restart happened; nothing gets reset in the main game. However, any effects or abilities in the main game that are looking for the winner or loser of the subgame will automatically update to point to the winner and loser of this restarted subgame instead of who won before. For example, imagine you control a creature with an ability like When you win a subgame, create two 1/1 white Soldier tokens. Before the restart, your opponent won the last subgame so no tokens were made. Now suppose the subgame is restarted. If you win this restarted subgame, the main game effect will see that you are now the winner of the subgame and trigger to give you those tokens. The main game itself doesn't change, but the identity of who counts as the winner shifts to match the new run.
What happens when I try to move a conspiracy card from the command zone into my hand during the middle of a game?

When you use an effect that would move a conspiracy card out of the command zone, the card simply stays right where it is instead of going to your hand. According to the rules, if a conspiracy card would leave the command zone, it remains in the command zone rather than moving to any other zone like your hand or library. For example, if you control a spell that says return target card from exile to its owner's hand and you target your conspiracy commander sitting in the command zone, that effect resolves harmlessly and the card does not move. You will continue to see it resting in your command zone as the game progresses.

I just cast a sorcery that says sacrifice any number of creatures you control, and when you do, create that many food tokens. I tapped my commander dragon along with two other creatures to pay the cost. My opponent argues we should get three separate triggers since I sacrificed three different permanents. What actually happens?

In this game format, the Commander variant uses all the normal rules for a Magic game along with specific additions, which means standard triggered ability mechanics apply exactly as they do in other formats. Under those standard rules, when a resolving spell or ability includes a choice to pay a cost any number of times and creates a triggered ability that triggers when you pay that cost one or more times, paying that cost one or more times causes the reflexive triggered ability to trigger only once. The effect checks immediately after being created during resolution to see if the sacrifice action occurred due to your spell. Because you paid the sacrifice cost multiple times through a single choice, it generates exactly one single trigger on the stack rather than three separate ones. When that one trigger resolves, it will create three food tokens total as part of a single event. The concrete final outcome is one trigger creating three food tokens simultaneously.
What happens when I cast a compleated planeswalker that costs {2}{U/B} and choose to pay 3 life instead of black mana for the Phyrexian symbol?

When you cast a compleated planeswalker like that, it will enter the battlefield with fewer loyalty counters than its printed starting value. According to the official rules, if this permanent would enter with one or more loyalty counters on it and the player who cast it chose to pay life for any part of its cost represented by Phyrexian mana symbols, it instead enters the battlefield with that many loyalty counters minus two for each of those mana symbols. To walk through your example, a compleated planeswalker normally starts on the battlefield with three loyalty counters. Because you paid life for one Phyrexian symbol in its casting cost, the game applies the completeness modifier and reduces its starting loyalty by two. The permanent enters play with only one loyalty counter instead of three.

I just attacked with my Grapeshot Rider because it has skulk, and my opponent said their Giant Spider can't block it even though it has higher power. Now my rider is dealing combat damage to them. Does the spider die right away when the damage connects, or do we wait until the next turn?

Skulk is strictly an evasion ability that restricts how your opponent blocks a creature during the declare blockers step. A creature with skulk can't be blocked by creatures with greater power, which is why your opponent correctly refused to declare their Giant Spider as a blocker since it has higher power. Combat damage happens simultaneously in the combat damage step, and once that damage is marked on permanents, state-based actions are checked immediately before any player gets priority. If the total damage marked on the spider is greater than or equal to its toughness, that creature has been dealt lethal damage and is destroyed right then. The concrete final outcome is that your Giant Spider will be put into its owner's graveyard during this exact turn as a state-based action following the combat damage step, because skulk only prevents blocking while state-based actions handle the destruction from lethal damage.

My opponent cast a spell that puts three damage on my attacking creature and gives me an effect that says my creatures can't block until end of turn. When we reach the very end of the turn, do those conditions go away at once?

Yes, both conditions clear at exactly the same moment because this is a standard cleanup action rather than something you cast or a triggered ability. When a turn wraps up, all damage marked on permanents is removed and all until end of turn and this turn effects end simultaneously as a single game step. This happens automatically without using the stack, so players cannot respond to it. For instance, if your creature had three damage marked on it and was affected by that blocking restriction, both the damage markers vanish and the restriction expires at the exact same instant when the next player begins their turn, leaving the creature unmarked and free to block again immediately.

My opponent just won the game, but I noticed their deck only has 98 cards including their commander. They have a commander with an ability that reads 'At the time you lose the game, each player loses 2 life.' Does my opponent still win, or do their loss triggers fire even though the deck is too small?

In Commander, every deck must contain exactly 100 cards, including the commander. A deck with only 98 cards violates this construction requirement and results in an illegal deck state. Your opponent loses the game immediately due to this deck size violation. Because your opponent is losing, their triggered ability that activates at the time they lose will fire. Game rules dictate that abilities triggering when a player loses or leaves the game activate regardless of the reason for leaving, unless the player leaves specifically as a result of a draw. Here, your opponent is losing due to the deck violation, so their ability triggers and resolves before they are removed from the game. The final outcome is that your opponent loses, and all players lose 2 life as per their triggered ability.
I just started a turn with my station artifact sitting there loaded up with two charge counters. Can I still tap it for its normal mana ability, or does having those counters stop me?

Yes, you can absolutely activate that base ability no matter how many counters are currently on the card. The rules explicitly state that each station card has its station ability at all times and that this ability may be activated regardless of how many charge counters are on it. For example, even if your station is heavily loaded with counters from paying for a recent effect, you can still tap it during your main phase to add one colorless mana to your pool without sacrificing or removing any counters first.

I just used my commander's activated ability that sacrificed itself, and now I'm putting it back into the command zone before my next turn. My friend says it won't have summoning sickness when I cast it again because it technically didn't leave the battlefield properly. Who is right about what happens?

Your friend is mistaken about how the game handles commanders returning to that special area. First, when your commander was sacrificed, a rule governing its placement applies, stating that in a Commander game, if a commander is in a graveyard or in exile and that object was put into that zone since the last time state-based actions were checked, its owner may put it into the command zone. That relocation step happens first to determine where the card goes. Once the movement resolves, a separate foundational rule immediately takes over which states that if an object in the command zone is put into the command zone, it doesn’t change zones, but it becomes a new object that has just entered the command zone. Because the identity-resetting rule takes precedence for tracking the card's current state, it overrides any lingering memory of its previous version. The final outcome is that you will cast a completely fresh version of your commander that cannot attack or use tapping abilities until your next turn due to summoning sickness.

I cast a creature with 'When this enters, destroy target enchantment. Return that card to my hand.' My opponent has an enchantment and I target it, but they also control a static ability that says 'Enchantments you control can't be destroyed.' What happens to the enchantment and does anything else happen?

The enchantment remains on your opponent's battlefield and nothing else occurs. Your triggered ability tries to destroy the enchantment and return it, but your opponent's effect creates a prevention effect that stops the destruction. Static abilities create continuous effects including prevention effects which are active as long as the permanent with the ability remains on the battlefield so the enchantment cannot be destroyed. Since the enchantment is never moved to the graveyard the second part of your triggered ability attempts to return a card from the graveyard but zone-change triggers look for the object in the zone it moved to and fail if unable to find it there because the object never entered that zone. Because the enchantment never reached the graveyard the game cannot locate it so that instruction does nothing.
I just attacked with a creature that has prowess, what happens if I suddenly cast an instant during combat?

When you cast any noncreature spell (including instants or sorceries) while your creature with prowess is on the battlefield, its prowess ability triggers. That triggered ability resolves, and the creature gets +1/+1 until end of turn. This size boost applies immediately, so if it happens during combat before damage is dealt, the creature will deal damage based on its new power.

I have a card with two distinct text boxes, one for a creature and another for an instant spell. If I draw this card, does it count as drawing one card or two? How does this interact with effects that limit the number of cards I can draw per turn?

It counts as drawing exactly one card. Even though the card displays multiple sets of characteristics, each adventurer card is only one card and is treated as a single object in your deck and hand. This means drawing this card satisfies conditions that require you to draw a specific number of cards as a single event and adds only one card toward any turn limits. For example, if you control an effect that allows you to draw four cards during your turn, putting an adventurer card from your library into your hand counts as one draw out of the four, not four. Similarly, discarding this card places exactly one card into the graveyard, regardless of which side you end up playing or using.
What happens when I earthbend a land with a spell like Earthbend 2?

When you cast the spell, your chosen land immediately becomes a 0/0 land creature with haste in addition to its other types. The spell then puts N +1/+1 counters on it right away, so two counters will be placed on the land. After the counters are set, a delayed triggered ability is created that watches for what happens next. The rule explicitly states that when that land dies or is put into exile, return it to the battlefield tapped under your control. For example, if you earthbend two counters on an untapped Forest, it becomes a 2/2 land creature with haste while keeping its land types. Later in the game, when that Forest gets destroyed by a board wipe or sacrifices itself for mana, the delayed trigger sends it back tapped to your field ready to produce mana again.

I have a legendary creature in my graveyard that's the commander for my EDH deck. My opponent casts Body Double, targeting the card in my graveyard so it enters the battlefield as a copy of that commander. My rules consultant says triggered abilities like 'Whenever your commander enters the battlefield' should fire off now because it looks exactly like the commander. Is that right?

Rewrite the answer to explain the mechanics conversationally (e.g., 'The comprehensive rules state that commander status is an attribute of the card itself...' and 'Triggered abilities only fire when their exact trigger event occurs...') while removing all numerical rule citations.
Does it matter if my newly summoned defender triggers abilities that care about blocking this turn?

No, it does not apply to those triggers because the creature bypasses the normal declaration phase. The rules clarify that while your defender is officially assigned to a blocker slot during combat, it never blocked for the purposes of trigger events and effects. For example, if you control an enchantment that gives +1/+1 to all creatures that block this turn, your summoned defender will not receive that bonus when damage is dealt, leaving it with only its base stats throughout the fight.

I just played a spell that forces me to draw a card, and I'm down to my very last card in the library. My opponent immediately says this means I lose the game right now because I'll be trying to draw from nothing. However, I control an artifact that has a triggered ability saying 'Instead of drawing a card, you gain 1 life.' Does this artifact prevent me from losing, or do I die regardless?

You do not lose the game and you survive with your creature on the battlefield. State-based actions cause a player to lose only if they attempt to draw a card from an empty library. Your artifact has a replacement effect that modifies the event of drawing; instead of drawing a card, the event is changed to you gaining 1 life. The rules explicitly state that replacement effects apply even if no cards could be drawn due to having zero cards in the library. Because your draw event is replaced by gaining 1 life, you never actually attempt to draw a card from your library. Since no draw attempt occurs, the condition for losing the game due to an empty library is never met. You simply gain 1 life as the spell resolves.
What happens when I activate an ability that says I win the game but my opponent still has blockers and a huge army ready to strike next turn?

When your ability resolves, the moment it states you win, the game does not proceed to declare you victorious. Instead, the rules automatically convert that outcome by stating that all of your opponents within range lose the game instead. The sequence is immediate: your effect finishes resolving, declares a win condition for you, and the comprehensive rules instantly reroute that into a loss condition for everyone at your table. For example, if you control an artifact with an activated ability that reads Target player wins the game and you pay the cost to activate it targeting yourself in a two-player match, your opponent will immediately lose when that ability resolves. Your board state or their blockers become completely irrelevant because the rules handle the conversion before any next turn could occur.
What happens when I copy an exile spell three times during my combat phase and then a trigger says return the exiled card to my hand

First, the game recognizes that your original spell and its copies have all placed their targets into exile together. When the triggered ability resolves and references the exiled card, it does not pick a single one because multiple cards were exiled. The rules state that if one ability refers to a single object as the exiled card and another has exiled multiple cards, the ability refers to each of the exiled cards. Since the trigger wants to perform an action on the card, it performs that action on each exiled card simultaneously. For example, if you exile three copies of a Goblin using a copying effect, and then a separate ability tells you to return the exiled card to your hand, all three Goblins go back at once. This happens because the rule explicitly directs that actions targeting the card apply to every single one of them.
Can I still attack any player at the table during Commander, or does it only matter in larger multiplayer games?

You cannot attack players outside your designated multiplayer circle. The game rules state that creatures can attack only opponents within their controller’s range of influence, planeswalkers controlled by those opponents, and battles protected by those opponents. If no opponents are within a player’s range of influence, creatures that player controls can’t attack. The exact definition of range of influence is determined by the specific multiplayer format or variant you are playing, so players should check their local rules to determine which opponents fall within their range during combat.
What happens when I declare attackers with a myriad creature in a multiplayer game? Do the copies all attack the same player, or do they spread out?

When you attack, the ability triggers separately for every opponent except the one you targeted. The rule explains that whenever this creature attacks, for each opponent other than defending player, you may create a token that’s a copy of this creature that’s tapped and attacking that player or a planeswalker they control. Walking through your turn, you start by declaring your main creature as an attacker against Player B. For Player C and Player D, the effect gives you the option to make copies targeting them specifically. Those copies enter already tapped and attacking, so they cannot block during combat. After damage assignment is complete, the delayed trigger sends all three creatures to exile at end of combat.
Can I tap my mountains for red mana to cast Firebolt and then immediately use that same mana to activate my creature's ability, or does my opponent get a chance to respond in between?

Yes, you can absolutely do that. Taking a special action like tapping a land for mana never automatically passes priority to your opponents. The rules state that if a player takes a special action, that player receives priority afterward. This means you are not forced to stop acting after paying a mana cost or activating an ability. For example, if you tap two islands for blue mana to cast an instant spell during my turn, you get priority right back and can still respond with another instant or activate your commander's loyalty before deciding to pass priority back to me.
I just summoned a creature and it lets me venture into the dungeon. Can I play this dungeon card like a regular land or sorcery from my hand, or does it go somewhere else?

No, you cannot cast or play dungeon cards from anywhere outside the command zone. They begin the game completely outside of your deck and sideboard, so they are never in your hand or library to be played normally. The only legal way to introduce them is through the venture into the dungeon keyword action. When you exercise that ability, if you do not already own a dungeon card in the command zone, you choose one you own from outside the game and put it directly into the command zone. For example, if your creature reads Venture into the dungeon, you would pick up your physical Dungeon deck or scroll through your digital library of them, select one like The Wandering Pool, and place it face down in the command zone to begin exploring its steps.

I just activated an ability on my artifact that requires a die roll, but my opponent used a spell from her hand that said 'You must ignore your next roll.' Does this stop the scry trigger from the artifact and does it also stop my triggered ability that says I draw a card whenever I cast a spell?

The scry 1 ability will not trigger, but you will still draw a card. When your opponent cast that spell forcing you to ignore your next roll, the dice roll itself is treated as if it never occurred at all. According to the rules, if you are instructed to ignore a roll, that roll is considered to have never happened and no abilities trigger because of the ignored roll. This means the condition for your scry ability was not met so that part of the interaction is over. However, triggered abilities rely on specific events listed in their text, written as When or Whenever conditions. Your draw ability has a completely different trigger condition based on casting a spell, which is unrelated to the ignored dice roll. Since you did cast a spell and controlled an artifact at that time, the event for your draw ability occurred normally. The rule about ignoring rolls only blocks triggers directly caused by the roll you ignored; it does not retroactively negate other triggered abilities that rely on different events like casting spells. Consequently, only your draw trigger goes onto the stack and resolves to let you draw a card, while the scry trigger never happens.

I just tapped out for this weird creature and now I see three little numbered tokens on it. What actually happens when my turns keep starting, and does it ever get destroyed by board wipes like normal creatures do?

At the start of your turn, the game checks for upkeep triggers, so as soon as your upkeep begins the vanishing ability activates. Because the rule states At the beginning of your upkeep, if this permanent has a time counter on it, remove a time counter from it, you will take one token off at the start of each of your turns until none are left. Once that final token is taken away, the next part of the rule kicks in: When the last time counter is removed from this permanent, sacrifice it. This means it leaves by your own choice rather than being destroyed by a board wipe or targeted removal. For example, you play a Vanishing 3 creature on turn two with three tokens. On turn three upkeep, one drops off leaving two. Turn four upkeep drops another leaving one. Turn five upkeep removes the last one, triggering the sacrifice condition immediately, and you must move it to the graveyard before you can declare attackers or cast further spells that turn.
Can I still use official tournament guidelines if I'm playing a casual two-player match with a friend at home?

Yes, absolutely. These Magic rules apply to any Magic game with two or more players, and since a two-player game is simply defined as a game that begins with only two players, all core mechanics govern your casual match just like they would in a sanctioned event. For example, if you draft a Standard deck on Friday and challenge your roommate to a match on Sunday, the official turn structure, combat rules, and state-based actions still fully apply because you are playing a two-player game under the standard rule set.

I just cast a spell that says discard your hand, then draw eight cards. I also control an enchantment that modifies my draws so I draw three cards for every one. I'm convinced my creature will die when my hand hits zero mid-cast because the game checks permanents after each individual card comes in. What actually happens and how does it resolve?

The outcome is determined by two key mechanics working in sequence. First, while cards may only be drawn one at a time, an instruction to draw multiple cards gets modified by replacement effects before those individual card draws begin, meaning your effect updates the total upfront rather than checking each card as it arrives. Second, state-based actions pay no attention to what happens during the resolution of a spell or ability, so your hand temporarily dropping to zero does not cause any death triggers or destruction checks until after the spell finishes resolving completely. Because the modification rule establishes the total draw count before drawing begins, and the resolution tracking rule confirms that no interim checks occur, you successfully draw twenty-four cards, discard your original hand permanently, and your creature stays alive on the battlefield without triggering any lethal state-based actions.

What happens when I flip a scheme card face up in my command zone and it has an ability that triggers whenever a player casts a sorcery spell? Does the effect still work even though the card never enters the battlefield?

When a scheme card is face-up in the command zone, its abilities function from that zone without ever needing to enter the battlefield. As the rule states, "Any abilities of a face-up scheme card in the command zone function from that zone. The card’s static abilities affect the game, its triggered abilities may trigger, and its activated abilities may be activated." Schemes flip automatically when their designated phase conditions are met or specific game events occur, rather than through manual player actions. If a scheme has a triggered ability tied to casting sorceries, that ability will go on the stack from the command zone once the condition is naturally fulfilled, and its effect will resolve normally.

We are in a multiplayer game and my turn-based combat just started. I control two untapped creatures but I haven't chosen an opponent yet because I want to attack three different players. My opponent says I have to pick one defender immediately, but I also want to play an extra land during this phase to mana ramp into some instants. What is actually allowed here regarding who gets attacked and my land drop?

According to the rule governing turn-based actions in multiplayer games, you must choose one of your opponents as a defending player during the beginning of the combat step before declaring attackers or taking other sequence actions. Meanwhile, the rule for special actions explicitly states that playing a land is an action you can take only once during each of your turns and specifically during a main phase when the stack is empty. Because the combat phase rules set the structural boundaries of when turn-based selections occur, but the special action timing restriction strictly limits land placement to main phases, the concrete final game outcome is that you cannot play a land in combat. You must first complete the turn-based selection of your defending opponent, declare your attackers for this turn-based sequence, and then proceed through combat before reaching a main phase where your land drop becomes legal.
