Can I exile my own creature with a spell just to get rid of it permanently, and if I accidentally exile the exact same card again from the exile zone later, will it still be gone forever?

Replace the hallucinated example with a clear, mechanically sound illustration that aligns strictly with the provided rule text without inventing card effects. For instance: 'Yes, exiling permanently removes a permanent from the game. If you later use another effect to exile that same object while it is already in exile, it will remain gone. This works because if an object in the exile zone is exiled, it doesn’t change zones, but it becomes a new object that has just been exiled. Simply put, re-exiling something already exiled does nothing meaningful; it just resets its status as a new exiled object and keeps it out of play.'

I just activated a creature ability that lets me sacrifice an artifact and then says whenever I do, draw two cards. My opponent immediately tried to shoot the creature with a removal spell before my draw trigger resolved, but the rules judge said they could not interrupt it at that moment. Why does the trigger wait instead of going on the stack right away like normal triggered abilities?

The confusion comes from how linked abilities function compared to standard triggers. Because this card pairs a static permission with a specific condition in the same paragraph, they work as a single unit rather than independent parts. The relevant rule states that these objects combine the abilities into one paragraph, meaning the sacrifice happens during resolution and the trigger only registers after that exact sequence completes. At that moment, standard queue rules take over, applying the principle that each time all players pass in succession, the spell or ability on top of the stack resolves. The linked evaluation takes precedence first by dictating exactly when the trigger is created, while the stack rule then manages the response timing. The final outcome is that you successfully sacrifice the artifact, draw two cards, place the draw trigger on top of the stack, let everyone pass priority until it fully resolves, and only then does your opponent get a legal window to cast their removal spell.
Can I cast my Lightning Bolt first and then play a card later in the same turn that says other spells cost one mana more to cast? Will the bolt suddenly cost four mana instead of three?

No, your bolt will remain at its original cost. When you announce a spell and pay its initial cost, that amount is locked in and placed on the stack. The game rule clearly states that casting a spell that alters costs won’t affect spells and abilities that are already on the stack. This means any cost modification effects only apply to spells you cast or abilities you activate after those effects resolve. For example, if your opponent casts something like Cost Increase after your Lightning Bolt is already on the stack resolving for one red mana, it does not retroactively raise your bolt's cost. The effect only changes the cost for future spells you might cast from that point forward.

My opponent cast a spell that would normally destroy my creature, but my creature has a static ability that says if it would be destroyed, exile it at the beginning of the next end step instead. Does the destruction happen immediately when the spell resolves, or does the creature just sit there? I'm confused about whether the exile effect is instant or happens later.

The destruction does not happen immediately, and the creature does not go to exile right away; it remains on the battlefield until a specific future time. Static abilities create continuous replacement effects that are active as long as the permanent with the ability stays on the battlefield, so this static ability intercepts the destruction and replaces it with a delayed action. The rules state that when a replacement effect creates a delayed triggered ability, that ability will not trigger until it has actually been created and the specific trigger event occurs again; here, the trigger event is the beginning of the next end step. Because the creature must be on the battlefield for the static ability to function as a replacement effect during the spell resolution, and because the delayed trigger waits for its designated time, the concrete outcome is that your creature stays on the battlefield unchanged when your opponent's spell resolves, and at the beginning of your next end step, the delayed triggered ability will trigger and exile the creature.
What happens when I cast an effect that puts a creature onto the battlefield face down and it has an enters-the-battlefield ability like searching my library for a basic land? Does it still trigger?

When you use that effect, the game performs two actions in sequence. First, it turns the object face down. Second, that face-down object enters the battlefield. Because the card is already reversed before it actually arrives, its enters-the-battlefield abilities never see it entering with their true identity and will not trigger or go on the stack. This happens because objects that are put onto the battlefield face down are turned face down before they enter the battlefield, so the permanent's enters-the-battlefield abilities won't trigger. For example, if you cast a spell that puts Joraga Treespeaker onto the battlefield face down through an alternative cost effect, it will not trigger its search ability upon arrival because it was already flipped over by the time the game registered its entry.

We are playing a combo deck and I just activated an ability on one of my creatures to set up a big finisher, but before I could chain my next steps, my opponent stole that creature with a spell. Can I still use the original activation for my combo piece that requires me to have activated an ability of a permanent I controlled this turn?

Yes, your combo will still work. The sequence of events follows priority first because the game rules state that if a player takes a special action, that player receives priority afterward, which is why you are able to chain multiple steps together without your turn ending immediately. Once that sequencing is established, the tracking rule locks in your history, as the guidelines clarify that when an effect looks for a permanent that was activated this turn, it means the permanent was the source of an ability that was activated this turn, regardless of whether that permanent still has that activated ability or the player who activated it is still in the game. Priority governs the turn structure and action chain first, while tracking preserves the mechanical history afterward. The concrete final outcome is that your combo successfully resolves because you maintained priority to chain the steps and the tracking rule keeps the original activation valid despite the opponent taking control of the creature.
What happens to the game state, my hand, and our life totals if someone actually casts the ultimate ability of Karn Liberated while we are deep into a round?

When Karn Liberated's ultimate ability resolves, the game immediately restarts. As stated in the rules, "One card (Karn Liberated) restarts the game. All players still in the game when it restarts then immediately begin a new game." This ends the current match and returns all remaining players to the beginning of a fresh game without carrying over any previous state or cards.

I just paid the cost to craft my creature, exiling a land and an artifact as materials. It returned transformed and gained flying because a card is now exiled with it. Right as it enters, my opponent’s spell tries to give all creatures -2/-2 until end of turn. Does the flying work while the size change happens, and what are its exact stats when combat starts?

When you activate craft, you exile the permanent itself along with specific materials and return the card transformed under your control. The rules note that this process refers to cards in exile that were exiled to pay the activation cost of the craft ability that put this permanent onto the battlefield. Because it arrives as a fresh object, it receives a timestamp at the time it enters a zone. Your opponent’s spell generates its own continuous effect when it resolves. The craft ability executes first to resolve the cost and put the transformed card onto the battlefield, but the timestamp system takes precedence for calculating overlapping continuous effects. Since within a layer or sublayer determining which order effects are applied in is usually done using a timestamp system, an effect with an earlier timestamp is applied before an effect with a later timestamp. The transformed creature's static ability effect receives its timestamp upon entry and establishes the baseline characteristics first, while the spell effect arrives slightly later in the calculation sequence and modifies those established values. The concrete final outcome is that the creature will enter with flying, then immediately receive the negative size modifier from the opponent’s spell layered on top of its transformed stats, resulting in a smaller but still flying combatant ready to attack.
What happens when the target of a permanent spell gets removed before that spell finishes resolving?

When you cast a spell with a target and that target becomes illegal, the game stops processing it entirely and sends it straight to its owner's graveyard. The rules explicitly state that if an object has an illegal target during resolution, the spell doesn't resolve. It is removed from the stack and put into its owner's graveyard. For example, if you cast Stone Golem targeting your opponent's Ashiok Dream Reaver, but they use Disenchant to destroy Ashiok before your spell finishes resolving, your Stone Golem will simply land directly in your graveyard instead of bouncing to hand or entering play.

I am mid-game in a commander match and my opponent cast Heart-Piercer Manticore. It enters the battlefield and has the option to sacrifice another creature for its damage trigger. I chose to sacrifice my own commander as that other creature, but because it is a commander, it immediately went back to the command zone instead of sitting in the graveyard. They insist the damage ability still goes on the stack and deals full damage. Is that actually how this works?

Yes your opponent is correct and here is exactly how the mechanics interact during resolution. The first relevant rule states that a resolving spell or ability may create a triggered ability that triggers only when you sacrifice another creature due to the original triggered ability and it checks immediately after being created based on whether the trigger event occurred earlier during the resolution of the spell. The second relevant rule confirms that in this variant game if a commander is in a graveyard or in exile and that object was put into that zone since the last time state-based actions were checked its owner may put it into the command zone. These rules interact through strict timing precedence because reflexive triggers are evaluated during the active resolution of your spell while the commander relocation function applies afterward as part of post-resolution state management. The concrete final outcome is that the damage trigger resolves successfully dealing damage equal to your commanders power to a target of your choice and your commander permanently moves to the command zone where it can be cast later or stay as a permanent option.

I'm defending against an attack where the opponent has a creature with Swampwalk and tapped two Swamps during their turn, but I don't control any Swamp lands myself. Can I block that attacker with my Knight?

Yes, you can block this creature without restriction from its landwalk ability. Landwalk is an evasion skill that prevents blocking only based on the resources controlled by the defending player. The relevant rule dictates that a creature with landwalk cannot be blocked as long as the defending player controls at least one land with the specified type. Since you are the defender and you do not control any Swamps, the condition for evasion is not met, regardless of how many Swamps your opponent controls or tapped for mana. For example, even though your opponent has ample Swamp mana available to cast spells, their attacker can still be legally blocked by your Knight because the blocker's legality depends entirely on your own land types; as long as all your lands are Forests, Islands, or other non-Swamp permanents, the Swampwalk ability offers no protection against your blocks.

I have a spell that says I can activate an ability of a creature this turn as though it had haste. My own creature is face-down due to Morph. Can I use the spell to activate the cost to turn my creature face up so it can attack?

No, you cannot use the spell to turn your creature face up. Turning a face-down creature face up is a special action, not an activated ability. The rules define that turning a face-down permanent face up is a special action a player can take any time they have priority, distinct from activating abilities. Your spell grants permission to activate an ability, but it cannot be used for a special action because the game treats these as fundamentally different categories of actions. Furthermore, when another card refers to a permanent that was activated this turn, it tracks permanents that were the source of an activated ability, which does not include special actions like turning a creature face up. Since you cannot activate the turn-face-up process, your spell has no effect on the Morph state of your creature, and it remains face-down with summoning sickness, unable to attack unless another source grants haste or changes its condition through different means.
I just joined a game where someone mentioned they are the archenemy, but before my turn started, it was already their turn to play. What is happening here? Did we skip a turn or make a mistake?

When a game uses an archenemy designation, the normal dice roll or coin flip to decide who goes first is completely skipped. Instead, rather than a randomly determined player, the archenemy takes the first turn of the game. This means your opponent starts immediately with an untap step and draw step while you wait for your second turn. For example, if you are playing at a casual table and one player declares they are the archenemy, they will untap, draw a card, and play their first land before you even take your first turn.
What happens if I cast something like Corpse Connoisseur by paying its evoke cost instead of its full mana cost?

When you cast a spell with evoke by paying the alternate evoke cost rather than its printed mana cost, it still enters the battlefield normally. The moment it arrives, its triggered ability sees that you paid the evoke cost and triggers. You do not get to choose whether it stays; the effect reads as When this permanent enters, if its evoke cost was paid, its controller sacrifices it. For example, if you cast Corpse Connoisseur by paying {3}{R} instead of {4}{B}, it hits your battlefield, then immediately triggers its sacrifice ability. After any players get priority to respond, the trigger resolves and you must move Corpse Connoisseur into your graveyard from the battlefield. This happens automatically because the rule states that casting a spell this way creates a triggered ability that forces a sacrifice upon entry.
Can I activate my planeswalker's +1 ability and then its −2 ability in the same turn if I have enough time to cast them?

No, you cannot activate multiple loyalty abilities on the same permanent in a single turn. The rules state that you may activate a loyalty ability of a permanent you control any time you have priority and the stack is empty during a main phase of your turn, but only if none of that permanent’s loyalty abilities have been activated that turn. This means once you use one of its abilities, the planeswalker becomes locked until your next turn. For example, if you tap Tamiyo for her +1 ability to draw a card and place a loyalty counter on her, you cannot immediately tap her again later in the same turn to activate her −2 ability, even if no spells are on the stack and you have mana available. You must wait until your next main phase to use any of her other abilities.

I just tapped my mana rock to cast a spell that exiles one of my opponent's creatures and sets a timer for it to bounce back at the start of my next upkeep. My opponent argues that if his creature gets turned into a land or an artifact before then, the timer breaks and he keeps it forever. What actually happens when that delay runs out?

The timer will still resolve exactly as written, regardless of any type changes your opponent makes. First, the linking mechanic takes precedence to establish identity: because your spell has one ability that causes cards to be exiled and another that refers to the exiled cards, these abilities are strictly linked, meaning the return effect only tracks the specific object exiled by that first ability. Once that tracking is locked in, the delayed trigger mechanism governs timing and resolution. Delayed triggered abilities wait for their specific event to occur and will affect the permanent even if it changes characteristics while in exile. Because the creature never left the exile zone, the trigger does not fizzle. Your opponent's attempt to change its type fails to stop it, and when your upkeep begins, the creature will return to its owner's hand exactly as planned.

I'm currently in a match and want to know if my creature can still block an enemy attack later if I used it to attack today. Can I have my creature both attack my opponent and block their creatures in the same game, or do I have to pick one permanently once I commit?

Yes, you can absolutely have a creature both attack and block across different turns. The rules clearly establish that creatures can attack and block, meaning there is no restriction forcing you to choose only one action for the rest of the game. This works because attacking happens during your Declare Attackers Step while blocking happens during your opponent's Declare Blockers Step in their respective combat phases. To put this into practice, imagine you control a Goblin Raider on your second turn. During your turn, you declare Goblin Raider as an attacker against your opponent for three damage. When your opponent declares their attackers in the next turn, you can then declare that same Goblin Raider is blocking one of their creatures during the Declare Blockers step. The creature remains on the battlefield throughout this process and fulfills both roles across separate combat phases without penalty.

I just tapped my creature to activate its ability, and before passing priority, I cast an enchantment that says any damage dealt to it would instead be dealt to the opponent's blocker. My opponent immediately responded by destroying their own blocker with a cheap removal spell. Does my creature still take the original damage or does the redirect fail because their creature died? We're stuck on whether tapping first locked things in or if they can still mess it up.

The redirect fails and your creature takes the full damage. Tapping is considered a special action, and as stated in the rules, if a player takes a special action, that player receives priority afterward, meaning you gained control of the stack to cast your enchantment while your opponent could respond with removal. Since they destroyed the blocker before combat damage was dealt, the replacement effect now checks what is on the battlefield when the damage would actually redirect. The rules state that some effects replace damage dealt to one creature with the same damage dealt to another, but if one of those permanents is no longer on the battlefield when the damage would be redirected, or is no longer a creature when the damage would be redirected, the effect does nothing. Because the special action rule dictates when you can set up your continuous replacement effect and pass priority, it establishes the timing window, but the redirection rule ultimately takes precedence at the exact moment combat damage would occur. Since the target blocker left play during your opponent's response phase, the replacement effect simply does nothing as written, and your creature still goes through its combat damage step unchanged.
I have a card that says it can only be cast after blockers are declared, but my opponent isn't attacking with anything. Can I still cast it during their combat phase?

No, you cannot cast it during their combat phase. The mechanic that determines this is whether the declare blockers step actually occurs on the battlefield. The rules explicitly state that if a spell states it may be cast only during combat after blockers are declared, but the declare blockers step is skipped that combat phase, then the spell may not be cast during that combat phase. For example, if your opponent taps out with no attackers because they have no creatures or are completely tapped down, the declare blockers step never happens. Since that prerequisite action is missing, the timing window never opens, leaving you unable to cast your card until a future turn where blocking actually takes place.
What happens if I attack with my Grizzly Bears and you block it with your Vampire Nighthawk which has afflict 1? Do I lose life?

Yes, you lose life immediately when the blocking is declared. The rule states that Afflict is a triggered ability meaning Whenever this creature becomes blocked, defending player loses N life. When you declare your attacker and I assign my Nighthawk to block it, your Bears becomes blocked right then, so the afflict 1 trigger goes on the stack and causes you to lose 1 life before any combat damage is dealt.

I'm in the middle of my turn in a multiplayer game and want to tap a creature to attack, but right before combat starts another player's life total hits zero and they leave. Does their stuff just vanish instantly, or do I still get to go through with my special actions like declaring attackers?

Special actions are defined as actions a player may take when they have priority that don't use the stack. However, tapping a creature to attack is a turn-based action during combat, not a special action. When another player leaves the game, their objects leave and their control effects end immediately. This process happens as soon as they leave and does not pause the current turn or freeze priority for other players. Priority simply passes to the next active player in turn order if needed, allowing you to continue declaring attackers and taking actions normally without interruption.
What happens when I cast a creature with prototype and choose to use its alternate power and toughness?

You make this choice as you put the spell on the stack, before paying any costs. The rule states that a player who casts a spell with prototype can choose to cast that card prototyped, and if they do, the alternative set of its power, toughness, and mana cost characteristics are used. You pay the new mana cost, and the spell retains those alternate stats while on the stack until it resolves. For example, if you cast Tuktuk Grunt in its prototyped mode, you will pay two generic mana and one red mana instead of just one red mana, and the spell will enter the battlefield as a 3/5 creature rather than a 2/1 because the alternative characteristics are locked in once you make the prototype choice.

I cast a sorcery that puts two creatures onto the battlefield. Each has an enters-the-battlefield ability. Do these abilities happen one right after the other instantly so I can chain them, or does my opponent get a chance to do something in between?

The spell resolves and both creatures enter the battlefield as the rules dictate that a permanent spell with no targets becomes a permanent and enters the battlefield under your control. Because they enter at the same time, their triggered abilities trigger simultaneously. However, these abilities do not happen instantly during resolution. The rules for triggered abilities state that once an ability has triggered, it waits until the next time a player would receive priority before its controller puts it onto the stack. This means your opponent will get priority right after all creatures have entered and all triggers are registered, allowing them to respond with instants or activated abilities before any of the enters-the-battlefield effects resolve. The final outcome is that the spell resolves, the creatures enter the battlefield, and then your opponent receives priority to act before you can use the triggered abilities.

I tapped lands and cast spells until my mana pool was empty, then my opponent played something that drains my unspent mana and puts it into their pool. What exactly ends up in their mana pool now? Do they get generic colorless mana, or do they keep the original colors?

When you lose unspent mana to that effect, your mana pool empties completely, and exactly the same mana moves into their pool. The game tracks which permanents, spells, or abilities produced that mana, so the colors, types, and any restrictions attached to it stay exactly as they were. For example, if you had three red mana and one blue mana floating in your pool from casting a fire spell, your opponent would receive three red mana and one blue mana in their pool with those same restrictions intact. They cannot convert them to colorless or use them for anything the original mana was restricted against, because the rule states that which permanents and spells produced the mana are unchanged along with any restrictions or additional effects associated with it.
I am in the middle of my turn and have already played my regular land, but my commander just gave me an extra play each turn. Can I still drop another one now?

Yes, you can as long as a continuous effect specifically increases your allowance. Normally the game only permits one land per turn, but effects on the battlefield can override that limit. The official rule states that to determine whether a play is legal, you compare the number of lands you can play this turn with how many you have already played, and if the number you can play is greater, the play is legal. For example, if your commander grants you one extra land play for a total of two, you could easily play your main land early in your turn and then drop a second land later using a spell like Rampant Growth.
Can I hold back a lightning bolt to cast it right as my untap phase finishes, so I can hit your blocker before combat?

No, you cannot cast instants during the untap step itself. The game automatically untaps your permanents and immediately proceeds to the draw step because any phase that does not give players priority concludes instantly once its built-in actions are finished. Since the untap phase gives you no chance to play spells, you must wait until combat or a main phase to respond. For example, if you tapped out last turn and now want to cast a lightning bolt right as your lands flip upright, the game simply skips that window, completes the untap action, and moves straight to your draw step before you finally get priority.

I have this creature that makes me draw a card whenever I control zero enchantments on the battlefield. My opponent casts a spell that exiles my only enchantment and then puts another enchantment from their graveyard onto the battlefield right after. During that whole sequence, does my draw trigger happen? And since the new enchantment looks exactly like my old one, will any of its enter-the-battlefield abilities know about the exile?

Your state trigger will resolve and you will draw a card immediately after the spell finishes resolving, not during it. This happens because triggered abilities that watch for a game state is true rather than triggering when an event occurs wait until priority returns before placing themselves on the stack. Since no one gets priority while the spell resolves, your ability holds off through the exile and replacement steps. Meanwhile, the enchantment that leaves is completely severed from its previous existence as soon as it crosses into exile, because any object moving between zones becomes a new object with no memory of or relation to its previous self. This means the returned card enters with zero linkage to its prior life. When both rules interact, the zone identity rule takes precedence during resolution as cards cross boundaries, while the state trigger rule governs what happens afterward when priority returns. The concrete final outcome is that you control one enchantment at the end of the spell, your ability meets its condition and puts a card draw on the stack right before your opponent gets priority again, and the returned enchantment functions as an independent permanent with no linkage to its prior life. You draw exactly one card.
What happens when my venture marker finally lands on the very last room of a dungeon card, but I haven't finished resolving its ability yet?

When your venture marker reaches the bottommost room, the game automatically checks a specific condition. If that dungeon is not currently the source of a room ability waiting on the stack, it gets removed from the game as a state-based action. However, if the final room trigger has already been placed on the stack, the dungeon remains in your hand until that ability finishes resolving, and then it is immediately removed once the stack empties. For example, if you roll the last room of Temple of the Eye and its ability to draw a card goes on the stack, the dungeon stays with you just long enough for the spell to resolve. Right after you actually draw that card, state-based actions trigger and remove the dungeon from your hand because no pending room abilities remain.

I just tapped my lands and sacrificed my creature to cast a big sorcery, but before it resolved, my opponent played an instant that exiled the exact same creature. When my spell goes off, does the sacrifice part fizzle because it is gone? The guy at my table said I wasted my turn since you can't pay costs for targets or effects after you start casting if they get removed.

Your sorcery resolves completely and does everything it says on the card without fizzling. The game handles this by strictly separating the casting process from the resolution window, which means responses cannot retroactively change what already happened during payment. First, when you propose the spell, announce your choices, determine the total cost, and lock it in, the rules require you to pay all costs immediately as part of that casting sequence. This includes sacrificing your creature and paying mana through activated abilities before anyone else gets a chance to act. Because the sacrifice happens during the cost payment step, the permanent is already moved to its graveyard and the cost is locked in before priority passes. Once the casting steps finish, the spell becomes the topmost object on the stack. Your opponent then responds by exiling something else entirely. When both of you pass without taking any actions in between passing, the rule about passing priority triggers and causes the spell on top of the stack to resolve exactly as it was cast. Since the sacrifice was already paid and locked in during the casting phase, the game does not check for it again at resolution, so your sorcery resolves fully and successfully. The casting mechanics take precedence first by establishing what is on the stack and locking costs, and only then does the passing mechanic allow it to resolve later.
What happens when I roll a die and two different cards try to modify my result at the same time? Do they just add up automatically or does something else happen?

When you roll a die, the number showing on the top face before any changes is called the natural result. If multiple effects try to modify that roll simultaneously, you do not just stack them all together. The rules state that if two or more effects are attempting to modify the natural result, the player who rolled chooses one to apply, following specific steps. First, you consider any effects that reroll the die. Second, you consider any effects that increase or decrease the result by a specified amount. After you pick which modifier applies, that chosen effect resolves and sets your final number. For example, imagine you are playing a dice-based card game and you roll a 4. An opponent spell says it will reroll your die, while your own aura says it will increase the result by 2. You must choose whether to let it reroll or add two to the four. If you pick the increase, your final result is six. If you pick the reroll, you roll again and use that new number.

I'm in a match and I control a Grizzled Outrider that says whenever it is dealt damage, you may draw a card. My opponent swings their only blocker and deals lethal damage to mine. Earlier this turn I cast an instant spell that gave my Outrider a regeneration shield. Does my Outrider actually survive or does it get put into the graveyard anyway? And do I get to choose whether to draw that card, or does it just happen automatically?

Your creature survives and stays on the battlefield while you retain full control over the card draw. The game resolves this by applying a replacement effect first. Regeneration is strictly a destruction-replacement effect, meaning instead of going to the graveyard, you remove all damage marked on it and its controller taps it. Because the damage event still officially registers in the game state, abilities that trigger from damage being dealt still trigger even if the permanent regenerates. That triggered ability immediately goes onto the stack when combat damage resolves. Since the ability contains the word may, it follows the rule for optional triggers where these abilities go on the stack when they trigger, regardless of whether their controller intends to exercise the option or not, and the choice is made when the ability resolves. The replacement effect takes precedence initially to keep the creature alive, followed by the triggered ability going on the stack where the optional rule gives you the chance to decide at resolution time. You will successfully save your Outrider and can freely choose whether to draw a card when the trigger resolves.
Can I win or lose a coin flip if my spell only cares about whether it comes up heads or tails?

No, you cannot win or lose that flip because the effect only cares about whether the coin comes up heads or tails to determine its specific outcome. According to the rules, some effects that instruct a player to flip a coin care only about whether the coin comes up heads or tails, which means no player wins or loses a coin flip for this kind of effect. When you are dealing with an outcome-only scenario, you simply follow whatever the result says without tracking a win or loss tally. For example, if you control an artifact that reads Flip a coin. If it comes up heads, draw two cards; otherwise put a +1/+1 counter on a creature you control, you simply look at which side lands face up and resolve that instruction without ever tracking a flip win or loss.
If a spell causes each player to sacrifice a creature, do we all select our losses simultaneously without anyone seeing the others' choices?

Replace the Lightning Greaves example with a neutral scenario: 'If you control two creatures and your opponent controls one, and an effect says each player sacrifices a creature, you choose first. You might sacrifice Creature A to save Creature B. Your opponent sees this and chooses whether to sacrifice their creature or another token. Then both choices resolve simultaneously.'

I just cast a spell that destroyed all creatures on the battlefield while my opponent had three creatures with death triggers on the field. We are arguing about whether one creature died first or if their triggers go on the stack at different times, and they want to rearrange the dead cards in the graveyard to make it look like a specific order. What actually happens here?

The rules state that the game looks back in time to determine if triggered abilities activate, using the existence and appearance of objects immediately prior to the event, which means all three creatures are registered as dying simultaneously rather than sequentially. This temporal check applies first to calculate exactly what triggers exist before any cards leave the battlefield. Once those creatures move to the graveyard, each graveyard is kept in a single face-up pile where you can examine the cards at any time to verify what died, but you normally cannot change their physical order. The look-back evaluation takes precedence because it establishes trigger timing and conditions before physical zone changes occur. The concrete outcome is that all three death triggers go onto the stack simultaneously and will resolve one at a time in active player priority order, with the unified face-up pile serving only as a verification tool that preserves whatever order the cards naturally fall into during the simultaneous mass destruction.

I'm in the middle of a game and my opponent just asked to see what card I'm actually using behind this generic white border card sleeve I put on my Fetchland. They're claiming I can't use that sleeve. Is she allowed to ask for that?

Yes, your opponent has every right to inspect the actual card because you are not permitted to use a substitute card like a generic white border sleeve unless it represents a double-faced or meld card. The rules state that if you use a substitute card, the real card must be set aside before the game and remain available throughout, so anyone can verify which real card is being substituted for at any time. Since a Fetchland is a normal single-faced card, it does not qualify for the exception that allows substitutes like sleeves or painted cards. For example, if you attempted to play with a plain white card as a proxy for your Storm-Scarred Citadel, your opponent can stop the game and request to see your set-aside cards; if you cannot produce the real Citadel or prove it is a double-faced card eligible for a substitute, this would be considered an illegal deck composition.
What happens if I have a scheme card face up in my command zone after using its ability, and no one responds to it? Does it just sit there until I decide to use it again?

No, the card does not stay face up waiting for your decision. The next time any player would receive priority, that non-ongoing scheme card will automatically be turned face down and placed on the bottom of its owner's scheme deck. This occurs as a state-based action provided there are no triggered abilities of any scheme currently on the stack or waiting to be put on the stack. For example, if you resolve the first phase of a scheme during your main phase, wait for your opponent to respond, and then pass priority while your opponent also passes, the game immediately checks these conditions before allowing you to cast another spell. The scheme is flipped over and moved to the bottom of your deck right at that moment, so you cannot use it again until you draw or otherwise retrieve a new copy from your deck.

What happens when I tap a permanent that has an ability preventing damage and also includes an extra effect, right as an attacking creature would deal combat damage to me? Does the extra effect happen before the damage is prevented or at the exact same moment?

When you activate such an ability to block incoming damage, the prevention occurs exactly when the original damage event would have happened. The extra effect takes place immediately afterward according to how replacement effects modify events. This timing split matters because any abilities watching for damage see the zero damage happen first, while your new effect resolves in the next moment of resolution. For example, if you block with a creature that has an ability that says prevent the next 3 damage that would be dealt to this creature and then draw a card, the damage is replaced by zero at the moment combat damage deals. Your opponent sees no damage trigger or life loss happen, and then right after that sequence finishes, your card draw happens separately.
Can I counter an artifact land if my opponent plays it from their hand?

No, you cannot counter it. This rule clarifies that any object combining the land type with another card type can only be played as a land and absolutely cannot be cast as a spell. Since lands never go on the stack, there is no spell on the stack for your counterspell to target or respond to during the window of play. For example, if your opponent plays an artifact land like Arcane Sanctum during their main phase, you cannot use Cyclonic Rift to bounce it or counter it when cast, because dual-type lands are placed directly onto the battlefield as a standard land drop rather than cast from hand or library.

I am attacking with a ten power creature and my opponent blocks it with two smaller creatures. I want to put eight damage on the bigger blocker and only two on the smaller one so both go down. Can I split the damage exactly like that during this step, and once the numbers are set, how does the game actually decide which ones die first or if they even survive?

You can distribute your attackers combat damage among multiple blockers however you choose, because the rules state that when two or more creatures are blocking it, the controller divides the assigned damage among them as they prefer. The combat assignment phase happens entirely first, locking in those numbers before anything else occurs. After the assignments are locked, all combat damage deals simultaneously to the creatures involved. Following that simultaneous deal, state-based actions are checked throughout the game and are not controlled by any player, meaning an automatic check immediately scans for creatures marked with lethal damage and moves them to the graveyard. The concrete outcome is that both blockers strike your attacker for their full power at the exact same time, and then the automatic check removes whichever blocker received enough damage marks to equal its toughness while leaving the other defender standing on the battlefield.
I just cast Vesuvan Doppelganger to copy a Runeclaw Bear on the field, and now I'm playing Clone. What happens to the copied information if my Clone copies that Doppelganger?

When you make a copy, the new permanent takes on exactly what the original currently is at that moment. The official guidance says that the copy’s copiable values become the copied information as modified by its status, and any objects that later copy it will use these new copiable values. Your Clone enters the battlefield matching the Doppelganger exactly. It becomes a 2/2 blue Bear named Runeclaw Bear with the upkeep triggered ability that the Doppelganger currently possesses. If someone else casts a second Clone later targeting yours, that new Clone will also become the 2/2 blue Runeclaw Bear with the upkeep ability, proving that the information updates and travels forward through each copy chain.

I turned my morph creature face up by paying its cost as a special action. My opponent claims they could have cast instant spells before that happened because playing a land and morph actions don't go on the stack, but I thought once I finished the action it was too late? Also, my card says 'When this turns face up, create a token. Sacrifice another creature to create two tokens instead.' We have Doubling Season. Do we get two or four tokens?

You cannot respond to the costs of turning a creature face up because costs cannot be responded to, but after you take a special action like turning a morph creature face up, the rules for special actions dictate that you immediately receive priority again. This means your opponent can cast instant-speed spells or activate abilities right after you finish turning it face up, though they could not stop the action itself while you were paying the cost. Regarding the tokens, the text on your card that says 'create two tokens instead' is a self-replacement effect that modifies the token creation event of its own triggered ability. When multiple replacement effects apply to an event, self-replacement effects are applied before other replacement effects like continuous doublers. Since self-replacements happen first, your ability attempts to create two tokens, and then Doubling Season replaces that with creating four tokens. The final outcome is that you create four tokens, and your opponent has priority immediately after the turn face up action completes to take any actions before the triggered ability resolves.
What happens if my opponent casts a spell that destroys one of my creatures during its resolution? Does the death trigger go on the stack right away so I can respond to it?

When you cast a spell like Lightning Strike targeting my Krenko, the moment it deals damage during resolution, Krenko's death trigger goes off. However, nothing actually happens right then because triggered abilities wait until the next time a player gets priority before going on the stack. This means your Lightning Strike will fully resolve and deal its damage before Krenko's ability even has a chance to be placed on the stack for you to respond to it. Once your spell finishes resolving, you get priority first, then I put Krenko's triggered ability on the stack, and that is when we get a chance to interact or let it resolve. The rules specify that while abilities trigger at any time during casting or resolution, nothing actually happens at the moment they trigger, so all waiting triggers pile up until priority passes.
What happens when a creature I control ends up with three +1/+1 counters and five -1/-1 counters on it? Will the excess ones stay or does everything get wiped out?

When you check the battlefield during any step of the game, the rules automatically scan for state-based actions and see that your creature carries both types of counters. The mechanic dictates that opposing counter types neutralize each other in pairs until only one variety remains. Specifically, N +1/+1 and N -1/-1 counters are removed from it as a state-based action, where N is the smaller of the number of +1/+1 and -1/-1 counters on it. In your situation, three matching pairs will instantly vanish during that check, leaving the creature with exactly two -1/-1 counters remaining while all the +1/+1 counters disappear completely.
When one of my soulshift creatures dies, does it go straight back to play or what exactly happens next?

When your soulshift creature is put into your graveyard from the battlefield, it triggers its soulshift ability before any other players can cast spells or activate abilities. According to the comprehensive rules, soulshift is a triggered ability and soulshift n means when this permanent is put into a graveyard from the battlefield, you may return target spirit card with mana value n or less from your graveyard to your hand. This means the creature does not return to the battlefield; instead, the game checks your graveyard first, and if you choose to use the ability, you move one matching spirit directly into your hand. For example, if you control Grim Lavamancer and sacrifice it to pay for another spell, its soulshift 2 triggers. You could then target an ancient zephid from your graveyard, which has a mana value of 2, to put it directly into your hand rather than letting the lavamencer stay dead or return itself.

I have Graf Rats and Midnight Scavengers on the battlefield. If I activate their abilities to meld them, what happens to these cards? Do they just turn over like double-faced cards, or do both stay on the battlefield?

When you meld two cards in a pair, they do not simply flip over. Instead, the rules state that to meld, you must 'put them onto the battlefield with their back faces up and combined,' resulting in 'a single object represented by two cards.' This means the two halves merge into one permanent on the battlefield. For instance, if an effect tried to meld Midnight Scavengers with a token copy of Graf Rats, neither would successfully meld because tokens cannot be melded, so they would remain exiled per the rule's example.

I’m piloting a mill deck mid-game and finally forced my opponent to draw two cards while they only had one left in their library. They had a legendary creature on the battlefield that says whenever they draw a card, they win the game, but instead of winning, they just lost. Why did losing happen before their trigger could go on the stack?

The situation happens because the loss condition is handled during a mandatory game check that always occurs before other actions. When your opponent attempts to draw a card from a library with no cards in it, they meet the exact condition for losing the game the next time a player would receive priority. The game resolves this by first performing a state-based action check every time priority becomes due. During this check, it looks for that specific condition and applies the loss as a single event before anything else happens. Because this state-based action phase takes strict precedence over triggered abilities, your opponent loses immediately during that check window. Their creature’s trigger never gets a chance to go on the stack or resolve. The concrete final outcome is that your opponent loses the game right then and there with zero cards left in their library, and their win condition does not resolve.
Can I cast an instant like Lightning Bolt right at the beginning of my turn before anything else happens?

No you cannot cast an instant immediately when your turn begins because priority has not yet passed to any player. The mechanic determining this is that the game automatically resolves a mandatory draw before allowing gameplay to start. This aligns with the official guidance that First, the active player draws a card. This turn-based action doesn’t use the stack, meaning you cannot intercept it with instant speed spells. For example if you start your turn holding Lightning Bolt, you must wait until after your library automatically shrinks by one card and the game passes priority to you before you can legally cast your spell.
What happens when an artifact like Paradise Plume has a color choice plus two other abilities that both rely on that same initial decision?

When you cast the card and pick a color, the game permanently ties that choice to every other ability that needs it, allowing you to track multiple effects simultaneously. The comprehensive guidelines state that an ability may be part of more than one pair of linked abilities. This mechanism ensures each connected effect shares your original selection without needing separate triggers. For example, if you cast Paradise Plume choosing red, casting a Red spell later puts the life gain trigger on the stack, and when you later activate its mana ability, it correctly produces {R} because the color choice is linked to that activated ability as well.

I just cast an enchantment that says whenever you cast a spell, you may draw a card. At the same time, my opponent controls a permanent that says players cannot draw cards. I had exactly one card left in my library and used it up on my previous turn so now my library is empty. Does the game immediately declare me as having lost or stopped progressing because of my empty library, or do we still put triggered abilities on the stack before anything happens?

When your library reaches zero cards, the game does not end or pause based solely on that condition. Instead, the ability you cast will resolve and look at your situation. Since an effect says that a player cannot draw cards and another effect offers that player the choice to draw a card, that player cannot choose to do so. You simply cannot take the draw action despite having no cards left. Only after that triggered ability finishes resolving does the game check for state-based actions as a single event. Once those checks are done, all waiting triggered abilities get put on the stack before any player gets priority. The concrete final outcome is that you do not lose immediately, your library remains empty, you make no draws from that trigger, and the turn proceeds normally as players receive priority to respond after the stack empties.
We just started a Two-Headed Giant match and I am losing track of when my partner gets to tap creatures for combat. Do we still take separate attack phases, or does our turn work differently now?

You cannot split your team into separate attack phases because the official guidelines confirm this variant uses the combat rules for the shared team turns option. This mechanic forces your entire partnership to act as one unit during the damage step rather than rolling initiative on individual creature groups. For example, if you control two soldiers and your partner controls one archer, you must declare all three attackers together in a single step, ensuring no partner ever taps or deals damage out of sequence with the team turn structure.

We are playing Commander and my opponent attacked me with their commander this turn, dealing exactly 20 points of combat damage. On their next turn they control an ability that creates a delayed effect which says the commander will deal combat damage equal to its power when it untaps. If I let it trigger, does that final point make them lose the game immediately?

Yes, they lose the game immediately. The rule governing delayed triggered abilities states that "A delayed triggered ability will trigger only once—the next time its trigger event occurs—unless it has a stated duration," meaning this effect will fire exactly one time when the commander untaps rather than repeating continuously. That single point of damage is added to the 20 they already assigned this turn. The specific rule for the commander variant confirms that "A player who’s been dealt 21 or more combat damage by the same commander over the course of a game loses," which operates as a state-based action checked continuously throughout the match. State-based actions take precedence and are evaluated before any player receives priority to respond. The concrete outcome is that your opponent loses the game the exact moment that delayed trigger resolves and deals the final point of combat damage, with zero opportunity for them to interact or attempt an alternate win condition.
Does the game consider colorless to be one of the five colors, or can I convert my white and green mana into it to pay for generic spells?

No, colorless is considered a type of mana rather than one of the five colors. However, you absolutely can use your white or green mana to pay for generic costs like {1}. The reference notation confirms that generic mana symbols accept any color or colorless mana. For example, if you have a Plains producing white mana and want to cast an artifact with a casting cost of {1}, that single white mana perfectly satisfies the requirement. You only need dedicated colorless mana sources for spells or abilities that specifically ask for colorless mana symbols ({C}), not for standard generic costs.

I am playing a standard game and down to three life. My opponent just attacked with a creature that has two damage already marked on it and has three toughness. I have an instant spell in my graveyard that can deal four damage to any target, but it does not have mana in its normal cost because it is meant for my hand. Can I use it right now to stop the attacker, and what happens to that card after it finishes resolving? Also, will the creature with the two damage on it die immediately?

You can absolutely cast that spell from your graveyard by paying its alternate cost rather than its normal mana cost, which allows you to play it there even during your opponents turn. Once on the stack and resolved, the spell deals damage to your opponents creature. The creature with two damage marked will not die immediately because state checks only happen between actions and before players receive priority. When the game pauses for state checks, it evaluates conditions like the rule that says if a creature has toughness greater than zero and the total damage marked on it is greater than or equal to its toughness, that creature is destroyed. Meanwhile, regarding your card placement, you followed the rule stating that if the flashback cost was paid, you exile the card instead of putting it anywhere else any time it would leave the stack. The concrete final outcome is that the attacking creature takes lethal damage and is put into its owner graveyard, while your instant card bypasses the graveyard entirely and ends up exiled after resolving.

I just played a Station artifact during my turn and noticed these faint horizontal lines splitting the printed text into sections. What happens when multiple triggered abilities appear above and below those lines, and do they resolve independently?

When you cast or activate that permanent, all of its triggered abilities go onto the stack simultaneously regardless of where they sit on the card. The game processes these as part of one continuous sequence because the faint lines are purely visual guides and do not split the text box into multiple sections. As the comprehensive rules explicitly state, these striations have no game significance other than clearly demarcating which abilities and which power/toughness box are associated with which station symbol. For example, if you play Mausoleum Guard and its entry trigger causes two different effects to happen, both triggers are placed on the stack at once using normal priority order. They resolve independently one by one, but they are mechanically grouped within a single text box rather than separate divided areas.
I just drew a card and then my opponent made me discard two cards at the end of the turn. Can I cast that spell from my graveyard next turn using its mayhem ability?

No, you cannot use it on a future turn. The mechanic that determines this answer is a strict timing window tied to your current game phase, because the rule specifies As long as you discarded this card this turn, you may cast it from your graveyard by paying [cost] rather than paying its mana cost. This means the discard must occur during the active turn for the permission to activate. For example, if a hand-cruising spell forced you to discard a three-mana sorcery during your opponent's last turn, that discard happened previously, so the condition expired and you cannot cast it from the graveyard now even though the card is sitting there waiting to be used.

I'm in a game and want to use a spell to move my Equipment from my attacker to a blocker. If the spell targets a creature that technically can't have this equipment on it, does the gear disappear or just stay put?

Can I Question: You can attempt the action, but if the target is illegal, the equipment simply stays put. The governing mechanic requires a valid attachment relationship before an effect can move the permanent. According to the rules, if an effect tries to attach an Aura, Equipment, or Fortification to an object or player it cannot be attached to, the Aura, Equipment, or Fortification doesn't move. For example, you control a Steel Leash on your Goblin Guide and cast a spell that says Attach that gear to target creature, but you accidentally select a Mountain Goat instead. The equipment will refuse to leave your Goblin Guide because the Goat is an illegal target for it, so it remains attached to the original creature.

My opponent attacks with a Goblin that has an ability that says 'Whenever this creature deals damage to you, draw a card.' I have a spell in hand that lets me prevent the next 2 damage that would be dealt to any target. When the attack happens, do I still draw a card from the Goblin's ability, or does preventing the damage stop the trigger?

Remove all rule number citations and rephrase mechanically. Explain that replacement effects modify events as they happen; because the spell prevents the damage event entirely, the condition 'whenever this creature deals damage' never actually occurs. Since the trigger condition is never met, the ability never goes on the stack and no card is drawn.

I control a giant beetle with rampage two and my opponent declares three creatures to block it. During the declare blockers step, one of those blocking beetles gets bounced back to its owner's hand before damage happens. What happens to the rampage bonus?

The rampage bonus is calculated only once per combat, when the triggered ability resolves. Adding or removing blockers later in combat won’t change the bonus. As soon as you declare attackers and your opponent declares blockers, the rampage ability triggers immediately and locks in the exact boost based on how many creatures are currently blocking it beyond the first one. Even if a blocker is removed from play before damage steps, that initial calculation remains unchanged for the rest of the turn. For instance, if your Rampage 2 Beetle becomes blocked by three Scorpion Devils, the ability triggers and adds a +4/+4 bonus to its stats right away. If you later use a removal spell to bounce one of those devils before attackers can strike, your beetle still fights with that full +4/+4 boost because the bonus was set in stone the moment it became blocked.

I just cast a spell that puts two creatures onto the battlefield at the same time. One of them says As this enters, choose a color, and the other has an ability that reads Whenever you control no permanents of that color, draw a card. When exactly do I pick the color, and does the draw trigger go on the stack right after the first creature arrives or do I wait until both are down? What actually happens at the table?

You make the color choice before either creature enters the battlefield. The game evaluates replacement effects that modify how a permanent enters by checking its characteristics as it would exist once on the board, and any required choice for those effects is made before the permanent actually arrives. Once your spell finishes resolving and both permanents are settled, state triggers evaluate the board. The draw trigger will fire exactly once because state triggers trigger when a game state becomes true rather than triggering when an event occurs, and they go onto the stack at the next available opportunity. Crucially, a state-triggered ability doesn't trigger again until the ability has resolved, has been countered, or has otherwise left the stack. The concrete outcome is that you lock in the color choice immediately during resolution, the permanent enters with those chosen characteristics, and the draw trigger fires once after your spell fully resolves, sitting on the stack ready to resolve before any other triggers repeat.

During a game, an opponent casts Dominate and takes control of my creature. While they are deciding what to do with mine, can I still cast spells and activate abilities on my own side of the battlefield?

Yes, you absolutely can. While gaining control of one of your creatures temporarily changes who makes decisions for it, you retain full agency over everything else on your side of the battlefield. The rule text governing this type of shared control situation specifies that a player who controls another player also continues to make their own choices and decisions. In practice, because spells only take control of a single creature, you continue making all decisions for your own permanents, spells, and life total as normal. For example, if your opponent takes control of my Goblin Guide during my turn, they make decisions for that specific creature until the effect ends, while I still maintain complete control over my other creatures and can cast instants like Lightning Bolt targeting them.
I'm playing with some phenomenon cards and my opponent just left the game. Does the phenomenon just stay there, or does someone else take control of it?

When your opponent leaves the game, you do not lose control of any phenomenon cards that are on the battlefield. If the current planar controller would leave the game, instead the next player in turn order that wouldn’t leave the game becomes the planar controller, then the old planar controller leaves the game. This means control transfers automatically to keep the phenomenon active rather than disappearing from play. For example, if you are Player One and your opponent is Player Two, and Player Three (the current planar controller) leaves the match, control of their phenomenon would transfer first to Player Two as they are the next in turn order. If Player Two also leaves or is unable to accept it, it would then pass to you.

During my turn I cast an instant that forces all my attackers to attack this turn. Then I sacrificed a creature as part of another effect that creates a damage trigger based on sacrificing. My opponent claims the damage trigger doesn't count because my creatures didn't actually have to attack anyway since they were already attacking. Does my forced attack effect change how the sacrifice trigger resolves?

The forced attack effect and the sacrifice trigger operate on completely separate game mechanics and do not interact. The check for whether creatures 'had to attack' only determines if they fulfilled a combat requirement during the declare attackers step, while the sacrifice trigger is a reflexive ability that checks specifically for the action of sacrificing another creature during an effect's resolution. Because these mechanics function independently across different phases and game states, the forced attack status has absolutely no bearing on the sacrifice trigger. The damage trigger will resolve normally based on the sacrificed creature's power, making your opponent's claim incorrect.
What happens when one of my creatures dies and goes to my graveyard? Does its recover cost trigger immediately, or can I do other stuff first?

When one of your creatures dies and goes to your graveyard, the recover ability triggers immediately and goes on the stack. Because it uses the stack, you get priority to cast instants or activate abilities before the trigger resolves. Once you pass priority and the trigger begins to resolve, you may pay its recover cost. If you do, the card returns from your graveyard to your hand. If you choose not to pay the cost, the card is exiled instead. For example, if a creature with recover dies, you could cast an instant spell in response before deciding whether to pay the recover cost to bring it back.
what happens when I use a copy effect on a permanent that was already created by another copy effect?

When you resolve a copy effect on top of another permanent that was already created by a copy effect, the new permanent copies all the updated values because some copy effects cause the copy to gain an ability as part of the copying process and this ability becomes part of the copiable values for the copy. You can walk through the sequence by looking at what each effect does in order. First, your first creature enters. Second, a copy effect makes a second permanent become a copy of it, but the effect also gives that second permanent an additional triggered ability as part of the process. Third, when you cast another copy effect targeting that second permanent, the new object copies everything including the newly gained ability. For example, if Quirion Elves is on the battlefield and Unstable Shapeshifter copies it, the Shapeshifter now has a triggered ability that says whenever another creature enters, this creature becomes a copy of that creature. If you then cast Clone targeting the Shapeshifter, the Clone becomes a perfect copy of the Shapeshifter including its new copying ability. The sequence matters because the copiable values update instantly after each resolution.
What happens when a spell gives all my creatures +2/+2 until end of turn, but I cast another creature spell later that same turn? Does the new creature get the bonus?

When you resolve a spell that creates a continuous effect modifying characteristics like power and toughness, the game locks in exactly which permanents are affected at that precise moment. The rules state that if a continuous effect modifies the characteristics of any objects, the set of objects it affects is determined when that continuous effect begins and will not change afterward. Because your buff changes object characteristics, only the creatures you controlled the exact moment the spell resolved will receive the bonus for the rest of the turn. Any creature that enters later, even if it shares a name or type with the earlier ones, stays unchanged. For example, if you cast Giant Growth on three 1/1 Goblin tokens to make them 4/3, they are permanently 4/3 for the turn. If you then play a fourth Goblin from your hand, it enters as a normal 1/1 and never receives the buff because it was not part of the set determined when Giant Growth resolved.

I just cast two separate one-mana burn spells on my opponent's creature in a single turn. It only had two toughness, so both spells together did way more damage than it needed to die from. I knew it used its regeneration ability earlier, but someone told me the extra damage should bounce back or do something special since it went over lethal. What actually happens to that leftover damage and does the creature survive?

First, you must look at how the game handles multiple sources hitting one permanent at once. The rule regarding excess damage states that when sources together deal an amount of damage to a creature greater than lethal damage, excess damage equal to the difference was dealt to that creature, so you add those two spells up and record the surplus right after they resolve. After that calculation finishes, the regeneration effect takes precedence because regenerating means that the next time a permanent would be destroyed this turn, instead all damage marked on it is removed and its controller taps it or removes it from combat. The excess damage assessment happens chronologically first to establish what was dealt, but the regeneration replacement effect intercepts the lethal state check to save the creature. The concrete final outcome is that your creature remains on the battlefield tapped with zero damage counters on it, any abilities that trigger whenever it is dealt damage still fire based on the total amount crossed, and the calculated excess damage simply has no additional mechanical impact since the replacement effect successfully prevented destruction.
Can I still activate an ability on a detained permanent after my untap step?

Corrected Answer: No, you cannot activate abilities on a detained permanent during your turn right after it enters or is detained. The rule states that a detained permanent 'can’t attack or block and its activated abilities can’t be activated' until the next turn of the spell’s controller. This means the restriction applies to both the current turn and the caster’s immediate next turn, lifting automatically when that next turn begins.

I just played a spell on my legendary commander to copy an opponent’s creature, and later this turn it blocks and kills that creature dealing three combat damage to them. My opponent claims those attacks no longer count toward the twenty-one damage limit, and when their commander eventually dies while still copying something else, they can’t move it back to the command zone because it looks like a different card now. Is my opponent right?

Your opponent is incorrect based on how the game handles permanent identity versus its current appearance. The rules clearly state that the commander designation is not a characteristic of the object represented by the card; rather, it is an attribute of the card itself, and the card retains this designation even when it changes zones or copies another card. This continuous identity determination takes precedence because it defines what the permanent actually is before any automatic evaluation happens. When you pass priority and the game runs its automatic checks, those checks rely on that persistent identity to resolve two specific outcomes: a player who has been dealt 21 or more combat damage by the same commander over the course of the game loses the game, and if a commander is in a graveyard or in exile and that object was put into that zone since the last time state-based actions were checked, its owner may put it into the command zone. The concrete final outcome is that your three points of combat damage absolutely count toward the twenty-one point threshold required to lose, and if the permanent eventually dies or is exiled while still copying another creature, its owner will successfully move it to the command zone instead of letting it remain in the graveyard or exile pile because the identity rule permanently overrides the visual copy effect for all tracking and replacement purposes.
What happens if a creature moves from my exile into play instead of going directly from my hand? Does it still count as entering?

When you move a permanent from exile, hand, library, or any other zone, only the exact moment it arrives on the playing field counts as an enter event. The game ignores temporary stops in other zones because it tracks the final destination rather than intermediate steps. This is why the official wording specifies that the term enters is short for enters the battlefield. For example, if you cast a spell that creates three Fire Elemental tokens directly from exile onto the field, all three tokens will trigger enter-the-battlefield abilities like those on Blood Artist, even though they briefly existed in exile moments earlier. They only register as entering once they physically hit the battlefield.
Can I put multiple sets of counters on a creature that shows three separate power and toughness numbers because it has a striated text box?

No, you cannot track multiple stat sets on this permanent. The presence of those three boxes does not allow for separate counter tracking or simultaneous applications; it exists solely to display the different starting power and toughness values tied to your initial level choice. This is because each leveler card has a striated text box and three power/toughness boxes, and the text box contains two level symbols, meaning the layout is strictly there to show your casting options before resolution. When you resolve the spell, you pick one level, apply that single set of base stats to the creature, and any subsequent modifiers modify that total normally. For example, if you choose the middle level on a card where that box shows 4/4, it enters as a 4/4. If a later effect gives it a +2/+2 counter, it becomes a 6/6, and you completely ignore the other two boxes printed on the face.
Can I tap my Forests for mana before I officially declare my blockers if one of them requires sacrificing a token to block?

No. The rules state that you must first determine the total cost required for each chosen creature to block, and once that cost is determined it becomes locked in. Only after the costs are locked in does the defending player get a chance to activate mana abilities like tapping lands. This means you have to decide which creatures are blocking and what they will pay before you can actually generate the mana. For example, if you control a Krenko's Mob with a restriction that says it can only block if you sacrifice a 1/1 creature token, you must first choose all your blockers and declare that you are sacrificing the token for the Krenko's Mob to block. Only after those costs are set do you tap your lands for red mana.

We are mid game and my opponent just attacked with multiple creatures while I also paid several costs that make me lose life simultaneously. My life total goes to zero right after combat. I have a card that says if I would lose the game, instead I shuffle my library and graveyard into my library, draw seven cards, and my life total becomes twenty. Do I actually lose the game immediately or do I get a chance to do something?

When combat damage and costs resolve, any abilities that triggered on damage being dealt are put onto the stack before you get priority, which prevents your opponent from ending the game immediately while responses are still legal. After those triggers resolve, the game checks for state-based actions afterward. If multiple conditions would cause you to lose the game at that exact moment, a single replacement effect replaces all of them rather than creating separate defeat events. Because triggers enter first and priority passes next, you can respond to the damage triggers, then the state check occurs where your safety card catches the unified loss condition, shuffling your library and graveyard into your library, drawing seven cards, and setting your life total to twenty while keeping you in the game.
I have a triggered ability on the stack like Rhystic Study, and my opponent just cast an effect that skips my next upkeep. Does this empty the stack or cancel the thing waiting to resolve?

Your triggered ability remains on the stack unaffected because abilities already placed on the stack exist as independent objects that do not disappear when steps or phases are skipped. When a triggered ability activates, it becomes an object on the stack with its own text and persists until it resolves or is removed by an effect; it is not merely a scheduled event waiting for a step to begin. The skipping effect acts as a replacement effect that intercepts scheduled occurrences and replaces them with nothing, but this only applies to events programmed to happen during the game flow, not to abilities that are already active objects on the stack. Consequently, your ability will resolve completely before any skip effects take hold or modify future timing.
What happens if I phase a permanent out until my next end step? Does it just come back automatically when the end step starts?

Remove the rule citation and phrase mechanically: 'When a permanent is phased out until a specific event occurs, a separate one-shot effect automatically returns it right after that event happens.' Replace the Cloudpost example with a correct illustrative scenario, such as phasing out a creature until your opponent sacrifices an artifact, which will cause it to return automatically once that sacrifice resolves.

I have my legendary commander on the battlefield with two +1/+1 counters and a shiny equipment attached to it. My opponent casts a spell that targets my commander but says I can put it into its command zone instead of returning it to hand. I choose the command zone option. When I cast my commander again from the command zone, do the counters and the equipment stick with it? Also, does this move count as leaving the battlefield so other triggers on my board fire?

When your opponent's spell allows you to put your commander into the command zone, this is permitted by Commander rules that allow legendary commanders to reside in that zone. Once the card goes there, a specific rule applies stating that when an object is put into the command zone, it doesn't change zones for tracking purposes but becomes a new object that has just entered the command zone. Because it becomes a brand new object, any physical modifications like counters or attachments from the previous instance do not transfer over; you are starting with a clean commander and the equipment separates and likely goes to your graveyard or hand depending on the spell's full text.
