Regarding leaving, even though the rule mentions the object doesn't change zones in terms of zone transition tracking, the fact that it becomes a new object means the old instance ceased to exist on the battlefield. Triggers that care about your commander leaving the battlefield will definitely fire because the original permanent is gone, replaced by this new entity now residing in the command zone ready to be cast again.
What happens to abilities that trigger when blockers are declared? Do they go on the stack immediately or do I get a chance to respond right away?

All triggered abilities that fire because you declared blockers will be placed onto the stack together before anyone gets priority. According to the comprehensive rules, any abilities that triggered on blockers being declared or during that specific process are put onto the stack before the active player gets priority, and the order in which they triggered does not matter. For example, if your opponent attacks with a creature that has an ability like when this is blocked draw a card, and you block it with two creatures that each have an etb trigger from being cast earlier, all three abilities will be placed on the stack simultaneously. You do not get to respond to the first one before the second or third are added; you simply receive priority only after every blocker related trigger has been queued up, allowing you to then cast instant spells or activate abilities in response to whichever resolves first.
I have Altar of the Pantheon in play and my opponent asks if my God of the Forge is actually a creature right now. Does that altar really make it count as red mana?

Yes, the altar absolutely counts toward your red mana count even though it has no red in its cost. The game calculates devotion by looking at all permanents you control and counting the colored symbols in their mana costs. Crucially, this calculation happens after effects that change text like Altar of the Pantheon's ability have applied, but before any effects that try to change what a permanent actually is. This ensures that static abilities modifying your devotion value are fully considered when checking conditions based on devotion. For example, if you control Altar of the Pantheon along with another red permanent costing {R}{R}{R} and Purphoros costs {3}{R}, your devotion calculation includes the altar's boost plus the symbols from your other permanents. In this scenario, your total devotion to red becomes five due to the altar. Because the count reaches five, Purphoros's condition that it stops being a creature only triggers when devotion is less than five, so you keep playing with a flying artifact god attacking for damage.

I am in the middle of a battle and swing two creatures at my opponent's face blocker. One attacker deals three damage and has an ability that says whenever it deals combat damage to a creature, draw a card. The other attacker deals three damage but has no trigger. After combat ends, the blocker goes to the graveyard and I am wondering if I still get to draw the card since it died from both attackers combined. What actually happens?

When your attackers deal damage simultaneously, the game follows a strict sequence determined by how state checks and triggers interact. First, whenever a player would get priority, the game checks for conditions like lethal damage being marked on creatures, then performs all applicable state-based actions simultaneously as a single event. This means the blocked creature instantly dies from having six damage marked on it during that check. However, because triggered abilities are not placed on the stack until after this specific sequence completes, your ability is not cancelled by the blocker dying. Next, the rule about damage tracking applies: if an ability triggers on damage being dealt by a specific source or sources, and the effect refers to the damage dealt, it refers only to the damage dealt by the specified sources and not to any damage dealt at the same time by other sources. Because your trigger specifies a single attacker, the game only counts its three damage when determining how many times the ability resolves. The concrete final outcome is that the blocked creature goes to the graveyard immediately during the state-based action check, and your triggered ability goes on the stack separately to make you draw exactly one card.
What happens when my attacker with Wither damages a blocker instead of leaving traditional damage marks on it?

When your creature deals combat damage, you do not track red damage squares on the blocked unit. The rules state that damage dealt to a creature by a source with wither isn't marked on that creature. Rather, it causes that source's controller to put that many -1/-1 counters on that creature. Here is how it plays out mid game: you tap your twelve power Witherbloom Beast and deal three damage to their four toughness defender. Instead of recording combat damage, you immediately place three minus one over one counters onto the blocker. The creature will eventually die from having zero or negative remaining toughness because the counters reduce its base stats directly. This sequence happens automatically every time wither deals damage because the mechanic strictly replaces damage markers with permanent stat reductions.

I just cast a spell that deals three damage to all creatures and makes me lose four life at the same time. My opponent has one card in their library, three life, and a creature with a regeneration shield active from earlier this turn. We argued about whether they actually lose the game twice or if their creature still dies anyway. What actually happens?

When a spell resolves and creates multiple dangerous conditions at once, the game checks state-based actions and replacement effects before anything else happens. If your opponent controls an artifact that replaces game loss, the rule states that if multiple state-based actions would have the same result at the same time, a single replacement effect will replace all of them. This means you do not lose twice; instead, one combined event triggers, the replacement effect swaps your hand, graveyard, and permanents into your library, draws seven cards, and sets your life total to twenty. Regarding the creature, regeneration is explicitly defined as a destruction-replacement effect. The next time that permanent would be destroyed this turn, instead all damage marked on it is removed and it taps. Because regeneration only replaces the destruction event and not the damage itself, abilities that trigger from damage being dealt still trigger even if the permanent regenerates. The concrete final outcome is that your opponent survives exactly once due to the merged loss condition, resets to twenty life with seven new cards, the creature clears its damage markers and stays on the battlefield tapped, and any damage triggers enter the stack. State-based actions and replacement effects are evaluated first, followed by destruction replacements, before any triggered abilities are placed on the stack.

I just saw my opponent use a card during combat that adds {S}{S} to their mana pool to cast a spell. I've never seen the snow symbol work like that before mid-game. Does that actually turn into colorless mana, or is there something else going on?

That is perfectly legal and here is exactly what happens when the ability resolves. The game looks at the symbols being added to your opponent's mana pool and applies a specific conversion rule. If an effect would add mana represented by one or more snow mana symbols to a player’s mana pool, that much colorless mana is added to that player’s mana pool. Because of this conversion, those two snow symbols become two units of colorless mana rather than colored or wildcard mana. For example, if you control a creature with an activated ability that costs {1}{U} and your opponent has one blue mana and two converted snow mana in their pool, they can spend all three to pay the cost. The snow mana does not interfere with the blue requirement because it simply sits in the mana pool as generic colorless resources alongside your colored mana.

I just cast a giant spider with amplify two while holding four other spiders in my hand. At the same time I have two different ongoing effects that give me protection from different colors, and the one giving me protection from red entered after the one for green. My opponent wants to block with their blue creature but claims I am no longer protected because the red effect is newer. What actually happens?

Your amplifier spider will enter with six plus one plus one counters because you reveal any number of cards sharing its type as it enters and place N plus one plus one counters per revealed card, which gives you two base plus four additional counters. The game locks in these object characteristics immediately before evaluating your status effects. All continuous effects affecting players are applied in timestamp order after the determination of objects characteristics, meaning your protections layer onto your game state without canceling or overriding each other based on recency alone. Both protections remain active according to when they entered, and neither retroactively changes the creature stats that were already set. The concrete final outcome is that your spider enters as a heavily buffed permanent with six counters, and both protection effects continue running in their original sequence without interfering with the blocker or altering the creature.
What happens when a Clone enters the battlefield copying a double-faced creature and then I try to flip it over with an effect like Moonmist?

When a cloning effect places a new permanent onto the battlefield as a copy, that new permanent is not actually represented by a double-faced card or token, so any attempt to change its faces will fail completely. The game mechanics specify that only permanents represented by double-faced tokens and double-faced cards that are not meld cards can transform or convert. If a spell or ability instructs a player to transform any permanent that isn’t represented by a double-faced token or a double-faced card, nothing happens. To see this in action, imagine you cast Clone to copy the back side of Wildblood Pack. Your Clone is now a single solid creature with no mechanical link to either side. If you then play Moonmist telling all Humans to transform, your Clone will sit still and do absolutely nothing because it lacks the physical representation required to flip over, whereas your actual double-faced card would successfully change faces.

I just cast a sorcery that says Target player may draw two cards. When they do this way, you draw one card. My opponent has zero cards left in their library but chooses to draw anyway so the effect triggers. Does it actually work and what happens at the end?

The game first checks if the drawing action is legal despite your opponent having zero cards left. The rules state that if there are no cards in a player library and an effect offers a choice to draw, that player can choose to do so. Since there is no restriction preventing it, their decision to draw two cards is valid. Next, we apply the mechanics for reflexive triggers. A resolving spell creates a triggered ability tied to that specific action, and these abilities are checked immediately after being created and trigger based on whether the event occurred during resolution. Because your opponent actually drew the cards, the condition is met instantly. The drawing legality check takes precedence by establishing whether the initial action can happen, which then allows the reflexive timing check to evaluate. Concrete final outcome: Your opponent legally draws two cards despite having no library left, and the reflexive ability fires right away, putting exactly one card from your library into your hand as instructed.
Can I tap a creature that just entered the battlefield this turn to enlist my attacker if it doesn't have haste?

Keep the accurate core explanation but replace the specific card names with generic terms or correctly named creatures that actually have Enlist, e.g., "For instance, if you attack with a creature that has enlist and try to tap a fresh creature without haste, you cannot do so; however, tapping an older creature would grant +X/+0 until end of turn."

In Commander, my opponent's Griselbrand has been hitting me for combat damage, and I've taken 20 points so far. On their turn, they declare attackers and one of them is Griselbrand again. During the declare blockers step, I want to cast this instant spell that says 'Prevent the next 1 damage your commanders would deal you.' I know replacement effects happen before damage, but someone at my table said the game ends the instant I take the 21st point and there's no window for me to cast anything once damage starts resolving. Can I actually cast this spell?

You can absolutely cast that spell during the declare blockers step as long as you have priority. The confusion often stems from misunderstanding when state-based actions occur versus when players receive priority. First, the rules clarify that there are no special restrictions on casting a spell or activating an ability that generates a replacement effect, so your spell is perfectly legal to cast and will establish a prevention effect while it resolves. Second regarding the loss condition, in a Commander game the rule states that a player loses the game if they have been dealt 21 or more combat damage by the same commander; this check happens as part of state-based actions which only occur when a player would receive priority, not during the flow of combat itself. When Griselbrand deals damage, state-based actions are checked immediately after damage is dealt to see if the count reaches 21. Since you have cast your spell with a replacement effect beforehand, that prevention will modify the damage event, meaning only 0 or less damage counts toward the commander damage total, so you stay at 20 or whatever the modified amount is. The concrete final outcome is that your spell resolves successfully and prevents enough damage to keep your commander damage count below the threshold, so you do not lose the game and remain in play.
I'm mid-combat and my opponent attacks with a huge creature. Can I still block it with my Unleash fighter if I chose not to put the +1/+1 counter on when it entered?

Yes, you can completely block with it. When a creature enters the battlefield with Unleash, you make a single choice during its entry to either put an additional +1/+1 counter on it or leave it off. The rule clarifies that this permanent cannot block as long as it has a +1/+1 counter on it, so skipping the counter entirely means the restriction never activates. For example, if you cast a creature with Unleash and intentionally enter it without the counter to keep its stats low, it functions exactly like a normal fighter and is fully allowed to step up and block any attacking creatures during combat.
I just started a multiplayer match and my opponent is pulling cards out of their deck to put them in a weird zone before we even draw. What's happening with those extra cards?

When a game begins after determining the starting player, several setup steps happen immediately before anyone draws. If players use sideboards or substitute cards, those are set aside first, and each player’s deck is considered their starting deck. For companion abilities, a player may reveal no more than one card from outside the game only if their deck fulfills the condition of that ability, but the revealed card remains outside the game for the entire match. In Commander games, players also put their commander directly from their deck into the command zone during this phase. For example, if you are playing a constructed match and own Ixalan Discovery as your companion, you reveal it before shuffling your starting deck, but because the rules state the revealed card remains outside the game, it never enters your hand or library and is only used to check deck construction requirements.

I'm attacking with a creature that has double strike and it got blocked by a regular creature with no first strike. The double striker dealt enough damage to kill the blocker in that first combat phase, but my opponent insists the blocker should still get to deal combat damage back because creatures usually wait until the end of combat to die. Who is right and what actually happens?

Your opponent is incorrect regarding the timing of death and subsequent damage assignment. The rules for combat damage establish that when a creature has first strike or double strike, those creatures assign their damage in an initial combat damage step. After that step concludes, the phase proceeds to a second combat damage step where remaining attackers and blockers that lacked first strike or double strike can assign damage. Simultaneously, the rules regarding damage marking state that damage marked on a creature remains until the cleanup step and that if the total damage marked is greater than or equal to its toughness, that creature has been dealt lethal damage and is destroyed as a state-based action immediately. In this scenario, the double striker assigns lethal damage in the first step. The game checks state-based actions and sees the blocker has lethal damage, destroying it right then and there. Because the blocker is removed before the second combat damage step begins, it is no longer a remaining blocker eligible to assign damage. Concrete outcome: The blocker is destroyed immediately after taking the first strike damage and deals zero combat damage to your double striker.

I just cast a spell that deals damage to each modified permanent, and right now there is a triggered ability on the stack waiting to resolve. I also have a card with suspend in my hand that I really want to exile immediately to start counting down its time counters. Can I exile it right now even though something is on the stack, and will my creature with three plus one plus one counters still be considered modified when my spell finishes resolving?

Yes, you can handle both completely normally. Exiling a card with suspend is explicitly listed as a special action that allows you to take it any time you have priority, even while other spells or abilities sit on the stack. This immediate action moves your card to exile and begins counting down without altering battlefield permanents. Your creature stays exactly as it is. The rules state that a permanent is modified if it has one or more counters on it, and since your creature still holds those three counters, it maintains that designation through the entire resolution window. When the stack clears and your spell resolves, your creature will be evaluated again and found to be modified, so it takes damage as written. The special action timing rule dictates when you may manipulate cards in hand, while the permanent modification rule continuously checks battlefield states first, ensuring your targets remain valid before your spell resolves.

I always assume that whenever multiple creatures tap or block at the same time, each one creates a separate slot on the stack so I can respond between them, but my game partner says they all happen instantly as a single phase before anything uses the stack. Is that correct, and how does that change whether my trigger abilities see one event or multiple events?

Declaring attackers and blockers are actually turn-based actions that do not use the stack, meaning opponents cannot respond between individual assignments once declared. After those declarations finish, the game applies the event rule, where one happening may be treated as a single event by one ability and multiple events by another based on its exact wording. This precedence means the declaration completes immediately without interruption, and only then do triggered abilities look at the event count to determine triggers. The concrete final outcome is that you cannot cast spells between block assignments, and your abilities will generate one or multiple triggers strictly based on whether they reference total blocking or individual creatures, all going onto the stack simultaneously after priority passes.

I am piloting a creature that says, You may reveal the first card you draw each turn. Whenever you reveal an artifact card this way, create a 1/1 white Soldier token with haste.' I drew a card earlier this turn and chose not to reveal it because I was hiding my hand. Now, later in the turn, my opponent casts a spell that forces me to show my hand to them. The person at the table is incorrect on both points. First, regarding the forced hand reveal, your creature combines a static ability with triggered abilities that are linked together. This link means the triggers for creating tokens only occur when you reveal a card as part of your creature's specific rule about revealing the first draw. When your opponent forces you to reveal your hand, that is a completely different event caused by their spell, not by your creature's instruction. The linked triggers ignore this external reveal, so no token was created. Second, regarding drawing the card, when an effect gives you the option to reveal as you draw, you are permitted to look at the card before making your choice. You do not have to display it to anyone during the decision process. You peeked at the card first, saw what it was, and decided not to reveal it in response to your creature's effect. Because you chose not to reveal in that context, the trigger did not fire. The final outcome is that no token appeared, and you kept the card secret until your opponent's spell required you to show your hand later.

I just cast a legendary creature from my hand while I already control another one of the same name. It definitely triggered its enters-the-battlefield effect before we noticed the second one was on the field, but now both cards are in the graveyard and that trigger fizzled out when it tried to resolve. What exactly happened here?

When you cast the legendary creature, it successfully entered the battlefield, which caused its enters-the-battlefield ability to trigger and go onto the stack. The game checks these triggers at the exact moment the permanent arrives on the battlefield. After the spell finishes resolving and before either of you gets priority to take other actions, the game automatically checks for state-based actions. This is where the rule about legendary permanents kicks in: since you control two or more legends with the same name, all except one are put into their owners graveyards. That automatic check happens first, so both creatures end up in the graveyard before anyone can activate anything else. Later, when your enters-the-battlefield trigger goes to resolve, it attempts to do something to that permanent, but because the card left the battlefield during the state-based action check and moved directly to the graveyard, the ability cannot find it anymore. The rule states that if an object leaves the battlefield before the triggered ability resolves, the ability looks for it in the new zone and simply fails to find it. The concrete outcome is that you choose one legendary creature to remain on the battlefield while the other goes to the graveyard, and your library and hand remain untouched, but the triggered ability resolves harmlessly against nothing because it cannot locate the permanent that moved zones before resolution.

We're playing Commander. My opponent cast a spell that destroys all creatures on the battlefield. My commander was among them. I want to know if my other creature with the ability Whenever a creature dies, you gain 3 life will trigger, and whether I can send my commander back to the command zone instead of the graveyard. Does it matter which happens first?

Both your triggers and your placement option apply to the same game event. The look-back rule states that for leaves-the-battlefield abilities, the game looks back in time to determine if those abilities trigger, using the appearance of objects immediately prior to the event. Because your commander was on the battlefield just before it was destroyed, the death trigger activates normally and goes on the stack. At the exact moment the zone change occurs, the commander rule applies a state-based action where if a commander is in a graveyard, its owner may put it into the command zone instead. The look-back evaluation runs first to validate triggers, and the state-based action replacement applies second as the card physically moves zones. Your death trigger resolves fully, your commander bypasses the graveyard entirely by going straight to the command zone, and no permanent actually lands in any other player's graveyard.

I'm playing a multiplayer format where two players on each team take turns acting together as a single group. My opponent controls a card that says opponents can't cast spells with even mana values. I have a spell in my hand that costs {X}{R}{R} and want to set X to one. My teammate is also sitting there waiting for me to do something, but we're not sure if I'm actually allowed to start casting this or if the restriction blocks us entirely. What happens here?

When you are playing a format where two players on each team take turns acting together as a single group, the rules state that teams rather than individual players have priority. This means your teammate and you coordinate, and only one of you actually announces the spell to start the process. Because you hold shared priority for the team, you can proceed with casting the spell. Regarding the opponent's restriction, the rules clarify that a player can begin to cast a spell only if no effect prohibits it, but when an effect prohibits spells with certain qualities, you may consider any choices made during that spell proposal that may cause those qualities to change. If choosing X equal to one makes the mana value odd and bypasses the prohibition, you are legally allowed to start casting the spell. The shared team priority rule takes precedence by establishing who gets to act for the group first, while the casting permission rule evaluates your chosen values afterward to determine legality. Once both conditions are satisfied, you cast the spell with X set to one, it resolves completely, and its effect is applied to the board.

I just attacked with my only creature this turn and my opponent blocked it. Later in the fight I destroyed their blocker, but my ability that says whenever a creature I control attacks alone it deals damage didn't trigger back then. Does it trigger now that they are gone? Or do I get to declare attackers again?

Combat declaration takes strict precedence because it locks your attacker status before any triggers can even look at the battlefield. The rules for solo combat state that a creature is attacking alone only when it is attacking but no other creatures are, meaning your solo condition is permanently fixed during the declare attackers step. The triggered ability guidelines clarify that an ability triggers only once each time its trigger event occurs and explicitly note that an event that is prevented or replaced will not trigger anything. Because the declaration phase establishes your attacker count first, followed by the trigger evaluation rules confirming no solo attack event actually took place to activate your effect, you cannot retroactively claim a mid-combat trigger. The concrete outcome is that your creature deals zero extra damage and combat continues normally with your attacker still assigned to its block.

I have a legendary enchantment named 'Auramancer' on the battlefield. My opponent casts an instant that creates a Token and says, 'This token enters the battlefield as a copy of target permanent.' They target my Auramancer. The token appears next to it. Does the token get exiled immediately due to the legend rule, or does it stick around? I feel like copying something shouldn't make you legendary too.

When a token enters the battlefield as a copy of another permanent, it copies all characteristics of that permanent, including the legendary supertype. Since your Auramancer is explicitly a legendary enchantment, the token will also be legendary. State-based actions are then checked, and because you control two legendary permanents with the same name, the legend rule applies. You must choose one to remain on the battlefield, and the other is put into its owner's graveyard.

I control Felidar Sovereign and my opponent attacks with a massive creature. My life total is currently thirty-nine, but they have an ability that says whenever their creatures deal combat damage to you, prevent that damage and draw cards equal to the damage prevented instead. When their upkeep step begins, do I win the game right away because of all the card draws from the prevention effect, or does something else happen first?

You do not win during the opponent upkeep because two separate timing layers must be processed in a specific order. First, the replacement effect modifying the damage follows a strict sequencing rule where any parts of the original event that haven’t been replaced occur first, then the card draws happen one at a time. This means your life total does not spike from the prevention until after any un-replaced combat portions finish resolving. Second, Felidar Sovereign uses an intervening if clause that requires the controller to check whether you have forty or more life when the upkeep begins. If you do not meet it then, the ability never triggers at all. Even if you had reached forty life earlier, the ability would go on the stack and check your life total again as it resolves. The replacement sequencing rule establishes exactly when draws occur and prevents instant life total changes during the initial trigger window. The final outcome is that your Sovereign does not win the game because your life stays at thirty-nine through combat, fails the first condition check at upkeep start, and therefore never puts an ability on the stack to resolve.

I cast a spell that exiles a card from outside the game and says 'You may return that card to your hand.' My opponent interrupts with a countercard. Is this possible, or does the return happen instantly like a special action because it's bringing back an external card?

No, the return is not instantaneous, and your opponent can counter the spell. Bringing a card from outside the game via a spell effect is not a special action; it is part of resolving a spell that uses the stack. The rule defining special actions clarifies that these are specific non-stack actions taken when you have priority, whereas casting a spell and having its effect return a card follows normal stack interactions, allowing responses like counterspells before resolution. Furthermore, even if the effect resolves successfully, the rule regarding Commander format restrictions on external cards applies: you cannot bring back a card that shares a name with any card in your starting deck, matches a card owned by you that is currently in the game, or has a color identity outside your commander's. The final outcome is that the spell can be countered as normal, and if it resolves without being countered, the card returns only if it passes the format restrictions.

I'm playing with my commander deck and my opponent suddenly cast an instant that moved eight cards from my library directly into my hand without using the word draw. My library is now completely empty. I have a creature on the battlefield that says whenever you draw a card it fights top card of my library, and another enchantment that says when you lose the game you get two poison counters. Right after this happens, a combat damage spell hits me for lethal and I go down to zero life. Do the combat triggers fire or does the loss just happen without any abilities going on the stack?

First the library movement resolves and because an effect moved cards from your library to your hand without using the word draw you did not actually draw those cards which stops your creature ability from triggering and prevents a deck out check. The rule states that if an effect moves cards from a player’s library to that player’s hand without using the word draw, the player has not drawn those cards and this makes a difference for abilities that trigger on drawing cards as well as empty library checks. Next taking lethal damage causes you to lose the game as a state based action before any player could take priority. Even though your life total hit zero from combat rather than drawing your enchantment will still trigger because some triggered abilities trigger specifically when a player loses the game and these abilities trigger when a player loses or leaves the game regardless of the reason unless that player leaves the game as the result of a draw. Since you lost from damage and not a draw your lose the game ability goes on the stack and resolves before you leave the battlefield giving you two poison counters before you are removed from the game. The concrete final outcome is that combat damage hits, state based actions immediately mark you as losing the game, your poison counter trigger fires and resolves placing two counters on you, and then you leave the match with those counters in place.

I just cast my commander spell that told me to roll two dice and I got doubles, which triggered my enchantment's ability that says 'When this happens, you may draw a card.' My opponent is shouting that since the condition was met instantly, I have to declare that I'm drawing the card right now before they can even cast a countering spell. Is that true?

Your opponent is incorrect about when you make your choice, but the order of operations matters. First, you determine if the dice result meets the condition by checking whether both dice show the same number, which confirms that you rolled doubles and the trigger for your enchantment exists. Once this check occurs, the mechanics for optional abilities take over. Triggered abilities containing 'may' still go on the stack even if you might not use them, and the choice to draw a card is made when the ability resolves rather than when it triggers. This means the dice check resolves immediately to put the trigger on the stack where your opponent can respond, but you retain the freedom to decide whether to draw until that trigger is resolving. The final outcome is that you do not declare the choice now; the trigger goes on the stack and you choose to draw or not at resolution.

I just started my turn with plenty of creatures sitting in my graveyard and I want to cast this two-mana red creature that has infect. The spell also says delve, so I began exiling three cards from my graveyard instead of paying the one generic mana cost. My opponent interrupts and claims that because I paid for it by exiling graveyard cards, the damage it deals on attack won't actually put poison counters on me like normal infect would. What exactly happens with my exile choices and how does the combat damage resolve?

You correctly follow the delve mechanic, which is defined as a static ability that functions while the spell with delve is on the stack and allows you to exile cards from your graveyard rather than pay generic mana in the spell's total cost. This payment step resolves first during casting. Once the creature enters the battlefield and deals combat damage, the outcome shifts entirely to the damage result framework, which states that damage dealt to a player by a source with infect causes that source's controller to give the player that many poison counters instead of normal life loss. Because these are separate game steps with the cost payment clearly taking precedence during the casting phase, your exile choices do not alter combat mechanics. The concrete final outcome is that your opponent will receive poison counters equal to the creature's power based on its infect keyword, completely unaffected by how you paid for the spell earlier.

I just activated my commander ability that says Roll a planar die. When you roll one or more dice, you may exile target creature card from a graveyard. My opponent says the ability fizzles immediately because the planar die does not have usable numbers for targeting comparisons, but I want to keep it on the stack. What actually happens and do I get to choose whether to exile it?

The ability triggers normally the moment you roll the planar die because the rule states that rolling a planar die will cause any ability that triggers whenever a player rolls one or more dice to trigger. This triggered ability immediately goes onto the stack according to the rule that optional triggered abilities go on the stack when they trigger, regardless of whether their controller intends to exercise them later. During resolution, precedence is given first to the rule that effects referring to a numerical result of a die roll, including ones that compare results or exchange values, ignore the rolling of the planar die, which means your specific roll value is legally disregarded for comparisons. Once that exclusion is applied, you make your decision because the rule specifies that the choice is made when the ability resolves rather than when it triggers. The concrete final game outcome is that the trigger does not fizzle immediately, it stays on the stack for players to respond to, and upon resolution you decide whether to exile the creature while any numerical comparisons tied to your roll are ignored by the game.

I am attacking with my legendary creature general and just dealt five points of combat damage to a player who had already taken twenty from that exact same commander earlier this game. My opponent immediately reaches for an instant spell to try and save himself before the turn phase ends, but I told him he loses right now. Are we actually checking the game state in the middle of combat like that?

You are correct that the player loses immediately because Magic uses variant-specific checks that some players don't realize run constantly. The rules state that a player who has been dealt 21 or more combat damage by the same commander over the course of the game loses, but this threshold is only enforced when variant games include additional state-based actions that aren't normally applicable in other formats. Because those checks happen immediately after any action resolves and before priority is given to players, the moment your general deals that final point of damage, the loss condition triggers before your opponent can respond. The cumulative damage tracking meets the format requirement, and the variant-specific checks enforce it first in sequence, declaring your opponent the loser and ending the match right then.

I just activated my commander ability to draw three cards, but I realized my library has no cards left after we removed them earlier this turn. My opponent says the game ends right then and there, but I feel like I should get a chance to do something since the effect already resolved. What actually happens at the table?

Your opponent is technically correct about when the match ends, though your intuition comes from not knowing how the game evaluates conditions behind the scenes. When your ability resolves and you attempt to draw cards you don't have, the game does not end instantly in real time, but it will end before either of you gets priority to respond or take further actions. The rules state that whenever a player would get priority, the game checks for state-based actions first and performs all applicable ones simultaneously as a single event. This mandatory check happens before the game moves to let players interact. Because this process runs right when priority would pass, it catches the condition where a player who attempts to draw a card from a library with no cards in it loses the game next time a player would receive priority. The precedence clearly favors this automated evaluation over any active responses. You never get a window to activate abilities or counter anything after the draw resolves. The concrete final outcome is that you lose the game immediately during that automatic check sequence, ending the match with your opponent winning before anyone can act further.

I just tapped three islands to cast a spell, but my opponent didn't respond and passed back to me. Can I tap another land now to save the mana for later, or does tapping use up my action for the turn?

You might think tapping lands ends your turn or consumes your action, but the rules clearly state that a player may activate an activated ability any time they have priority. Once your opponent passes back to you after resolving their response, you regain priority in an open window. The guidelines also note that if a cost includes a mana payment, the player paying the cost has a chance to activate mana abilities as part of following casting steps. Priority dictates the turn sequence and opens windows for general actions, while cost-payment timing governs specific moments during spell declaration. When both interact, priority determines turn order and window availability first, establishing your right to act, after which you are free to use mana abilities freely. Concrete outcome: You may tap another land right now to add mana to your pool, but that mana will automatically empty from your pool at the end of each step and phase, so it cannot be carried over to save for a later turn or different action.

We're playing Commander and I just cast a spell that shuffles my library, then my opponent targets it with a spell that puts cards from my graveyard into the battlefield. My friend said I can rearrange the cards in my graveyard to put the ones they want on top first, but another player said we aren't allowed to touch the order. What actually happens?

The Commander format operates under a foundational framework where each deck is led by a legendary creature designated as that deck commander, and this variant uses all the normal rules for a Magic game with targeted additions. Because the official guidelines state that the order of objects in a graveyard cannot be changed except when effects or rules explicitly allow it, you are strictly prohibited from rearranging cards regardless of what your friend suggests. While players are generally permitted to arrange other zones however they wish for convenience, that flexibility never extends to libraries or graveyards where fixed sequencing dictates how spells interact with your pile. The standard zone ordering restriction takes precedence over casual house rules, so the concrete final outcome is that your opponent spell resolves using whatever card currently sits in the targeted position of your unchanged graveyard, and no one may touch the sequence until a card effect explicitly permits shuffling or reordering.

I just started my turn and realized I have this car mechanic card on the battlefield but haven't used it yet. Do I automatically gain some momentum right at the beginning before I can actually play a card or attack?

The card rule explicitly states that if you control a permanent with start your engines! and have no speed, their speed becomes 1 as a state-based action. Because state-based actions are game actions that happen automatically whenever certain conditions are met and do not use the stack, they take precedence over any spells or abilities you might want to play. This automatic check resolves first before priority is passed, so you definitively start your turn with 1 speed already in place, ready to act.

My opponent attacks and I block, then during our second main phase I have a modal spell with an optional extra cost that says if you pay it, you pick as many modes as you like. I also just exiled one of my cards face down earlier this turn to trigger its suspend ability. When I cast the spell now, do I have to choose my first mode before deciding to pay the extra cost, and was my timing right for exiling that card during combat?

The rules explicitly allow you to rearrange your announcement order when casting a spell because some options may only be available if other choices are made that would normally be decided later, meaning you may consider any other choices to be made in that step. You do not have to pick a mode first; you can decide to pay the extra cost immediately and select multiple modes right away. Regarding your card exile, putting that card into exile with time counters is defined as a special action that you may take anytime you have priority, which includes during combat before or after blockers are declared. Because special actions fall outside the spell casting process, they must be completed fully before you begin announcing the choices for your next spell. The concrete outcome is that your exile timing was legal, and when you cast the modal spell, you will announce all chosen modes alongside your intent to pay the extra cost at the exact same moment. Special action rules take precedence in sequencing because they occur entirely outside the casting steps, while the flexible announcement rule only governs choices made during a single cast event.

I just cast a spell that makes me roll two dice and I got two sixes, but my opponent is insisting it's not 'doubles' because he read somewhere that you have to roll them simultaneously for the effect to trigger. He's also claiming the ability won't go on the stack at all now. What actually happens here?

The game rules explicitly define that a player has rolled doubles if the result of each of those rolls is equal to the other, so getting two sixes counts as doubles regardless of timing or rolling method. This triggers your ability immediately because the condition is met by the equality of the results. The rules for triggered abilities then dictate that once an ability has triggered, you must put it on the stack as an object when you next receive priority. Your opponent is mistaken about both the definition of doubles and the mechanics of putting abilities on the stack. The concrete outcome is that your doubles effect successfully triggers and will be placed on the stack to resolve.

I just declared my attackers and my opponent blocked with a first strike creature, but after initial damage goes off we got confused because an ability on my double striker triggered again during the second damage phase. Why does it trigger twice and how do we count the damage without messing up the stack?

The combat timing mechanism applies first to establish the sequence, stating that if at least one attacking or blocking creature has first strike or double strike, only those creatures assign combat damage in the initial step, followed by a second combat damage step where remaining attackers and blockers without first strike assign their damage, along with any creatures currently with double strike. This creates two separate windows for damage assignment, which is why your creature fires its trigger twice instead of once. Once the phases are established, source tracking applies to evaluate the ability, noting that if an ability triggers on damage being dealt by a specific source and refers to the damage dealt, it only counts the damage dealt by that specified source and not to any damage dealt at the same time by other sources. The concrete final outcome is that your creature deals lethal damage to the blocker in phase one and then its full power as combat damage to the opponent in phase two, causing the ability to trigger exactly twice per combat, with each trigger counting only the exact amount of damage that specific double striker dealt during its respective phase.

I just played Doubling Cube and tapped it to double my three red mana that can only be used for creature spells. Now I have six red mana restricted to creatures. My opponent is thinking about casting a combat trick on their attacker. Should I cast my creature spell before they get priority again, or will it still work if I wait until the whole stack clears?

The restriction applies immediately when Doubling Cube resolves because the rules explicitly state that any restrictions or additional effects created by the spell or ability will apply to all mana produced when replacement effects increase the amount. This modification locks in first during resolution and governs exactly what you can pay with later. Meanwhile, the priority system controls whether those mana points survive long enough to be spent: if all players pass in succession without taking any actions in between passing, the spell or ability on top of the stack resolves or, if the stack is empty, the phase or step ends. Since phases automatically advance when consecutive passes occur, unspent mana vanishes at that exact moment. The concrete outcome is that your six red restricted mana remains fully locked to creature spells and will be completely lost if you pass priority first and the turn advances without you casting a creature spell; you must pay for the spell while priority is still active to prevent it from disappearing.

I'm attacking with two Goblin Warriors that each have toughness 2, and my opponent blocks one of them with a Knight that has toughness 2. Both Goblins deal damage to the Knight and take lethal damage back from it. My opponent argues that the first Goblin should die first so the second Goblin doesn't have to assign lethal damage, or that I can wait to see the first Goblin die before dealing damage to the Knight? We're arguing because everyone seems to be dying and we don't know if the damage assignment order matters here.

Both Goblin Warriors are put into their owners' graveyards simultaneously along with the Knight. All combat damage that has been assigned is dealt at the same time, meaning there is no moment where one creature dies before another receives its damage and you cannot assign damage based on whether a creature will die from earlier assignments in the same combat step; this simultaneous dealing happens without using the stack so no player can act between assignment and resolution. After all damage is dealt automatically, state-based actions occur where creatures with lethal damage are destroyed immediately without using the stack, and since all three creatures received their full assigned damage at once, they are all removed from the battlefield together at the exact same moment.

I just played a card that makes three separate abilities trigger, and each one says my opponent draws a card. I looked at my deck and realized I only have two cards left. If those triggers resolve one by one, when exactly do I lose the game? Do I drop out right after the first draw fails, or do I keep playing until all of them are done?

You will not lose the game immediately when the first attempt to draw fails. The rules clearly state that a player who attempts to draw a card from a library with no cards in it loses the game the next time a player would receive priority. This is a state-based check that only runs when priority passes, not instantly during resolution. In the meantime, each of those instructions functions as a triggered ability that goes onto the stack. Triggered abilities have a trigger condition and an effect, and they resolve one at a time before the game checks for state changes. Because these three separate triggers must finish resolving first, you will attempt to draw from zero cards multiple times while the stack clears. The triggered ability rule takes precedence in timing by allowing all stack events to complete, while the empty library rule applies second to determine that you lose the game exactly once priority passes after the last trigger resolves.

I just took lethal damage in my Commander game and am leaving the match, but I realize now that my deck actually has a card with a color outside my commander's identity because I misread it during deck building. My opponent controls an enchantment that says whenever you leave the game, they get to take one of your commanders. Do I still give them my commander, and what happens to that wrong-colored card?

Before resolving anything about leaving the match, we must address your deck construction. The rules require that every color in any non-land card's identity matches the commander's identity, meaning you cannot include cards with colors outside that range. That misplaced card is completely illegal and must be taken out of play immediately because only cards matching your commander's specific color palette are allowed. Once we remove it, the game proceeds normally. The rules state that triggered abilities looking for a player losing will still trigger whenever that player leaves the game, regardless of the reason, unless they leave as the result of a draw. You are conceding to lethal damage, so the leave trigger goes on the stack and resolves exactly as written. Your opponent gets to take your commander, the game ends, and you walk away with only legal cards. The deck construction restriction takes precedence by filtering out invalid cards before any game-ending triggers can possibly interact with them.

I just cast a spell that reduced my opponent's life total to zero and they had a commander ability saying when a player leaves the game you gain 5 life. They claim the trigger doesn't go on the stack because it happens too fast, but I thought all triggers wait for a response window. What exactly happens here?

When your opponent's life total reaches zero, the game automatically performs a state check rather than waiting for players to act. As the rules state, state-based actions are game actions that happen automatically whenever certain conditions are met and they do not use the stack. This means the loss occurs instantly without giving anyone priority. Because you have now lost, any abilities designed to respond to that event activate immediately. Some triggered abilities trigger specifically when a player loses the game and these abilities trigger when a player loses or leaves the game regardless of the reason. The automatic state check takes precedence by resolving first through an instant elimination effect, followed by your loss-triggered ability going onto the stack. Your opponent will immediately lose the game at the end of that sequence, but the trigger you mentioned will still resolve and grant you the five life before they are removed from play.

I just finished casting a sorcery on my turn and have open mana left. I want to play a forest, but there is an ongoing effect that says instead of putting lands onto the battlefield from your hand, exile them instead. Does this change when I can do it or what actually happens?

Playing a land is a special action that you are allowed to take any time you have priority and the stack is empty during a main phase of your turn, so you are perfectly timed to attempt this right now. However, replacement effects modify events at the moment they occur because if an event is replaced it never happens and a modified event occurs instead. The replacement effect takes precedence over the standard result of your action since it rewrites the outcome before the land enters play, while your permission to attempt the action remains locked to the timing windows of the special action rules. The concrete final game outcome is that you successfully execute the special action during your main phase, but the forest goes directly into exile instead of entering the battlefield, and any triggered abilities will register a modified event rather than a permanent entering play.

I just cast my turn and attacked with my creature that has an ability reading whenever this creature is put into exile you draw a card. My opponent responded by casting a spell that exiles it, so the trigger went on the stack to let me draw. Then they cast another spell targeting that same creature to exile it again while it was sitting in their exile zone. Do I get to draw another card from that second spell or does something weird happen with the trigger?

You only get to draw one card from the first trigger, and you will not draw a second card. When your opponent cast the second spell targeting your creature while it was already exiled, the object became a new object because of the rule that says if an object in the exile zone becomes exiled it does not change zones but becomes a new object that has just been exiled. Because the creature did not actually move between zones for the second spell, no event occurred where the creature was put into exile. Triggered abilities are defined as having a trigger condition and effect written as when or whenever a trigger condition occurs, and since the condition of being put into exile requires a zone change that never happened, no new triggered ability is created on the stack. The first trigger resolves normally and gives you one card draw, while the second spell merely makes the creature a new object in exile without triggering its ability again.

I keep getting confused when opponents claim that trigger phrases on different lines of a card resolve completely separately from each other. For example, my opponent cast something that says whenever you cast an instant or sorcery, sacrifice a land, and also has a tied ability that triggers when you sacrifice a land to look at your library. They think these are two independent chains, but I read somewhere they are actually treated as one combined effect. On top of that, when lands go to the graveyard from this, can the opponent shuffle them around before the second part of the combo resolves?

These abilities are treated as a single cohesive block rather than independent chains because these objects combine the abilities into one paragraph, with the static ability first, followed by each triggered ability that is linked to it, so they share timing and resolve together without splitting into separate logical events. The combined effect processes all conditions in sequence within that same resolution window, meaning any land sacrifice required or caused by the first trigger immediately feeds into the second linked part before anything else can interrupt. Once those lands are moved to the graveyard, you cannot rearrange them because each graveyard is kept in a single face-up pile and players normally cannot change their order at any point during gameplay. The ability combination rule establishes how the triggers link and resolve first, which dictates the exact cards that will be placed down, and then the graveyard ordering rule takes precedence to prevent any shuffling or reordering once those cards arrive. In this scenario, your opponent resolves one unified effect that sacrifices the land and looks at the library simultaneously, and all lands that enter the graveyard must remain stacked exactly as they were placed with zero shuffling allowed before any further actions are taken.

I'm at 0 life and my library is empty while it's my turn to draw. I have a creature with lethal damage on it from combat, and my opponent has a blocker with lethal damage marked too. I control Lich's Mirror. Does the damage destroy anything, and does Lich's Mirror save me from losing even though there are two reasons I should lose?

Damage does not destroy creatures; instead, state-based actions check after damage is dealt and put creatures with lethal damage into the graveyard due to that result of the damage, so your creature and the opponent's blocker move because the game checks for lethal damage. You have zero life which causes you to lose the game, and you are required to draw from an empty library which also causes you to lose the game. These are multiple state-based actions with the same result of losing the game. Lich's Mirror replaces what happens when you would lose the game. Because multiple state-based actions lead to the same outcome, a single replacement effect replaces all of them rather than triggering twice. The final result is that your creature and the opponent's blocker go to their graveyards because state-based actions check for lethal damage from the combat, but Lich's Mirror activates once to replace the combined loss caused by both your life total and the draw requirement, keeping you in the game with a full library and 20 life.

I have a Goblin with four damage marked on it and a power of two. My hand is empty but I have other mana, and I want to cast Harmonize for three generic mana and one green mana. Can I tap this damaged Goblin to pay the harmonize cost and get the discount? Will the game kill the Goblin before I can even tap it because of the four damage?

Yes, you can tap the Goblin and get the discount. The game will not kill the Goblin immediately when you tap it, so you can complete the action without issue. The rules for Harmonize state that you may pay an alternative cost by tapping an untapped creature you control rather than paying the spell's mana cost, and if you do this, the total cost is reduced by an amount of generic mana equal to that creature's power, which means your three generic mana becomes one generic mana. Regarding the damage, the rules specify that objects can deal damage to creatures and that damage affects them detrimentally, but a creature is only put into its owner's graveyard due to lethal damage after state-based actions are checked. Tapping the creature to pay the cost happens before those checks occur, so the Goblin exists and can be tapped despite having lethal damage marked on it. The concrete outcome is that you pay one generic mana and one green mana, the Goblin remains on the battlefield until state-based actions are checked later at which point it will be put into its owner's graveyard due to the four damage exceeding its toughness, and your Harmonize spell goes onto the stack for resolution.

My opponent's commander has been hitting me for 18 damage earlier in the game. During my turn, it attacks and hits me for another 5 points of damage. I still have mana open and a spell with Suspend in my hand that I was planning to use. Can I take the special action to exile this card with Suspend now to avoid losing?

You lose the game immediately and cannot take any actions. The rule for commander damage states that a player loses the game when they have been dealt 21 or more combat damage by the same commander over the course of the game. This loss is a state-based action, which means it is checked and resolved instantly before any player receives priority. The ability to exile a card with suspend is a special action that requires you to have priority to perform. Because the state-based action causing your defeat is checked and applied before you would ever be granted priority, you never reach the window to activate the special action. The game ends right at that moment, and no further actions or responses are possible.

During a game, I had a card on the battlefield that set my maximum hand size to three. Then my opponent brought in another permanent with a static ability that created a replacement effect saying players can't discard cards during their cleanup step. When my turn reached the cleanup phase, how many cards do I actually have to get rid of, and why?

The concrete outcome is that you must discard down to three cards. This happens because both mechanics interact through a specific sequence of application. Your opponent's permanent generates a static ability that creates a continuous effect, which functions for as long as the permanent with the ability remains on the battlefield and has the ability. However, when another effect directly modifies a fundamental game rule like your maximum hand size, it does not follow the normal continuous effect timeline. Instead, effects that change game rules are applied after all other continuous effects have been applied. Because the rule-modifying effect applies last in this sequence, it establishes the final limit for your hand at three cards during cleanup. Even though the active replacement effect attempts to block discards, the timing dictates that the rule-changing effect takes precedence, forcing you to discard until you meet that final boundary.

I just brought out my legendary creature from command zone for the first time and it only cost its printed mana. Tomorrow I want to play a land I drew and cast that same commander again, but I'm worried playing the land might mess up the timing or make him more expensive. Can I do both this turn, and does the order matter?

The concrete outcome is that you will play your land for its normal cost, put it onto the battlefield, and then cast your commander paying an additional two mana because it is now the second time you have cast it from command zone. To understand why, first you apply the commander rule which states that a commander cast from the command zone costs an additional two for each previous time the player casting it has cast it from the command zone that game. This tax calculation happens immediately when you attempt to cast it and is completely independent of other actions. After the tax is determined, you then follow the special action rule which says playing a land is a special action that can be taken any time you have priority and the stack is empty during a main phase of your turn. The precedence here is clear because both rules share the exact same timing window. You take the land special action while holding priority with an empty stack, resolve it, and then immediately use your remaining priority in that same main phase to cast your commander. Neither rule overrides the other; they simply run sequentially during your main phase, allowing you to maximize resources before opening the stack.

I just cast an effect that copies my commander onto the battlefield to block a creature, and while it was attacking with another thing later, it took enough damage to be destroyed. My opponent says the copy isn't actually my commander anymore since it's a new object on the battlefield, so when it dies from that combat damage, it should go to the graveyard like any other creature. Is my opponent correct about where it goes?

Your opponent is completely correct, and the concrete outcome is that the copied permanent travels directly to your graveyard rather than the command zone. This happens because automatic game checks run before any special replacement effects apply. First, a state-based action happens automatically whenever certain conditions like lethal damage are met, moving damaged permanents to the graveyard without using the stack. Second, even though it is on your battlefield, the rules explicitly state that a permanent copying a commander is not a commander because the commander designation is an attribute of the card itself and does not carry over to new copies. Because the automatic check moves it based on its physical zone path and its copied status strips away its special identity, it follows standard creature rules and ends up in your graveyard where it stays until a later effect removes it.

I just cast a spell that lets me exile up to three target creatures from my graveyard onto the battlefield, and each one has an enters-the-battlefield ability that says 'When you exile this creature this way, create two 1/1 White Soldier tokens.' My opponent claims I have to arrange the order of those triggers in reverse, and wants me to shuffle my graveyard first so they don't know which creatures will trigger. What actually happens with the order and the timing?

You may arrange cards in your graveyard however you wish as long as control and tapped status remain clear to everyone, but the official rules state that the order of objects in a graveyard can’t be changed except when effects or rules allow it. Once your spell resolves and targets those creatures for exile, the effect creates reflexive triggered abilities for each exile event. These reflexive triggers are checked immediately after being created and trigger based on whether the triggering event occurred earlier during the resolution of the spell that created them. The zone arrangement restriction applies first to establish legal boundaries before any targeting occurs, while the reflexive timing mechanism takes precedence during resolution to determine immediate placement on the stack. Because all three exiles happen in sequence during the same spell resolution, the triggered abilities are generated and evaluated instantly for each card, resulting in exactly six 1/1 White Soldier tokens entering the battlefield before anyone receives priority. You choose their stacking order, but mechanically they resolve as part of that single event with no intervening turns allowed.

I’m in the middle of a game and I tapped my Snow-Covered Swamp to pay for a two-mana spell that needs to be black mana, but my opponent’s creature just died from combat damage and has an ability that lets me draw a card when it dies. I want to know if I get to respond to my own spell before that draw trigger happens, and whether the snow mana actually counts as black since the land is black. What’s the actual outcome here?

Snow mana from your land becomes colorless rather than black, meaning you cannot pay a black mana cost with it unless you have other black mana available. Regarding timing, state-based actions happen first when the creature dies, then its death trigger is placed on the stack. Crucially, after that trigger goes on the stack, priority is given to you. This provides a concrete window for you to cast your spell (if you can pay the cost with other mana) or respond to the draw trigger before it resolves and gives you the card.

We just started our four-player match and it is my turn first on turn one. My friend insists we skip drawing a card this turn because we go first, but I also want to tap a land for mana right after I declare attackers so I can pay for an instant. Someone at the table claims that tapping the land goes on the stack so they can counter it or respond. What actually happens here?

The starting player never skips their draw step of their first turn in any multiplayer game except Two Headed Giant, so you will absolutely draw your opening card right after untapping with no delays. When you tap a land for mana you are performing a special action that players may take when they have priority and these actions deliberately do not use the stack or allow responses. The opening draw sequence applies first by confirming your turn structure remains intact, and the special action mechanic takes precedence during combat because it overrides any assumption that mana payment enters a response window. The concrete final outcome is that you successfully draw your card, declare attackers, tap your land for mana safely during combat, and pay for your instant without opponents being able to interrupt or counter that specific action.

I just turned on my Vehicles living metal ability and they become creatures this turn. I have one with zero power attacking a creature that also has zero power. We both think we should destroy each other in combat, but nothing happens. Can you explain what actually goes on here?

Your vehicle becomes a creature during your turn because of its living metal ability, which means it is eligible to attack and block just like any other creature. When your zero power vehicle attacks the other zero power creature, combat damage is theoretically assigned, but there is a crucial rule about zero damage that applies here. If a source would deal 0 damage, it does not deal damage at all. This prevents any combat damage event from actually occurring. Because no damage is dealt, state based actions do not check for lethal damage, so neither permanent is destroyed and they both remain on the battlefield. Additionally, if either had an effect that would increase the damage, it would have nothing to replace since the damage event never happens in the first place. The living metal ability establishes the creature type early in the turn, while the 0 damage rule applies during the combat damage step and takes precedence by completely removing the damage event before it can trigger anything or destroy permanents. The concrete final outcome is that both permanents survive combat intact and no triggers occur.

I have a creature that is currently 0 power and 0 toughness because of an effect from a spell cast earlier this turn. My opponent activates an aura swap ability using an aura card in their hand and attaches it to my creature. The new aura says 'Target creature gets +1/+1.' Everyone at the table is arguing whether the creature stays dead at 0/0 or wakes up as a 1/1. Can you settle this?

The opponent successfully activates the aura swap ability, which exchanges the aura on the battlefield with the aura card in hand according to the rule that allows trading a permanent for an aura card in hand when both parts can be completed. Once the new aura is attached, it generates a continuous effect that modifies power and toughness. Rules for continuous effects dictate that multiple modifiers are applied simultaneously but in a specific order based on layers. An effect that sets power and toughness to zero applies in an earlier layer than an effect that simply adds +1/+1. Because the game calculates layers from first to last, the zero-setting effect is applied first, resulting in a base of 0/0, and then the aura's +1/+1 modifier is applied in a later layer on top of that result. The final outcome is the creature becomes a 1/1 creature. It remains on the battlefield with a power of 1 and toughness of 1 until whatever effect made it 0/0 expires or is removed.

I have Valduk, Keeper of the Flame on the battlefield and my opponent has a creature. On my turn, I play a Mountain for mana and then cast Lightning Bolt targeting their creature. My opponent claims that playing the land also triggered Valduk because it feels like doing something game-related, but I want to know exactly what counts here.

Only the Lightning Bolt triggers Valduk; playing the Mountain does not trigger it. Playing a land is classified as a special action that allows you to put a land onto the battlefield from your hand once per turn during a main phase when priority is empty, and this action is strictly distinct from casting spells or activating abilities. Committing a crime requires casting a spell, activating an ability, or putting a triggered ability on the stack that targets at least one opponent, any permanent, spell, or ability your opponent controls, or any card in your opponent's graveyard; since playing a land uses none of these mechanics and does not target anything, it cannot commit a crime. Your Lightning Bolt is casting a spell that targets a permanent your opponent controls, which satisfies the targeting requirement for committing a crime, so Valduk sees one crime. Concrete outcome: Valduk triggers exactly once from the Bolt, and playing the Mountain produces no crime or trigger.

I just cast Draw Two during my main phase, but I also control an artifact that says Instead of drawing a card you may exile it instead. My opponent claims this replacement effect completely stops my enchantment from triggering because no actual cards are drawn, but my other friend argues the enchantment still triggers and I should get the bonus draw since the linked ability only cares about the original instruction. We really need to know who is right here.

Clarify that since you control the artifact, you may choose to exile cards instead of drawing them; however, because the replacement effect completely overrides the draw event, the linked ability's trigger condition (revealing a drawn card) is never satisfied, resulting in zero bonus draws for you and no trigger for your opponent.

We have a disagreement at the table. I control a creature with deathtouch attacking their blocker. They used an instant that prevents all damage that would be dealt to creatures this turn. My opponent argues that since my creature has deathtouch, the blocker should still die because it is just 'one hit,' even though no damage actually gets through. Is my opponent right that the blocker dies from deathtouch despite the prevention?

Your opponent is incorrect; the blocker will survive this combat. Deathtouch creates an ability that makes one damage from a source with deathtouch enough to destroy the blocked creature, but this ability only applies when damage is actually dealt. In this case, the prevention spell reduces the damage to zero. According to the rules, if a source would deal 0 damage, it does not deal damage at all. This replacement effect takes precedence because it stops the damage event from occurring entirely before any results are processed by the game state. Without damage being dealt, there is no damage instance for deathtouch to evaluate for lethality, as lethality checks happen only after damage is marked on a creature. The sequence confirms that since no damage occurs, no destruction results from the combat. The blocker remains on the battlefield unchanged, and no players lose life.

I’m attacking with two creatures at the same time. One of them has an ability that says Whenever this creature deals combat damage to you, create X tokens equal to the damage dealt by it. My opponent responds with a spell that says The next 3 damage that would be dealt to you by sources you don't control is prevented instead. When my first creature's ability goes on the stack and resolves, how many tokens do I actually get?

First, we must determine what happens during combat resolution when multiple effects interact. Replacement effects always modify events before triggered abilities evaluate them. As the comprehensive rules state, if an event is replaced, it never happens and a modified event occurs instead. This means the prevention spell rewrites the damage assignment so that original damage event is entirely erased and replaced with zero damage being dealt. Next, we apply the specific tracking mechanic for triggered triggers: when an ability triggers on damage being dealt by a specific source or sources, and the effect refers to the damage dealt, it refers only to the damage dealt by the specified sources and not to any damage dealt at the same time by other sources. Because the prevention replacement already removed the original event entirely, the trigger looks solely at that creature and counts exactly what occurred in the modified timeline. The concrete final outcome is that you create zero tokens, since no combat damage was actually dealt by that specific source after the replacement took precedence.

I just attacked with my creature that has the annihilator two ability and a reward trigger for dealing combat damage. My opponent played an effect last turn that halves all combat damage my creatures would deal to zero. We are arguing about whether they sacrifice permanents and whether I get to draw. What actually happens?

When you declare attackers, the creature attacks and immediately triggers its annihilator ability, which functions as a triggered ability meaning whenever this creature attacks, the defending player sacrifices two permanents. This activation happens instantly upon the attack declaration and does not look ahead at combat damage. During the damage step, your opponents effect reduces the assigned damage to zero. At this point, the comprehensive rule for zero damage applies and states that if a source would deal 0 damage, it does not deal damage at all. Because the damage event is completely nullified, any abilities that trigger on damage being dealt won’t trigger.
