The annihilator trigger resolves first based on the attack declaration phase, and the zero damage rule then prevents any subsequent combat damage interactions from occurring. Your opponent sacrifices two permanents, but you do not draw cards or receive any other rewards since no actual combat damage ever hits.

I had a Thragtusk on the battlefield with two points of damage from an earlier block, and my opponent cast Lightning Bolt to finish him off so they could get value from their own abilities. Everyone at the table argued whether the state-based actions killing the creature prevents the death trigger or if the spell kills it first. What actually happens and do I draw any cards from Thragtusk's ability?

The Lightning Bolt resolves successfully and you receive the benefit of Thragtusk's ability. The sequence works in your favor because spells and triggered abilities coordinate properly regarding game state changes. When Lightning Bolt resolves, it puts three damage on Thragtusk, which exceeds his toughness and moves him to the graveyard due to the spell's effect. This event causes the when this creature dies trigger to go onto the stack. State-based actions also check for lethal damage automatically whenever a state change occurs, but since the spell already moved the creature to the graveyard, the state-based action has no damaged creatures on the battlefield to handle and simply passes through without interfering. Your triggered ability watches for the creature entering the graveyard, which happened here, so you resolve it and return two creature tokens to the battlefield. The prior damage does not stop anything; the outcome is that Thragtusk goes to the graveyard and you get your tokens.

I control a creature with the ability When this attacks alone, you draw two cards. My opponent controls three creatures but none of them attack. I declare my creature as the only attacker. During combat, before damage is dealt, my opponent activates an ability to sacrifice one of his non-attacking creatures and then tries to argue that my trigger shouldn't resolve because his creatures are still on the battlefield. What happens?

The trigger resolves and you draw two cards regardless of what happens later in combat. The rule for attacking alone states that a creature attacks alone if it is the only creature declared as an attacker during the declare attackers step, meaning having other creatures on the battlefield that are not attacking does not prevent this condition from being met. This condition is evaluated and locked in when attackers are declared, so your opponent's actions afterward cannot retroactively change whether your creature was attacking alone. Additionally, the rule for special actions clarifies that declaring attackers is a turn-based action handled automatically by the game, whereas activating abilities or taking other actions requires priority and does not happen during the declaration phase itself. Since the trigger goes on the stack immediately after you finish declaring your attacker, your opponent can take actions later in combat, but those actions cannot undo the fact that the trigger already fired based on the state at declaration. The final outcome is that your creature attacked alone, the trigger resolved successfully, and you draw two cards even if your opponent sacrificed a creature afterward.

I just played with a card that makes something happen the instant I take priority, and it doesn't go on the stack. At the same time, I want to cast a spell that has different effects depending on whether I pay an extra cost or choose a specific mode. Can I hold off picking which mode to use until after my card effect resolves so I know what works best?

No, you cannot delay your choice. During the casting process, you follow a structured announcement phase where even though some options may be available only if other choices are made later in that step, you may consider any other choices to be made in that initial planning window and declare all modes together upfront. Meanwhile, your card effect is classified as a special action, which means it is an action you may take when you have priority that doesn't use the stack and happens immediately outside the normal casting sequence. Because special actions bypass the stack entirely, they cannot be interjected between your spell announcement decisions. The lookahead allowance during casting takes precedence for structuring your declaration, meaning you must lock in all your spell choices before taking that immediate action. Outcome: You simultaneously declare your chosen mode and all associated costs, then immediately take your non-stack special action afterward. Your spell enters the stack fully declared with no mid-announcement pauses allowed, and your special effect happens separately without interfering with how your spell was cast.

I'm playing a four-player Commander match and my opponent cast something that says Shuffle all cards from target player's library into their graveyard. They targeted the guy sitting across the table from me. Is that allowed even though they're so far away? And does it only shuffle half the deck or what?

In Commander multiplayer games, the official format explicitly establishes the default multiplayer setup is the Free-for-All variant with the attack multiple players option and without the limited range of influence option, meaning no physical distance restrictions block legal targets anywhere at the table. This layout rule takes precedence first by validating that any opponent can be targeted regardless of seating arrangement. Once the spell is legally cast, a separate mechanic governs how it resolves: some effects instruct a player to do something to a zone like a library, and when that happens, that action is performed on all cards in that zone rather than letting you pick specific ones or just a portion of them. The format rule clears the path for targeting across the table, while the zone rule dictates the exact scope of the shuffle during resolution. Final outcome: The effect is completely legal against the player across from you, and every single card in their library gets shuffled into their graveyard, leaving that library empty.

I just tapped my Forest for green mana to pay a cost, but before that mana hits my pool, my opponent uses an effect that replaces the tap with two colorless instead. Then he says his triggered ability should resolve before mine because he went last. We are arguing about which effect actually changes what happens and who gets priority on the triggers. What is the correct sequence?

Tapping your land for mana simply means activating a mana ability that includes the rotate card symbol in its activation cost, and the game treats this action as resolving and producing mana once that specific ability completes. When a replacement effect applies to a permanent tapped for mana, it modifies the mana production event while such an ability is resolving and producing mana, meaning the amount and type change immediately during that resolution window before anything else interacts with the result. Meanwhile, when a player casts a spell or activates an activated ability while another spell or ability is already on the stack, the new action has been cast in response to the earlier one and it will resolve first because it is placed on top of the existing stack. The stacking rule takes precedence for determining interaction order, so any triggered abilities that went onto the stack afterward follow reverse chronological ordering with your opponents latest response resolving first. The concrete final outcome is that your land produces two colorless mana instead of green mana immediately during its own resolution, and all subsequent triggers resolve in top down stack order where the most recent response finishes before your other effects go off.

My opponent just tapped one of my creatures to activate an ability that tries to bring a card from outside the game into play, and they did it right after attacking. I want to respond with removal, but someone told me I have to wait for them to finish their whole turn first. Also, they said the card is black but their commander only has white and blue colors in it, so it can't be brought in anyway. What happens here?

You actually receive priority immediately after your opponent taps the creature because the game dictates that if a player takes a special action, that player receives priority afterward. This means you do not have to wait for their turn to end; you can respond instantly if you have a removal spell ready. However, even if you choose not to respond and their ability resolves, the commander restriction takes precedence when it tries to move the card. The regulations clearly state that if a player is allowed to bring a card from outside the game into a Commander game, that player cannot bring a card into the game this way if any color in its color identity isn't in the color identity of the player's commander. Since the black card lacks the required white and blue colors, the game completely blocks its entry. The concrete final outcome is that you may respond immediately due to priority rules, but regardless of your response, the external card will never enter the battlefield or hand because it violates the color identity restriction.

I'm in a Commander game with Wort, the Raidmother as my commander and I am completely mana-screwed. I want to add a Plains card from my side of the table into my deck so I can cast a white spell. My opponent says that is not allowed, but I argue that since it is my turn now and I plan to play the land and then receive priority afterward to use it, that timing makes the action valid. What happens?

Adding a card during the game is strictly prohibited in Commander regardless of whose turn it is or what you plan to do next. Your deck must be constructed with exactly 100 cards before the game starts, and every card's color identity must fall within your commander's red-green identity, which excludes white from Plains entirely. Basic lands are only permitted if all mana colors they produce match your commander's identity, so a Plains is illegal in a Wort deck even though other basic lands like Mountain or Forest are allowed. Although you would receive priority after taking special actions like playing a land, receiving priority governs the flow of in-game interactions and never validates an action that violates pre-game deck construction requirements; the legality of cards depends on the deck list established before play begins, not on turn-based timing. The concrete outcome is a game loss for adding an additional card from outside the constructed deck and attempting to play an illegal card.

My opponent claims that even if an effect prevents all damage from a source, the damage event still counts as happening so triggers should fire. I have an ability that reduces incoming damage by the number of cards I drew when the game started, and my opponent deals 3 damage to me. What actually happens?

The rules for the start of the match establish that each player draws a hand of seven cards once the starting player is determined, so your reduction applies to subtract those seven cards worth of protection from the incoming three damage. This calculation reduces the potential damage to zero. The relevant rule states that if a source would deal zero damage, it does not deal damage at all, and replacement effects have no event to replace. This means the damage never occurs as an actual event. Your opponent is mistaken; the triggers do not fire because there was no damage dealt to trigger them. The concrete outcome is that you take zero damage and no damage-based abilities resolve.

I'm in a match and I cast Damnation to destroy all creatures. My opponent controls a permanent that says Reveal the first card from your graveyard each turn and has a triggered ability that draws a card whenever you reveal a creature with mana value 2 or less. Before they use that ability, I realize we can put multiple cards into our graveyards at once because of the spell. Can I arrange the order of my own creatures in my graveyard so I can make sure a cheap creature isn't on top when the ability resolves?

Yes, you can rearrange your cards to control what is revealed. When Damnation resolves, it puts multiple creature cards from the battlefield into their owners' graveyards at the same time. The rules state that if an effect puts two or more cards into the same graveyard simultaneously, the owner of those cards may arrange them in any order they choose. This arrangement happens as part of the simultaneous placement before any triggered abilities are put on the stack. Your opponent's permanent has a static ability that links to a triggered ability; the static portion tells you to reveal the first card from the graveyard, and the linked trigger watches for a specific result. Because you get to order your cards in the graveyard first, you can place your expensive creatures above your cheap ones. When the static ability resolves after everyone gets priority, it will reveal whatever is now on top, allowing you to avoid revealing a creature with mana value 2 or less and preventing the linked trigger from drawing a card.

I have a creature on my battlefield with an ability that triggers when it dies. My opponent suspended a copy of that creature card in their hand. They claim that by suspending the creature, it triggered my creature's ability because the card was removed from the game zone. Is that right?

No, the ability does not trigger. Suspending a spell is a special action that allows a player to exile it from their hand rather than casting it, which can be done anytime they have priority provided they could begin to cast the card. The suspended creature goes to the exile zone with time counters and does not leave the hand until it eventually resolves. The game defines dying strictly as being put into a graveyard from the battlefield. Since the suspended card was never on the battlefield and did not go to the graveyard, it has not died under the rules. Your creature's ability only triggers when a permanent dies by leaving the battlefield for the graveyard, so suspending the copy in hand produces no trigger and your existing creature remains safe on the battlefield without generating any effect.

I just tapped my lands during our team turn and saw a dragon with {R}{G} on it. My partner also wants to cast an instant at the exact same time, but we keep getting interrupted by opponents or confused about who acts when. Can we pay for the dragon using any combination of mana, and why can't we just take turns casting our spells separately during this phase?

Mana symbols strictly define what can be paid, and according to game rules, mana symbols also represent mana costs, meaning {R}{G} demands exactly one red and one green rather than generic substitutes or colorless gems. Additionally, during your turn phase, teams rather than individual players have priority, which blocks you from taking separate actions. The cost requirement must be established before the priority window determines who can legally act. You will pay one red and one green mana to cast the dragon, your partner queues their instant behind it, and neither of you acts independently because only your whole team shares a single priority window until all cards are played or passed. The concrete outcome is that you successfully cast the dragon by paying the exact required colors, your teammate waits for the shared priority queue, and once you both pass as a unit, the spell resolves without further interruptions.

I have Flash granted to me by an enchantment, and it's your turn with priority passed, so I start casting a sorcery that normally can only be cast on my turn. I tap my forests for mana and sacrifice a creature as part of the cost. You respond by destroying the enchantment granting Flash. Can I still finish casting this spell even though I lost the Flash ability now, or does the game undo everything I did?

The outcome is that your spell successfully casts and goes onto the stack, and your mana and sacrificed creature are not returned. First, the priority system establishes that you may cast instant spells or activated abilities any time you have priority, and noninstant spells during your main phase when the stack is empty. By having Flash granted to you, you met the condition allowing you to cast this spell during your opponent's turn once they passed priority, so you were permitted to begin the casting process. The rules regarding illegal actions include a specific protection for flash-like conditions: once a player has begun casting a spell because certain conditions like Flash were met, they may continue to cast that spell even if those conditions stop being met later in the process. This means the destruction of your enchantment does not make the casting illegal because the game validates your right to finish the cast based on the state when you started. The validation rule takes precedence here by allowing the cast to complete, so the spell enters the stack after your costs are paid and your opponent can respond from there.

I attacked with my two toughness creature last turn and it took three damage. Today I used a spell that makes my creatures phase out, and now in the untap step they automatically phase back in. Do they go to the graveyard right away because they took damage? My opponent says yes, but I thought phasing just made them disappear temporarily.

Your opponent is correct about the creature dying, but not for the reason you think. While the creature is phased out, its status changes and except for rules that specifically mention it, a phased-out permanent is treated as though it does not exist on the battlefield. Because of this, state-based actions do not check it while it is gone, and counters including damage markers stay attached since phasing never moves the permanent to another zone. When the untap step arrives and the creature phases back in, the game once again treats it as though it exists. At that exact moment, state-based actions check the battlefield. The rules clarify that damage dealt to a creature does not destroy it directly. Rather, state-based actions may destroy a creature due to the results of the damage dealt. Since phasing happens first during the untap step without removing counters, and state-based actions run immediately after permanents phase in, the three damage markers are still present on a two toughness creature. The concrete final outcome is that the creature phases back into play and immediately goes to its owner's graveyard as a result of a state-based action, before either player receives priority.
I just tapped my Meteor Crater during my opponent's turn to try to cast a spell, but I got zero mana back. My opponent says he can respond now even though it was a land ability. Is that right?

Your opponent cannot respond, and here is how the rules determine the outcome. First, regarding priority, the general rules state that the active player receives priority at key points and after taking actions like activating abilities, which allowed you to activate the ability when it was your turn or during a phase where you held priority. However, Meteor Crater's ability requires you to choose a color of a permanent you control. Because you controlled no colored permanents at that moment, the ability would produce mana of an undefined type. The authoritative rule for this situation states that if an ability would produce one or more mana of an undefined type, it produces no mana instead. This means your activation resolved with no effect on your mana pool, but it does not trigger any response window because Meteor Crater is a land and its activated mana ability never uses the stack. The concrete outcome is that you gained no mana, the Crater remains tapped, and since mana abilities resolve instantly without going on the stack, priority returns to you immediately after the activation so you can take further actions if you have other resources available.

I control a creature called 'Giant Spider' which is printed as a 2/2. My opponent controls an Aura that says 'Enchanted creature gets +5/+0.' Then my opponent casts 'Mirror Entity' which copies one of my creatures. The Mirror Entity becomes a Giant Spider but it looks like just a regular spider with normal stats! Does the copy not get the big boost from the Aura? I thought copies only get what's printed on the card.

No, the copy does not get the +5/+0 bonus. Copy effects only replicate the printed characteristics of the creature being copied, starting with its copiable values. While static abilities from Auras produce continuous effects that are simply true while attached, those enchantments remain attached to the original creature and do not transfer to newly created copies. Because copies start with only their printed values before any continuous effects apply, the copy will enter the battlefield as a base 2/2 without the Aura's power/toughness boost.

I just cast a spell that forces me to draw a bunch of cards and my library only had four left. The spell is still resolving but I can see I'm about to empty my deck. Do I lose right now or does the game wait? And what happens once it resolves?

This comes down to timing and precedence. First, the rule for state-based actions applies and takes precedence by stating they pay no attention to what happens during the resolution of a spell or ability, which means the game will not check your library status while you are drawing. Once the spell finishes resolving, the empty library rule applies next, which explicitly says that a player who attempts to draw a card from a library with no cards in it loses the game next time a player would receive priority. The concrete final outcome is that you survive the entire resolution phase without losing, but you will definitely lose the match the moment you pass priority or your opponent starts their turn.

I just tapped my artifact for mana that shows up as a half-red half-white symbol on its activation cost. I let it resolve and now I have some colored mana sitting in my pool. My opponent says they can respond, but I thought the turn just moved to them automatically since we're still in combat. Can they actually respond at this point, or did the phase already move past that?

Yes, your opponent absolutely gets a chance to respond before the phase ends. First, when that ability resolves and adds mana to your pool, you must choose exactly one half of the hybrid symbol, meaning either one red mana or one white mana is added depending on which side you picked. This choice happens during resolution, so your mana pool is already updated before turn order matters. After it resolves, priority returns to you because you just activated an ability. Once you have priority and decide not to take any further actions, you must pass by announcing exactly what mana is sitting in your pool at that moment. Then the next player in turn order receives priority, which is why your opponent gets a response window right now. Your concrete outcome is that they get one chance to cast an instant or activate an ability after you announce your one colored mana and pass, and only after both of you repeatedly pass without acting will the game proceed to your attacker phase.

I have two artifacts in my Commander game that make damage creatures deal double instead of its normal amount, and I just declared an attack against three different opponents. You deal quadruple your base damage to each opponent, not infinite damage. The rules state that replacement effects get only one opportunity to affect an event or any modified events, which prevents looping and means your two double damage effects multiply your base damage by four rather than escalating forever. Your Commander game defaults to a Free-for-All format where you may attack multiple players, so you distribute that calculated quadruple damage to each of the three opponents you attacked, resulting in a finite total for everyone involved.

I just cast a board wipe that destroys all my creatures on the field. Once the trigger is generated and the creatures actually move to your graveyard, a different rule takes over which states that if an effect puts two or more cards into the same graveyard at the same time, the owner of those cards may arrange them in any order. This arrangement step directly controls your follow-up options. Concrete final outcome: You will gain 1 life from the triggered ability going on the stack. When both permanents hit your graveyard, you may place whichever card you want on top so you can legally target it with next turn's spell. The look-back-in-time mechanic always resolves first to create triggers, and the arrangement rule takes effect only after the cards land in the graveyard zone.

I have a three-toughness creature with a regeneration shield ready. My opponent just cast a spell that deals exactly three damage to it. They say it gets destroyed and goes to the graveyard, but I told them it taps up instead because of the regen. Who is right?

Because this replacement rule takes precedence over the state-based check for lethal destruction, your creature never dies. It survives combat fully healed and in a tapped state, staying on the battlefield until you untap it during your next untap step.

I’m in the middle of a Commander game and it’s my turn. My only creature on the battlefield is my commander. I tap it and declare it as an attacker, my opponent doesn’t block it, and they claim I win right away because of commander damage. What actually happens step by step?

The concrete final outcome is that your commander deals its normal unblocked combat damage to your opponent and both players proceed through the turn without ending the game immediately, with the twenty-one point threshold continuing to track forward until it is eventually reached.

I just exiled a creature from my hand because I wanted to use its plot ability during my main phase. Once the creature enters play, the two ongoing modifiers apply simultaneously as independent continuous effects. Since both effects are active before it enters, they will modify it based on when those effects came under your control. The precedence here is straightforward: the plot mechanic first determines how and when you legally cast the spell from exile, and then the continuous effects rule dictates how battlefield modifiers apply once it resolves. The concrete final game outcome is that the plotted creature resolves onto the battlefield with the +2/-0 boost and has lost flying, remaining in that exact state until a newer effect changes or removes those modifications.

I just cast two different spells on my turn that each exile a creature at the beginning of my next end step. The physical tracking rule applies first because you must organize the game state correctly before timing matters, meaning those cards go into separate zones since rules require that exiled cards that might return to the battlefield or any other zone should be kept in separate piles to keep track of their respective ways of returning. This separation establishes independent identity for each permanent. Once tracked, the timing rule takes precedence during phase transitions because a delayed triggered ability is created during the resolution of spells and will trigger only once when the next time its trigger event occurs. When your end step arrives, those two independently created delayed abilities activate on separate instances of the stack without combining. The final outcome is that both creatures return to the battlefield individually during your end step as distinct permanents, with their original exiled zones emptying exactly after each independent delay resolves.

I just tapped out my only creature to attack and triggered 'Riftbolt Elf's' effect because I was attacking alone, but then my opponent declared two blockers with it! The game determines whether you are attacking alone based on which creatures were declared as attackers at the moment you finished declaring your attackers, not on what blockers show up later. A rule states that a creature attacks alone if it's the only creature declared as an attacker during the declare attackers step, meaning the condition is fixed once declaration ends. Because this triggered ability checks for a game state rather than an event, it functions as a state trigger that fires immediately when the game recognizes that attacking alone is true. The ability went onto the stack based on your declaration and its outcome is independent of subsequent changes like blockers being assigned, so you gain the full benefit of the effect.

I just declared attackers with a creature that says it deals 3 damage to the defending player when it hits. My opponent controls a legendary artifact that says artifacts you control can't be damaged by sources you control. Does the artifact actually take the damage from its own controller's permanent?

The relevant mechanics state that any object can deal damage, and each attacking creature deals combat damage equal to its power during the combat damage step. However, the opposing artifact's ability creates a permanent restriction that must exist before the appropriate event occurs, meaning it cannot go back in time to change something already happened. This type of can't effect takes precedence over any prevention mechanics and simply blocks the event from ever starting. The concrete final outcome is that the artifact suffers zero damage, no triggered abilities fire, and your attacker remains on the battlefield dealing no damage.

My opponent just cast a sorcery that says Each player draws four cards, and I have an empty library. The game has not ended yet, so I am confused about the timing. Does the game stop right now when I try to draw, or does everything happen after? Can my opponent respond to me losing?

When your opponent cast that spell, it resolved and attempted to make you draw four cards from your empty library, but the loss does not occur instantly upon the attempt. The rules state that a player loses the game the next time they would receive priority after attempting to draw from an empty library, which means the spell finishes resolving completely before the loss condition is checked. This delay occurs because these outcomes are governed by state-based actions that are monitored throughout the game and are not controlled by any player, so the game performs this automatic check only after the current event concludes. Consequently, your opponent cannot respond to you losing because the loss is the result of an automatic game check rather than a triggered ability with a stack, resulting in you losing the game once the spell finishes resolving and the state-based action is processed.

I attacked with a creature and its ability went on the stack to let me put the top card of my graveyard into my hand. I saw when the ability triggered that there was a bad card on top, but my opponent yelled that I have to do it anyway because the trigger already happened. What are they talking about?

Your opponent is mistaken. The rules regarding optional triggered abilities state that if an ability includes the word may, it goes on the stack when it triggers regardless of whether you intend to use it, and your choice of whether to exercise the option is made only when the ability resolves. This means triggering does not commit you to using the effect; you retain the right to decline until resolution time. The precedence here is that the optional trigger rule governs the timing of your decision, while the examination rule ensures you had full access to the necessary information at that moment. The concrete final outcome is that when the ability resolves, you can choose not to put the card into your hand, leaving the bad card in your graveyard and preserving your hand as it was.

I just had my commander die in a group slay and it went straight to exile instead of graveyard. Why didn't its death trigger go on the stack first? Also, I'm worried because now that commander isn't technically in my 100-card deck anymore, does this break my deck construction limits mid-game?

State-based actions happen automatically whenever certain conditions are met and do not use the stack, which is why the exile replacement effect resolves immediately before any death triggers can even be placed on the pile. Abilities that watch for a specified game state are triggered abilities, not state-based actions, meaning your commander's death trigger will wait to resolve while the automatic check finishes first. Deck construction rules require each deck to contain exactly one hundred cards including its commander, but these limits are static parameters checked only during initial deck preparation and do not dynamically shift during play. The concrete final outcome is that the commander remains in exile as required by legendary rules, your death trigger will successfully resolve on the stack after other responses finish, and your deck construction status remains completely unchanged because pre-game building limits never override or reset based on mid-game state changes.

We just started our first game as Team A in Two-Headed Giant. Our team goes first but my friend says we have to wait until our second turn to even play a land or use cards like Companion since we skip drawing a card. Is that true? What exactly can we do on this first turn?

Even though the team who plays first skips the draw step of their first turn in a Two-Headed Giant game, the rest of the turn still proceeds into your main phases where special actions are permitted. The turn structure rule applies first to establish that your first main phase still occurs, after which the rules for special actions take precedence by stating that playing a land is only allowed during a main phase when the stack is empty and you have priority, and other specific actions require those exact same conditions. Because skipping the draw step does not remove your first main phase, you remain fully eligible to act. The concrete final game outcome is that your team will successfully put one land onto the battlefield and activate any other eligible special actions during your first main phase this turn, despite never drawing a card at the start of the turn.

I just pulled off a deck building idea where my commander says instead of drawing your opening hand you draw five cards, but my friend at the table says we still play out the normal seven card start and then draw five later. Can you tell me what actually happens at the very beginning of our match?

The official starting procedure explicitly states that once the starting player has been determined each player sets their life total to 40 and draws a hand of seven cards as the baseline for the game. However replacement effects act like shields around whatever they are affecting and apply continuously as events happen, using keywords like instead to completely substitute the original action with a new one. This replacement effect takes precedence because it actively monitors the opening draw event and overrides the default setup instruction before any game state is locked in. As a concrete final outcome you begin the match with exactly five cards in hand and forty life, you are not allowed to mulligan or redraw, and the first turn proceeds immediately from that starting state.

I just cast a bunch of spells that deal one damage to my own creatures, and at the same time I take two points of poison and my life drops to zero. I have an enchantment that says if I would lose the game, I shuffle my hand and graveyard into my library instead. My friend says I should only shuffle once for all the things that are killing me, but then asks if I can keep my library in a specific order since I spent turns setting it up last turn. What actually happens?

Because your life total hit zero and you also took poison damage at the exact same time, you are facing multiple conditions that would cause you to lose simultaneously. When this happens, the rule for simultaneous losses applies directly and states that if multiple state-based actions would have the same result at the same time, a single replacement effect will replace all of them. This means your friend is correct that you only shuffle once instead of shuffling repeatedly for each separate loss condition. However, the rule about keeping library order intact explicitly notes that the order of objects in a library, in a graveyard, or on the stack cannot be changed except when effects or rules allow it, which means your previous carefully arranged card order is permanently lost because the enchantment's instruction to shuffle overrides that restriction. The concrete final outcome is that you survive the turn, you perform exactly one shuffle of your hand and graveyard into your library, all simultaneous game-loss conditions are prevented by that single replacement effect, and the replacement effect takes precedence here since the simultaneous losses trigger the shuffling before you would ever need to worry about maintaining zone order.

My opponent just passed priority in my main phase, but I want to activate an ability on my artifact that says 'Tap: Add {3} to your mana pool' and then use that mana immediately to cast a spell with cost {U}{3}. A few people at the table are arguing whether I have to wait for them to pass priority to activate this ability or if I can do it right now, and they also keep debating whether this generic {3} counts as colorless mana or something else. What is the actual ruling on both timing and what kind of mana I will get?

You can activate the ability immediately because you currently have priority, and the active player may always take actions like activating abilities when it is their turn. Regarding the mana type, if an effect adds mana represented by a generic symbol to your mana pool, that exact amount of colorless mana is added. This means you will gain three units of colorless mana. However, colorless mana cannot be used to pay for colored costs like blue {U}; it can only cover the generic portion of a cost. To cast your spell for {U}{3}, you must spend the three colorless mana on the generic cost and find one additional source of blue mana to cover the remaining blue requirement. Your final outcome is that you activate the artifact now, gain three colorless mana, but still need to produce or locate one blue mana to successfully cast the spell.

I just started a Commander game with an artifact commander that has no color identity. During my turn, I tapped a card for one mana and immediately tried to play a Swamp from my hand before passing priority. My friend said I can't do that because I have to wait until my main phase, but another player argued that since the deck only needs exactly one hundred cards and everything must match the commander's identity, any land type is fair game here. A completely colorless commander restricts a Commander deck to cards that have no color identity, making a Swamp (which is black) illegal regardless of timing. Even if the land were legal, playing it is a special action that you may take only when you have priority, the stack is empty, and you are in a main phase. Because you attempted this outside those conditions, the play is illegal and the land remains in your hand until your next eligible main phase.

I just played a creature with haste from my hand and attacked with it this turn. My opponent blocked it for lethal damage during combat. The creature gets destroyed. Does the creature go to the graveyard right away, or can I use an instant spell on it after it takes damage but before it moves?

When you cast a creature with haste, the rule for haste allows it to attack even though it entered the battlefield this turn, specifically because if a creature has haste, it can attack even if it hasn't been controlled by its controller continuously since their most recent turn began. After combat damage is assigned and dealt, the game performs state-based actions automatically. State-based actions are game actions that happen automatically whenever certain conditions are met and do not use the stack. Because the creature now has lethal damage, a state-based action checks and moves it to the graveyard immediately. These checks occur before any player receives priority, meaning you cannot respond with an instant spell between the time damage is dealt and the creature dies. The concrete outcome is that the creature is destroyed and placed into the graveyard instantly after combat damage resolves; you have no chance to save it at that moment, though you could have acted earlier in the turn.

I'm in a multiplayer game where our group allows casting spells from exile or something weird, but my opponent says I can't play a land during combat because of the 'stack empty' rule. You cannot play a land during combat regardless of format unless a specific rule explicitly modifies timing. Playing a land is defined as a special action you can take only when you have priority and the stack is empty during a main phase. The requirement for an empty stack prevents you from using this action in response to spells or during combat steps. You cannot assume your group's general leniency overrides specific timing restrictions without a written rule confirming it. Concrete outcome: You must wait until a main phase with an empty stack to play your land; you have no special action available during combat to play a land, and no informal house rule can bypass this unless officially adopted per the tournament rules reference.

We are in the middle of a Commander match and my opponent casts a board wipe that exiles my commander. You must handle the automatic game state changes before attempting any discretionary special actions, because the game processes replacements immediately after a spell resolves and before handing priority to players. The Commander format rules establish that if a commander is in exile and that object was put into that zone since the last time state-based actions were checked, its owner may put it into the command zone instead as a replacement effect. Once your commander safely moves to the command zone through that automatic check, you then gain priority to take special actions like paying three mana to move a companion from outside the game into your hand. The replacement effect applying to your commander happens first during the mandatory state check, and only after that step completes do you get the window to choose your companion action. Your final outcome is that your commander returns to the command zone on its own accord, and you may subsequently pay three mana to place your companion card into your hand or decide not to take that special action at all.

We’re in combat and I activated my creature’s tap ability to deal damage equal to the number of enchantments I control. The special action rule applies first because you must complete the tap and receive priority before any damage evaluation or response windows open. Regarding the damage, replacement effects require an actual event to modify. Even though protection prevents the original damage from landing, the game state still processes the attempt. However, if a source would deal 0 damage, it does not deal damage at all. Replacement effects that would increase the damage dealt by that source have no event to replace, so they have no effect. The concrete final outcome is that you tap the creature, gain priority to act or pass, your opponent’s protection resolves first, and your creature deals exactly zero damage with no replacement effect applying.

I just went into combat with two attackers and my opponent blocked both of them with creatures that deal equal damage back. The sequence of events follows a strict order where combat damage resolves before any dead creatures are removed from play. Because every creature received lethal damage at the exact same moment, they all transition to the graveyard together during this automatic check. The concrete final outcome is that both of your blockers and both of your attackers die at once, leaving you with zero creatures left on the battlefield for that combat phase.

The timing and priority system establishes the foundational window for taking actions first, but the casting rules handle the specific characteristic choices within that framework. I have two creatures attacking, and my opponent blocks with one creature that deals lethal damage to both attackers simultaneously. Both creatures die at the exact same time, creating death triggers for me and my opponent that go onto the stack. When creatures are marked with lethal damage, state-based actions are checked automatically without any player control, causing both creatures to be put into graveyards simultaneously and creating death triggers for each controller. These triggers are placed on the stack according to turn order rules. The rule regarding object order strictly forbids changing the position of cards once they are there except when specific effects or rules allow it, which means you cannot insert a new card between two existing objects on the stack. Casting an instant puts your spell on top of the entire stack, not inside it. The concrete outcome is that all three objects resolve in a fixed order: your new instant resolves first because it sits on top, then one of the death triggers resolves based on active player priority, and finally the other death trigger resolves. You cannot manipulate the relative order of the original triggers by playing spells.

I just untapped my turn and played a commander that gives all my creatures +2/+2. Then I cast a creature with an ability that says This creature has base power and toughness 1/1. Your opponent is misinterpreting how bonuses interact. The guidelines for static permanents clarify that static abilities create continuous effects, and these effects remain active as long as the permanent with the ability remains on the battlefield and has the ability. Because the characteristic-defining text establishes the baseline immediately, it takes precedence over later modifiers. Once that 1/1 base is locked in, the commander plus two plus two applies since it entered first, followed by the Aura plus one zero because it entered second. These bonuses stack in the order they arrived rather than replacing each other. The final outcome is a permanent with exactly 4 power and 3 toughness on the battlefield.

I just lost my commander to a board wipe and put it into the command zone, but my opponent hit it with an effect that turned it face down. Replace explicit rule citations with conversational descriptions of the mechanics. I'm in Planechase and my artifact reads 'Tap, Pay {U}: Roll a six-sided die. Whenever you roll a 4 or higher this way, draw a card.' I tapped it and got a 2, so I didn't draw. No. Your artifact combines a static ability and a triggered ability into one paragraph where the trigger is linked to the action of rolling. The phrase 'this way' ties the draw effect strictly to the result of rolling that specific six-sided die, meaning only the d6 roll provides numbers for this check. Additionally, Planechase rules dictate that while abilities triggering whenever you roll a die will trigger from the planar die, any effect that refers to a numerical result ignores the rolling of the planar die. I’m playing a three-person game and it’s my turn. In a multiplayer game where not all opponents automatically become defending players during combat, you must choose one opponent as your defending player as a turn-based action during the beginning of combat step before anyone can act. The rules state that unless opponents automatically become defenders, the attacking player chooses one of their opponents as a turn-based action during the beginning of combat step, and this happens immediately without using the stack. After that mandatory choice resolves, players receive priority. For special actions like paying three generic mana to retrieve a companion, the rules specify you can take this action any time they have priority and the stack is empty during a main phase of your turn, meaning it cannot be used once combat starts. However, other flexible abilities that trigger anytime you could cast an instant may be used once priority passes after defender selection. The concrete final game outcome is that you pick your defending opponent first during the beginning of combat, and only afterward do you gain priority to attempt the non-phase-restricted special actions.

I just declared I want to cast Lightning Bolt targeting their creature, but before I actually pay the red mana and move it to my library, my opponent says Okay I pass priority. Does that mean my Bolt goes on the stack now, or does passing automatically resolve things?

The cost resolution step takes precedence because a cost is an action or payment necessary to take another action and you must carry out the instructions specified before the spell can exist on the stack. Your opponent passing priority does not skip this requirement. Instead, his pass simply gives you another opportunity to finish paying the mana or declare that you are done. The interaction happens when you complete the cost, at which point the rule about consecutive passing applies: if all players pass in succession without taking any actions in between passing, the spell or ability on top of the stack resolves. Since neither action has happened yet, nothing triggers automatically. Concrete final outcome: Your Lightning Bolt does not go on the stack until you pay the red mana, your opponent receiving priority changes nothing until that payment is made, and once the spell is properly placed on the stack, consecutive passing without further responses will cause it to resolve and destroy their creature.

My opponent claims that sacrificing a creature doesn't trigger abilities that say 'When this leaves the battlefield' because sacrifice isn't dying or destroying. They said those triggers only happen from combat damage or destruction effects. Is my opponent right?

Your opponent is incorrect. When you sacrifice a creature, that action puts the permanent into its owner’s graveyard. This movement from the battlefield to another zone satisfies the condition for leaves-the-battlefield triggers. The game rules define these as zone-change triggers that activate whenever a permanent moves from the battlefield to any other zone, regardless of whether it dies in combat, is destroyed, or is sacrificed. Because the sacrifice places the card directly into the graveyard, the leaves-the-battlefield ability will trigger normally on the stack and resolve just like it would if the creature had been killed by combat or a destruction effect. The final outcome is that the triggered effect resolves fully, making your opponent’s claim incorrect.

I just cast a red creature with devour 3, and my opponent has two black and red source effects on the board that would each give it devour 5 as it enters. When you cast that creature, first apply all replacement effects that modify how it enters the battlefield. After those entry replacements finish resolving and the spell completes, the game checks state-based actions. At this point, multiple conditions might want you to lose the game due to zero life and an empty library. However, a single replacement effect will replace all of them at the same time. Because Lich's Mirror covers every game loss instance simultaneously, it triggers and saves you. Concrete final outcome: The creature enters with exactly three or five counters based on your choice, you sacrifice the Bear once, and Lich's Mirror fully replaces the game loss, leaving you at 20 life to keep playing.

I’m trying to cast a sorcery for five generic mana during my main phase, and I have three lands that tap for one colorless each plus an artifact that taps for two colorless. You can activate all four tap abilities at once. When you pay, each unit of mana keeps its identity as the rules state that the source of mana is the specific ability that produced it, meaning your commander trigger will correctly see exactly which land or artifact generated the mana.

My opponent attacked with a creature that has lifelink, but I have a blocker that has an ability saying if damage is dealt to it, N of that damage is prevented. Does my opponent still gain life for the amount of damage that gets prevented?

No, your opponent gains no life for the damage that is prevented. The ability you described acts as Absorb, which is a static ability that prevents a specific amount of damage from being dealt by a source. The game rules state that damage dealt by a source with lifelink causes its controller to gain life in addition to other results. However, because your Absorb ability prevents the damage before it is actually dealt, that damage never reaches the game state where it triggers or applies results. Since the damage is prevented, the condition for gaining life is never met, and your opponent gains zero life for that portion of the attack.

I have a commander sitting in my command zone and my opponent used an effect to turn it face down while it was still there. Now I want to cast it as my commander this turn. Does its enters-the-battlefield ability trigger when I cast it, and if so, when does that ability actually go on the stack during the spell resolution process?

When your opponent turned your commander face down while it remained in the command zone, the game immediately treats it as a new object, exactly matching the rule that states if a face-up object in the command zone is turned face down, it becomes a new object. Because it is now a completely fresh entity, casting it from the command zone will cause its enters-the-battlefield ability to trigger normally without any connection to its prior state. That triggered ability does not go on the stack right away; once an ability has triggered, its controller puts it on the stack as an object that’s not a card the next time a player would receive priority. The precedence is clear: the face-down transformation happens first and creates a new object, and only after you finish casting the commander does the timing rule step in to handle the trigger placement. The concrete final outcome is that your commander enters the battlefield successfully, its ability triggers based on the fresh identity, and the game waits for the next priority window to place that trigger onto the stack where you control it and can respond before anything resolves.

I just cast a spell that creates a token copy of my opponent's attacking creature onto the battlefield. They also control an artifact that says permanents enter tapped. The copied creature has an activated ability where you tap it to deal 3 damage to any target. Can the copy use that ability immediately, or does it have to wait until next turn?

The token copy will enter tapped due to the artifact's replacement effect. Because of both summoning sickness and already being tapped, the creature cannot tap itself immediately to pay for its activated ability. Tapping is required for the cost, so the player must wait until their next turn's untap step to refresh the creature and remove summoning sickness before activating it. The 3 damage is dealt as a spell or ability effect, not combat damage, meaning any object can deal it once the activation conditions are met.

I control a commander with the ability At the beginning of your upkeep you may draw a card. It started my turn and that effect automatically went onto the stack even though I had not decided to take any action on it yet. I am currently tapping a swamp for black mana but someone told me I could just choose to discard this trigger from the stack since I am taking a special action with my land. Can I do that or does it stay?

The ability stays on the stack because optional triggered abilities go on the stack when they trigger regardless of whether their controller intends to exercise the option or not and the choice is made when the ability resolves. This mechanic applies immediately when the upkeep begins and operates independently from your current mana tapping sequence. Regarding timing precedence, triggers are placed on the stack based on game state changes before any new actions occur so the commander effect remains waiting while you handle your land. The rule for special actions only clarifies that if a player takes a special action that player receives priority afterward which simply allows you to cast instants or activate abilities between taps without passing the turn to your opponent. The concrete final outcome is your optional draw trigger remains safely on the stack unchanged by your mana tapping you finish tapping your lands and casting any spells you want during your retained priority and when the commander trigger resolves during upkeep phase sequence you make your definitive choice to draw a card or skip it.

I control a creature with both a +1/+1 counter and a -1/-1 counter on it. My opponent casts an effect that destroys the creature and sends it to my graveyard. Later, I find a way to return that creature card from the graveyard to the battlefield tapped. I thought since it comes back as a brand new card, all those counters would disappear and leave it with its base stats only. Is that correct?

It is a common misunderstanding that returning a permanent resets all its modifications like counters, but the rules distinguish between damage and counters when objects move zones. When your creature was destroyed and moved to the graveyard, it became a completely new object with no memory of past damage or effects, so any marked damage would indeed disappear. However, +1/+1 and -1/-1 counters are physical markers that move along with the card as it changes zones. When you return that card from the graveyard to the battlefield, an effect can locate the object in that public zone and bring it back as a new permanent carrying all the counters it had. As soon as this new creature enters the battlefield, state-based actions are checked immediately. The game sees that the creature has both a +1/+1 counter and a -1/-1 counter on it at the same time, which triggers a rule requiring an equal number of each type to be removed. Since there is one of each, they are both removed before any player could act. Your creature returns tapped with all counters gone, resulting in a creature with only its printed power and toughness.

I'm mid-game and just attacked with two creatures while my opponent blocks each one. One of his blockers has three damage marked on it and a plus one plus one counter on it, and it dies after combat. My attacker has an ability that triggers whenever it deals combat damage to a creature, putting counters equal to the damage dealt. Do I get counters for all five damage from both attackers, or just mine? And when that blocker goes to the graveyard with its death trigger on the stack, does the game see the plus one plus one counter still attached?

When multiple effects resolve at once, the game checks state-based actions before any triggered abilities resolve. If a state-based action results in a permanent leaving the battlefield at the same time other state-based actions were performed, that permanent’s last known information is derived from the game state before any of those state-based actions were performed. This means your blocker leaves with the plus one plus one counter clearly visible, so its death trigger sees it exactly as it was right before dying. After creatures move to the graveyard, triggered abilities go on the stack and resolve individually. For your attacker's ability, if an ability triggers on damage being dealt by a specific source or sources, and the effect refers to the “damage dealt,” it refers only to the damage dealt by the specified sources and not to any damage dealt at the same time by other sources. You do not combine the attacks for this calculation. Your attacker gets exactly three counters from this trigger, and your blocker enters the graveyard with its counter remaining visible while its death ability resolves separately.

I just attacked with a weird creature that says its power is equal to the number of lands I control, and it also has this melee keyword. I attacked my opponent with two different creatures this turn. How big does the melee buff make it get exactly?

Clarify that the characteristic-defining ability sets your creature's base power and toughness continuously based on your land count before combat begins. Then, when you declare attackers, the Melee keyword triggers because it reads 'Whenever this creature attacks...' and grants +1/+1 until end of turn for each opponent you attacked with a creature this combat. Since you attacked one opponent using two creatures, Melee applies exactly once. The interaction is straightforward: the characteristic-defining rule establishes the starting numbers first, and the combat trigger modifies those established numbers afterward, resulting in a final size equal to the base value plus exactly one.

I control two artifacts that both have abilities where you sacrifice an artifact to get a benefit like adding mana or drawing cards but I only have one artifact left on the battlefield can I sacrifice that single artifact to activate both abilities at the same time so I can get both benefits?

No, you cannot sacrifice a single artifact to pay for two different costs at the same time. Each payment of a cost applies to only one spell, ability, or effect, meaning one sacrificed permanent cannot cover multiple separate activations. Instead, you must sequence these actions using priority. You activate the first ability by sacrificing the artifact, then pass priority. After it resolves, you receive priority again and can attempt to activate the second ability, but since sacrificing the artifact moves it to the graveyard immediately, the second activation will fail unless you have a way to return or duplicate the artifact before activating that cost.

I just tapped all my artifacts for mana early in my main phase, but then my opponent cast a counterspell during combat. I wanted to respond later in the same turn, only to find out my unspent mana was completely gone when we checked it at the end of the phase. Why couldn't I just hold onto that mana to respond whenever I wanted?

When you generate mana, it goes into your mana pool where you can use it immediately to pay a cost or leave it as unspent mana. However, the rules clearly state that each player's mana pool empties at the end of each step and phase, and the player is said to lose this mana once that boundary is reached. When handling responses, casting something after an opponent's spell means the new spell has been cast in response to the earlier spell or ability, and it will resolve first before priority moves back down the stack. The precedence here belongs to the stack mechanics during active turns because they dictate exactly when you can legally insert a response, while the mana pool expiration rule only acts as a hard cleanup step that clears resources when phases conclude. Because you waited until the phase ended rather than responding while priority was active, both your timing window closed and your unspent mana was permanently lost. The concrete outcome is that the opponent's spell resolved successfully and all unused mana vanished from your pool due to the phase ending.

I just activated an ability on my artifact that told me to roll two dice, and I got two fives! But right after rolling, my opponent cast a spell that exiles everything on the battlefield. I have another permanent that says whenever a creature dies, you gain one life. My friend said the life trigger won't work because everything is gone now, but I think it still goes on the stack. Also, does my dice ability even count as doubles if everything vanished before checking? What actually happens?

You successfully rolled doubles because the game defines that outcome as occurring when the result of each of those rolls is equal to the other, checked at the exact moment you roll them regardless of board state changes afterward. The life trigger still works because triggered zone-change abilities operate on a look-back-in-time principle, meaning the game uses the appearance of objects immediately prior to the event to verify the trigger fired rather than scanning the empty battlefield now. For precedence, the dice evaluation happens first during your activation to lock in the matching numbers. Once that resolves and the board wipe hits, the look-back rule applies second to confirm the death trigger remains valid based on what existed right before the wipe resolved. Concrete final outcome: Your two fives count as doubles so the associated effect resolves normally, and you will still gain one life from the creature death trigger because the game checks the prior state to validate it.

I just killed three creatures in a row with a board wipe. One of them has a death trigger that searches my graveyard for that specific creature card and puts it into my hand. My opponent claims they can reshuffle their graveyard right now to mess up which card the ability is looking for. What actually happens?

When those creatures die, each one creates a triggered ability that goes on the stack. As each trigger resolves, it looks for the exact creature card that just moved into your graveyard during that specific event. The rules state that during resolution, these zone-change abilities look for the object in the zone that it moved to, and if the object is unable to be found there, the part of the ability attempting to do something to it will fail completely. However, normal play dictates that each graveyard is kept in a single face-up pile and a player normally cannot change their order at any time. Because the rule requiring a fixed, face-up graveyard structure applies first and locks the physical location of every card without allowing shuffling or reordering, the game state remains unambiguous before resolution occurs. This allows the zone-change trigger to successfully locate that exact creature card right where it landed. You resolve the ability correctly, find the specific creature card in your face-up graveyard, and put it into your hand while the other triggered abilities resolve separately without interference.

I control a commander that has an ability triggering when it dies. My opponent casts a spell targeting my commander that says 'Destroy target creature. If a creature dies this way, return it to its owner's hand.' Since the spell wants to send my commander back to my hand, does the death trigger still happen, or does the commander just go to the command zone and skip dying? Also, another player has a creature with 'Whenever a creature dies, create a 1/1 rat token' that triggers at the same time. Who decides which of these effects goes on the stack first?

Yes, your death trigger still happens. The rule for commanders allows you to put it in the command zone instead of the graveyard or hand when it would go there, but this replacement effect only changes the destination zone; it does not prevent the creature from leaving the battlefield and dying. Triggers that care about a creature dying see the event occur regardless of whether the body ends up in the graveyard or the command zone, so both your trigger and the other player's rat token trigger will fire. Regarding the order, all triggered abilities go on the stack at the same time when the commander dies. The rules state that once an ability has triggered, its controller puts it on the stack as an object next time a player receives priority. For multiple abilities triggering simultaneously, each player places their triggered abilities on the stack in Active Player, Non-Active Player order, and within that turn order, you can put your own multiple triggers in any order you choose. The final outcome is that both your death trigger and the opponent's rat token trigger will resolve, with the order determined by whose turn it is and who controls the triggers; if you are the active player, you place your trigger first on the stack, followed by the opponent's trigger, or vice versa if they are active.

I just cast a spell that reduces target creature's toughness by five, and my opponent retaliates with an ability that makes it deal damage equal to its power to my face. Our table is arguing because the creature showed zero toughness for a split second during resolution, so they think it died instantly. Also, we're debating whether the damage it dealt counts as combat damage since it was already on the battlefield and attacking. What actually happens?

The creature does not die, and the damage is non-combat damage. This outcome relies on two game mechanics working together to determine timing and classification. First, state-based actions pay no attention to what happens during the resolution of a spell or ability; they only check once the entire effect finishes resolving and players receive priority. Even though your creature temporarily dropped to zero toughness in the middle of resolution, it survives because the game does not destroy it until after the sequence completes. Second, any object can deal damage, but combat damage is specifically dealt during the combat damage step as a result of an attack or block. Since your opponent's effect made the creature deal that damage outside of the combat damage step, it is classified as non-combat damage from a spell or ability effect. The state-based action timing rule takes precedence in determining survival because it dictates when lethality is actually checked, while the damage source rule applies immediately afterward to classify how that damage interacts with shields and counters. In the concrete final outcome, your creature remains on the battlefield after resolution finishes, and the damage successfully dealt as non-combat damage hits your face without triggering combat-specific responses.

I'm at two life, my opponent casts a spell that makes me draw three cards and lose three life. I also have five poison counters from earlier. Do I lose the game three separate times before drawing, or do I just die once? Also, does it matter if I check after each card?

State directly that you lose the game exactly once after the spell resolves. Explain that while cards are drawn one at a time, state-based actions like losing life are not checked between draws but only after the entire spell finishes resolving. Clarify that without a replacement effect, going from two life to negative life triggers a single game loss, and poison counters remain unchanged because they function independently of life total or library changes.

I just cast a spell that tells me to draw three cards, but my opponent stopped me saying I should only get one because I already drew a card earlier this turn and I can only ever draw one per turn. Right after that resolves, two of my creatures with exactly one toughness will take damage and die at the exact same time. One of them has an ability that says it triggers when it dies if it has no counters on it. What actually happens with the cards and does that creature trigger?

You will draw zero additional cards from the spell, and neither creature will trigger its ability. When you are instructed to draw multiple cards, cards may only be drawn one at a time as individual card draws, but any replacement effect that limits how many you can draw modifies that instruction before considering any of those individual pulls. Because your per-turn limit was already used, the instruction is partially carried out until it hits zero, leaving you with no more cards to receive. The drawing portion resolves fully on the stack first, which takes precedence over subsequent game state checks. Once the spell finishes resolving, state-based action results in permanents leaving the battlefield at the same time other state-based actions were performed when both creatures reach zero toughness simultaneously. For this simultaneous departure, that permanent last known information is derived from the game state before any of those state-based actions were performed. Since each creature retained a counter right before that checkpoint, their condition fails entirely. The concrete final outcome is you keep your original hand size and neither death trigger activates or resolves.

I just cast Lightning Helix targeting my opponent's legendary commander on the battlefield, and they say because of Commander rules it actually goes to their command zone instead of the graveyard. Does that stop my card from resolving and trigger any death abilities?

The Commander variant establishes that each deck is led by a legendary creature designated as its commander and notes that this format uses all normal game rules with specific additions for that leader. When your spell resolves and attempts to destroy the permanent, replacement effects evaluate the upcoming event first. Since if an event is replaced it never happens and a modified event occurs instead, the replacement effect shifts where the creature will go before the destruction finishes. The Commander variant addition takes precedence in modifying the destination because it intercepts the movement from battlefield to graveyard. The final outcome is that your Lightning Helix fully resolves dealing damage and destroying the creature, but the permanent is redirected straight to the command zone, so no death triggers fire and the opponent can later cast their commander from there with any additional costs.

We are in combat and my opponent declared two attackers with a combined total of twelve damage against my commander that only has ten toughness. I want to know exactly what happens when the next person gets a chance to play spells. Does it die right now, or does it stay until later? Also, my friend said it goes to the graveyard like any other creature. What is the actual result at the table?

Whenever a player would get priority, the game checks for state-based actions and performs them simultaneously. Because your commander took lethal combat damage, the game immediately checks its condition. The commander replacement rule then applies: if it would be put into a graveyard or exile from anywhere, you may choose to put it into the command zone instead. The concrete final outcome is that your commander moves directly to the command zone rather than the graveyard, and any combat damage marked on it is immediately removed as it leaves play.

I just attacked with my two-headed demon and declared two blockers. Its first ability says whenever it becomes blocked it destroys one blocker, and its second ability says whenever it becomes blocked by a creature it draws a card. But I also tapped it earlier this turn to activate an extra damage ability as a special action before combat started. My opponent says the triggers go on the stack together and destroy both blockers at once. What actually happens with those triggers and who gets priority?

When you activated that extra damage ability before combat, you completed a special action, and per the timing rules, you receive priority afterward. This means your opponent had the chance to respond to that activation before attackers were even declared, establishing a clear window for interaction before blockers are assigned. Moving into combat, declaring two blockers is handled differently depending on the exact wording of the triggered abilities. The rule defining what counts as an event states that one happening may be treated as a single event by one ability and as multiple events by another. Specifically, your demon becoming blocked is one single event for its first trigger, but because it was blocked by two distinct creatures, it becomes a separate event for each blocker regarding the second trigger. The priority rule takes precedence chronologically by determining when players may act after the special action finishes, while the event counting rule subsequently dictates how many independent triggers form during that combat phase. Your opponent cannot merge them into one destruction effect. The final outcome is that you draw two cards as two separate instances resolve, destroy exactly one blocker, and your demon survives with the remaining creature still assigned to it.

I just played a creature that says Flip a coin. If you win the flip, at the beginning of your upkeep, you may draw two cards. My opponent used an effect earlier this turn that said to completely ignore all coin flips. During my upkeep, I set it up to put the draw trigger on the stack since optional effects always wait until resolution anyway. But they argued nothing happens because the flip was ignored. What is the actual game outcome?

The actual outcome is that you will not draw any cards and no ability ever enters the stack during your upkeep. Even though optional triggered abilities normally go on the stack when they trigger regardless of whether you intend to exercise the option later, a coin flip that is instructed to be ignored is treated as if it never happened at all. Because the game treats the roll as nonexistent, the condition required for your creature ability to trigger never occurs. Since the triggering event was wiped from existence first, the ability never activates in step one, which means there is nothing left to place on the stack or make optional later. The final result is that your upkeep phase proceeds normally with zero triggers and no cards drawn.

We're playing a team format with shared turns. I just cast an instant spell that produces some mana as part of its effect, and my teammate is excited to use that mana right away. An enemy player suddenly yells out that they can counter the spell because it is technically their turn in the initiative rotation to respond. My teammate argues that since we are teammates, we get to act together now. Who is right about who can respond, and what happens next?

The enemy player is incorrect regarding individual initiative turns. In this multiplayer game using the shared team turns option, teams rather than individual players have priority, which means the opposing team must act as a single unit when deciding to respond; they cannot rely on individual player turn order or initiative rotations to determine who gets a chance to act. The opposing team decides together which of their players will cast the counter or take other actions. As for your spell, a spell that produces mana is still a spell and goes on the stack while resolving. According to the rules, a spell or ability that produces mana instructs a player to add that mana, and if mana is produced by a spell, the source of that mana is that spell. The interaction order is that you cast the spell, which creates a response window where the opposing team has priority as a group under the shared team turns mechanic. The final outcome is that the opposing team collectively chooses whether to respond with the counter. If they do not choose to respond, your spell resolves, the source of the mana is identified as your spell, and the game instructs you or your teammate to add that mana to their mana pool for use. If the opposing team does respond and wins priority, the counter may resolve before your spell, potentially preventing the mana production entirely based on how they play the interaction as a team.
