I just cast a spell that exiles my opponent's creature, but I have another card that says whenever any creature is put into a graveyard from the battlefield, I gain life. My opponent says I don't get life because it was exiled, not destroyed. Who is right?

You are correct that you do not gain life; your opponent is right. When a spell exiles a creature, it moves to a different zone than the graveyard. The rules specify that actions described as removing an object from the game or setting it aside result in exile. Because the creature goes to exile, the event of it being put into the graveyard never happens. Triggered abilities only activate if their specific trigger event actually occurs, and events that are replaced by other outcomes will not trigger anything. Since your card looks for creatures entering the graveyard and the spell replaced that event with exile, the trigger condition is never met.

I’m mid-combat and just declared a single creature as my blocker against an attacker. My opponent then casts an instant that destroys one of my other, non-blocking creatures before damage is dealt. At the end of combat, my blocker has an ability that draws a card if it blocked alone. Does it still count as blocking alone even though my battlefield changed during the phase?

Yes, your blocker still counts as blocking alone. The game determines this strictly based on declarations made in a specific step, meaning a creature blocks alone if it’s the only creature declared as a blocker during the declare blockers step. State-based actions are checked throughout the game and are not controlled by any player, so they automatically move your destroyed creature to the graveyard without affecting combat mechanics you already locked in. The declaration establishes the combat status first, while continuous state-based checks handle automatic battlefield cleanup afterward without overriding what was already declared. Final outcome: Your blocker successfully met the blocking alone condition and will draw a card when its end of combat ability resolves.

I just cast Serum Visions on my turn and have two creatures with whenever you draw a card triggers. My friend thinks the triggers pop up instantly before I even see the cards, but I think they wait until after. What actually happens at the table when this resolves?

First, you follow the drawing rule which states that a player draws a card by putting the top card of their library into their hand, and this action happens immediately as part of the effect of the spell you cast. Once the spell fully resolves and priority is returned to you, the triggered ability rules take precedence for sequencing, noting that once an ability has triggered, its controller puts it on the stack as an object the next time a player would receive priority. This means the drawing happens completely before any triggers are placed into play. The concrete final outcome is that you draw both cards first, then both triggered abilities go onto the stack in an order of your choice, and they will resolve sequentially afterward without you being able to respond to the drawing itself.

I just cast a spell that lets my opponent choose to draw a card or lose, and they have zero cards in their library. They are panicking and saying they just take the loss automatically, but I want to know if they can even make that choice, and if they do end up losing, will their exile trigger actually happen since they never drew?

Even though your opponent has no cards left, the game rules state that if there are no cards in a player’s library and an effect offers that player the choice to draw a card, that player can choose to do so. This means they are allowed to select the draw option despite having nothing to draw, or they may decline it. Since they have the full choice available, they can opt not to draw, which will cause them to lose the game. Regarding your second question, the rules explicitly state that abilities triggering when a player loses the game trigger when a player loses or leaves the game, regardless of the reason, unless leaving results from a draw. The empty library rule is evaluated first to confirm they had the legal option to decline the draw and accept the loss. Once they lose, the loss condition takes precedence in state evaluation and immediately triggers your exile effect. Your ability will go on the stack and resolve normally unless something else interacts with it, so you will not automatically skip that trigger simply because they had an empty library when making their choice.

We have a common misconception in our shared team turns matches. One teammate thinks that because we are on the same team, if one of us controls a card granting permission to cast spells with flexible mana payment, the whole team can use that permission and treat all our mana pools as interchangeable colors when deciding who casts what? Where does the rule actually draw the line between team timing and individual resources?

Remove references to "Rule 118.14" and "Rule 117.6". Rephrase as: "When an effect grants flexible mana payment and casting permission, it applies only to the player who controls that effect, not their teammates. In shared team turns, priority belongs to the team rather than individuals, which consolidates timing for passing and responding, but this does not merge individual mana pools or extend card-specific permissions across the team. Consequently, each player must use their own resources and cannot share another teammate’s casting permission or flexible payment allowance."

I just cast a creature that has an enters-the-battlefield ability granting it protection from destruction, but my opponent's board wipe destroyed it the moment it landed. Why didn't the protection save it?

The ability on your creature is a triggered ability, which means it uses trigger words like when or whenever and goes onto the stack before its effect resolves, creating a delay between the creature entering and the protection becoming active. Replacement effects must exist before the appropriate event occurs and cannot go back in time to change something that has already happened. Because the destruction event happens as the creature enters the battlefield, your triggered ability has not yet resolved to provide the replacement effect at that exact moment. The board wipe resolves first since no valid replacement effect was present to intercept it, and the creature is put into the graveyard without surviving. Your protection failed because the trigger arrives too late to affect a simultaneous destruction event.

I control an artifact that has a 'Once you have played six lands' ability, and at the end of my turn I must 'set aside' this artifact. My opponent claims their card saying 'Whenever an artifact is put into your graveyard from the battlefield...' will trigger because setting it aside counts as destroying or discarding. Is that right?

No, your opponent is mistaken. The outcome depends on how specific old game terms map to current zones and what events actually happen when those zones are used. First, under the current rules, text on older cards that says 'set aside' has been updated in the official card database to mean exile; this means when your artifact's effect resolves, that artifact is exiled, not put into the graveyard. Because the artifact moves directly to exile, the event of it being put into the graveyard never actually occurs. Triggered abilities only trigger if their trigger event matches a game state change, and an event that is prevented or replaced will not cause any triggers to fire. Since the destination is exile rather than graveyard due to the mapping rule, there is no graveyard event for your opponent's ability to see. The final outcome is that the artifact ends up in the exile zone and your opponent's triggered ability does not trigger at all.

During my group’s match using the shared team turns option, my teammate tapped lands and activated an ability before passing priority, then said it was my turn to cast a spell. I wanted to use another untapped land for blue mana to counter an opponent’s instant. Is that allowed, or did we blow our chance?

In this format, the game operates on a simple foundation where mana is the primary resource in the game and players spend mana to pay costs whenever they are allowed to act. Since you are playing under the shared team turns option, teams rather than individual players have priority, meaning your entire side gets one unified window to respond or cast spells before the other side can intervene. Because your team currently holds that window and no opponents have responded yet, you are completely permitted to tap additional untapped lands for blue mana and use it to pay the casting cost of your counter spell. The concrete final outcome is that your counter spell successfully resolves, sending the opposing instant to the graveyard and ending the exchange in your favor. Team priority takes precedence first because it establishes who gets to act at all, and once established, the mana payment rules apply freely to any team member during that same window.

I have a spell with improvise on the stack and my opponent casts an effect that changes all artifacts into lands until end of turn in response. Can I still tap that artifact to pay for the generic mana on my spell?

No, you cannot tap that artifact because it is no longer an artifact when the game calculates its characteristics. Continuous effects are applied in a specific order, and type-changing effects happen early in the sequence of calculations, meaning the object's type is determined before ability checks are evaluated. The opponent's effect changes the permanent to a land during this sequence, so it loses the artifact type required for your spell's ability. Improvise allows you to tap an untapped artifact you control rather than pay generic mana, and since the continuous effects determine the permanent is now a land and not an artifact, it cannot be tapped for improvise. You would need to use other artifacts that remain artifacts or pay the generic mana normally.

I'm attacking with a creature that has double strike, and my opponent blocks me with a creature that has first strike. My attacker has an ability that reads "Whenever this deals combat damage, exile target blocking creature." If the trigger resolves after the first round of damage but before the second, will the blocker still deal damage to my attacker in the second step?

The outcome depends on the timing of the two separate combat damage steps created by double strike and the status of the blocker. The rule regarding first strike and double strike states that if a creature has double strike when the combat damage step begins, it is the only one assigning combat damage in that initial step, and after that step, a second combat damage step occurs where remaining attackers and blockers with neither ability assign damage as well as remaining double strikers. This structure defines two distinct windows for dealing damage. Additionally, the rule about combat damage specifies that each blocking creature deals combat damage equal to its power during a combat damage step. Because your attacker has double strike, it deals damage in the first step, triggering its ability. If that trigger exiles the blocker before the second combat damage step begins, the blocker leaves the battlefield. Since the blocker is no longer on the battlefield, it cannot assign damage in the second step under the rules for combat damage assignment. Your attacker survives the entire combat phase without taking damage from the blocker.

I just cast a spell during combat and my opponent sacrificed their blocking creature right before damage hits, but they also had regeneration set up earlier that turn. We disagreed about what happens when the destruction effect resolves since the creature regenerated instead of dying, and whether I get to act again immediately after they tapped and sacrificed it. Can you break down the ruling?

When your opponent tapped and sacrificed their creature, they took a special action, which means that player receives priority afterward before anyone else can act. Since regeneration is a destruction-replacement effect where the next time the permanent would be destroyed this turn it instead removes all damage marked on it and its controller taps it, the creature avoids going to the graveyard entirely. Even though it regenerates instead of dying, abilities that trigger from damage being dealt still trigger even if the permanent regenerates. The priority rule applies first by dictating the timing window for actions after a special action, while the regeneration replacement takes precedence during resolution to alter how destruction is handled. Your opponent sacrifices normally, passes priority through your spell resolution, and when destruction would occur, the replacement effect applies. The creature stays on the battlefield tapped without dying, and all damage-based triggers from earlier in combat go on the stack as normal.

I’m attacking and my opponent assigns blockers. Right in the middle of their blocker assignment, I try to cast an instant that says it can only be cast after blockers are declared. My opponent says I'm too late because they already put creatures out, but another player at our table claims I can still cast it since we haven't dealt damage yet. The card also says whenever you cast it during combat you get a +1/+1 counter on your attacker. Who is right and what actually resolves?

First you must evaluate the timing window because according to official guidelines a spell that states it may be cast only after blockers are declared refers specifically to the turn based action of declaring blockers and may be cast only before or after that step begins regardless of whether any blockers are actually declared. This means your opponent is correct since the legal casting window closed the moment they began assigning blockers. Next you apply the rule for combined abilities which states that when a static permission is paired with a triggered effect they are combined into one functional paragraph and operate as a single linked unit. Since the foundational timing restriction from the first rule makes the cast illegal, the second part of the linked ability never gets to trigger. Concrete final game outcome: You lose priority for that instant, your attacker remains unchanged, combat proceeds directly to the combat damage step where your attacker deals lethal damage and destroys the blocker, and no counters are created.

I’m in the middle of a game and my commander has this trigger that says it gains +1/+1 every time I commit a crime. On my turn, I have priority and I decide to turn one of my creatures face down using its special action instead of casting a spell or activating an ability. My friend says that counts as a crime since I’m taking an action with priority. What actually happens for the trigger?

Your friend is mixing up taking priority with actually putting things on the stack. When you turn your creature face down, you are taking a special action, which the game defines as actions a player may take when they have priority that don’t use the stack. Because this movement bypasses the stack entirely, it does not meet the criteria for triggering crime effects. The rules clearly state that a player commits a crime as that player casts a spell, activates an ability, or puts a triggered ability on the stack and that spell or ability targets at least one opponent. Since your face-down flip never hits the stack, you do not commit a crime that turn. The determination of whether this is a special action takes precedence over any trigger checks because it defines the nature of the event itself before the game evaluates for triggers. The concrete final outcome is that your commander does not gain +1/+1, no crime counters are added, and the battlefield only reflects your creature turning face down with no other effects occurring.

I'm in a game and I control a creature that has an ability that triggers when it dies, checking if it had any positive counters on it before damage killed it. My opponent casts a spell that deals enough damage to kill three of my creatures at once. At the same time, their spell causes me to draw a card right in the middle of them casting it. When all this resolves, does the ability trigger for my creature, and what will the card I drew actually look like when I finally see it?

The game processes state changes simultaneously before any triggered abilities go on the stack. Because multiple creatures are dying from damage at the exact same time, the rules specify that when a state-based action results in a permanent leaving the battlefield at the same time other state-based actions were performed, that permanent last known information is derived from the game state before any of those state-based actions were performed. This means your creature will be checked with all its counters still on it as they existed just before dying, so if it had a plus counter despite taking damage, its ability will trigger as expected. Regarding the card you drew while the opponent was casting their spell, the rules state that if a spell or ability causes a card to be drawn while another spell is being cast, the drawn card is kept face down until that spell becomes cast. You will not see it during the casting process, and once the opponent finishes casting their spell and it resolves, you will reveal your drawn card normally. State-based actions and last known information calculations take precedence immediately after effects resolve before any triggers are placed on the stack, while the drawing rule simply governs the visibility window until the casting process fully completes. The final outcome is that your creature triggers its death ability based on its pre-death state, and your drawn card remains face down until the opponent completes casting, after which you turn it over and put it into your hand.

I’m attacking with my Golem, and my opponent casts a spell that puts three 2/2 Construct artifacts onto the battlefield attacking me. I tried to tap my Mountain for mana to cast something in response, but they told me I couldn't because those Constructs already entered tapped and attacking. What actually happens here?

The rule governing special actions takes precedence for determining the immediate sequence of play. Special actions are actions a player may take when they have priority that don’t use the stack, which means you cannot tap lands or activate abilities while an effect is actively resolving on the stack. You must wait until priority returns after resolution before taking any actions. Once the spell finishes putting permanents onto the battlefield, the combat entry rule determines their official status. If an effect would put a noncreature permanent onto the battlefield attacking or blocking, the permanent does enter the battlefield but it’s never considered to be an attacking or blocking permanent. The concrete final outcome is that you get priority after the spell resolves to tap your mountain and cast your response, and the three Constructs will enter the battlefield tapped but will strictly not count as attackers and will deal zero damage during combat.

We're playing a multiplayer game where our whole squad takes turns together instead of each person going individually. During my teammate's turn phase, I want to use an old card from my collection that says play a creature from my hand. The opposing team says they can cast instant speed removal before it happens because the wording is old and technically a different action. Who actually gets to act first, and does the word play change anything about how or when we can do this?

First you must determine who has the opportunity to take an action, which means recognizing that in your format teams rather than individual players have priority during your block. This structural rule takes precedence because it establishes exactly whose turn it is and defines the active window for all decisions before any specific card text matters. Once you know your squad controls that window, you resolve the terminology question by applying the standard definition that playing a card means playing that card as a land or casting that card as a spell, whichever is appropriate. Because of this equivalence, your old card functions identically to modern language and does not require a separate timing track. The concrete final outcome is that your squad holds priority during the shared block, you may begin the process using the older card normally, and the opposing team gets their interrupt opportunity only after you have cast it and passed priority back to them, meaning they can successfully respond if they have instant speed removal ready before the creature resolves.

I'm in a Commander game with a double-faced card commander and just attacked with a creature that has an ability saying whenever it deals damage you may redirect that damage to another target of your choice. During combat, before the redirection effect tries to happen, my opponent's blocking creature moved or got removed from play. What actually happens to the damage, and does the color identity rule matter here?

The principle that color identity of a double-faced card includes its back face when determining deck legality means your entire card pool was locked in before match start. During combat, replacement effects that replace damage dealt to one battle, creature, planeswalker, or player with the same damage dealt to another take precedence over standard damage assignment. The governing text specifies that if one of those permanents is no longer on the battlefield when the damage would be redirected, or is no longer a valid permanent type when the damage would be redirected, the effect does nothing. Chronologically and mechanically, the color identity rule applies first during deck construction to verify legality, while during combat resolution replacement effects take precedence to determine if redirection can successfully trigger. The concrete final outcome is that your deck remains legal since the double-faced commander's identity was properly calculated before play began, and because the new target left the battlefield before redirection could apply, the redirect fails completely and deals zero damage.

I’m at one life and my opponent cast two different spells that deal two damage each simultaneously on my turn. We both agree that normally that would make me lose the game multiple times, but I have a card like Lich’s Mirror out. How exactly does this work, and what happens to my hand and graveyard during all this?

You do not lose the game because when multiple state-based actions would have the same result at the same time, a single replacement effect replaces all of them. Your protective permanent triggers once to prevent the game loss from both spells simultaneously, moving your hand and graveyard into your library. Since library and hand are hidden zones even if their cards were previously revealed, the shuffle process keeps every card private regardless of battlefield transparency. This single replacement effect resolves, you draw seven cards, your life total becomes twenty, and the game continues with no further penalties.

I'm playing a deck with a huge dragon that costs {5}{R}{R}. My opponent cast an instant card right after I announced my dragon, and the instant says it reduces the mana cost of target spells by two generic mana. He thinks this means my dragon will only cost three mana total since his spell resolved first. Why is he wrong about the cost?

Your opponent is incorrect because the game locks in costs the moment a spell is cast, and effects cannot reach back to change them after the fact. The rules establish that casting a spell that alters costs won't affect spells and abilities that are already on the stack, which means your dragon's cost was fixed as {5}{R}{R} when you announced it, before your opponent had priority to cast his instant. Although the rules dictate that your opponent's instant goes on top of the stack and resolves first because it was cast in response, this resolution order does not grant the power to retroactively modify a cost that is already determined. The instant resolving first simply means its ability applies before your dragon resolves, but since no cost-altering effect can target a spell on the stack, the instant has no valid effect on your dragon's cost. The final outcome is that your opponent's instant will resolve and do nothing regarding the dragon's cost, then go to the graveyard, and your dragon will resolve and enter the battlefield for its original {5}{R}{R} cost exactly as you paid at the start of casting it.

I just cast a spell that looks at the top two cards of my library and puts them into exile, and it has an ability that says whenever I put a land into exile from anywhere, if I have three or more lands in play, I draw a card. My opponent argues that the trigger wont work because they cant see what was in my library or how many lands I actually control right now. What happens?

The trigger will resolve normally based on actual game state rather than what anyone can see. First, the zone visibility rules apply by establishing that libraries are hidden zones in which not all players can be expected to see the cards faces, while exile is a public zone where all players can see the cards faces. This creates a clear information boundary where your opponent cannot watch exactly what you drew or track its type as it leaves, but that lack of sight does not pause the game state. Next, the triggered ability rule applies by stating that when the trigger event occurs, the ability checks whether the stated condition is true, and if it triggers, it checks the stated condition again as it resolves to ensure it still holds before having any effect. The zone definition sets up private information boundaries first, but the conditional trigger mechanic operates objectively within those boundaries second to determine the result. Your opponent will draw a card if your land count meets the requirement when the ability triggers and again when it resolves, completely unaffected by visibility limitations.

My opponent's commander just hit me for damage over the last few turns. On my turn, I cast something that draws three cards and lets me show one as I pull it from my deck. Can I check what the card is before I decide whether to show it? Also, does taking all that commander damage mess with my drawing or reveal choice?

You are allowed to peek because when an effect gives a player the option to reveal a card as they draw it, that player may look at that card as they draw it before choosing whether to reveal it. Your commander damage does not interrupt this process. Game actions happen first, meaning you will complete the draw and make your reveal choice during your turn. Only after those actions finish does the game check for matching conditions. At that moment, a player who’s been dealt 21 or more combat damage by the same commander over the course of the game loses the game. The concrete outcome is that you see your cards, decide not to show them if you prefer, but then immediately lose the match due to the commander damage limit. The drawing and reveal rule executes first during the action phase, while the loss condition triggers afterward as a state-based check.

I am playing Commander and my opponent's commander card started face up in their command zone at the beginning of the match. During combat it attacked me for 15 damage but then got exiled by a board wipe. Today it comes back and attacks again for 10. Does that count as 22 and make me lose, or does exiling it reset the tracker?

The tracking does not reset because of how your game was initialized and how ongoing state checks work. At the start of play, the rules require that each player puts their commander from their deck face up into the command zone to establish the game identity for that card. That setup procedure permanently ties the damage record to the exact object you placed there. The continuous loss condition explicitly states that in a Commander game, a player who has been dealt 21 or more combat damage by the same commander over the course of the game loses the game, which means the tracker follows that specific card regardless of whether it sits on the battlefield, in exile, or back on top of the command zone. State-based action checks happen first at any pause in priority, locking in your accumulated damage before replacement options or new casting can interfere. The concrete final outcome is that you have 25 tracked damage against that commander, so you lose the game immediately once those state-based actions are checked after combat ends.

My opponent cast a board wipe that destroys all creatures, and I have a commander with a death trigger along with another creature that also has a death trigger. They argued that the triggers shouldn't happen because everything died at the exact same time. Do both triggers fire, and where exactly do the cards go in my graveyard?

Both triggers will fire normally despite the simultaneous destruction because the game uses a special timing rule for triggered abilities that look back in time to determine if trigger conditions were met by the event involving objects that existed immediately prior to the state change. This means your commander ability will trigger for each creature that died even though they left the battlefield simultaneously, so you will get two separate death triggers on your stack. Regarding where the cards go, the rules dictate that any object that is destroyed is put on top of its owner's graveyard rather than being shuffled randomly or placed in a different zone, which ensures both creatures are accessible and ordered at the very top of your graveyard pile. The concrete outcome is that you have two death triggers resolving and both destroyed creatures reside on top of your graveyard.

I’m playing Commander with three other people at the table. It’s my turn and I tap down my commander for combat, but the opponent sitting across from me says I have to formally pick him as the defender right now before I can target his planeswalker. He also mentioned that if I hit him with enough commander damage he’ll be out of the match immediately after this phase. Is that how it actually works?

Your opponent is completely correct about the timing sequence. During the beginning of the combat step in a multiplayer game, you must take a turn-based action to choose one of your opponents as the defending player unless the specific variant automatically assigns all opponents into that role. You cannot legally attack a planeswalker until that player has been formally selected as your defender for this phase. Once you have made that choice and declared attackers, combat damage resolves normally. Only after damage assignment and resolution does the game check state-based actions. At that exact moment, if your commander has dealt twenty-one or more combat damage to that specific player over the course of the entire game, that player loses the match immediately. The concrete final outcome is that you must declare him as your defender at the very start of combat, the attack sequence proceeds fully as declared, and he is permanently removed from the game right after the combat damage step because the loss condition triggers via state-based checks.

We're playing Commander Free-for-All and I used a dragon that has the ability to attack multiple players. It hit two opponents who both blocked, and my creature died with a +1/+1 counter on it. I have an Undying card in play. Does the dead creature come back? We're arguing because one of us thinks taking damage from multiple people matters for the return.

The outcome depends on how counters are handled when the creature takes damage and dies, which involves both the multiplayer structure of your game and the rules for last known information. In this Commander Free-for-All game, the rules allow your dragon to attack multiple opponents simultaneously, which explains why it can take combat damage from two sources at once. When that damage is dealt, it is marked on the creature and does not create permanent -1/-1 counters that would interact with the +1/+1 counter. The rule for state-based actions states that if a permanent leaves the battlefield at the same time as other state-based actions, its last known information comes from the game state before those actions happen. Because the +1/+1 counter remains on the creature until the moment it dies, the last known information includes that +1/+1 counter. Undying checks for counters in that last known information and will not trigger because there is a +1/+1 counter present. The concrete final outcome is that your dragon stays in the graveyard and does not return.

I just played a modal card that lets me choose between creating tokens or dealing damage to an opponent, and it has an escalate ability that costs two mana more for the second mode. My opponent already has an enchantment that says players can't be dealt red damage. Do I have to pay the extra cost to get the second option, and will the damage still happen?

You must pay the extra two mana immediately, because escalate is a static ability of modal spells that functions while the spell with escalate is on the stack, meaning you pay an additional cost for each mode you choose beyond the first as you cast the spell. The damage prevention enchantment is a continuous effect affecting players rather than objects, so it does not interfere with your casting or cost payment; instead, all such effects are applied in timestamp order after the determination of objects characteristics when the spell resolves. You must pay the escalate cost to unlock both options, but because the continuous effect is already active, the second mode will fail to deal its red damage while the token creation portion of the spell still resolves successfully.

I’m in a match and my opponent has an instant ready to tap my creature so it can’t block. I have an equipment attached to it. Can I just click the creature to make it tapped before they cast their spell, or do I have to wait for them to go? Does the equipment change anything about this?

You get to act whenever you have priority, and tapping a creature you control is a special action that happens when a player has priority and does not use the stack. Because it bypasses the stack entirely, your opponent cannot respond with an instant spell once you tap it. The equipment on the creature simply makes it a modified permanent because a permanent is modified if it has one or more counters on it, if it is equipped, or if it is enchanted by an Aura that is controlled by that permanent’s controller. This modified status is just a static game state definition and does not create any timing restrictions or interfere with how special actions resolve. The rule governing special actions takes immediate precedence in resolving timing, as it dictates when the tap happens and blocks all stack responses, while the rule defining modified permanents simply establishes a continuous game state that does not interfere with that resolution. You successfully tap the creature first, and since it is already tapped, the opponent's instant spell targeting it to make it tapped will resolve with no visible effect.

I'm casting Inscription of Abundance and really want to kick it so I can choose any number of modes, but my opponent keeps saying they can interrupt me while I'm deciding whether to pay the extra mana, claiming I have to pick a mode before committing to the kicker. Are they right that I must lock in a mode choice without knowing if I'll kick?

The rules allow you to make decisions during spell announcement in any order that makes logical sense, meaning you can consider choices like kicking alongside mode selection even if one technically happens later in the process. You do not have to pick a mode first; you can decide to pay the kicker cost and select any number of modes simultaneously. Regarding priority, the rules state that the active player receives priority after casting a spell, which includes the completion of all announcements for modes and costs. If your opponent has not already used priority to cast an instant before you started announcing this spell, they cannot interrupt your decision-making. The concrete outcome is that you announce the kicker and your mode choices all at once, paying the full mana cost, and only after this announcement is complete does priority pass, allowing your opponent to respond to the fully formed spell.

I just cast a board wipe that deals damage to all creatures and my opponent sacrificed one at the same time. Three of my creatures died together, each triggering a draw effect. My opponent says they can rearrange the stack so their triggers resolve after mine, but I thought you couldn't change order mid-stack. What actually happens?

When the game reaches that moment, it first checks for state-based conditions and performs all applicable state-based actions simultaneously as a single event, which causes all damaged and sacrificed creatures to die at once. This simultaneous movement to the graveyard triggers the death abilities for every creature at exactly the same time, and those waiting triggered abilities are then put onto the stack before any player gets priority. Once placed, the sequence is fixed because the order of objects on the stack can’t be changed except when effects or rules allow it. The precedence here is clear: the simultaneous state-based check happens first to determine what enters the graveyard and triggers, and once those abilities hit the stack, zone-ordering rules lock them in place for resolution. The concrete final outcome is that all three death triggers enter the stack at once, neither player can shuffle or reorder them, your opponent can only respond by casting instant spells on top of the stack, and everything resolves strictly bottom-up in the exact order they were placed.

I have a Commander deck with a double-faced card as my commander. During the game, it flips to its back face, which is a different color. I'm worried now that my deck is illegal because my commander has changed colors, or maybe I can't play certain cards anymore? Also, when it flipped, I had some damage on it. Does the flip change how that damage works? What happens?

The game state resolves normally with no deck penalty and standard combat rules apply. According to the color identity regulations, a commander's allowed colors are fixed before the match starts and include all colors from both faces of double-faced cards, meaning flipping your commander mid-game never alters its legality or restricts the cards you built into your list. Since this identity is locked in during deck construction, the change on the battlefield has zero impact on whether your deck is valid or what spells you can cast. Meanwhile, combat and damage resolution follow automatic state checks that occur whenever relevant thresholds are reached, operating outside the stack and independent of color attributes. These immediate game actions determine if a permanent is put into a graveyard based on its current characteristics like toughness and damage marked. The definitive outcome is that your deck stays legal forever once constructed, and if your commander had lethal damage when it flipped or anytime afterward, the game automatically moves it to its owner's graveyard as a state-based action before anyone could take further steps.

I just got poisoned for lethal damage and my life hit zero. I have a card with an ability that triggers when you lose the game and puts cards back into my graveyard in a specific order. My opponent is tapping the table yelling that they can now shuffle my graveyard however they want because I lost, and they think my ability doesn't trigger anymore because I'm gone. What actually happens here?

Your opponent cannot shuffle or change the order of your graveyard. The rules state that each graveyard is kept in a single face-up pile and a player can examine the cards at any time but normally cannot change their order. Your opponent's claim about shuffling is false; they can look through it, but the order remains fixed. Regarding your ability, it does trigger. The rules specify that triggered abilities trigger specifically when a player loses the game or leaves the game regardless of the reason, unless the loss results from a draw. Since you are taking lethal damage and losing, your ability triggers and goes onto the stack even though you are about to leave the game. The concrete outcome is that your ability will resolve and put the cards into your graveyard in the specified order before the game ends or your cards move, and your opponent can only look at your current graveyard pile without changing its sequence.
I have one card left in my library and three life. My opponent casts a spell that forces me to draw two cards. What happens when that spell resolves?

You will successfully draw exactly one card and then immediately lose the game, meaning the second draw instruction never completes and you cannot take any further actions. The resolution begins with you performing the drawing action defined by the rules as putting the top card of your library into your hand, which happens for the first card without issue. However, once that card leaves your library, it becomes empty while the spell still requires you to draw a second time. At this point the game does not wait for players to respond or pass priority; instead it checks for automatic conditions known as state-based actions which happen instantly and do not use the stack. Because you are forced to draw from an empty library, this specific game state is detected by a state-based action rather than allowing the spell to simply fail quietly. This automatic check takes precedence and results in your loss immediately after the first card moves to your hand, so the concrete outcome is that one card enters your hand and you lose the game before any further resolution occurs.

I just sacrificed my commander to a legend rule death trigger that says you may draw a card. My opponent and I got into an argument about whether I can tap creatures or take other immediate actions before that draw actually happens, or if I have to wait until the whole thing resolves. What is the correct ruling?

The correct sequence depends on how stack placement and immediate actions interact. First, because the trigger contains may, it follows the rule that some triggered abilities effects are optional and these abilities go on the stack when they trigger, regardless of whether their controller intends to exercise the ability option or not. This places the draw option in a waiting queue while priority passes. Meanwhile, special actions are actions a player may take when they have priority that don't use the stack. Because special actions bypass the stack entirely, they take immediate precedence over waiting for a triggered ability to resolve. You will place the draw trigger onto the stack, then immediately take any special actions you want since those resolve right away without interrupting the trigger. When priority returns to the draw ability on the stack and it finally resolves, you will evaluate your options and decide whether to actually draw a card at that moment. The final result is that all special actions happen instantly before the optional trigger ever evaluates, and you make your draw decision only when the stack clears.

I have a creature that attacked this turn and has a boast ability that deals damage equal to the number of artifacts I control, but I don't control any artifacts so it would deal zero damage. Can I still activate the boast? If I do, does anything happen with things like abilities that trigger when a source deals damage?

You can activate the boast even though it results in zero damage. The rule for boasting allows you to activate that ability one time each turn if your creature attacked this turn, and there is no restriction that prevents activation based on the damage amount being zero. When the ability resolves, the game calculates the damage, which comes out to zero. A core rule states that if a source would deal 0 damage, it does not deal damage at all. This means your ability resolves successfully and your creature has boasted for the turn, but no damage is actually dealt. Since no damage is dealt, any abilities that trigger on a source dealing damage will not trigger. The concrete outcome is that you pay the cost, the boast resolves, nothing deals damage, and no triggered abilities go on the stack.

I just had my opponent block three of my attackers with a single blocking creature, and all four creatures ended up dealing combat damage to each other at the exact same time. Do the death triggers and damage triggers go on the stack one by one so we can respond, or do they all just pile up together? And when exactly can I cast an instant to stop it?

When combat damage is dealt and causes creatures to reach zero toughness while simultaneously dealing damage, the game does not give you priority immediately. The rules state that whenever a player would get priority, the game checks for any listed conditions for state-based actions, then performs all applicable state-based actions simultaneously as a single event. If any state-based actions are performed as a result of a check, the check is repeated until none are needed. Only after that loop finishes are all waiting triggered abilities put on the stack, and specifically, any abilities that triggered on damage being dealt or while state-based actions are performed afterward are put onto the stack before the active player gets priority. The rules also note that the order in which they triggered doesn't matter. Because state-based action checks take precedence and must complete first, the triggers are batched together rather than handling one at a time. The concrete final outcome is that all death triggers and combat damage triggers pile onto the stack simultaneously in any order you choose, you do not get to respond between individual triggers, and both players receive a single shared window to cast instants only after the entire group of triggers has been placed on the stack.

I just cast a spell that instructs me to sacrifice any number of creatures I control, and it says when I do, each sacrificed creature deals damage to its controller equal to its power. My opponent keeps saying each sacrifice should be tracked separately in my graveyard so we can reference them later, but I wanted to shuffle them together. Does the game track them as separate triggers, and can I just arrange the sacrificed creatures however I want in the graveyard to set up a future effect?

First, the game treats this as a reflexive triggered ability because the spell instructs you to take an action and creates a trigger for when you do that action. The rules clearly state that these reflexive triggers are checked immediately after being created and trigger based on whether the event occurred during the resolution, meaning sacrificing multiple creatures will create exactly one damage trigger for each creature sacrificed. Second, regarding zone arrangement, the rules explicitly state that the order of objects in a graveyard cannot be changed except when effects or rules allow it. Because your spell does not grant permission to rearrange cards, they simply stack in the exact order you sacrificed them. In terms of precedence, the reflexive trigger creation rule applies first during resolution to determine how many triggers enter the game, and then the zone ordering rule immediately locks the physical placement of the cards with no rearrangement allowed. The concrete final outcome is that you will have a separate damage trigger on the stack for each creature sacrificed, and those creatures will remain in your graveyard in a strict fixed order with no ability to shuffle or manipulate them for future effects.

I have a land that taps for {C} and I want to cast a spell with cost {X}{R}. My opponent says I can't use the {C} from my land to help pay for X because it's colorless mana. Is he right, or can I actually set X equal to the mana I generate and pay the whole cost?

Your opponent is incorrect and you can proceed with this plan. The casting process requires you to first announce the value for X when you put the spell on the stack, after which the total cost is determined and locked in before any payments are made. Once costs are locked, you activate abilities to generate mana and then pay. Regarding the type of mana, if an effect adds generic mana or {C}, that amount becomes colorless mana added to your mana pool. Colorless mana can be used to pay for generic symbols like X in the locked cost. You announce X based on your available resources, generate three {C} which converts to three colorless mana, and then pay the total cost using that colorless mana for the generic portion and separate red mana for the {R}, resulting in a valid cast.

We're in a game and I have this enchantment that reads 'You may reveal cards from your library while casting your first spell each turn. Whenever you cast a spell this way, copy it and you may choose new targets.' I just cast a sorcery, revealed the top card, and then my opponent stopped me and said the copy trigger won't happen because the card I'm revealing is still in the library which is a hidden zone so I shouldn't be allowed to see it. He thinks the trigger can't fire if the information isn't legally available. What actually happens?

Your opponent is incorrect about the outcome. The game rule for public and hidden zones establishes that your library is a hidden zone where you are not expected to see card faces, but this does not prevent an effect from revealing cards. When a card explicitly instructs you to reveal, that action takes precedence over the general hidden status, moving the card's information to a visible state for that moment. The text structure of your enchantment combines a static ability with a triggered ability that is linked to it, which allows the trigger to look back at the specific action defined by the static part. The linked text means the trigger checks whether you revealed a card using the permission granted by the static instruction. Since you performed the reveal, you legally viewed the card face and created the game event of revealing. The concrete outcome is that the triggered ability sees that you revealed a card this way and resolves, creating a copy of your sorcery. You are allowed to see what you revealed, so your opponent cannot block the trigger based on hidden zone restrictions.

I attacked with a dethrone creature targeting the player tied for the highest life total. Right after declaring attackers, I took damage from an opposing card that dropped my life to one. My friend claims the game instantly checks for automatic conditions right then and cancels my dethrone trigger because life totals changed. How do these mechanics actually interact here, and what happens?

Dethrone is a triggered ability that activates the exact moment a creature is declared as an attacker, meaning the life totals are locked in at that second. The official wording states that dethrone means whenever this creature attacks the player with the most life or tied for most life, put a +1/+1 counter on this creature. This check happens immediately upon declaration and places the effect on the stack. Automatic checks for game conditions are state-based actions that happen automatically whenever certain conditions are met, but they explicitly do not use the stack and are only checked when players pass priority or steps conclude, never instantly during an action sequence. The triggered ability applies first because it resolves as part of the declare attackers step process, while the automatic state-based checks wait for the next priority window. Even though the life total changed afterward or a state-based check eventually runs, the dethrone trigger already exists on the stack and is completely unaffected. Your creature will successfully receive a +1/+1 counter when the trigger resolves.

I just attacked with a creature that says whenever it leaves the battlefield, you draw a card. My opponent responded by casting a spell that exiled it from the battlefield instead of letting it die or be destroyed. When does my trigger actually happen, and will I still draw the card even though the creature is now in exile?

Your trigger still resolves and you will draw the card. Here is how the mechanics interact: First, the ability goes on the stack because once an ability has triggered, its controller puts it on the stack as an object that remains there until it is countered, it resolves, a rule causes it to be removed from the stack, or an effect moves it elsewhere. This establishes precedence, as the trigger locks in before any zone changes occur. Next, the exile effect applies. To exile an object is to put it into the exile zone from whatever zone it is currently in, which immediately relocates your creature away from the battlefield. Because the triggered ability was already placed on the stack during the initial trigger check, it continues to exist independently of the creature moving to exile. The final outcome is that you will draw one card, and the creature permanently remains in the exile zone.

I have a creature with an ability that says At the beginning of combat, you may draw a card. My opponent just cast something that skips my next combat phase. I figured since we are skipping combat, I can just ignore this trigger and not even think about drawing cards. Is that right?

Your reasoning is slightly off because of how skip effects interact with triggered abilities in sequence. The game rules state that anything scheduled for a skipped step, phase, or turn will not happen, and a skip effect functions as a replacement that does nothing instead of performing the action. Because the combat phase is replaced by a do-nothing event, the beginning of combat never actually arrives, meaning the ability never triggers. This directly overrides any thoughts about whether you want to use its optional effect later. The rule for optional triggered abilities explains that they go on the stack when they trigger, regardless of whether their controller intends to exercise the ability’s option or not, but that timing rule only activates once the triggering event occurs. Since the skip replacement effect takes precedence by preventing the step from starting, the ability never triggers, so nothing goes on the stack and you simply skip drawing cards. The concrete final outcome is that you draw zero cards, the creature enters combat without gaining any additional benefits, and your opponent's attack proceeds normally without interruption.

I cast a creature card that says When this creature enters the battlefield, draw a card, but my opponent countered the spell right before it resolved. Does the ability still trigger and put me on top of my library to draw?

No, the ability does not trigger and you do not draw a card. The ruling starts with determining the destination of the countered spell. The rule for the graveyard states that any object that's countered is put on top of its owner's graveyard, so the creature card moves directly from the stack to the graveyard without ever entering the battlefield. This establishes the game state change where the object is now in the graveyard. Next, you evaluate if a triggered ability activates. The rules for triggered abilities explain that an ability has a trigger condition and an effect and is written as When or Whenever followed by the specific event. Because the creature card was placed in the graveyard per the first rule without entering the battlefield, the When this creature enters condition never occurred. The destination rule places the object, but the absence of the entry event means the triggered ability requirement is not met, resulting in no trigger and no card draw.

I just cast a creature spell that has a continuous buff like +2/+2 and also says Whenever you cast this spell, scry 1. My opponent used an effect to remove all static abilities from target permanent spell on the stack. When it resolves, do I still get to scry 1 even though the buff is gone, or does removing the static part break the connection to the trigger?

You do still get to scry 1. Triggered abilities like "Whenever you cast this spell" go on the stack independently of the spell itself and resolve based on priority, completely separate from any continuous effects or static abilities modifying the creature. Removing static abilities from the spell on the stack only alters how that object will exist once it moves to the battlefield; it does not erase or prevent already-triggered abilities from resolving. The cast trigger has already happened and is waiting on the stack, so removing the static buff has no impact on its resolution.

We are in a tight game and I just cast an instant that says you may draw two cards. My opponent has zero cards left in their library, and they control a creature whose toughness is exactly equal to the number of cards in their hand. They also currently have one card in hand. During my resolution phase I watched them discard down to zero because of a side effect of my spell, and now their creature looks like it should crumble. They are trying to decide whether to draw from that empty library while their beast has zero toughness mid-resolution. Can they actually make that choice, and will the creature survive until after my spell finishes?

Yes, your opponent can absolutely choose to draw those two cards even though their library is empty, and yes the creature will safely survive the whole resolution. When determining the outcome, two key principles apply in sequence. First, state-based actions pay no attention to what happens during the resolution of a spell or ability and only check the game state after everything finishes settling, so a temporary drop to zero toughness during the middle of your spell will not cause the creature to be put into the graveyard mid-resolution. Second, regarding the library draw, if there are no cards in a player’s library and an effect offers that player the choice to draw a card, that player can choose to do so unless an effect explicitly says they cannot draw cards. Since nothing is stopping them from drawing and the rules allow choices even with an empty library, they get to make the decision and draw what happens, then the game checks again afterward. The concrete final outcome is that the creature remains on the battlefield throughout the resolution, your opponent successfully chooses to draw the cards, and the spell resolves completely without dying prematurely.

I just attacked with a creature that already had three damage marked on it from blocking earlier, and my opponent blocked it with a two-power creature. My attacker also has three power. We argued about whether my attacker deals its combat damage or if it's too damaged to fight back. Also, do I still get triggers for dealing the damage?

Your creature deals combat damage regardless of the damage already marked on it. During the combat damage step, attacking and blocking creatures deal damage simultaneously equal to their power, so your attacker successfully deals three combat damage to the two-power blocker. State-based actions are automatic game actions that check for conditions like lethal damage only after damage is dealt and do not interrupt the damage event. The concrete final outcome is that both creatures receive lethal damage and are put into their owners' graveyards simultaneously. Any triggered abilities from dealing combat damage or dying are placed on the stack afterward and resolve normally.

I just attacked with a black creature that has intimidate and my opponent blocked it with a black artifact creature. He then cast Awe Strike targeting my attacker to prevent the next 5 damage. My attacker is a 4/4. What actually happens to combat and the prevention effect?

The block is legal because artifact creatures and creatures sharing a color can block intimidated attackers. During the combat damage step, all combat damage is dealt simultaneously. The prevention effect applies as damage would be dealt, stopping the attacker's damage from being marked and granting you life equal to what was stopped. Since your attacker only deals 4 damage, the effect prevents exactly 4, giving you 4 life. The blocker remains in play and deals its full combat damage to your attacker during that same simultaneous step.

I am in a four-player game where my opponent wants to sacrifice a permanent as part of a combo to trigger an effect, but they claim they can just remove it from the battlefield without paying costs because multiplayer formats allow flexible resource management. Meanwhile another player at the table says that since the action skips the stack it happens automatically. What actually resolves?

Remove all references to specific rule numbers and rephrase the explanation conversationally. Clarify that multiplayer tournament guidelines only add external paperwork rules like deck construction and cannot override core game actions or allow bypassing costs. Explain that actions taking priority without using the stack are special actions, but sacrifices are typically paid as costs for abilities or effects that use the stack. Conclude that unless a card explicitly changes these rules, the sacrifice must be paid according to standard cost requirements and will use the stack if it is an activated ability.

I just attacked with my opponent's commander and took twenty-one points of damage from it during combat. Even though the attack phase is still going on and I thought I had time to tap my lands for mana or cast a removal spell, I lost the game right away. Why did I lose immediately instead of getting a chance to respond after taking the damage?

Combat damage is dealt simultaneously, and state-based actions are checked immediately after damage finishes because no player receives priority during combat damage resolution. The rule for commander damage states that if a player has been dealt twenty-one or more combat damage by the same commander over the course of the game, that player loses as a state-based action. Since this check happens instantly upon the damage being dealt, you lose before priority is ever passed. Special actions and casting spells require priority, which you do not receive until after state-based checks complete. The concrete outcome is that you take twenty-one damage, the game detects the loss condition, and you lose the game immediately with no opportunity to tap lands, cast spells, or take special actions.

I just sacrificed my enchantment to pay a cost, and it had a continuous boost on our main creature. The creature drops to its base stats instantly. Does the game remember the boosted numbers for anything, like triggers or combat math? Also, we have another static effect on the battlefield that was put down after mine, and now they are the only ones left. How do we figure out the final state?

Replace the fabricated 2/3 stats with a placeholder like its original power and toughness. Clarify that the game does not remember previous boosted numbers; triggers and combat math always use the creature current up to date characteristics on the battlefield. Explain that because static abilities cannot use last known information, removing the enchantment immediately strips its modifier. Then apply the remaining effects using timestamp order, noting that effects modifying actual game rules resolve after all other continuous effects, leaving the newer static effect as the only active modifier determining the creature final stats.

I attacked with a creature that has undying and put a counter on it when it entered. My opponent cast an effect that gave all creatures negative power and toughness before combat damage. Both my attacker and their blocker ended up with zero or less toughness at the same time. Does undying trigger, and does a card ability that says whenever this creature dies, if it attacked alone this turn see my creature as having attacked alone?

First, you need to understand the order of events in a turn. The combat declaration phase happens early, while the check for dying and returning creatures happens much later after state-based actions process. A creature attacks alone if its the only creature declared as an attacker during the declare attackers step. That status is locked in immediately when blockers are assigned, long before damage or replacement effects resolve. When your opponent's effect puts creatures at zero toughness, they die simultaneously from state-based actions. If a state-based action results in a permanent leaving the battlefield at the same time other state-based actions were performed, that permanent's last known information is derived from the game state before any of those state-based actions were performed. Because the game uses that preserved information to evaluate death triggers, it sees your creature with the counter still on it and as having attacked alone. The final outcome is that undying does not trigger because the counter existed in last known information, but the death ability correctly recognizes the unopposed attack condition, goes on the stack, and resolves normally in a later phase.

I am playing at 2 life and my opponent taps their mana to activate an ability that says it deals 3 damage to me. At the exact same time, they control a creature with a triggered ability that says whenever you lose the game, draw a card. What actually happens here and in what order?

State-based actions are game actions that happen automatically whenever certain conditions are met and they do not use the stack. Because your life total drops to zero or less, the game instantly performs these automatic checks and moves you to the losing state. Once that happens, the second rule applies. Some triggered abilities trigger specifically when a player loses the game. These abilities trigger when a player loses or leaves the game regardless of the reason. The concrete final outcome is that you lose the game immediately, after which your opponent's creature ability is placed onto the stack and resolves normally. Automatic checks take precedence and resolve first, followed by the trigger.

We are in the middle of a game and I activate a creature that says it adds one mana of a color among permanents I control. Right now I only have a basic land out. As soon as I tap it, my opponent plays an instant that makes everything cost one extra mana. Does the activation still go on the stack and what actually happens when it resolves?

The activation goes onto the stack with its original tapping cost intact. When determining the order of operations, the cost alteration rule takes precedence at the moment of declaration because casting a spell that alters costs will not affect spells and abilities that are already on the stack. Your opponent's instant resolves after your activation is already sitting there, so the cost increase never applies to it. At resolution, the undefined mana rule takes over since you control no colored permanents. If an ability would produce one or more mana of an undefined type, it produces no mana instead. The concrete final outcome is that the activation resolves successfully without being cost-increased, but it generates exactly zero mana.

I'm attacking with a 4/4 Gorgon, and my opponent blocks with a 2/2 Soldier. Their player says they're casting Flash Hulk to dodge, but I already declared the blocker. Does the damage still go through, or does the flash in time stop it? Also, if my gorgon takes 2 damage and is going to die, can they still respond before my gorgon goes to the graveyard?

Your opponent cannot cast Flash Hulk and you both have no timing windows to respond. All combat damage that has been assigned is dealt simultaneously, and this turn-based action doesn’t use the stack. No player has the chance to cast spells or activate abilities between the time combat damage is assigned and the time it’s dealt. This combat damage rule applies first, meaning the damage phase completes without handing control to either player. Immediately after the damage finishes dealing, state-based actions are checked throughout the game and are not controlled by any player. Because these checks happen right away, any creature with lethal damage is put into the graveyard at that exact moment. The concrete final outcome is that both the Soldier and your Gorgon take their assigned damage at the same time, both die before priority is returned to players, the Flash Hulk spell fizzles as the combat phase ends, and you simply proceed to the cleanup step with nothing having happened in response to the damage.

I'm in a two-player team format where my whole team shares a turn. My teammate is trying to cast Rolling Thunder from our hand while our opponents control a card that says opponents can't cast spells with even mana values. They're arguing that the spell can just be cast normally, but I think they have to pick the X value first. Also, since it's my team's turn, can my other teammate suddenly cast a sorcery while my teammate is figuring out this spell?

Team priority must be established first, as the rules state that in a shared team turns format teams rather than individual players have priority. This means your other teammate is completely locked out and cannot cast any spells until both you and the active player pass priority together. Once priority is assigned to your team, the casting proposal rule applies: a player can begin to cast a spell only if no effect prohibits it, and players may consider choices made during proposal that may cause those qualities to change. Because their opponent restricts spells with even mana values, your teammate can choose X to be one during proposal to make the total mana value odd, which legally permits the cast. The concrete outcome is that your teammate successfully casts Rolling Thunder by setting X to one, and your other teammate must wait until the opposing team passes priority as a group before taking any action.

I just tapped a Mountain and played an Island, then cast Lightning Strike for four mana because my opponent said the extra two was cheaper than my actual spell cost. They told me they could force me to not pay the extra before it resolves. What actually happens?

Your opponent cannot interfere with your payment choice once you have begun casting. The rules state that any number of additional costs may be applied to a spell as it is being cast, and the controller must announce their intentions to pay them at the same time they pay the mana cost. Because this announcement and payment step happens entirely before the spell reaches the battlefield stack, your opponent only receives priority to react after you have already finished paying everything. Cost declaration takes precedence over later responses, so your Lightning Strike successfully pays the extra amount, enters the stack with that modification locked in, and resolves normally regardless of their protests.

My opponent just dealt damage to me and I reached zero life, so I should be losing the game. My deck includes a card that says when you lose the game, put it from your graveyard into your hand and you may cast it, but it also has a line at the bottom saying you can't cast this card unless you control an artifact. I had no artifacts on the battlefield, so am I stuck with this card in my graveyard or does the lose-the-game effect let me ignore that restriction and cast it right away?

When you reached zero life and left the game your triggered ability fired because it triggers whenever a player loses or leaves the game regardless of the reason which means your card moved to your hand and gave you permission to cast from that zone however the restriction is a static ability that limits casting in any zone you could cast the card from so when you attempt to cast it from your hand the requirement to control an artifact still blocks you and since you do not meet that condition you cannot cast the spell and it remains in your hand
What happens if I exile a card that has two different sides, like a transforming creature, but it ends up face down?

When a card with two sides is exiled face down, it remains hidden. Because a double-faced card that is exiled face down remains hidden, you must use a face-down substitute card and/or opaque sleeves to represent it. For example, if an opponent exiles your transforming creature face down, you would place a blank card or a sleeve over it in the exile pile so that its identity stays secret.
We are starting a game with teams of three players instead of two. How much life and how many poison counters should we use?

In a Three-Headed Giant game, your team receives bonuses to both life and poison thresholds. Because for each player a team has beyond the second, the starting life total is increased by 15 and the number of poison counters required for the team to lose is increased by five. For example, if a standard Two-Headed Giant game starts at 60 life and 10 poison, your team of three would start with 75 life and require 15 poison counters to lose.
What happens if my creature attacks your artifact? Can I just deal damage to it to destroy it?

When the attack is declared, no damage will actually be dealt to the artifact. Damage can only be dealt to battles, creatures, planeswalkers, and players. Because an artifact is not one of those types, it cannot receive damage. For example, if you attack with a 3/3 creature against an opponent's Artifact like a Mana Vault, your creature will deal no damage to that Mana Vault because damage can't be dealt to an object that's not a battle, a creature, or a planeswalker.
What happens if my teammate's life total reaches zero during an opponent's turn?

Your entire team loses the game immediately because players win and lose the game only as a team, not as individuals. Since if either player on a team loses the game, the team loses the game, your partner hitting zero triggers that loss for both of you. For example, even if you have 30 life, your team is defeated the moment your teammate's life total becomes zero.
I have a Case card on the table that has an ability starting with 'Solved', but I haven't finished the requirements to solve it yet. Can I still use that ability?

No, you cannot. For an activated ability, the rule specifies that you may activate the ability only if this Case is solved. For example, if you have a Case card that says Solved - Pay 2 mana to draw a card, you must first complete the conditions to solve the case before you are allowed to pay the mana and draw the card.
What happens to ownership of a scheme card when it is moved from the command zone and played face-up on the battlefield?

The owner becomes the player who currently controls it. Because the controller of a face-up scheme card is its owner, the status changes once the card is no longer in the command zone. For example, if Player A has a scheme card in their command zone and plays it to the battlefield face-up, Player A remains the owner because they are also the controller.
My creature has a level symbol that says Level 2-4 and it currently has 5 level counters on it. Does it still have the power and toughness listed in that section?

No, it does not. For a level range, the power, toughness, and abilities only apply as long as the creature has at least the first number of counters but no more than the second number. For example, if a creature has a Level 2-4 symbol with 3/3 power and toughness, it will only have those stats while it has 2, 3, or 4 level counters on it. Since it has 5 counters, it has exceeded the maximum number in that range, so those specific stats and abilities no longer apply.
I have a card I set aside at the start of the game for my companion ability. Can I just take it and put it in my hand whenever I want?

No, you cannot do this at any time. You can only perform this action once per game, and you must follow specific timing requirements where you have priority, the stack is empty, and it is your main phase. For example, if you set aside a card at the beginning of the match, you must wait for your own turn to come around and ensure no other spells are currently resolving before you pay 3 to get that card into your hand.
What happens when my teammate and I are sharing a turn but I want to cast a spell before they do?

When using shared team turns, priority is held by teams rather than individual players. This means that instead of you acting and then your partner acting separately, the team acts as one unit to manage the stack. For example, if you and your partner are a team, the team must collectively decide when to cast a spell or pass; you cannot claim priority for yourself independently of the team.
Can I play this creature with flash even though it is my opponent's turn and not my main phase?

Yes, you can. Flash means you may play this card any time you could cast an instant. Since instants can be played during your opponent's turn, you can also play a card with flash then. For example, if your opponent casts a spell, you can play a creature with flash to respond to it, or you can play a creature with flash to block an attacker if that creature has haste.
What happens if my card says I can do something that isn't normally allowed?

The card's instruction will occur. First, you identify a conflict between the card and the rules. Then, because whenever a card's text directly contradicts the rules, the card takes precedence, you follow the card. It only overrides the rule that applies to that specific situation. For example, if a card says you can cast a sorcery during your opponent's turn, you follow the card instead of the standard rule about casting timing.
What happens if I move an Aura from one creature to another using a spell?

When you move an Aura, the ability that was modifying the first creature stops applying to it and starts modifying the new one. This is because the static abilities of Auras modify the object they are attached to without targeting them. For example, if you have an Aura like Rancor on a Bird and you move it to a Wolf, the Bird loses its +2/+0 bonus and the Wolf gains that bonus instead.
I am playing a game where a card says to flip a coin, but I do not have any coins with me. Can I use a different item to decide the outcome?

Yes, you can substitute another object or method. The rules acknowledge that casual variants often allow additional items such as specially designated cards or nontraditional Magic cards to resolve effects when standard components are unavailable. For instance, if a spell requires you to flip a coin but you lack one, you could use a marked token or a basic land card flipped face up and face down to represent heads and tails before resolving the effect.
How can I tell if this new card I just played is actually a station?

You can identify it by looking at the card's text box. Station cards have a striated text box that contains one or two station symbols and they usually possess the station keyword ability. For example, if you play a card like Vanguard Depot, check the striated text box for those station symbols to be sure.
