What happens if I have a Saga card on the table when my turn starts?

When you reach your precombat main phase, you put a lore counter on each Saga you control that has one or more chapter abilities. This happens automatically at the start of that phase and does not use the stack. For example, if you control a Saga enchantment like Journey to Eternity, it will automatically receive its next lore counter as soon as your precombat main phase begins.
What happens if my creature with afterlife dies?

When a permanent is put into a graveyard from the battlefield, you create N 1/1 white and black Spirit creature tokens with flying. For example, if your creature with Afterlife 3 is destroyed by a spell, you will trigger the ability and then create three 1/1 white and black Spirit creature tokens with flying.
Can I still use a card to prevent damage if my creature was just hit?

No, you cannot. Prevention effects must exist before the appropriate damage event occurs and they cannot go back in time to change something that has already happened. For example, if a creature deals 2 damage to your creature during combat, playing a spell like Fog after the damage has been dealt will not stop that damage from occurring.
What happens if I attack with an islandwalk creature while my opponent has an Island, but they also have their own islandwalk creature ready to block?

Your creature will be unblockable. When you declare attackers, the game checks the defender's lands to see if the evasion condition is met. A creature with landwalk can't be blocked as long as the defending player controls at least one land with the specified land type. For example, if you attack with an islandwalk creature and your opponent controls an Island, they cannot block that creature even if they have their own islandwalk creature in their way.
What happens if I have two enchantments that say damage dealt by my creatures is doubled, and my 2/2 creature deals damage?

It will deal 8 damage. When an event like dealing damage occurs, each replacement effect gets only one opportunity to affect an event or any modified events that may replace that event. First, the first enchantment replaces the 2 damage with 4 damage. Then, the second enchantment sees that new event of 4 damage and replaces it with 8 damage. For example, if you have two copies of Fiery Emancipation on the battlefield, a 2/2 creature attacking will deal 8 damage instead of just 4.
What happens when my turn starts if I have two rad counters?

At the beginning of your precombat main phase, you will mill a number of cards equal to the number of rad counters you have. For each nonland card milled this way, you lose 1 life and remove one rad counter from yourself. For example, if you have 2 rad counters and you mill a Forest and a creature, you will mill 2 cards total, but you will only lose 1 life and remove 1 rad counter because the Forest is a land.
What happens if we roll the chaos symbol on the planar die?

When you roll that symbol, the chaos ability on the current plane card triggers. According to the rules, this ability triggers if the chaos symbol is rolled on the planar die. For example, if Zendikar is the active plane and someone rolls the chaos symbol, the current planar controller resolves the specific chaos effect listed on the Zendikar card.
What happens if I have to reveal a face-down card for a spell, but an enchantment is currently making all my cards blue?

The card will not be counted as blue for that effect. If a spell or ability needs information about a revealed face-down permanent, it uses the characteristics of that object ignoring any continuous effects that may be applying to it. For example, if you reveal a face-down red card while an enchantment is making all your permanents blue, the spell will see the original red color of the card rather than the blue color from the enchantment.
What happens if an effect says my opponent skips their next turn? Do they still get to do anything during that time?

When a turn is skipped, the game moves directly to the next player's turn. Because skipping a turn means you proceed past it as though it did not exist, the player whose turn was skipped does not get to perform any actions. For example, if a card forces your opponent to skip their next turn, they do not draw a card, they do not untap their permanents, and they cannot cast spells; the game simply moves on to your turn.
If I am attacking in a game with three players, does everyone's damage happen at the same time?

No, the damage is not assigned for everyone simultaneously. Combat damage is assigned in APNAP order, which means the active player assigns their damage first, followed by the non-active players. For example, if it is your turn and you are attacking, you will assign your combat damage to your targets before any of your opponents assign their damage to theirs.
What happens if I roll a 4 on a card that says roll a d6, and the table shows 1-3 is nothing and 4-6 is draw a card?

You will draw a card. After you roll the die, you must use the result to determine which effect listed on the results table happens. Because your roll of 4 falls within the 4-6 range, you apply the effect associated with that result. For example, if a card says roll a d6 and shows a table where 1-3 results in nothing and 4-6 results in drawing a card, rolling a 4 means you immediately draw a card.
Can I use an ability that says I can use it any time I could cast a sorcery if I don't actually have any sorceries in my hand?

Yes, you can. When an ability says you can use it any time you could cast a sorcery, it is only checking if you have priority, if it is your main phase, and if the stack is empty. You do not need to actually have a sorcery in your hand or be able to cast one. For example, if you have an enchantment on the battlefield that prevents you from casting sorcery spells, you can still activate the ability because effects that would preclude you from casting a sorcery spell do not affect your capability to perform that action.
What happens if I use an ability that says deal 2 damage to target artifact?

The artifact will not take any damage. Because damage can only be dealt to battles, creatures, planeswalkers, and players, the game checks the target and determines that since an artifact is not one of those things, it cannot receive damage. For example, if you use a spell that deals 2 damage to a land, the land remains completely unaffected because a land is not a battle, creature, planeswalker, or player.
Can I still use my enchantment after I cast it, or does it go to the graveyard first?

No, it does not go to the graveyard first. When an enchantment spell resolves, its controller puts it onto the battlefield under their control. This means the card moves from the stack directly to the table as a permanent rather than being discarded. For example, if you cast Sphere of Safety, once the spell finishes resolving, it becomes a permanent on the battlefield for you to use.
Can I use a spell that targets all artifacts to destroy my opponent's emblem?

No, you cannot. An emblem has no characteristics other than the abilities defined by the effect that created it, meaning it has no types. Since it does not have the artifact type, it will not be affected by spells that target only artifacts. For example, if you cast a spell like Vandalblast to destroy all artifacts, your opponent's emblem will stay on the battlefield.

If my opponent plays a creature with an ability that says When this enters the battlefield, target player sacrifices a permanent and this ability can't be countered, can I still use a spell like Counterspell to stop it?

No, you cannot. Even though the instruction that it cannot be countered is not technically part of the ability's effect, it stays with the ability while it is on the stack and functions to prevent it from being countered. For example, if a creature enters the battlefield and its ability says target player loses 3 life and this ability cannot be countered, your counterspell will fail because that instruction limits what can happen to the ability while it is waiting to resolve.
I just played a card that says it has split second. Can my friend cast an instant to stop it?

No, they cannot. As long as a spell with split second is on the stack, players can't cast other spells. This means your friend cannot cast an instant like Counterspell to try and negate your play. However, they can still tap their lands for mana because players may activate mana abilities while a spell with split second is on the stack. For example, if you cast a spell with split second, your friend is stuck waiting for it to resolve, but they can still tap their Islands for blue mana.
What happens if I play a creature that says it enters the battlefield with three +1/+1 counters on it?

The creature enters the battlefield already having those counters. This is because effects that read [this permanent] enters with... are replacement effects, meaning the event of the creature entering is replaced by an event where it enters with those counters. For example, if you play a 1/1 creature that enters with three +1/+1 counters, it becomes a 4/4 at the exact moment it arrives on the battlefield.
What happens to the planes I am controlling if I have to leave the game mid-match?

If you leave the game, you first cease to be a planar controller, and then each face-up plane or phenomenon card that you controlled is put on the bottom of its owner's planar deck. For example, if you are controlling the Battle for Zendikar plane and you leave, that plane goes to the bottom of its owner's deck instead of staying on the table.
We just decided who starts, but my hand is still empty. What happens when we finish picking the starter?

Once that decision is made, you must follow a specific sequence where each player sets their life total to 20 and draws a hand of seven cards. For example, if you and your friend flip a coin and you win, you both immediately set your life to 20 and draw seven cards from your decks before the first turn begins.
Can we play an alternating teams game if three of us team up against the fourth person?

No, you cannot. For these games, players must be divided into two or more teams of equal size. In a four-player game, you would need to have two teams of two players each instead of one team of three and one team of one.
I have this card with a symbol that says {3+} and it shows flying and 4/4, but it only has one charge counter on it right now. Is it still a creature?

No, it is not a creature right now. The card only becomes a creature with that power and toughness once it has 3 or more charge counters on it. For example, if you have a station card that says {3+} Flying 4/4 and it currently only has 1 charge counter, it stays as its base type like an artifact or enchantment without any flying or power and toughness until those extra counters are added.
Can I use any two creatures I have on the battlefield to pay for a conspire cost?

No, you cannot. As an additional cost to cast this spell, you may tap two untapped creatures you control that each share a color with it. For example, if you are casting a red spell with conspire, you must tap two untapped red creatures. If you only have one red creature and one blue creature available, you cannot pay the conspire cost for that red spell.
What happens if I want to get rid of a scheme card that is currently affecting the game?

You turn the scheme card face down and put it on the bottom of its owner's scheme deck, but this is only possible if you are playing an Archenemy game and the scheme is currently face-up and ongoing. For example, if an Archenemy player has a face-up scheme in play and wants to stop it, they would flip the card face down and slide it to the bottom of their deck.
What happens if a card tells me to shuffle my whole hand into my library? Does that mean I dont have a hand anymore?

You still have a hand, it just becomes empty. When an effect instructs you to do something to a zone, that action is performed on all cards in that zone, but the zone itself is not affected. For example, if you have two cards in hand and use an ability to shuffle your hand into your library, those two cards move to your library and you are left with a hand containing zero cards.
I have an effect that tells me to blight 2, but I don't have any creatures on the field right now. Can I still use it?

No, you cannot. To blight N means to put N -1/-1 counters on a creature you control. If you are given the choice to blight but are unable to put those -1/-1 counters on a creature you control, typically because you do not control any creatures, you cannot choose to blight. For example, if an opponent plays a spell that requires you to blight 2 and you only have lands on the battlefield, you are unable to perform the action.
I see an enchantment on the table that says it is also a Saga. Does it still count as an enchantment?

Yes, it does. Some enchantments have the subtype Saga, which means they are still enchantments but with a specific subtype. For example, if you play The Kami War, it functions as an enchantment that specifically carries the Saga subtype.
Does a cost reduction from an effect like Heartless Summoning apply before or after I use convoke?

The reduction applies first. Convoke is not an additional or alternative cost and applies only after the total cost of the spell is determined. For example, if you cast Siege Wurm which costs 5 generic and 2 green mana, but Heartless Summoning makes it cost 2 less, your new total cost is 3 generic and 2 green. You then use convoke to tap creatures to pay for that new total cost.
Can I still cast my sorcery if my opponent just played an instant to destroy my creature?

Yes, you can cast your sorcery once the current spell has finished resolving and there are no other spells or abilities left on the stack. You may cast a sorcery from your hand during a main phase of your turn when the stack is empty. For example, if your opponent casts Lightning Bolt to kill your creature, you must wait for that Bolt to resolve and for any subsequent responses to clear before you can cast your sorcery, like Commune with Lava.
What happens if my creature deals way more damage than a planeswalker has loyalty?

If those sources together deal an amount of damage to a planeswalker greater than that planeswalker's loyalty before the damage was dealt, excess damage equal to the difference is dealt to that planeswalker. For example, if you attack with a 5/5 creature against a planeswalker with only 2 loyalty, the planeswalker receives 2 damage to satisfy its loyalty, and the remaining 3 damage is considered excess damage.
Can I include two copies of a card like Sol Ring in my deck if I really need the mana?

No, you cannot. Other than basic lands, each card in a Commander deck must have a different English name. This means you are limited to one copy of any specific card per deck. For example, even if Sol Ring is essential for your strategy, you may only include exactly one copy in your 100-card deck.
I see this card has a plus sign instead of bullets. Can I pick more than one option to do at once?

Yes, you can. The spree ability means you choose one or more modes, and as an additional cost to cast the spell, you pay the costs associated with those modes. For example, if a card costs 2 mana and has two spree modes that each cost 1 mana, you can pick both modes by paying 4 mana total for that single spell.
What happens if I want to flip a coin for a card effect but we don't have a coin at the table?

You can use something else instead of a coin as long as there are two possible outcomes that are equally likely and everyone agrees on it. For example, if a card effect requires a coin flip, you could roll a standard six-sided die and designate that even numbers represent heads and odd numbers represent tails.
What happens to my creature's +1/+1 counters if it gets destroyed and I play it again from my graveyard?

Those counters will not come back with the creature. Counters on an object are not retained if that object moves from one zone to another, meaning they simply cease to exist during the move. For example, if you have a 1/1 creature with two +1/+1 counters that is destroyed, and then you use a spell like Reanimate to bring it back to the battlefield, it will enter as a plain 1/1 without any counters.
What happens if my opponent plays a card that says everyone has to sacrifice a creature?

You do not all pick at the same time. The active player makes their choice first, then the next player in turn order makes their choice, and finally any remaining players make theirs. Once all choices are made, the actions happen simultaneously. For example, if it is your turn and a spell forces everyone to sacrifice a creature, you will pick your creature first, then your opponent will pick theirs, and only after both have chosen will both creatures be sacrificed at once.
What happens if I have two different creatures that both reach zero toughness at the exact same time, do they die one after the other or all at once?

They die all at once. The game performs all applicable state-based actions simultaneously as a single event. For example, if an effect deals 3 damage to two different creatures that only have 2 toughness each, both creatures are moved to the graveyard at the same time rather than one after another.
What happens if I cast a spell that creates a single token while having one effect that doubles the number of tokens and another that exiles any tokens I create?

First, the game identifies the event of creating a token. Because replacement effects apply if an effect would create one or more tokens, and they also apply if another replacement or prevention effect does so, even if the original event being modified wasnt itself an effect, both effects will modify the outcome. The sequence results in two tokens being created, and because the exile effect applies to those tokens as they are being created, they both enter the battlefield exiled. For example, if you cast a spell that creates one 1/1 Soldier while Doubling Season and an exile effect are on the field, you create two Soldiers and both are immediately exiled.
If an opponent plays a card that deals 4 damage to each player in a Two-Headed Giant game, does my team take 4 damage or 8?

Your team takes a total of 8 damage. Damage, loss of life, and gaining life happen to each player individually, but the result is applied to the team's shared life total. For example, if an opponent plays a card that deals 4 damage to each player, both players on that team take 4 damage, which means the opposing team as a whole loses 8 life.
If I play a card that has an ability that triggers at the beginning of the end step, but I play it right as my turn is about to finish, will that ability still trigger this turn?

No, the ability will not trigger during your current end step. If a permanent with an ability that triggers at the beginning of the end step enters the battlefield during the end step, that ability won't trigger until the next turn's end step. For example, if you play an enchantment during your end step that says At the beginning of the end step, draw a card, you will not draw that card this turn; it will only trigger at the next turn's end step.
What happens if I try to use an effect that tells me to assemble a contraption during a regular game?

In a standard game, you generally cannot perform this action because the Assemble keyword is part of the Unstable set. This keyword action puts Contraptions onto the battlefield, but since mechanics from the Unstable set are not included in standard rules, you won't be able to do it unless you are playing with those specific silver-bordered cards. For example, if you are playing a game of Standard and an effect mentions assembling a contraption, that action is not possible because the mechanic is not part of the rules for that format.
I want to play this Forest card, but I don't see any mana symbols on it like my other cards. Do I still have to pay something to put it into play?

No, you do not pay anything to play a land. Some objects have no mana cost, which normally includes all land cards, and having no mana cost represents an unpayable cost. For example, when you play a Mountain, you do not spend any mana from your pool to put it onto the battlefield; you simply play it.
What happens if I turn my face-down creature face up after it has been a copy of my opponent's dragon?

Once you turn the permanent face up, its copiable values become the values it copied from the other permanent. While it was face down, its copiable values were those of the dragon as modified by its face-down status. For example, if your face-down creature was a copy of a 5/5 Dragon, turning it face up results in a permanent with the copiable values of that 5/5 Dragon.
Can I search my library for an Omen card using a spell that specifically looks for Omens?

No, because in every zone except the stack, an omen card has only its normal characteristics. This means while it is sitting in your library, it is treated as a standard card rather than an Omen. For example, if you cast a spell that says search your library for an Omen card, you cannot find that card in your deck because it only has its normal characteristics while it is in the library.
What happens if I have an enchantment that gives me protection from red, but my opponent plays a card that says players can't be targeted by red spells?

First, the game determines the characteristics of all objects on the battlefield, such as creatures and artifacts. After that, continuous effects that affect players are applied in timestamp order. This means the sequence is determined by when each effect was played. For example, if your enchantment was on the field before your opponent's card, your protection is processed based on its earlier timestamp.
Can I turn my face-down creature face up whenever I want?

Yes, you can. Any time you have priority, you may turn a cloaked permanent you control face up. This is a special action that does not use the stack. To do this, you must show all players that the card representing that permanent is a creature card and what its mana cost is, pay that cost, and then turn the permanent face up. For example, if you have a face-down card that was cloaked from a creature with a mana cost of {U}, you would show that it is a creature card, pay one blue mana, and then turn the permanent face up to regain its normal characteristics.
I used two blue mana and two colorless mana to pay for this card. How many counters does it get when it enters the battlefield?

It will enter with two counters because sunburst counts each color of mana spent to cast it. If the object is entering as a creature, ignoring any type-changing effects that would affect it, it enters with a +1/+1 counter for each color of mana spent. Otherwise, it enters with a charge counter for each color of mana spent. For example, if you cast a creature spell costing two blue mana and two colorless mana, it will enter with two +1/+1 counters because two pieces of colored mana were spent.
I just played a card that told me to sacrifice it unless I exile another creature, so I exiled my dragon. What happens to my dragon if this new card gets destroyed?

When your new card leaves the battlefield, you return the exiled card to the battlefield under its owner's control. This is because the champion mechanic includes a linked ability that states when the permanent leaves the battlefield, you return the exiled card to the battlefield. For example, if your new creature is destroyed in combat, your dragon will immediately enter the battlefield again.
Can I still attack my opponent's planeswalker if they are sitting way over on the other side of the room?

No, you cannot. The mechanic at play is that creatures can only attack opponents within their controller's range of influence, as well as planeswalkers controlled by those specific opponents. If the player is not within your range, their planeswalker is unreachable. For example, if an opponent moves to a different area of the room that is outside your range of influence, your creatures cannot attack their planeswalker.
I just found this card that says it is a Plane, can I still put it in my deck?

No, you cannot. A plane is a card type seen only on nontraditional Magic cards and is used only in the Planechase casual variant. For example, if you try to add a Plane card into your Commander deck, it would be an illegal card because that type is restricted to the Planechase format.
Can I still use the prowl cost of a spell if the creature that dealt the damage is destroyed right after combat?

Yes, you can. The rule states that you may pay the prowl cost if a player was dealt combat damage by a source that, at the time it dealt that damage, was under your control and had any of the spell's creature types. Since the requirement only cares about what the creature was and who controlled it at the moment the damage occurred, its current status does not matter. For example, if your 2/2 Goblin deals combat damage and then is destroyed by a spell, you can still pay the prowl cost for a Goblin spell because the source was a Goblin under your control when the damage hit.
What happens if the card that created my emblem is destroyed?

The emblem stays in play because an emblem is a marker used to represent an object that has one or more abilities, but usually no other characteristics. For example, if a player uses a spell to create an emblem that gives all creatures +1/+1, and then the player's commander is destroyed, the emblem remains on the battlefield and continues to provide the bonus.
Do I get to decide where the counters go if I cast a spell that brings a creature into play with three +1/+1 counters, even if my opponent controls it?

No, you do not. If the effect does not specify a player, the object's controller puts those counters on it. For example, if you cast a spell that brings a creature into play with three +1/+1 counters and your opponent controls that creature, your opponent is the one who must place them on it.
What happens when I play an Altar of the Pantheon while I already have two red creatures on the field?

Your total red devotion increases by one. Devotion is calculated as the number of mana symbols of that color among the mana costs of permanents you control, and Altar of the Pantheon specifically increases your devotion to each color. For example, if you control two creatures costing {R} each, your current red devotion is 2, and playing the Altar brings your total red devotion to 3.
What happens if I attack with a creature that has flanking and my opponent blocks it with one of their regular creatures?

The blocking creature gets -1/-1 until the end of the turn. This occurs because flanking is a triggered ability where whenever the creature becomes blocked by a creature without flanking, the blocking creature gets -1/-1 until end of turn. For example, if you attack with a 3/3 creature that has flanking and your opponent blocks it with a 2/2 creature that does not have flanking, that 2/2 will become a 1/1 for the rest of the turn.
What happens if we start playing a whole new game in the middle of this one?

You stop the current game for a while. The main game is temporarily discontinued while the subgame is in progress and it resumes when the subgame ends. For example, if you cast a spell that starts a subgame, you would put your current decks and board states aside to start a completely fresh match. Once that new game is over, you return to the exact same spot in your original game.
What happens to my card if an opponent exiles my double-faced creature face down?

The card is placed in exile face down, which means it remains hidden. You then use a face-down substitute card and/or opaque sleeves to represent it so that no one can see the actual card. For example, if an opponent exiles your transforming creature face down, you would place a different, unimportant card face down in the exile zone to act as its placeholder.
What happens if I use an effect to put a double-faced card onto the battlefield face down? Can it still flip over later?

When a double-faced card enters the battlefield face down, it takes on the characteristics assigned to it by the effect that made it face down. While it is face down, the card cannot transform or convert. For example, if you use an effect to play a double-faced creature face down, it will stay hidden and cannot flip to its back side until an effect turns it face up. When it is eventually turned face up, it will show its front face.
What happens if a plane card says all players draw a card while we are playing a four-player game?

All players will draw a card as the effect resolves. Since plane cards and phenomenon cards are exempt from the limited range of influence option, their abilities and the effects of those abilities affect all applicable objects and players in the game. For example, if a plane says each player draws a card, all four players at the table will receive one card.
Can I still play a card with flash during my opponent's turn?

Yes, you can. Flash means you may play this card any time you could cast an instant. For example, if your opponent is casting a spell during their turn, you can respond by playing a creature from your hand that has flash.
What happens when I scry 3?

To scry 3 means you look at the top three cards of your library, then put any number of them on the bottom of your library in any order and the rest on top of your library in any order. For example, if you see a Forest, an Island, and a Mountain, you could put the Forest and the Island on the bottom and leave the Mountain on top.
I just cast a spell to copy my opponent's card. Can I treat my copy as if it were the actual card itself?

Yes, you can treat it that way because each spell has all the characteristics of the card associated with it. For example, if you use a spell to copy an opponent's Thalia, Guardian of Thraben, your copy is also a Thalia, Guardian of Thraben and possesses all its original properties.
What happens if an opponent tries to destroy my creature while it has a shield counter on it?

The creature stays on the battlefield because one or more shield counters on a permanent create a single replacement effect that protects the permanent. Specifically, if this permanent would be destroyed as the result of an effect, instead remove a shield counter from it. For example, if your 3/3 Knight has a shield counter and an opponent casts a spell to destroy it, the destruction effect is replaced by the removal of the shield counter, and the Knight remains on the battlefield.
Can I still use a spell that targets land types on a card like Dryad Arbor?

Yes, it applies. When a card has multiple card types, each subtype is correlated to its appropriate card type. Since Dryad Arbor is a Land Creature, the Forest subtype belongs to its land type and the Dryad subtype belongs to its creature type. For example, if an effect targets all land types, Dryad Arbor is included because Forest is one of its land subtypes.
Does it matter what color the card frame is? I have a card with no colored mana in its cost, but the border looks like it should be a color.

It does not matter. An object is the color or colors of the mana symbols in its mana cost, regardless of the color of its frame. For example, a card with a mana cost of {2} is colorless even if it has a blue-colored border.
Who is in charge of the plane card right now?

The planar controller is typically defined by who is currently taking their turn. Normally, the planar controller is whoever the active player is. For example, if it becomes your turn and there is a face-up plane card in play, you become the planar controller because you are now the active player.
What happens to my opponent's starting life if their vanguard card has a -5 modifier?

Their starting life total is adjusted during setup. Since each player's starting life total is 20 plus or minus the life modifier of their vanguard card, the modifier is applied to the base number before play begins. For example, an opponent with a -5 modifier will begin the game with 15 life instead of 20.
If my opponent has a card that says all damage from creatures is prevented, can I still use a creature's special ability to deal damage?

You can still use the ability, but the damage itself will not happen. Prevention effects apply to damage from a source, meaning it does not matter if the damage comes from a combat attack or a special ability; as long as the creature is the one causing the damage, it will be stopped. For example, if your opponent has an enchantment that prevents all damage from creatures and you use a creature's activated ability to deal 2 damage to them, that 2 damage is still prevented because the creature is the source of the damage.
What happens if the creature that was haunted stops being a creature later in the game?

The haunt effect stays on the object. When a permanent is put into a graveyard, it exiles a target creature haunting it, but the phrase creature it haunts refers to the object targeted by the haunt ability, regardless of whether or not that object is still a creature. For example, if a haunt ability targets a creature and then that creature is turned into an artifact by a spell, the exiled card still haunts that artifact.
What happens when I use an Embalm ability on a creature that is sitting in my graveyard?

When you activate an Embalm ability, you pay the cost and exile the card from your graveyard to create a token that is a copy of that card, except it is white, has no mana cost, and is a Zombie in addition to its other types. For example, if you have a black creature in your graveyard with Embalm, you can exile it to create a white Zombie token version of that creature.
What happens if my creature is attacking, but my opponent prevents all combat damage and I have an effect that doubles all damage dealt by my creatures?

No damage will be dealt. Because the prevention effect ensures the source would deal 0 damage, the event of dealing damage never actually occurs. Since a source that would deal 0 damage does not deal damage at all, replacement effects that would increase the damage dealt by that source have no event to replace and therefore have no effect. For example, if your creature would normally deal 3 damage but is prevented from dealing any, your doubling effect has no event to act upon and does nothing.
What happens when my creature token gets exiled?

The token moves from the battlefield to the exile zone and immediately ceases to exist. Because a token that is in a zone other than the battlefield ceases to exist, you cannot interact with it or bring it back later. For example, if your opponent uses a spell to exile your 1/1 Soldier token, that token is effectively wiped from the game and you cannot use a card like Reanimate to get it back since it no longer exists.
I just played For Mirrodin!, what exactly happens next?

When you play For Mirrodin!, its triggered ability goes on the stack. When that ability resolves, you first create a 2/2 red Rebel creature token, then attach this Equipment to it. This sequence is required by the wording of the ability. For example, if you cast For Mirrodin! during your turn, you will immediately have a 2/2 red Rebel token on the battlefield with the equipment already attached to it.
Can I look at the card first if an ability says I can choose to reveal it after drawing?

Yes, you can. When an effect gives a player the option to reveal a card as they draw it, that player may look at that card as they draw it before choosing whether to reveal it. For example, if you use an ability that says draw a card and then choose to reveal it, you would pick up the card from your library, look at its face, and then decide whether or not to show it to your opponent.
Can I still play a land if I decide not to attack this turn?

Yes, you can. Even if you choose to skip your combat phase, the rules specify that all other main phases are postcombat main phases, which includes the second main phase of a turn in which the combat phase has been skipped. This ensures that skipping combat does not prevent you from accessing your postcombat actions. For example, if you have a Forest in your hand and decide not to declare any attackers, you can still play that Forest during your second main phase.
Can I use an effect to grab a card from outside the game if I already have a copy of it in my graveyard?

No, you cannot. If a player is allowed to bring a card from outside the game into a Commander game, they cannot bring a card that has the same name as a card that the player owns in the current game. For example, if you have a Sol Ring in your graveyard and an effect allows you to add a card from outside the game to your hand, you cannot choose Sol Ring because you already own a card with that name in the current game.
What happens if we try to start an Archenemy match with a scheme deck that only has fifteen cards?

The game would not be played according to the rules because an archenemy needs a supplementary scheme deck of at least twenty scheme cards. For example, if a group attempts to start with only fifteen cards, they must stop and add five more scheme cards to the deck before the match can proceed correctly.
What happens if an opponent's commander deals a lot of damage to me over several different turns?

If an opponent's commander deals a total of 21 or more combat damage to you across multiple turns, that player immediately loses the game. This is because a player who has been dealt 21 or more combat damage by the same commander over the course of the game loses the game. For example, if an opponent attacks you with their commander for 10 damage on turn three and then another 11 damage on turn five, they will lose the game as soon as that second attack resolves.
What happens when a player activates an ability on a creature and then that creature is destroyed before the ability resolves?

The ability will still resolve because once an ability is activated or triggered, it exists on the stack independently of its source. For example, if you activate a creature's ability to draw a card and your opponent destroys that creature before the ability resolves, the ability remains on the stack even though the creature is gone, so you will still draw the card.
I have a creature that is both a Rogue and a Wizard. Does that count as two different members of my party?

No, it only counts as one member. If a creature has multiple creature types for which it could be the party member, it is counted as the party member for only one of those types. If there are different ways to count such a creature that results in different numbers of creatures in your party, it is counted in such a way to get the highest result. For example, if you control a single creature that is both a Rogue and a Wizard, along with a Cleric, your party size is 2.
Can we still play Commander if there are only two of us?

Yes, you can, because a Commander game may be a two-player game or a multiplayer game. For example, if you and your friend decide to use your legendary creatures to play against each other, you are following the rules.
What happens when I try to play a land while my opponent is casting a spell?

You cannot take that action at that moment. Playing a land is a special action that can only be taken any time you have priority and the stack is empty during your own main phase. For example, if your opponent casts a spell and you want to play a Forest from your hand, the game will proceed with your opponent's spell resolving, and you must wait until your turn begins and you reach your main phase before you can put that land onto the battlefield.
What happens when I choose which creature to target with a spell? Does that choice go on the stack?

When you pick a target, that choice does not go on the stack as its own separate thing. This is because choosing a target is a special action, which is an action a player may take when they have priority that does not use the stack. For example, if you cast a spell that targets a creature, you select the target during the casting process, and then the spell enters the stack as a single entity.
I thought we were supposed to start with 20 life for this Brawl match, but my opponent says it should be 25. Who is right?

Your opponent is correct. In a two-player Brawl game, each player's starting life total is 25. For example, if you are playing a heads-up match against a single opponent using your Brawl decks, you should both begin the game with 25 life instead of the standard 20.
What happens if I try to use Garth One-Eye to copy a card that is sitting in my graveyard?

You create a new token representing that card outside of the game. Because the ability instructs you to create a copy of a card defined by name rather than an object to be copied, you do not need the physical card on the table for it to work. Instead, you use the Oracle card reference to determine its characteristics and then generate the copy. For example, if you want to copy a creature in your graveyard, you look up its official text and then place a new version of that creature onto the battlefield.
What happens when I cast a spell that fateseals 3?

The opponent looks at the top 3 cards of their library, then puts any number of them on the bottom of that library in any order and the rest on top of that library in any order. For example, if they look at three cards and see a land, a creature, and an instant, they can put the land on the bottom and keep the creature and instant on top to draw them next.
Can my teammate and I keep our own separate life totals while playing against the Archenemy?

No, you cannot. The opposing team has a shared life total that starts at 60 life rather than individual life totals. For example, if your teammate takes 15 damage from an attack, your combined life total drops to 45, affecting both of you.
If my opponent has a card in their graveyard, can I just use an ability to grab it from any graveyard?

No, you cannot. While the battlefield and stack are common areas, each player has their own library, hand, and graveyard. For example, if you use a spell that lets you search a graveyard, you must choose which specific player's graveyard you want to look in.
Can I still tap my lands for mana if it is my opponent's turn and they are currently casting a spell?

Yes, you can. Because some activated abilities are mana abilities, they do not use the stack and can be activated even if you do not have priority. For example, while your opponent is in the middle of casting a spell, you can tap your Forest or a Llanowar Elves to produce mana so you are ready to react.
What happens if I use a spell to change my creature's color? Does it lose its bonuses?

The creature will gain or lose bonuses based on its new color. First, the color change is applied; because the game continually and automatically performs the application of continuous effects, the creature's characteristics update instantaneously. For example, if you have a 2/2 black creature and an enchantment that gives white creatures +1/+1, turning that creature white will cause it to become a 3/3. If its color is later changed to red, the enchantment no longer applies and it returns to being a 2/2.
What happens to the cards while my opponent is deciding how to split them into piles? Are they out of the game for a moment?

No, the cards stay exactly where they were during the process. While an opponent is separating revealed cards into piles, those cards are still in their owner's library. They do not leave the library until they are actually put into their owner's hand or graveyard. For example, if you cast Fact or Fiction and your opponent is choosing which cards go to the hand and which go to the graveyard, those five cards remain in the library until the separation is finished and they are moved.
If a creature enters the battlefield with an ability that says "create a 1/1 Bird token and sacrifice it," can I use an instant to destroy the token after it appears but before it is sacrificed?

No, you cannot. These are linked abilities because one part causes an action (creating the token) and the second part refers directly to the object affected by that first action (the token). Because they are linked, they function as a single event. For example, if a creature says "When this enters the battlefield, create a 1/1 Bird token and sacrifice it," your opponent cannot cast a spell to destroy the token after it enters the battlefield but before the sacrifice happens.
It's my turn and I'm in my main phase, can I play an enchantment card from my hand?

Yes, you can. During your main phase, you can cast an enchantment card from your hand as a spell, provided the stack is empty. For example, if you have an enchantment like Sphere of Safety in your hand, you can cast it during your main phase and it will be placed on the stack to resolve.
Can I still use a creature with decayed to block my opponent's attack?

No, you cannot. The decayed ability includes a static effect that means this creature can't block. For example, if your opponent attacks you with a 2/2 creature and you have a 5/5 creature with decayed on the battlefield, you are not allowed to declare that creature as a blocker.
I see this infinity symbol on my opponent's card with some text next to it. Does that ability work all the time?

No, that ability only works while the permanent is being harnessed. The rule dictates that as long as this permanent is harnessed, it has the ability listed after the symbol. For example, if a card has the infinity symbol followed by Reach, the creature will only have reach during the specific period it is currently being harnessed.
What happens to my Siege card after the last defense counter is taken off it?

When the last defense counter is removed from the permanent, the card is exiled, and then you may cast it transformed without paying its mana cost. For example, if your opponent uses a spell to remove the final defense counter from your Siege, you will exile that card and can immediately cast its transformed side for free.
I just rolled a 1, but my card says I have to ignore the lowest die. Does that 1 still count for any of my other abilities?

No, it does not count. When a player is instructed to ignore a roll, that roll is considered to have never happened, which means no abilities trigger because of the ignored roll and no effects apply to it. For example, if you had an ability that triggers whenever you roll a 1, that ability will not trigger because the 1 is treated as if it never occurred.
How do we choose who our creatures are attacking when we are playing as a team?

Since you are the active team, you declare your attackers as a single group. During the declare attackers step, for each attacking creature, your team must announce which defending player, planeswalker, or battle that creature is attacking, and the entire set of attacking creatures must be legal as a whole. For example, if your team has two creatures and the opponent team has two players, you could declare one creature attacking Player A and the other creature attacking Player B.
What happens when I turn a face-down creature face up that has an ability that triggers when it enters the battlefield?

The ability will not trigger. Because the permanent has already entered the battlefield, any abilities relating to the permanent entering the battlefield don't trigger and don't have any effect when it is turned face up. For example, if you turn a face-down creature face up that has an ability saying 'When this creature enters the battlefield, draw a card', you will not draw a card.
What happens when I play a card that has a little guild icon in its text box? Does it trigger something special?

When you play the card, the icon is simply visible in the text box but does nothing to change the card's functions. Because icons like a guild icon appearing in the text box of many Ravnica cards have no effect on gameplay, you just resolve the card's written abilities as normal. For example, if you play a creature with a Boros icon in its text box, it enters the battlefield and performs its listed abilities without any extra bonuses from that symbol.
If I'm attacking two different people at the same time, how do we decide which one gets to pick their blockers first?

The order is determined by the turn order between the active and non-active players. The first defending player declares all their blocks, then the second defending player, and so on. For example, if it is my turn and I attack both you and our friend Sam, you will declare all your blocks first before Sam gets to declare any blockers for his creatures.
What happens if my creature with poisonous 2 deals combat damage to an opponent?

When your creature deals combat damage to a player, the poisonous ability triggers and will eventually grant those counters to the player. For example, if you attack with a creature that has poisonous 2 and it is not blocked, the defending player will receive 2 poison counters because the ability triggers whenever the creature deals combat damage to a player.
If my creature becomes a copy of another card, does it keep being tapped or flipped?

When a permanent is made a copy of something else, it changes its characteristics to match the new card but keeps its current physical state. A permanent retains its status until a spell, ability, or turn-based action changes it, even if that status is not relevant to it. For example, if you have a flipped creature and use an effect to make it a copy of a non-flip card, the new creature will stay in its flipped state.
What happens when we start a new match and nobody has played any cards that change the time of day yet?

The game starts with neither designation, so it is currently neither day nor night. A designation is gained when an effect makes the game day or night. For example, if you are playing a match and no one has cast a spell or used an ability that affects the time of day, the game does not have a day or night status.
Can I use an ability on a creature that just entered the battlefield if its cost requires me to untap it?

No, you cannot. A creature's activated ability with the untap symbol in its activation cost can't be activated unless the creature has been under its controller's control continuously since their most recent turn began. For example, if you play a creature called Ironclad Warden that has an ability costing {Q}: {1} to add mana, you cannot use that ability on the same turn it enters the battlefield because it hasn't been under your control since the start of your turn.
What happens if I play a creature with Echo and then my turn ends?

Nothing happens immediately when your turn ends because the ability only triggers at the beginning of your upkeep. Since the permanent came under your control since the beginning of your last upkeep, you will have to pay the cost or sacrifice it once your next upkeep starts. For example, if you play a creature with Echo 2 during your main phase, you can finish your turn normally, but you must pay 2 mana at the start of your next upkeep or the creature is sacrificed.
What happens when a creature gets enough minus one minus one counters to die while it already has other counters on it?

If a creature's death is one of several state-based actions occurring simultaneously, its last known information is derived from the game state before any of those state-based actions were performed. For example, if Young Wolf has a +1/+1 counter and receives three -1/-1 counters from a spell, it has both types of counters on it immediately before state-based actions are checked. However, if its death happens as part of a set of simultaneous state-based actions, its last known information would be the state from before those actions began, meaning it is treated as only having the +1/+1 counter and undying will not trigger.
Can my teammate sit right next to me if we are playing an alternating teams game?

No, you cannot. Players must be seated so that no one is next to a teammate and each team is equally spaced out. For example, if you and another player are both on Team A, there must be at least one person from a different team sitting in the chair between you.
What happens if I play a dragon that is clearly shown flying in the picture, but my opponent says it can be blocked by a regular foot soldier?

In this situation, your opponent is correct because the illustration on a card has no effect on gameplay. Even if a creature is depicted as flying, it does not have the flying ability unless stated in its rules text. For example, if your dragon card shows it soaring through the air but the text box lacks the word flying, it must follow the standard rules for non-flying creatures and can be blocked by any creature without flying.
Can I use my planeswalker's ability more than once in a single turn if I have ways to activate it?

No, you cannot. A player can only activate a loyalty ability if none of that permanent's loyalty abilities have been activated that turn. For example, if you use a planeswalker to draw a card with its plus ability, you cannot use its minus ability later in the same turn.
What happens if I cast a spell that says when my creature leaves the battlefield I draw a card, but my opponent destroys that creature while the spell is still on the stack?

You will not draw a card because the ability never gets created. A delayed triggered ability will not trigger until it has actually been created, even if its trigger event occurred just beforehand. In this situation, because the creature leaves the battlefield before the spell creating the effect finishes resolving, the ability is never created. For example, if you cast a spell that says 'When this creature leaves the battlefield, draw a card' and your opponent uses a removal spell to kill that creature while the first spell is still resolving, the trigger event happened before the ability existed, so nothing happens.
Can I still get the discount for an opponent who lost but is still sitting at the table?

No, you cannot. Undaunted means the spell costs 1 less to cast for each opponent you have, but players who have left the game are not counted when determining how many opponents you have. For example, if your friend loses their last life and is no longer in the match, they do not count as an opponent, so you would not get the mana reduction for them even if they are still present.
What do I do if I need to know the color of a card but there is no mana cost in the corner?

You should look for a circular symbol filled in with one or more colors. This indicator is printed to the left of the type line directly below the illustration. For example, if you have a blue enchantment that has no mana cost, you will see a blue circle next to the word enchantment to show its color.
What happens when an old card says it removes my creature from the game? Does it go into the graveyard?

The creature goes to the exile zone. Even though older cards use different wording, any card printed with text that removes an object from the game actually exiles that object. For example, if you play an older card that says it removes a permanent from the game, that permanent is placed in the exile zone instead of the graveyard.
What happens if my enchantment is destroyed but the effect says it should endure 2?

When an enchantment is instructed to endure 2, you have a choice to ensure its presence remains on the battlefield. You can either create a 2/2 white Spirit creature token or put two +1/+1 counters on that permanent. For example, if your enchantment is destroyed but told to endure 2, you could choose to create a 2/2 white Spirit token instead of the enchantment simply going to the graveyard.
Can I mulligan my starting hand in a multiplayer game without having to reduce my hand size?

Yes, you can. In a multiplayer game, the first mulligan a player takes does not count toward the number of cards that player will put on the bottom of their library or the number of mulligans that player may take. For example, if you are playing in a four-player game and draw seven cards but want to try again, you can mulligan and still receive a full hand of seven cards.
What happens when I use an ability to create a token? Does it get all the same powers as my card?

When you use an ability to create a token, the game defines the token based only on what that specific ability says. The spell or ability that creates a token may define the values of any number of characteristics, and those become the token's text. A token has no characteristics not defined by the spell or ability that created it. For example, if you use Jade Mage to create a 1/1 green Saproling creature token, that Saproling will have no rules text or abilities because the ability did not define them.
What happens when a Clone enters the battlefield as a copy of a Vesuvan Doppelganger that is already copying another creature?

First, the Clone enters as a copy of the Doppelganger. Because the copy's copiable values become the copied information, the Clone then adopts the characteristics the Doppelganger has already taken from its target. For example, if a Vesuvan Doppelganger is currently copying a 2/2 green Bear, the Clone will enter the battlefield as a 2/2 blue Bear named after that Bear and will also have the Doppelganger's upkeep ability to become a copy of another creature.
I just played this Vehicle card, but it's not a creature yet. Can I attack with it right away?

No, you cannot attack with it while it is only an artifact. A Vehicle has its printed power and toughness only if it is also a creature. You must use the crew ability to turn it into an artifact creature before it can participate in combat. For example, if you play a Vehicle with crew 2, you need to tap two other creatures to make it a creature so that it can attack.
Can I still use a card's Scavenge ability if it is sitting in my graveyard instead of being on the battlefield?

Yes, you can. Scavenge is an activated ability that functions only while the card with scavenge is in a graveyard. For example, if you have a creature with 3 power that has Scavenge in your graveyard, you can pay its cost and exile it to put three +1/+1 counters on another creature you control.
I just played an equipment with living weapon. What actually happens to the board?

When you cast an equipment with living weapon, a sequence of events occurs. First, the ability triggers because the equipment is entering the battlefield. This triggers the effect to create a 0/0 black Phyrexian Germ creature token, then attach this equipment to it. For example, if you cast Batterskull, you will first see a 0/0 black Phyrexian Germ token appear, and then Batterskull will immediately attach itself to that Germ, making it a 4/4 creature.
Can I use the text in the middle of the card to identify what it is called?

No, you cannot because the name of a card is printed on its upper left corner. For example, if a card has an ability that says This creature is a Dragon, you must still look at the top left corner to find the actual name of the card.
What happens to the way we pass packs when we move from the first round to the second round of drafting?

The direction of passing changes for the middle round. In the first and third draft rounds, booster packs are passed to each player's left, but in the second draft round, they are passed to each player's right. For example, if you were passing your pack to the person on your left during the first round, you will instead pass it to the person on your right when the second round starts.
What happens if I cast an enchantment that targets a creature, but my opponent destroys that creature before the enchantment actually resolves?

The enchantment will not enter the battlefield. When a spell resolves, it checks whether its target is still legal. If the target is no longer legal, the spell does not resolve and is instead removed from the stack and put into its owner's graveyard. For example, if you cast an enchantment like Aura of Luminous Ambition targeting an opponent's creature, but they use a spell like Murder to destroy that creature in response, your enchantment will fail to resolve and go directly to your graveyard.
What happens when my opponent destroys the land I just earthbent?

When that land dies or is put into exile, return it to the battlefield tapped under your control. For example, if you use an effect to earthbend a Plains and your opponent plays a spell to destroy all creatures, your Plains will be put into the graveyard but will immediately come back to the battlefield tapped.
I'm the monarch right now, but my opponent just played a card that makes them the monarch too. Do we both get to draw an extra card at the start of our turns?

No, you will not both draw the extra card. Only one player can be the monarch at a time, and as a player becomes the monarch, the current monarch ceases to be the monarch. For example, if you are currently the monarch and your opponent plays a spell that makes them the monarch, your status ends immediately when that spell resolves, meaning only they will draw the extra card at the start of their turn.
What happens if I use two different cards that both say they add an extra combat phase right after my main phase?

When you use effects that add phases, they are added directly after the specified phase. If multiple extra phases are created after the same phase, the most recently created phase will occur first. For example, if you cast a spell that adds a combat phase after your main phase and then cast another spell that also adds a combat phase after your main phase, the combat phase from the second spell will happen before the combat phase from the first spell.
My opponent just played a card that destroys all permanents. Does my emblem get destroyed too?

No, your emblem stays on the field. When the spell resolves, it looks for permanents to destroy, but because an emblem is neither a card nor a permanent, it is not affected by the effect. For example, if you have an emblem and your opponent casts a spell like Wrath of God that destroys all creatures, your emblem remains because it is not a permanent.
What happens to my creatures when I play an enchantment that says they all get flying?

The creatures gain the flying ability because an ability can be defined by an object's rules text or by the effect that created it. When the enchantment resolves, the effect modifies the creatures to include that new characteristic. For example, if you have a 1/1 creature with no abilities and play an enchantment that grants flying, that creature now has the flying ability.
What happens when I have an enchantment that forces me to attack and another effect that makes my creatures unblockable?

The game applies effects that change game rules, such as a requirement to attack, after all other continuous effects have been applied. This means the game first determines the state of your creatures, such as them being unblockable, and then applies the rule that you must attack. For example, if you have an effect making your creatures unblockable and an enchantment like Archon of Coronation forcing an attack, the game first processes the unblockable status before applying the mandatory attack requirement.
What happens if I have an effect that turns my artifacts into 2/2 creatures, and then another effect that gives them +1/+1? Do they both work even though they weren't creatures to begin with?

When multiple effects apply to an object in different stages, the game applies the parts of the effect in their appropriate ones. If an effect starts to apply in one stage, it will continue to be applied to the same set of objects in each other applicable stage, even if those objects change. For example, an effect that makes all noncreature artifacts 2/2 artifact creatures is both a type-changing effect and a power-and-toughness-setting effect. The game first turns them into creatures and then applies the 2/2 power and toughness to those same objects.
What happens if I play a creature while my opponent has a Space Sculptor on the field?

When a permanent with space sculptor and creatures without a sector designation are on the battlefield at the same time, players choose a sector designation for those creatures. For example, if your opponent controls a Space Sculptor and you cast a creature, that creature enters without a designation. Because these conditions are met, you will get to choose whether that creature is in the alpha, beta, or gamma sector.
Can I still use the adventure part of an adventurer card if it is sitting in my graveyard?

No, you cannot. In every zone except the stack, an adventurer card has only its normal characteristics. This means that while the card is in your graveyard, it does not function as an adventure spell. For example, if Brazen Borrower is in your graveyard, you cannot cast its adventure portion because the card only possesses its normal characteristics in that zone.
What happens to a creature when I use a spell to make a copy of another creature spell?

When the copy of a permanent spell resolves, it becomes a token. This is because a copy of a permanent spell becomes a token as it resolves and has the characteristics of the spell that became that token. For example, if you use a spell to copy a creature spell that is a 2/2 Red Goblin, the resulting token will be a 2/2 Red Goblin.
What happens if I exile a card? Does my opponent get to see what it is?

By default, any card you exile is kept face up and may be examined by any player at any time. For example, if you use a spell to exile a creature from your graveyard, that card stays face up so everyone can see its name and abilities.
I have four copies of Lightning Bolt in my main deck, can I put one of them in my sideboard to swap it out later?

No, you cannot do that. In constructed play, the four-card limit applies to the combined deck and sideboard. Since you already have four copies of the card in your main deck, you cannot add any additional copies to your sideboard. For example, if you have four copies of Counterspell in your main deck, you are not allowed to have a fifth copy in your sideboard.
What happens when a card says I get an emblem with a special power?

When you receive an emblem, you put that emblem into your command zone. This is because the rules state that the player gets an emblem that is both owned and controlled by them. For example, if a spell says you get an emblem with all your creatures gaining flying, you place that emblem in your command zone to begin using that ability.
What happens if a spell says the player with the most life wins, but two people are tied at exactly 20 life?

There is no automatic way for the game to decide who wins in that situation. If an effect could result in a tie, the text of the spell or ability that created the effect will specify what to do in the event of a tie. Because the Magic game has no default for ties, you cannot assume the person who reached that life total first or the active player is the winner unless the card explicitly says so. For example, if a card simply says 'the player with the most life wins' and two players both have 20 life, the game does not have a built-in rule to break that tie.
My commander just got exiled by an opponent's spell. Can I get him back into my command zone right away?

Yes, you can move your commander back to the command zone. In a Commander game, if a commander is in exile and it was put there since the last time state-based actions were checked, its owner may put it into the command zone. For example, if an opponent casts a spell that exiles your commander, you can take that commander from exile and place it back in your command zone during the next check.
We chose the limited range of influence option, but this plane effect says everyone gets a bonus. Does it really hit every player?

Yes, it does. Plane cards and phenomenon cards are exempt from the limited range of influence option, meaning their abilities affect all applicable objects and players in the game. For example, if a plane card says each player draws a card, every player at the table will draw a card even though you have chosen to limit the range of influence for other effects.
What happens if someone uses an effect to restart the game while we are playing with limited influence? Does everyone have to start over or just the people that player was interacting with?

Everyone in the game is involved in the restart. Even if the person who controls the ability that restarts the game only has a limited range of influence, all players in the game are involved. For example, if four players are playing and Player A's abilities only affect Player B, but Player A then uses an effect to restart the game, Players C and D must also participate in the restart.
What happens if I see a card that says Plane — Serra's Realm? Does it have two subtypes?

You treat the entire phrase after the dash as one unit. Because all words after the dash are, collectively, a single subtype, you do not count them as separate types. For example, on a card labeled Plane — Serra's Realm, you identify the entire phrase Serra's Realm as its one and only subtype.
What happens if I have three Demons on the battlefield and one face-down Demon, but my win condition requires me to control four Demons with different names?

The win condition does not trigger. Because the group of creatures includes one with no name, those creatures do not count as having different names. To satisfy such a requirement, every object must have at least one name and no two objects can share a name. For example, if you control a Demon named Rakdos, a Demon named Belial, and a nameless face-down Demon, you only have two Demons with different names.
What happens if we are playing a little side game for a bonus and that game gets restarted?

When a subgame is restarted, the main game remains unaffected, but any effects in the main game that refer to the winner or loser of the subgame will now refer to the winner or loser of the restarted subgame. For example, if you have an enchantment that says You gain 3 life if the winner of the side game has more creatures than you, and the side game restarts, that effect will now trigger based on whoever wins the new side game.
What happens if my creature hits a planeswalker for 3 damage?

When you deal damage to a planeswalker, that many loyalty counters are removed from it. For example, if you attack with a 3/3 creature and choose the planeswalker as the target for combat damage, you will remove 3 loyalty counters from that planeswalker.

What happens if I am about to lose the game because my life hits zero and I also run out of cards in my library at the same time, but I have a card that says instead of losing, I shuffle and draw seven?

You will not lose. When state-based actions are checked, the game identifies all reasons you would lose at that moment. Because if multiple state-based actions would have the same result at the same time, a single replacement effect will replace all of them, your card handles all those losses with one effect. For example, if you have Lich's Mirror and an event causes you to hit zero life and run out of cards in your library simultaneously, the mirror replaces that loss with its shuffle-and-draw effect.
Can I still use the abilities on my scheme card if it is sitting in the command zone instead of being played?

Yes, you can. The mechanic is that any abilities of a face-up scheme card in the command zone function from that zone. This means its static abilities affect the game, its triggered abilities may trigger, and its activated abilities may be activated. For example, if your scheme card has a static ability that says all creatures you control get plus one plus one, that bonus still applies to your creatures even while the card is in the command zone.
My teammate and I can't decide which of our creatures should attack. Who gets to make the final choice?

If you and your teammate cannot agree on a choice, such as which creatures attack, the responsibility falls to a designated primary player. This person is defined as the player seated in the rightmost seat from that team's perspective. For example, if you are playing on a two-person team and you and your partner disagree on whether to attack with a 2/2 creature or a 3/3 creature, the person sitting furthest to the right from your team's point of view decides.
My friend and I are playing Two-Headed Giant, but he is sitting all the way on the other side of the table from me. Can we still take our turns together as one team?

No, you cannot use shared team turns in that arrangement. Shared team turns can be used only if the members of each team are sitting in adjacent seats. For example, if you are playing Two-Headed Giant but your teammate is sitting directly across from you instead of right next to you, you must take separate turns rather than sharing a single team turn.
What happens if I use an ability to boost a Vehicle's power while it is still just an artifact?

The effect is created even though it does not do anything until the permanent becomes a creature. Because a noncreature permanent has no power or toughness, even if it has numbers printed on it, the modification is applied to the object so that it is ready once the Vehicle is crewed. For example, if you cast a spell to give an uncrewed Skysovereign, Intervention Supreme +2/+2, the bonus will be waiting and apply as soon as you crew the Vehicle and it becomes a creature.
What happens to my planeswalker's loyalty when I use an ability that costs minus 2 loyalty?

When you activate such an ability, you are removing loyalty counters from the card. Because a planeswalker's loyalty on the battlefield is equal to the number of loyalty counters on it, the loyalty value changes to match the new counter count. For example, if your planeswalker has 5 loyalty and you use an ability that costs minus 2 loyalty, the card will then have 3 loyalty counters on it, meaning its loyalty is now 3.
What happens to my Sagas when I reach my first main phase?

During your precombat main phase, you put a lore counter on each Saga you control that has one or more chapter abilities. This is an automatic turn-based action. For example, if you have The Eldest Reborn on the battlefield, you will add its first lore counter as soon as you enter your precombat main phase.
What happens if I sacrifice a creature to pay for the casualty cost on my spell?

When you cast a spell with casualty and pay that cost, the rule states that you copy the spell and, if the spell has any targets, you may choose new targets for the copy. For example, if you cast a spell with Casualty 3 that targets an opponent's creature, and you sacrifice a 3-power creature to pay the cost, you will have both the original spell and a copy of it on the stack, allowing you to pick a different target for the copy.
What happens if I try to use a Treasure token to get some mana?

To use a Treasure token for mana, you follow its specific instructions. A Treasure token is a colorless Treasure artifact token with {T}, Sacrifice this token: Add one mana of any color. This means you tap the token and sacrifice it to move it to your graveyard, which then allows you to add one mana of any color you choose to your mana pool. For example, if you have a Treasure token and need to cast a green spell, you tap the token, sacrifice it, and add {G}.
What happens if I cast a creature with Squad 2 and decide to pay 6 mana for the squad cost instead of just 2?

You will end up with four creatures total: the original creature you cast and three token copies. This is because paying a squad cost is an additional cost that you may pay any number of times when casting the spell, and when the creature enters, if its squad cost was paid, you create a token that is a copy of it for each time its squad cost was paid. For example, by paying 6 mana for a Squad 2 ability, you have effectively paid the cost three times, which results in the original creature plus three tokens.
If I use an effect that converts a creature to its other face, will it trigger my opponent's ability that says 'Whenever a permanent is turned face down, draw a card'?

No, it will not trigger. Although converting uses the same physical action of turning a card over, they are different game actions. Abilities that trigger when a permanent is turned face down won't trigger when that permanent converts. For example, if your opponent has an enchantment that triggers whenever a creature is turned face down, and you use an effect to convert one of their creatures directly to its other face, that enchantment will not trigger.
We decided to add a rule where everyone draws an extra card and another rule where creatures get bigger when they attack. What happens if we try to use both at the same time?

Both rules will be active in your game. This is because the rules consist of a series of options that can be added to a multiplayer game, meaning you can layer multiple additions on top of each other. For example, during your turn, you would first draw your extra card and then move to combat where your creatures receive their size bonus. You can use as many options as you like, but you must ensure you are only using one variant style of play.
What happens if my opponent casts a spell and it finishes resolving? Can I play something now, or do they get to go again?

After a spell or ability resolves, the active player receives priority. This means if your opponent is currently taking their turn and a spell they cast finishes resolving, they get the first chance to take an action before you can respond with your own spell. For example, if your opponent casts a spell that draws them a card and it resolves, they receive priority immediately after, which might allow them to cast another spell before you have the opportunity to play anything.
What happens when I flip over a phenomenon card from my planar deck?

When you move a phenomenon card off a planar deck and turn it face up, you encounter it, which triggers that card's ability. For example, if you have a phenomenon card titled Great Flood that says When you encounter Great Flood, destroy target creature, the destruction effect happens as soon as you flip the card from the deck and turn it face up.
Can I search for a land that is an Island if my spell says I need to find a basic land?

You can only do so if that Island also has the supertype basic. Any land that does not have the supertype basic is a nonbasic land, even if it has a basic land type. For example, if you use a spell to search for a basic land and you only have an Island that lacks the supertype basic, you cannot select that land.
What happens when I tap three lands for three mana but only spend two to cast a spell?

When an effect instructs a player to add mana, that mana goes into your mana pool and it can be used to pay costs immediately or stay in your mana pool as unspent mana. This mana will remain available until the end of the current step and phase. For example, if you tap three lands to add three blue mana during your main phase and only use two to cast a spell, you can keep that remaining one blue mana to cast another spell later in that same main phase.
