My friend says my deck is illegal because of some tournament rules, but I don't see those rules anywhere in this book. What happens when there's a disagreement like this?

A disagreement like this occurs because many multiplayer Magic tournaments have additional rules not included here, including rules for deck construction. To resolve the conflict, you would need to check the most current Magic: The Gathering Tournament Rules at WPN.wizards.com/en/rules-documents to find the specific requirements for your event. For example, if you bring a deck with 100 cards and the tournament organizers have added a rule that all decks must be exactly 60 cards, the judge will use those additional rules to declare your deck illegal.
What happens when I use Magar of the Magic Strings to copy a creature that had its power increased by an effect right before it died?

First, you note the name of the card in the graveyard. Then, you create the copy by using the characteristics of that card as it last existed in the graveyard to determine the copiable values. This ensures any modifications are included. For example, if a 2/2 creature had its power increased to 4 right before being put into the graveyard, your copy will be a 4-power creature.
What happens when I cast a creature using its Blitz cost? Does it stay on the battlefield permanently?

When you pay the blitz cost, the creature enters the battlefield with haste and a card-draw ability. However, because you paid that specific cost, a delayed trigger will occur where you must sacrifice the permanent at the beginning of the next end step. For example, if you cast a creature using its blitz cost during your turn, it will stay on the battlefield through your combat phase, but you will be forced to sacrifice it once the next end step begins.
I have a card with Transfigure on it. If I decide to use that ability, what exactly does it do?

When you use Transfigure, you must pay the required cost and sacrifice the permanent you are using. Then, you search your library for a creature card that has the same mana value as the one you just sacrificed and put it onto the battlefield. Finally, you shuffle your library. For example, if you have a 2-mana creature with Transfigure and you activate it, you sacrifice that creature and then search your deck for any other creature that costs 2 mana to put into play.
I just pulled this new card and it has these weird lines in the text area and some icons. Is there a specific way to tell if it is one of those station cards?

You can identify them by looking for a few specific features. Each station card has a striated text box and will contain one or two station symbols within that text box. For example, if you play a card called Frontier Outpost that has a striped-looking text area and a single station symbol, you know it functions as a station card.
What happens to my spells after they finish working?

After an instant or sorcery spell finishes resolving, it moves from the stack to your graveyard. The rules specify that any instant or sorcery spell that has finished resolving is put on top of its owner's graveyard. For example, if you cast a Fireball and the damage is dealt, the card moves from the stack into your discard pile.
Can I cast this card from my graveyard by just tapping a creature instead of paying its mana cost?

It depends on the specific harmonize cost. If a card has a harmonize cost, you may cast it from your graveyard by paying that cost and tapping an untapped creature you control instead of paying the spell's normal mana cost. However, you do not just tap a creature; you also pay the mana specified in the harmonize cost, which is then reduced by the tapped creature's power. For example, if a card has a harmonize cost of 2, and you tap a 2/2 creature, your total cost for the spell would be 0 generic mana rather than 2.
I am playing a card that affects all creatures with a certain name, but my version looks different. Does the effect still work on my creature?

Yes, it does. For the purposes of all rules, abilities, and effects that refer to a card name, objects with interchangeable names have the same name. For example, if an ability targets every creature named Silver Dragon and you play a version of Silver Dragon that has an interchangeable names indicator, the effect will treat it as having that name.
What happens if a card says something is supposed to happen right when my turn ends? Can I use a spell to stop it?

It depends on whether the effect is a turn-based action or a triggered ability. Turn-based actions happen automatically when steps or phases begin or end and do not use the stack. However, most cards use triggered abilities, such as an enchantment that says At the beginning of your end step, sacrifice this artifact. Because this ability watches for a phase to begin, it is a triggered ability that goes on the stack, meaning you can use spells to respond to it.
What happens when a card says my life becomes 5, but I already have 12 life?

You lose 7 life. When an effect sets your life total to a specific number, you lose the necessary amount of life to end up with that new total. For example, if you have 12 life and a card says your life becomes 5, you lose 7 life so that your life total ends at exactly 5.
I have a card in my graveyard that says Aftermath on it. Can I actually play it from there?

Yes, you can. The Aftermath ability means you may cast this half of this split card from your graveyard. For example, if you have a spell with Aftermath in your graveyard, you can pay its mana cost to cast it directly from the graveyard rather than needing to draw it into your hand first.
I just played a card that says it has Daybound, but it's night in our game. Does it stay as the front side or does it flip over right away?

It flips over immediately. The Daybound ability states that if it is night and the permanent is represented by a double-faced card, it enters transformed. For example, if you cast a creature with Daybound while it is currently night, it will enter the battlefield already transformed into its back face.
If I don't want to play any cards or attack, do I still have to go through all those different parts of the turn?

Yes, you must go through every stage. The rules specify that each of the five phases—beginning, precombat main, combat, postcombat main, and ending—takes place every turn, even if nothing happens during the phase. For example, if you have no lands to play and no spells in hand, you still move from the beginning phase through the precombat main phase before your turn officially ends.
If I use the monstrosity ability on my creature, can I use it again later in the game?

No, you cannot. The rule states that if this permanent isn't monstrous, you put N +1/+1 counters on it and it becomes monstrous. Once a permanent becomes monstrous, it stays monstrous until it leaves the battlefield. For example, if you have a creature with Monstrosity 3 and you activate its ability, it gets three +1/+1 counters and is now monstrous. You won't be able to trigger that ability again even if you have extra mana because the creature is already monstrous.
What happens to my teammate when I play a card that gives me an extra turn in Two-Headed Giant?

Your teammate will also take that extra turn. Because you are on the same team, any effect that gives a player an extra turn or adds a phase or step to that player's turn means that player's team takes the extra turn. For example, if you cast a spell in Two-Headed Giant that says you take an extra turn, your teammate will proceed through that extra turn along with you.
What happens to my cards and the current plane if I have to leave the game?

When you leave the game, all objects you own, including your lands and creatures, leave the game. If this process includes leaving a face-up plane card, the planar controller must turn the top card of their planar deck face up. For example, if you are playing on a plane called Zendikar and you leave the match, your entire board state is removed from play, and the next plane in the deck is flipped over to become the new active plane.
My opponent just played a card that says I skip my next turn. Can I still cast spells and tap lands during the rest of my current turn?

Yes, you can. Once a step, phase, or turn has already started, it can no longer be skipped. Any effect that causes you to skip your next turn will wait until the next occurrence of a turn. For example, if your opponent casts a spell to skip your next turn while you are currently in your combat phase, you will finish your current combat phase and the rest of your current turn as normal. The skip effect will only take effect when your next actual turn begins.
What happens when I finish my mulligans and realize I have a card that should be on the battlefield immediately?

Once the mulligan process is complete, you may take any such actions in any order. If the card allows you to begin the game with it on the battlefield, you put that card onto the battlefield. The starting player performs these actions first, and then each other player follows in turn order. For example, if you are the starting player, you would place your special permanent on the table right after your mulligans are done but before your first turn begins.
What happens when I play a card that tempts the Ring but I don't have an emblem yet?

If you do not have an emblem named The Ring at the time the Ring tempts you, you get an emblem named The Ring before choosing a creature to be your Ring-bearer. For example, if you cast a spell that causes the Ring to tempt you for the first time, you will immediately gain The Ring emblem and then select one of your creatures, such as a 2/2 Goblin, to become your Ring-bearer.
What happens if I try to use a spell to move an Aura from my creature onto a Land?

Nothing happens. If an effect tries to attach an Aura to an object it cannot enchant, the Aura does not move. For example, if you have an Aura like Rancor attached to a creature and you use a spell that says attach target Aura to target land, the Rancor stays on the creature because it cannot be attached to an object it could not enchant.
What happens if I want to use a battle card from my hand during my turn?

You can cast the battle card as a spell during your main phase as long as the stack is empty. For example, once you have finished playing your lands and other spells and there are no more actions waiting to resolve, you can cast the battle card which then goes on the stack for players to respond to.
Can I build a deck with 150 cards for a regular tournament?

Yes, you can. This is because while formats have a minimum deck size that must be met, there is no maximum deck size for non-Commander decks. For example, if you are playing Modern and must have at least 60 cards, you could legally build a deck with 150 cards.
I have a creature with no abilities, and I have a card out that gives +2/+2 to creatures with no abilities. If I use an enchantment to give that creature flying, does it still get the +2/+2 bonus?

No, the creature will no longer get the +2/+2 bonus. When you use an enchantment to give a creature flying, you are granting it an ability. The rule clarifies that an effect that grants an ability is different from an effect that simply states a quality of an object. Once the creature has the flying ability, it no longer meets the requirement of having no abilities. For example, if you enchant a Runeclaw Bear with an Aura that gives it flying, it will not get the +2/+2 bonus from Muraganda Petroglyphs.
If my opponent plays a spell that destroys all artifacts, can they destroy the ones in my sideboard?

No, they cannot. This is because cards in a player's sideboard are outside the game, and cards outside the game cannot be affected by spells or abilities. For example, if your opponent plays a spell that destroys all artifacts, none of the artifacts you have sitting in your sideboard will be destroyed because they are not in any of the game's zones.
Why does the player playing the archenemy have so much more health than us? We only started with 20.

In this game format, the archenemy's starting life total is 40 and each other player's starting life total is 20. For example, if you and your teammate are playing against one opponent, you both begin with 20 life while that single opponent starts with 40 life.
What happens to the owner of a scheme card once it is turned face up?

Ownership shifts to whoever is currently controlling the card. While the player who started with the card in their command zone is typically the owner, once it is flipped face up, ownership is determined by who controls it. For example, if Player A has a scheme card in their command zone and it is flipped face up, they own it, but if Player B takes control of that face-up card, Player B becomes the owner because the controller of a face-up scheme card is its owner.
What happens if it is day and my opponent goes through their whole turn without casting anything?

The time of day will change to night. If it is day and the previous turn's active player didn't cast any spells during that turn, it becomes night. For example, if your opponent passes their turn without playing any cards while it is daytime, the game will transition to night.
Wait, since we have extra people playing on each side now, do we change how far apart everyone sits?

Yes, you must adjust the range of influence if the teams have more than three players. A general's range should be the minimum number that allows one opposing general to begin the game within their range, and an emperor's range should be the minimum number that allows two generals from opposing teams to begin within their range. For example, in a game with two teams of four players, the emperor has a range of 3, the second general (General 2) has a range of 2, and the first and third generals have a range of 1.
I have a creature with 3/1 on it. If my opponent attacks me with a 2/2, will my creature survive?

No, your creature will be destroyed. The second number on the card is its toughness, which is the amount of damage needed to destroy it. Since your creature only has 1 toughness and the attacking creature deals 2 damage, it will not survive. For example, if you had a 3/3 creature instead, it would survive because 2 damage is less than its toughness of 3.
If I am forced to discard a card with Madness, do I just put it in the graveyard or can I do something else?

Instead of putting the card into your graveyard, you exile it instead. When this card is exiled this way, its owner may cast it by paying the madness cost rather than its mana cost. If you choose not to cast it, you put the card into your graveyard. For example, if you have a card with Madness 3 in hand and an effect forces you to discard it, you exile that card and can then pay 3 mana to cast it immediately.
What happens if I hit my opponent with a creature that has toxic 2?

When combat damage is dealt to a player by a creature with toxic, you give that player a number of poison counters equal to the creature's total toxic value, in addition to the damage. For example, if your creature with toxic 2 deals 3 damage to an opponent, they will receive 2 poison counters.

I have a card that makes tokens and another that untaps my creatures whenever a token enters, and it's going to take forever. Can I just tell everyone I'm going to do this a thousand times so we don't have to go through every single step?

Yes, you can suggest a shortcut by describing a sequence of game choices that may be legally taken based on the current game state. This sequence can include a loop that repeats a specified number of times. For example, if you control a creature that creates a 1/1 token when tapped and an artifact that untaps all creatures whenever a creature enters, you can suggest a shortcut by saying you will repeat the sequence of tapping the creature, letting the token ability resolve, and letting the untap ability resolve 999,999 more times. Each other player then has a chance to either accept your proposal or name a point where they would make a different game choice. If everyone accepts, the game advances to the end of that sequence.
What happens if we need to decide who starts the game?

You must randomly determine which emperor goes first, and then the turn order goes to the players' left. For example, if you flip a coin and it lands on heads for Player A, the person sitting to their left will be the next one to take a turn.
Can I still say I attacked you if my creature gets destroyed before it hits you?

Yes, you can, because a player has attacked if they declare one or more creatures as attackers attacking the second player. For example, if you declare a 2/2 creature as an attacker but your opponent uses a spell to destroy it before it deals damage, you still technically attacked them during that combat phase.

If I am casting a spell that costs two mana and also requires me to sacrifice a creature, but I have a card on the table that makes my spells cheaper, do I calculate the discount before or after the sacrifice?

You calculate everything together before you pay anything. When casting a spell, you first propose the spell and then determine the total cost. This process involves taking the mana cost, adding any additional costs like a sacrifice, and subtracting any cost reductions. Once this calculation is finished, the resulting total cost becomes locked in. For example, if you are casting Altar's Reap which costs {1}{B} and has an additional cost of sacrificing a creature, and you have Thunderscape Familiar on the battlefield that makes your black spells cost {1} less, you determine the total cost as {B} plus the sacrifice. After that, the cost is locked in, and then you proceed to pay it.
I have a creature with Support 2 on the field. Can I use its ability to put a counter on itself and another creature?

No, you cannot. When Support N is on a permanent, it means you put a +1/+1 counter on each of up to N other target creatures. Because the rule specifies other target creatures, the creature providing the support cannot be one of the targets. For example, if you have a 2/2 creature with Support 2, you can choose two other creatures to receive counters, but you cannot choose that same 2/2 creature as one of your targets.
What happens if I do not have any creatures ready to attack this turn? Do we still have to go through the part where my opponent picks blockers?

No, you skip those steps. If no creatures are declared as attackers or put onto the battlefield attacking, you skip the declare blockers and combat damage steps. For example, if you only have a single creature that has summoning sickness and cannot attack, you move straight from the beginning of combat to the end of combat without anyone choosing blockers.
What happens when I use a spell that tells me to put a card from my library into my hand?

The card moves from your library to your hand area. This occurs because while the hand is where a player holds cards that have been drawn, cards can also be put into a player's hand by other effects. For example, if you cast a spell like Brainstorm that allows you to put a card from your library into your hand, that card becomes part of your hand immediately.

My opponent just cast a spell that requires them to sacrifice one of their creatures as part of the cost. They have another ability on a different permanent that also asks them to sacrifice a creature to activate it. They tried to tap a single creature and say it counts for both because it gets put into the graveyard anyway. What actually happens here, and how do we handle the timing of any death triggers?

The player cannot use that single creature sacrifice to pay for both the spell and the activated ability at the same time. The game rules clearly state that each payment of a cost applies to only one spell, ability, or effect, meaning you cannot sacrifice just one permanent to satisfy the separate costs of two different things. You must choose which cost to actually pay before putting that choice on the stack. Regarding timing, when the chosen spell begins resolving, no player has priority while a spell or ability is resolving. This means the sacrifice happens completely automatically during resolution without interruption. Any triggered abilities that look at the creature dying will notice the event, but nothing actually happens at the time an ability triggers; those death triggers simply wait until after the current spell fully finishes resolving and you receive priority again. The concrete final game outcome is that only the sacrificed cost for your chosen spell resolves, the creature moves to the graveyard, your spell effect happens immediately, and all related death triggers remain pending until after resolution ends, at which point active play continues normally.
Can I use a spell that destroys artifacts to get rid of an emblem my opponent just made?

No, you cannot. An emblem has no characteristics other than the abilities defined by the effect that created it, which means it has no types like artifact or enchantment. For example, if you cast a spell that says destroy target artifact, the emblem is not a legal target because it does not have the artifact type.

I just cast this spell that says Create a 2/2 Golem token with haste. Whenever you create a Golem token this way, roll a d6 and put +1/+1 counters on it equal to the result. My opponent wants me to use a physical six-sided die, but I only have my phone random number generator app. Also does the counter placement happen instantly or wait for priority?

When you create the Golem token, the effect that tells you to roll a die and place counters triggers. Like all triggered abilities, this waits to resolve on the stack, so the counters are placed when that trigger resolves rather than instantly during the initial spell. Regarding the die, players may agree to use an alternate method like a digital random number generator app instead of a physical six-sided die, as long as the chosen method has the exact same number of equally likely outcomes.

I just played my basic forest this turn to generate mana, and then I tried to activate an ability on a creature that triggers whenever I play a land. My opponent claimed the triggered ability shouldn't fire because playing a land is a special action and doesn't use the stack. Is my opponent right, or does the ability still trigger?

Your opponent is incorrect; the ability will definitely trigger. Playing a land is an action that does not use the stack, which means no player can respond to the act of playing the land itself. However, the game still registers the event of the land entering the battlefield. According to triggered ability rules, these abilities look for specific events or states to occur. Since the land has now entered the battlefield as a result of your action, the condition for the triggered ability is met. The ability goes onto the stack independently after the land play is complete, and your opponent will get priority to respond to that triggered ability once it is on the stack. The concrete outcome is that your triggered ability resolves normally unless countered by a spell or ability in response.
What happens if I show a card from my hand to pay for a spell? Does it stay face up until the spell is finished?

The card remains revealed from the time the spell is announced until the time it leaves the stack. For example, if you cast Silvergill Adept by revealing a Merfolk card from your hand as an additional cost, that Merfolk card stays visible while the spell is being cast and resolved.

I just cast a cascade spell and exiled a creature that attacks and deals combat damage to me during my turn. I have an enchantment that says I can choose any source of damage on the battlefield and deal 3 damage to it. My opponent points at their cascaded creature, but I argue the damage is actually coming from them personally or the original spell since cascade lets you cast it without paying its mana cost. Who is actually dealing the damage and what happens?

When your opponent cast their initial spell, the cascade ability resolved first by exiling cards from the top of their library until they found a nonland card whose mana value was lower, allowing them to cast that card without paying its mana cost. This placed the creature onto the battlefield under their control as a permanent game object. Later when combat damage is dealt, the rule for sources of damage applies next and states verbatim that the source of damage is the object that dealt it. Because cascade resolves first to place the creature into play, and then the source identification rule takes precedence when the damage actually occurs, the attacking creature itself is legally considered the source dealing that damage, not your opponent personally or their original spell. The concrete final game outcome is that they can successfully target their own cascaded creature with the enchantment effect, dealing 3 damage to it.
What happens if my creature gets turned face down by an opponent's spell?

Your creature stays on the battlefield, but its identity becomes hidden. Because some cards allow spells and permanents to be face down, the card remains that specific permanent, but you cannot see its name or abilities. For example, if an opponent uses a spell to turn your creature face down, it is still that same creature, just in a state where its power, toughness, and abilities are not visible until it is flipped back up.

I just tapped my creature to activate an ability that copies another activated ability I control, and then immediately cast a charm that makes the next instant or sorcery spell I cast this turn cost zero mana. My opponent claims the copied object should now be free because the charm resolved right after my tap ability started. Who is correct and what actually happens?

Your opponent is incorrect about how the game resolves this sequence. First, you must understand priority flow, which dictates that if a player takes a special action, that player receives priority afterward. This means you have full control over the timing of your actions in your main phase. However, when you look at how cost changes interact with the stack, the game rules explicitly state that casting a spell that alters costs won’t affect spells and abilities that are already on the stack. Because you activated your copying ability before casting the cost reducer, that ability was already sitting on the stack waiting to resolve. When the charm resolves later, its effect only applies forward-moving targets on the stack or future spells; it does not retroactively modify things already there. The priority rule governs when you can chain these actions together, but the cost alteration rule dictates the actual mechanical outcome and takes precedence for determining final costs. Final outcome: Your copying ability resolves exactly as originally printed without any mana reduction applied to it, your opponent cannot claim a discount on that copy, and they will receive their priority window only after your charm finishes resolving or you pass priority back to them.
If I search my library for a card and then shuffle, does the card I just found get mixed in with everything else while I am shuffling?

No, you do not include the found cards in the shuffle. All the cards in your library except those found are shuffled, and then the found cards are put into their new zone or position. For example, if an effect tells you to search for a land and then shuffle your library, you shuffle all the other cards first, and then you put the land you found into its designated spot.

I just cast a permanent that costs absolutely nothing to play during my turn, and it has an enters-the-battlefield trigger. At the end of my turn, after all my other triggers resolve, the game pauses for a moment before giving me priority again. Do I automatically get another zero-cost spell onto the battlefield right then, or do I need to wait? My opponent says since it costs zero, the rules handle it automatically during that gap between steps.

The pause you are seeing is actually the game processing triggers before anyone gets a chance to act. According to the turn-based sequence, each time a player would get priority, the game first performs all applicable state-based actions as a single event and repeats this process until no further state-based actions are performed and no abilities trigger, then the player receives priority. Because a spell whose mana cost is {0} must still be cast the same way as one with a cost greater than zero, it won't cast itself automatically. The turn-based timing sequence takes precedence first because it establishes when you actually have legal opportunities to take actions, whereas the zero-cost casting rule only dictates how the spell is executed during those windows. You must wait until you receive actual priority in your next phase to formally declare casting the spell. Once you announce it during a valid window, it will resolve normally without costing any resources.
Can I use a creature that is already tapped to pay for the harmonize ability?

No, you cannot. To use the harmonize ability, you must tap up to one untapped creature you control instead of paying the spell's mana cost. For example, if your only creature on the battlefield is a 2/2 that is already tapped from attacking, it does not meet the requirement of being an untapped creature to pay for the ability.

I just declared combat with my infect creature against an opponent who is sitting at zero life because of damage I dealt earlier. They argued that since my attacker only gives them poison counters instead of reducing their life total, they should stay alive long enough to use a counter spell or gain life from a blocker. Are they right that the game continues, and when do we actually check if someone loses?

Your opponent is incorrect because of how damage replacement effects interact with loss conditions. When your attacker deals combat damage, the rule for infect specifies that it causes the source’s controller to give the player that many poison counters instead of reducing their life total. However, state-based actions are checked immediately after all combat damage resolves to see if anyone has met a losing condition. The rule regarding life totals states that if a player has 0 or less life, that player loses the game. Because your opponent was already at zero life before your infect creature dealt its damage, and infect does not change life totals, the loss condition is met right then. You lose nothing from the infect mechanic in this specific case because the prior damage already put them at zero, triggering a loss before poison counters are even added. The concrete final game outcome is that your opponent loses the game immediately after the first combat damage step resolves, and the turn ends.
What happens when I tap an Exotic Orchard to add mana of any color my opponent could produce, but they only have one Island on the battlefield?

When you tap your Exotic Orchard, it will produce blue mana because that is the only type of mana your opponent's Island could produce. The rule states that the type of mana a permanent could produce includes any type of mana that an ability of that permanent would produce if the ability were to resolve at that time. Since an Island can produce blue mana, that becomes the available type for your Orchard.
If I offer to pay for my opponent's spell, can I still cast an instant right after making that offer?

Yes, you can. This works because if a player takes a special action, that player receives priority afterward. For example, if you offer to pay the mana cost for an opponent's creature, you get priority back immediately and can choose to cast an instant spell before they even respond to your offer.

We were playing a game and I tried to cast an instant from my hand during my opponent's turn because I had a creature on the battlefield that said it gives me flash. I put the spell on the stack and started paying the mana costs, using some Phyrexian mana symbols to pay with life instead of colored mana. Right after I tapped my lands but before I finished paying all the costs, my opponent destroyed my flash-creature. The game paused because we weren't sure if the spell still goes through or if I get refunded everything I already paid. What happens here?

The spell continues to resolve and your mana payments are final. Once you have moved past the proposal stage by putting it on the stack and beginning to pay costs, you may continue casting it as though it had flash even if those conditions stop being met, so destroying your creature does not rewind the game state or refund your life or mana. With the casting legally locked in, your cost payment is processed next under the mana addition rule, which states that if an effect would add mana represented by a Phyrexian mana symbol to a player’s mana pool, one mana of the color of that symbol is added to that player’s mana pool. Because the continuation permission applies first and locks your action in place, the Phyrexian mana resolves normally and completes your costs, so the spell will resolve fully after this step finishes.

I have this artifact that says whenever I sacrifice a creature, if my life total is 10 or less, I roll a d8 and draw cards equal to the result. My opponent forced me to gain 1 life so now I have 11 life. The ability went on the stack when I was at 10, but then I gained life before it resolved. Does my opponent think I still get to roll the die? Everyone is arguing about whether the roll happens.

The trigger checks your life total twice using an intervening if clause, not just once when the sacrifice occurs. When you sacrificed the creature, your life was 10 or less, so the ability triggered and went on the stack. However, before it resolves, the game checks the condition again because the text requires your life total to be 10 or less at resolution time. Since you now have 11 life, the condition is false when the ability attempts to resolve, causing the ability to be removed from the stack without resolving. This means you never reach the part of the ability that instructs you to roll the die. The rules also dictate that when an ability tells you to roll dice without providing a results table, you use the result exactly as indicated by the text, but that instruction is only reached if all intervening conditions are true at resolution. Since the life total condition failed, the trigger fizzles completely and you draw no cards or roll any dice. Your opponent is correct.

We have a heated argument at the table involving my commander. I want to use the Commander rule ability to move my commander to the command zone, and someone argued that because this is a special action, my opponent can cast an instant in response to me trying to do it since moving a creature usually triggers things. Another player countered that special actions don't go on the stack so you can't respond. Who is right, and how do these rules actually work together regarding timing?

The player who argued that special actions cannot be responded to is correct. Under the Commander variant additions to the normal rules, moving your commander to the command zone is allowed as a special action. This action type is governed by mechanics stating that special actions are things you may take when you have priority that do not use the stack and are separate from turn-based or state-based actions. Since moving your commander uses this special action classification, it does not enter the stack at any point. Your opponent cannot cast an instant in response to you initiating the move because there is no event on the stack to target. The concrete outcome is that once you have priority and declare the special action to move your commander, the movement occurs immediately without opportunity for responses. Your opponent can only act after you finish moving the commander and pass priority back to them, at which point they may attempt to interact with the board state or the commander now sitting in the command zone.

I'm mid-game and just attacked with my blue wizard that has intimidate. My opponent blocked with their gray artifact golem. The fight deals damage to both, but my wizard ends up with zero toughness while keeping a plus-plus counter on it. It also has undying. I know intimidate limits blocking, but I'm confused about whether the death trigger cares about that zero toughness or the counter it had before combat resolved. What actually happens?

The block is fully legal because the rule for this ability explicitly states that a creature with intimidate can’t be blocked except by artifact creatures and/or creatures that share a color with it, meaning your opponent’s gray artifact blocker bypasses that restriction entirely. When combat damage resolves and game rules check for lethal state changes, your wizard hits zero toughness and is put into the graveyard by the game board. At this point, the mechanics for death triggers take over by establishing that if a permanent leaves the battlefield this way, its last known information is derived from the game state before any of those state-based actions were performed. Because the game processes all simultaneous board checks completely before triggered abilities like undying can wait on the stack, the ability looks back at your wizard right before it died to count the tokens on it. It still had that plus-plus counter in that pre-death snapshot, so the trigger fires correctly. The final outcome is that your wizard safely returns to your hand carrying the plus-one counter.

I have two creatures attacking your planeswalker during my turn and you respond by using an instant that deals enough damage to kill one of my attackers. We both think the destroyed blocker just stays on the battlefield until the entire fight phase is over so I can use its last-minute abilities, but I am not sure how the timing actually works or if changing the combat flow affects who gets to attack or defend for the rest of this turn. What happens here?

The game does not wait for the entire combat phase to finish before removing damaged permanents. During the combat phase, the active player is the attacking player whose creatures may attack, while in a two-player game the nonactive player is the defending player whose planeswalkers they control and battles they protect may be attacked. However, removal does not pause for phase completion because state-based actions are checked throughout the game and are not controlled by any player. This continuous checking rule takes immediate precedence over the assumption that damaged creatures linger until combat closes. The exact moment lethal damage is dealt, the automatic check runs and puts that creature into your graveyard instantly. The concrete final outcome is that the destroyed attacker leaves the battlefield right away, it never reaches the end of the combat step to trigger last-minute abilities, you continue resolving combat with your remaining creatures against the same defending player, and the phase continues normally without any delay.
What happens when my opponent plays both Word of Command and Opposition Agent at the same time?

When Word of Command and Opposition Agent are both in play, they allow a player to exert control over an opponent for a short time. For example, if Player A has both cards active, they can use their combined effect to dictate the actions or turns of Player B for a limited duration.

I just cast a creature that rolls two dice when it enters the battlefield and keeps those numbers written on itself. It has an ability that says whenever this creature attacks, you may put plus one plus one counters on it equal to the sum of those stored numbers, unless it is already tapped. My opponent insists I have to make my decision right as it triggers, but I know I get to wait. How exactly do we track those dice and when does everything actually happen?

Your ability goes onto the stack immediately when it triggers because optional triggered abilities that say may go on the stack when they trigger, regardless of whether their controller intends to exercise the ability or not. You track the numbers by noting both the kind of die rolled and the result of that roll, which makes them a stored result permanently noted on the card, and any other ability referring to those notes is considered linked to this storage. The stacking order takes precedence for timing, so you wait until that trigger resolves to make your choice, at which point the game will use those specific stored numbers to calculate the effect unless the tapped condition interrupts it. Since it is untapped when you declare attackers, the ability will successfully resolve and you get to apply counters based on those exact stored results.

I just cast a sorcery that targets my opponent's Goblin and a Forest they control. Right before it resolves, an effect changes the Goblin's color to make it illegal for one part of the spell, but they sacrifice the Forest to something else. When my spell resolves, does it just fizzle completely like that triggered ability on our stack that says Whenever you attack with a creature, if it has trample, draw a card, which lost trample before resolving? Why do they handle this differently?

When your spell reaches resolution, the game follows its instructions and checks targeting legality first. The rules state that a target no longer in its zone or with changed characteristics is illegal, and only the parts of the effect tied to that illegal target are ignored while other sections resolve normally against valid targets. In contrast, an ability with an intervening if clause checks whether its condition is true when it triggers, goes onto the stack, then checks again as it resolves. The rules explicitly note that this mirrors the check for legal targets, but if the condition is false at resolution, the entire ability is removed from the stack and does nothing. The targeting legality evaluation happens during the resolution step to allow partial effects, while the intervening if clause acts as a strict double gatekeeper that cancels the whole effect when conditions shift. The concrete final game outcome is that your spell successfully resolves its remaining parts against legal targets, and the triggered ability completely fizzles leaving no tokens or cards drawn.
What happens when I try to read the text on an Omen card?

You read the instructions by looking at both sections of its unique visual layout. Omen cards have a two-part card frame, with a smaller frame inset within their text box. For example, when you play an Omen card, you will see that part of its effect is located in the main text area while another part is placed inside that smaller inset frame.

I’m in the middle of a match and my opponent just cast an effect that says all future spells they cast cost extra mana to play. They didn’t have anything else ready, so I’m trying to figure out what happens with the spell I already put on the stack earlier this turn, and whether I can still tap my creatures for mana right now before they get a chance to do anything else. What actually happens here?

The spell you already put on the stack will cost exactly what it originally said to cast because casting a spell that alters costs wont affect spells and abilities that are already on the stack. Regarding tapping your creatures, you have priority while their effect is waiting to resolve, and since tapping creatures for abilities or mana is treated as a special action rather than a spell, special actions are actions a player may take when they have priority that don't use the stack. Because special actions bypass the stacking system entirely, you can tap those creatures immediately right now. The rule governing special actions applies first in this timeline since it determines what you can legally do while your opponent’s effect sits on the stack, and once their effect resolves, the cost alteration rule takes full effect for all future casting attempts. Your pending spell resolves at its original cost, and you successfully tap your creatures right now to generate mana or activate abilities before moving forward.
What happens if I attack with a creature that has Mentor and I target another attacking creature that also has Mentor?

The target creature will get a counter, and then its own mentor ability will trigger. An ability that triggers when a creature mentors another creature triggers whenever the mentor ability resolves. For example, if you attack with a 3/3 with Mentor and target a 2/2 with Mentor, the 2/2 gets a counter when your 3/3's ability resolves, which then triggers the 2/2's own Mentor ability.
What happens to the life I should get from my lifelink creature if my opponent uses a spell to prevent some of the damage?

The amount of life you gain is based on the damage that is actually dealt after any prevention is applied. Damage is processed in a sequence where, second, damage is dealt as modified by prevention effects, and then, third, the results like lifegain are calculated. For example, if a 3/3 creature with lifelink is blocked by a 2/2 and an opponent prevents 2 damage to the blocker, the damage event is modified so only 1 damage is dealt. Since the results of the damage event are calculated from that 1 damage, you would only gain 1 life.

I have a face-up legendary creature in my command zone that got dealt twenty points of combat damage earlier this game. My opponent just cast something that turns it face down while it is still sitting in my command area. Right after that resolves, I also drop to negative life from one spell and hit ten poison counters from another at the exact same time. Do I lose from the old commander damage now that it flipped over, and do I actually die multiple times from all these things happening at once?

When a face-up object in the command zone is turned face down, it becomes a new object, which completely wipes all prior damage tracking and identity markers. This means your earlier commander damage disappears instantly as the card resets to zero. Meanwhile, dropping to negative life and hitting ten poison counters simultaneously triggers multiple loss conditions during the same state-based action check. The rules state that if multiple state-based actions would have the same result at the same time, a single replacement effect will replace all of them. This bundles your simultaneous deaths into one event so Lich's Mirror activates once to save you. First because the command zone reset changes what the permanent is before the game evaluates loss conditions. Next, the simultaneous loss bundling occurs during state-based resolution. Your final outcome is that you keep playing with a fully reset commander carrying zero tracked combat damage, and your replacement effect successfully replaces every simultaneous life total and poison loss to restore you to the game.
I am about to play a one-on-one match and I won the die roll to go first. What happens when my turn starts?

You skip your draw step. In a two-player game, the player who plays first skips the draw step of their first turn. For example, if you are playing a duel and decide to play first, your very first turn will consist of an untap step followed immediately by your main phase, without a draw occurring.
What happens if I use a creature's ability to add mana and then that creature is destroyed before I play a card that looks for a permanent that was activated this turn?

If the creature has been destroyed, it is no longer a permanent on the battlefield. Therefore, if a card requires you to target or choose a 'permanent that was activated this turn,' you can no longer select that creature because it no longer meets the requirement of being a permanent. For example, if you tap Llanowar Elves to add {G} and then Llanowar Elves is destroyed in response, you cannot cast a spell that targets 'a permanent that was activated this turn' by choosing Llanowar Elves, as it is no longer a permanent.

We just finished drafting our Commander Draft games decks and are ready to start. I feel like my mana is unbalanced compared to my opponent, can I take a special action at the beginning of the game to swap one card from my deck for a basic land so we both have equal resources?

Special actions occur when a player has priority but do not use the stack and cannot alter your deck. Commander Draft rules lock cards into a player's card pool once the draft ends, with deck construction following fixed parameters. Because neither special actions nor draft rules allow mid-game deck changes, the request to swap a card for a land is denied.

What happens if I have an enchantment that makes all my creature tokens 3/3 instead of 1/1, and then I use a spell that says instead of creating a 1/1 Zombie, create a 2/2 Zombie? Does it become a 3/3?

Yes, it becomes a 3/3. The sequence works like this: the spell first replaces the 1/1 Zombie with a 2/2 Zombie. Then, your enchantment sees that a token is being created and modifies that new event. This happens because replacement effects apply if an effect would create one or more tokens, and they also apply even if another replacement or prevention effect is the one creating the token. For example, if you have an enchantment that makes all tokens 3/3 and you play a spell that says instead of a 1/1 token, create a 2/2 token, the final result is a 3/3.

I'm playing Commander and my opponent has been attacking me with their commander for three turns straight. It says something like 'If this creature would deal combat damage to you, prevent that damage and put three +1/+1 counters on it instead.' The numbers add up to exactly twenty-one combat damage during those fights. Did I lose the game yet?

No, you did not lose. The creature uses a replacement effect that modifies its own combat damage output, which qualifies as a self-replacement effect that replaces part or all of that spell or ability’s own effect. When determining how to handle this event, these effects are applied before other replacement effects when checking for replacements, meaning the prevention happens first and the damage never actually reaches you. Because no damage is dealt to you, it does not count toward the commander damage tracking rule. That rule explicitly states that a player who’s been dealt 21 or more combat damage by the same commander over the course of the game loses the game. Since the damage was entirely replaced before dealing, zero points are recorded against your commander damage total. The concrete final outcome is that you remain in the game and survive indefinitely as long as no unmodified combat damage from that commander reaches you.

I just played a spell that forces all my creatures to attack if they can, but every single one of them already tapped for mana this turn so none actually attacked during combat. My opponent claims the ability that rewards me when creatures attack should still trigger because my creatures were forced to go in. What actually happens here and how does the game handle forced movement versus automatic checks?

Explain mechanically without citing rule numbers: When attackers are declared, the forcing effect satisfies the condition for any abilities that check if a creature 'had to attack.' However, tapped creatures cannot declare attackers, so they never actually enter combat. Because triggered abilities that care about attacking require the creature to actually declare and attack, those specific rewards will not fire. State-based actions simply check game states at static times and do not intervene in combat declaration or trigger timing.
What happens when a haunted creature stops being a creature, like if it turns into a land?

The enchantment still haunts the object. The rule states that the phrase creature it haunts refers to the object targeted by the haunt ability, regardless of whether or not that object is still a creature. For example, if an enchantment exiles a creature and then a spell like Karn, the Great Creator turns that creature into a land, the enchantment continues to haunt that land.

I attacked with a creature and my opponent blocked it with another one. After both sides figured out the damage exchange, I wanted to cast an instant spell at their artifact before combat damage triggered abilities resolved, but someone told me I have to wait for the triggers first. Also, one of my creatures has a triggered ability that says whenever it deals combat damage I can deal 2 damage to target noncreature permanent. Can I use that ability to destroy their land or enchantment now?

During the combat phase, any abilities that triggered on damage being dealt are put onto the stack before the active player gets priority, so you must wait for those triggers to resolve completely before casting your instant spell. Furthermore, objects can deal damage only to battles, creatures, planeswalkers, and players, which means damage simply cannot be dealt to an artifact, enchantment, or land. Because the timing rule applies first, your blockers trigger resolves and you receive priority afterward, but when you attempt to target the artifact with your creature ability, it fails immediately since artifacts cannot receive damage from objects. The combat triggers will resolve first, your damage effect will do nothing due to targeting restrictions, and then you finally get priority to cast your instant spell at a legal object.
My opponent just played a planeswalker. Can I attack that instead of them?

Yes, you can. Since planeswalkers can be attacked, you simply choose the planeswalker as your target during the combat phase. For example, if your opponent has a planeswalker on the field, you can declare an attack against that planeswalker with one of your creatures rather than attacking the player directly.

I just cast Giant Growth on my creature during combat so it gets +3/+3 until end of turn. My opponent blocks it with a creature that has wither and deals 4 damage to mine. Everyone is arguing about whether the +3/+3 disappears entirely or if my creature survives as something other than a zero toughness monster. What actually happens?

Your creature ends up as a one-over-one permanent. Even though Giant Growth temporarily boosts your creature, wither changes how combat damage resolves because wither dictates that damage dealt to a creature by a source with wither isnt marked on that creature but instead causes its controller to put that many minus one over minus one counters on it. Those counters represent a characteristic modification rather than unmarked damage. Under the continuous effect rules, the values of an object characteristics are determined by starting with the actual object and then applying all applicable continuous effects in a series of layers in the following order, with power or toughness changing effects processed together in Layer 7. Because both the temporary boost and the counter penalties fall into this same layer, they are mathematically added or subtracted simultaneously rather than one overwriting the other. Your creature started as a base two over two, gained three over three for a total of five over five, and then lost four from each stat due to the counters, leaving it at a final power and toughness of one over one. It remains on the battlefield until checked by state-based actions.
What happens when I flip a creature over during my turn?

When you flip a creature, you must ensure that it is clear at all times whether that permanent you control is flipped or not, both when it is untapped and when it is tapped. To achieve this, you should use common methods for distinguishing between flipped and unflipped permanents, such as using coins or dice to mark the object. For example, if you flip a creature using a morph ability, you should place a small die on top of it so your opponent knows its status.
What happens when a card tells me to flip a coin but I don't have one?

You can substitute another method of randomization, provided there are two possible outcomes of equal likelihood and all players agree to the substitution. For example, if you are resolving an effect from Akroan Skyguard, you and your opponent can agree to roll a six-sided die where even results count as heads and odd results count as tails.

We are playing a multiplayer Commander game and it is my first turn. I want to play one of my lands and then exile a card from my hand using the plot mechanic to generate mana for a combo finisher, but my friend said I have to wait until after drawing cards before taking any actions. Can I do those special moves right after untap, and will skipping or drawing cards change what I can do?

In a multiplayer Commander game, you do draw on your first turn because the starting player only skips the draw step in Two-Headed Giant formats. You must finish that draw step before reaching your main phases, which is when you get priority to take special actions. Both playing a land and using the plot mechanic are special actions you can take whenever you have priority and the stack is empty. Playing a land is limited to once per turn, while plotting just requires exiling a card from your hand during your turn. Plotting doesn't produce mana; instead, it exiles the card to trigger whatever unique one-time effect that specific card has on the battlefield. You can play your land and then plot sequentially in your main phase to run your combo.
If an opponent plays a spell that turns all my lands into creatures, will the land cards in my graveyard also become creatures?

No, they won't. Effects like turning lands into creatures apply only to permanents unless the card specifically states it affects other zones. For example, if you have a Plains in your graveyard and an opponent plays a spell that turns all lands into creatures, that Plains remains a land because it is no longer a permanent on the battlefield.

We are playing a Cube game and I cast an effect that brings a permanent directly from outside the game onto the battlefield. The effect specifically puts it onto the battlefield with damage marked on it equal to its toughness, so it should be at lethal state immediately. My opponent argued that since it dies instantly to automatic checks before it can do anything, it won't trigger any enters-the-battlefield abilities. However, I feel like the trigger should still happen. Who is right and what actually happens?

You are correct that the triggers will go on the stack even though the creature dies immediately. When your spell resolves and brings the card from outside the game into play, the permanent enters and its enters-the-battlefield ability creates a trigger. At this moment, no player has priority yet. The game performs a state-based action check before anyone gets a chance to act. This check sees the permanent with lethal damage and puts it into its owner's graveyard instantly. Only after all state-based actions are completed does the game look for triggered abilities waiting to go on the stack. Because the trigger was created when the card entered, and triggers go onto the stack after the state-based action loop finishes, your ability will still resolve successfully. The concrete outcome is that the creature dies upon entry due to lethal damage, but its enters-the-battlefield effect occurs anyway, allowing you to chain powerful abilities off a card that never stays alive.
We are playing as teams, but does that mean I am only allowed to attack one person at a time?

No, you can actually choose to attack more than one person. In the Team vs. Team variant, the attack multiple players option is used. For example, if you and your partner are facing two opponents, you can send your creatures to attack both of them during your combat step.
What happens if I roll a 4 to visit my attractions and the Grand Bazaar card has a lit-up 4?

The effect on that card will trigger. A visit ability triggers whenever you roll to visit your Attractions and the result matches one of the lit-up numbers. For example, since your roll of 4 matches the lit-up number on Grand Bazaar, you will resolve that specific effect.

My opponent cast a creature with four generic mana on it, but I have an effect that reduces generic costs by two. They paid the reduced cost and then claimed their enters-the-battlefield trigger should go right onto the stack immediately so they can respond to it before their spell finishes resolving. Is that correct?

Correct the math to show a four generic mana cost reduced by two becomes two. Clarify that the spell resolves first, state-based actions are checked, and only then does the next player receive priority to place the triggered ability on the stack.

I just blocked with my creature that has 'Whenever this creature becomes damaged, if it has been dealt damage by a single source this turn equal to or greater than its toughness, destroy that source.' My opponent attacked with two creatures. The first one did 2 damage and the second one did 3 damage to my blocker at the exact same time. My blocker has toughness 5. Did my ability trigger to destroy one of the attackers?

No, your ability does not trigger. State-based actions are checked immediately after combat damage is dealt. Your blocker has 5 damage marked on it in total from both attackers combined, which meets its toughness requirement, so it is destroyed and put into the graveyard due to lethal damage. This state-based action occurs before triggered abilities are put on the stack. For your ability to resolve, you must apply the rule regarding damage from multiple sources, which states that if an effect refers to the damage dealt by a specific source, it counts only that damage and ignores damage dealt simultaneously by other sources. Your ability requires damage equal to toughness from a single source. The first attacker dealt 2 damage, which is less than the blocker's toughness of 5. The second attacker dealt 3 damage, which is also less than 5. Even though the blocker died because the total damage reached its toughness, neither individual source dealt enough damage on its own to satisfy your condition. Therefore, no trigger occurs.
I am reading this card and it says to exile my creature, but I usually just put things in the graveyard. Does exile mean something different?

Yes, it does. When you resolve an effect that uses a specialized verb, you follow its specific definition as a game term rather than relying on standard English definitions. For example, if a card says to exile a creature, the creature is removed from the game entirely instead of being put into the graveyard. This happens because these keywords are specialized verbs used to trigger precise mechanical actions.
What happens if I play a card that makes me control my opponent's next turn, but then someone else plays a spell that skips their turn?

The effect stays active and waits for them. Any pending player-controlling effects wait until the player who would be affected actually takes a turn. For example, if you use a card to take control of your opponent's turn, but then an opponent plays a spell that skips that player's turn, you will still control their turn as soon as they finally get to take one.

I just cast an effect that makes me draw three cards, but I have two replacement effects on the battlefield modifying this draw event. One replaces a portion of it with creating tokens, and another changes one of those draws into putting counterstuffs on permanents. When exactly does the game check if my life total is too low or if my library runs out? Does it check after every single replacement?

The sequence follows a strict order where replacement resolution happens before any automatic game checks. First, if there are any parts of the original three-card draw event that haven't been replaced, those parts occur first. After those unreplaced draws finish, each card draw resulting from your replacement effects happens one at a time. State-based actions are checked throughout the game and are not controlled by any player, but they only trigger after the entire sequence completes rather than during it. Therefore, you will successfully create all your tokens and place all your counters before any loss conditions or library-empty checks occur. You will end up with the full board state you intended, plus whatever cards remain in your deck after the draw sequence finishes, and the game will only check for zero life or other death conditions at that exact moment.
If I force my opponent to discard a card, does it go into my graveyard or theirs?

The card goes into your opponent's graveyard. This is because each player has their own hand and graveyard. For example, if you cast a spell that forces an opponent to discard, the card moves from their hand into their personal graveyard rather than yours.

I’m in the middle of casting a spell that costs three total mana, but before I can actually tap my lands or pay anything, an effect on the board empties all the unspent mana sitting in my pool and gives it to my opponent instead. Can I still go through with casting this spell?

The game dictates that you must first determine and lock in the total cost of the spell before doing anything else related to payment. The rules for casting spells explicitly state that once the total cost is determined, any effects that directly affect the total cost are applied, then the resulting total cost becomes locked in, and if effects would change the total cost after this time, they have no effect. This lock-in step applies first and takes precedence over mana pool changes. Meanwhile, the rule for transferring unspent mana says that one card causes one player to lose unspent mana and another to add it, which empties the former player’s mana pool and causes the mana emptied this way to be put into the latter player’s mana pool. Because your pool is emptied by that transfer effect before you reach the step where you activate mana abilities or pay costs, you are left without any resources to cover the locked-in amount. Since partial payments are not allowed, you cannot complete the casting process. The concrete final outcome is that your attempt to cast the spell fails entirely and the spell never goes onto the stack.
Can I still use an Omen card's alternative name if a spell asks me to choose a card name?

Yes, you can. If an effect instructs a player to choose a card name and the player wants to choose an omen card's alternative name, the player may do so. For example, if you are playing a card that asks you to choose a card name and you have an Omen card with an alternative name, you can choose that alternative name.
What happens if I use an ability to exile a creature token?

When a token is moved to any zone other than the battlefield, such as being exiled or put into a graveyard, it immediately ceases to exist. This happens because a token that is in a zone other than the battlefield ceases to exist. For example, if you use an ability to exile a 1/1 Soldier token, that token does not stay in exile like a regular card; it simply disappears from the game entirely.

We are in a multiplayer game with four players and during my friend's turn, they just declared three attackers for each of us individually. Can I tap one of my untapped lands for mana right now to cast a counter-spell since it feels like the action is happening across the board?

Because your game involves more than two players, you are playing a multiplayer game which relies on optional rules for turn structure and priority passing that maintain distinct phases even when combat impacts multiple opponents simultaneously. Special actions are defined as actions a player may take only when they have priority and these actions do not use the stack, meaning you must be in a specific moment where the game grants you priority to perform any special action like tapping a land for mana. The requirement for priority in special actions takes precedence over the visual of simultaneous declarations; you do not hold priority during another player's declaration step regardless of how many players are affected. You cannot tap the land at this time, and once the attackers are declared, the game will proceed to the next step without your intervention. Final outcome: You lose the opportunity to tap the land, and you must wait until a later phase or turn where you receive priority before attempting special actions.
What happens if I cast an artifact with sunburst using only colorless mana?

The artifact will enter the battlefield with no counters on it. Sunburst only adds counters if one or more colored mana was spent on its costs. For example, if you cast a 3-mana artifact with sunburst using three colorless mana from lands like Ancient Den, it enters with zero counters because no colored mana was used.

I'm mid-cast and my opponent activated an effect that adds {R/G} mana to my pool while resolving their spell. I wanted to wait until after they were done to decide whether to take the red or generic half, but they told me I had to pick right then. They also said I couldn't respond by doing something else first. Am I stuck with whatever I pick at that moment?

When an effect adds mana represented by a hybrid symbol to your pool, you must choose one half of that symbol immediately as the effect resolves. Because no player has priority while a spell or ability is resolving, you cannot wait until resolution finishes to decide or cast spells in response. The choice locks in right then, adding either colored mana or colorless generic mana based on your selection.

I just attacked with a creature and my opponent activated an ability that says 'Redirect lethal damage from target creature to another target creature,' choosing my attacker as the source and their Commander as the destination. Their Commander has 5 toughness and takes the redirected lethal damage, ending up in the graveyard. My opponent then announced they are putting their Commander into the command zone. I argued that since the damage was redirected, the Commander shouldn't have actually died or triggered the command zone rule. Who is right?

Your opponent is correct, and their Commander goes to the command zone. The redirection effect replaces the lethal damage that would hit your attacker with the same lethal damage dealt to their Commander instead, so the Commander takes the damage and is destroyed. Because the permanent moved to the graveyard since state-based actions were last checked, the owner may put their Commander into the command zone as a replacement effect. The redirection did not prevent the death; it simply changed which permanent took the damage, resulting in the Commander dying and being eligible for the command zone return.
I'm trying to cast a spell that costs two generic mana and one red mana, but my opponent has an effect that reduces all costs by two blue mana. Do I still have to pay the red mana?

Yes, you still have to pay the red mana. Because the cost does not require blue mana, any reduction of colored mana that is not required by the cost is treated as generic mana. Since effects that reduce a cost by generic mana only affect the generic mana component, the two generic mana reduction will reduce your two generic mana to zero, but it will not affect the red mana component.
What happens when an opponent deals damage to my partner in a team game?

When your partner is dealt damage, the entire team's health decreases because each team has a shared life total that starts at 30 life. For example, if an opponent attacks your partner for 5 damage, your team's single life total moves from 30 down to 25.
What happens to a creature's abilities when I use the prototype cost instead of paying its full mana cost?

When you cast a spell using prototype, the card resolves and enters the battlefield with all its original abilities intact. This is because a prototype card's characteristics other than its power, toughness, and mana cost (and other than color) remain the same whether it was cast as a prototyped spell or cast normally. For example, if you cast a 4/4 creature with Trample using its prototype cost, it will still have Trample once it enters the battlefield.
What happens to the sequence of a turn when playing Commander?

The turn follows the standard rules because the Commander variant uses all the normal rules for a Magic game, with certain additions. One addition is that each deck is led by a legendary creature designated as its commander. For example, your turn will still proceed through the usual sequence of untapping, drawing a card, and then playing lands or casting spells.

My opponent is playing a commander and has already cast it once this game. He's trying to cast it again, but I have an enchantment on the field that says whenever a permanent enters the battlefield, its controller chooses between it entering with flying or being an artifact. He's confused about whether he pays the extra two mana he owes for his commander before or after he makes that choice, and if the choice changes how much he has to pay.

The player must pay the additional two mana for the commander tax during the casting process, because the tax is an additional cost required to cast a commander from the command zone. The replacement effect that allows the choice of flying or being an artifact only modifies how the permanent enters the battlefield, which happens after the spell has been cast and successfully resolves. Therefore, the player must pay the total mana cost including the extra two mana first. Once the commander actually enters the battlefield, the replacement effect will apply, and the player then makes their choice between flying or being an artifact before the permanent fully enters.

My opponent played a card that triggers whenever a creature enters the battlefield, and the trigger says to search my library for a creature and exile it. I just cast my commander, so when the trigger happens, can I pick my commander out of my deck?

No, you cannot pick your commander. At the start of the game, your commander is placed in the command zone and only the rest of your cards are shuffled into your library. Because of this, your commander is not part of your library. When the trigger resolves, it looks specifically for an object in the library as instructed. Since the rules for zone-change triggers state that an ability looks for objects in the specific zone it is directed toward, and your commander is currently in the command zone, the search will fail to find it. The final outcome is that you must search your library for a different creature, or the ability will do nothing if no other creatures are found.
My opponent just put a land down on his turn and then immediately cast a huge dragon. I told him he had to let me react to the land first, but he said I can't. Who is right?

Your opponent is correct. The rules distinguish between playing a card as a land and casting a card as a spell. Because playing a land is not casting a spell, it is handled as an action that does not grant your opponent priority to respond. Once the land is on the battlefield, the active player receives priority and can then choose to cast a spell. When your opponent casts the dragon, they are now casting a spell, and once that spell is on the stack, the rules state that the active player must pass priority to you before the spell resolves. The distinction of whether they are playing a land or casting a spell determines when you actually get your chance to react. The final outcome is that the dragon is on the stack and you can now cast a counterspell.

My opponent played a spell that gave my creature negative toughness so it has zero toughness now. I have another card out that says if any creature would go to the graveyard, it gets exiled instead. Does my creature still count as being put into the graveyard for some reason, or does it just get exiled?

The replacement effect applies first because it changes the event itself as it is happening. Replacement effects watch for a particular event that would happen and completely replace that event with a different one. Because your card uses the word instead, the event of the creature being put into the graveyard is replaced by the event of it being exiled. Since the replacement effect has changed the event, the state-based action that normally checks for creatures with zero toughness and puts them into the graveyard is looking at an exile event instead. The final outcome is that your creature goes directly to the exile zone.

I just cast this spell that costs one red mana or two life, and it says I choose a mode, but my opponent gets to pick the target if I choose the second one. My friend thinks that because I am paying life instead of adding red mana to my pool, I lose the right to go first when picking the modes. What actually happens?

Your friend is mistaken. The choice to add one mana of the color of the symbol to your pool or pay life is part of paying the cost for the spell. Once that cost is paid, the rules for opponent choices apply. If a spell requires both the caster and an opponent to do something at the same time, the caster always goes first. The final outcome is that you first decide how to pay the cost with mana or life, then you choose which mode you want, and finally, your opponent chooses the target while the spell is still being cast.

My friend is playing Commander and his big dragon is in the command zone. I used a spell to destroy it, but he says he can use a regeneration ability to keep it on the field. Since it's his commander, does it still work like a normal creature?

Yes. At the start of the game, each player puts their commander from their deck face up into the command zone and shuffles the rest of their deck to become their library. Once that commander is played onto the battlefield, it follows all standard rules for creatures, including regeneration. Regeneration is a replacement effect, which means that the next time the creature would be destroyed, instead of going to the graveyard, all damage marked on it is removed and its controller taps it. If it was attacking or blocking, it is also removed from combat. The final outcome is that the dragon stays on the battlefield, but it will be tapped and have no damage marked on it.

My opponent attacks with a creature that has Mentor and it targets one of my attacking creatures. My creature already has 2 damage marked on it and its toughness is 2. Does my creature die immediately because of the damage, or does the Mentor ability save it?

Your creature survives. When your opponent declares their attacker, the Mentor ability triggers and resolves to put a +1/+1 counter on your creature. This increases its toughness from 2 to 3. Although the damage is already marked on the creature, the game checks if the total damage marked on a permanent is greater than or equal to its toughness to see if it should be destroyed. Because the new toughness of 3 is now greater than the 2 damage marked on it, the creature does not have lethal damage and stays on the battlefield.

I just transformed my double-faced creature and realized it has an 'As this transforms' ability on its back face. Does that ability trigger when I flip the card, or does it wait until after the transformation is done?

This ability triggers during the transformation process itself, not after.
