The game rule states that if a double-faced card has an As transforms ability even if that ability applies after the transform occurs, the effect is applied while the permanent is transforming or converting, rather than afterward. For example, if you control a creature whose back face includes an ability like As this permanent transforms, create a 1/1 white Spirit token, triggering that transformation will cause the token to be created as part of the transform event, allowing you to use that token for costs or triggers immediately linked to the transformation, rather than waiting for the new face to fully enter the battlefield.

What happens if I attach a sticker to my attacking creature and it gets destroyed and sent to the graveyard before combat damage resolves? Will the sticker still be there when it comes back next turn?

No, the sticker will not follow it. According to the rules, stickers on an object are not retained as that object moves to a hidden zone like the graveyard, hand, or library. They only persist when moving to public zones such as the battlefield, exile, or command zone. This means the moment your creature hits the graveyard, all stickers attached to it are lost. For example, if you attach an enhancement sticker to your Goblin in the main phase and an opponent uses a removal spell to send it to the graveyard, the sticker is not retained with the card. If you later use a resurrection spell to return that exact card from the graveyard to your battlefield, it will enter completely blank without any stickers because the zone transition stripped them away.
Can I include a Vanguard card in my starting deck for our weekly draft tournament?

No, you cannot use that card outside of its designated format because the official guidelines clearly state that only the Vanguard casual variant uses vanguard cards. Draft requires a specific pool of legal cards, so any card excluded from that environment simply cannot be played. For example, if you open three booster packs and find a red and black Vanguard card alongside your draftable creatures, you must immediately set it aside and build your thirty-card deck using only the remaining eligible cards until you have enough to play legally.
What happens when I accidentally start to pay for a spell but realize mid-way that I don't actually have the mana or conditions to finish it?

When you realize your play is illegal after starting it, the game immediately undoes everything in a strict sequence. First, any payments you already made get canceled and returned to you. Second, no abilities trigger and no effects apply as a result of that undone action. Third, if you were casting a spell, it simply returns to the zone it came from. The rules confirm this by stating that the entire action is reversed and payments are canceled, with exceptions only for library-related actions. For example, imagine you tap three lands and put two generic mana into your pool to cast a sorcery, but then notice you forgot an additional colored mana requirement in the cost. Once you realize the mistake, the game reverts your tapped lands to untapped, removes the mana from your pool, and sends the spell back to your hand. Since the action is fully reversed, nothing else changes on the board and no triggered abilities go on the stack.

I am still trying to wrap my head around how this match started. We are playing with four people, and when I took that first mulligan, did I actually have to put cards on the bottom? And after I finished shuffling, why did I get to act before anyone else instead of the turn just moving on?

Since you are playing in a multiplayer game, the rules state that your first mulligan does not count toward the number of cards you must put on the bottom of your library or the number of mulligans you may take. This rule applies first to determine how many cards you keep during the mulligan process. Once you have completed the shuffle, because taking a mulligan is a special action, you receive priority afterward. This means that instead of the turn immediately passing, you are the one who gets to act next. The final outcome is that you keep your full hand size and you are the player who receives priority to act next in the game.

What happens when a spell turns my creature into a copy of another card but specifically instructs it to change its name to something new? Will abilities that trigger off my original creature still work?

When the continuous effect resolves, the game immediately updates the permanent identity in the current state. This changes the text that represents the object’s name, and that object loses any names it had and has only the specified name. Because the identifier is replaced, any new triggers that look for your original creature by name will fail to match, though abilities already on the stack from previous turns remain valid. For example, if your Tarmogoyf had its name changed to Bird by a continuous effect, an ability that triggers whenever Tarmogoyf attacks would no longer recognize it, but a spell that targets a Blue creature would still work because the creature's color has not changed.
Can I tap my lands for mana right in the middle of resolving a spell that costs multiple colored mana, or do I have to pay everything before it starts resolving?

You certainly can. According to the rules, a player may activate a mana ability whenever they are casting a spell or whenever a rule or effect asks for a mana payment, even in the middle of casting or resolving a spell. This means you can tap lands to pay costs at any point during these processes. For example, if a spell is resolving and its text says 'Pay {1}: Target creature gets +1/+1', you may tap a land for mana to pay that {1} while that part of the spell's resolution is happening.

We are playing a four-player Conspiracy Draft and I have a creature that can assign combat damage to more than one opponent. If I want to block an attacker, can my blocker engage a creature coming from someone sitting across the table, or is there a restriction based on where players sit?

Yes, your blocker can absolutely engage an attacker from across the table. This format treats every player as being within range of everyone else, so seating distance does not restrict combat or targeting. Because the game defaults to a Free-for-All setup without limited range of influence, you can block any attacker regardless of position, and your creature can attack multiple opponents in the same combat phase if its ability allows it. For example, imagine Player A has a creature that wants to attack; Player C, sitting directly opposite Player A, is fully eligible to declare their own creature as a blocker for that attacker, and Player A can assign damage from that creature to both Player C and another opponent simultaneously.
What happens if a card says my life becomes 10 and I already have 15?

When an effect sets your life total to a specific number, you gain or lose the necessary amount of life to end up with that new total. For example, if you are at 15 life and a spell says your life becomes 10, you will lose exactly 5 life to reach that new total.
What happens if I use an ability that tells me to sacrifice a creature with three +1/+1 counters to put its counters on another creature?

The counters do not actually move from one object to the other. Instead, you put the same number of each kind of counter the first object had onto the second object. For example, if you sacrifice a creature with three +1/+1 counters to an ability that puts its counters on a target creature, the original creature is sacrificed and goes to the graveyard, and then you place three new +1/+1 counters on the target creature.
What happens if I have a card that says at the beginning of my upkeep, if I have 40 or more life, I win the game, but an opponent uses a spell to make me lose life before it actually happens?

The ability will not resolve. When the trigger event occurs, the ability checks whether the stated condition is true. If you have 40 life, the ability triggers and goes on the stack. However, as it resolves, the game checks the stated condition again. If your life is now 39, the ability is removed from the stack and does nothing. For example, if you have 40 life at the start of your upkeep, the ability triggers. If an opponent plays a spell to make your life 39 before the ability resolves, you will not win.
What happens when I make a token and then my opponent takes control of it?

First, you use a spell or ability to create the token, and the token enters the battlefield under your control. Because the player who creates a token is its owner, that token belongs to you. If your opponent then uses an effect to take control of it, they control it, but you remain the owner. For example, if I create a 1/1 Soldier token, it is mine; if you use a spell to take control of that Soldier, it still belongs to me.
If my spell says to target an object, can I choose my opponent's creature or a land they have?

Yes, you can. An object is a broad term that includes many different things in the game, such as cards, tokens, spells, and permanents. Since creatures and lands are both considered permanents, they qualify as objects. For example, if you cast an instant that targets an object, you could choose to target a creature or a land on the battlefield.
Can I find dungeon cards if I am opening booster packs for a regular tournament set?

No, you cannot. Because dungeon is a card type seen only on nontraditional Magic cards, these cards do not appear in standard drafting or tournament-legal booster packs. For example, if you are opening a pack from a traditional set like Bloomburrow, you will never find a card with the dungeon type inside.
I just used an ability that says incubate 3. What exactly is this token I just got, and how do I make it a creature?

When you incubate 3, you create an Incubator token that enters the battlefield with three +1/+1 counters on it. This token is double-faced; its front face is a colorless artifact with the ability {2}: Transform this token, and its back face is a 0/0 colorless Phyrexian artifact creature named Phyrexian Token. To make it a creature, you must pay 2 mana to transform it. For example, if you incubate 3, you first get an artifact with three +1/+1 counters. You can then pay 2 mana to flip it over, turning it into a 0/0 creature that still has those three counters, making it a 3/3.
What happens if I go first in a one-on-one game? Do I still get to draw a card?

You will not draw a card on that turn. In a two-player game, the player who plays first skips the draw step of their first turn. For example, if you are playing a match against one opponent and you go first, your turn begins, you pass through the draw step, but you do not take a card from your library.
What happens if I have a creature copying my dragon, and it uses an ability that mentions the dragon's name, but then the creature stops being a copy of the dragon? Does the ability still work?

The ability will still work. When an effect refers to a permanent by name, the effect still tracks that permanent even if it changes names or becomes a copy of something else. For example, if an Unstable Shapeshifter is copying Olivia Voldaren and uses an ability that says Olivia Voldaren deals 1 damage to another target creature, the Shapeshifter will still deal that damage even if it is no longer a copy of Olivia Voldaren when the ability resolves.
What happens to my spell if my opponent uses a counterspell on it?

When a spell is countered, it is put on top of its owner's graveyard. The rules specify that any object that is countered is put on top of its owner's graveyard. For example, if you cast a creature spell and your opponent plays Counterspell, that spell goes directly to your graveyard instead of entering the battlefield.
What happens when we try to add several different house rules like extra card draws and also use a specific way of playing called King of the Hill?

You can combine many different house rules if they are considered options, but you must stick to only one style of play. The rules consist of a series of options that can be added to a multiplayer game and a number of variant styles. This means you can use multiple options, such as adding an extra card draw, while playing the King of the Hill variant, but you cannot add a second variant like Team Play because a single game may use multiple options but only one variant.
What happens when I cast a spell that says at the beginning of my next upkeep I draw a card? Do I get to draw it right away?

No, you do not draw the card immediately. The spell creates an effect that instructs a player to do something later in the game rather than as the spell itself resolves. For example, if you cast a spell with that text, the spell first resolves and moves to your graveyard without you drawing anything. You then wait for your next upkeep to begin. When that upkeep starts, the delayed ability triggers and finally tells you to draw the card.
Can I use the special abilities of an Omen card while it is still in my hand?

No, you cannot. An omen card has only its normal characteristics in every zone except the stack, and even on the stack, it must be acting as an Omen to have those special properties. For example, if you are holding an Omen card in your hand, it is just a normal card and does not possess any of its special Omen traits until it is on the stack being played as an Omen.
What happens if I have a card turned face down and then use an ability to make it a copy of my opponent's creature? Does it stay a copy when I turn it face up?

When you turn the permanent face up, its copiable values become the values it copied from the other permanent. For example, if your face-down creature is copying an opponent's 5/5 Dragon and you play a spell to turn it face up, it will become a 5/5 Dragon with all the characteristics of that Dragon.
I have a card in my hand that has foretell on it. Do I have to wait until my main phase to pay the two mana and exile it face down, or can I do it whenever I want during my turn?

You can do it at any point during your turn as long as you have priority. A player who has a card with foretell in their hand may pay {2} and exile that card face down as a special action, and they may take this action any time they have priority during their turn. For example, if you have a card like Temporal Trespass in your hand, you do not need to wait for your main phase; you could pay {2} and exile it face down during your combat step instead.
What happens if an effect turns one of my enchantments face down?

When a face-up permanent is turned face down by an ability that does not list any characteristics for that object, it becomes a 2/2 face-down creature with no text, no name, no subtypes, and no mana cost. For example, if you have an enchantment like Sanguine Bond on the battlefield and an effect turns it face down without specifying new traits, it is now just a 2/2 creature that has no abilities or name.
If I have a card in my hand that has two different faces, am I allowed to look at the back of it?

Yes, you are. Players who are allowed to look at a double-faced card may look at both sides of that card. For example, if you have a card like Delver of Secrets in your hand, you can look at both its creature side and its transformed side whenever you want.
What happens to my commander at the very beginning of a Commander game?

Instead of being shuffled into your deck, your specially designated cards will start the game in the command zone because Commander is one of the casual variants where this occurs. For example, if you are playing with a legendary creature as your commander, it sits in that command zone waiting to be cast rather than being hidden in your library.
What happens if I try to use a spell to attach an Aura that normally only works on creatures onto a land instead?

The Aura will not move. An Aura, Equipment, or Fortification cannot be attached to an object or player it could not enchant, equip, or fortify. If an effect tries to attach an Aura to an object it cannot be attached to, the Aura does nothing and stays where it is. For example, if you try to use a spell to attach an Aura like Bear Umbra onto a Forest, the Aura will remain in its current location instead of moving to the land.
What happens to my creature's damage and its temporary power boost when the turn ends?

At the end of the turn, two things happen simultaneously: all damage marked on permanents is removed and all until end of turn and this turn effects end. This action does not use the stack. For example, if your 2/2 creature took 1 damage from a spell and you also gave it +2/+2 until end of turn with an enchantment, the 1 damage is wiped away and the +2/+2 bonus disappears at the same time.
What happens if I play an Attraction card during my turn?

When you control one or more Attractions and it is your precombat main phase, you roll to visit them. This is a turn-based action that does not use the stack, so it occurs automatically as part of the turn sequence. For example, if you play The Grand Labyrinth during your first main phase, you will perform the roll to visit it during that same precombat main phase.
I'm using a creature that explores and I reveal a land card on top of my library. Do I still get the +1/+1 counter?

No, you do not get the +1/+1 counter if you reveal a land card. When you explore, if a land card is revealed, you put that card into your hand instead of putting a +1/+1 counter on the permanent. For example, if your creature explores and reveals a Forest, you put the Forest into your hand, but the creature does not get a +1/+1 counter.
I found some scheme cards while playing with my friends; can anyone just pick one up and start using it?

No, you cannot. Only a scheme card may be set in motion during an Archenemy game, and only the archenemy is allowed to set a scheme in motion. For example, if you are playing a standard game of Magic that isn't specifically an Archenemy game, no one can use these cards. Even in an Archenemy game, a player who is not the archenemy cannot set a scheme in motion.
What happens if a spell makes my creature's toughness zero? Do I get a chance to respond?

Certain game actions happen automatically whenever certain conditions are met and do not use the stack. This means you cannot respond to them because they occur as soon as the condition is satisfied. For example, if you cast a spell that reduces a creature's toughness to zero, that creature is moved to the graveyard immediately without any opportunity to cast an instant in response.
Can I use my creatures to attack my opponent?

Yes, you can. Because creatures can attack and block, they are able to participate in combat by attacking. For example, if you have a 2/2 Soldier on the battlefield, you can declare it as an attacker during your turn to try and deal damage to your opponent.
What happens when I am done with all my spells and just want to let the next person play?

To end your turn, you must pass through the ending phase. The ending phase consists of two steps: the end step and the cleanup step. For example, if a card effect requires you to discard down to your hand size at the end of your turn, that would occur during the cleanup step.
If a spell lets me put a land onto the battlefield, can I still play a land from my hand this turn?

Yes, you can. Effects that allow you to put lands onto the battlefield are not the same as playing a land and do not count as a land played during the current turn. For example, if you use a spell to put a Mountain onto the battlefield, you are still allowed to play a Forest from your hand as your normal land for the turn.
What happens if it is daytime and I end my turn without casting any spells?

It will become night during your opponent's untap step. The game checks to see if the previous turn's active player cast any spells, and if it is day and the previous turn's active player did not cast any spells during that turn, it becomes night. For example, if you play a land and then pass the turn without casting anything else, the sun will set during your opponent's next untap step.
My friend thinks we should start with 20 life since we are playing Commander, but that doesn't seem right. Is it actually 20?

No, in a Commander game, each player's starting life total is 40. For example, if you sit down to play a multiplayer Commander match, you and your opponents should all begin the game with 40 life rather than the standard 20.

I have a spell with convoke that costs {2}{G}. I have two green creatures and a blue creature on the field. Can I tap both green creatures to pay for the {G} part, and then use the blue creature to help pay for the {2} part?

Yes, you can. Convoke allows you to tap an untapped creature of a specific color to pay for each colored mana in a spell's total cost, while any untapped creature can be used to pay for generic mana. For example, with a spell costing {2}{G}, you would tap one green creature for the {G} and then use your other green creature and your blue creature to pay for the {2} generic mana.
Can I still trigger an ability that says 'whenever you attack a player' if my creature is blocked immediately?

Yes, you can. This is because a player has attacked a player if they declared one or more creatures as attackers attacking the second player. For example, if you declare a creature to attack and your opponent blocks it with a 1/1, you have still attacked because the declaration of those attackers is what triggers the effect.
I see this pawprint symbol on my spell, do I have to pay some kind of special energy or mana for it?

No, you do not need to pay anything for that symbol. The pawprint symbol is used to indicate the modes on some modal spells and does not represent a cost or mana. For example, if you cast a spell with the pawprint symbol that lets you choose between drawing a card or destroying an artifact, you do not spend any mana to use that symbol; you just use it to decide which effect occurs.
Can my teammate sit on the opposite side of the table to watch the other players?

No, you cannot. Each team sits together on one side of the table. For example, if you and your partner are playing as a team, you must both be seated on the same side of the table instead of sitting across from each other.
If I am attacking, can I pick one creature to hit a planeswalker and another creature to hit a player?

Yes, you can. When declaring attackers, you choose a defending player, a planeswalker controlled by a defending player, or a battle protected by a defending player for each creature to attack. For example, if your opponent has both a Planeswalker and a Battle on the field, you can declare one of your attacking creatures to target the Planeswalker and another to target the Battle.
What happens if I play a card that has a green circle next to its type line but the mana cost only shows generic numbers?

The card is treated as a green card. Because a color indicator is a circular symbol that appears to the left of the type line, and the color of that symbol defines the card's color or colors, the card enters the battlefield as a green permanent. For example, if you play a creature with a green circle and a cost of 4 generic mana, it will be affected by effects that target green creatures.
What happens to my creature if an effect turns it face down?

When a face-up phenomenon card is turned face down, it becomes a new object, meaning the previous version of the card has been replaced on the battlefield. For example, if you have a face-up phenomenon card and an effect turns it face down, the new face-down card is not that same card anymore.
What happens if I want to play with a specific legendary creature as my leader?

If you choose to do that, each deck is led by a legendary creature designated as that deck's commander. You select that creature to lead your deck, and then the game proceeds using all the normal rules for a Magic game. For example, if you pick Atraxa, she becomes the designated leader of your entire deck.
My opponent has Void Winnower on the battlefield, so they cannot cast spells with even mana values. I have a Rolling Thunder in my hand that costs XRRR. Can I still start casting it?

Yes, you can. Even though Void Winnower prohibits casting spells with even mana values, you are allowed to begin casting if the choices made during the spell's proposal could cause those qualities to change. Because the value of X is a choice you make and choosing an odd number for X would result in an odd mana value, you may legally begin to cast the spell.
What happens when we start a game of Conspiracy Draft?

When you begin a Conspiracy Draft, the game is set up as a multiplayer Free-for-All where you have the option to attack multiple players and there is no limited range of influence. This means that once your turn reaches the combat phase, you can immediately declare attacks against multiple opponents. For example, if there are four people playing, you could declare an attack against the player on your left and then also declare an attack against the player on your right.
What happens if my commander gets exiled?

If your commander is put into exile, its owner may put it into the command zone because if a commander is in exile and was put into that zone since the last time state-based actions were checked, its owner may put it into the command zone. For example, if an opponent casts a spell that exiles your commander, you can move it back to the command zone instead of it staying in exile.
I am attacking with an Islandwalk creature and my opponent has an Island out. Can they block me with their big creature?

No, they cannot. A creature with landwalk can't be blocked as long as the defending player controls at least one land with the specified land type. For example, if you attack with a creature that has islandwalk and your opponent has an Island, that creature cannot be blocked by their big creature or any other creature.
What happens if I play a card that gives me two extra turns at once?

If you are given multiple extra turns, the extra turns are added one at a time. This means you will finish your current turn and then take your first extra turn, followed by your second extra turn immediately after the first one ends. For example, if a spell grants you two extra turns, you would complete your current turn, play through an entire extra turn, and then start another one.
What happens when I have a card that says I must attack with everything, but another card makes my creatures unable to tap?

You cannot attack because your creatures are unable to tap. This is because certain continuous effects affect game rules rather than objects, such as an effect that says a creature must attack this turn if able. These effects are applied after all other continuous effects have been applied. For example, if you have an enchantment that forces an attack but also have a card like Sleep that prevents tapping, the rule-changing requirement is applied last, and since the creatures cannot tap, they cannot attack.
My enchantment says I can sacrifice it to make my opponent draw cards, but they exile it before the ability finishes. Do they still get the cards?

No, they do not draw the cards. The ability requires you to sacrifice the enchantment as a cost. If the enchantment is exiled before the ability resolves, you are unable to pay that cost. Because you cannot complete the action, the 'If you do' clause fails. For example, if you have Standstill and an opponent exiles it in response to its trigger, you can no longer sacrifice it when the ability resolves, so your opponents will not draw any cards.
I have an enchantment that gives my creatures +1/+1, but then I attach an equipment to a creature that says it loses all abilities. Which effect is applied last?

The equipment effect is applied last. An Aura or Equipment receives a new timestamp each time it becomes attached to an object, and because effects are applied in order of their timestamps, the newer effect is applied after the older one. For example, if you have an enchantment that grants +1/+1 and then attach an equipment that says a creature loses all abilities, the equipment's effect will be applied after the enchantment's effect because it received a new timestamp upon attachment.
What happens when I turn a face-down creature face up that has an ability saying 'As this creature is turned face up, create a 1/1 token'?

You create the token during the process of turning the card. The rule states that if a face-down permanent would have an ability starting with 'As [this permanent] is turned face up...' after it's turned face up, that ability is applied while that permanent is being turned face up, not afterward. For example, as you flip the creature over, the token is generated during that transition rather than as a separate event once the card is already fully face-up.
What happens if I have ten cards in my hand at the start of my turn?

If your hand contains more cards than your maximum hand size, you must discard enough cards to reduce your hand size to seven. This is a turn-based action that does not use the stack. For example, if you start your turn with ten cards in hand, you will immediately discard three cards to bring your hand back down to seven before any other actions can be taken.
What happens if my creature with ingest hits an opponent during combat?

When your creature deals combat damage to a player, that player exiles the top card of their library. For example, if you attack with a creature that has ingest and it successfully deals damage to your opponent, they must exile the top card of their deck rather than putting it into their graveyard.
What happens once I've paid the cost to exile a card using suspend?

When you use suspend, you move the card to the exile zone with time counters on it. At the beginning of your upkeep, if this card is suspended, remove a time counter from it. You repeat this process each of your turns. When the last time counter is removed from this card, if it's exiled, you may play it without paying its mana cost if able. For example, if you suspend a creature with 3 counters, you will remove one at the start of your first upkeep, one at the start of your second, and when the third is removed, you can cast the spell for free.
What happens to a card that says whenever a player rolls one or more dice, they draw a card, when someone rolls the planar die?

The ability will trigger. When the planar die is rolled, it counts as rolling one or more dice, which causes any ability that triggers whenever a player rolls one or more dice to trigger. For example, if you have an enchantment with that text, the player will draw a card immediately after the planar die is rolled.
Can I include two copies of a powerful card like Sol Ring in my Commander deck?

No, you cannot. Other than basic lands, each card in a Commander deck must have a different English name. This means you are limited to one copy of any non-land card. For example, even though Sol Ring is a very common card to use, you can only include exactly one copy in your 100-card deck.
What happens to my creature's power if an opponent plays an enchantment that says all creatures are 1/1s?

Your creature's power becomes 1 immediately and stays that way as long as the enchantment is on the battlefield. This occurs because a continuous effect modifies characteristics of objects for a fixed or indefinite period. For example, if you have a 5/5 dragon and your opponent plays an enchantment like Humility, your dragon becomes a 1/1 and remains a 1/1 until Humility leaves play.
Can I pick two different players to attack during a Grand Melee match?

No, you cannot. In the Grand Melee variant, the option to attack multiple players is not used. This means when you declare attackers, you must choose one single opponent as your target. For example, if you have a group of creatures ready to attack, you have to pick one player to face them all rather than splitting your forces between two different opponents.
I have a spell that says target two creatures. Can I just pick my one huge dragon twice?

No, you cannot. Because the word target is only used once in that instruction, you must select two different creatures. The rules state that the same target cannot be chosen multiple times for any one instance of the word target. For example, if a spell says target two creatures, you must pick two separate creature cards on the battlefield.
If an effect tells me to put a card onto the battlefield transformed, does it land face up or face down?

It enters the battlefield with its back face up. If a spell or ability puts a double-faced card onto the battlefield transformed or converted, it enters the battlefield with its back face up. For example, if an effect says a creature enters the battlefield transformed, you would place it on the table showing its back side.
What happens if I cast a spell that deals damage to my opponent, but I want it to hit their planeswalker instead?

The damage will go directly to your opponent. A previous rule allowed for a redirection effect where noncombat damage that would be dealt to an opponent could be dealt to a planeswalker under that opponents control instead, but this has been removed. For example, if you cast Lightning Bolt and target a player, the damage must hit that player and cannot be redirected to any planeswalkers they might have.
What happens when an opponent plays a spell that ends the combat phase while my creature has a buff that lasts until end of combat?

The buff will expire immediately. When an effect ends the combat phase, effects that last until end of combat expire as the game skips straight to the next phase. For example, if you have a creature with a +2/+2 bonus that lasts until end of combat and your opponent plays a card that ends the combat phase, that creature will lose its bonus immediately.
Can I turn my creature face up whenever I want if it was turned face down by an opponent?

No, you can only do so if the effect that turned it face down also granted you that ability. The rules state that the ability or rules that allow a permanent to be face down may also allow the controller to turn it face up, but they do not guarantee it. For example, if an opponent uses a spell to turn your creature face down and that spell does not mention turning it face up, you cannot flip it back over yourself.
I have a card that says 'Whenever you expend 3, gain 3 life.' If I cast a 2-mana spell and then a 1-mana spell, does the life gain happen?

Yes, it does. The ability triggers if you pay a cost to cast a spell and the amount of mana spent this turn before paying that cost was less than 3 but becomes at least 3 after paying it. In your example, before casting the 1-mana spell, you had only spent 2 mana. After paying for that 1-mana spell, you have spent a total of 3 mana this turn, which means you have now spent at least 3 mana and triggered the ability.
My creature has an aura on it that says it protects it from being destroyed. If my opponent uses a spell to destroy my creature, does the creature die?

No, the creature stays on the battlefield. Because of the umbra armor ability, if the enchanted permanent would be destroyed, instead all damage marked on it is removed and the aura itself is destroyed. For example, if your creature has 3 damage marked on it and an aura with umbra armor, and an opponent casts a spell like Murder to destroy the creature, the creature remains alive, the 3 damage is wiped off, and the aura goes to the graveyard instead.
Can I rearrange the cards in my graveyard so that a specific card is on top before I use an effect to look at it?

No, you cannot. The order of objects in a graveyard can't be changed except when effects or rules allow it. For example, if you have a Forest and a Lightning Bolt in your graveyard, you are not allowed to move the Forest to the top to ensure it is the first card you see when you use an effect that looks at the top card of your graveyard.
What happens if I play a card face down and then realize I forgot what it was?

You can simply look at the card because you are allowed to look at a face-down permanent you control. For example, if you have a creature that was played face down and is sitting on the battlefield, you can look at it to confirm its identity and abilities.
What happens if the person controlling the plane leaves the game?

If the current planar controller would leave the game, the next player in turn order that wouldnt leave the game becomes the planar controller, and then the old planar controller leaves. For example, if Player A is the active player and current planar controller but must exit the game, the next player in turn order who is still playing will become the new planar controller before Player A actually leaves.
What happens if an artifact asks me to pick a color when it enters, but then has two different abilities that use that same color? Do I have to make a second choice?

You only make the choice once. Because an ability may be part of more than one pair of linked abilities, your initial selection is used to satisfy all dependent effects. For example, when you play Paradise Plume and choose Blue, that single choice is immediately applied to both the life gain trigger and the tapping ability to add Blue mana.
I cast a spell to destroy a creature, but before it actually happens, my opponent gives that creature protection from the color of my spell. Does the spell still work?

No, the spell will not resolve. When a spell or ability begins to resolve, it checks whether its targets are still legal. If a target is no longer in the zone it was in or if its characteristics have changed, such as gaining protection from the color of your spell, the spell cannot resolve and is put into its owner's graveyard. For example, if you cast Sorin's Thirst to deal 2 damage to a creature and gain 2 life, but that creature gains protection from black before the spell resolves, the entire spell fails and you do not gain any life.
What happens if I use an ability that says Whenever you draw a card, target player loses 1 life, and this can't be countered? Can my opponent still use a spell to stop the life loss?

Yes, the instruction that the ability cannot be countered works while the ability is on the stack. Even though the instruction itself is not considered part of the effect, it still functions to prevent your opponent from using a spell like Counterspell to stop the life loss. For example, if you play a creature with an ability that says Whenever you draw a card, target player loses 1 life and this ability cannot be countered, your opponent cannot use a spell to stop that life loss from happening.
What happens if my creature's toughness becomes 0? Can I cast a spell to save it before it dies?

The creature is moved to the graveyard because state-based actions are checked throughout the game and are not controlled by any player. This means that once the toughness reaches zero, the game automatically processes the death before anyone can take another action. For example, if an opponent casts a spell that gives your 1/1 creature -1/-1, the creature will be put into the graveyard immediately after the spell finishes resolving, and you cannot cast a spell to save it in response to its toughness hitting zero.
Can I still use the abilities on my plane if it is sitting in my command zone?

Yes, you can. As long as a plane card is face up in the command zone, its static abilities affect the game, its triggered abilities may trigger, and its activated abilities may be activated. For example, if your plane in the command zone has an activated ability that says tap to add one mana, you can still use that ability even though it is not currently in play.
If I use a spell that deals 3 damage to a planeswalker, what happens to its loyalty counters?

Damage dealt to a planeswalker results in that many loyalty counters being removed from it. For example, if you cast a spell that deals 3 damage to a planeswalker with 5 loyalty, you remove 3 loyalty counters, leaving that planeswalker with 2 loyalty remaining.
My friend and I are playing together against another pair of players. Can I split my attacks so that one creature hits one opponent and another creature hits the second opponent?

Yes, you can. In a team vs. team match, the attack multiple players option is used by default. For example, if you control a Knight and a Wizard, you can declare the Knight attacking the first player and the Wizard attacking the second player on the opposing team.
What happens if an opponent targets a creature in my graveyard with a spell? Since it is not on the battlefield, who is controlling it?

A card does not have a controller unless that card represents a permanent or a spell. When an opponent targets a creature in your graveyard, they are targeting a card that is neither a permanent nor a spell. If an effect asks for the controller of such a card, you use its owner instead. For example, if an opponent plays a spell that requires them to interact with the controller of a creature in your graveyard, the game treats you as the controller because you are the owner.
I have an effect that lets me pick a source to prevent damage from next. Can I pick a creature spell that is still on the stack before it enters the battlefield?

Yes, you can. When an effect requires a player to choose a source of damage, they may choose a spell on the stack. If the player chooses a permanent spell, the effect will apply to any damage dealt by that spell and any damage dealt by the permanent that spell becomes when it resolves. For example, if you choose a Llanowar Elves spell on the stack, the next time that spell or the Llanowar Elves creature deals damage to you, that damage will be prevented.
Can I pick the name of a token when a card asks me to choose an artifact card name?

No, you cannot choose the name of a token unless it is also the name of an actual card in the Oracle reference. Even if there is a Treasure token on the battlefield, you must choose the name of a real artifact card. For example, if you use Dispossess and need to choose an artifact card name, you could pick Sol Ring, but you cannot pick Treasure because Treasure is a token name rather than the name of a specific card.
Hey, since we are already halfway through this match, can we decide that the winner gets my most expensive card instead of just winning the game?

No, you cannot change the terms of the game to include ante once a match is underway. While playing Magic games for ante is considered an optional variation on the game, it is strictly forbidden under the Magic: The Gathering Tournament Rules. For example, if you are in the middle of a sanctioned tournament match, you cannot decide mid-game to wager cards as part of the outcome.
What happens to a creature's characteristics when it flips over to its back face?

The creature takes on the characteristics of its back face. While a nonmodal double-faced permanent has its back face up, it has only the characteristics of its back face, though its mana value is still calculated using the mana cost of its front face. For example, if a creature with 2 toughness transforms into a creature with 5 toughness, it will have 5 toughness while the back face is up.
What happens when an effect makes my creature have no power value at all?

The creature's power is treated as 0. Because if a creature somehow has no value for its power, its power is 0, the game assigns that value immediately so combat can proceed. For example, if you use an effect to remove your creature's power, it will enter the combat phase and then deal 0 damage to any creatures it fights.
Can I stop an ability from triggering if it says I may do something?

No, you cannot prevent the trigger by deciding not to use it. Triggered abilities that contain may go on the stack when they trigger, regardless of whether their controller intends to exercise the ability's option or not. The choice is made only when the ability resolves. For example, if you have an enchantment that says At the beginning of your upkeep, you may draw a card, the ability will still go on the stack even if you decide you do not want to draw a card.
Can I add plane cards to my deck when playing a regular game of Magic?

No, you cannot. Plane is a card type seen only on nontraditional Magic cards and is used specifically for the Planechase casual variant. For example, if you are playing a standard game of Modern and try to include a Zendikar plane in your deck, it would be an illegal inclusion because planes are not part of traditional Magic formats.
If I have an enchantment that gives me extra mana whenever I tap a land, can I use that extra mana to pay for the spell I am currently casting?

Yes, you can. Triggered mana abilities resolve immediately after the mana ability that triggered it, without waiting for priority. This means the additional mana is added to your pool right away and can be used to pay for the spell you are currently in the middle of casting. For example, if you are casting a spell that costs {3}{U} and you tap a land while an enchantment says "Whenever you tap a land for mana, add one {U}", that extra {U} is added immediately so you can use it for that same spell.
I'm playing a double-faced card but I only have the front side available right now. Can I use a regular card with a normal back to represent it?

Yes, you can use a substitute card to represent a double-faced or meld card. A substitute card is a game supplement that is used for this purpose and it has a normal Magic card back. For example, if you are playing Delver of Secrets but only have the front side available, you can use any other standard card with a regular back to represent its presence on the battlefield.
I am looking at my planeswalker and it has a symbol with a plus sign and a 2 next to it. Do I actually add anything to the card?

Yes, that is a positive loyalty symbol. Using a [+N] symbol means you put N loyalty counters on this permanent. For example, if you activate an ability with a [+2] symbol, you will place 2 loyalty counters on that planeswalker.
What happens if my opponent uses a spell to destroy all artifacts but I have an artifact creature on the table?

The artifact creature will be destroyed. When the spell resolves, the object is recognized as an artifact because objects with more than one card type combine the aspects of each of those card types and are subject to spells that affect either or all of those types. For example, if you have a Metalwork Colossus on the battlefield, it will be destroyed by a spell like Shatter even though it is also a creature.
What happens if I have two different creatures that both reach zero toughness at the exact same time?

Both creatures will be put into the graveyard simultaneously. Whenever a player would get priority, the game checks for any of the listed conditions for state-based actions and then performs all applicable state-based actions simultaneously as a single event. For example, if an effect deals 3 damage to a 1/1 creature and 2 damage to a 2/2 creature at the same time, both will be moved to the graveyard in one single step before any other things happen.
I have a few creatures on the board. Can I hit more than one person at the same time?

Yes. In games that allow for it, you can choose to attack multiple other players. For example, if you have three creatures, you could send two of them to attack Player A and one of them to attack Player B.
What happens when my creature is attacking a player but gets destroyed before its ability resolves?

The ability will still target the original player. If a creature is no longer attacking, the defending player it refers to is the player that creature was attacking before it was removed from combat. For example, if you attack Player A and your creature is destroyed by a spell during combat, an ability targeting the defending player will still target Player A.
What happens when I have a card that lets me start the game with it on the battlefield?

Once your mulligan process is complete, you take action by putting that card onto the battlefield. The starting player puts their card on first, and then each other player in turn order does the same. For example, if you are playing a card like Leyline of the Void, you would place it on the field after deciding how many cards to keep, but before the first turn starts.
If I tap my flipped creature, how do my opponents know it is still the flipped version and not the original one?

You must ensure that it is clear at all times whether a permanent you control is flipped or not, both when it is untapped and when it is tapped. To avoid confusion, players often use common methods like coins or dice to mark flipped objects. For example, if you flip a creature and then tap it to attack, you should place a small die on the card so your opponent knows it is still in its flipped state.
If a card says {2}, {T}: Draw a card, can I just pay the 2 mana and draw it without tapping the creature?

No, you cannot. The activation cost is everything before the colon in an ability, and that cost must be paid by the player who is activating it. For example, if a creature has an ability that reads {2}, {T}: Draw a card, you must pay both the two mana and tap the creature to successfully activate that ability.
What happens when I play a card that is listed as both an Elf and a Creature?

The card will behave like a regular creature. Because each kindred card has another card type, casting and resolving a kindred card follows the rules for the other card type it possesses. For example, if you play an Elf creature, you follow the standard process of paying its mana cost and it enters the battlefield as a permanent that can eventually attack or block.
If I cast two spells this turn and then cast a spell with Storm, how many times does that Storm spell resolve?

The spell will resolve three times in total. When you cast a spell with Storm, it copies itself for each other spell that was cast before it this turn. If you have already cast two spells, the Storm ability triggers and creates two copies of the spell, resulting in the original spell plus those two copies resolving. For example, if you cast two cheap instants and then cast a spell with Storm, you will end up with three versions of that spell on the stack.

I'm trying to cast a spell that costs {1}{U}. I have two Islands tapped and one Swamp untapped, but I also control a card that makes my blue spells cost one less to cast. Do I need that third land to pay for the generic mana, or does the discount change what mana I actually need to spend?

The game processes casting by first calculating the total cost before you pay anything. According to the rules, when determining the total cost of a spell, you start with the mana cost and apply all cost reductions. The text notes that once the total cost is determined, any effects that directly affect the total cost are applied and then the resulting total cost becomes locked in. This happens before you activate mana abilities or pay costs. Your card making blue spells cost one less applies here. The printed cost is {1}{U}, but with your reduction, the total cost locks in as {0}{U}. Now looking at mana definitions, the game distinguishes that {U} represents blue mana while {1} represents generic colorless mana that can come from any source. Since your locked-in cost is only {0}{U}, you only need to produce one blue mana. You do not need the third land because the generic portion was reduced to zero. You tap two Islands, pay {U}, and cast the spell successfully without spending any generic mana or using the Swamp.

We're mid-game and I just tapped out for a card that says Whenever you cast an instant or sorcery spell, you may draw a card. My deck is completely empty, and my opponent has a lock piece saying Players can't draw cards. The trigger went on the stack even though I had no cards left and drawing was banned. At resolution, what actually happens with this choice?

Optional triggered abilities go on the stack when they trigger, regardless of whether their controller intends to exercise the option or not, so the ability proceeds normally even if you plan to decline it later. When it resolves, the game checks your library state alongside all active restrictions. Because your deck contains zero cards but there is an active effect stating that players cannot draw cards, the rule for empty libraries explicitly states that if an effect says a player can’t draw and another offers the choice to draw, you cannot exercise that choice. The ability resolves safely without drawing any cards, leaving your library empty and continuing the game until a state-based action triggers later.
I just cast a spell that tells my creature to connive. What actually happens?

When a permanent connives, you draw a card and then discard a card. If a nonland card is discarded this way, you put a +1/+1 counter on the conniving permanent. For example, if you have a 2/2 creature and it connives, you draw one card and discard one card; if that discarded card is a Sorcery, the creature gets a +1/+1 counter and becomes a 3/3.

I control this robot creature that rolls dice for its triggered ability. During my upkeep, it has an ability that says roll two dice and you may put a token onto the battlefield if you rolled doubles. My opponent thinks I have to declare whether I'm going to use the word may before I even roll the dice, but I want to wait until I see the result. Who is right about the timing of this decision and what happens at the table?

Your opponent is incorrect about the timing of your decision. Because your ability includes the word may, the triggered ability goes on the stack immediately when the upkeep starts, regardless of whether you intend to use the option or not. This rule regarding optional triggered abilities dictates that the game waits for players to pass priority before moving forward, meaning the choice is made much later when the ability resolves. When the ability finally reaches resolution and players stop receiving responses, that is the moment you roll the two dice. You have rolled doubles if each of those rolls is equal to the other. If the rolls match, you now make your choice whether to put the token onto the battlefield. The outcome is that the ability goes on the stack first where your opponent can respond, it resolves after both players pass priority, you roll the dice during resolution, and once you confirm the rolls are a matching pair, you choose to create the token or not.
My card says I need to roll a d6, but I only have a d20. Can I just use that instead?

No, you cannot use a different die because an effect that instructs a player to roll a die will specify what kind of die to roll and how many of those dice to roll. The die must have N equally likely outcomes, numbered from 1 to N. For example, if a card tells you to roll a d6, you need a six-sided die with outcomes 1 through 6. A d20 would not work because it has twenty different outcomes instead of the six required by the instruction.

I just started casting an enchantment that says on cast, my opponent chooses one of my creatures to attack me this turn if able, and I'm tapping three forests for mana at the same time to pay half the cost. My forests have abilities that say whenever they're tapped for green mana, draw a card. Which event resolves first and do I draw cards before or after my opponent picks the creature?

Remove all rule number references, explain the interaction conversationally using only the provided mechanics, and clarify that mana abilities resolve as costs are paid (placing triggers on the stack), after which the simultaneous casting instruction occurs with you acting first.
What happens when we pick a team to decide who goes first but that team has an even number of players?

First, you randomly choose a team. If that team has an even number of players, the player to the left of its midpoint goes first. For example, if you are playing two-on-two and your team is selected, and your team consists of two players, the person sitting to the left of the midpoint between those two players would take the first turn.

I just cast a spell that says my opponent picks the targets for it, but before they picked, I tried to tap a creature for mana to cast something else. The judge said I couldn't do that until after they made their choice. Is that right?

The casting procedure rule takes precedence over general timing because opponent selections are part of the spell itself rather than separate events. According to the guidelines, if a spell specifies that an opponent does something you would normally do while it is being cast, the opponent does so when you normally would during that phase. Under normal timing rules, unless a spell or ability instructs a player to take an action, players can only cast spells or activate abilities when they have priority. However, priority never passes until the entire casting process finishes. Because the target selection happens before the spell reaches the stack, you get no opportunity to act in between. The final outcome is that your opponent must choose the targets immediately, and only after they do so will you receive priority to tap creatures or cast instants.

I have a 2/2 creature in play. My opponent plays an instant that says give target creature -3/-3 until end of turn. In response, I cast this card with the Tiered ability. I choose the first mode which puts two +1/+1 counters on target creature, and I pay the additional mana required by the tiered ability. After everything resolves, my creature is a 1/1 and goes to the graveyard from combat damage or state-based actions. Why didn't the counters save it? Shouldn't the counters make it stronger than the -3/-3 effect?

The order of resolution determines the outcome here even though you responded first. Because your spell was on the stack above your opponent's instant, it resolves first and creates a continuous effect that puts two +1/+1 counters on your creature. This effect receives an earlier timestamp than the effect from your opponent's instant which will resolve next. However, within the layer system, effects with earlier timestamps apply before effects with later timestamps. The +1/+1 counters apply to your 2/2 creature first, making it a 4/4. Then the -3/-3 effect from your opponent's spell applies to that 4/4 result because its timestamp is later, reducing it to a final power and toughness of 1/1. The Tiered ability simply allowed you to choose this mode and pay extra mana to cast the spell, but it does not change how timestamps are calculated or give your effect priority over others based on investment. Your creature ends up as a 1/1 and dies.
My opponent just cast a spell with split second. Can I use my ability to sacrifice a creature to save myself before it hits the table?

No, you cannot. As long as that spell is on the stack, players can't cast other spells or activate abilities that aren't mana abilities. For example, if your opponent casts a spell with split second, you are unable to activate an ability like a creature's ability to sacrifice itself to gain life. You must wait for the spell to resolve.

I attacked with a face-down morph creature that had an ability dealing damage to me at end of turn. My opponent cast something turning all my creatures into enchantments before end of turn. Does the face-down card deal damage even though it is now an enchantment and not a creature?

Yes, the damage will be dealt. The interaction relies on how the game identifies objects when their characteristics change versus what qualifies for special actions. Turning a face-down creature face up is a special action that requires priority and follows specific timing rules, which establishes the permanent's status on the battlefield. However, the delayed ability refers to this object based on its initial identity. The authoritative text explains that if an ability uses a phrase such as this [something] to identify an object, it refers to that particular object even if it isn't the appropriate quality at the time. Because the ability identified the permanent when it was on the battlefield, the reference holds true even after the opponent's effect changed it from a creature to an enchantment. The final outcome is that the delayed trigger resolves and deals damage to you.
What happens when I play an old card that has the Tribal type printed on it?

The game identifies the card as its specific intended type rather than a Tribal because cards printed with that type have received errata in the Oracle card reference. For example, if you play an old card that says Tribal but is officially a Dragon in the Oracle database, the game will treat it as a Dragon for all interactions, such as being targeted by Dragon-specific spells.

In combat, my creature has first strike and deals damage to your blocking creature first. My blocker doesn't have first strike but still has enough power to kill me back. Everyone thinks my creature will die in the second damage phase because it takes counterdamage, but it actually survives. What's happening here?

This happens because the combat damage phase is split into two parts, and automatic cleanup checks run immediately after the first part ends. The rules state that if at least one attacking or blocking creature has first strike, only those creatures assign combat damage in that step, and after that step completes, the phase gets a second combat damage step for remaining attackers and blockers. However, state-based actions are game actions that happen automatically whenever certain conditions are met, which includes putting any permanent marked with lethal damage into its owner's graveyard before anyone can take priority. Once your first strike creature deals damage in the initial step, your blocker is immediately marked with lethal damage. Before either player gets a chance to respond or before the second combat damage step begins, those automatic checks run and remove the blocked creature from the battlefield. Because it is already gone, it never exists to assign or deal damage in the second phase, so your original creature survives untouched. The automatic removal takes precedence over the expectation of counterdamage, directly following the first strike timing structure.
What happens if I use an ability to exert my creature, and then I exert it again later in the same turn? Will it stay tapped for two turns?

No, it will not stay tapped for two turns. If you exert a permanent more than once before your next untap step, each effect causing it not to untap expires during the same untap step. For example, if you have a creature that lets you exert it to deal damage, and you exert it once to attack and a second time using a different spell, both exertions will resolve during your very next untap step, allowing the creature to untap normally then.

I just tapped a forest for two green mana in my main phase, then my opponent attacked me and I declared blockers. After combat ended, we both passed priority twice so their turn technically continued while they were untapping. I forgot to use those two mana before moving to the end step. Can I still save them to cast a spell later this turn or do I lose them?

When you and your opponent pass priority in succession without taking any actions in between passing, the spell or ability on top of the stack resolves or the phase or step ends. Once that phase or step officially concludes, each player’s mana pool empties at the end of each step and phase and you are said to lose this mana. The timing rule regarding passing applies first to close out the turn structure, which then directly triggers the mana pool drainage. Therefore, you completely lose those two green mana and cannot use them to cast spells or activate abilities later this turn or in any future phase.

I control a creature called Maro that has toughness equal to the number of cards in my hand, and my opponent casts a spell that forces me to discard my hand then draw seven cards. I'm panicking because my hand count goes down to zero for a moment during resolution before I draw the new cards. Does Maro die when the count hits zero? Also, since my hand is usually hidden, how would anyone even know it hit zero in the middle of the spell?

Maro survives and ends up with toughness seven because state-based actions only check for lethal conditions after a spell or ability finishes resolving completely. The rules dictate that unlike triggered abilities, state-based actions pay no attention to what happens during the resolution of a spell or ability, so the temporary drop in hand size is ignored for survival purposes. Furthermore, your hand remains a hidden zone throughout this entire process because library and hand are defined as hidden zones even if all cards happen to be revealed by an effect. This means your opponents cannot see the moment your hand count hits zero; they only see the final result where you hold seven cards and Maro is alive with toughness equal to seven.
I have a card with this infinity symbol on it, but I can't use the ability. What happens when I harness the card?

When you harness the permanent, the ability listed after the symbol becomes active. The rule is that infinity followed by an ability means as long as this permanent is harnessed, it has that ability. For example, if you have an artifact with infinity and an ability to add mana, the artifact will only gain that mana-producing ability once you harness it.
What happens if my creature with infect hits you for 5 damage?

Instead of causing life loss, damage dealt to a player by a source with infect causes that source's controller to give the player poison counters equal to the damage dealt. For example, if you attack with a 5/5 creature with infect and it deals 5 damage to your opponent, they receive 5 poison counters instead of losing 5 life.

We are in the middle of my opponent's turn and they just cast a combat trick targeting one of my creatures. I want to tap two of my snow-covered islands before their spell resolves to pay for a {2}{U} mana ability on my commander so I can counter it, but I am confused about whether I can actually activate lands during someone else's turn and what kind of mana those snow symbols will actually give me since they look blue on the card.

You can absolutely activate those abilities right now because the game operates on a strict priority system where A player may activate an activated ability any time they have priority, which fully covers responding to instant spells on the stack. This timing rule takes precedence by establishing your legal window to act first, and once that window is open, the snow conversion clause directly controls the result by stating that If an effect would add mana represented by one or more snow mana symbols to a player’s mana pool, that much colorless mana is added to that player’s mana pool. Consequently, tapping both lands adds four colorless to your pool rather than blue, meaning you have sufficient generic resources but still need an additional source of blue to fully pay the {2}{U} cost before their spell resolves.

I just cast a creature spell that has an enters-the-battlefield ability. Does the creature actually enter first, or does the ability happen immediately? And can my opponent respond to it before it resolves?

When you cast a permanent spell, it resolves step by step rather than triggering effects instantly. First, the resolution instructions place the card onto the battlefield under your control as a permanent. Only after that permanent is actually on the battlefield do any of its triggered abilities look for their trigger events. The rules state that whenever a game event or game state matches a triggered ability's trigger event, that ability automatically triggers but does nothing at this point and waits to be placed on the stack. Because the creature enters completely before the trigger activates, your opponent receives priority to respond after entry but before the enter-the-battlefield ability resolves. The concrete final outcome is that the creature enters the battlefield, then its enters-the-battlefield trigger goes on the stack, so you must wait for all responses to resolve before the spell cycle finishes. Permanent spell resolution takes precedence by establishing the permanent's presence first, which then allows the triggered ability framework to evaluate and place the trigger on the stack afterward.
I have a spell with tiered on it. Can I pay the mana for the spell first and then pick which mode to use once it is on the stack?

No, you cannot. Tiered means that as an additional cost to cast the spell, you must choose one mode and pay the cost associated with that mode. This decision and payment happen at the same time you are casting the spell, before it even reaches the stack. For example, if a spell has Tiered where you can choose to either pay 2 extra colorless or 2 extra red, you must pick your option and pay that specific mana immediately when you cast it; you cannot wait to see what happens before deciding.

I have a creature on my side of the board that has two abilities printed on it. The first is a static ability that says Creatures you control get +2/+2, and the second is a triggered ability that says Whenever this creature dies, create a 2/2 Zombie creature token. My opponent casts a spell that destroys all creatures, so my creature leaves the battlefield at the exact same time as several others. Do those death triggers still go on the stack even though everything dies together, and does the static buff somehow carry over into the graveyard or affect things after they leave?

The backward-looking trigger check takes precedence during the event phase, applying first to determine if abilities trigger before any zone changes occur. The game uses the exception that lets certain triggered abilities look back in time to determine if those abilities trigger, using the appearance of objects immediately prior to the event, so each death ability recognizes the creature as present right before leaving and successfully goes on the stack. Afterward, the static ability follows the rule that static abilities cannot use an object's last known information for purposes of determining how their effects are applied, which means its +2/+2 effect instantly stops once the creature leaves the battlefield. The concrete final outcome is that all triggers resolve normally creating tokens based on pre-death characteristics, while the static buff vanishes completely with no lingering impact in other zones.
What happens when I cast a spell that adds mana to my pool?

You cast the spell, it resolves, and then you add the specified amount of mana to your pool. The source of this mana is the spell itself because if mana is produced by a spell, the source of that mana is that spell. For example, if you cast Pyretic Ritual to add three red mana, the ritual is the source.
What happens to my creature if a card says it removes it from the game? I dont see an exile zone on my table.

The creature is moved to the exile zone. The rules state that cards printed with text that removes an object from the game are treated as exiling that object. For example, if you use an old spell that removes a creature from the game, that creature is placed in the exile zone instead of the graveyard.

I’m mid-combat and I have a creature with transfigure on the battlefield. My opponent just cast an enchantment that says “All creatures get +2/+0” and also has a triggered ability that gives me protection from green. I activate transfigure to swap my creature for a green one. When the new green creature enters, does it stay tapped or untapped, and how do my opponent’s enchantment and my protection interact with it?

Correct the transfigure cost to “[Cost], Sacrifice this permanent” without tapping. State clearly that creatures enter untapped by default unless an effect explicitly states otherwise. Explain that continuous effects like +2/+0 and player protection are applied in timestamp order after the creature’s base characteristics are determined, which finalizes its stats and combat interactions on the battlefield.
Can I still target my artifact creature with a spell that only says it targets artifacts?

Yes, you can. Some objects have more than one card type, and such objects satisfy the criteria for any effect that applies to any of their card types. For example, if you cast a spell like Shatter which says destroy target artifact, it will work on an artifact creature because the card satisfies the requirement for being an artifact.

I just played Centaur of Attention and rolled my dice, getting a high result that made me draw a card. The ability went on the stack immediately. Later in combat, I wanted to reroll that stored result to lower it and save myself from an attack, but now the game says my first draw is gone too. Did I lose the card because I changed the number?

The card you drew is yours to keep; changing the stored result does not undo effects that have already triggered. According to the rules for storing results on permanents, when you reroll, the results you rerolled stop being stored results and you store the results of each new die roll on that permanent. This action changes the current values on the creature, but it cannot retroactively affect abilities that are already waiting to resolve. Once the ability triggered from storing the high result, it must go on the stack as an object that is not a card the next time a player would receive priority. Triggers placed on the stack exist independently of their source and will resolve even if the stored result changes afterward. The precedence is that the triggering event occurs first based on the stored value, placing the effect on the stack, and only then can you use an ability to reroll which modifies the permanent's state but leaves existing stack objects alone. Your concrete outcome is that you drew your card as indicated by the first trigger, and rerolling the die afterwards only changes the values currently noted on Centaur of Attention without removing anything already resolved or on the stack.
I have a huge creature with trample attacking, but it gets blocked by a tiny 1/1. Does all the extra damage go straight to my opponent?

Yes. Once you assign enough damage to the blocking creature to deal lethal damage, any excess damage is assigned as you choose among those blocking creatures and the player you are attacking. For example, if you attack with a 5/5 with trample and they block with a 1/1, you must assign at least 1 damage to that blocker first, then you can assign the remaining 4 damage directly to your opponent.

I just untapped my creatures and tapped them to attack on my turn, then cast a spell that says As this creature enters, exile up to one target permanent. My opponent claims they can respond to the tap for attack or stop the exile with an instant. What actually happens?

Tapping creatures to declare attackers is a special action per the provided rules. Because these actions are taken when you have priority but do not use the stack, neither you nor your opponent can cast instants or activate abilities in response solely to the tap itself. When you cast your creature spell, it goes on the stack during your turn (typically after attackers are declared but before blockers or end of combat), and opponents may respond to the spell itself at that point. If the spell is not countered and resolves, its exile ability becomes a replacement effect that modifies how the creature enters the battlefield. Per the provided rules, while applying this replacement effect, you choose one target permanent to change zones simultaneously as the creature enters. Since replacement effects modify entry rather than use the stack, opponents cannot respond with instant-speed spells at this step. The final outcome is that your creatures attack successfully; if no one counters the spell on the stack, your creature enters the battlefield and exactly one permanent of your choice moves to exile.
Wait, I thought I could only play one land each turn, but this card says I can play two. Is that okay?

Yes, that is perfectly fine. Whenever a card's text directly contradicts the rules, the card takes precedence and overrides only the rule that applies to that specific situation. For example, if you use a card like Oracle of Mul Daya which allows you to play extra lands, that card's instruction overrides the standard rule about playing only one land per turn.

My opponent just cast a sorcery that forces me to discard my hand until I have zero cards, then draws seven for me. While this is resolving, I control a creature whose toughness equals cards in my hand, and I also have an enchantment that says whenever I lose the game, I get an extra turn. Someone at the table said my creature dies immediately when I hit zero cards mid-resolution, which stops its ability from triggering before I even lose. Is that true, or does the creature stick around? How does the game actually time these events?

The creature does not die during resolution because state-based actions pay no attention to what happens during the resolution of a spell or ability. The spell finishes resolving, restoring the seven cards to your hand and instantly restoring your creature's toughness before state checks occur. After resolution ends, if you lose the game for any reason, triggered abilities that trigger specifically when a player loses or leaves the game will still activate. Your enchantment goes on the stack as you depart and resolves successfully while you are leaving, granting you an extra turn.

My opponent has a permanent out that says opponents cant cast spells with even mana values. I want to cast a spell from my hand that costs XRR. If I declare X equals one, is it legal to cast? Also, once it resolves and deals damage, when do the damage triggers actually go on the stack so my opponent can respond?

Yes, it is perfectly legal. During the proposal phase of casting, you may consider any choices made that cause those qualities to change, meaning you can pick X equals one to make the mana value odd and bypass the restriction. This casting legality step happens first while you are declaring how to cast the spell. After the spell resolves, triggered abilities do not resolve immediately. The game rules state that nothing actually happens at the time an ability triggers, and each time a player would receive priority, each ability that has triggered is put on the stack. Since no one receives priority while a spell or ability is resolving, your opponent will only get a response window after the spell fully leaves the stack. The concrete final game outcome is that the spell casts successfully, resolves dealing damage as declared, and all resulting triggers wait in the trigger queue until you next receive priority, at which point they are placed on the stack for your opponent to respond to.
What happens when my cards get messy or disorganized during a game? Can I tidy them up?

You can tidy them up at any moment. Because a player may arrange their hand in any convenient fashion and look at it at any time, you simply take a moment to reorganize.
