For example, if your cards are scattered on the table, you can gather them into a neat pile or line them up so you can see each one clearly.
Can I try to cast a spell if its cost is something impossible to pay?

Yes, attempting to cast a spell or activate an ability that has an unpayable cost is a legal action, but attempting to actually pay that unpayable cost is an illegal action. For example, if an effect requires you to pay the mana cost of a token, that cost is considered unpayable because tokens do not have a mana cost. You can legally make the attempt to cast the spell, but you cannot actually pay any mana for it.

I just attacked with my two-power beast and realized two other players control permanents that each say if a creature you control would deal damage to a permanent or player, it deals double that damage instead. Someone claims we get priority after the first doubling so they can respond, while another says it doubles twice for four total. What actually happens during this interaction?

Replacement effects modify events exactly as they occur without using the stack, meaning opponents cannot respond between doublings. The first effect changes two damage to four, and the second immediately modifies that modified event to eight, resulting in exactly eight damage dealt.
Can I tap my lands to pay for a spell that needs specific colors of mana?

Yes, you can. The rules allow this because if a cost includes a mana payment, the player paying the cost has a chance to activate mana abilities. For example, if you want to cast a spell that costs {U}{U}, you can tap two Islands to produce that blue mana.

We are playing a two-player team match where we take turns as one unit. I tapped my lands for {2}{U} and announced I was casting a sorcery. My teammate immediately started tapping another land to try and activate an ability, claiming that since we share a turn and a mana pool, they can act whenever they want. But the game director said they had to wait. What actually determines who gets to take actions at this moment, and how does the way mana costs are defined factor into whether my teammate could pay for that ability right then?

Under shared team turn formats, teams rather than individual players have priority, meaning your entire group acts as a single decision maker until the opposing team responds. Because you announced the sorcery, you passed the team window to allow the opponent to act. The rules state that mana is represented by mana symbols and mana symbols also represent mana costs, so your teammate would need to pay generic and blue mana symbols to activate anything, but they cannot even attempt to do so because the team no longer holds priority at this moment. The priority rule takes precedence first by dictating who gets to act when. Since opponents now have priority, your teammate must wait until they pass back or until the stack empties and priority returns to your team. Final outcome: Your teammate is legally required to hold their activation until the opposing team passes priority back or your sorcery resolves and leaves the stack. You will then pay {2}{U} for the spell as announced, and only after priority cycles back to your team can your teammate activate their ability.
What happens if I move my marker to the very last room in a dungeon and nothing happens?

The dungeon card is removed from the game because your venture marker is on the bottommost room and that dungeon card isn't the source of a room ability that has triggered but not yet left the stack. For example, if you move your marker to the final room of the Lost Mine of Phandelver and no abilities have triggered yet, the dungeon card is removed from the game as a state-based action.

I'm at 1 life with my hand full. My opponent attacks with two creatures and I also have to draw extra cards from a separate effect on the stack. If both things happen at once, do I die twice or does one card save me?

The game handles this by processing damage in a strict four-part sequence during the resolution of effects. First, excess damage is calculated. Second, damage is dealt as modified by replacement and prevention effects that interact with damage. Third, damage that has been dealt is processed into its results, which means life loss occurs here alongside your card draw. Finally, the complete damage event occurs. Because both your life total dropping to zero and exceeding your hand limit happen simultaneously after step three finishes, multiple loss conditions trigger at once. When multiple state-based actions would have the same result at the same time, a single replacement effect will replace all of them. The damage processing rule applies first because it dictates how effects modify the hit before any loss triggers occur, followed by the simultaneous state-based check, and finally your mirror resolves to cover every condition at once. You safely shuffle everything into your library, draw seven cards, set your life total to twenty, and completely avoid losing the game.

I'm in combat and my opponent cast a spell that made all of my creatures attack if they could, but before I got to declare attackers, I tapped a land which emptied my hand for a split second while a permanent on the battlefield triggered off having zero cards left. We're arguing about whether one of my creatures actually had to attack this turn or not, since that trigger went on the stack right when my hand emptied. What's the actual ruling here?

The creature did have to attack this turn, and you must declare it as an attacker if it is legally able to do so. Here is why both mechanics interact this way. When your opponent created a mandatory attack requirement, that effect applied immediately. Later, when your hand size dropped to zero, the permanent triggered because a game state is true rather than triggering when an event occurs, and it went onto the stack at the next available opportunity. Because this state trigger does not resolve instantly and waits for its controller to gain priority or for the step to progress, the mandatory attack requirement still stood when you entered combat declaration. The relevant rule explicitly states that a creature had to attack if one or more effects were requiring that creature to attack at the time attackers were declared in that combat. Since the state trigger was waiting on the stack and had not yet changed control of that creature, the mandatory condition remained active. Therefore, you must declare that creature as an attacker during combat declaration, and once it attacks, it satisfies the requirement regardless of what happens when the empty hand trigger eventually resolves.
If my card says 'create a legendary 2/2 red Warrior creature token named Firebrand', what actually happens when that token enters the battlefield?

The token enters as a 2/2 red Warrior with the name Firebrand. This is because an instruction to create a legendary token is the same as an instruction to create a token with the listed characteristics that has the given name. For example, you are not just getting a generic warrior; you are getting a specific legendary creature named Firebrand.

I just put my commander back onto the battlefield from the command zone this turn, but my opponent has an enchantment that says all creatures enter with a counter and lose their activated abilities as they enter. Does my commander still get its enters-the-battlefield ability to trigger? I thought being a commander protected it from normal creature rules.

Your commander is not protected from standard game mechanics just because it is the deck leader, since the Commander variant explicitly uses all normal rules for a Magic game alongside specific additions. The opponent's continuous effect will modify your commander exactly when it hits the battlefield, and rule text confirms that continuous effects modifying characteristics do so the moment the permanent is on the battlefield and not before then. Because the creature loses all abilities at the precise instant of entry, its enters-the-battlefield triggered ability never exists to go on the stack. The continuous modification takes precedence over the timing of triggered abilities because static and continuous effects apply immediately upon presence on the battlefield, while triggers wait for resolution after the event. Your commander enters with counters but zero abilities, so it will not trigger anything and remains completely inert until an effect specifically grants it new abilities.
What happens when my opponent is exiled from the game? Does my card that says I win if they lose the game still work?

Your ability will trigger and you will win. Triggered abilities that trigger specifically when a player loses the game also trigger when a player leaves the game, regardless of the reason. For example, once an opponent is exiled from the game by a spell, the game recognizes they have left, which triggers your ability just as if they had lost via zero life.

We are in combat and I attack with two creatures for five damage each. My opponent blocks one of them with their blocker, but lets my second creature hit them directly for five as well. Right before all the damage resolves, we both realize this means we drop to zero life at the exact same time. I thought my opponent might get a chance to cast something or that one of us would lose first since they blocked a creature. What actually happens and how do these rules interact?

In this situation, the rules work together to produce a specific outcome. First, during the combat damage step, all assigned damage resolves at once. As stated in Rule 510.2, 'all combat damage that’s been assigned is dealt simultaneously' and 'no player has the chance to cast spells or activate abilities between the time combat damage is assigned and the time it’s dealt,' so neither of you can respond after assignment. Once that simultaneous damage is dealt and both life totals drop to zero, the game immediately checks state-based actions. Since both players would lose the game from having zero or less life at the exact same moment, there are no replacement effects unless specifically granted by a card on the battlefield (like Lich's Mirror). Because neither condition prevents the loss, the game ends immediately as a draw for both players.
Can I put two counters on an artifact creature if my Modular 2 creature dies?

Yes, you can. Modular means the permanent enters with N +1/+1 counters on it, and when it is put into a graveyard from the battlefield, you may put a +1/+1 counter on target artifact creature for each +1/+1 counter on this permanent. For example, if your creature has Modular 2, it enters with two +1/+1 counters. When it is put into the graveyard, you can choose one target artifact creature and put two +1/+1 counters on it.

I just cast a spell that draws three cards and lets me reveal one of them to copy it. My hand limit is seven, and I had four before casting it. Do I get to look at the three new cards before deciding which one to reveal, and does my opponent get a chance to mess with the spell in between?

When you cast that spell, it resolves completely before any player receives priority, so your opponent cannot interact with it while it is on the stack. As the rules state, if an effect gives a player the option to reveal a card as they draw it, that player may look at that card as they draw it before choosing whether to reveal it, allowing you to inspect the three cards and resolve the reveal effect during resolution. After the spell finishes, the game checks for state-based actions per the rules that whenever a player would get priority the game checks for listed conditions for state-based actions and performs them simultaneously. However, hand limits are not state-based actions and do not trigger during resolution or when priority is passed; instead, you only need to reduce your hand to exactly seven cards during the cleanup step if it remains above that limit. The concrete final outcome is that you look at the three cards, reveal one for its effect as the spell resolves, finish resolving completely, and then both players receive priority to cast instants or activate abilities on your turn. You will discard down to seven cards only later in the cleanup phase, not immediately upon drawing.
I just played a creature that can tap itself for mana, but it's not letting me use it. Why?

You cannot activate a creature's activated ability with the tap symbol in its cost unless the creature has been under your control since the start of your most recent turn. The only exception is if the creature has haste. For example, if you play a creature that has an ability to tap itself for mana, you cannot use that ability on the same turn it enters the battlefield unless it has haste.

I'm in a Commander game and my opponent attacks with their commander, dealing the 21st point of combat damage to me from that specific creature. I block it with a creature that deals lethal damage to their commander at the same time. Since the damage kills me instantly, does the game end before anything else happens, or does their commander still move? If it moves, where does it go?

When you are dealt 21 or more combat damage from a single commander, you lose the game immediately. Because losing the game ends play instantly, no state-based actions can resolve afterward, so the commander does not move. Additionally, note that the replacement effect to redirect a commander only applies when it would go to your hand or library, not your graveyard.
What happens to my party size if I play a creature that is both a Cleric and a Wizard?

Your party size only increases by one. If a creature has multiple creature types for which it could be a party member, it is counted as the party member for only one of those types. However, if there are different ways to count such a creature that results in different numbers of creatures in a player's party, it is counted in such a way to get the highest result. For example, if you control a Rogue, a Cleric, and a Warrior, and then play a Wizard-Cleric, your party size becomes four because the game will count that new creature as a Wizard to give you the highest possible number.

I cast my commander from the command zone while an instant is on the battlefield that makes all creatures lose their abilities. My commander has a powerful enters-the-battlefield trigger. Does the trigger happen this time, and how much mana does it cost?

Your commander will not trigger its enters-the-battlefield ability because continuous effects modify characteristics the moment a permanent is on the battlefield and take precedence over triggered abilities checking for those characteristics; the effect removing abilities applies instantly upon entry so your commander never gains the enters-the-battlefield ability to trigger. Regarding the cost, casting your commander from the command zone costs an additional {2} for each previous time you have cast it from the command zone this game. The concrete outcome is that you must pay the calculated commander tax to cast your creature, but its enters-the-battlefield ability will be absent and will not go on the stack.
If my Vanguard card says +2 to my hand size, do I still only draw 7 cards if I decide to mulligan?

No, you would draw nine cards. A player's starting hand size is seven cards, as modified by the hand modifier of their vanguard card, and when you take a mulligan, you draw a new hand equal to that same modified starting hand size. For example, with a +2 modifier, you start the game with 9 cards, so if you shuffle your hand back to mulligan, you will draw 9 new cards instead of the standard 7.
If my card flips over into a creature and then I use a spell to return it to my hand, will it still be that creature when I play it again?

No, it will go back to being the original card. When a flipped permanent leaves the battlefield, it retains no memory of its status. For example, if you flip a land into a creature and then use a spell like Unsummon to return it to your hand, when you play it again from your hand, it will be the original, unflipped version.

I'm in the middle of my turn trying to cast a creature with Flash that costs {U}. I activated my Island for blue mana and placed it in my mana pool, but before I could declare casting the spell, my opponent responded by targeting my land with an effect that destroys its ability to produce mana and stops all other lands from doing so too. He claims I can't cast the spell because the land is ruined and I can't pay the cost anymore. What happens here?

Replace all explicit rule number citations with conversational descriptions (e.g., 'The general mana rules state...' and 'The spell casting continuity rule states...'). Clarify that while the provided text defines mana spending and casting initiation, the specific rule about mana persisting after a land is disabled is a standard game rule not detailed in the excerpt. State: You successfully cast the creature. The general mana rules establish that players spend mana to pay costs, and once mana is generated it sits in your pool independently of its source, so disabling lands cannot retroactively remove mana you already possess. The spell casting continuity rule addresses what happens next: once you have begun casting a spell with flash because conditions were met, you may continue the cast even if those conditions stop being met or external effects disrupt your permanents after initiation. The concrete outcome is that you pay the blue mana from your pool and the creature enters the battlefield.

My opponent's commander attacked me last turn for 6 damage. Then they cast a spell that exiles it until their next upkeep, with an effect that creates a delayed trigger saying 'When this permanent leaves exile, return it to the battlefield tapped.' Today it returned and attacked again for 5. Do these damage totals add up toward the twenty-one rule, or does returning it reset the counter because it is technically a new creature?

You are asking how zone changes interact with cumulative damage tracking. The rules clarify that if an object leaves a zone and then returns it becomes a new object, which explains why many players assume counters reset after exile and return. However, the commander damage mechanic tracks the specific card identity across the entire game rather than the individual battlefield object. That delayed triggered ability simply moves your opponent's commander between zones without breaking the ongoing tally. Because the rule governing commander damage explicitly states a player loses when dealt 21 or more combat damage by the same commander over the course of the game, this threshold operates as a continuous state-based action that accumulates independently of object identity changes. The commander damage check takes precedence because it continuously monitors the running total regardless of temporary zone travel or new object creation. Yes, the hits stack together for a final tracked total of eleven points.
What happens if I have an enchantment on my opponent and then they leave the game?

The enchantment will be moved to your graveyard immediately. Because an Aura cannot enchant a player that is outside its controller's range of influence, the attachment becomes illegal once the player is gone. For example, if you have an enchantment targeting an opponent and that opponent leaves the game, the enchantment is put into your graveyard as a state-based action.

I control a creature with an ability that reads "When you lose the game, if this creature attacked alone this turn, you win the game." During my combat phase, I tap only this creature to attack by itself. My opponent then casts a spell dealing lethal damage, and my life total drops to zero. I feel like I just lost instantly and the ability cannot trigger because I am gone. Does my win condition activate?

Yes, you win the game. First, during the declare attackers step, you tapped only this creature to attack while no other creatures attacked. According to the rules regarding combat declaration, a creature attacks alone if it is the only creature declared as an attacker during that step. This confirms your creature satisfied the condition of attacking alone when the trigger event occurred. Although you lost the game due to lethal damage, triggered abilities do not simply disappear when a player leaves the game. The rules specify that certain triggered abilities trigger specifically when a player loses the game, and these abilities trigger when a player loses or leaves the game regardless of the reason. Because your creature attacked alone as defined by the combat declaration rule, the condition for your win ability is met. The sequence establishes that you attacked alone first based on your declarations, and then when you lost, the ability triggers based on that established state. Concrete outcome: You win the game.
What happens if a card lets me choose to draw a card but I have no cards left in my deck?

You can still choose to draw. If an effect offers a player the choice to draw a card and they have no cards in their library, that player can still choose to do so. For example, if you use an ability that lets you choose to draw a card but you have zero cards left in your deck, you can still pick that option as part of the resolution.
Can I cast a spell right after my combat phase ends but before my opponent's turn starts?

No, you cannot. The game follows a strict sequence where no game events can occur between steps, phases, or turns. This means there is no period of time outside of a defined step or phase where you can act. For example, if your combat phase ends, you must move immediately into your end step without any gap in between for casting spells.

I just cast a spell that lets me roll one die and check a results chart. The chart says if I roll a four or higher, I put a time counter on my opponent blocking creature, and then it creates an effect that exiles that creature at the beginning of its controller next end step. My opponent sacrificed the creature to another card before that end step arrived. Does the exile still happen?

No, the exile will not happen. Precedence starts with the dice resolution phase, where the rule states that you use your roll result to determine which striation on your results chart applies, establishing the timing window first. Once that spell finishes resolving, it creates a delayed triggered ability for that end step. The interaction between these mechanics means the dice rule sets up the effect, but the delayed trigger rule dictates that if that permanent left the battlefield before then, the ability simply will not do anything. Since your opponent sacrificed the creature before the end step arrived, the object is no longer in the expected zone, so the exile effect completely fizzles.
Wait, we're playing alternating teams but my brother just joined our side, so now it's three of us against one person. Is that still okay?

No, that is not allowed. An alternating teams game must be played with two or more teams of equal size. Since your team now has three people and the other team only has one, the sizes are no longer equal. For example, to keep it legal, you would need to have two players on each team for a total of four players.

I control an artifact that says counters I cast cost one less to cast, and my opponent has a creature with the ability 'Whenever a spell is countered, draw a card.' I just cast Counterspell targeting their creature. Do I pay less mana for it, and does their trigger still activate even though my artifact has some wording about static abilities on the stack?

Yes, you pay one less mana because static abilities modifying costs apply while a spell is on the stack. Even though your Counterspell targets their creature and both would leave play simultaneously, that creature’s triggered ability looks back in time to check if it was present when your spell was countered, so it successfully triggers and you draw a card.
What happens if my creature is attacking a player, but then an effect lets me change the target to a planeswalker? Does it stop attacking the player?

The creature does not stop attacking the original player. When you change the target, the creature is now attacking the reselected player or permanent, but it is still considered to have attacked the player or permanent chosen as it was declared as an attacker. For example, if your 3/3 Goblin attacks Player A, and then you use a card to make it attack Jace instead, that Goblin is now attacking Jace, but it is also still considered to have attacked Player A.

My opponent just cast an ability that lets them put a target creature card from any graveyard into their hand, and they picked my commander which was sitting in their own graveyard. What actually happens and where does it end up?

In the Commander variant, each deck is led by a legendary creature designated as that deck’s commander, which establishes strict ownership tracking for these permanents throughout the match. When determining the final destination of the card, the universal zone relocation rule applies first and takes precedence over the ability’s intended target. The comprehensive rules state that if an object would go to any library, graveyard, or hand other than its owner’s, it goes to its owner’s corresponding zone instead. Because the effect attempts to place your commander into your opponent’s hand rather than yours, this mandatory redirection immediately triggers. As a result, the commander bypasses your opponent entirely and ends up directly in your hand as the final game state.
If an opponent uses a spell that asks me to choose a card name, can I pick the whole split card name like Fire//Ice?

No, you cannot pick both names at once. If an effect tells you to choose a card name, you must choose one of those names and not both. An object is considered to have the chosen name if one of its individual names matches your choice. For example, if you are playing Fire//Ice and need to pick a name, you must choose either Fire or Ice to successfully target that card.

I'm mid-game in a Commander match and my attacker with exile replacement effects and combat damage triggers gets blocked by two creatures simultaneously. Both blockers die from combat damage. My opponent claims their total combat damage trigger counts for all four attackers on the field, but I want to know if I can activate the second ability on both sets of exiled cards. What actually happens here?

The game evaluates each source independently during the combat damage step. When your blockers die, a replacement effect causes one creature along with specific associated cards to be exiled instead of going to the graveyard, and a separate linked ability restricts you to only interacting with exactly those specific exiled cards rather than mixing them with others because an object may have one ability printed on it that generates a replacement effect which causes one or more cards to be exiled, and another ability that refers either to the exiled cards or to cards exiled with this object are permanently linked. Combat damage triggers are also strictly scoped, meaning your opponent's trigger only sees the combat damage from their own attacker that actually dealt it, ignoring all other creatures dealing damage at the exact same time since if an ability triggers on damage being dealt by a specific source, it refers only to the damage dealt by the specified sources and not to any damage dealt at the same time by other sources. The replacement and exile tracking happens first as the event resolves, establishing which cards are legally tied to the permanent before any triggered abilities check the battlefield state. Your opponent gains life from only one of their attackers' damage. You may activate the second ability on just one set of exiled cards, specifically the ones put into exile with that single source, and no other exiled cards can be accessed through that link.

I just cast a spell that would destroy a creature my opponent controls. They responded by tapping it for mana, then cast an instant that says if this creature would be destroyed it is instead tapped. My opponent claimed the tap was too late because spells go on the stack, but we are stuck wondering if the destruction actually happens or not. What is the real sequence?

Replace the unsupported priority claim with text explaining that when multiple instants respond to the same event, they are placed on the stack in Last-In-First-Out order, so the last response cast will resolve first. This allows the replacement effect to exist before the destruction event occurs, successfully modifying it and leaving the creature tapped but alive.
I just found this card and it has three different numbers at the bottom for attack and defense. Is this one of those leveler cards?

Not necessarily, you need to check a few more things first. Each leveler card has a striated text box and three power/toughness boxes, and the text box of a leveler card contains two level symbols. For example, if your card has those three sets of numbers but is missing the two level symbols in its text area, it is not a leveler.

I just attacked with a creature that has three damage marked on it, and I want to activate an ability that says put a sorcery card from my hand onto the battlefield. My opponent says I can't do either thing right now. Are they correct, and what actually happens?

State-based actions are checked throughout the game and are not controlled by any player, which means the automatic evaluation happens continuously before you get a chance to activate abilities or take other actions. Because your creature already has lethal damage marked on it, that state-based check happens immediately and puts the creature into the graveyard before your ability resolves. Even if timing allowed the effect to attempt its action, an instant or sorcery card cannot legally enter this area according to zone rules; specifically, if an instant or sorcery card would enter the battlefield, it remains in its previous zone. Because you are trying to move it from your hand, it simply stays there and the effect does nothing to the board. The concrete final outcome is that the damaged creature is destroyed and placed into your graveyard due to continuous automatic checks taking precedence, and the sorcery card remains safely in your hand.
I have this card that is both a land and an enchantment. If I play it like a land, which side shows up on the table?

When you play a modal double-faced card as a land, you choose one of its faces that is a land before putting it onto the battlefield. It then enters the battlefield with that chosen face up. For example, if you play a card like Agadeem's Awakening, which has a spell on one side and a Swamp on the other, you choose the Swamp face so it enters the battlefield as a land.

We're playing our first ever Commander match with four of us, and the rulebook says it's a default Free-for-All game. I just cast Sutured Ghoul from my hand at the same time I bounce three creatures back to their owners' hands and then replay them with a mass ritual effect. One of those returning creatures is also a Sutured Ghoul that wants to exile cards from its controller's graveyard as it enters. My opponent claims they can choose one of the other two Sutured Ghouls entering at the same time for their ability, but I said that's illegal because they're all arriving together. Who is right and what exactly happens with those abilities?

You are correct to stop them from choosing the other simultaneous arrivals. The rule for replacement effects modifying how a permanent enters explicitly states that you can’t choose the object that will become that permanent or any other object entering the battlefield at the same time as that object. This restriction takes precedence during zone change resolution because simultaneous entries are processed together before individual replacement effects make their selections. Additionally, the default multiplayer setup is the Free-for-All variant with the attack multiple players option, which means each player tracks their own graveyard independently rather than sharing zones across the table. The concrete final outcome is that the opponent cannot target the other entering Ghouls for the exile requirement. The Ghoul enters the battlefield with zero exiled creatures from this interaction, and you will proceed to declare attackers normally in this format where players attack multiple opponents independently.

I have a three power creature attacking your two blockers, a four toughness one and a two toughness one. Your second blocker has an ability that triggers when it takes damage from combat. I tried to split the damage one each to avoid triggering it, but the game told me I had to assign two to the first and one to the second, or three to the first and zero to the second. If I put three on the big one and leave the small one completely alone, will its trigger still pop off because I technically assigned damage that way?

Let us walk through how the game resolves this step by step. First, when you declare your blockers and damage split, standard combat rules apply which state that each blocking creature assigns combat damage divided as its controller chooses among them, and once you finish assigning, the total damage assignment is checked to see if it complies with those requirements before anything proceeds. In your scenario, putting all three power on one blocker and leaving the other with zero is perfectly legal. However, right after that compliance check passes, a separate foundational rule immediately takes over which dictates that if a source would deal 0 damage, it does not deal damage at all. This means abilities that trigger on damage being dealt simply will not trigger because there is no actual damage event to attach to. The concrete final outcome is that the targeted blocker takes your full three combat damage and survives with one toughness remaining, while the other blocking creature suffers absolutely nothing from this attack and remains on the battlefield untouched.

I just started playing Commander and my opponent kept saying we can shuffle our graveyards before the game to make things fair, and they also tried to rearrange their library cards while discussing strategies. I told them that was against the rules but they insisted Commander must have different rules since it is a variant format. Can players reorder their libraries or shuffle their graveyards in Commander?

Remove the sentence about error penalties for accidental reordering. The corrected answer should simply state that players may not shuffle graveyards or reorder libraries casually under Commander rules, as both formats prohibit changing zone order unless a specific effect or rule explicitly allows it, and no such casual permission exists.
Can I still pick an option if it is impossible, like exiling a creature that is not on the battlefield?

Yes, you can. While facing a villainous choice, a player may choose an option that is illegal or impossible. In that case, they perform as much of the action as is possible. For example, if a card tells you to face a villainous choice between drawing two cards or exiling target creature, and your opponent has no creatures on the battlefield, you can still pick the exile option; since there are no creatures to target, you simply do nothing for that part of the choice.

I just cast two creatures at once that say as either enters exile target creature and my opponent warned me I cannot use the same permanent for both but then immediately after they hit the battlefield a creature of mine with zero toughness died and went to the graveyard all on its own why did this happen

When you cast multiple creatures that enter simultaneously the game applies replacement effects that modify how they enter first and you cannot pick the exact same permanent twice because the official wording states the same object can never be chosen to change zones more than once when applying replacement effects that modify how one or more permanents enter the battlefield. Once those replacements finish resolving the permanents actually arrive on the battlefield and immediately afterward the game automatically evaluates the board state since state-based actions are checked throughout the game and are not controlled by any player. Because your creature now has zero toughness it is put into its owner's graveyard right away before anyone receives priority. The concrete final outcome is that only one opponent creature was exiled while the other entered safely and your zero-toughness creature ends up in your graveyard due to an automatic game check.
I just saw a card say to investigate. What actually happens to my board?

When you investigate, you create a Clue token. This means you resolve that instruction by placing a single Clue token onto the battlefield. For example, if a creature's ability tells you to investigate, you will add one Clue token to the battlefield.

I'm playing a game and I have a creature on the battlefield with an ability that says 'Whenever you draw a card, create a 1/1 Soldier token.' My opponent casts an instant spell that says 'Target player draws a card.' It's my turn, but I look at my library and realize I have zero cards left. My opponent says they can't cast this on me because I have no cards to draw from, so the ability won't trigger anyway. Is my opponent right? Can I still get the token if we go through with this?

Your opponent is incorrect; you will still get the token even though your library is empty. The rules actually allow you to draw a card in this specific situation whenever you are offered a choice to do so. The authoritative rule regarding drawing cards states that if there are no cards in a player's library and an effect offers that player the choice to draw a card, that player can choose to do so. Because your opponent's spell gives you the opportunity to draw, you are permitted to take that choice despite having zero cards. Once you make this choice, the game event of drawing occurs as a concrete action. With that event now happening, we look at how triggered abilities work. The rules for triggered abilities explain that whenever a game event matches a triggered ability's trigger event, that ability automatically triggers. Since the draw event took place thanks to your choice being valid under the drawing rule, your creature's condition is met and the ability fires immediately. The final outcome is that your opponent casts the spell, you choose to draw (even though nothing enters your hand), and your creature creates a 1/1 Soldier token as normal.
If I see a card with Planeswalker — Jace Beleren, does the whole thing after the dash count as one single subtype?

No, it is not treated as one single thing. The rules state that planeswalker subtypes are always a single word and each word after the dash is a separate subtype. For example, on a card that says Planeswalker — Jace Beleren, you would identify Jace as one subtype and Beleren as another.

My opponent just played a card that exiles creatures as they enter the battlefield instead of putting them onto the battlefield. I had a creature in my hand with an ability that triggers when it enters the battlefield, but my opponent said the exile replacement happens first so my creature never actually enters and doesn't get to trigger its ability. Is that true?

Yes, your opponent is correct. When a spell or ability tries to move a permanent from another zone to the battlefield, replacement effects are applied to that event before the move completes. The rule states that if an object would move and replacement effects apply, they are applied to the event of moving the object. In this case, the replacement effect changes the destination from the battlefield to exile during the move process. Because the creature is moved directly to exile by a replacement effect, it never enters the battlefield. Triggered abilities only trigger if their specific trigger event actually occurs. Since the event of entering the battlefield was replaced and did not happen, the enter-the-battlefield ability does not trigger. The final outcome is that the creature ends up in exile and no enter-the-battlefield triggers occur.
What happens when a battle is on the field but nobody is attacking it and no one is listed as its protector?

The controller of the battle chooses an appropriate player to be its protector. If no player can be chosen to be the protector, the battle is put into its owner's graveyard. For example, if you play a new battle card and it has no protector assigned, you would choose one of your opponents to be its protector so the battle remains on the battlefield.

I'm attacking my opponent's planeswalker with a creature that gets X/X based on how many cards I have in hand. I currently have six cards, so it's a six-to-six attacker. My opponent responds by casting an instant that says to discard your hand and then draw two cards while my creature is resolving combat damage. He argues that because my hand hits zero for a split second during the spell, my creature shrinks to zero toughness and dies before hitting his planeswalker. Does my creature survive to deal the damage?

Your creature survives and deals combat damage to your opponent's planeswalker. Your opponent is incorrect about the timing of destruction because state-based actions pay no attention to what happens during the resolution of a spell or ability; they only check the game state once the spell has fully resolved. Even though your hand size temporarily becomes zero while the spell resolves, the creature never actually exists as a zero-toughness permanent in a way that would cause it to be put into the graveyard, and it will reappear with a toughness of two after the spell finishes. The rules regarding combat roles confirm that during the combat phase, the active player is the attacking player and may attack players, planeswalkers, or battles, so your surviving creature completes its assignment and assigns damage as defined by those turn actions once state-based actions are finally evaluated.
What happens if something is supposed to change automatically at the start of my turn? Can I use a spell to stop it?

These changes are turn-based actions that happen automatically when certain steps or phases begin or end. Because they don't use the stack, you cannot respond to them with spells or abilities. For example, when your untap step begins, all your tapped lands untap automatically without anyone being able to cast an instant in response.

I control a Heart-Piercer Manticore and my opponent cast a spell that said Roll a d6. If the result is 4 or greater, you may sacrifice a creature. I rolled a natural 3, but I have an effect that lets me add 1 to a die roll. Can I use that to bump it up and make my Manticore trigger?

Yes, your Heart-Piercer Manticore will trigger. The process begins with the die roll mechanics which determine whether the condition for sacrifice is met. According to the rules for die rolls, modifiers may increase or decrease the natural result, and after considering all applicable modifiers, the final number is the result of the die roll. You apply your effect to add 1 to the natural 3, making the final result 4. Because the final result meets the threshold, the spell instructs you to take the action of sacrificing a creature. Once that instruction exists, the reflexive triggered ability rules come into play. These rules state that a resolving spell can create a triggered ability that triggers when you take an action, and this trigger is checked immediately based on whether the event occurred earlier during the resolution of the spell that created it. Since you sacrifice a creature due to the instruction resulting from the final die roll, the condition for the reflexive trigger is satisfied. The concrete final outcome is that you sacrifice a creature, and your Heart-Piercer Manticore triggers, allowing you to deal damage equal to that creature's power to any target.
What happens when an ability says I draw a card? Do I just pick any card from my deck?

You cannot pick any card you want. To draw a card, you must take the top card of your library and put it into your hand. This can be done as part of an effect of a spell or ability. For example, if you play a spell that says draw a card, you look at the very top card of your deck and move it to your hand.

We are in combat and my opponent attacks with a two-power creature while I block with my Undying zombie that has no counters on it. The damage swaps, both creatures take lethal damage, but I was told the zombie just stays dead while mine bounces back. What actually happens at the table?

State-based actions take precedence because the game checks for lethal damage and destruction before any triggered abilities can resolve. The rule states that if a creature has been dealt damage equal to or greater than its toughness, it is destroyed and put into its owner’s graveyard. Because this mandatory event happens first, both creatures move to their owners’ graveyards simultaneously, which then triggers the undying ability on your zombie. When that triggered ability resolves afterward, it returns the permanent to the battlefield under its owner’s control with a plus-one-plus-one counter on it. The concrete final outcome is that your blocker dies and immediately comes back as a new one-toughness creature carrying a single counter. It does not gain haste from returning this way, so it will have summoning sickness and cannot attack or use tap abilities until your next turn begins.
What happens when the archenemy starts their turn and reveals a new scheme?

Immediately after the archenemy's precombat main phase begins, that player moves the top card of their scheme deck off that scheme deck and turns it face up. This is called setting that scheme in motion. For example, as soon as the archenemy enters their precombat main phase, they will flip over the next card from their scheme deck, such as a card named Dark Decree, to set it in motion.
What happens when I use a spell that tries to flip my creature, but the back side of the card is actually an instant?

Nothing happens to the permanent. When the spell attempts the transformation, the game checks the resulting face, and because the face that permanent would transform or convert into is an instant or sorcery card face, nothing happens. For example, if you cast a spell to flip a creature but the back of that card is an instant, the creature stays on the battlefield exactly as it was.
I have a creature that turns into a copy of something else every turn, and then I play a Clone to copy it. Does my Clone also get that ability to change every turn?

Yes, the Clone will inherit that ability. When an object copies another, its copiable values become the copied information of the original object. For example, if you use a Vesuvan Doppelganger to copy a creature and then play a Clone to copy that Doppelganger, the Clone becomes a copy of the Doppelganger. This means the Clone will also have the Doppelganger's ability to become a copy of another creature during its upkeep.
What happens if I attack with a blue creature and then immediately use a spell to turn it green? Will my enchantment that says 'Whenever a green creature attacks, destroy it' still trigger?

No, the ability will not trigger. Abilities that trigger on a creature attacking trigger only at the point the creature is declared as an attacker. Because your creature was blue at the moment you declared it as an attacker, it did not meet the condition for the enchantment to trigger, even if it becomes green immediately afterward.

I am at two life in the middle of my turn and I control Lich's Mirror. My opponent casts an instant that deals four damage to me and makes me draw three cards even though my library is already empty. We keep arguing about whether the damage or the card draw makes me lose first, and I heard triggers might not happen at all. What actually resolves?

When the spell finishes resolving, the game checks state-based actions. Both your life total dropping to zero or below and drawing from an empty library would normally cause you to lose simultaneously. Because multiple state-based actions would have the same result at the same time, a single replacement effect replaces all of them. Lich's Mirror's ability reads 'If you would lose the game, instead shuffle your hand, your graveyard, and all permanents you own into your library, then draw seven cards and your life total becomes 20.' This replacement effect applies once, completely preventing you from losing the game. Since triggered abilities watching for a player to lose specifically trigger when that event happens, and you never actually lose due to the replacement, those abilities do not trigger at all. The concrete final outcome is that you survive the turn, your library is shuffled with your hand and permanents into it, you draw seven cards at a life total of twenty, and no game-loss triggers resolve.
What happens if my creature has an Aura on it and then I give it protection from enchantments?

First, the creature gains the protection ability. Then, because a permanent with protection cannot be enchanted by Auras that have the stated quality, any Auras currently attached to it that have the stated quality are put into their owners graveyard as a state-based action. For example, if your creature is enchanted with an Aura like Ethereal Armor and you cast a spell that gives it protection from enchantments, the Ethereal Armor will immediately be moved to the graveyard.
Can I still block an opponent's creature that has flying by using my creature with reach?

Yes, you can. A creature with flying can't be blocked except by creatures with flying and/or reach. For example, if your opponent attacks with a 3/3 bird that has flying, your 2/2 spider with reach is able to step up and block it.
If I use an effect to search my library for a legendary creature, can I pick my flip card even if it hasn't flipped yet?

No, you cannot. In every zone other than the battlefield, and also on the battlefield before the permanent flips, a flip card has only the normal characteristics of the card. For example, if your flip card is currently a nonlegendary creature in your library, a search for a legendary card will not find it because it has not yet flipped into its legendary version.
I just drew this card and it says it is a Scheme; can I play it in our current game?

No, you cannot. Scheme is a card type seen only on nontraditional Magic cards and is used specifically for the Archenemy casual variant. For example, if you are currently playing a standard game of Commander and draw a Scheme card, you cannot add it to your play because that card type is not meant for traditional formats.
Can I use Unearth to bring a creature back and attack with it the same turn I use it?

Yes, you can. The ability grants the card haste, which means it ignores summoning sickness and can tap or attack the moment it enters the battlefield. For example, if you unearth a creature during your main phase, you can immediately use it to attack before your turn is over.
What happens if a spell costs 5 life but I only have 3 life left?

When you try to pay a cost that exceeds your current life, you cannot complete the action. A player may only pay an amount of life greater than 0 if their life total is greater than or equal to the amount of the payment. For example, if you attempt to cast a spell that requires 5 life but you only have 3 life, you are unable to meet the requirement and cannot cast the spell.
What happens if I play a creature with Bloodthirst 3 right after I use a spell to deal 2 damage to my opponent?

The creature will enter the battlefield with 3 +1/+1 counters on it. This is because Bloodthirst N means the permanent enters with N +1/+1 counters if an opponent was dealt damage this turn. As long as any amount of damage was dealt to an opponent, you get the full value of N. For example, if you deal only 1 damage to an opponent and then cast a creature with Bloodthirst 3, it still enters with all 3 +1/+1 counters.
Can I use an effect that tells me to blight a creature if I don't have any creatures on the battlefield?

No, you cannot. To blight means to put -1/-1 counters on a creature you control, and if you are unable to put those counters on a creature because you control no creatures, you can't choose to blight. For example, if an opponent plays a spell that forces you to blight one creature and you have no creatures on the battlefield, you cannot perform the action.
What happens to my opponents when it is my turn?

They are categorized as nonactive players. The active player is the player whose turn it is, and all other players are nonactive players. For example, if you are currently taking your turn, you are the active player and your opponents are nonactive players.
If I have a card that says Learn, do I always have to throw away a card in my hand to get a new one?

No, you have a choice. You can either discard a card and then draw a card, or if you did not discard a card, you may reveal a Lesson card you own from outside the game and put it into your hand. For example, if you are playing a deck with many Lesson cards in your sideboard, you can choose to skip the discard-and-draw step to specifically pick one of those cards for your hand.
What happens when I activate the ability to meld my two cards?

The ability exiles both the card and its counterpart, and then you put them onto the battlefield with their back faces up and combined. This process creates a single object represented by two cards. For example, if you trigger a meld ability, both components will be moved to exile before being placed together on the table as one unified permanent using their back sides.
Can I keep playing if my life total drops to zero while my teammate has a Platinum Angel on the field?

Yes, you can. In Two-Headed Giant, players win and lose the game only as a team, and any effect that says a player cannot lose the game applies to the entire team. Because your teammate controls Platinum Angel, which states that you cannot lose the game and your opponents cannot win the game, neither player on your team can lose while that card is on the battlefield. For example, if your individual life total reaches 0, your team does not lose because the protection from the Platinum Angel extends to both you and your teammate.
What happens when an ability tells me to sacrifice a creature?

When you sacrifice a permanent, its controller moves it from the battlefield directly to its owner's graveyard. For example, if you use an ability like the one on Greater Good that requires you to sacrifice a creature to draw cards, you choose one of your creatures and move it from the battlefield directly to your graveyard.
What happens if I suddenly get the initiative during my opponent's turn?

As soon as you take the initiative, you immediately get to start your journey through the dungeon because whenever a player takes the initiative, that player ventures into Undercity. For example, if your opponent attacks you and you manage to take the initiative through some other effect, you will immediately venture into Undercity even though it is not your turn.
What happens if my artifact is told to endure 2?

When a permanent is told to endure N, you choose between two options. You can either put N +1/+1 counters on that permanent or create an N/N white Spirit creature token instead. For example, if an effect says your artifact endures 2, you would first decide whether you want to add two +1/+1 counters to the artifact or just create a new 2/2 white Spirit creature token.
My opponent played a spell that says we both vote for a color, and they get two votes while I only get one. Do I have to pick my choices one after another?

No, you do not pick them one at a time. If an effect gives a player multiple votes, those votes all happen at the same time the player would otherwise have voted. For example, if a spell says players vote for a color and gives one player two votes, that player makes both of their selections simultaneously during their turn in the voting order, before the next player makes their single choice.
What happens if my creature has a shield counter on it and an opponent tries to destroy it?

The creature will stay on the battlefield. One or more shield counters on a permanent create a single replacement effect that says if this permanent would be destroyed as the result of an effect, instead remove a shield counter from it. For example, if your opponent casts a spell like Murder on your creature that has a shield counter, the creature remains on the battlefield and you simply remove one shield counter instead.
I am looking at this card and it does not have any mana cost in the top right corner, but there is a little colored circle under the picture. Does that mean the card has a color?

Yes, that circular symbol indicates the card's color. The color indicator consists of a circular symbol filled in with one or more colors and is located to the left of the type line directly below the illustration. For example, if you play a card that has no mana cost but features a single red circle under its artwork, that card is considered a red card for all game purposes.
I just met the requirement for my Case card by playing a third land. Does it solve right away?

Not immediately. The rule states that if the condition is met and the Case is not already solved, it becomes solved at the beginning of your end step. For example, if your Case says To solve — if you control three lands, and you play your third land during your main phase, you must wait until the beginning of your end step for the Case to become solved.
What happens to my planes when I move them into the planar deck?

They stay in your command zone. You move the plane card from its starting area into the planar deck, but all plane and phenomenon cards remain in the command zone throughout the game, even while they are part of a planar deck. For example, if you move a plane card into the planar deck to be drawn later, it is still considered to be in your command zone.
If I tap a land for mana and it also does something else, can my opponent react to the second part of that ability?

No, they cannot. Mana abilities resolve immediately. If a mana ability both produces mana and has another effect, the mana is produced and the other effect happens immediately. For example, if you use a land that taps for one green mana and also lets you draw a card, the mana enters your pool and you draw the card at the same time, leaving no window for an opponent to respond.
What happens when my creature with afterlife 3 is destroyed?

When the permanent is put into a graveyard from the battlefield, you create three 1/1 white and black Spirit creature tokens with flying. For example, if your creature is destroyed by combat damage, it moves to the graveyard, which triggers the ability to create three 1/1 white and black Spirit creature tokens with flying.
What happens if I try to use an effect that replaces a card draw, but my deck is already empty?

The replacement effect is applied even if no cards could be drawn because there are no cards left in your library. For example, if you have an effect that says instead of drawing a card, you look at the top card of your library and put it into your hand, that action still happens even if your library is empty, though there will be no card to move.
What happens if I want to play a card that says I have to pay an extra {1} mana?

When you cast the spell, you pay the printed mana cost and the extra amount simultaneously. Any additional cost listed in an object's rules text or imposed by an effect isn't part of the mana cost, but such costs are paid at the same time as the spell's other costs. For example, if a spell costs {2}{R} and has a requirement to pay an extra {1}, you must pay {3}{R} all at once when you begin casting it.
Can I use the new abilities on the bottom of my card before it actually flips?

No, you cannot. The characteristics on the bottom half of a flip card, such as its text box, name, power, and toughness, are used only if the permanent is flipped. For example, if your creature has 1/1 stats on the top half and 4/4 stats on the bottom upside-down half, you must continue to use the 1/1 stats until the specific conditions to flip the card have been met.
What happens to my plane card if an effect turns it face down?

As the effect resolves and turns the card over, the face-up plane card that is turned face down becomes a new object. This change means the card's previous identity is gone. For example, if you have a plane named Sky Garden and an effect turns it face down, the resulting face-down card is technically a different entity from the original Sky Garden.
Can I cast a spell to give my creature protection from red if it already has protection from blue?

Yes, you can. There are no special restrictions on casting a spell that generates a prevention effect, so having one active does not stop you from using another. For example, if your creature already has protection from blue because of an enchantment, you can still cast a spell that grants protection from red. The new effect will work alongside the existing one until its duration has expired.
If I hit something with a creature and an ability goes off, do I have to wait for that ability to finish before I can do anything else?

No, you do not have to wait. Any abilities that triggered on damage being dealt or while state-based actions are performed afterward are put onto the stack before the active player gets priority. This means that if it is your turn, those triggers will be waiting on the stack for you to interact with once you get priority. For example, if your creature deals damage to an enemy creature that has an ability triggered by damage, that ability goes on the stack first, and then you get priority to cast a spell or activate an ability in response to it.
Can I still use the name of my card's other side if it flips? If an effect asks me to pick a name and my creature has transformed, can I pick that new name?

Yes, you can. When an effect instructs a player to choose a card name, the player may choose the name of either face of a double-faced card. For example, if you have a transforming creature like Delver of Secrets and it has already changed into Insectile Aberration, you can choose Insectile Aberration as your chosen name.
I only have blue mana from my islands right now, but this card says I can pay the cost with mana of any type. Can I use my blue mana to pay for a spell that normally costs red mana?

Yes, you can. When an effect says that mana of any type can be spent, it means that players may spend mana as though it were colorless mana or mana of any color to pay that cost. For example, if you have one blue mana available and an effect allows you to pay its cost with mana of any type, you can use that blue mana to pay for a spell that costs one red mana.
My opponent has a big bird with flying and I only have this small ground goblin. Can my goblin stop it from hitting me?

No, you cannot block that creature. A creature with flying can't be blocked except by creatures with flying and/or reach. Since your goblin lacks both of those abilities, it cannot intercept the attacker. For example, if your opponent attacks with a Pegasus and you only have a Goblin Warrior on the battlefield, the Pegasus will bypass your goblin and deal damage to you directly.
I have a spell that says I can cast it only after my opponent declares attackers. But what if they don't actually attack with anything? Can I still use it?

Yes, you can still use it. The rules state that a spell which can be cast only after attackers are declared refers to the turn-based action of declaring attackers, and this applies regardless of whether any attackers are actually declared. For example, if your opponent chooses not to attack with any creatures during their combat phase, the declare attackers step still occurs, meaning you can cast your spell during that window.
What happens if I use a card that lets me play cards exiled with it, but I actually used a different spell to exile those cards instead?

The ability to play the cards will not work for them. Since these abilities are linked, the second ability refers only to cards in the exile zone that were put there as a direct result of the replacement event caused by the first ability. For example, if a card has an ability saying whenever it attacks, instead exile target creature, and another ability saying you may play cards exiled with that card, you can only play the creatures moved to exile by that attack effect. If you use a spell like Path to Exile to exile a creature, the card's ability will not see that creature because it was not put there by the specific replacement effect on that card.
Does a battle card have any defense value if it is still in my hand?

Yes, even before it reaches the battlefield, the defense of a battle card not on the battlefield is equal to the number printed in its lower right corner. For example, if you are holding a battle card that has 5 printed in the bottom right corner, its defense is considered to be 5.
What happens if my opponent uses a spell to prevent the next 3 damage dealt to me, and then attacks me with two creatures at once?

The effect works like a shield where each 1 damage prevented reduces the remaining shield by 1. Since the damage is coming from two sources at the same time, you get to choose which damage the shield prevents. For example, if one creature deals 2 damage and another deals 2 damage simultaneously, you can choose for the shield to prevent the 2 damage from the first creature and 1 damage from the second. This leaves 1 damage that is dealt normally to you.
What happens if an enchantment says cards go to exile instead of the graveyard, but my creature has an ability that shuffles it into its owner's library if it dies?

You get to decide which effect occurs. Since both are replacement effects attempting to modify how the event affects the object, the controller of the creature chooses one to apply. For example, if you control a creature with an ability that shuffles it into your library when it dies while an enchantment is active that exiles cards instead of putting them in the graveyard, you choose whether the creature shuffles or gets exiled.
What happens if I have a creature that says 'As this permanent transforms, draw a card' and I use a spell to flip it?

You will draw the card during the transition. Since an ability that triggers as a permanent transforms is applied while that permanent is transforming or converting, not afterward, the effect occurs during the actual change of faces. For example, if you use a spell to flip a creature with this ability, the card draw happens at the same time the card is being turned over.
I just played an Instant on my opponent's turn and it finished resolving. Why can't I immediately play another card?

After a spell or ability resolves, the active player receives priority. This means if you cast an Instant during your opponent's turn, once that spell finishes resolving, the priority goes to your opponent first because they are currently the active player. For example, if you cast a removal spell on their creature and it resolves, your opponent gets the first chance to act, perhaps by casting a spell to protect another creature, before you get a chance to respond.
What happens once we know who is starting?

After you have decided which player starts, the sequence is that each player sets their life total to 20 and then draws a hand of seven cards. For example, if you and your opponent decide that you will go first, you both immediately set your life totals to 20 and draw seven cards from your decks to prepare for the game.
I just put an art sticker on my creature. Does it give the creature any extra powers or abilities?

No, it does not. An art sticker on a permanent has no effect on game play other than to act as a marker that other spells and abilities can identify. For example, if you place a dragon art sticker on a 1/1 Goblin, that Goblin does not gain flying or any other combat abilities.
I have a card with dredge 7 in my graveyard. I am about to draw a card, but I only have 4 cards left in my deck. Can I use the dredge ability to mill cards and get that creature back into my hand?

No, you cannot. The dredge ability only works as long as you have at least N cards in your library. Since you only have 4 cards left and the card requires 7, you cannot mill any of them this way. For example, if you had a card with dredge 7 in your graveyard but your library only had 4 cards remaining, you would simply draw the card normally instead of milling.
I just played a card that says skip my next untap step, but I feel like I missed out on something. Does the game just act like that step never happened?

When a step is skipped, the game proceeds past it as though it did not exist. This means you do not get to perform any actions associated with that specific part of the turn sequence. For example, if your untap step is skipped, you move from your end step directly into your upkeep step without your permanents being untapped first.
Can I cast a spell from my graveyard that has jump-start by only paying its mana cost?

No, you cannot. To use the jump-start ability, you must discard a card as an additional cost to cast it from your graveyard. For example, if you have a spell with jump-start in your graveyard and want to cast it, you must choose one card in your hand and discard it while casting that spell.
Can my creature keep getting more counters from renown every time it hits a player?

No, it cannot. The ability triggers when the creature deals combat damage to a player, if it isn't renowned. Once a permanent becomes renowned, it stays renowned until it leaves the battlefield. For example, if you have a creature with Renown 2 and it hits an opponent, it gets two +1/+1 counters and becomes renowned. On its next successful attack, it won't get any more counters from that ability because it is already renowned.
What happens to an omen card after its effect happens? Does it go to my graveyard like a normal spell?

It does not go to your graveyard. As an Omen spell resolves, its controller shuffles it into their library instead of putting it into their graveyard. For example, if you cast an Omen card and its effect resolves, you will shuffle that card back into your deck rather than placing it in the graveyard.
Can a non-planeswalker ever use a loyalty ability?

Yes, it can. While normally only planeswalkers have loyalty abilities, any activated ability with a loyalty symbol in its cost is a loyalty ability. For example, if a special artifact had an ability that cost one loyalty, that ability would be treated as a loyalty ability despite the card not being a planeswalker.
What happens if someone uses an ability that restarts the whole game, even if we are playing with those rules where players only have a limited range of influence?

The entire game is restarted for every person playing. Even if you are playing with limited range of influence, if a game is restarted, all players in the game are involved regardless of the range of influence of the player who controls the ability that restarted the game. For example, in a four-player game where your abilities only reach two people, using an effect that restarts the game would still force everyone at the table to restart.
I just played this Battle card, but can I actually attack it myself if I'm the one who played it?

That depends on the type of Battle. While a battle's protector can never attack it, there is an exception where a Siege battle can be attacked by its own controller. For example, if you play a Siege card and choose yourself as the protector when it enters the battlefield, you are still allowed to attack that Siege.
Can I use a creature's Outlast ability to get a counter while my opponent is playing their turn?

No. Because the ability can only be activated as a sorcery, you cannot use it during your opponent's turn. You must wait until it is your turn and the stack is empty. For example, if a creature has Outlast 3, you cannot tap it to get a counter during your opponent's end step; you can only do so during your own main phase.
If I have enough mana, can I just pay for the level 2 ability right away instead of going through level 1?

No, you cannot skip levels. The activation part of the bar means you can only activate a level N ability if the class is currently level N-1. For example, if a card has Level 1 and Level 2 bars, you must first pay the cost to make the class level 1 before you are allowed to pay the cost for the level 2 ability.
Can I use my station ability to get more counters while it is my opponent's turn?

No, you cannot. The station ability can only be activated as a sorcery, meaning you can only use it during your own turn when the stack is empty. For example, if an opponent casts an instant spell during your main phase, you must wait for that spell to finish resolving before you can tap a creature to use the station ability.
I just played a creature with discover 2. I keep exiling cards and they are all big spells or lands. What happens if I can't find a card that is small enough?

When you use a discover effect, you exile cards from the top of your library until you exile a nonland card with mana value N or less. If you cannot find a card that meets this requirement before running out of cards, you have still completed the discovery process. Any cards you exiled during this process are then put on the bottom of your library in a random order. For example, if you have discover 2 and your library only contains a land and a spell with mana value 5, you will exile both cards and then place them on the bottom of your library in a random order.
What happens when I use an ability that targets a card in my opponent's graveyard? Does it count as a crime?

First, you activate the ability and put it on the stack. At that moment, you have committed a crime because you activated an ability that targets at least one card in an opponent's graveyard. This triggers any cards you have that react to crimes being committed. For example, if you use an ability to exile a specific card from your opponent's graveyard, you commit a crime as soon as that ability is on the stack.
What happens to the regular rules once we start playing this Archenemy version where one person is the boss?

The game still functions mostly the same way you are used to. The rule explains that the Archenemy variant uses all the normal rules for a Magic game, with only specific additions like scheme cards. For example, even though there is a special setup, you still have to follow the standard rules for tapping lands and casting spells during your turn.
What happens if I use Volrath's Shapeshifter to copy a card like Kokusho, the Evening Star? Does it actually become that legendary creature with the same name and color?

If you use Volrath's Shapeshifter to copy Kokusho, the Evening Star, the Shapeshifter first gains the ability to be that card. Then, because it has the full text of the other object, it changes not just the text that appears in its text box and type line, but also changes the name, mana cost, color indicator, power, and toughness. This means your creature becomes a black legendary creature named Kokusho, the Evening Star with its specific power and toughness.
If my friend is playing a game for me because I am busy, can they just decide that we lose and give up?

No, they cannot. The controller of another player cannot make that player concede. Even though your friend is making decisions for you, a player may concede the game at any time, even if they are controlled by another player. For example, if your friend decides to surrender during a match you are supposed to be playing, you can still choose to stay in the game and finish it yourself.
Can I look at my teammate's hand so we can coordinate our next turn?

No, you cannot look at their hand because a team's resources like cards in hand are not shared. The only exception is if teammates are sitting next to each other, which allows them to review hands. For example, if your teammate is sitting across the table from you, you must rely on what they tell you verbally rather than looking at their actual cards.
What happens if my opponent casts a spell and I don't have any responses? Do we just skip to my next turn or does the spell happen first?

When all players pass in succession, the top spell or ability on the stack resolves. This means the spell must finish its effect before the game can move forward. For example, if your opponent casts a spell to destroy a creature and you both pass, the creature will be destroyed before the game transitions to the next phase.
What happens when I want to use a spell that says I can cast it after my upkeep step? Do I have to wait for my main phase?

First, you complete your upkeep step. Once that step ends, the condition is satisfied, allowing you to cast it at any point during the rest of the turn. For example, if you have a spell that says you may cast it after your upkeep step, you can cast it during combat or during your second main phase because the rule allows it to be cast any time after that first upkeep step ends.
Can I tap a creature for mana the same turn it enters the battlefield?

No, you cannot. A creature's activated ability with the tap symbol in its cost can't be activated unless the creature has been under your control continuously since your most recent turn began. For example, if you cast a Llanowar Elves this turn, you cannot use its ability to add green mana until your next turn starts.
What happens to our game if we started with three people but one player just had to leave?

The game remains a multiplayer game. Since a multiplayer game is defined as a game that begins with more than two players, the classification is established at the very start of the match. For example, if Alice, Bob, and Charlie begin a match and Charlie leaves on turn four, it is still considered a multiplayer game.
What happens if I play another Role aura on a creature that already has one?

The previous Role will be put into your graveyard. This is because if a permanent has more than one Role controlled by the same player attached to it, each of those Roles except the one with the most recent timestamp is put into its owner's graveyard. For example, if you have a creature with a Fighter role and then you attach a Scout role to that same creature, the Fighter role will be moved to your graveyard so that only the most recent role remains.
If I want to use the effect on a card with casualty 3, do I have to sacrifice my creature, or is it optional?

You do not have to sacrifice a creature because casualty is an additional cost that you may pay. However, if you do sacrifice a creature with power 3 or greater, then when you cast this spell, if a casualty cost was paid for it, copy it. For example, if you have a 3/3 Dragon and cast a spell with casualty 3, you can choose to sacrifice the Dragon to get a second copy of that spell.
