What happens when an opponent tries to counter my spell after I have already paid its mana cost and it is sitting on the stack, if I have a permanent that prevents countering?

The attempt to counter your spell will fail. Once the spell is placed on the stack, it is still subject to static abilities that refer to countering a spell. For example, if you have an enchantment that says spells cannot be countered, your spell remains protected from any opponent's counterspells because those static abilities apply while a spell is on the stack.
What happens if I have a card that triggers at the start of my turn? Does everything happen all at once?

When a new step or phase begins, any turn-based actions associated with it are automatically dealt with first. This occurs before triggered abilities are put on the stack and before players receive priority to act. For example, during your untap step, all your permanents will untap before any of your triggered abilities are put on the stack for you to respond to.
When I play a creature that has Tribute 2, what actually happens?

As the creature enters the battlefield, you choose an opponent. That player then has the choice to put two +1/+1 counters on the creature as it enters. For example, if you play a creature with Tribute 2 and select your opponent, they can decide to add those two counters or choose not to add any at all.
What happens if I only use these rules to prepare for my tournament and ignore all other documentation?

You may end up with an illegal deck because many multiplayer Magic tournaments have additional rules not included here, including rules for deck construction. To find the correct guidelines, you must see the most current Magic: The Gathering Tournament Rules at WPN.wizards.com/en/rules-documents. For example, if a tournament requires a specific number of cards and you only follow these basic rules, your deck could be disqualified during registration.
What happens when an opponent plays a card that counters all activated abilities?

Planeswalker abilities will be countered because loyalty abilities are a type of activated ability. For example, if an effect counters all activated abilities, a Planeswalker's loyalty abilities will also be countered.
Can I cast my second partner commander without paying extra if I already cast my first one?

Yes. Except for determining the color identity of your commander, the two commanders function independently. When casting a commander with partner, you ignore how many times your other commander has been cast. For example, if you have two partner commanders and you cast the first one, the second commander will still cost its base mana cost to cast because its tax is calculated separately.
What happens when my opponent is forced to discard a card?

To discard a card, it is moved from the owner's hand to their graveyard. By default, effects that cause a player to discard a card allow the affected player to choose which card to discard. For example, if your opponent has a Forest and a spell in hand and you play a spell that makes them discard, they will choose which of those two cards is moved from their hand to their graveyard.
Can my 2/2 creature still be treated as a 2/2 if I attach an equipment that gives it +3/+3?

No, you cannot. The mechanic at play is that a nontoken permanent's characteristics are the same as those printed on its card, as modified by any continuous effects. For example, if you attach an equipment that gives +3/+3 to a 2/2 creature, the creature's current characteristics are 5/5 because of the equipment's effect.
Can my teammate and I just sit next to each other if we are playing in a three-team game?

No, you cannot sit next to your teammate because players must be seated so that no one is next to a teammate and each team is equally spaced out. For example, if you are on Team A, you should have players from Team B and Team C between you and your teammate.
What happens to my creature once I finish casting the spell?

When a creature spell resolves, its controller puts it onto the battlefield under their control. This means the card moves from the stack to the table as a permanent. For example, if you cast a 2/2 Goblin, once the spell finishes resolving, you place that Goblin onto the battlefield under your control.
Can my tiny 1/1 creature kill your huge 10/10 dragon if it has deathtouch?

Yes, it can. Any nonzero amount of combat damage assigned to a creature by a source with deathtouch is considered to be lethal damage. For example, if your 1/1 with deathtouch attacks my 10/10 dragon and they both deal combat damage, the dragon will be destroyed because it was dealt damage by a source with deathtouch since the last time state-based actions were checked.
I see this card says it is a Saga. Does that mean it is something else besides an enchantment?

No, it is still an enchantment. The rules specify that some enchantments have the subtype Saga, so it remains an enchantment while also having that special subtype. For example, if you use a card like Sanctum Weaver to produce mana, it will still count your Saga as an enchantment.
What happens when I use an ability on my creature that costs mana?

The ability is put on the stack. An activated ability has a cost and an effect, and you can activate it whenever you have priority. For example, if you have a creature that lets you pay one mana to draw a card, you pay the mana, the ability goes on the stack, and then it resolves.
What happens if my prototype spell gets countered and goes back to my hand?

When a prototype spell is countered, it moves from the stack back to your hand. Since in every zone except when it is being cast as a prototyped spell, a prototype card has only its normal characteristics, the card reverts to its standard form during this transition. For example, if you attempt to cast a creature using its prototype cost but it is countered, once that card is back in your hand, it is simply the regular version of the card and you must pay its full mana cost to cast it again.
I'm trying to venture into a dungeon but I realized I don't have any dungeon cards in my command zone. What happens then?

If you are instructed to venture into the dungeon while you do not own a dungeon card in the command zone, you choose a dungeon card you own from outside the game and put it into the command zone, placing your venture marker on the topmost room. For example, if you trigger a venture effect but your command zone has no dungeons, you can take a card like Lost Mine of Phandelver from your collection, move it to your command zone, and place your marker on the first room of that dungeon.
Can I still use an effect to make someone lose life if they are sitting two seats away from me and my range of influence is only one?

No, you cannot. Your range of influence covers things like making choices or dealing damage, and it is measured in player seats. If your range of influence is 1, it means that only you and the players seated directly next to you are within your range of influence. For example, if you are at a table where the person you want to affect is two seats away, they fall outside that limit and cannot be impacted by your abilities.
What happens to a battle spell after it finishes its effect?

Instead of being put into the graveyard, the controller puts the battle onto the battlefield under their control. For example, if you cast a card that is a battle, once it has finished resolving, it stays on the field as a permanent rather than going to your graveyard like a sorcery would.
What happens if I play a card with space sculptor while my opponent already has creatures on the field?

When a permanent with space sculptor and any creatures without a sector designation are on the battlefield at the same time, players choose designations for those creatures. This is a state-based action that occurs immediately. For example, if you play Space Beleren and I have a creature that hasn't been assigned a sector yet, you will choose a sector for your creatures and I will choose a sector for mine.
What happens when my next upkeep starts if I have a creature with Vanishing 2 on the battlefield?

At the beginning of your upkeep, if the permanent has a time counter on it, you remove one time counter from it. Since the creature entered with two time counters, you will remove one during your upkeep, leaving it with one counter remaining. For example, if you play a creature with Vanishing 2, it enters the battlefield with two time counters, and at the start of your next upkeep, you remove one, so the creature stays on the battlefield.
What happens when a spell destroys my creature?

When a card or token is moved to another zone by an effect or rule, it stops being a permanent. For example, if you play a creature like Llanowar Elves and your opponent casts a spell to destroy it, the creature moves from the battlefield to the graveyard, causing it to stop being a permanent.
What happens when we set up an Archenemy game?

You first identify which player is the archenemy and then assign the correct life totals. The archenemy's starting life total is 40 and each other player's starting life total is 20. For example, if you are playing against a single archenemy, you would set your life to 20 and their life to 40 before beginning play.
If a spell lets me choose two different options, am I allowed to just pick the same option both times?

You can only do that if the card specifically says you may choose the same mode more than once. Normally, a player cannot choose the same mode more than once. For example, if a card says Choose two modes. You may choose the same mode more than once. and one of the modes is Target player loses 2 life, you could choose that mode twice to make a player lose 4 life.
Can I still cast spells right after my combat ends but before anything else happens?

Yes, you can. Once the end of combat step begins, the active player gets priority. This means you are the first to have the chance to act. For example, if you just finished an attack and want to cast a spell like Boros Charm, you can do so immediately as the end of combat step starts.

My opponent has been chipping away at me with their commander over the last few turns, and I've already taken about twenty combat damage from it. Today I control a permanent that says whenever I have no artifacts on my battlefield, I draw three cards. My only artifact just got destroyed by an attack right now. Do I get to draw those cards, or does taking that last bit of damage end the game first?

State triggers check when your battlefield state matches the condition and go onto the stack at the next available opportunity. State-based actions are then checked automatically by the game; since commander damage is an SBA, it checks immediately after the combat damage/destroy event and causes you to lose before any abilities currently on the stack can resolve.
What happens if I play a spell that says I gain 5 life?
When the spell resolves, your life total is adjusted accordingly to reflect the increase. For example, if you have 10 life and the spell causes you to gain 5 life, your new life total will be 15.

My opponent just tapped me out for lethal damage so my life total hit zero, but I have an artifact that says 'Whenever you lose the game, exile target creature card from your graveyard' and also has a separate line saying 'You may cast cards exiled by this artifact without paying their mana costs.' My opponent insists that since I'm dead, the artifact is discarded and I can't do anything. Can I still cast a creature from the exile zone, and if so, how does the game handle the order of things?

You can definitely cast the creature. Your opponent is misunderstanding how the game handles losing combined with linked abilities. Even though you took lethal damage, triggered abilities that trigger when a player loses the game are put on the stack immediately and resolve before you leave the game. This means your artifact's loss trigger fires while you are still in play, exiling the creature to the artifact's exile zone. The two abilities on your artifact are linked together; this means the permission to cast applies only to cards that were exiled by the first ability on this specific object and ignores any other cards in exile from other sources. The order of events is critical here: your opponent deals lethal damage, you reach zero life and lose, the loss trigger resolves while you are still in the game, the creature is exiled into the linked zone, the game grants you permission to cast that specific card, you cast and resolve it, and only after all triggers resolve are you removed from the match. The concrete outcome is that you get to cast the exiled creature despite losing the game due to combat damage.
What happens when we get caught in a loop where a creature keeps entering and leaving the battlefield infinitely? Do we have to physically move the cards every time?

When you encounter an infinite loop, you do not have to physically perform every single repetition. Instead, shortcut rules can be used to determine how many times those actions are repeated without having to actually perform them, provided both players understand what is happening. For example, if a combo involving a creature and a sacrifice outlet creates an infinite sequence of entering and leaving the battlefield, you can skip the physical movement and simply agree on the final outcome or the number of triggers that occur.

We were arguing about this commander that can change colors based on what you play, and someone said that if it changes to red during the game, I should suddenly be able to put red spells into my deck from my hand. I also tried casting a spell that replaces drawing cards with scrying, but got confused about how many cards actually get put back. How do I figure out what's legal and what actually happens?

The confusion comes from thinking a commander can change deckbuilding rules mid match. Color identity is established before the game begins and remains fixed throughout the entire session, even if the commander changes zones or has abilities that shift its battlefield colors. This means you cannot suddenly add non matching cards to your deck. Regarding your draw replacement sequence, if an effect replaces a draw within a sequence of card draws, all actions required by the replacement are completed, if possible, before resuming the sequence. Additionally, if an effect would have a player both draw a card and perform an additional action on that card, and the draw is replaced, the additional action is not performed on any cards that are drawn as a result of that replacement effect. The deck construction restriction establishes legality first, while the replacement mechanics dictate the exact step by step resolution during gameplay. Your final result is that your deck stays strictly bound to your initial color choices, the replacement action finishes completely without triggering conditional bonuses, and any leftover draws resolve normally using only legal cards from your preconstructed pool.
I have this artifact called a Fortification and I want to attach it to my Forest. Am I allowed to do that?

Yes, you can attach a Fortification to a land. Much like how Equipment attaches to creatures, Fortifications use the fortify keyword to attach to lands. For example, if you have a Fortification artifact and a Plains, you can use its ability to attach it to that Plains.

I attacked with a Swiftfoot Knight and a Goblin Firebug. My opponent blocked the Knight with their only blocker, a Silvercoat Lion. The Knight has first strike, so we swap damage before anything else happens, right? After that exchange, does the Silvercoat Lion get to deal any more damage or stay around to threaten me later?

Yes, the Swiftfoot Knight deals damage first because it has first strike, which means it assigns combat damage in the initial step while normal creatures wait. If the Knight deals enough damage to reduce the Silvercoat Lion's toughness to zero or less, state-based actions check immediately and put the Lion into its owner's graveyard due to lethal damage. After that check, if the Knight survived and has no first strike remaining, it would assign damage in the second combat damage step, but since the blocker is destroyed, there is no creature left blocking to receive damage from the Knight's return fire. The final outcome is that the Silvercoat Lion is destroyed by lethal damage during the first strike step and deals no further damage, while the Swiftfoot Knight remains on the battlefield alive.

I am casting a creature that requires me to exile some cards as part of the cost, and then the creature has an ability that lets me look at cards exiled with it. Does that ability let me see the cards I used to pay for the spell?

Yes, it does. If a permanent spell has an ability that allows cards to be exiled while paying a cost to cast it, and the permanent that spell becomes has an ability that refers to cards exiled with that object, those abilities are linked. This means the second ability refers specifically to the cards you exiled to pay for the spell. For example, if you cast a creature that costs two generic mana plus exiling three cards from your graveyard, and that creature has an ability saying "Look at cards exiled with this creature," you can look at those three cards.
What happens if a planeswalker's loyalty reaches zero?

When a planeswalker's loyalty is 0, it is put into its owner's graveyard. This happens automatically as soon as the loyalty hits that amount. For example, if you have a planeswalker with 2 loyalty and you use an ability that costs -2 loyalty, the planeswalker will be moved to your graveyard immediately after that ability finishes resolving.

I attack with two creatures for three damage each. My opponent blocks one with a creature that has a death trigger to draw a card, but I also control an effect that replaces my next card draws with revealing the top two cards of my library instead. Both the attackers' triggers and the blocker's death happen simultaneously. How does this resolve and what is the final board state?

First, combat damage is processed simultaneously across all attackers and blockers. When multiple sources deal damage in that step, you combine them to see if the permanent survives. The rules state that if those sources together dealt an amount of damage to a creature greater than lethal damage, excess damage equal to the difference was dealt to that creature. This calculation happens first and confirms the blocker is destroyed while leftover damage stays marked on it. Next, the death trigger goes on the stack. When you resolve it, you would normally draw a card, but replacement effects take precedence over the actual drawing action when the trigger resolves. Since some effects replace card draws, your enchantment modifies what happens before the game attempts to put a card into your hand. Because an effect would have a player both draw a card and perform an additional action on that card, and the draw is replaced, the additional action is not performed on any cards drawn as a result of that replacement effect. Final outcome: The blocking creature is destroyed with lethal plus excess damage, you do not draw cards from the death trigger, your hand remains completely unchanged, and you only follow the instructions of the replacement effect without triggering secondary card-handling abilities.
What happens to my creature if an effect says it phases out until the end of the turn?

When the end of the turn occurs, a second one-shot effect is created immediately after that specified event to cause the permanent to phase in. It is important to note that a permanent that phased out this way does not phase in as a result of the turn-based action during a player's untap step. For example, if you cast a spell that causes your creature to phase out until the end of the turn, it will phase back in once the end step occurs because the specified event triggers a new effect to bring it back.
I just cast this with its blitz cost. If it gets sacrificed at the end of the turn, do I still get to draw a card?

Yes, you will. Because you paid the blitz cost, the permanent has haste and the ability 'When this permanent is put into a graveyard from the battlefield, draw a card.' Even though you must sacrifice the permanent at the beginning of the next end step because its blitz cost was paid, it is still entering the graveyard from the battlefield. For example, if you cast a creature with Blitz 3 and it is sacrificed at your end step, you will draw a card as it hits the graveyard.
What happens if our game ends in a draw? Who picks who starts the next round?

When a game results in a draw, the player who made the choice in that game makes the choice in this game. For example, if you and your opponent play a game that ends in a tie, and you were the person who decided whether you or your opponent would go first, you are also the one who chooses who starts the next game.

I'm playing commander with a mono-white commander. My opponent just told me I can't cast this card from my hand because it has a red mana symbol in its triggered ability and that makes the whole deck illegal. Also, the spell exiles me for three life and I already had exactly ten cards in library before it resolved, leaving me at one life and zero cards. I have Lich's Mirror on the battlefield. Will I lose the game from both conditions or does my mirror save me?

Before play begins, color identity is established before the game starts to define legal deck composition, and reminder text is ignored when determining a card's color identity during that process. Since the red symbol appears in an ability text rather than as part of a color indicator, it correctly counts toward your commander's limits and makes the spell legal. When you cast it and trigger both zero life and zero library conditions together, the rule that states if multiple state-based actions would have the same result at the same time, a single replacement effect will replace all of them takes over during resolution. Deck identity rules naturally precede in-game checks because they are locked in before the match starts. Because Lich's Mirror covers that combined loss event exactly once, you do not lose, instead shuffling your hand, your graveyard, and all permanents you own into your library, then drawing seven cards and setting your life total to twenty while continuing the match.

My opponent controls a creature called Ironclad Crusher with an ability that says other creatures you control get +2/+0. I cast a spell that gives my attacker +3/+3 and changes its text so it no longer cares about creature types. We disagree on whether the bonus still applies or if one effect overwrites the other, especially since we swapped control of the Crusher mid-combat with another spell earlier this turn. What actually happens?

Change the final statement to state that the creature receives a combined bonus of +5/+3 (plus five power and plus three toughness), which is added to its original stats for combat damage calculations.
Can my opponent block my blue creature with intimidate using their red creature?

No, they cannot. A creature with intimidate can't be blocked except by artifact creatures and/or creatures that share a color with it. Since your creature is blue and their creature is red, the red creature cannot block unless it is also an artifact creature. For example, if you attack with a blue creature with intimidate, an opponent cannot block it with a red Dragon, but they could block it with a blue Dragon or an artifact creature like an Ornithopter.

I just tapped my creature for an ability that exiles my opponent's blocker as a replacement effect instead of dealing damage, and the card text says at the beginning of the next end step you may return that card to the battlefield under its owner's control. My opponent changed their blocker into a 0/4 with trample using a quick instant before damage resolved. Will the trigger still bring back my blocked creature, or does changing its power and toughness mess it up? Also, can I use this exile ability on multiple creatures and return them all at once?

The game handles this using two specific mechanics that work together in a set order. First, the rule for linked abilities explicitly states that when an object has one ability generating a replacement effect that causes cards to be exiled and another ability referring to those exiled cards, they are strictly bound so the second refers only to cards put there as a direct result of that first event. This happens first in the ruling sequence to establish exactly which exile contents belong to your specific trigger. Second, once tracking is established, the delayed triggered ability rules take over and note that such an ability will affect the named object even if it changes characteristics, but it will not affect it if the permanent leaves the expected zone before resolution. Because the linking rule locks down object identity before the timing rules evaluate the return window, a single activation only creates one independent loop rather than a shared pool. The concrete final outcome is that exactly one delayed trigger will fire at the beginning of your next end step to attempt to return exactly the one blocker you originally exiled, and it will succeed as long as that specific card remains in exile up until that moment, completely ignoring any power or toughness changes it underwent.

We are playing a free-for-all multiplayer game and my turn has come up. I start attacking with a creature that has undying, but during combat damage I accidentally let it take lethal damage from two blockers before realizing what happened. It goes to the graveyard now, but does its undying ability trigger based on its power and toughness right as it died, or something else? Also, since we are in multiplayer, does the rule about picking a defending player at the start of combat change how this resolves?

First, the foundational combat restriction applies immediately before any damage is dealt because multiplayer matches require you to lock in your target early. The official guideline states that during multiplayer games, the attacking player chooses one of their opponents as a turn-based action during the beginning of combat step, which establishes who is defending and validates your attackers for this phase. Once combat proceeds and your creature takes lethal damage, it triggers simultaneous state checks upon hitting zero toughness. At that exact moment, if a state-based action results in a permanent leaving the battlefield at the same time other state-based actions were performed, that permanent’s last known information is derived from the game state before any of those state-based actions were performed. This means the returning ability ignores mid-combat damage or altered counters and looks strictly at its pre-damage board state to determine if conditions are met. The concrete final outcome is that your attack remains assigned to the originally chosen defender, the creature’s death trigger evaluates its exact configuration just prior to leaving, and it successfully returns to the battlefield with its original counters intact because the earlier turn-based defender selection made the combat valid and the subsequent last known information rule preserved its true stats.
What happens if I pick a creature to block, but then the attacker gets flying before I actually pay for the block?

The block remains valid. After you choose which creatures will block and verify they meet all restrictions, the block is set. The rules state that if an attacking creature gains or loses an evasion ability after a legal block has been declared, it does not affect that block. For example, if you declare a non-flying creature to block an attacker without flying, and then your opponent plays a spell to give that attacker flying, your blocker is still blocking the attacker.
Can I use the powers on my scheme card if it is just sitting in the command zone?

Yes, you can. As long as a scheme card is face up in the command zone, its static abilities affect the game, its triggered abilities may trigger, and its activated abilities may be activated. For example, if your scheme card has an activated ability that lets you pay 2 mana to draw a card, you can still do that even if the card is not on the battlefield.

I control a creature with recover and it has an ability that reads 'when this creature dies, if it had +1/+1 counters on it, draw a card.' My opponent cast a spell that put three -1/-1 counters on my creature and also gave it lethal damage at the same time. State-based actions are about to check, and my friend says the -1/-1 counters reduce toughness to zero first via state-based actions, so by the time the death trigger looks for counters, they're gone? Does recover still fire in this mess? What's the actual result?

Your friend is misunderstanding how last known information works when multiple state-based actions coincide. When state-based actions cause a permanent to leave the battlefield at the same time as other state-based actions, such as lethal damage and zero toughness from counters, the game uses last known information derived from the game state before any of those state-based actions were performed. This means your death trigger checks the creature with the +1/+1 counters still present, so you will draw a card. Meanwhile, the creature is put into your graveyard from the battlefield, which triggers its recover ability independently of damage or counters. The rule for recover states that when a creature is put into your graveyard from the battlefield, you may pay the recover cost to return this card from your graveyard to your hand; otherwise it is exiled. Because the move to the graveyard occurs regardless of why it died, recover triggers correctly. The final outcome is both abilities go on the stack: your death trigger sees the +1/+1 counters due to last known information, and you get a recover trigger that lets you pay mana to save the card or let it exile if you choose not to pay.

I just cast a sorcery that returns all creature cards from my graveyard to my hand while two of my creatures have lethal damage marked on them. Does it drag the damaged creatures into my hand too, or just the one already buried?

When your spell resolves, it performs its instruction on all cards in that zone exactly as they exist at that moment, meaning only the one already buried creature returns to your hand. Right after the spell finishes resolving, state-based actions happen automatically whenever certain conditions like lethal damage are met, and these checks don't use the stack. Because those two battlefield creatures now meet the damage condition, they are put into your graveyard as a separate game action rather than being pulled by your spell. The concrete final outcome is one creature in your hand and two creatures sitting in your graveyard, with priority returning to the active player to continue the turn.
What happens if a card says I have to draw a card as an upkeep cost, but another card lets me skip that draw instead? Did I actually pay my cost?

Yes, you have still paid the cost. Even if the actions performed do not match the actions that are called for because they were modified by an effect, the cost has still been paid. For example, if you control Psychic Vortex which has a cumulative upkeep cost of draw a card, and you also control Obstinate Familiar which lets you skip that draw instead, choosing to skip the draw means the upkeep cost is still considered paid.
Can I just decide to stop using a scheme card if it is not helping me?

You can only do this if you are playing an Archenemy game and the scheme card is currently face-up and ongoing. If those conditions are met, you abandon the card by turning it face down and putting it on the bottom of your scheme deck. For example, if an Archenemy finds a face-up scheme too difficult to deal with, they can choose to abandon it by flipping the card over and moving it to the bottom of their scheme deck.

I just swung with my creature that has both soulshift and lifelink, and my opponent blocked it with their creature. After combat ends, both of our creatures are in the graveyard and I gained life from combat damage, but I was expecting my soulshift effect to trigger when mine died. Did something go wrong or does it not work like that?

Your soulshift ability absolutely triggered, you just may have missed it because multiple things happen at once. First, combat damage is dealt simultaneously, and the lifelink mechanic applies here because the rules state that damage dealt by a source with lifelink causes that source’s controller to gain that much life, in addition to the damage's other results. That is why you gained life during combat. Next, state-based actions check for lethal damage, see both creatures have taken more than enough damage to destroy them, and put them into their controllers' graveyards. This move to the graveyard is exactly what activates your soulshift ability, which states that when this permanent is put into a graveyard from the battlefield, you may return target Spirit card with mana value N or less from your graveyard to your hand. The lifelink damage modification happens first during the combat phase, and once the creatures are moved to the graveyard as a result of those damage results, the soulshift triggered ability goes on the stack. Your concrete final outcome is that you gain life equal to the combat damage dealt, both creatures are placed into their respective graveyards, and your soulshift ability resolves allowing you to target and return a matching Spirit card from your graveyard to your hand.

I just played a creature spell and my opponent responded by tapping one of my artifacts to make it stop being a creature until end of turn. Their enchantment says all creatures get +2/+2. Does my creature still get the boost even though it is not a creature right now, or does the boost disappear immediately?

Continuous effects from multiple sources do not apply simultaneously but instead follow a strict ordering system based on dependency. An effect depends on another if applying one would change what the other does or applies to, and when that happens, the dependent effect waits until just after all of those independent effects have been applied, which overrides any normal timestamp calculations. In your scenario, while the enchantment continuously modifies characteristics, static abilities strictly evaluate the game state in real time. Because static abilities cannot use an object's last known information for purposes of determining how their effects are applied, they do not remember that the permanent was a creature moments ago. They only care about what currently exists on the battlefield after all continuous effects resolve in their dependency order. The concrete final outcome is that your permanent immediately stops receiving the +2/+2 boost the instant it ceases to be a creature, as the static ability instantly reevaluates based on its new current type rather than past state, and the dependency system simply ensures all type and characteristic modifiers calculate in a fixed sequence before that evaluation occurs.

I have a 1/1 Goblin on my side of the board that took two damage during combat, so it should die. Can I activate Reinforce 3 targeting that Goblin and add three counters to save it, or does it die immediately when the damage is dealt?

Yes, you can activate Reinforce to save it, and the creature will survive. When you activate Reinforce, you pay the cost by discarding the card from your hand and put the ability on the stack to add the counters. The game does not check if creatures die until after the ability resolves and players receive priority. At that point, the Goblin has received three +1/+1 counters, making it a 4/4 with two damage marked on it. The game then checks for state-based actions simultaneously: the condition for destruction requires damage greater than or equal to toughness, but now the Goblin's toughness is 4 and its damage is only 2. Since the damage is no longer lethal, the state-based action does not move the creature to the graveyard, and the Goblin remains on the battlefield.

I just dropped a legendary creature with an enters the battlefield ability that says to roll a d6 for X damage. My opponent immediately flashes in something that makes all creatures lose all abilities when they enter the battlefield. What actually happens with the damage and the dice roll?

The rules state that continuous effects that modify characteristics of a permanent do so the moment the permanent is on the battlefield. Because your opponents effect causes all creatures to lose all abilities as they enter, your creature loses its triggered ability simultaneously with entering, which means the enters the battlefield trigger never occurs. Even though the rules allow players to agree to use an alternate method for rolling a die as long as the method has the same number of equally likely outcomes, no die is rolled here because the triggering condition is suppressed by the characteristic modification taking precedence during the entry event. The concrete final outcome is that your permanent enters with no triggered abilities, you do not roll any die, and zero damage is dealt.
I have three artifacts on the table right now. If I want to play a card that has affinity for artifacts and costs 4 mana, do I still have to pay the full 4 mana?

No, you do not. Because the spell has affinity for artifacts, it costs 1 less to cast for each artifact you control. Since you control three artifacts, the cost is reduced by 3, meaning you only pay 1 mana to cast the spell.

I have a permanent that says whenever you control no face-down cards in exile, draw two cards. My opponent just used an effect to exile three of my creatures face down. Then they activated another ability that lets them choose one of those exiled cards and cast it without paying its mana cost. When does my trigger go on the stack, and does it trigger again when they reveal that card during resolution? What is the final outcome?

The game handles this by checking your triggered ability the moment those three creatures are exiled because your exile zone goes from having no face-down cards to having three. At that exact moment, a triggered ability goes onto the stack at the next available opportunity. Because this trigger is already on the stack, it will not trigger again during the rest of that activation or resolution. Even if revealing the chosen card changes your exile count back down to zero face-down cards while the spell is resolving, the game prevents duplicate triggers in this window. Additionally, when your opponent pays the mana and additional costs for their ability, they must follow the rule about face-down exiled cards: they can only choose a specific card if they are allowed to look at that card; otherwise, they may choose an entire pile of face-down exiled cards, and then a card is chosen at random from within that pile. The chosen card remains hidden and is not revealed until after that cost is fully paid. Your trigger fires first, and its presence on the stack takes precedence by blocking any potential second trigger during resolution. Final outcome: You draw two cards immediately when the exile happens, your opponent picks a random card from a pile without looking at it during payment, they reveal it exactly when casting costs are complete, and no additional draw triggers occur during that sequence.
We are playing a four-player game and my friend and I want to team up to win. Can we be treated as a single unit?

No, you cannot. In Free-for-All multiplayer games, a group of players compete as individuals against each other. This means that you and your friend must maintain separate game states such as life totals and hands. For example, if your friend is defeated and loses the game, you do not lose with them; you remain in the game as an individual player.

I just cast a creature that says As this enters the battlefield, you may sacrifice another creature. When you do, it deals damage equal to its power to any target. At the same time, there is another effect on the board that modifies how red creatures enter and says they also get plus two over plus two if you sacrificed a permanent. I sacrificed my only other creature to trigger the first ability. My opponent claims the second effect should also count and give me counters because I sacrificed it anyway. Is that right?

The game resolves this by prioritizing replacement effects during entry before evaluating post-resolution triggers. The rule states that while applying an effect that modifies how a permanent enters, you may have to choose a number of objects that will also change zones. Crucially, the same object can’t be chosen to change zones more than once when applying replacement effects that modify how one or more permanents enter the battlefield, so your single sacrifice only fulfills one replacement modification and cannot be duplicated for the second effect. Immediately after resolution completes, reflexive triggered abilities follow rules stating they trigger only when you sacrifice another creature due to the original triggered ability and not if you sacrifice a creature for any other reason. Replacement modifications take precedence during entry, and once locked in, they determine whether the reflexive condition is met. The concrete final game outcome is that your creature enters without extra counters, and it deals damage equal to its power to a target of your choice, while the second replacement effect provides zero bonuses because the sacrifice was exclusively applied to the first modification.
Can I still tap my Command Tower for Blue if an effect turns it into a Forest?

No, you cannot. When an effect sets a land's subtype to a basic land type, the land no longer has its old land type and loses all abilities generated from its rules text. It then gains the appropriate mana ability for the new type. For example, if you have a Command Tower and an effect makes it a Forest, it will lose its ability to tap for any color and instead gain the ability to tap for Green mana.

I just resolved a spell that temporarily reduces a creature's toughness to zero for a split second, and at the same time another part of my combo tries to put a fresh card from my sideboard onto the battlefield. My opponent insists the zero-toughness creature dies immediately and shuffles back into my deck or graveyard right then, preventing my combo from finishing. Is that correct?

No, your creature stays on the battlefield until after both effects finish resolving. First, the rule governing cards outside the game applies because it sets the boundaries for what can legally move or be targeted; cards outside the game cannot be affected by spells or abilities except for characteristic-defining abilities printed on them and spells and abilities that allow those cards to be brought into the game, meaning your sideboard card is completely untargetable until its specific entry effect finishes. Once that movement completes, the rule regarding resolution timing takes precedence to determine if any deaths occur; state-based actions pay no attention to what happens during the resolution of a spell or ability, only evaluating once everything finishes. Because dropping to zero toughness was just an intermediate step mid-cast, the creature does not die prematurely. The concrete final outcome is that your creature survives with its normal stats once resolution ends, your sideboard card successfully becomes a permanent you control, and neither object moves to any graveyard or exile zone during this sequence.

I'm playing a Commander game and my opponent attacks me with their legendary commander plus two other creatures. My commander takes lethal damage in return, but my opponent wants to sacrifice their commander right after combat damage is dealt to save it for the command zone or activate an ability. Does combat happen simultaneously, or can they get a window to do something before losing from taking 21 damage?

When your opponent attacks with multiple creatures, all combat damage that has been assigned is dealt simultaneously and no player has the chance to cast spells or activate abilities between the time combat damage is assigned and the time it’s dealt. Because of this rigid timing, the game immediately moves to check state-based actions after the damage hits. Commander rules specifically state that a player who has been dealt 21 or more combat damage by the same commander over the course of the game loses the game as soon as that condition is met. The rules establish that the simultaneous damage dealing takes place first, and the variant Commander loss condition triggers second during the state-based action check. There is no window to intervene before this sequence completes. Your opponent will lose the game immediately and cannot activate their commander or save it from the battlefield.
Can I use a card that lets me cast spells on my opponent's turn to cast a spell in my hand that says 'Cast this spell only during your turn'?

No, you cannot. The restriction on your card still applies because certain abilities follow the card in any zone where you could normally cast or play it. Because the text specifically says 'Cast this spell only...', that limitation stays with the card regardless of other effects. For example, if you have a spell that says 'Cast this spell only during your turn', you cannot use an opponent's ability to cast spells on their turn to bypass that rule.
What happens when I use a spell that turns all my lands into creatures if I have a land in my graveyard?

When the spell resolves, it identifies all lands currently on the battlefield and changes their type to creature. Because effects apply only to permanents unless the instruction's text states otherwise or they clearly can apply only to objects in one or more other zones, the spell does not affect cards that are not permanents. For example, your lands on the battlefield will become creatures, but your land cards in your graveyard will remain as lands.
What happens if I put a lore counter on my Saga and it reaches the last chapter number?

Once the ability for that final chapter triggers and finishes resolving, you must sacrifice the Saga. This happens because the number of lore counters is greater than or equal to its final chapter number and it is no longer the source of a chapter ability that has triggered but not yet left the stack. For example, if you have a Saga with two chapters and you add a second counter, you first let the second chapter ability resolve, and then you immediately sacrifice the Saga.

I just attacked with two creatures, one that deals 4 damage and another that deals 3 damage. My opponent blocked the smaller attacker with a single 5 toughness creature. They told me their creature has a trigger that gives them a token whenever it takes excess damage. Does the trigger see both hits as a single event or do they happen one after the other? Also, could my opponent cast an instant spell like Shock to kill the blocker before the second attacker deals its damage?

Both attackers deal their damage at the exact same moment because all combat damage that has been assigned is dealt simultaneously, and no player gets a chance to cast spells or activate abilities between the time combat damage is assigned and when it is actually dealt. This simultaneous dealing rule establishes the timing framework first, which means priority windows are completely locked during the damage step. Once that single event finishes, the excess damage calculation takes precedence for resolving triggers by checking how those sources together dealt an amount of damage greater than lethal damage, then determining that excess damage equal to the difference was dealt to the creature, which comes out to exactly 2 extra points beyond its toughness. The timing rule runs first to lock in the sequence, and the excess math runs after to calculate trigger amounts. The final outcome is that your opponent cannot cast any mid-hit spells, the blocker survives combat, and a single trigger resolves for exactly 2 excess damage.
Wait, I just flipped the coin and it was heads, but my card says I win the flip anyway. Do I still have to follow what the coin shows?

No, you do not follow the coin. If an effect states that a certain player wins a coin flip, you ignore the actual results of that flip and use the indicated result instead. For example, if you play a card that says flip a coin and you win the flip, even if the physical coin lands on heads, you treat it as a win as dictated by the card.

I just tapped my land with an ability that says 'When this land is tapped for mana, create a 1/1 creature.' My opponent tried to blast the land with an instant right after I tapped it but before the creature appeared. They argued that since they saw me tap it, they could respond. Also, one of my creatures had damage on it from earlier turns, did that matter at all? What is the correct order of events?

Your opponent cannot respond to you tapping the land or during the activation itself. Tapping for mana is a mana ability, and the rules clarify that an ability triggers when such a mana ability resolves and produces mana, not when you perform the tap action. Since mana abilities do not use the stack, there are no responses allowed between tapping and resolution. Your opponent can only interact after the land produces mana. Furthermore, once the mana is produced, the game does not immediately go to priority. The rules state that each time a player would get priority, the game first performs all applicable state-based actions as a single event. If your damaged creature had lethal damage, it would be put into its owner's graveyard at this moment. Only after state-based actions are performed and no further ones apply does the game put triggered abilities onto the stack. In your case, the 1/1 creature trigger is placed on the stack now. After the triggers are on the stack, priority passes to your opponent. Concrete outcome: The land produces mana safely, any damaged creatures die immediately via state-based actions, the creature token trigger goes on the stack above any other triggers from that event, and your opponent gets a chance to respond only after all of this is complete. They cannot remove the land in response to the tap, nor can they interrupt the sequence between tapping and the trigger going on the stack.
What happens if my top card is revealed, then I shuffle my library, and that same card ends up back on top and is revealed again?

It becomes a new object. If an effect causes a player to play with the top card of their library revealed, and that particular card stops being revealed for any length of time before being revealed again, it becomes a new object. For example, if you have your top card revealed and then shuffle your library, the moment that card is no longer visible, it ceases to be that specific revealed object. Even if that exact same card ends up back on top, it is considered a new object for game purposes.

My opponent just attacked me with their black dragon commander and dealt 10 combat damage, putting me at 20 total from that card. They immediately used an effect to return the dragon to their hand for a shuffle, claiming this resets my count because the card isn't on the battlefield anymore to keep tracking. Is the reset valid?

No, the reset is not valid and you remain at 20 damage from that commander. The governing rule for commander damage tracks cumulative hits over the entire duration of the match rather than just current presence; specifically, a player loses if they have been dealt 21 or more combat damage by the same commander over the course of the game, meaning the damage count persists regardless of where the commander moves after dealing the damage. Although the hand is a hidden zone where players cannot see all cards, and the command zone is public, this visibility distinction does not impact the tracking mechanism because the damage accumulation follows the permanent itself based on game history, not its current location or who can see it at that moment. Concrete outcome: Your commander damage counter remains at 20 against that dragon, so if it ever attacks you again and deals combat damage, you will reach 21 total and lose the game.
I have an old card that says I can play a spell, but my newer cards always say cast. Is there a difference?

There is no functional difference in how you perform the action. Older cards that were printed with the word play have received errata in the Oracle card reference so they now refer to casting that spell. For example, if an old card says you may play a creature from your graveyard, you are simply casting that creature onto the stack just like a modern card would say.

I control Volcano Hellion and my life total is at 8. My opponent hits me with a spell that drops me to 5 life. Later in the turn, I attack with it while controlling another permanent that somehow became both a creature and a planeswalker (toughness 3, loyalty 4). I deal 4 damage to that multi-type permanent. What happens with the echo cost later on, and how is the damage calculated?

In this situation the variable cost for the echo ability will not lock in when the upkeep step begins but will instead adjust to match your life total at the exact moment the ability resolves because the governing text states that for keyword abilities with variables based on characteristics or other information about the game state the value of that variable is constantly reevaluated. Meanwhile the damage portion follows a separate calculation that happens immediately after combat damage occurs. The relevant guidelines specify that some triggered abilities check whether a permanent has been dealt excess damage by comparing the total damage to toughness and loyalty separately. Since your target is both a creature and a planeswalker the game calculates the difference for each type then determines that the excess damage dealt to that permanent is the greatest of the calculated amounts for each of the card types it has. The concrete final outcome is that your echo cost becomes exactly equal to your current life total when the ability resolves, and exactly one point of excess damage is recognized for the multi-type permanent regardless of how much was dealt over the higher threshold. These mechanics follow a strict sequence where the excess damage calculation settles immediately during the combat phase to set battlefield totals, while the variable cost reevaluation occurs later during the upkeep step when the triggered ability resolves on the stack.
Can I shuffle my friend's deck once we decide who is going first?

Yes, you can. After the starting player is determined, each player shuffles their own deck so that the cards are in a random order, and then each player may shuffle or cut their opponents' decks. For example, if you and your friend have finished deciding who goes first, you can take your friend's deck and give it a good shuffle or perform a cut to ensure it is randomized before you begin.

Im mid-game in Commander and my opponents commander has already dealt me twenty combat damage this game. They attack with it and i have an instant spell ready to counter one of their blockers, but they respond by trying to pay an ability to redirect the damage back at them. Can i just push my response through after theirs so they dodge the win condition?

You cannot change the sequence of responses once they are placed on the stack. The core game rule states that the order of objects on the stack cannot be changed except when effects or rules allow it, meaning you must wait for each ability to resolve in the exact reverse order it was cast or triggered without rearranging them. After all spells and abilities have finished resolving, the game then checks state-based actions based on the variant regulations, which specify that a player who has been dealt twenty-one or more combat damage by the same commander over the course of the game loses the game immediately. The rule governing stack resolution takes precedence first to lock in what actually happens during the turn, while the win condition check only occurs afterward as a final state check. The concrete final outcome is that your response chain must resolve exactly as entered without interruption, and if the total damage crosses the threshold once that last spell resolves, you lose the game right away.
Can I use my creature's ability to target that spell my opponent just cast?

No, you cannot. Only permanents are legal targets for spells and abilities unless the ability specifies it can target a spell or an object in another zone. Because the spell is currently being cast and has not yet entered the battlefield, it is not a permanent. For example, if you have a creature with an ability that says target creature gets plus 1 plus 1, you cannot use that on an instant your opponent is currently casting.

We're mid-game and my opponent's commander has already hit me for 14 combat damage over the past three turns. He just sacrificed it to pay some costs, then put it back into the command zone from his graveyard before it would normally go there. Now he's trying to cast it again and adding up six extra mana because it had been played from command twice before. I told him the commander tax resets every time it dies so he only has to pay the base cost, and that sending it back early doesn't change the fact I still only need seven more damage to win. Who is right?

Your understanding is mostly correct, but there is a small math adjustment needed. When determining the outcome, you must look at how the permanent cost tracking interacts with the zone change replacement effect. The rules state that if a commander ends up in a graveyard or exile, its owner may put it into the command zone instead. This rule governs where the card physically goes when it leaves play. However, this zone choice does not reset persistent counters because the casting rule also specifies that a commander cast from command costs an additional two for each previous time that player has cast it from command that game. Tracking damage and tax takes precedence over temporary zone movement because both are continuous match conditions that survive permanent transitions. Since your opponent moved it back to command while carrying a four mana penalty from its two prior casts, he must pay the base cost plus four extra mana next time he casts it. You will lose the game if that exact commander deals seven or more additional combat damage to you over the course of this match.
My commander just got destroyed and went to my graveyard. Can I still play it or is it lost?

Yes, you can. If a commander is in a graveyard or in exile and that object was put into that zone since the last time state-based actions were checked, its owner may put it into the command zone. For example, if your Urza, Lord High Artificer is destroyed by a spell like Lightning Bolt, you can move it from the graveyard to the command zone.

I cast a spell that instructed me to roll a six-sided die and put charge counters on an exiled creature equal to the result, then created a delayed triggered ability saying at the beginning of my next end step that creature deals damage equal to those counters to their controller. After I rolled and set the counters, my opponent activated an ability to remove three charge counters from that card before the end step arrived. When the turn ended, does the damage still happen, and if so, how much is it for?

The damage happens because the delayed triggered ability remains attached to the exiled creature and resolves normally despite the change in characteristics. Rules for delayed abilities state that they affect the specific object even if that object changes characteristics later, provided it stays in the zone where the ability expects it to be at resolution time. Since the creature remained in exile, the delay fires at the beginning of your end step and looks at the current game state to determine the damage amount. The rule for rolling dice without a results table confirms that your die roll was used correctly to establish the initial counter count, but those instructions do not freeze the value in time; the ability checks the number of counters present when it resolves. You deal damage equal to the reduced number of charge counters on the card at the moment the delay resolves.

I have a creature with an ability that reads At the beginning of your upkeep, you may exile target creature. My opponent has a large blocker and I want to remove it, but they cast an instant spell targeting my source creature to destroy it before the ability resolves. They argue they can kill the source because I haven't put the ability on the stack yet since I was just announcing my plan, and once resolved, they claim the target goes to the graveyard so their own return-from-graveyard cards will work. Is my opponent right about the timing? And does the creature actually end up in the graveyard?

Your opponent is right about the timing because optional triggered abilities go on the stack when they trigger regardless of whether the controller intends to exercise the option, so the ability is already on the stack and open to response before any choice is made. The creature does not end up in the graveyard; if the ability resolves and you choose to exile, the creature moves to the exile zone, which functions as a holding area for objects that is distinct from the graveyard, meaning spells that return creatures from the graveyard cannot retrieve an exiled creature.
If I use an ability to airbend my lands, can I ever get them back?

When you airbend, you exile those permanents. For each card exiled this way, as long as it remains exiled, its owner may cast it by paying {2} rather than paying its mana cost. For example, if you airbend a Forest and a Swamp, you can cast those specific Forest and Swamp cards from exile for {2} each.
I just cast a planeswalker and the spell is finished. Where does it go?

When a planeswalker spell resolves, its controller puts it onto the battlefield under their control. For example, if you cast Ajani, Mentor of Heroes and the spell finishes resolving, Ajani moves from the stack directly to the battlefield where you can immediately start using his abilities.

I am playing a two-player Brawl game and my opponent has twenty-five life total. I just attacked with a creature for four damage and they blocked it, but now we are wondering if dealing exactly twenty-one points of combat damage from our commander ever wins the game instantly in this format like it does in Commander. My friend says the game ends right at zero life automatically, but I am not sure when that check actually happens during a complex turn sequence with multiple spells and triggered abilities going on the stack. What is the actual outcome once the damage resolves?

In Brawl, the commander lethal tracking mechanic does not apply because a specific format exception removes the continuous check that causes a loss from dealing 21 combat damage with a commander as its source. Instead, winning normally relies on reducing your opponent's life total to zero. Since two-player Brawl games start each player at 25 life, dealing 21 points of combat damage leaves them at 4 life rather than ending the game instantly. The continuous checks for loss conditions or other state-based actions happen automatically throughout the game without waiting for a player to take an action, allowing the game to proceed with remaining spells and abilities on the stack while the opponent still has 4 life.
Can I cast spells cheaper if my Assassin just hit someone?

Yes, you can. You may pay the freerunning cost rather than the spells mana cost if a player was dealt combat damage this turn by a creature that was an Assassin at the time it dealt that damage. For example, if your Assassin deals combat damage to an opponent, you can then cast a spell with freerunning by paying its alternative cost instead of its normal mana cost.

I am playing a Commander game and I just cast a spell that put four plus one plus one counters on my creature while my opponent replied by placing two minus one minus one counters on the exact same permanent. We got into an argument about whether the creature immediately dies or if I can try to counter their spell. What actually happens and when do we figure out who wins this interaction?

State based actions do not trigger during the casting of spells or while anything remains on the stack, so the counters simply sit on your permanent right now with no destruction occurring yet. The official Commander rules state that in the Commander variant each deck is led by a legendary creature designated as that decks commander and the Commander variant uses all the normal rules for a Magic game which means board checks only happen when priority passes to both players after the stack empties. Once that moment arrives the game evaluates your counters by removing N plus one plus one and N minus one minus one counters where N is the smaller number leaving your creature with two remaining positive bonuses safely on the battlefield. Because normal rules apply in this format you will not get another window to respond since state based actions resolve instantly without passing priority, so the creature stays in play with its leftover power boost until someone takes a new action.

My commander says I can't draw more than one card per turn, but I cast a spell that says 'Discard your hand, then draw seven cards.' My creature's power and toughness match my hand size exactly. Does the creature die when I discard, and do I get to keep drawing all those cards?

You are restricted by your commander's effect that limits drawing to one card per turn, which means the instruction to draw seven cards is carried out only partially, allowing you to draw just one card despite the spell asking for seven. As the spell resolves, you discard your hand, but state-based actions do not check what happens during resolution and only look at the game state after the spell finishes resolving, so your creature does not die when your hand count hits zero mid-effect. After the spell completes, you have drawn one card due to your commander's restriction, leaving you with exactly one card in hand. Your creature becomes a creature with power and toughness equal to one and remains on the battlefield alive.
What happens if my life total hits zero during an opponent's turn?

As soon as your life total reaches 0 or less, you lose the game as a state-based action. This means the game checks for this condition constantly and resolves it automatically without anyone needing to cast anything. For example, if an opponent's creature deals enough damage to bring your life from 2 down to 0, you lose the game immediately at that moment.

My opponent cast a sorcery that reads 'Deal 5 damage to target creature. Instead, deal 0 damage if you paid 3 life.' I paid the life, so the second part of the text applied. My creature has an enchantment that says 'Whenever this creature deals damage, create two Treasure tokens.' Do I get any Treasures from this spell resolving?

No, you do not get any Treasures. When the spell resolves, the self-replacement effect that says to deal 0 damage applies first as part of the spell's own resolution. This modifies the event so the source is now attempting to deal 0 damage rather than 5. Because the damage amount becomes zero, no damage is actually dealt at all. Since no damage is dealt, abilities that trigger on damage being dealt will not trigger, so your Treasure creation effect does nothing. The final outcome is that zero damage is dealt and no tokens are created.

I control a creature that dies and triggers an ability, so now there's a triggered ability sitting on the stack. I want to play my mountain this turn. My friend said because I have priority and it's my main phase, I can just play the land whenever I want regardless of what's on the stack. Is he right?

Your friend is incorrect. While playing a land is something you can do when you have priority during your main phase, there is a strict requirement that the stack must be empty before you can take this action. Since the triggered ability from the dying creature is currently on the stack, you cannot play your mountain yet. You must wait until that triggered ability resolves or is countered so that the stack becomes empty. Once the stack is clear and you still have priority during a main phase, you can then play your land. The restriction on playing lands prevents you from doing so while any object is waiting on the stack, even if it's just one trigger from another permanent leaving. The concrete outcome is that you cannot play the land until the trigger finishes resolving, at which point the stack becomes empty and you may perform the special action of playing your land.
What happens when I cast a spell with an enchantment that makes my spells draw a card, but then my opponent destroys that enchantment before my spell actually resolves?

You will still get to draw the card. The effect of the static ability begins to apply to appropriate spells at the time you put the spell on the stack. For example, if you cast a Fireball while an enchantment is active that says all your spells draw a card, the Fireball gains that ability the moment it hits the stack. Even if the enchantment is destroyed before the Fireball resolves, the Fireball keeps its new ability.
What happens if I cast a spell with bargain and decide to sacrifice an enchantment? Do I still get to pick targets for the extra abilities?

When you declare your intention to sacrifice an enchantment as an additional cost, the spell is considered bargained. The rules specify that if part of a spell's ability has its effect only if that spell was bargained and that part includes any targets, the controller chooses those targets only if the spell was bargained. For example, if you cast a spell with bargain that says 'If this spell was bargained, target creature gets +1/+1', you will choose the creature to receive the bonus at the time you cast the spell because you fulfilled the bargain cost.

I just cast a spell that shuffles my entire library onto the top of my opponent's library, but when they start drawing cards, nothing from those new cards is showing up in their hand or triggering on them. Did something go wrong with the spell?

When you shuffle your library into your opponent's, the cards actually belong to you. The game has a specific rule that says if any card would go to a player's hand, graveyard, or library when it isn't theirs, it goes to their owner's corresponding zone instead. This means as soon as your opponent tries to draw those shuffled cards, they are instantly redirected to your hand rather than staying in their deck or skipping over them. Commander construction rules don't apply here since this is an in-game movement effect, not a deck-building restriction.
I just played a creature with multiple power and toughness numbers on it, but it has no level counters yet. What happens to its stats?

You use the power and toughness shown in the uppermost box. If the number of level counters on a leveler creature is less than the first number printed in its level symbol, it has the power and toughness denoted by its uppermost power/toughness box. For example, if a creature has a {LEVEL 3-5} symbol and its top box says 1/1, it will remain a 1/1 until it reaches at least 3 level counters.

I just cast an instant and triggered my commander's ability, which says Whenever you cast a spell, create two token creature tokens. Sacrifice any number of artifacts for each token created this way. For each artifact sacrificed this way, put a +1/+1 counter on each token. At the same time, my other permanent has an effect that changes how counters are placed. My playgroup is split on whether the counters still get modified when they come from my commander's ability, or if the replacement effect breaks the chain since it's not a direct spell anymore. What actually happens here?

This scenario involves two mechanics working together to determine the final board state. First your commanders ability uses a linked structure exactly as described when some objects combine the abilities into one paragraph with the static ability first followed by each triggered ability that is linked to it. This ensures the token creation and counter placement function as one unified event. Second replacement effects that change how many counters are placed apply if another replacement or prevention effect does so even if the original event being modified was not itself an effect. Regarding precedence the linked triggered ability resolves first and establishes the base counter placement event. The counter modification replacement effect then evaluates that specific step and adjusts the number accordingly. Because both mechanics are designed to layer this way your tokens will enter with the fully adjusted counter count leaving them stronger than expected when combat begins.
What happens when I cast an artifact that has a red mana symbol in its cost? Does being an artifact make it colorless?

The card is treated as a red permanent. While most artifacts have no colored mana symbols in their mana costs and are therefore colorless, artifacts may be colored. For example, if you cast a red artifact, any effect that targets red permanents will still see it as red.
Can I still play the game if I mulligan down to two cards?

Yes, you can still play, but your deck size must be sufficient. You will lose the game if you have fewer than seven cards in your library when state-based actions are checked during the upkeep step of the first turn. For example, if you mulligan to two cards and your deck only has six cards left, you will lose during your very first upkeep.

I'm in a four-player game and have priority on my turn. I want to take an extra turn so I can attack with everything, but right then my opponent decides he has no answers and wants to leave the table. Do I still get to take that extra turn, or does his departure change things?

Special actions are actions a player may take when they have priority that don’t use the stack, which means they cannot be responded to directly on the stack. However, multiplayer departure rules handle player exits instantaneously and override pending game states. As soon as your opponent decides to leave, all objects owned by that player leave the game and any effects which give that player control of any objects or players end immediately. This departure process takes precedence over any special action attempts because the multiplayer framework updates priority and turn structure the exact moment a participant departs. The concrete final outcome is that your extra turn attempt is completely voided, your opponent permanently leaves with all their permanents going to the appropriate zones, and the remaining three players continue your turn normally until someone takes a voluntary action or a phase concludes.

I cast a two-part spell that deals 4 damage to my opponent's blocker, then gives that same creature -2/-2 until end of turn. Does the creature die right away when it takes the damage, or does it wait until my spell is completely finished?

The creature remains on the battlefield until your spell finishes resolving. To understand why, you have to look at how both mechanics work together. First, damage dealt to a creature doesn’t destroy it; rather, state-based actions are what actually move damaged creatures to the graveyard based on those results. Second, state-based actions pay no attention to what happens during the resolution of a spell or ability, meaning they completely ignore temporary changes like marked damage or reduced toughness while your effect is still playing out. These checks simply wait until your spell completes and control passes back. Once resolution ends, state-based actions finally run, see both the 4 damage and the zero toughness, confirm the destruction criteria are met, and move the creature to its owner's graveyard as the definitive outcome. The timing rule takes precedence by suspending all checks during resolution, so nothing happens until the spell is fully done.
What happens when an effect checks the power of a creature that says its power is equal to the number of lands I control, but the creature is in my graveyard?

The effect will see the power as being equal to the number of lands you control. Since the creature's power is set by a characteristic-defining ability, it functions everywhere, even outside the game. If the ability needs to use a number that can be determined, such as the number of lands you control, you use that number. You only use 0 if the ability needs to use a number that cannot be determined.

I just cast a spell that puts two creature tokens onto the battlefield attacking my opponent. Right after casting it, I tried to turn one of my face-down creatures face up so it would get +2/+2 before combat, but my opponent said I can't do that while the spell is resolving and the creature isn't even attacking yet anyway. Is he right?

Your opponent is correct on both counts. First, turning a face-down creature face up is a special action that requires priority and does not use the stack, meaning you cannot perform it while resolving a spell or attempting to change targets. Second, even if you waited until your turn, creatures entering the battlefield via an effect 'do enter the battlefield, but it’s never considered to be an attacking creature.' Because they lack the official attacking designation and are affected by summoning sickness, they cannot attack this turn regardless of being turned face up.
What happens if I cast a spell and my opponent responds by activating an ability? Do they both use cards on the table to show what is happening?

Not necessarily. When you cast a spell, the physical card is put on the stack. However, when an ability is activated or triggers, it goes on top of the stack without any card associated with it. For example, if you cast a Fireball spell, you would place that card on the stack, but if your opponent responds by tapping a creature for an activated ability, that ability is simply an effect on the stack and does not require a physical card to represent it.

I just set up a combo where tapping my lands and activating creature abilities gives me enough mana, but I also control a high mana cost God that stops being a creature if my devotion drops below five. My opponent argues that because attacking and paying costs are actions you can take when you have priority that don’t use the stack, the game doesn’t actually check what type of permanent it is until everything resolves. What happens?

Special actions are actions a player may take when they have priority that don’t use the stack, which means those moves happen immediately without waiting for a response window or spell resolution. When determining whether your God becomes a creature, you must follow the devotion calculation order rather than assuming characteristics change later.
