The rules state that devotion to each color is equal to the number of mana symbols in the costs of permanents you control, and this count is calculated after considering any copy, control, or text-changing effects but before other continuous effects like type changers are applied. Special actions simply bypass the stack for timing purposes, while devotion priority dictates exactly which effect evaluates first during that same window. Because continuous effect ordering takes precedence in determining permanent characteristics right when you take your special actions, your God’s creature status resolves immediately. Concrete final outcome: Your God immediately becomes a creature the moment you hold priority and take those special actions, allowing it to attack, block, or be targeted as normal without any delay.
What happens if I have a card that makes my planeswalkers' abilities cost an extra loyalty counter, but I want to use an ability that normally takes away four counters?

If you have an effect that adds an additional [+1] to your planeswalkers' loyalty abilities, and you try to activate an ability that normally costs [-4], you will only remove three loyalty counters instead of four. When the total cost to activate a loyalty ability contains multiple costs to add or remove loyalty counters, those costs are combined into a single cost to add or remove loyalty counters. For example, if you control a planeswalker with three loyalty counters and use an ability that normally costs [-4], the additional [+1] effect means you only remove three counters from that permanent.

I just cast a spell that exiled my opponent's creatures face-down into exile, and then they cast a spell that says 'Choose one face-down card in exile and return it to the battlefield.' My opponent is arguing they should get to pick which creature comes back because those are their cards. What actually happens here, and does the returned creature trigger any abilities when it hits play?

When you choose which card to return, the rules for managing hidden exile cards dictate the process first. Face-down cards in exile should be kept in separate piles based on when they were exiled and how they were exiled. Since you are not allowed to look at face-down exiled cards during selection, you must choose a pile of face-down exiled cards, and then a card is chosen at random from within that pile. This selection precedence happens before any permanent triggers interact with the returning object. Once that selected card resolves and moves zones, the rules for zone-change triggers take over. During resolution, these abilities look for the object in the zone that it moved to. Because the card arrives on the battlefield, each time an event puts a permanent onto the battlefield all permanents on the battlefield including the newcomer are checked for any enters-the-battlefield triggers that match the event. The final concrete outcome is that you randomly select a pile to determine your choice, the chosen creature returns face-up (as per standard game rules), and its enters-the-battlefield ability successfully triggers and goes on the stack under the control of its owner/controller, not the player who cast the return spell.
What happens when I use an old card that tells me to put a creature into play?

The creature goes onto the battlefield. Because cards printed with text containing phrases like into play or from play are referring to the battlefield, you resolve the effect by moving the card from its current zone to the battlefield. For example, if a card says return a creature into play, you take that creature from the graveyard and place it on the battlefield.

I'm attacking with three creatures and my opponent controls Lich's Mirror. Their life total is at 3, and they only have one card left in their library. The damage connects, but then I heard a rules debate because multiple things seem to happen at once. What actually resolves?

During the combat damage step, your attacking creatures deal damage equal to their combined power to your opponent. This reduces their life total to zero or below while they have only one card remaining in their library. The next time state-based actions are checked, two separate conditions attempt to make them lose the game simultaneously. Your opponent's Lich's Mirror acts as a single replacement effect that applies to both simultaneous state-based actions, replacing the game loss entirely. They shuffle their hand, graveyard, and permanents into their library, draw seven cards, and their life total becomes 20, allowing the game to continue.
What happens when a card effect says I take control of my opponent? Do I get to choose their moves?

If an effect says you take control of an opponent, you make all the decisions and choices for that player, such as deciding which creatures to attack with or which lands to tap. This is different from an effect that might give a player control of themselves; in those instances, that player will still make their own decisions and choices as normal. For example, if a card gave you control of your own permanents, you would still be the one choosing how to use them.
What happens if an opponent separates my revealed cards into two piles? Are they still technically in my library while they are being moved?

While the cards are being separated, they have not actually left their original zone. The rules state that objects grouped into piles don't leave the zone they're currently in until they are actually put into another zone. For example, during a spell like Fact or Fiction, the five revealed cards are still considered part of your library while your opponent is deciding how to split them.

I just untapped my lands and I'm up against a board control deck with a creature that costs five mana to cast. My opponent hasn't moved yet but is staring at me like they expect me to end the turn so they can go again, but I haven't declared attackers yet. Do I have to attack before I can cast spells? Also, when exactly does my turn actually finish—are we done once I decide I don't have any more moves?

Clarify that mana availability for casting spells and the priority passing required to end turns are sequential processes within a phase, where players can freely cast creatures using mana before declaring attackers, and the turn only concludes when both consecutively pass actions without intervening moves.

I just cast a spell that puts two creatures onto the battlefield at the exact same time. Both of them have enter-the-battlefield triggers, but my opponent keeps saying theirs goes first because they control the board space. We both have instant spells we want to play. What actually happens with those triggers and can I do anything while they are waiting?

When two creatures enter simultaneously, their enter-the-battlefield triggers go on the stack during your next priority step in a specific order: as the Active Player first, then the Non-Active Player, with each player choosing the order of their own triggers. You do not need to worry about controlling board space, as turn order dictates this. Both you and your opponent get priority between the time the spell resolves and when the first trigger resolves. During these sequential priority windows, you can cast instant spells, which go on the stack above the triggered abilities and can target or counter them. The triggers will resolve in reverse order of how they were placed on the stack, allowing you to respond to each one before it resolves.
What happens to a creature with no text if I play an enchantment that says it cannot be blocked?

The creature will continue to be treated as having no abilities. This is because stating a quality of an object, such as saying a creature cannot be blocked, is different from granting an ability. Since the enchantment is simply stating a quality rather than granting an actual ability, the creature's status remains unchanged for other effects. For example, if you have a Runeclaw Bear with no abilities and you enchant it with an Aura that says the creature cannot be blocked, it would still qualify for bonuses from cards like Muraganda Petroglyphs which reward creatures with no abilities.

My opponent cast a spell that says At the beginning of your next turn, you may draw two cards, but I only have one card left in my library. Is the trigger just going to do nothing because I'm about to lose anyway? Or does it not even go on the stack?

The ability will go onto the stack and resolve normally. Triggered abilities that contain may go on the stack when they trigger regardless of whether their controller intends to exercise the option or not. This means the ability is already on the stack waiting for you to make a choice at resolution time, and it does not care about your library size at the moment it triggers. When the ability resolves, you must decide whether to draw. Regarding your library count, if there are no cards in a player's library and an effect offers that player the choice to draw a card, that player can choose to do so. The same principles apply if the library has fewer cards than the amount offered; you can still make the choice even though it will lead to drawing from zero cards eventually. The concrete final game outcome is that the ability resolves and you face the decision. If you choose to exercise the option, you will draw your last card and then immediately lose the game because you attempted to draw from an empty library. If you choose not to draw, you keep your one card and avoid the loss. The trigger does not fizzle or get prevented by your low library count.
Can I just grab my companion card from outside the game and put it in my hand whenever I want during my turn?

No, you cannot. Once during the game, any time you have priority and the stack is empty, but only during a main phase of your turn, you may pay 3 mana and put that card into your hand. For example, if you are playing with Emrakul, the Aeons Torn as your companion, you cannot use this ability in response to an opponent's spell; you must wait until it is your main phase and nothing else is happening on the stack.

My opponent attacks with a Goblin that has First Strike and I block with a creature without First Strike. The Goblin kills my blocker instantly. Does my blocker still get to deal damage back because it successfully blocked?

No, the blocking creature deals no damage back to the Goblin. The rules state that when a creature has First Strike, combat damage is handled in two separate steps within the combat phase. In the first combat damage step, only creatures with First Strike or Double Strike assign and deal damage. This means your opponent's Goblin deals its damage immediately while your blocker cannot assign any damage yet. Once that first damage step ends, the game checks for state-based actions simultaneously as a single event. Since your blocker received lethal damage from the Goblin, it is destroyed and put into the graveyard before the second combat damage step can begin. Because the blocker is removed from play by state-based actions, it does not exist for the second step and therefore deals zero damage to the Goblin.
If I use a card with splice to add its effect to another spell, does the new spell get that card's color and name too?

No, the spell keeps its own identity. When you splice, the spell has the characteristics of the main spell, plus the rules text of each of the spliced cards. This means the spell does not gain any other characteristics like the name, mana cost, color, or card types of the spliced cards. For example, if you splice a red Glacial Ray onto a blue Reach Through Mists, the resulting spell is still a blue spell named Reach Through Mists, even though it now has the ability to deal 2 damage to any target.

I attacked with three creatures and all three got blocked for lethal damage at the exact same time. My sideboard card says whenever a creature dies, put a +1/+1 counter on another creature we control. Do we get to pick which trigger goes on the stack first? Can my opponent shuffle the order of those triggers while they are waiting to resolve?

The creatures dying does not use the stack at all; it happens automatically whenever certain conditions like lethal damage or zero toughness are met, and it never enters the stack so nobody gets priority to respond to the death itself. Once they land in the graveyard, their placement is fixed because you cannot change the order of objects in that zone unless a rule or specific effect explicitly allows it. After the automatic check finishes, each creature dying creates a triggered ability rather than functioning as a state-based action, and those abilities go on the stack in turn order starting with the active player. The final concrete outcome is that three separate triggers are placed on the stack one after another in a set sequence, you cannot rearrange them once they resolve or wait to place them later, and your controller resolves all three triggers sequentially to place three counters total. The automatic game action takes precedence first during the appropriate step, and the fixed ordering rule immediately locks in the placement of those resulting triggers on the stack.
What happens if I see a symbol on a card that I do not recognize?

You can identify the set by checking the official website. First, you would go to the Magic website and locate the Card Set Archive section where the full list of expansions and expansion symbols can be found. For example, if you have a card with a snowflake icon, you would navigate to that archive to see which specific expansion it belongs to.

I cast a spell that destroys two lands I control, and I have an enchantment that lets me draw a card whenever a land dies. After the spell resolves, I still have one card left in my library. Can I take the choice to draw from both triggers? If so, what is my final number of cards?

When your spell resolves and puts both lands into the graveyard, your enchantment's triggered ability triggers twice because triggered abilities trigger once for each time the event occurs during the resolution of a spell or ability. These two separate triggers go onto the stack, and you control them. Regarding your library, even if you had zero cards, you would still be allowed to take the choice to draw cards; the rules state that if there are no cards in a player's library, that player can choose to draw a card. Since you have one card remaining, you can definitely take the choices. You resolve the first trigger by choosing to draw, adding one card to your library for two total. You then resolve the second trigger by choosing to draw again, bringing your library to three cards. The concrete final outcome is that you end up with three cards in your library after both triggers resolve and you take the draws.
I am looking at this new Class card, but the picture is all the way to one side. Is there something wrong with my card?

No, there is nothing wrong with your card. The design for these cards dictates that the illustration is vertically oriented on the left side of the card. For example, if you are looking at a Class card, you will see the art running down the left side rather than being in the middle.

I just attacked with a creature that has an ability meaning whenever it deals combat damage to a player, you put two +1/+1 counters on it. My opponent instantly cast something that says instead of dealing damage, create a 2/2 token and put a counter on it. Nothing happened to my counters! Why didn't I get them?

When your creature attempts to deal combat damage, the opponent's replacement effect intervenes first and changes the game event entirely. The replacement rule states that if an event is replaced, it never happens and a modified event occurs instead. Because the damage was swapped out, the actual event of dealing damage simply does not occur. Next, the triggered ability rule applies, specifying that an ability triggers only if its trigger event actually occurs, explicitly noting that prevented or replaced events won't trigger anything. The replacement effect takes precedence by rewriting what actually happens before the game checks for triggers. The concrete final outcome is that your creature receives zero counters from its combat trigger, while the replacement instruction to create a token resolves normally and may activate any enter the battlefield abilities on other permanents you control.
My creature has first strike and it is attacking my opponent's creature that does not have first strike. Do they both deal damage to each other at the same time?

No, they do not deal damage at the same time. When combat damage begins, if at least one creature has first strike, the only creatures that assign combat damage in that step are those with first strike or double strike. After that step, instead of proceeding to the end of combat step, the phase gets a second combat damage step where the remaining attackers and blockers that had neither first strike nor double strike assign their damage. For example, if your 2/2 creature with first strike attacks an opponent's 2/2 creature without first strike, your creature will deal its damage during the first step, and then the opponent's creature will deal its damage during the second step.

I cast a spell that duplicates my legendary creature on the battlefield so now there are two of them. My opponent started going through my graveyard cards and pointed out one of our legends just moved there, saying he's totally allowed to look since it's his turn too. I argued that players can't peek at each other's graveyards like they can hands. Can he really flip through my graveyard without permission?

A state-based action checks for duplicate legendary permanents controlled by the same player and moves all but one into their owners' graveyards, which happens automatically as part of the game rules before any player receives priority. Once the extra legend moves to that zone, the visibility rules define the graveyard as a public zone where all players can see the cards' faces without restriction for this scenario. The final outcome is that your opponent is absolutely correct and may look through your graveyard at any time, including examining the legendary card you just sacrificed. Precedence: The state-based action first moves the card to the graveyard, and then the zone definition establishes its public status allowing visibility.
What happens if I cast a spell with Awaken 3 but decide to pay its normal mana cost instead of the awaken cost? Does it still turn my land into a creature?

If you choose to pay the regular mana cost instead of the awaken cost, you do not get the land-to-creature effect. The rule states that the controller only chooses a target for the awaken spell ability if they chose to pay the awaken cost; otherwise, the spell is cast as if it did not have that target. For example, if you cast a spell with Awaken 3 and pay its standard mana cost instead of the awaken cost, your lands will remain regular lands and will not receive any counters or become creatures.

We're in combat and my two toughness creature with first strike is blocking an opponent's two toughness attacker without first strike. They deal damage in that first phase step, but now we're arguing whether my double striker still gets to hit twice since the blocker died. Can you clarify the exact sequence?

The sequence is governed first by the combat damage rules, which state that if at least one attacking or blocking creature has first strike or double strike as a combat damage step begins, the only creatures that assign combat damage in that step are those with first strike or double strike. After that step ends, the phase gets a second combat damage step for the remaining attackers and blockers without those abilities. This phase structure takes precedence in determining when damage can be assigned. In your scenario, both creatures assigned lethal damage during that initial step. Immediately after the step concludes, state-based actions are checked before the second step begins. When these actions cause permanents to leave the battlefield simultaneously, the rule dictates that a permanent’s last known information is derived from the game state before any of those state-based actions were performed. This means both creatures are moved to the graveyard at exactly the same moment using their pre-removal state for any triggered abilities. Because they are removed before the second combat damage step starts, your double striker ceases to exist and cannot assign or deal additional damage. The concrete final outcome is that both creatures go to the graveyard right after the first combat damage step, and the double strike ability deals zero extra damage.
What happens if a card tells me to put my opponent's cards into my hand?

The cards will not move to your hand; instead, they will stay with your opponent. This is because if an object would go to any library, graveyard, or hand other than its owner's, it goes to its owner's corresponding zone. For example, if you play a card that says target player puts all cards in their hand into your hand, the cards will actually just stay in the target player's hand.

I control a creature with an ability that says whenever this creature dies, I may roll the planar die and gain life equal to the result. My opponent just destroyed my creature in combat. When it goes to the graveyard, does my triggered ability still resolve so I can try to roll for life? And if I roll, do I actually get that much life?

The ability will trigger even though the creature is already in the graveyard because abilities that trigger when a permanent leaves the battlefield look back in time to check if the object had that ability right before it left. This means your opponent's destruction event causes the ability to go on the stack based on the state of the creature just prior to dying. When you roll the planar die, however, the game rules state that any effect referring to a numerical result ignores the rolling of the planar die. Since gaining life equal to the result depends on a numerical value from the roll, the planar die roll is ignored for this calculation, meaning you gain zero life regardless of what side comes up. The final outcome is that you may announce and roll the die as part of resolving the trigger, but you gain no life because the numerical result is disregarded by the rules governing planar dice.
We are playing this team game, can we change who we attack after the match has already started?

No, you cannot change those rules mid-game because any multiplayer options used are determined before play begins. For example, if you decided at the start that players would only attack left, you cannot suddenly decide to attack a player on your right once the match is underway.

We're in the middle of a skirmish and I just tapped for mana to cast my removal spell targeting their only creature. Their commander has an ability that generates tokens whenever they control zero creatures. During the resolution, we had to roll a d6 and ignore it per our group's rule. My opponent says because their creature count technically hit zero when my spell resolves, their token ability should fire multiple times or interact weirdly with the dice check. What actually happens here?

In this situation, the instruction to ignore a roll takes absolute precedence over any intermediate game state checks. Under the rules, that specific die result is considered to have never happened and no abilities trigger because of the ignored roll, which completely nullifies any hypothetical token creation tied to that dice effect. Because the dice portion is retroactively erased, the game evaluates your spell resolution as a clean sequence without interference. Their commander ability is designed to trigger when a game state is true rather than triggering when an event occurs, meaning it only activates once the actual battlefield condition stabilizes at zero creatures. A state-triggered ability doesn't trigger again until the ability has resolved, has been countered, or has otherwise left the stack, and since your spell permanently removes their last creature, the condition matches exactly once. The final outcome is that their commander leaves play via exile, a single token generation ability goes onto the stack, you get one token at end of turn, and the ignored dice roll completely disappears from history without affecting anything.

I just sacrificed my creature to activate an ability and it goes to the graveyard triggering a death effect, but my opponent claims they can respond the moment I sacrifice it before anything else happens. Is that right?

The game defines dying as being put into a graveyard from the battlefield, which confirms your permanent qualifies for its triggered ability the instant it leaves play. This definition must be evaluated first to determine whether a trigger actually exists and should go on the stack. Following that check, the rules state that if a player takes a special action, that player receives priority afterward. Because sacrifice is classified as a special action rather than a spell or ability on the stack, this priority rule takes immediate precedence over normal turn-passing expectations. The concrete final outcome is that your opponent cannot respond during the sacrifice. You complete the action, the creature enters the graveyard, your death trigger goes on the stack, and priority returns directly to you. You may cast additional instant-speed spells or activate more abilities, but your opponent only receives a chance to interact once you choose to pass priority.
What happens when I play a Class card that has text at the top but I haven't leveled it up yet?

The ability at the top is active immediately. Any ability printed on a Class card that is not preceded by a class level bar is treated normally and is available at all times. For example, if you play a Class card with a static ability at the top that says creatures you control get +1/+1, those creatures will receive the bonus as soon as the card enters the battlefield, even without any level-up mana being spent.

I just tapped all my mana to cast a spell that turned my opponent's legendary enchantment creature colorless. They had an aura attached to it that specifically says Enchant white creature. What happens right now on the battlefield?

When state-based actions are checked, the game evaluates both effects in sequence. First, the characteristic-defining rule states that Devoid means this object is colorless, which permanently overwrites the creature's previous color and makes it fully colorless on the battlefield. Second, because the creature is no longer white, it becomes an illegal target for the attached enchantment. State-based action rules immediately dictate that if an Aura is attached to an illegal object or player, that Aura is put into its owner’s graveyard. The game engine processes the color change first, recognizes the attachment violation, and automatically moves the aura to the graveyard without any player needing to take an action. The final outcome is that your opponent's enchantment is instantly removed from play, leaving their creature on the battlefield but stripped of the aura's benefits.
What happens when an ability tells me to add {B/P} to my mana pool?

When the ability resolves, you do not choose between life and mana; instead, because the effect adds mana represented by a Phyrexian mana symbol, one mana of the color of that symbol is added to your mana pool. For example, if an ability says add {B/P}, you simply add one black mana to your pool.

I just tapped my twelve-power creature to attack your two blocking creatures during combat. I assigned one damage to each blocker and eight to you, but you said the assignment is illegal because those blockers will die anyway. How does the game actually decide if an assignment is valid or not?

First, assigning combat damage is a turn-based action that does not use the stack. When blocked by two or more creatures, you may assign its combat damage to those blockers divided as you choose among them, including uneven splits. However, each creature must assign combat damage exactly equal to its power; a twelve-power creature must assign exactly twelve damage total. Once you announce the assignment, the game checks whether it complies with these rules. If it does not comply (e.g., assigning only ten damage total), the assignment is illegal and the game returns to the moment before you began assigning combat damage. Second, state-based actions are strictly delayed until whenever a player would get priority rather than resolving during the declaration phase. When priority is eventually granted after combat concludes, the game checks for applicable conditions and performs all state-based actions simultaneously as a single event, which is when creatures with zero or less toughness are put into graveyards before waiting triggered abilities go on the stack. Concrete outcome: The assignment of one damage to each blocker and eight to you (totaling ten) is illegal because it does not equal the creature's twelve power. The game returns to the start of the combat damage assignment phase, allowing you to reassign exactly twelve damage as permitted by the rules.
What happens if we want to play with four people?

You will organize into groups because Two-Headed Giant games are played with two teams of two players each. For example, you and one partner will combine to form the first team, and the other two people will combine to form the second team.

My opponent controls a creature that keeps changing size because of two static enchantments on it. One gives it +3/+3, and the other sets its power to 2. Then my opponent sacrifices one of those enchantments during combat, and we're arguing whether the creature's power goes back to zero or if it stays at whatever it was a moment before the sacrifice resolved. What actually happens on the table?

The game recalculates the creature's stats using only what is currently on the battlefield because static abilities cannot use an objects last known information for purposes of determining how their effects are applied. This means no ghost of past stats lingers once a permanent changes state, and all continuous calculations run fresh against the current board. Meanwhile the layer system dictates exactly how those remaining stats stack: effects that set power and/or toughness to a specific number or value are applied before effects and counters that modify power and/or toughness but don't set them to a specific number or value. Once the set-to-two enchantment leaves, only the additive modifier remains in its layer so the creature simply becomes whatever its base toughness plus three equals while its power becomes five. The concrete final outcome is that the creature ends combat as a modified single-stat creature calculated strictly from active board state, never retaining a memory of previous stats. The layer framework determines the step-by-step mathematical order of calculation, while the static ability restriction removes any possibility of using past stats as a starting point, meaning current state always takes precedence over historical snapshots.
If I want to get a bunch of copies of this creature, can I just keep paying the squad cost while I'm casting it?

Yes, you can pay the cost as many times as you want. Squad is an additional cost that you may pay any number of times as you cast the spell. For example, if a creature has Squad {2}, you could pay {2} once to get one token, or you could pay the cost twice to get two tokens in addition to the original creature.

I control a creature that entered face down with a morph cost. My opponent declares two attackers. Can I turn my creature face up to pay its morph cost and make it block one of them, or does the timing pass me by? We are arguing because we both know morph happens at instant speed, but I feel like blockers have to be declared immediately.

You can absolutely turn your creature face up and then declare it as a blocker. Turning a face-down creature face up is classified as a special action, which means it is an action you may take when you have priority that does not use the stack. This stands in contrast to casting spells, which follow the proposal process where choices are made and the spell goes on the stack for responses. After your opponent declares attackers, they pass priority to you before blockers are declared. You can use this window to take the special action of turning your creature face up by paying its mana cost. Because this is a special action rather than a cast spell, it does not require going through the stack mechanics and resolves as soon as you complete the action. The concrete outcome is that you turn your morph creature face up during the attack phase after attackers are declared but before blockers, and then you may declare it as a blocker against one of the attacking creatures using its new characteristics.
If I play a spell that says the Ring tempts me, but I don't have any creatures on the battlefield, do I still get the emblem and anything else from it?

Yes, you still receive the benefits. The Ring tempts a player whenever they complete the actions required, even if some or all of those actions were impossible. If you do not have an emblem named The Ring at the time, you get one before the process finishes. For example, if you cast a spell that says the Ring tempts you while your board is empty, you still receive the emblem and the total number of times you have been tempted increases, even though you could not choose a creature to be your Ring-bearer.

I'm playing with Lich's Mirror on the battlefield and my life total is 20. My opponent attacks me with two creatures, each having an ability that says when it deals combat damage to you, you lose half your life rounded up. I block one of them with my creature and leave the other unblocked. How does damage assignment work here? If the attacker assigns all its damage to my blocker and it dies, do I still take damage from the second attacker? And if both attackers manage to deal damage, will Lich's Mirror save me from losing the game twice at once?

Combat damage assignment follows a strict turn-based order based on block status. A blocked creature assigns its combat damage to the creatures blocking it; if exactly one creature is blocking it, it assigns all its combat damage to that creature. Therefore, your first attacker can assign all its damage to your blocker, potentially killing it without dealing damage to you. Your second attacker is unblocked and will assign its combat damage directly to you as per the rules for unblocked creatures. If both attackers deal combat damage, multiple triggers will cause you to lose life simultaneously. State-based actions are checked after combat damage is dealt and resolve simultaneously. Even though two separate sources cause you to lose half your life rounded up at the same time, state-based actions see this as multiple potential game losses occurring at the same instant. A single replacement effect replaces all of them. Your Lich's Mirror replaces that combined game loss event entirely. Concrete outcome: You take damage only from the second attacker (or both if you choose to assign lethal to your blocker and let remaining damage go through, though the first attacker cannot deal excess damage unless it has an ability allowing it). If you lose half life twice, Lich's Mirror saves you from losing the game, shuffling everything into your library, drawing seven cards, and setting your life total to 20. You survive the combat phase.

I have a creature on the battlefield that says 'When this creature dies, draw a card.' My opponent attacks with a 2/2 and I cast a spell that says 'Prevent the next 2 damage.' We're arguing whether I draw a card when the fight is over or not. What happens?

You do not draw a card. When your prevention spell resolves, all of the damage intended for your creature is prevented and does not mark the creature. According to the rules, an ability triggers only if its trigger event actually occurs and an event that is prevented will not trigger anything. Because the damage is prevented, no damage remains on your creature to cause it to die. State-based actions are game actions that happen automatically whenever certain conditions are met, such as a creature having lethal damage marked to be moved to the graveyard. Since prevention kept the damage off your creature, the condition for this state-based action is not met, meaning the creature stays on the battlefield and never moves to the graveyard. Because it never dies, the triggered ability never starts to resolve. Final outcome: Your creature remains alive on the battlefield and you do not draw a card.
What happens if I have a way to make hundreds of tokens and want to skip the part where we go through each one individually?

You can suggest a shortcut by describing a sequence of game choices that may be legally taken based on the current game state and predictable results. This sequence can be a loop that repeats a specified number of times or even cross multiple turns. For example, if you have a creature that creates a token when tapped and an enchantment that untaps all creatures whenever a creature enters, you could propose that you repeat the process of tapping the creature, letting the trigger resolve, and untapping all creatures 99 more times, ending just after the last token-creating ability resolves. Each other player can then either accept your proposal or shorten it by naming a place where they would make a different choice.

I’m playing a mono-red commander and I have this creature that taps for red mana. I cast another spell, it resolves, then I tap my commander for mana right away because I read that players keep priority after tapping special actions. My opponent says they can interrupt me, but I want to chain into attacking before they get a chance. Is that legal? Also, I’m trying to run three copies of a land in this deck to fuel the combo.

Deck construction rules are evaluated first at game start and strictly govern what can legally enter play. The official guidelines state that each deck must contain exactly one hundred cards and that except for basic lands, each card in a commander deck must have a different English name. Because you attempted to run three copies of a nonbasic land, your list would be flagged as illegal before the game even begins. If you adjust your list to meet those exact construction limits, then timing mechanics take over during play. The priority guidelines explicitly confirm that if a player takes a special action, that player receives priority afterward. This means tapping for mana does not end your turn or give control to your opponent. Concrete outcome: You are limited to one copy of each nonbasic land per the singleton limit, and once your deck passes construction checks, tapping your commander grants you ongoing priority, allowing you to successfully attack and cast additional spells without giving your opponent a window to respond.
Can I still cast other spells after one of my spells with Epic resolves?

No, you cannot. Once a spell with epic resolves, for the rest of the game, you can't cast spells. For example, if you cast a spell with epic that targets an opponent's creature, you will be unable to cast any more sorceries or instants for the remainder of the match.

I just tapped my Aether Vial for two mana and want to cast a creature that costs three generic and one blue, but I don't have any blue sources in play right now. Can I use the two mana from Vial for the blue part since it says generic mana? Also my opponent is tapping his lands and holding up what looks like counter magic but hasn't done anything yet; does that mean he's about to cast something or will the phase just end?

The two mana generated by Aether Vial are strictly colorless because effects that add generic mana symbols result in colorless mana being added to your pool, and colorless mana can only pay for generic costs or the {C} symbol; it cannot satisfy colored requirements like blue, so you cannot use these sources for the {U} portion of the creature cost. Your opponent tapping lands is a game action that does not automatically place spells on the stack; he is likely generating mana or activating abilities and has not cast anything yet. The turn continues normally as long as priority has not passed twice in succession with an empty stack, which means your opponent retains the full opportunity to cast spells or activate abilities at any time before both of you pass without taking actions between passes.
What happens if my only opponent leaves the game? Do I win immediately?

You win the game immediately. A player still in the game wins if that player's opponents have all left the game, and this happens immediately, overriding any effects that would preclude that player from winning. For example, if your opponent has an effect active that says you cannot win the game, that effect is ignored the moment they leave the game because the rule about opponents leaving takes precedence.
What happens when an effect reduces a spell's cost by two blue mana, but the spell only costs one blue and two generic?

The blue component becomes zero and then the extra reduction is applied to the generic mana. If a cost is reduced by an amount of colored mana that exceeds its mana component of that color, the color component is reduced to nothing and the generic mana component is reduced by the difference. For example, if you are casting a spell that costs {U}{2} and an effect reduces its cost by two blue mana, the blue part becomes zero and the remaining one blue reduction applies to the generic part, leaving a final cost of {1}.

I just played an artifact that reads Whenever you roll a six-sided die, if you control three or more permanents, draw a card. My opponent rolled a natural six on their turn, so my artifact triggered and went onto the stack. Then my opponent used a spell that told them to ignore that die roll. Since the trigger is already on the stack, does it still resolve and let me draw?

When a roll is instructed to be ignored, it is considered to have never happened. Because the triggering event did not actually occur, no abilities trigger from it, meaning nothing goes on the stack and no cards are drawn.
What happens to my creature if its toughness becomes zero?

If a creature has toughness 0 or less, it is put into its owner's graveyard. For example, if an opponent uses a spell that gives your 2/2 creature a -2/-2 effect, its toughness becomes 0, and the creature is immediately moved to the graveyard. Even if you have an ability that allows you to regenerate that creature, regeneration cannot replace this event, so the creature still dies.

I just started my combat phase in a three-player game and was about to tap creatures to attack when my opponent mentioned that my creature with lethal damage should have already died since those automatic checks happen all the time. Does that change who I can officially target for this whole combat step, or do I pick my defending player first?

The rules clearly state that state-based actions are checked throughout the game and are not controlled by any player, meaning they resolve instantly as soon as conditions like lethal damage are met rather than waiting for a spell or ability. This continuous checking happens first and takes precedence in timing because it operates independently of player initiative, automatically moving your damaged creature to its owners graveyard before you can take any actions. After that permanent leaves the battlefield, the multiplayer combat rules apply during the beginning of the combat step where the attacking player chooses one of their opponents as a turn-based action to become the defending player for this phase. The concrete final game outcome is that your creature dies immediately upon meeting the damage threshold, and you then officially select your defending opponent and declare attackers with only the remaining creatures on the board.

I cast Kiki-Jiki to copy my opponent's Ashiok, Dream Eater, and create a token of it. The original Ashiok has an ability that creates a delayed triggered ability dealing damage later in the turn. I'm controlling the token now, but when that damage trigger resolves, can I target my opponent with it? Also, if my opponent tries to prevent that damage by naming the source, can they name the original Ashiok on the battlefield instead of the token since the token is just a copy?

The token enters the battlefield as its own permanent and becomes a new object. Replacement effects that modify how a permanent enters determine its characteristics based on what it would be on the battlefield, so when you create a token copy, the token gains the printed abilities of the creature it copies and acts independently. The delayed triggered ability was created by the token, making the token the object dealing the damage. Rules regarding sources of damage clarify that the source is the object that dealt the damage, and you may choose a permanent as the source; in this case, the source is the token on the battlefield. The original Ashiok is not the source because it did not deal the damage, nor does the delayed trigger refer to it. The outcome is that the token deals the damage to your target, and any prevention or replacement effect must identify the token as the source of that damage, not the original Ashiok or the spell that created the token.
What happens when a card has one sentence that tells me to do something every turn and another sentence that says 'whenever' I do that thing, something else happens?

Those are actually linked abilities that combine into one paragraph, with the static ability coming first followed by each triggered ability that is linked to it. For example, if a card says 'Reveal the first card you draw each turn. Whenever you reveal a basic land card this way, draw a card,' you first perform the static action of revealing the card, and then the game checks if that specific reveal satisfies the trigger condition to allow the draw.

I just cast an instant that exiles my entire library and puts my commander into exile as well, but I also have a permanent on the battlefield that says whenever I have no cards in hand, draw a card. As the spell resolves, it briefly empties my hand before the library parts finish happening. What actually happens with both the commander and that trigger?

First, as the instant resolves, it puts your library and commander into exile. Immediately after the spell finishes resolving, state-based actions are checked. Because the commander is now in exile and was just put there, the owner may choose to move it to the command zone via this state-based action. Meanwhile, because your hand became empty during the spell's resolution, the game state matched the condition for your battlefield permanent. Its state-triggered ability goes onto the stack at the next available opportunity (before state-based actions or before you get priority), resolves independently, and draws a card. The final outcome remains the same: commander moves to the command zone after the spell resolves, and the trigger successfully resolves drawing a card.
What happens if I am the monarch but it is my opponent's turn?

You will not draw a card during your opponent's turn. The sequence of events is that your opponent goes through their main phase, combat, and then moves to their end step. Since at the beginning of the monarch's end step, that player draws a card, you must wait until your own turn for that to happen. For example, if your opponent is the monarch and they reach their end step, they draw a card, but you receive nothing because it is not your end step.

I just cast a big red sorcery that deals four damage to my opponent's two toughness creature. The spell resolved and is sitting in their graveyard now, but before I got priority to cast my follow-up spell, I saw the creature still on the battlefield with damage counters on it. Why didn't it drop right away, and how does the game remember what dealt that damage for my trigger effect?

When a spell resolves, its effects apply immediately so the four damage is marked on the creature right then. However, the game does not constantly check if permanents should die because state-based actions are only checked whenever a player would get priority, such as when you finish casting your sorcery or when your opponent gets priority to respond. At that exact moment, the rules check each creature to see if the total damage marked on it is greater than or equal to its toughness, and if so, that creature has been dealt lethal damage and is destroyed unless a replacement effect like regeneration intervenes. Because state-based actions only happen at those specific timing windows, the creature stayed put until you passed priority. Even though your damaging spell already moved to the graveyard, the game still tracks exactly what dealt that damage. The source of damage is the object that dealt it, and a source doesn't need to be capable of dealing damage to be a legal choice for tracking purposes. The state-based action check takes precedence in physically moving permanents to zones, while the source tracking rule operates continuously in the background to support other mechanics. As a result, when your trigger event occurs later, the game correctly identifies the resolved spell in the graveyard as the source that dealt the damage, and the creature will have moved to the graveyard the moment you passed priority after the spell resolved.

We're in a long game and I finally have enough mana to cast my commander from the command zone again, but it has an ability that says whenever it becomes tapped, I draw a card. Some guy told me because a battlefield effect made it enter already tapped, I should get to draw extra cards right away since it's entering a tapped state. Is he right? Also, do I have to pay that extra cost for casting it again?

No, your opponent is mistaken about the trigger. You are required to pay extra mana because the rules state that a commander cast from the command zone costs an additional two mana for each previous time you have cast it from that zone during the game. This payment happens first and takes precedence, meaning you must pay the increased cost before the creature ever leaves your hand or deck. Once you pay it and it resolves, the game checks its triggered abilities. The rules specify that abilities using the word becomes trigger only at the time the named event happens and do not trigger if a permanent enters the battlefield already in that state. Because your commander entered tapped rather than transitioning from untapped to tapped during this turn, the trigger never fires. Concrete final outcome: You pay the increased mana cost to cast it, it enters with summoning sickness in a tapped state, and you draw zero cards.
What happens when I roll two 2s and a 5, but the card says to ignore the lowest result?

You first identify the lowest value. If multiple results are tied for the lowest, you choose which of those rolls is ignored. For example, if you roll a 2, a 2, and a 5, you pick one of the 2s to be the ignored result. Because that roll is considered to have never happened, no abilities or effects will trigger from that specific die.

During a Commander game, I just used a board wipe that killed everything on the battlefield. A card I control says whenever I have no creatures, draw two cards. My opponent claims it only triggers once per wipe but I think it keeps going off. What actually happens?

This situation plays out under the Commander variant where each deck is led by a legendary creature designated as that deck’s commander and the format uses all the normal rules for a Magic game alongside specific additions. The ability you described functions as a state trigger rather than an event watcher. According to the established mechanics, these triggered abilities activate when a game state is true rather than triggering when an event occurs, and they will go onto the stack at the next available opportunity without triggering again until resolved or removed from the stack. Precedence belongs to the continuous state check, which overrides your opponent’s claim that it acts as a one-time event trigger. Because your board wipe emptied the battlefield simultaneously, the new game state immediately fires the ability. The concrete final outcome is that you will draw two cards now, and as soon as that effect finishes resolving, the game checks the state again, sees you still control zero creatures, and places another copy of the draw effect on the stack automatically, repeating this exact cycle until you summon a creature or the trigger leaves play.

I just cast a two-mana creature that says When this enters the battlefield you may draw a card. My opponent cast something on the stack but it resolved before my creature did. Now we are arguing about whether my creature actually entered or if its drawing ability is already waiting to be resolved. What happens next and what's the final result?

The permanent spell resolution rule applies first and takes precedence, meaning your creature card must resolve completely before any triggered abilities can even exist. The rules state that the steps for making a permanent spell become a permanent and putting it onto the battlefield under your control are always performed first, so your creature successfully enters play right now regardless of earlier resolutions. Only after that happens do triggered abilities interact with the process. The rule for triggered abilities states that optional effects containing may go on the stack when they trigger regardless of whether their controller intends to exercise the ability's option or not. Because resolving the permanent spell takes precedence, your creature is already on the battlefield and its draw-a-card effect has been placed on the stack above your opponent's last action. The concrete final game outcome is that your creature remains on the battlefield under your control and its optional trigger waits on the stack until you explicitly choose to draw a card when it resolves.
What happens if my friend starts playing as the Archenemy but only has 15 scheme cards in their deck?

The setup will be considered invalid because the archenemy needs a supplementary scheme deck of at least twenty scheme cards. For example, if your friend attempts to start a game with only 15 schemes, they must first add at least 5 more cards to their deck before the match can begin.

I just cast a spell that lets me choose multiple modes, and it has a kicker cost to choose even more effects. When I was casting it, I set up two modes but didn't mention the kicker because I wasn't sure if my teammate would have enough lands untapped later in the turn to afford it. After we passed priority as a team and went back to check mana, I realized we definitely had the mana. Can we go back and add the kicker now to get all the effects, or are we stuck with just the two modes?

You are stuck with only the two modes you originally chose. During the announcement process for your spell, the rules allow you to consider whether you will be able to pay additional costs like kicker when you are choosing your modes, which means you can look ahead and decide to commit to paying that cost before you finish announcing. However, once you have finished announcing the spell and passed priority as a team, all choices including the decision on kicker become final and cannot be changed. The rule governing announcement choices lets you plan for future costs while setting modes so everything is decided at once, but it does not allow changes after the announcement closes. Your team sharing priority means your teammate can act after you pass, but it does not grant the ability to revise a spell's announcement that has already been locked in by passing priority. The concrete outcome is that your spell resolves with only the two modes you announced and does not receive the extra effects from kicker because the decision to pay or not pay was fixed during the initial announcement phase.

I control a creature that says whenever you expend three mana this turn, create a 1/1 white Soldier token. I tapped all my lands for mana and passed priority so I could cast Incinerate. My opponent argued they could destroy my creature with their instant spell before the token would be created because I hadn't spent the mana yet. Who is right about the timing of this interaction?

Your opponent is mistaken about the timing because tapping lands for mana is a special action that does not use the stack, meaning no player can respond to you generating mana during those actions. Special actions are resolved immediately without passing priority until after they are complete. After you finish tapping your lands, you receive priority again and may cast Incinerate. When you pay the cost for Incinerate, the game evaluates your cumulative spending on spells this turn at that exact moment. If paying for Incinerate causes your total spent to reach three or more, the creature's ability triggers and is placed on the stack. Your opponent cannot respond to the land tapping or stop the trigger from happening; their only window to interact is after the spell is cast and the trigger resolves on the stack. The concrete outcome is that your opponent cannot destroy your creature in response to you tapping lands, and the token creation trigger will go on the stack once you pay for Incinerate provided you have now spent three mana total on spells this turn.
What happens when my precombat main phase starts if I have an Attraction on the board?

As your precombat main phase begins, you immediately perform a roll to visit your Attractions. This occurs because as a player's precombat main phase begins, a player who controls one or more Attractions rolls to visit their Attractions. For example, if you control an Attraction named Marketplace, the moment your precombat main phase starts, you must roll for it before you can take any other actions like casting spells.

I'm attacking with two creatures at once. My first creature has an ability that says when it deals combat damage to you, you gain life equal to the damage dealt by attackers you control. I expected this to include my second attacker hitting at the same time so I get extra life, but my opponent says it doesn't work that way. Also, after they both hit face, can I sacrifice one of them in response to that trigger?

Your opponent is correct on both counts based on how combat damage and triggered abilities interact. First, when multiple creatures deal damage simultaneously, all their triggered abilities are placed onto the stack before any player gets priority. This means you cannot intervene between hits or act before the triggers appear because there are no distinct moments to do so; the game deals damage for all attackers at once and immediately creates the triggers. Second, even though all your creatures deal damage simultaneously, there is a specific rule for abilities that trigger based on a source. If an ability triggers on damage dealt by a specific creature and refers to "damage dealt," it only counts the damage from that specific creature, not any other simultaneous damage from your attackers. Your trigger is tied to the first creature, so it calculates life gain using only that creature's damage, ignoring your second attacker completely. However, you can absolutely sacrifice a permanent in response to the trigger once it is on the stack. The rule about triggers going on the stack before priority ensures the trigger exists and waits for responses, so after combat damage resolves and the trigger appears, you receive priority and can sacrifice your second creature to activate abilities or pay costs linked to that trigger.
What happens if my opponent and I both lose all our life at the same time?

The game results in a draw. If all the players remaining in a game lose simultaneously, the game is a draw. For example, if we both have 1 life and use a spell that deals 1 damage to everyone at once, we both reach 0 life at the same moment, which results in a draw.
What happens if I use a spell with haunt and the creature I pick turns into something else, like an artifact, before the effect finishes?

The haunt effect will still work. First, you target a creature with the haunt spell; then, even if that target changes types, the haunt ability still triggers when the spell goes to the graveyard. The rule states that the phrase creature it haunts refers to the object targeted by the haunt ability, regardless of whether or not that object is still a creature. For example, if you cast a spell with haunt targeting a creature and your opponent turns that creature into an artifact before the spell resolves, the spell will still exile it haunting that artifact.

I'm playing a Commander deck with a purely white commander, and I just cast a creature that costs one generic and two red mana. It has an ability that says when this enters the battlefield, create a 1/1 blue Soldier token. My playgroup is arguing about whether this card is actually legal in my deck since it's outside my commander colors, and also what happens to the token generation if I have another enchantment on the field that makes all permanents white right as it hits the table. What's the ruling here?

In Commander, deck legality is determined by your commander's color identity and any mana symbols in your cards' costs or rules text, not by continuous effects that change colors once they hit the battlefield. Because this creature has a red mana symbol in its cost, it adds red to your deck's color identity, making it illegal if your purely white commander lacks red. Regarding the token: continuous effects that modify permanents take effect the exact moment they enter the battlefield. If an enchantment makes all permanents white as yours enters, the creature becomes white upon entry, but its triggered ability explicitly says to create a 'blue' Soldier token. Since the ability defines the token's color independently of the permanent's current color, it will still produce a blue token unless the continuous effect specifically overrides that instruction.
Can I still use an ability to protect my creature if my opponent has already cast a spell to destroy it?

Yes, you can. If you activate an ability while another spell is already on the stack, that ability is considered to have been activated in response to the earlier spell and will resolve first. For example, if your opponent casts a spell like Murder to destroy your creature, you can respond by activating an ability that gives your creature indestructible. The indestructible effect resolves first, and then the Murder spell resolves against the protected creature.

I'm mid-game and control an artifact that says 'Permanents enter tapped.' I play a Mountain from my hand that has an ability reading 'As this enters, you may choose one — it enters with two charge counters or it enters flying.' Does the Orb make my land enter tapped? Also, when do I get to pick between counters and flying?

Playing a land is a special action, which means it is an action taken when you have priority that does not use the stack and happens immediately without players being able to respond during the action itself. However, even though playing the land is a special action, replacement effects still apply to the permanent as it enters the battlefield. The rules for how permanents enter specify that replacement effects can come from other sources like your Orb and modify the entry state, so the Orb applies and the Mountain defaults to entering tapped. Additionally, the rules regarding choices for entry modifications state that if an effect requires a choice as a permanent enters, that choice must be made before the permanent enters the battlefield. Your land's ability triggers this requirement, so you must choose between counters or flying before the Mountain resolves onto the battlefield. The concrete outcome is that you make your choice during the special action resolution but before the Mountain becomes a permanent on the battlefield. If you choose counters, the Mountain enters with two charge counters and is tapped due to the Orb; if you choose flying, it enters with flying and is also tapped. The choice happens first in terms of determining the permanent's characteristics, and the replacement effect from the Orb then applies to set the entry state.
What happens when I trigger Bolster 2 while I have a 3/3, a 2/2, and a 1/1 on the field?

When Bolster triggers, you must choose a creature you control with the least toughness or tied for least toughness among creatures you control. Because the 1/1 has the lowest toughness of all your creatures, it is the only valid target, so two +1/+1 counters are placed on it to make it a 3/3.
Can I use the Warrior tokens created by Mobilize to block during my opponent's turn?

No, you cannot. The Mobilize ability says those tokens enter tapped and attacking. Because they are already attacking, they are committed to combat and cannot be used as blockers. For example, if you attack with a creature that has Mobilize 2, the two 1/1 red Warrior tokens you create will be attacking, so they cannot block your opponent's creatures.

I’m mid-game and just cast a sorcery with that cascade mechanic for three mana. It pulled a two-mana creature from my deck, so I cast it for free right away. At the same time, my opponent resolved an effect that turns all creatures black until end of turn, and my own enchantment gives white creatures plus one plus one. When the cascaded creature hits the battlefield, does it get the stat boost at all? It feels weird because I didn't pay mana for it or anything.

The cascade mechanic triggers when you cast your original spell, which means you must exile cards from the top of your library until you exile a nonland card whose mana value is less than this spell's mana value, and then you may cast that exiled card without paying its mana cost. This resolution happens first while the creature is still transitioning to the battlefield. Once it arrives, continuous effects apply next according to the layer system. The game continually and automatically applies these effects, meaning all resulting changes to an object’s characteristics are instantaneous. Color calculations happen first, so your opponent's effect turns the creature black immediately. Because its color changed, the enchantment that boosts white creatures stops applying to it, and it returns to its base statistics. Casting for zero mana via cascade does not alter this sequence. Your creature ends up on the battlefield as a standard two-mana creature with no stat boost at all.
I just drew a cool sorcery card, but my opponent just played an enchantment. Can I cast my sorcery right now while that enchantment is waiting to happen?

No, you cannot. The mechanic that determines this is that you may only cast a sorcery card from your hand during a main phase of your turn when the stack is empty. Since your opponent's enchantment is currently on the stack, it is not empty. For example, if your opponent casts a spell and it is still waiting to resolve, you must wait for that process to finish before you can cast a sorcery like Blasphemous Act during your own main phase.
What happens when a phenomenon card is revealed if we are playing with the limited range of influence option turned on?

The phenomenon card will still affect every player. Plane cards and phenomenon cards are exempt from the limited range of influence option, meaning their abilities affect all applicable objects and players in the game. For example, if a phenomenon card says all players draw a card, everyone draws a card regardless of your limited range setting.

I am down to my last card in the library and my opponent casts a spell that makes me draw two cards. There is also an effect on the battlefield that replaces one of my draws with me searching my graveyard for a card instead. Do I lose the game because I have no cards left when I try to draw?

Yes, you lose the game. The rule regarding replacement effects states that if an effect replaces a draw within a sequence of card draws, all actions required by the replacement are completed before resuming the sequence. This means your search action resolves fully first. Once that is done, you still need to complete the second draw from the sequence. Since your library has no cards, this second draw causes you to attempt drawing from a library with zero cards. The state-based action for losing the game triggers when a player attempts to draw a card from a library with no cards since the last check. You do not survive because the replacement only altered one part of the sequence; the subsequent draw attempt is still made and fails due to the empty library, leading to your loss.

I'm playing a combo deck with a bunch of draw spells and I accidentally empty my library on purpose to set up an attack. My opponent tried to stop me from winning by saying I lose immediately when my library runs out, but I thought the game just goes to my next turn? We're confused about what actually happens right after the last card is pulled into my hand versus when the loss triggers.

When you draw your final cards into hand using spell effects described in the first rule, your library empties but you do not lose immediately. State-based actions are checked throughout the game and are not controlled by any player, which means they only evaluate specific game states when triggered rather than continuously for zero cards. You will keep playing until your next turn arrives at your draw step, where you would need to put the top card of your library into your hand. Since your library is empty at that exact moment, state-based actions evaluate the condition right then and you lose the game immediately during that draw attempt, not before it or in a different phase.
Can my opponent use a spell to stop me from playing a land during my turn?

No, they cannot. Playing a land is a special action that does not use the stack, which means it is never a spell and players cannot respond to it with instants or activated abilities. For example, if you want to play a Plains during your main phase, your opponent cannot cast a spell like Negate to prevent that land from being played.

I've taken 20 damage from my opponent's Commander Grist, the Hunger Tide, but they just used an effect to turn him face down in the command zone. He attacks me again next turn and deals 2 more damage. Do I lose the game now?

You do not lose the game because the combat damage counter resets to zero when the commander becomes a new object. The rule for losing states that a player loses if they have been dealt 21 or more combat damage by the same commander over the course of the game, but this tracking depends on the commander maintaining its identity as the source of the damage. When your opponent turned their commander face down in the command zone, the game rules state that it becomes a new object. This transformation happens immediately and creates a completely distinct entity that has no connection to the previous one. Because the old object is replaced by this new object for all game purposes, any combat damage dealt before the transformation does not carry over. The commander damage total is tied to the specific object, so when your opponent attacks again with 2 more damage, you have only suffered 2 damage from this new commander. You are safe and will only lose if this new object alone deals 21 combat damage in the future.

I just cast a spell that says Return all creatures from your graveyard to your hand. In Commander Draft, I managed to grab like five copies of the same creature since we can take as many as we want with the same name. Does this spell bring them all back at the exact same time, or do I have to choose which ones go back first? Also, does my library being bigger than usual change anything?

Commander Draft explicitly states that a player’s deck may include any number of cards from that player’s card pool with the same name, which explains why you have five copies of that creature in your graveyard. When your spell resolves, the zone instruction rule takes precedence by defining how the game handles instructions affecting entire areas: some effects instruct a player to do something to a zone and that action is performed on all cards in that zone simultaneously. Because the spell targets the graveyard as a whole, every single creature card currently there will move to your hand at once rather than one by one. The deck construction rule establishes the starting quantity of cards before the game begins, but the zone rule takes precedence during resolution to dictate the actual movement timing. You will end up with all five creatures immediately in your hand ready for future turns, and your library size remains completely unaffected by this exchange.

I just activated an ability that puts a creature card from my hand onto the battlefield instead of casting it. Immediately after, my opponent casts a spell saying all players draw cards equal to their devotion, followed by another effect giving creatures +2/+0 but also targeting players with a side effect that says they can't block. When do these different effects actually apply and will my creature survive this turn?

The ability that places the card directly on the battlefield bypasses normal casting entirely, but if you had cast it, any restrictions or permissions would only matter while the card was in your hand because some static abilities apply while a card is in any zone that you could cast or play it from and are strictly limited to those read as You may cast this card, You cant cast this card, or Cast this card only. Once on the battlefield, the drawing and blocking effects are continuous effects affecting players rather than objects, which means all such effects are applied in timestamp order after the determination of objects characteristics. Because the creature placement happens before these player effects resolve, the zone based casting permission takes precedence over any player wide continuous effects that apply later in the turn structure. The concrete final outcome is that the creature enters safely with its printed power and toughness, and the player effects only determine your draw count and blocking legality afterward, leaving your permanent fully intact on the field.

I have a creature with three points of damage marked on it from an earlier combat, and it has two toughness. My opponent claims the game rules destroy this creature immediately via state-based actions so it cannot die for my triggered ability that lets me draw a card when it dies. They argue the trigger is lost because the creature was put into the graveyard by the game state check rather than being destroyed by another effect. What actually happens here?

Your opponent is incorrect about the outcome even though they are right that the game destroys creatures with lethal damage. The game checks state-based actions first and puts a creature into its owners graveyard if it has been dealt damage greater than or equal to its toughness, but this event still counts as the creature dying for triggered abilities. Once the creature is removed by the state check, the death event causes the ability to go onto the stack regardless of whether you intend to exercise the option, because triggered abilities always go on the stack when they trigger even if optional and contain may or unless clauses. After the state-based action completes and the creature moves to the graveyard, the ability resolves and you make your choice. The concrete final outcome is that you may draw a card.
What happens if I cast a spell that destroys all permanents while my opponent has an emblem?

The emblem will not be destroyed. An emblem is neither a card nor a permanent, so it is not affected by spells that target or destroy things on the battlefield. For example, if you cast a spell like Wrath of God to destroy all creatures, any emblems in play will remain because they are not permanents.
What happens if I use a spell that destroys both a creature and an artifact that has an ability to trigger whenever a creature dies?

The ability will still trigger. When an event happens, the game normally checks the state of things after the event is over, but certain triggers are exceptions that look back in time to see what was happening immediately prior to the event. For example, if you have an artifact that says whenever a creature dies, you gain 1 life, and an opponent casts a spell that destroys all creatures and all artifacts at once, the artifact's ability will still trigger for every creature that died because the game checks the state of the battlefield just before that destruction happened.

I just cast a spell that deals damage to my opponent while simultaneously blocking with my creatures, and their life total dropped below zero exactly as I drew the last card from my library. I have Lich's Mirror on the battlefield. Do I lose because two things happened at once, or does the mirror keep me alive?

When your spell resolves and your blockers deal combat damage, the game applies the principle that objects can deal damage to battles, creatures, planeswalkers, and players. This is generally detrimental to the object or player that receives that damage, which immediately drops their life total while your draw empties your library. Once those effects finish resolving, the game checks its state-based actions across the battlefield. Because zero-or-less life and an empty library would cause you to lose at the exact same moment, the rule that says if multiple state-based actions would have the same result at the same time, a single replacement effect will replace all of them takes precedence over treating them as separate losses. The damage application establishes the game state first, then the simultaneous loss check evaluates second, and your mirror replaces every instance at once. Concrete final outcome: You do not lose the game, you shuffle your hand, graveyard, and all permanents into your library, draw seven cards, and your life total becomes twenty.
What happens if I try to use a spell on an opponent's creature but it is currently considered to be outside my range of influence?

If you attempt to cast a spell that requires a target, you will find you cannot select the creature. Because objects and players outside a player's range of influence can't be the targets of spells or abilities that the player controls, your choice is blocked by the rules. For example, if you try to cast Lightning Bolt targeting an opponent's creature that is outside your range of influence, you will be unable to legally pick it as a target.
What happens if my opponent casts a spell that destroys my creature, but I have an ability that triggers when a creature is destroyed?

It does not happen immediately. Although triggered abilities can trigger at any time, including while a spell is resolving, nothing actually happens at the exact moment the ability triggers. Instead, each time a player would receive priority, those triggered abilities are put on the stack.
