For example, if an opponent casts a spell to destroy your creature, your ability will trigger, but it will not be placed on the stack until the destruction spell has finished resolving and players are granted priority to act.

I just cast a spell that creates two fresh tokens with soulbond at the same time, and I already have one creature on the battlefield. Right after, my life total drops to zero and my library runs completely empty because of another part of that same spell. Do I need to shuffle right now or do the pairing happen first?

The pairing happens first, and here is exactly how it resolves. When your tokens enter the battlefield, two triggered abilities go on the stack. According to the soulbond mechanic, if you control both an entering creature and another unpaired creature, you may pair them for as long as both remain creatures on the battlefield under your control, and a creature can be paired with only one other creature. These triggered abilities resolve before any state-based actions are checked. Once the tokens successfully form their soulbond pairs, the game then checks for loss conditions. You notice that you would lose from zero life and also from having an empty library simultaneously. The rule for simultaneous identical results states clearly that if multiple state-based actions would have the same result at the same time, a single replacement effect will replace all of them instead. This means you only shuffle once, moving your hand, graveyard, and all owned permanents into your library, then draw seven cards and set your life total to twenty. The concrete final outcome is that both tokens lock into soulbond pairs, you trigger the protective replacement effect exactly one time, you keep playing with full resources, and neither game-loss condition ends your match.
What happens if I give my creature some extra power and then it flips over to its other side?

The creature will keep the extra power. First, the effect is applied to the front face of the card. Then, when the card transforms or converts, it does not become a new object, so any effects that applied to that permanent will continue to apply to it. For example, if you cast a spell to give your creature +2/+2 and then it transforms into its back face, it still has that +2/+2 bonus.

I just paid the extra mana to entwine my modal spell, which has three modes written on it in this order: first creates a creature token, second sets my maximum hand size to three, and third says creatures I control must attack if able. My opponent already had an enchantment on the field that sets my maximum hand size to six. What actually happens when this resolves, especially regarding the order of effects?

The mode resolution rule applies first to establish the exact chronological sequence of events. When it resolves, you must follow the text of each of the modes in the order written on the card when the spell resolves, meaning your creature token enters the battlefield immediately during the first phase, and then mandatory attackers are declared during the third phase. The continuous-effect rule takes precedence in determining which limit governs your hand at any given moment because continuous effects that affect game rules rather than objects are applied after all other continuous effects have been applied according to timestamp order. Since your spell just entered the battlefield, its limit effect carries a newer timestamp than your opponent's older enchantment and naturally overrides it. The concrete final outcome is that the creature token successfully enters the battlefield, your maximum hand size becomes three overriding the previous six, and all creatures you control are forced to attack this turn if able.

I'm in a game and my opponent just activated an ability that sacrificed their commander as part of the cost to let me draw two cards. I have a permanent with a replacement effect that says 'Instead of drawing a card, exile it instead.' My opponent argues that because he already sacrificed the commander and gained priority afterward, my replacement effect is now too late to apply since he made his decision. Is he right that I can't use my replacement anymore?

Your opponent is incorrect, and you absolutely can still use your replacement effect. The key to this situation involves understanding when replacements are applied versus when special actions and priority interact. Your opponent sacrificed the commander as a cost of activation; costs are paid without passing priority, meaning no one could respond to the sacrifice itself or stop the ability from going on the stack. Once the ability was activated and put on the stack, both players receive priority, but your replacement effect is not something you activate during that window—it is a static effect that modifies how the draw happens when the spell or ability resolves. According to the rule governing replacements on draws, if an effect replaces a draw within a sequence of card draws, all actions required by that replacement are completed before resuming the sequence. This means your replacement applies directly to the drawing step during resolution, regardless of what happened earlier when priority passed after the cost was paid. The final outcome is that your replacement effect fully applies: you do not draw either card; instead, each card that would be drawn is exiled instead.
I have a huge army ready to go, but I don't think I can reach the player on my left. Can I still send them in to attack?

No, you cannot. Creatures can only attack opponents within your range of influence, planeswalkers controlled by those opponents, and battles protected by those opponents. For example, if a card effect limits your range of influence to only the player sitting directly in front of you, you cannot declare an attack against the player sitting to your left.

We're in my end step and my opponent drops a Mountain after resolving several instants on the stack. Earlier they cast Fireball which required waiting for everything to clear, but this land drop seemed to happen instantly without going on the stack. I want to stop their next action with an instant spell targeting their next move. Are they allowed to keep putting lands down like that without triggering responses, and why did my counter-magic work on Fireball but not on this land?

When your opponent cast Fireball earlier, they were following the rule that previously referred to casting as playing but now clarifies that playing a card means playing it as a land or casting it as a spell, whichever is appropriate. Because it was a non-land card, they cast it and placed it on the stack, allowing you to respond before resolution. However, when they drop their Mountain during their main phase, they are executing a different mechanic because the special actions rules explicitly state that playing a land is a special action. Special actions do not use the stack, cannot be responded to with instant-speed spells or abilities, and resolve immediately upon announcement. The special action definition takes precedence over general casting procedures for lands because putting a land onto the battlefield is specifically carved out of the normal spell-casting system. Therefore, your opponent successfully put their Mountain into play without giving you a chance to respond, and any instant spell you cast targeting that land drop will simply fizzle since no spell ever entered the stack.

I just cast Doom Blade on my opponent's two Glistener Elves and they responded with a spell that completely prevents the next three damage this turn. My cards have an ability that triggers whenever a creature takes damage, but our table disagreed on whether those triggers go to the stack before or after their prevention spell resolves. What actually happens?

When you cast Doom Blade, the spell goes on the stack first, followed by your opponent's prevention spell placed on top of it due to priority rules. The evaluation step applies first and follows the exact principle that an ability triggers only if its trigger event actually occurs, but because the prevention effect modifies the damage event so zero damage is dealt, the triggers never see the required state. This means no triggered abilities enter the stack at all. Once both players pass in succession with nothing pending, the second rule takes precedence by stating that each time all players pass in succession, the spell or ability on top of the stack resolves, which simply moves your spells through their normal steps. The concrete outcome is that Doom Blade and the prevention spell resolve harmlessly, no damage triggers are created or resolved, life totals remain unchanged, and combat proceeds to the next phase.
What happens if my creature with 5 power attacks a battle that only has 2 defense counters?

When you deal damage to a battle, that many defense counters are removed from it. For example, if your creature with 5 power attacks a battle with only 2 defense counters, 2 defense counters are removed from that battle.

I just cast an older reprint that exiles a creature from my graveyard, and I have another permanent that triggers whenever a creature card is put into exile from anywhere. My opponent had a creature there when I played this spell. Does the effect actually happen even though the old printing originally used removed from game wording?

Yes, the effect will definitely trigger. Per official Oracle errata, older cards printed with 'removes [an object] from the game' or 'sets [an object] aside' wording now exile those objects to the standard exile zone. When the creature card moves there, it satisfies the trigger condition for your permanent, which activates '[When/Whenever/At]' a specified event. The ability goes on the stack and resolves normally, producing the permanent's printed effect.
What happens to all my stuff, like cards in my graveyard or in exile, once this extra game is over?

When a subgame ends, each player takes all their traditional cards that were in the subgame, which includes cards in the subgame's exile zone, and puts them into their main-game library, then shuffles them. For example, if you exiled a Mountain during this extra game, that Mountain goes back into your main deck and you shuffle your library before continuing the main game.

We are mid-combat and my opponent taps three creatures to attack me. I have an enchantment on the battlefield that reads whenever I control no creatures of any type, draw two cards. My opponent responds by sacrificing one attacker with a sacrifice ability, while I respond by destroying another attacker with a spot removal spell. Both attackers had a passive static ability that gave all other creatures +1/+0. After those permanents leave the battlefield, does my enchantment trigger and will the plus one zero bonus still apply to my other creatures?

The enchantment will trigger and you will draw two cards, and the plus one zero bonus will completely disappear from your other creatures once those attackers leave the battlefield. This happens because state triggers evaluate live conditions rather than waiting for events to finish, so the moment both attackers depart you control no creatures and the enchantment checks that exact reality. As the rules explain, triggered abilities tied to game conditions trigger as soon as the game state matches the condition before going onto the stack at the next available opportunity, and they will not trigger again until they resolve or leave the stack. At the same time, the passive plus one zero ability stops applying immediately because static abilities never look backward at what a permanent was doing before it left the zone. The rules clearly state that unlike spells and other kinds of abilities, static abilities can’t use an object last known information for purposes of determining how their effects are applied. When both mechanics overlap, the timing precedence is straightforward: the permanents change zones first, which forces all static modifications to vanish instantly based on current locations, and only then does the empty battlefield condition become true causing the state trigger to go onto the stack. The final outcome is that you draw exactly two cards and your remaining creatures lose the plus one zero boost entirely without any lingering effects.
My opponent just played a Siege card. How do they decide who protects it?

When a Siege enters the battlefield, its controller must choose its protector from among their opponents. Only an opponent of a Siege's controller can be its protector. For example, if you are playing in a three-player game and your opponent plays a Siege, they must pick either you or the third player at the table to be the protector.

I have a creature attacking their Battle. Opponent blocks with one creature and there's an artifact Golem on the field too. Can I split damage between the blocker and the Golem? If the blocker dies, does damage spill to the Battle?

First, the combat assignment rules require that a blocked creature assigns its damage only to the creatures blocking it, which immediately restricts your options to just the single blocking creature. This rule takes precedence in defining valid recipients during the assignment phase, meaning you cannot choose to split damage with objects that are not blockers. Furthermore, the general game rules state that objects can deal damage only to battles, creatures, planeswalkers, and players, so damage cannot be dealt to an artifact Golem even if it were a potential target. Since there is exactly one blocker, all combat damage must go to that creature. If the blocker is destroyed before damage assignment or removed from combat, the attacking creature assigns no damage at all; there is no spillover to the Battle because unassigned damage does not transfer unless a specific rule allows it, which none do here. The concrete outcome is that your entire combat damage is dealt to the blocking creature, while both the artifact Golem and the Battle take zero damage.
What happens if my dungeon goes into my command zone? Do I start over?

When you put a dungeon you own into the command zone, you put your venture marker on the topmost room. For example, if you were currently in the third room of a dungeon and that card was moved to your command zone, your marker would be placed on the first room at the top of the card.

I just cast a spell that gives all my creatures an ability like If this creature would die, exile it instead. Since two different cards gave them this, now I have two replacement effects trying to apply when they die. When they actually go to the graveyard or exile, what happens with the triggers that are supposed to go on the stack?

First, the game determines how the creatures move zones by applying replacement effects immediately during that event. If any effects or rules try to do two or more contradictory or mutually exclusive things to a particular object, you as the controller choose which effect to apply and what that effect does before the zone change completes. Once those permanents finish moving, the triggered abilities wait for the game to check for new triggers. Once an ability has triggered its controller puts it on the stack as an object that’s not a card the next time a player would receive priority. If multiple abilities have triggered since the last time a player received priority, they are placed on the stack in active player then nonactive player order, and you arrange your own simultaneous triggers however you like within your step. The zone movement replacement rule takes strict precedence because objects must finish transitioning zones before any new ability can legally enter the stack. The concrete final outcome is that you pick one replacement effect to apply to each creature, they never actually go to the graveyard if your choice was exile or another public zone, those specific triggered abilities go onto the stack in your turn priority window arranged by your chosen order, and the game proceeds with resolving them while the original destruction path is permanently ignored for that event.
Can I play my instant right after my opponent plays a spell?

Yes, you can. When it is your turn to act or after an opponent finishes casting something, a player who has priority may cast an instant card from their hand. When you do this, the instant becomes a spell and uses the stack, meaning it will resolve before any spells already waiting on the stack. For example, if your opponent casts Lightning Bolt to destroy your creature, you can respond by casting Counterspell to try and stop it.

I just had my attacker get boosted by two different enchantments that say damage it deals is doubled. It hit my opponent for what would have been just one damage, but they lost the game instantly and their creatures died too. Did that damage count as eight or just four? And why didn't their dying creatures trigger their death abilities until after the fight phase ended?

The damage counts as four because replacement effects multiply rather than add linearly (1 damage × 2 = 2, then 2 × 2 = 4), which aligns with the single-opportunity stacking rule for damage doublers. Their creatures died and triggered death abilities afterward because state-based actions check simultaneously and resolve first; once all applicable actions are performed, the game places waiting triggered abilities onto the stack before passing priority, ensuring you can respond to those deaths after combat damage resolves.
Wait, if we are already doing a mini-game and someone plays something that starts another one, do they both just happen at the same time separately?

They do not run separately; instead, they nest. A subgame can be created within a subgame, which means the existing subgame becomes the main game in relation to the new subgame. For example, if you are currently participating in a side-battle triggered by a card and an effect during that battle triggers a second mini-contest, that second contest is nested inside the first one, with the first battle serving as its main game environment.

I'm mid-combat and have been playing my turn for a while. I currently control just one creature left on the board because I used a removal spell earlier. I want to attack with it, but I also have this enchantment that says whenever I control exactly one permanent, I draw a card at the end of the turn. Do I get the draw trigger when I declare my attacker? Also, does my opponent care if I'm attacking alone for their blocking effects?

During your declare attackers step, combat rules establish that a creature attacks alone if it’s the only creature declared as an attacker during the declare attackers step. At the exact same moment you commit that single creature to attack, the game also evaluates your battlefield state for your enchantment ability. Rules for triggered abilities watching game states specify that they trigger as soon as the game state matches the condition and go onto the stack at the next available opportunity. The combat declaration rule applies first because you must formally declare attackers before the state is finalized and triggers can be placed on the stack. Concrete final outcome: your single attacker is officially recognized as attacking alone, any opponent blocker will be considered a lone blocker if they commit just one creature, and your enchantment trigger successfully goes onto the stack right after you finish declaring combat to resolve for the card draw.
If I cast a spell that gives me mana, am I using a mana ability?

No, you are not. A spell can never be a mana ability, even if it could put mana into a player's mana pool when it resolves. It is cast and resolves just like any other spell. For example, if you cast an instant that adds three colorless mana to your pool, it follows the standard rules for spells rather than being a mana ability.

We just started our game and are deciding how to set up our boards. My friend has a card effect that says they start with fifty life and draw nine cards, while I have a permanent that says any damage dealt to me gets redirected to my commander instead. How do those starting conditions and later redirection actually resolve when we begin playing?

The game strictly follows the established opening sequence because Once the starting player has been determined, each player sets their life total to 40 and draws a hand of seven cards which completely overrides your friend attempt to start with fifty life and nine cards. Later in the match during combat or other damage steps your redirection permanent resolves by replacing damage dealt to one battle, creature, planeswalker, or player with the same damage dealt to another battle, creature, planeswalker, or player as long as both remain valid targets on the battlefield. If one of those permanents is no longer on the battlefield when the damage would be redirected, or is no longer a battle, creature, or planeswalker when the damage would be redirected, the effect does nothing and you take the original damage, while if damage would be redirected to or from a player who has left the game the effect does nothing. Because the opening setup happens first it establishes your actual health pool and hand size, and the redirection mechanic then takes precedence later by altering where incoming damage lands rather than how much life you have overall. The concrete final outcome is that both players begin at 40 life with seven cards in hand, your commander absorbs redirected damage throughout the match as long as it stays on the battlefield, and you lose the game if redirection fails and you take enough damage to reach zero.

I’m going through my whole deck by sacrificing creatures to draw cards on purpose. Once my library is completely empty and I try to draw one more time, can my opponent still cast a spell or use an ability before the match actually ends?

Triggered abilities follow the rule that they have a trigger condition and an effect written as When or Whenever or At trigger condition or event followed by effect, meaning they continuously monitor gameplay and are placed on the stack after their triggering events occur. The empty deck rule states that a player who attempts to draw a card from a library with no cards in it loses the game the next time a player would receive priority. When you drain your library and attempt the final draw, the loss condition is deferred until priority passes, so the triggered abilities watching for the draw event take precedence during resolution and go on the stack first. The concrete final outcome is that your opponent gets to cast their instant spell, all triggers resolve normally, and you lose the game as soon as they finish their action and pass priority back to you.
Can I find the mana cost of a card by reading its text box?

No, you must look at the mana cost instead. The mana cost and the text box are distinct parts of a card. For example, if a card has {1}{U} in the top right corner, that is the mana cost required to cast it, whereas the text box contains special abilities like draw a card.

I control a permanent that says Each instant and sorcery card in your hand has base power and toughness 2/2. Whenever you cast an instant or sorcery spell this way, draw a card. My opponent just used an effect that tries to put an instant card from my graveyard directly onto the battlefield. Do I still get to draw a card? We are arguing because one of us thinks the triggered ability still happens since the static part said cast, but the other thinks it goes to the battlefield so it triggers. What actually happens in this situation?

When your opponent attempts to move that instant card directly onto the battlefield, it never leaves your graveyard because the game enforces a hard restriction that if an instant or sorcery card would enter the battlefield, it remains in its previous zone. This zone placement limit takes immediate precedence over any other effects trying to relocate the card, meaning the card stays put and never enters play. Additionally, your permanent uses a specific design structure where a static ability sets up a condition and a triggered ability monitors for a result, which means these components are linked and combine the abilities into one paragraph with the static ability first, followed by each triggered ability that is linked to it. Because the zone rule stops the card from moving, and the static portion of your combined block only references casting spells from your hand under its specific parameters, the linked trigger never receives a valid game state change to evaluate. The concrete final outcome is that the instant card remains in your graveyard unchanged, does not enter the battlefield, and you do not draw any cards because the zone restriction resolves first and breaks the tracking requirement for the linked ability.
What happens if my creature has an ability that says Whenever this creature blocks, draw a card, and it ends up blocking two different attacking creatures?

You will only draw one card. An ability that reads Whenever a creature blocks triggers only once each combat for that creature, even if it blocks multiple creatures. For example, if your creature is declared as a blocker against two different attackers during the same combat, the ability triggers when it becomes a blocker, but it will not trigger again for the second attacker.
What happens to my protection if the enchantment providing it is destroyed?

The protection ends immediately. Static abilities create continuous effects that are active as long as the permanent with the ability remains on the battlefield and has the ability. For example, if you have an enchantment that prevents all damage dealt to your creatures and that enchantment is destroyed, your creatures will immediately start taking damage again because the effect only lasts while the enchantment is on the battlefield.

I just sacrificed one of my creatures with afterlife three during combat to get three white and black flying spirit tokens. My opponent has two enchantments on the field: one says all creatures are red, and another says white creatures you control get plus one plus one. What exactly are these tokens going to look like when they enter, and do those effects even apply to them?

The afterlife rule states that When this permanent is put into a graveyard from the battlefield, create N 1/1 white and black Spirit creature tokens with flying. This trigger resolves first, placing three brand new spirits on the battlefield. However, their exact characteristics are immediately dictated by the layer system, which takes precedence for calculating stats because the application of continuous effects as described by the layer system is continually and automatically performed by the game. The rule dictates that color modifications are processed before power and toughness bonuses. Even though your opponent has an enchantment changing all creatures to red and another giving white creatures plus one plus one, the tokens first have their color altered to red, placing them outside the scope of the color-based buff. The continuous modification is applied second and simply does not trigger because the condition is no longer met. The final outcome is three untapped 1/1 red flying spirit tokens that sit on the battlefield without any stat boosts until the end of turn.
What happens when I turn a face-down creature face up? Do its enters the battlefield abilities trigger again?

The abilities do not trigger. When you turn a face-down permanent face up, it is a special action and any abilities relating to the permanent entering the battlefield dont trigger because the permanent has already entered the battlefield. For example, if you have a creature with morph that says 'When this creature enters the battlefield, draw a card,' you will not draw a card when you pay the morph cost to turn it face up.
What happens to my opponent's equipment if I take control of their creature?

When you take control of the creature, it is no longer within your opponent's range of influence. Because an equipment cannot equip an object outside its controller's range of influence, the equipment will automatically become unattached from that permanent as a state-based action. However, the equipment does not go to the graveyard; it remains on the battlefield. For example, if your opponent has a legendary sword attached to their dragon and you use a spell to take control of that dragon, the sword will simply fall off the dragon and stay on the battlefield as an unattached artifact.

I just cast Lightning Strike to deal three damage to my opponent's commander, but they responded with an artifact that prevents the next point of damage for each creature they control. We both thought their commander would still die and trigger its ability that says whenever a creature dies this turn draw a card, but now we are arguing about whether it actually goes on the stack. What happens in this situation?

The replacement effect handling damage modification takes precedence and must be evaluated first. When that prevention effect applies, the incoming damage is reduced to zero, and under replacement mechanics if a source would deal 0 damage it does not deal damage at all. Because that foundational event never happens, the game then evaluates triggers using the exception where normally objects that exist immediately after an event are checked but here the game looks back in time to determine if those abilities trigger by analyzing the appearance of objects immediately prior to the event. Since the damage was reduced before it could actually occur looking back in time reveals no destruction happened and the trigger condition was not met. The concrete final outcome is that your opponent commander takes zero damage survives unchanged and its death-triggered ability does not go on the stack or resolve.
What happens if my Battle card's defense gets reduced to 0 during a game?

When a battle's defense reaches 0, it is put into its owner's graveyard. However, there is one exception: if the battle is the source of an ability which has triggered but not yet left the stack, it stays on the battlefield. For example, if you cast a spell that reduces a Battle's defense to 0, the Battle will only move to the graveyard after any abilities it triggered have finished resolving and left the stack.

I'm playing Commander and I used an enchantment that says Creatures you control must attack this combat if able. My opponent claims my commander didn't actually deal lethal tracking damage because there were no legal blockers available, so they argue it wasn't forced to attack properly. Meanwhile, the damage total from that commander has reached twenty points against one of us. Does the damage count toward the loss condition, and how does the forcing mechanic work here?

At the exact moment attackers are declared, the game checks if an effect is compelling combat. Per the rules, a creature had to attack if one or more effects required it to attack at that time, so your commander was fully forced even if no legal blockers were available. After combat damage resolves, format-specific state-based actions are evaluated immediately. In Commander, a player loses the game only when they have been dealt twenty-one or more combat damage by the same commander over the course of the game. Since your commander has only dealt twenty damage so far, the loss condition has not yet been met. If you deal one more point of combat damage from this commander in any combat, that additional damage will trigger the state-based action and the targeted opponent will lose the game immediately.

I'm in combat right now and my opponent's four toughness creature has shroud because they cast an enchantment on it. I have a five power attacker and want to know if blocking with it will trigger my other card that looks for combat damage greater than lethal. Does the shroud stop the damage or the trigger?

Shroud is a static ability that means this permanent can't be the target of spells or abilities, so your opponent's enchantment successfully protects their creature from being targeted by your removal spells or counterspells. Because targeting restrictions are evaluated before damage assignment, and combat damage does not use targeting, shroud has no effect on how blockers interact. When your five power attacker blocks the four toughness defender, they deal damage simultaneously in combat. The game then applies the excess damage calculation to that result: because those sources together dealt an amount of damage to that creature greater than lethal damage, exactly one point is considered excess damage. That single excess damage point will successfully trigger your ability.
If I cast a spell that deals 5 damage to my opponent and they respond with an effect that tries to redirect that damage to a different player, does that other player still take the redirected damage?

No, not if that person is outside your range of influence. If a replacement effect tries to cause a spell or ability to affect an object or player outside its controller's range of influence, that portion of the event does nothing. For example, if you cast Lava Axe targeting your opponent Rob, and Rob casts Captain's Maneuver to redirect 3 damage to Carissa, but Carissa is not within your range of influence, the Lava Axe will deal 2 damage to Rob and no damage will be dealt to Carissa.

I have a massive 8/8 Golem attacking my opponent's board, and they block me with two different 4/4 creatures. Can I split the damage so that one takes 4 and the other takes 4? If I do exactly 4 to each, will both blockers die in combat?

Yes, you can assign the damage exactly that way or choose any other split. According to the rules, when an attacking creature is blocked by two or more creatures, its controller assigns combat damage to those blockers divided as it chooses among them. Assigning 4 damage to each of your opponent's 4/4 creatures is perfectly legal. After assignment, all combat damage is dealt simultaneously. The rules require each blocking creature to assign combat damage to the creature it is blocking, so both 4/4s will deal 4 damage back to your Golem. State-based actions are then checked throughout the game and are not controlled by any player, so once the damage is marked, both blocking creatures and your Golem will be destroyed for having lethal damage equal to their toughness. The final result is that all three creatures die in combat.
What happens if an opponent deals damage to just one person on my team?

Since each team has a shared life total, any damage dealt to any member of your team affects the whole group. Because the life total starts at 30 for the team, if an opponent's creature deals 4 damage to one teammate, your entire team's life total drops from 30 down to 26.
I just cast a spell that says the game is a draw between me and my opponent. Does the whole match end right now for both of us?

The match does not necessarily end for everyone. When an effect states the game is a draw, it only results in a draw for the controller of that spell or ability and any players within their range of influence. Those specific players leave the game, while all remaining players continue to play. For example, if you are playing a multiplayer Commander game and you cast a spell that causes a draw between you and the player to your left, you and that player would leave the match, but the other two players would keep playing against each other.

I just tapped my face-down creature to block and it got destroyed this turn. I know my commander took ten damage earlier from it while it was face-up, but now that its in my graveyard, can I still use the return option, and does that damage even count toward losing?

The card you control is still officially designated as your commander even though it has been turned face-down, meaning it retains that designation across all zones and game states. This identity check happens first to establish what we are tracking. Because it is still your commander, the combat damage it dealt earlier continues to count toward the rule where a player who has been dealt 21 or more combat damage by the same commander over the course of the game loses the game. State-based actions will evaluate that loss condition first. If you do not reach twenty-one points, state-based actions then check the zone change rule, which states that if a commander is in a graveyard and was put there since the last time state-based actions were checked, its owner may put it into the command zone. Final outcome: The damage fully counts toward the loss condition and is evaluated first, but since you are below twenty-one points, you will successfully return the card to the command zone when those actions resolve.
What happens if my opponent has less life than me right at the start of the game?

To determine starting totals, you take 20 and add or subtract the life modifier from your vanguard card, because each player's starting life total is 20 plus or minus the life modifier of their vanguard card. For example, if your vanguard card has a modifier of +3 and your opponent's has a modifier of -4, you would start with 23 life while they would start with 16.

I cast Lightning Strike and my opponent responds with Counterspell. Now I want to pay the additional {U}{U} cost for Shockwave so it doesn't counter, but he says I already lost the chance. Is that right? We argued because I thought I could just declare it whenever I have priority.

Remove the hallucinated reference to 'triggering Shockwave normally.' Replace the conclusion with a strict rules-based outcome: spells resolve exactly as they were declared when placed on the stack, meaning opponents cannot retroactively allow cost declaration after responding. State clearly that Lightning Strike resolves as cast (or is countered) based solely on the costs actually paid and announced during the initial casting phase.
What happens if I play a copy of my scheme card from my hand when that card has an ability that says 'this scheme draws you a card'?

When the copy triggers the ability, it will refer back to your original card in the command zone. Because an ability of a scheme card that includes the text 'this scheme' means the scheme card in the command zone that is the source of that ability, the effect applies to the original rather than the copy on the battlefield. For example, if you play a copy of Skyward Raid from your hand, the ability will trigger and then specifically identify the original Skyward Raid sitting in your command zone as the subject of the draw.

We are in combat and I attack with a creature. My opponent blocks it. They have an enchantment that says if your creatures would deal damage to this block, draw a card instead of dealing that damage. But they also control a commander that says whenever you draw a card, create a 1/1 white Soldier token. What happens exactly and in what order do the abilities go on the stack?

Replace all references to 'three' with 'one' (or explicitly note that multiple triggers apply only if multiple creatures attack). Correct the sequencing explanation: state that because the damage replacement happens as a single combat damage event, the triggered ability sits until the entire event finishes and players receive their first shared priority window. Once placed on the stack, it resolves normally to create exactly one 1/1 Soldier token.
What happens if my creature has an ability that triggers when it deals damage, but another creature also hits the same player at the exact same time?

Your creature's ability will only trigger based on the damage your specific creature dealt. Even though both creatures hit the player at the same moment, the effect refers only to the damage dealt by the specified sources and not to any damage dealt at the same time by other sources. For example, if your creature deals 2 damage and an opponent's creature also deals 3 damage to the same player during combat, your ability only considers the 2 damage from your specific creature.

I just declared attackers with a creature that scales in toughness based on my hand size. My opponent immediately taps it with an instant after the declaration step, then casts another spell mid-combat that temporarily reduces its toughness to zero while resolving. Does the tapped creature skip damage and get destroyed before end of turn?

No, your creature will deal its full combat damage and remain on the battlefield. First, tapping a creature that has already been declared as an attacker does not remove it from combat and does not prevent its combat damage, so the tap effect cannot stop the attack. Second, even though the creature temporarily has zero toughness while that second spell resolves, state-based actions pay no attention to what happens during the resolution of a spell or ability; they only evaluate once the entire spell finishes resolving. The sequence takes precedence in order: your attacker locks into combat upon declaration, so damage calculation runs unaffected by later taps, and lethal checks are deferred until resolution ends. By the time state-based actions finally check, the creature's toughness has already returned to a positive number, so it stays alive and your life total reflects the damage taken.
What happens to my creature if I remove a level counter from it?

It depends on the symbol. If the symbol is Level 3+ and you go from 3 counters down to 2, the creature loses its extra features because those abilities and stats only apply as long as the creature has 3 or more level counters on it. For example, if a creature has Level 3+ [4/4] [Trample] and you remove a counter so it only has 2, it will lose both Trample and its 4/4 power and toughness.

I just cast a creature with undying that has a coin flip effect when it enters. The flip gave me two plus one plus counters on it. My opponent then cast an instant that puts three minus one minus one counters on it right before combat. It dies to a blocker. Did it come back?

It will not return to the battlefield. The coin flip mechanic operates as a random event that determines whether you place positive or negative counters on the permanent when it resolves. When your opponent’s instant puts three minus one minus one counters on the creature, those negatives begin canceling out the existing positives, but the game does not move the creature to the graveyard until state based actions check. Before those actions finalize the move, the game records the creature’s last known information exactly as it appears on the battlefield. The undying ability triggers based on a specific rule that states when this permanent is put into a graveyard from the battlefield, if it had no +1/+1 counters on it, return it to the battlefield under its owner’s control with a +1/+1 counter on it. Because three negative counters only cancel out two positive ones until one remains, the last known information still shows that single plus one plus counter. The coin flip rule sets the initial count, and the undying rule checks the battlefield state before death takes precedence in evaluating whether the return condition is met. Since the condition requires zero positive counters to remain, the trigger fails and the creature stays dead permanently.
I want to cast a spell with delve but I am low on mana. Can I just use cards from my graveyard instead of spending mana?

Yes, you can. Delve means for each generic mana in the spell's total cost, you may exile a card from your graveyard rather than pay that mana. For example, if you are casting a spell that costs 3 generic mana and 1 blue mana, you could choose to exile three cards from your graveyard to avoid paying those three generic mana, and then pay the 1 blue mana normally.

I just tapped one of my creatures using a special action before combat so it could sit out this round, and now my opponent is arguing that my other creature doesn’t count as attacking alone because we didn’t formally pass turns during the declare attackers step. We’re playing right now and want to know who gets the trigger benefit.

The ruling depends on the strict sequence of priority actions versus automatic combat declarations. Special actions are actions a player may take when they have priority that do not use the stack, meaning you must tap your creature during a previous phase before combat begins. Declaring attackers is a turn-based action that happens automatically as the declare attackers step starts. Because special actions require active priority and happen first, tapping the creature beforehand legally removes it from consideration for declaration. During the declare attackers step, only one creature will be chosen to attack since the other is already tapped. A creature attacks alone if it’s the only creature declared as an attacker during the declare attackers step. Since the special action occurred earlier and prevented the second creature from entering combat, exactly one will be declared. The final outcome is that your single attacking creature officially attacks alone, triggers its effect immediately upon declaration, and proceeds through combat normally without opposition.
Wait, I see that card in your command zone. Can I also take some of my conspiracy cards from my sideboard and put them there?

Yes, you can, but only during the setup phase. At the start of a game, before decks are shuffled, each player may put any number of conspiracy cards from their sideboard into the command zone. For example, if you had two conspiracy cards in your sideboard when we started, you could have placed them in your command zone before we began shuffling our decks.

I'm mid-game and just attacked with a Young Wolf that has a +1/+1 counter on it. My opponent casts two spells targeting it simultaneously: one dealing three damage and another putting three -1/-1 counters on it. We both froze when the creature died. My opponent claimed Undying won't trigger because the counter was already gone, but I argued it should still go back. What actually happens and where does it end up?

When simultaneous state-based actions cause Young Wolf to die, its last known information is locked into the game state before those actions occur. As the provided guidance explains using this exact scenario, because the creature had a +1/+1 counter on it when it was last on the battlefield, Undying will not trigger. The creature simply moves to the graveyard and does not return.

I just used a card that exiles my last spell from hand, and now I have another effect that says Whenever you have no cards in your hand, draw two cards. The ability is sitting on the stack waiting to resolve. While it waits, I gain a card in hand from drawing or an ally giving me one, then my opponent uses a card to exile that new card too. Do I get the trigger to happen again while the first one is still waiting?

When you cast that spell, you followed the rule that says to exile an object is to put it into the exile zone from whatever zone it’s currently in, meaning your final card immediately left your hand and went to exile. This instantly created a new game state where your hand size hit zero. That change caused your draw ability to activate as a triggered effect, which will go onto the stack at the next available opportunity. The rule for these specific triggers states clearly that they do not trigger again until the ability has resolved, has been countered, or has otherwise left the stack. Because your first trigger is already waiting on the stack, the game ignores the second time your hand became empty while you exiled the new card. Once the original effect finishes resolving, if your hand remains empty at that exact moment, you will draw two cards one time and nothing else happens.
What happens when my turn starts if I have a creature that is currently phased out?

That creature will phase back onto the battlefield. At the start of a turn, all phased-in permanents with phasing that the active player controls phase out, and all phased-out permanents that the active player controlled when they phased out phase in. For example, if you have a creature like Thassa's Oracle that is currently phased out, it will phase in at the beginning of your turn. This occurs simultaneously with any of your other phased-in permanents phasing out and does not use the stack.

I just sacrificed a creature with an ability that reads Whenever this permanent dies, create a 2/2 black Zombie creature token to pay for a spell cost. The creature card immediately moved to the graveyard because of the sacrifice. Does that death trigger still happen since it is already gone when the game checks for triggers? Also, I have another permanent that says If an effect would create one or more tokens under your control, put two +1/+1 counters on target creature you control instead. Will that replacement effect apply to this death trigger even though the trigger came from a sacrifice rather than directly casting something that makes tokens?

The death trigger will definitely activate. The game handles this by using a process that looks back in time to determine if those abilities trigger, using the existence of those abilities and the appearance of objects immediately prior to the event, so leaves-the-battlefield abilities function correctly even though the permanent is already gone. When that ability resolves later, it will attempt to create tokens. At that point, your replacement effect will apply because these replacement effects apply if the effect of a resolving spell or ability creates a token or puts a counter on a permanent, and they also apply if another replacement or prevention effect does so, even if the original event being modified wasn’t itself an effect. The look-back mechanism takes precedence first to confirm the trigger exists before the permanent leaves, while the replacement mechanism takes effect second to alter the resolution. The concrete final game outcome is that you will create a 2/2 black Zombie creature token, which immediately becomes two +1/+1 counters placed on the target creature you choose due to the replacement effect.

I have a creature that has an ability triggering whenever it attacks. My opponent waits until after I declare attackers to cast a spell that destroys my creature. Does the attack trigger still go on the stack, or does it disappear because the creature is gone now?

Triggered abilities function based on when their specific condition occurs, not on the permanent remaining in that state. The rules state that a triggered ability has a trigger condition and an effect, and it triggers when the event happens. In your case, the event of declaring the creature as an attacker occurred during the declare attackers step, so the ability triggered at that moment and is now on the stack. Later, when your opponent destroys the creature, the permanent leaves the battlefield, which causes it to be removed from combat according to the rule that a permanent is removed from combat if it leaves the battlefield. However, removing the creature from combat or destroying it does not retroactively cancel triggers that have already occurred. The final outcome is that the attack trigger resolves successfully on the stack despite the creature dying, and you receive the full effect of the ability.
What happens when I cast a spell and then immediately activate an ability to reduce costs?

First, your spell is placed on the stack with its original cost. Then, when you activate the cost-reducing ability, that ability is also put on the stack. However, activating an ability that alters costs won't affect spells and abilities that are already on the stack. For example, if you cast a spell costing {3} and then activate an ability to make all spells cost {1} less, the spell already on the stack remains at {3}.

We are playing a Commander match right now and my opponent has been attacking me with three different creature commanders. They dealt ten damage to me from one of them earlier, but then they sacrificed it and relexiled it later in the same turn. I’m wondering if that damage still counts toward making me lose the game later, or if starting fresh with a new creature resets everything. What happens here?

Both the rule stating that a player who’s been dealt 21 or more combat damage by the same commander over the course of the game loses and the variant rule allowing owners to move commanders from graveyards or exile into the command zone are actively governing your situation. The damage tracking rule explicitly ties the loss condition to that specific card object permanently, meaning points do not reset when the creature leaves play or changes controllers. When your opponent returned it from exile, the movement rule simply resolved its location change without erasing the historical damage marker because both functions operate as part of the same simultaneous state-based action checking process. Since these checks occur together whenever a player would receive priority, neither rule takes precedence in timing, but they dictate separate aspects that work in tandem to preserve the damage total while permitting zone changes. The concrete final outcome is that you will lose the game exactly when that one commander reaches 21 cumulative combat damage, as the prior points remain locked to the card regardless of its sacrifice and return to the battlefield.
Can I play a card that makes things exile instead of die even if nothing is currently being destroyed?

Yes, you can. There are no special restrictions on casting a spell or activating an ability that generates a replacement effect. Such effects last until they are used up or their duration has expired. For example, if you cast a spell that says any creature destroyed this turn is exiled instead, that effect will stay active and wait for a creature to be destroyed, even if no creatures are in danger at the moment you cast it.
I am new to this format, how do we actually pick our cards during the draft?

In a Conspiracy draft, each player opens a booster pack, drafts one card by placing that card in a face-down pile in front of them, and then passes the remaining cards to the next player. This procedure continues until all cards in that draft round have been drafted. For example, if you are playing the first round, you would put your first card face-down in a pile and pass the rest of the pack to the person on your left, then repeat this process with the next pack passed to you.
I have Maelstrom Wanderer on the battlefield and I'm trying to trigger its ability by suspending Lightning Storm from my hand, but the counters aren't going up. Is this supposed to count as a crime?

No, suspending a card does not commit a crime. To determine the outcome, we first look at what action you are taking and how it is classified. The rules define special actions that are distinct from casting spells or activating abilities; specifically, exiling a card with suspend is a special action available when you have priority, allowing you to put the card into exile with time counters rather than casting it as a spell. Because this is a special action, you are not casting a spell nor activating an ability to put on the stack. Next, we check the definition of committing a crime. A player commits a crime only when they cast a spell, activate an ability, or put a triggered ability on the stack, and that spell or ability targets at least one opponent, a permanent they control, or a card in their graveyard. The rule regarding special actions takes precedence here because it classifies your action as something other than casting or activating, which immediately fails the criteria for crimes. Since suspending is neither casting a spell nor activating an ability targeting an opponent's resources, you do not meet the requirements to commit a crime. The concrete final outcome is that Maelstrom Wanderer does not receive a +1/+1 counter from your action of suspending Lightning Storm.

I just cast a spell dealing three damage to a two toughness creature while I control an enchantment that exiles permanents destroyed this way, and my opponent argues it goes to the graveyard first before the game checks if the damage was enough. What actually happens here?

The replacement effect takes immediate priority during event modification rather than waiting for any automatic evaluations. If an event is replaced, it never happens, and a modified event occurs instead, which may in turn trigger other abilities as written. After that modified sequence finishes, state-based actions are checked throughout the game and are not controlled by any player, meaning the system automatically scans the battlefield continuously to see if permanents meet fatal criteria like having damage equal to or greater than toughness. Because the modification rule steps in first, the continuous evaluation routine runs afterward on the updated board and simply sees a permanent without lethal damage remaining in play. Concrete final game outcome: Your creature is permanently moved to exile rather than dying, no death triggers activate from that spell, and the automatic evaluation system processes the new board state normally with that card safely removed from play.
What happens if a card tells me to put a sorcery from my hand onto the battlefield?

The sorcery will stay in your hand. When the effect attempts to move the card, the game sees that sorceries can't enter the battlefield, so if a sorcery would enter the battlefield, it remains in its previous zone instead. For example, if an ability says put target sorcery from your hand onto the battlefield, the sorcery stays in your hand.

I cast Krenko's Command to generate a bunch of Goblin Token creatures, but my opponent controls Gonti's Machete, which says if a creature would enter the battlefield, it enters tapped and attacking instead. I tried tapping my lands for mana in response to the spell going on stack, arguing that since tapping is a special action you get priority back, I could somehow interrupt the token creation or apply effects differently, but everyone got confused about whether tapping lets me respond to the Machete effect. What actually happens with the tokens and does my land-tapping give me any window to stop the replacement?

The Goblin Tokens will enter the battlefield tapped and attacking controlled by your opponent. Replacement effects like Gonti's Machete apply continuously and do not use the stack, so there is no window where you can respond or interrupt them once the effect creating tokens resolves. The rule regarding replacement effects states that these effects apply if an effect would create one or more tokens, and they also apply even if triggered by another replacement, meaning they happen automatically as part of the game state without using priority or the stack. While it is true that taking a special action like tapping a land for mana means you receive priority afterward, allowing you to cast instants or activate abilities immediately after paying mana costs, this priority window cannot be used to respond to replacement effects because replacements are not events on the stack that require timing; they simply replace the event entirely. Since Gonti's Machete replaces the token creation event before it happens in any meaningful sense for interaction, your special action of tapping lands only gives you priority to act around the spell resolution, but it does not prevent the replacement from modifying how the tokens enter.
My creature just died. This card has Recover on it, so can I use that to bring it back to my hand?

Yes, you can. The ability triggers when a creature is put into your graveyard from the battlefield. If you choose to pay the specified cost, you return the card from your graveyard to your hand. For example, if you have a creature with Recover 2 and it is destroyed, you can pay 2 mana to move that card from your graveyard back into your hand.

My library is empty and there's a permanent on the battlefield that says players can't draw cards. I attack with two creatures, and each has an ability that triggers when it attacks and reads 'You may draw a card.' When these abilities resolve, am I allowed to choose to draw from both of them even though my deck is empty?

Both triggered abilities go onto the stack as separate objects in the order you choose, following the standard process for multiple triggered abilities. As each ability resolves, it offers you a choice to draw cards. Although having no cards in your library would normally allow you to choose to draw even if the action is optional, the presence of an effect that prevents drawing cards changes this permission. The rules state that while an empty library does not stop a player from choosing to draw, a restriction that says a player cannot draw cards overrides that ability and blocks the choice entirely. Consequently, when each triggered ability resolves, you are prohibited from choosing to draw due to the continuous effect, so neither ability results in you gaining any cards and your library remains empty.
Can I target my creature with an Elf spell if it says Creature — Elf Warrior?

Yes, you can. A creature can have multiple subtypes, which are listed after the long dash. Because your card is a Creature — Elf Warrior, it counts as both an Elf and a Warrior. For example, if you cast a spell that targets an Elf, your Elf Warrior is a valid target because it has the Elf subtype.

I'm casting a spell that says I sacrifice a creature and my opponent sacrifices a creature at the exact same time as part of the cost. My opponent keeps hesitating, saying we should just do it together or let them go first so they can react to what I pick. Can I force him to wait until after I have sacrificed? What's the actual ruling?

No, you cannot wait for your opponent, and your opponent definitely cannot go first. When a spell requires both you and an opponent to take actions simultaneously while it is being cast, the rules explicitly state that the controller of the spell must act first. This is a specific exception to normal timing order. So, you must choose which creature you are sacrificing and move it to your graveyard before your opponent chooses theirs. Even though sacrificing a permanent is a special action that normally gives you priority afterward, this simultaneous casting exception dictates the sequence during the cast and prevents any priority window from opening between your actions. Once both sacrifices are completed as part of the casting process, the spell proceeds normally. The outcome is that you sacrifice your creature first, then your opponent sacrifices theirs.

I just brought in my second legendary commander through the partner ability, and now both are on the battlefield. My opponent has two creatures blocking them. Both of my commanders have regular damage and lifelink. Do I gain life for both attacks combined, or do they work separately? Also, how does the opponent track if either of them deals enough damage to make them lose the game?

When both of your partner commanders attack and are blocked, combat damage is dealt simultaneously to those creatures. The damage results framework establishes the initial values first by stating that damage dealt by a source with lifelink causes that sources controller to gain that much life, while unblocked or assigned damage to players causes them to lose life equal to the amount dealt. Because lifelink ties directly to the specific damage event, you will gain life separately for each commander based on exactly how many points of damage each one assigns. The partner pairing rules then take precedence for all long-term tracking and loss conditions, explicitly stating that except for determining color identity, the two commanders function independently and when determining whether a player has been dealt 21 or more combat damage by the same commander, you consider damage from each of your two commanders separately. The concrete final game outcome is that you gain life individually for each creature as it deals damage, and your opponent must maintain two completely separate damage ledgers. If one commander marks twenty-one damage and the other only marks twelve, only the first causes your opponent to lose the game right away, and neither value bleeds into the other's tracker.

I just attacked my opponent with a huge creature that deals lethal damage, leaving them at zero life. They have a card on the battlefield that says 'When you lose the game, draw three cards.' Do I win right away before they can use that ability, or does their trigger go on the stack?

You do not win instantly, and your opponent gets to put their trigger on the stack. The interaction is governed by the order of operations for state-based actions versus triggered abilities. Whenever a player would get priority, which occurs after your attack resolves, the game checks for state-based actions and performs all applicable ones simultaneously as a single event. In this case, the conditions include zero life or lethal damage, so the game performs these state-based actions to cause your opponent to lose the game. Only after all state-based actions are finished does the game check again and put triggered abilities onto the stack. Since triggered abilities trigger specifically when a player loses the game regardless of the reason, your opponent's ability triggers as a result of losing via state-based actions. The concrete outcome is that state-based actions resolve first to cause the loss, then your opponent's draw trigger is placed on the stack for you both to respond to before the game eventually ends.
I just played a Forest, but it doesn't say anywhere that I can use it to pay for spells. Can I still tap it for green mana?

Yes, you can. Any object with the land card type and a basic land type has the intrinsic ability to tap for its corresponding mana symbol even if the text box does not actually contain that text. For example, since Forest is one of the five basic land types, your Forest automatically lets you tap it to add {G} to your mana pool.
My opponent attacks with a creature that has flanking, and I block it with my normal creature. What happens to my creature?

When you block the creature, your creature will get -1/-1 until end of turn because flanking triggers whenever this creature becomes blocked by a creature without flanking. For example, if an opponent attacks with a 2/2 creature with flanking and you block it with a 2/2 creature that does not have flanking, your creature will become a 1/1 for the rest of the turn.

I used a cloning spell to copy an equipment on my battlefield that has the Living weapon ability. The copy appeared in play, but it didn't create a germ token or attach itself like the original does when cast. Did something go wrong?

When you use a cloning spell to copy an Equipment with Living Weapon, the copy enters the battlefield as a new permanent that copies all characteristics of the original, including the printed ability. Because it is a new permanent entering the battlefield, its "Living weapon" triggered ability will fire normally. The game resolves by creating a 0/0 black Phyrexian Germ creature token and attaching the Equipment to it. If you did not receive the token, check for other effects on the battlefield that might have prevented triggers (like abilities that stop creatures or permanents from entering or triggering), as the clone itself will always attempt to trigger Living weapon upon entry.
What happens when I use an effect to exile a card that is already in the exile zone?

The card remains in the exile zone, but the game treats it as a brand new object that has just been exiled. This happens because even though the object does not change zones, it becomes a new object that has just been exiled. For example, if you use an effect to exile a creature that is already in exile, the game sees it as a fresh instance of being exiled.
I am casting a big spell and realize I am one mana short. Can I tap my lands for more mana right in the middle of casting it, or do I have to wait until the spell is finished?

Yes, you can. You are allowed to activate an activated mana ability whenever you are casting a spell. For example, if you are casting a creature that costs five mana and you only have four mana available, you can tap a land to provide that final mana needed before you finish casting the spell.

I just realized my commander deck only has white mana sources, but during a game someone put one of my black lands onto the battlefield using a cross-color tutor effect. Now that land is tapping for black and moving to exile after we're done with it. Can I keep playing it like this since it's in different zones now?

Deck construction restrictions only apply when verifying deck validity before a game starts. They do not trigger or recheck when cards move between zones during play. Because zones are defined as places where objects exist during a match, and the rules do not state that legality resets upon zone changes, the black land remains fully legal on your battlefield and in exile for the rest of the current game. It would only need to be removed from your deck list before starting future matches.
What happens if a spell turns my Commander face down while it's still in the command zone?

When a face-up object in the command zone is turned face down, it becomes a new object. This means the original card is replaced by the face-down version and is no longer considered the same thing. For example, if your commander is a creature named Solitude and an effect turns it face down in the command zone, that object is no longer Solitude; it is a brand new face-down object.

I'm mid-game in Commander and my opponent swings their legendary commander at me for what would be lethal combat damage on my blocking creature. I have an enchantment that says instead of this creature being dealt combat damage, its controller gains life equal to the damage. Does my blocker still die when the game checks for dead creatures, and does this swing count toward the twenty-one commander damage rule if they did it three times earlier?

First, some replacement effects apply to damage from a source, which means your enchantment modifies the combat damage event before anything else happens. Because that damage is fully replaced with life gain, the creature never actually takes damage. After this modification completes, the game moves to state-based actions for variant formats. The rules specify that in a Commander game, a player who has been dealt 21 or more combat damage by the same commander over the course of the game loses the game. Since your enchantment prevented any actual damage from landing, those swings do not count toward that threshold. Replacement effects always apply during the damage event, while state-based action checks happen immediately afterward. The concrete final outcome is that your blocker remains on the battlefield alive, you gain life instead, and you do not lose the game from the commander damage rule because zero damage was dealt to you or your creatures.

We're playing multiplayer and I just picked Bob to be the defender at the start of combat like my card allows. My opponent says 'But you didn't choose Bob to be attacking yet, so he isn't really defending, your trigger won't work.' Is he right? Also, can I choose Bob if he's already the defender from a previous turn?

The card combines a static ability linked to triggered abilities into one paragraph, meaning the game treats the trigger condition as permanently connected to the text block and ready to monitor for the specified event. During multiplayer combat, the rules state that during the beginning of combat step, the attacking player chooses one opponent as the defending player via a turn-based action, and that chosen player becomes the defending player immediately upon selection. When you choose Bob in the beginning of combat, he transitions from not being the defending player to being the defending player at that moment. Because the card's triggered ability is linked to this state change, the condition of him becoming the defending player is satisfied instantly upon your choice. Your opponent is incorrect; the rule requires a choice during the beginning of combat, and that choice establishes the defending role before any attackers are declared. Regarding re-choosing Bob: if he already holds the defending status when you choose him again, he does not become the defending player because he already is, so the trigger condition requiring a change or new occurrence of becoming is not met. The outcome is that if Bob was not defending prior to your choice in the beginning of combat, the linked effect resolves and produces the result associated with his becoming the defender; if he was already defending, no result occurs due to lack of role change. The static-triggered linkage ensures the rules engine correctly identifies and responds to this specific transition defined by the turn-based action.
What happens if we start a Commander match with only 20 life each?

You should adjust your life totals mid-game because in a Commander game, each player's starting life total is 40. For example, if you and your opponent realize you both mistakenly started with 20, you should immediately update your life counts to 40 each to follow the correct format rules.

I'm attacking with my creature, but my opponent controls an artifact that says "If this permanent would be dealt damage, exile it instead." We keep arguing over whether my creature actually deals damage or not, and if a card in my hand that lets me choose a source of damage to draw a card for each instance can still target my attacker after the hit. What's the actual ruling here?

When your creature attempts to deal combat damage, replacement effects evaluate first. According to tournament guidelines, if an event is replaced, it never happens and a modified event occurs instead, which may in turn trigger abilities. This means your creature's damage transaction is completely overwritten by the exiling effect. Because the original damage event was successfully replaced and never occurred, no actual damage resolves. Even though the damage event did not happen, the object that would have dealt it remains legally recognized as the source of that hypothetical damage, following the principle that the source of damage is the object that dealt it and if an effect requires a player to choose a source of damage, they may choose a permanent or a spell on the stack regardless of later changes. The replacement rule takes precedence by modifying the event before anything else checks for triggers or state-based actions. In the end, the artifact is exiled immediately, your creature stays on the battlefield, and you may still legally choose your attacking creature as a damage source to satisfy your hand effect because replacement effects alter the outcome but do not erase the logical origin of the event.
Can I attack the player sitting two seats over on my left if we are using the attack left rule?

No, you cannot. If the attack left option is used, a player can only attack an opponent seated immediately to their left. If your nearest opponent to the left is more than one seat away, you cannot attack them. For example, in a four-player game where the person sitting directly to your left has already been knocked out of the game, you would be unable to attack the player who is two seats away from you.
Can I use my equipment to attach it to a creature during my opponent's turn if I have mana available?

No, you cannot. The equip ability is an activated ability that can only be activated as a sorcery. This means you can only use it during your own main phases when the stack is empty. For example, if you have a Sword artifact and want to attach it to a creature, you must wait until your turn to do so, even if you have plenty of mana available while your opponent is attacking.

I keep hearing players say that when you switch power and toughness, it just grabs whatever numbers are on the card at that exact moment and flips them, regardless of whether those numbers came from earlier modifiers or if a characteristic-changing effect like Devoid happens afterward. Is that true, and how does layering actually override this intuition?

That intuition is incorrect because the game calculates a creature's power and toughness in a strict order before a switch occurs. Characteristic-defining abilities that define power or toughness apply first, followed by effects that set those values, and finally modifiers and counters. Switches do not grab current printed numbers; instead, a later switching effect takes the values calculated up to that point (like a 1/4 after a +0/+1 modifier) and swaps them, making it a 4/1. Switches ignore later characteristic effects or printed text because they operate on the math already finalized by earlier sublayers.

I have a creature enchanted by a blue Aura that gives it +2/+2 and flying. My opponent has another aura that gives it -1/-1. I want to activate the aura swap ability on my blue aura using mana from my hand, but I'm not sure what happens to my creature's stats and abilities once the swap resolves. Does the new aura just replace the old one instantly, or do the buffs stack weirdly?

When you activate the aura swap ability, you are attempting to exchange this permanent with an Aura card in your hand. This activated ability resolves as a discrete game action first, checking whether you control both the battlefield permanent and the hand card, because if either half of the exchange can't be completed, the ability has no effect. If both conditions are met, the old Aura moves to your hand and the new one attaches to your creature. Immediately after this swap completes, the timestamp system takes precedence for calculating continuous effects. Because an Aura receives a new timestamp each time it becomes attached to an object or player, the newly swapped-in Aura's static ability is queued later than any existing modifiers on that creature. In the layer system, effects are applied in timestamp order, meaning earlier timestamps apply before later ones. The concrete final outcome is that your swap resolves successfully, your creature ends up enchanted by the new Aura, and its power and toughness are modified with all older effects calculated first and the fresh timestamp of the new Aura applying last.
What happens if an enchantment becomes a creature? Does it stop being an enchantment?

No, it does not lose its enchantment status. When an effect states that an object becomes an artifact creature, those effects also allow the object to retain all of its prior card types and subtypes. For example, if an effect turns an enchantment like Sanctum Weaver into a creature, it will be an enchantment creature and keep its enchantment type.

I just cast a spell with replicate three times so it hits my opponent's board, and I'm wondering where the copies go after they finish resolving. Do they pile up in the graveyard like regular spells? My friend says they disappear completely. What actually happens?

When you cast a spell with replicate and pay the extra cost multiple times, the game uses the rule that when you cast this spell, if a replicate cost was paid for it, copy it for each time its replicate cost was paid, and you may choose new targets for any of those copies.
