These copies travel down the stack alongside your original spell. Once they resolve and attempt to move into the graveyard or another zone, state-based actions are immediately checked. The rule explicitly states that if a copy of a spell is in a zone other than the stack, it ceases to exist. Because the copies leave the stack upon resolution, they never actually enter the graveyard as cards; they simply vanish from the game right after producing their effect. The final outcome is that the three copies resolve completely, apply their chosen effects to your opponent's board, and then immediately cease to exist off the stack before state-based actions can register them in any other zone.
What happens when I use the eternalize ability on a card in my graveyard?

You exile the card from your graveyard and create a token that is a copy of that card, except it is black, it is a 4/4, it has no mana cost, and it is a Zombie in addition to its other types. For example, if you use eternalize on a blue creature, you will get a 4/4 black Zombie token that acts as a copy of the original card.
What happens when I give a creature flying with one spell, and then another player plays a card that says all creatures have no abilities?

The creature will still have flying. Effects that add or remove abilities do not change the actual text of the objects they affect. Since the flying was added by an effect and was not part of the original printed text, any effect that changes the text of a creature cannot modify that granted ability. For example, if you use an enchantment to give a 1/1 Bird flying, and then a player plays a card like Humility which changes all creatures' text to have no abilities, the Bird will still keep its flying because the flying was an added ability and not part of the card's permanent text.

I just cast a spell that creates two token creatures, and my opponent controls an effect that says to double the number of tokens created. They also control another effect that says those doubled tokens enter tapped. My opponent claims only one replacement should apply, and argues we can respond immediately after the first token enters. Is that right?

Your opponent is incorrect about both points. First, the comprehensive rules explicitly state that replacement effects apply if an effect would create one or more tokens, and they also apply if another replacement effect does so, which allows your two doubling and tapping effects to chain together seamlessly during resolution. Because of this chaining mechanic, all four tokens will enter the battlefield tapped as a single simultaneous event. Second, the rules dictate that state-based actions are checked whenever a player would get priority, not during resolution. The game performs all applicable state-based actions simultaneously as a single event, repeats the check until none apply, and only then puts waiting triggered abilities on the stack before passing priority. As a result, all four tapped tokens arrive at once, any creatures meeting criteria for immediate death are put into graveyards simultaneously, your triggers wait to go on the stack, and only then does your opponent actually get a chance to respond.
What happens when I want to move to combat, but my opponent responds to my last spell with an instant?

The phase continues because a main phase ends only when all players pass in succession while the stack is empty. If your opponent casts an instant, the stack is not empty, so you remain in the main phase. For example, if you cast a creature and your opponent casts a counterspell, you cannot move to combat until that counterspell resolves and everyone passes priority while nothing remains on the stack.

My opponent just swung with his legendary dragon and it connected for exactly twenty-one damage total over the course of this game. He says he lost right that second, but I still have priority to cast something. Is he out of the game immediately?

The player taking the damage does not leave the game immediately because of how the timing system works in Magic. The specific rule for commander damage states that a player who has been dealt 21 or more combat damage by the same commander over the course of the game loses the game, and this is strictly categorized as a state-based action. However, state-based actions do not happen instantly when damage is dealt. Instead, the general process rule explains that whenever a player would get priority, the game checks for condition triggers first before performing all applicable state-based actions simultaneously as a single event. Because you still have priority after combat damage resolves, that evaluation window has not closed yet. You can absolutely cast your instant spell now. Once you pass priority to your opponent and they pass back, the game will check the conditions again. At that point, the commander damage condition will be met, and your opponent will lose the game. The concrete final outcome is that your opponent survives the exact moment of impact due to the priority window, but will definitely lose once priority cycles back around and state-based actions are evaluated.

I'm mid-battle and my opponent just played a card that says the next spell I cast costs one extra mana. I already had a creature spell on the stack from my last turn, but I just tapped lands to try and pay for it now. Does the extra mana cost apply to that spell sitting on the stack, or does it only hurt my future plays?

The extra mana cost does not apply to the spell already waiting on the stack. First, the timing of when actions enter play dictates everything: casting a spell that alters costs won’t affect spells and abilities that are already on the stack, so your creature spell locked in its price before their modification took effect. Next, you simply follow the core resource rule that players spend mana to pay costs when casting spells and activating abilities. Because your spell was already placed into play on the stack, you will tap lands to pay exactly its original printed cost. The increased price strictly applies forward, meaning you will only pay the extra mana for any new cards you cast after their card resolves.
What happens to my cards and the plane if I leave the game?

When you leave the game, all objects you own leave the game, except for abilities from phenomena. If this process includes a face-up plane card leaving the game, the planar controller turns the top card of their planar deck face up. For example, if a player leaves the game and the plane they were using leaves with them, the current planar controller will immediately flip the top card of their planar deck face up to become the new plane.

I just cast a creature with two abilities printed on it and my playgroup is arguing about how they resolve when multiple attackers hit simultaneously. The first ability is a replacement effect that exiles up to target creature when this permanent deals combat damage. The second is a triggered ability that reads whenever another creature deals combat damage to this permanent, you may cast spells from among the cards exiled with it. My opponent attacks me with three different creatures at once, one hits my blocked creature while the other two hit me directly, and I used the first ability to exile a card from each attacker. Does the second ability count all the damage together as one big trigger, or does it split them up? Can I use the exile cards now?

The concrete final outcome is that your triggered ability will fire exactly once per attacking creature rather than combining into a single trigger, each trigger will calculate its effect using only that individual attacker's damage amount, and you may absolutely use the exiled cards for those triggers. The specific damage tracking rule applies first to establish precedence by isolating simultaneous combat events, ensuring the game does not pool damage from different sources. The rules state that if an ability triggers on damage being dealt by a specific source or sources and the effect refers to the damage dealt, it refers only to the damage dealt by those specified sources and not to any damage dealt at the same time by other sources. This means each attacker processes its own separate trigger event with its own independent damage count. After the damage rule isolates the individual hits, the linked abilities rule takes over to govern resource access. Game rules specify that an object may have one ability printed on it that generates a replacement effect which causes one or more cards to be exiled, and another ability that refers either to the exiled cards or to cards exiled with this object, and these abilities are strictly linked so the second refers only to cards put there by the first on this exact permanent. They cannot link to any other ability regardless of what other objects have. Because your exile cards were all placed by this commander's first ability, they remain correctly tracked together for use across all three independent triggers. You will get three separate chances to cast from the linked exile zone, each tied to one specific attacker's damage.
What happens if I want to use a spell right as we start declaring attackers? Does my opponent get to jump in before me?

You get the first opportunity to act. When the game moves into the Declare Attackers step, the active player gets priority. This means you can cast spells or activate abilities before your opponent can respond. For example, if you want to use a spell that gives your creatures protection from black right as you are about to attack, you can do that before your opponent uses a removal spell.

I'm playing Commander with three other people and I want to tap five creatures to attack, sending two at my friend Alice and three at Bob. Bob has one blocker ready. Does the damage from the creatures attacking Alice somehow spill over and help kill Bob's blocker? Also, if all the damage Bob takes leaves him with zero life, can I cast 'Heroic Intervention' on him in response before he dies?

The default Commander rules allow a free-for-all game where players can attack multiple opponents simultaneously, so you are permitted to split your attackers between Alice and Bob. However, damage assignment follows specific combat rules where creatures attacking one player only deal damage to that player or creatures blocking them, meaning the two creatures assigned to Alice cannot deal damage to Bob's blocker; only the three creatures attacking Bob will damage his blocker and Bob himself. Regarding Bob's life total, if the combat damage brings him to zero life or less, state-based actions trigger automatically and instantly remove him from the game without using the stack. State-based actions occur before any player receives priority to play spells, so you cannot cast 'Heroic Intervention' in response to his death; the concrete outcome is that Bob's attacker deals damage only to Bob and his blocker, Alice's attackers deal damage only to Alice or her blockers, and if Bob reaches zero life from the damage he sustains, he dies immediately before any instants can be played.
What happens if an ability tells me to move counters from a creature to a land, but that creature gets destroyed before the ability actually resolves?

The ability still works. Since the object with the counters left the battlefield, you do not move counters from one object to the other; instead, you put the same number of each kind of counter the first object had onto the second object. For example, if a triggered ability says to move all +1/+1 counters from a creature to a land, and that creature is destroyed in response, you simply put the same number of +1/+1 counters that were on the creature onto the land.

We're playing a two-team multiplayer game with shared team turns. My teammate and I control a legendary creature that literally has no mana cost. We want to cast it from exile using an effect that lets us cast it without paying its mana cost, but we're not sure if we can do it during our turn since my teammate is currently the one taking actions for our group. Can we cast it, and who exactly gets to make the call?

Under shared team turns, teams rather than individual players have priority, so only the designated acting player makes decisions for your entire squad while teammates wait in line. This team-based priority framework establishes the active window first, after which you must evaluate whether the spell can legally be cast using the cost rules. As the rules state, some objects have no mana cost, which represents an unpayable cost. Attempting to cast a spell with such a cost is completely legal, but attempting to pay any mana for it would be illegal unless another effect applies an alternative cost. Your exile replacement effect supplies that necessary alternative cost, which overrides the default unpayable restriction. The concrete final outcome is that your designated acting teammate may successfully cast the legendary creature from exile during the team turn, it enters the battlefield normally, and neither participant can assign generic or colored mana to it unless a separate rule change modifies how the cost is paid.
Can I use a ninja with ninjutsu and still keep the creature that was attacking?

No, you cannot keep the creature because returning an unblocked attacking creature to its owner's hand is a required part of the cost. To activate the ability, you must pay the cost, reveal the card from your hand, and return an unblocked attacking creature you control to its owner's hand to put the ninjutsu card onto the battlefield tapped and attacking. For example, if you attack with a Goblin token and use a Ninja with ninjutsu, the Goblin goes back to your hand while the Ninja enters the battlefield tapped and attacking.
My friend and I are playing Two-Headed Giant and I play a card that gives me an extra turn. What happens next?

Your entire team takes the extra turn. The rules state that if an effect gives a player an extra turn, that player's team takes the extra turn. This means you and your teammate will act together during this additional time. For example, if you play Time Warp in Two-Headed Giant, your team receives one extra turn to play lands and cast spells.
I am attacking my opponent, but they have 10 life while another player at the table has 20 life. What happens with my Dethrone ability?

Nothing happens with the ability in this scenario. Dethrone triggers whenever the creature attacks the player with the most life or tied for most life. Because the player you are attacking has less life than another player, the condition is not met. For example, if Player A has 20 life and Player B has 10 life, attacking Player B will not result in a +1/+1 counter being placed on your creature.

I just got my commander out and want to grab a specific card from my sideboard during my main phase when nobody is doing anything. Can I just pull it out right then? What happens if someone tries to interrupt it with a counterspell or something?

You cannot simply pull a card from outside the game into your Commander deck or hand. Rule 903.11 explicitly states that cards from outside the game cannot be brought into Commander except through specific rules, special actions, or effects that call for it. Even if a rule or effect permits it, you must still follow the restrictions in Rule 903.11a, which forbid bringing in cards that match names in your starting deck or commander, or share color identity with your commander. Since pulling from outside the game is not a default special action you can initiate at will, and no specific rule or effect allows it here, the move is illegal. The question of stack interaction is moot because the action itself cannot be legally performed.
What happens if one of my friends loses in a four-player match? Does everyone just stop playing?

The rest of the players continue playing. When a player loses the game, that player leaves the game, but the multiplayer rules handle what happens to the others. For example, if Alice, Bob, Charlie, and Dave are playing and Alice loses, she leaves the game while Bob, Charlie, and Dave keep playing to find a winner.

I'm casting Lightning Helix targeting my opponent's player. My opponent has a Spell Queller with an activated ability that can bounce instant spells from the stack. When I tap my Mountain to activate its mana ability and generate red mana to pay the cost, can my opponent use their Queller now to bounce Helix while I'm still paying? They keep arguing that they get priority every time I perform an action related to paying.

No, your opponent cannot respond at this moment because you are in the process of paying costs and activating mana abilities, which is not a point where priority is given to opponents. The rule concerning mana payments clarifies that if a cost includes a mana payment, the player paying the cost has a chance to activate mana abilities, which means you complete all necessary steps to generate the required mana as part of casting without interruption. Once you have finished paying the cost including any activated mana abilities, Lightning Helix is then placed onto the stack and your opponent receives priority. The rule for resolution states that if all players pass in succession without taking any actions, the spell on top of the stack resolves or the phase ends. Since your opponent has not acted yet, they must wait until after Helix is on the stack to use their Queller. If neither you nor your opponent takes further action and both pass priority in succession, Lightning Helix will resolve dealing three damage to your opponent's player, and your opponent will be unable to bounce it because it has already resolved and gone to the graveyard.

I attacked with two creatures dealing three damage each, and my opponent had two 2/2s in play. One of the 2/2s has an enchantment that says if it would die, exile it instead of putting it into the graveyard. The other creature has the ability when this dies, draw a card. What actually happens here?

When combat damage is dealt, the game reaches a point where players would normally get priority, triggering a state-based action check. At this moment, the game performs all applicable state-based actions simultaneously as a single event rather than resolving them one by one. Because both 2/2s have lethal damage, they are evaluated together for death. For the enchanted creature, a replacement effect applies before that specific death event occurs. If an event is replaced, it never happens and a modified event occurs instead, so the creature is exiled and never actually dies in the game state. The other creature successfully dies and its ability triggers. After this unified simultaneous check finishes, all triggered abilities from those permanents are placed on the stack together. You only receive priority after every state-based action has been performed and all related triggers have been queued up. The concrete final outcome is that the enchanted creature goes to exile without triggering anything, the other creature dies normally and its trigger goes on the stack, and you get priority only once this entire sequence is complete.

We are playing a casual game and I just played Centaur of Attention, so its enter-the-battlefield ability put four dice values on it. Midway through the match I cast a sorcery that says At the beginning of your next end step, draw cards equal to half the sum of all stored results on target creature. Before that end step arrives, I use an effect to reroll two of those dice to higher numbers. Do I draw based on the original four rolls or the updated ones?

You will draw cards based on your newly rerolled dice rather than the original set. When you cast the sorcery, it creates a delayed triggered ability that waits until the beginning of your next end step to resolve. The rules for these abilities make it clear that an effect like this refers to a particular object and still affects it even if the object changes characteristics later in the game state. At the same time, when you actively reroll dice before that step arrives, the results you rerolled stop being stored results and you store the results of each new die roll on that permanent instead. The rerolling mechanic applies first to update the board state during your turn, and then the delayed trigger resolves at the end step evaluating that fresh information. Because the check happens after your reroll action completes, you will draw based on the updated totals when the spell finally goes off.
What happens if I pay the impending cost instead of the normal mana cost?

When you choose to pay the impending cost, the permanent enters the battlefield with time counters on it. As long as that permanent has a time counter on it and the impending cost was paid, it is not a creature. For example, if you play a spell with Impending 3 for its alternative cost, it will enter as a non-creature artifact or enchantment, and you must wait for those time counters to be removed before it becomes a creature.
Can I use an enchantment that says enchant creature to target my opponent's artifact?

No, you cannot. The enchant ability restricts what an Aura spell can target and what an Aura can enchant. Because the card specifically says enchant creature, it is limited to only targeting creatures. For example, if you have an Aura that enchants a creature, you would not be able to attach it to an opponent's Sol Ring because a Sol Ring is an artifact, not a creature.
What happens if I flip over a new plane card from my deck during the game?

When you move the top card of your planar deck off and turn it face up, you have planeswalked. This action causes any continuous effects that were set to last until a player planeswalks to end. For example, if you have an enchantment that provides +1/+1 to all creatures until you planeswalk, that enchantment's effect will stop working the moment you reveal your new plane card.
My card says I clash with my opponent. We both show our top cards at once, but how do we decide where they go?

When you clash with an opponent, you and that opponent each clash. Both players reveal the top card of their library at the same time. Then, in APNAP order, you both decide where to put those cards. This means the active player decides first, then the non-active player decides, and finally, the cards move to their chosen locations at the same time. For example, if it is your turn and you clash with an opponent, you will choose where to put your card first, then your opponent will choose for theirs, and then both cards are moved simultaneously.
What happens when I roll a 5 and the number 5 is lit up on my Attraction?

When you roll a 5 that matches a lit-up number, the visit ability triggers. If the card says to claim the prize, you then carry out the actions listed after the long dash because that text is part of its visit ability. For example, if you roll a 5 on an Attraction where 5 is lit up, and it says 'Claim the prize' followed by 'Prize — Draw a card', you will draw a card as part of that visit.
What happens if I use a spell that doubles my creature's power and toughness when it is already a 3/2?

If you use an effect that doubles a creature's power and toughness, the creature gets +X/+Y, where X is its current power and Y is its current toughness. This means it does not just set its stats to a specific number but adds the current values as modifiers. For example, if your 3/2 creature is targeted by an effect that doubles both, it will get +3/+2 and become a 6/4.
What happens if I make a token? Since it isn't a real card, does it even have anything else?

When you create a token, it functions as an object that isn't a card, but it has some of the parts of a card because those parts are also characteristics. For example, if you cast a spell to create a 2/2 Goblin token, the token enters the battlefield not as a card, but with the characteristics of 2 power and 2 toughness so it can attack and block.
I have a split card in my graveyard with Aftermath on one half. Can I still cast that part of the card?

Yes, you can. The Aftermath ability means you may cast this half of this split card from your graveyard. However, keep in mind that this half of this split card can't be cast from any zone other than a graveyard. For example, if you have an Aftermath-half split card in your graveyard, you can pay its mana cost to cast it directly from there.
I just cast an artifact, but it is still sitting there on the stack. What happens next?

Once the spell finishes resolving, its controller puts it onto the battlefield under their control. For example, if you cast a Sol Ring, once that spell resolves, you place the Sol Ring directly onto the battlefield and you are the one who controls it.
If my creature has an ability that prevents 1 damage and my opponent casts a spell that deals 2 damage to every creature, does my creature only take 1 damage?

Yes, your creature will only take 1 damage. The prevention effect refers to a specific amount of damage from a source, so it applies to the damage event caused by the spell. For example, if you have Daunting Defender and your opponent casts Pyroclasm which deals 2 damage to each creature, the Daunting Defender ability prevents 1 of that damage, meaning only 1 damage is actually dealt to your Cleric.

I just cast a spell with demonstrate on my turn and chose an opponent to copy it, so now there are two copies of the spell waiting on top of each other to resolve. Both copies deal damage that would put two of their creatures in the graveyard at the exact same time, and one of those creatures has a death trigger. Do I get to respond to that death trigger before the second copy resolves?

When you cast a spell with demonstrate, the mechanic means when you cast this spell, you may copy it and you may choose new targets for the copy, then an opponent copies the spell and may choose new targets for that copy. Your first copy resolves and deals damage, but before anyone gets priority to respond or pass, the game performs a mandatory check. The priority framework dictates that whenever a player would get priority, the game checks for applicable state-based actions, then performs all applicable state-based actions simultaneously as a single event. Because both creatures take lethal damage at once, they are both put into their graveyards during that one simultaneous check. Only after those checks complete does the game allow waiting triggered abilities to be put on the stack. You then get priority to respond to the death trigger. The concrete final outcome is that both creatures die together from a single simultaneous state-based action event, the death trigger is queued after that event, and you receive priority only once all triggers are stacked and no further checks are needed.
Does the rule for how creatures block change when using the shared turn option in Two-Headed Giant?

No, it does not change. The Two-Headed Giant variant uses the combat rules for the shared team turns option, meaning you follow the standard rules for how creatures interact during combat. For example, if you attack with a creature, your opponent still follows the regular rules to decide if they will block it with one or more of their own creatures.

We are mid-combat and I just cast a spell that makes each player draw three cards. Right as it resolves, my two blockers go to the graveyard from lethal damage at the exact same time my opponent's attacker also dies. The judge is confused about what triggers when and how many cards actually get drawn. What is the correct sequence?

The resolution follows a strict sequence that separates card drawing from battlefield state checks. First, the rule for drawing states that cards may only be drawn one at a time, and any replacement effects modify the total number before considering any of the individual card draws. In this scenario, all players finish their individual draws in turn order without pausing the spell resolution. Only after the spell fully resolves does the game check for state-based actions. At that moment, the rule about simultaneous permanent removal applies: if a state-based action results in a permanent leaving the battlefield at the same time other state-based actions were performed, that permanent’s last known information is derived from the game state before any of those state-based actions were performed. This means the timing of the draws does not affect how the dying creatures are evaluated. The concrete final outcome is that every player successfully draws their three cards in sequence, followed by all three creatures being placed into graveyards with their death triggers resolving using their exact stats and counters from right before those simultaneous state-based checks began.

I just resolved a spell with the ravenous ability using a high number, but my opponent paused us and said we have to look at the board state before anything else triggers. What is actually happening right now at the table?

When you resolve your spell, the Ravenous keyword immediately acts as a replacement effect that means this permanent enters with X +1/+1 counters on it according to its rules text. Before any triggered abilities can go on the stack or players get priority, the game must automatically check state-based actions first, which includes verifying if a creature has toughness 0 or less and putting it into its owner’s graveyard if that condition is met. This survival checkpoint takes strict precedence over the trigger because the game evaluates permanent legality before allowing abilities to resolve. If your chosen X value plus the creature's base stats keep its toughness above zero, it safely passes this initial check and then the Ravenous ability goes on the stack to see if your X was 5 or more for a card draw. The concrete final outcome is that your opponent correctly identified the mandatory survival checkpoint, your creature remains on the battlefield with enhanced stats, and you will draw exactly one card only after clearing that first check and confirming your chosen number reached five.
Can I play a spell with flash while my opponent is casting something on their turn?

Yes, you can. Flash means you may play this card any time you could cast an instant. Since instants can be played during your opponent's turn in response to their spells, a card with flash follows that same timing. For example, if your opponent casts a spell to destroy your creature, you can cast a creature with flash in response to try and create a new threat.

I just tapped my snow-covered mountains and swamps during my turn to cast a modal spell that lets me choose multiple effects. My opponent said I shouldn't have decided how many modes to pick before actually looking at my mana pool, because normally you pick modes after tapping lands. Also, I'm not sure if those snow taps even count toward the generic mana in the spell's cost. What actually happens here?

When casting a spell with multiple modes or optional costs, the rules state that while announcing choices, some options may be available to a player only if other choices are made that would normally be made later, and in that case you may consider any other choices to be made in that step. This means you are legally allowed to plan your mode count before tapping anything. After locking in your selection, the total cost is calculated and you move to payment. At this stage, the guidelines confirm that if an effect would add mana represented by one or more snow mana symbols to a player’s mana pool, that much colorless mana is added to that player’s mana pool. This conversion ensures your tapped sources provide valid generic mana. The announcement planning rule takes precedence first during casting declaration, while the snow conversion rule applies second during actual payment. You successfully cast the spell with your declared number of modes, and your snow lands legally cover the generic costs through colorless conversion.
What happens when I sacrifice a creature to cast a spell but my opponent counters that spell?

The creature remains in the graveyard. A cost is an action or payment necessary to take another action, such as casting a spell. To pay a cost, a player carries out the instructions specified by the spell, meaning the sacrifice occurs the moment you attempt to cast it. For example, if you sacrifice a Goblin to cast a spell and your opponent uses a counterspell, the spell is countered, but the Goblin remains in the graveyard because the cost was already completed to initiate the action.
Can I still pick a vanguard card and put it on the table if we are already halfway through the match?

No, you cannot. The rules require that each vanguard card is placed face up next to its owner's library before the game begins. For example, if you are already ten turns into a match and realize you forgot your card, you cannot simply pick one out and start using it now.

I just cast a spell that puts my legendary creature onto the battlefield copying an existing one, and it also has this text saying this permanent gains abilities from static sources while staying on the field, and whenever you copy it, put it into your hand. Right after it arrives, both show up for a second but then one disappears. I thought the copy would stay because it was created directly on the battlefield. Can you explain what is actually happening here?

The game automatically runs a cleanup step called state-based actions whenever a player would get priority, and this happens before anyone can respond or attack. The comprehensive rules state that if two or more legendary permanents with the same name are controlled by the same player, that player chooses one of them, and the rest are put into their owners graveyards. This applies immediately upon entry because copied permanents enter as new objects sharing the original name. Meanwhile, the text describing your permanent follows the design for linked abilities, where a static ability that is linked to one or more triggered abilities combine into one paragraph with the static part first followed by each triggered response. Even though the trigger created a copy and both legitimately entered simultaneously, the automatic legend rule cleanup overrides any expectation of them coexisting. Concrete final game outcome: One legendary remains on the battlefield while the other is permanently removed to its owner graveyard before priority was ever given.

I just played a sorcery that has the demonstrate ability and deals three damage to target creature. My opponent copied my copy as per the demonstrate rule and targeted one of my own creatures for two damage. Before those spells resolve, I flashed in an enchantment that turns one of those creatures into an artifact until end of turn. Do the damage marks disappear because it is no longer a creature, or do they still destroy them later? And how exactly does the copying work with demonstrate when we both change targets?

The demonstrate ability triggers exactly when you cast the spell, meaning you copy it and choose an opponent who then copies that copy with new targets, placing three independent damage events on the stack before anything resolves. Because those instances resolve separately, they each mark their respective permanents with damage. Even though one target stops being a creature due to your enchantment, damage marked on a creature remains until the cleanup step, even if that permanent stops being a creature. The demonstrate mechanic establishes the initial damage sources first, but the persistence rule takes precedence afterward to ensure those marks survive type changes and wait for state-based action checks. Since all damage markers stick around without fading away, the concrete final outcome is that both permanents retain their marked damage until the cleanup step, and any creature meeting the toughness threshold gets destroyed as a state-based action during cleanup.
Can I just pick colorless if a card tells me to choose a color?

No, you cannot. If a player is asked to choose a color, they must choose one of the five colors. Colorless is not considered a color for this choice. For example, even if your entire deck consists of colorless artifacts, you must still pick white, blue, black, red, or green when an effect asks you to choose a color.

I just cast an attack with my undying creature during a Commander Draft match and it took enough damage to die while sitting on one plus counter and two minus counters. My opponent says it should come back because there was still a plus counter left, but the rules lawyer at our table claims it stays dead because of how death triggers work. At the same time, we are arguing whether I can actually put four copies of my commander in this draft deck since standard magic usually only allows three per deck. What is the actual ruling?

The tournament regulations state that a player’s deck may include any number of cards from that player’s card pool with the same name, which directly overrides the standard three-card limit and allows you to legally run all four copies during your Commander Draft games. That deckbuilding rule establishes what cards enter play, but once they are on the battlefield, the state-based action sequence takes precedence for timing. The rules explicitly clarify that when a permanent leaves the battlefield due to damage or countering, its last known information is derived from the game state before any of those state-based actions were performed. This means the game evaluates your undying creature exactly as it existed right before death, and since it still carried a plus counter in that final pre-death snapshot, the requirement for triggering an undying ability is not met. The concrete outcome is that you may keep all four commanders in your draft deck without penalty, and your creature will permanently stay in the graveyard without returning.
I have a 3/3 creature, but my opponent played a card that makes it a 1/1. Can I still deal 3 damage with it?

No, you cannot. While the printed numbers show 3/3, power and toughness can be modified or set to particular values by effects. For example, if an opponent plays a spell that turns all creatures into 1/1s, your creature's power becomes 1, meaning it will only deal 1 damage in combat instead of 3.
What happens if I play a World Star but there are no other world permanents on the table?

When you play the World Star, its special abilities will not activate because the rule specifies that the effect applies to a permanent only if other world permanents are within its controller's range of influence. Since no other world permanents are present, the condition is not met. For example, if you have a World Star and your opponent plays a World Moon, both would then start functioning.

I cast Cryptbreaker and my opponent immediately tries to respond before I pick a card from the graveyard. He claims I must choose a target right when I put the creature on the battlefield, but he also says he has an instant that can force me to move a specific card to the front of the pile so I have no choice in the matter. Who is right about how this works?

Remove all references to specific rule numbers and rephrase those sentences conversationally. For example, change 'Rule 603.5 states that optional triggered abilities go on the stack...' to 'The rules for triggered abilities state that optional effects go on the stack regardless of intent, and the choice is made when the ability resolves.' Change 'rule 404.2 defines the graveyard...' to 'Regarding the graveyard, the rules define it as a single face-up pile where players can examine cards but normally cannot change their order.'

I just cast an enchantment that attaches to my creature and continuously gives it +2/+2 and makes it white, but my opponent immediately played a spell saying Until end of turn, you gain protection from white. We are mid-combat and arguing about what happens next. Does the creature lose its color change or its power boost, and can I still block with it? What is the exact state right now?

The exact state is that your creature remains white with a +2/+2 boost to its power and toughness, and you independently have protection from white. This outcome occurs because static abilities do something all the time rather than being activated or triggered, and they are simply true, so the creature traits are locked in as soon as the enchantment resolves. Once those object characteristics are determined, continuous effects that affect players rather than objects are applied in timestamp order after the determination of objects characteristics, meaning your protection effect is layered on top afterward without interfering with the creature. Because static abilities establish the baseline for all objects first and player effects follow strictly in the order they appeared, there is no conflict. Your creature attacks and blocks as a white +2/+2 boosted permanent, and you can use the protection to prevent red sources from targeting or damaging you, but it does not remove the color change from your own creature.
Can I make my Brawl deck 65 cards to have more options?

No, you cannot. A player's deck must contain exactly 60 cards, including its commander. This means the minimum deck size and the maximum deck size are both 60. For example, if you have a collection of 65 cards that you want to use, you must remove 5 of them to ensure your final deck is exactly 60 cards.

I cast a clone spell that copies my opponent's creature, which has an enters-the-battlefield ability that deals damage to all opponents. Before the copy resolves, they play an instant spell on the stack that says the copied creature has no triggered abilities. When the copy actually enters the battlefield, does it trigger its enters-the-battlefield ability and deal damage?

The copy will not trigger the ability and will deal no damage. Even though the original creature had a triggered ability, the clone becomes a new object upon entering, but effects from spells on the stack continue to apply to the permanent that spell becomes. This means the modification granting no triggered abilities persists through the resolution of the spell. When the copy enters, continuous effects modify its characteristics the moment it arrives on the battlefield. Because the persistent effect stripped all triggered abilities before the check, the copy enters with no triggers to fire. The game evaluates the object after these modifications are applied, so there is no ability present to trigger.

I'm playing Commander and my legendary creature commander has been attacking for four damage each turn, putting my opponent at twelve total combat damage against them. On my next turn, I tap out to cast a sorcery that says When this spell resolves, put three +1/+1 counters on your commander. Does the damage from future attacks still count toward the twenty-one threshold, or does it reset because its stats changed?

The damage tracking does not reset. The commander variant rules state that a player who’s been dealt 21 or more combat damage by the same commander over the course of the game loses the game, which establishes a cumulative total tracked across all instances that specific commander deals damage. Meanwhile, continuous effects that modify characteristics of a permanent do so the moment the permanent is on the battlefield, meaning those counters will increase its power immediately without altering its identity or clearing historical damage. When both rules interact, the characteristic modification rule applies first because static and modifying effects take effect instantly upon the permanent entering play, updating its power before any new combat damage is dealt toward the threshold. The concrete final outcome is that your opponent reaches the twenty-one threshold faster with the boosted damage, but the original twelve damage already dealt still counts toward that total, resulting in a game loss once the new cumulative combat damage meets or exceeds twenty-one.
What happens if I use an ability for zero mana and then my opponent casts a spell that makes all abilities cost two more mana?

Your ability will still only cost zero mana. When you activate an ability, its cost is determined the moment it is put onto the stack. Casting a spell that alters costs won't affect spells and abilities that are already on the stack. For example, if you activate a creature ability for zero mana and your opponent responds by casting a spell that increases all activated ability costs, your ability remains free because it was already on the stack before their spell was cast.

I just cast my spells this turn and decided to pay three mana to move a companion card from outside the game into my hand because I read it's a special action. My opponent says they can respond with instant speed cards to stop it, but I was told that special actions cant be responded to. What actually happens here?

When you attempt to move a card from outside the game into your hand using this mechanic, two distinct rule sets interact to determine the outcome. First, the action itself is governed by special action guidelines, which state that a player may take this action any time they have priority and the stack is empty during a main phase of their turn. Because it is formally classified as a special action, it does not use the stack and opponents cannot respond with instant speed cards or abilities to interrupt it. Second, once the timing conditions are met, Commander restrictions on external cards still apply strictly. The rule for bringing cards from outside the game explicitly notes that you cannot bring a card into the game if any color in its color identity is not in your commander's identity, or if it shares a name with a card in your starting deck or owned by you in the current game. Precedence works sequentially: you must first satisfy the timing requirement of the special action, and only then does the external card restriction check whether the move is legal. Final outcome: Your opponent cannot respond to this action at all. If your companion matches your commander's color identity and does not duplicate a card in your starting deck or current game, the card successfully moves into your hand immediately. If it violates any of those Commander restrictions, the action is illegal, you simply do not gain the card, and nothing happens.
If we are playing on a team, do we have to decide which of our opponents each creature is attacking, or can we just attack as a group?

You attack as a group, but you must still declare specific targets for every creature. For each attacking creature, the attacking team announces which defending player, planeswalker, or battle that creature is attacking. For example, if you and your teammate are both attacking an opponent named Sarah, you might declare your Knight attacks Sarah directly while your teammate's Bird attacks Sarah's Planeswalker instead.

I am in the middle of my turn with two lands on the battlefield and a land in hand. I have an instant that says it can only be cast before attackers are declared. I accidentally tapped all my creatures to attack. Now I realize I need the extra mana from my land, and I still want to cast the instant. Can I play the land first and then cast the spell?

You cannot do this because of how special actions and combat timing windows lock together during a turn. Playing a land is defined as a special action that allows you to put a land onto the battlefield from your hand. By default, you can only take this special action once per turn, specifically when you have priority and the stack is empty during a main phase of your turn. Once you tap creatures to attack, you are declaring attackers, which means you have already transitioned into the combat phase, so the window for that special action closes immediately. Regarding the instant spell, the rules clarify that when a card states it may be cast only before or after a particular point in combat, it is referring strictly to the turn-based action of declaring attackers. It may be cast only before the declare attackers step begins. Since you already declared attackers, you missed that window. The concrete final game outcome is that you cannot play the land and cannot cast the instant at this time; you must wait until your next main phase to play the land, and the opportunity to cast the instant before attackers are declared will not return until your next turn.
Can I just grab an extra copy of a card from my collection and add it to the game if I realize I forgot it in my deck?

No, you cannot. Traditional cards from outside the game cannot be brought into a Commander game except via rules, special actions, or effects that specifically bring cards into the game from outside the game. For example, if you are playing a match and realize you left a copy of Sol Ring in your deck box at home, you cannot simply reach into your collection and pull one out to play during the match.

I'm playing Two-Headed Giant and my opponent attacks with a creature that has infect for 6 damage and I have no blockers. I see poison counters piling up on my character, but do we lose the game right now or does it take more? How many poison counters actually end us?

When your opponent's infect creature deals damage to you in Two-Headed Giant, the damage produces specific results based on the source properties. According to the damage rules, when a source with infect deals damage, that source's controller gives the player that many poison counters rather than causing life loss. In Two-Headed Giant, any poison counters given to a player are added to their team's total counter pool. However, receiving these counters does not immediately trigger a game loss. The game outcome relies on state-based actions checked after damage and effects resolve. A specific variant rule states that if a team has fifteen or more poison counters, that team loses the game. Since you were dealt 6 damage, your team receives 6 poison counters added to your current total. If your team previously had 9 or fewer poison counters, gaining these 6 keeps your total at 14 or fewer and the game continues. Your team does not lose the game from this attack alone unless your team was already at 9 or more poison counters before this combat, in which case adding 6 brings the team to 15 or more and you lose the game as dictated by the variant condition.

We were in the middle of a game and decided to swap seats so we could see the board better. We both agreed to it, but then my opponent tried to declare his creatures as attackers right away. I told him he had to wait for the next turn because the seating change reset our priority. Is he allowed to do that?

You are incorrect. Because you and your opponent mutually agreed to the move, the new seating order is valid since players can use any agreeable method to determine where they sit. This seating change occurs first. Once the move is completed, the game continues normally. Declaring attackers is a special action, which means it is an action a player takes when they have priority that does not use the stack. Therefore, he can perform that action immediately upon having priority without needing to wait for a turn reset.

My friend and I are arguing. I have two different cards that say all my damage is doubled instead. I use an ability on one of my artifacts to deal 2 damage to him. Does it become 4 or does it double twice and become 8?

Any object can deal damage as an effect of a spell or ability, so your artifact will successfully deal the damage. Regarding the amount, replacement effects can apply to modified events. Because a replacement effect gets an opportunity to affect an event or any modified events that replace it, the first doubling effect replaces the 2 damage with 4 damage, and then the second effect applies to that new 4-damage event, replacing it with 8 damage instead. The final outcome is 8 damage.

I just played this creature that has first strike and draws a card when it hits. My friend has a card that lets them gain life whenever any creature deals damage. When they block my creature, do they get the life gain right away or is there another step?

He will gain life twice. Because your creature has first strike, combat is split into two separate damage steps. In the first step, your creature deals damage, which triggers both your ability to draw a card and his ability to gain life because his ability applies to any creature dealing damage. After that step is over, the game proceeds to a second combat damage step where his regular creature will deal damage, triggering his life gain ability a second time. The final outcome is that you draw one card during the first strike step, and he gains life twice—once during the first strike step and once during the regular combat damage step.

My opponent and I are arguing about a play. I have a creature that deals 2 damage, and we both have cards that double my creature's damage. My friend says it should hit for 8, but I thought it would only be 4 because it already doubled once. Also, my ability that lets me draw a card whenever a creature deals damage—does that trigger twice because of the two doubling effects?

Your friend is right on both counts. First, the doubling effects are replacement effects, meaning they change the event before it actually happens. Each effect gets one chance to modify the event, so the 2 damage is first replaced by 4, and then that modified event is replaced again to become 8. Second, because this all results in a single event of 8 damage being dealt by your creature, your draw ability only sees one instance of damage being dealt. Therefore, it triggers exactly once.

I am playing Commander and my library is empty. My opponent plays a card that says I can choose to draw a card. At the same time, my commander was just sent to the graveyard by an effect. Can I still choose to draw a card if I have none left, and what happens to my commander?

Yes, you can still choose to draw. Even if there are no cards in your library, if an effect offers you the choice to draw, you can still take that choice. This occurs as the effect resolves on the stack. After that resolves, the game checks state-based actions. Since your commander was put into the graveyard since the last time those checks were performed, you can move it back to the command zone. The final outcome is that you make the choice to draw (which results in no card being added to your hand) and then you move your commander back to the command zone.

My friend was playing Commander and used a spell that turned my commander face down while it was sitting in the command zone. Now I am trying to use an effect that lets me search my deck for my commander, but I can not find it because it is face down. Is it still my commander, and should I be looking in my deck?

Your commander is not in your deck. At the start of the game, you put your commander in the command zone and shuffle all other cards to form your library. Because your commander was turned face down in the command zone, it became a new object. Therefore, you cannot search for it in your deck because it is not there, and even if you look in the command zone, you are looking at a new object that is no longer your original commander.

I just played a creature that says 'When this enters the battlefield, draw a card' and my opponent used a spell to destroy it immediately. Does the drawing a card part still happen? We can't agree if it's too late.

Yes, you still draw the card. When your creature enters the battlefield, its ability triggers immediately because an enters-the-battlefield event occurred. Even if it is destroyed right away, the trigger has already been put on the stack to resolve. After the destruction happens, the creature moves to your graveyard as a result of being destroyed, which follows the rule that destroyed objects are put into the graveyard. Since the entering event happened before the destruction, the ability successfully triggers and will resolve.

I just cast a spell that can be copied for extra mana, and I paid for two extra copies. The spell gives a creature Flying. My opponent has an enchantment that gives all my creatures Lifelink. Do they both have it?

Yes, they will both have those abilities. When you pay the replicate cost, you create additional copies of the spell that resolve when you cast it. To determine which abilities a creature has, we apply effects in timestamp order. The enchantment's lifelink effect is applied first because it was already on the battlefield. Then, your three copies of the spell resolve, adding the flying ability. Because adding one ability does not replace another, the creature receives both. The final outcome is that the creature has both Flying and Lifelink.
My creature has double strike and is attacking, but my friend used a spell that prevents the next time a creature deals damage. Does my creature deal no damage at all this turn?

No, your creature will still deal damage during the combat. Because your creature has double strike, combat is split into two distinct combat damage steps. The first step is for creatures with first strike or double strike, and the second step is for remaining attackers as well as those that currently have double strike. When your opponent casts the prevention spell, it applies to the first damage event that occurs during that first combat damage step. According to the rules for how damage is processed, prevention effects modify a damage event before it is actually dealt. Once that first event is finished, the game moves to the second combat damage step. This creates a completely new, separate damage event. Since your opponent's spell was already used on the first event, your creature will deal its normal damage during this second step.

My opponent just played a card that makes me skip my next turn. I have some things I want to do right now, like playing a land or using an ability, but can I still do those things before the skip happens?

Yes, you can still perform special actions during your current turn. The skip effect only applies to your next occurrence of a turn. Since a skip effect is a replacement effect that says instead of your next turn happening, nothing happens, it does not affect anything occurring during your present turn. You can continue to play lands or use other special actions as long as you are still in your current main phase and have priority.

My friend used a card that says roll a die, if it is a 1 you lose, but if it is anything else roll again. He rolled a 4 and then a 1. I have a card that triggers when someone loses. Does my card work even though he was still in the middle of his dice rolling thing?

Yes, your card will trigger. Even though the instruction to roll again and the result that causes a loss are both part of one single ability, once the die shows a 1, the player loses immediately. Because losing the game is an event that triggers any abilities specifically watching for a player losing or leaving the game, those abilities will go on the stack right then. The final outcome is that the player loses and your card's ability triggers normally.

My friend cast a spell that makes me lose, but I have this card that lets me draw cards whenever I lose. I tried to counter his spell, but he said it would not matter because my draw when I lose thing would happen anyway. Am I still going to lose?

No, you will not lose. When you cast a counterspell, you are using an ability that applies while a spell is on the stack to prevent it from resolving. Because the counterspell resolves and stops your opponent's spell, the instruction for you to lose the game never actually happens. Since the trigger for your ability specifically occurs only when a player loses or leaves the game, and you never actually lose, the ability will not trigger. The resolution of the counterspell takes precedence by stopping the loss event before it can occur.

My teammate and I are playing on a team against two others using the shared turn rule. I just used an ability that gives us snow mana, but my opponent says we can't use it until our individual turns are over, and they also say snow mana isn't actually colorless so it doesn't work for generic costs. What happens?

Your opponent is incorrect. Because you are using shared team turns, your team holds priority as a single unit, meaning your teammate can act during the collective turn rather than waiting for an individual turn. Additionally, any effect that adds snow mana to a player's pool is treated as adding that much colorless mana. The final outcome is that the snow mana becomes colorless mana and your teammate can use it immediately during your shared team turn.

I was playing with a creature that has first strike, and it hit my opponent's regular creature and died. My opponent says he still gets to deal damage with his creature even though mine is already gone. Is he right?

Yes, your opponent is correct. The rules state that if any attacking or blocking creatures have first strike or double strike, the combat damage step is split into two parts. The first part is for those special creatures, and after that, the game has a second combat damage step where the remaining attackers and blockers that do not have first strike or double strike assign their damage. Before the game moves to that second step, it must perform state-based actions, such as moving your creature to the graveyard because its toughness reached zero. Once those actions are completed, the second combat damage step proceeds normally.

My friend played this card that says whenever you shuffle your library, you lose two life and it can't be countered. Then I used a spell that told me to shuffle my hand into my library. He says nothing happened because I didn't specifically shuffle the library, I just moved cards from my hand to it. Is he right?

Your friend is actually correct that nothing happens, though his reasoning is slightly off. While shuffling your hand into your library does indeed count as shuffling the library (as the action is performed on all cards in the zone), the trigger condition on your friend's card is 'whenever you shuffle your library'. Because that card is on the battlefield, 'you' refers to the controller of the card (your friend). Since you are the one shuffling your own library and not your friend, the trigger condition is never met. If the card had said 'whenever a player shuffles their library', then the ability would trigger and would be protected from being countered because that instruction functions while the ability is on the stack.

I attacked with my creature that has banding and one other guy at the same time. My friend blocked just the banding one. Does the other guy get blocked too, and do I get to decide how the damage is split?

Yes, your second creature is also blocked. When you declare an attacking band, if one member of that band is blocked, every other creature in that same band becomes blocked by that same creature as well. Regarding the damage, because the attacker has banding, the active player chooses how the combat damage from the blocking creature is assigned among your attacking creatures. While the amount of damage dealt remains equal to the blocker's power, you have the final say on which creature in your band receives that damage.

My opponent just cast a spell that says I can choose to draw a card, and if I do, I sacrifice a creature, and then when I sacrifice a creature this way, I deal 3 damage to them. I have no cards left in my deck. Can I still pick the draw option to get the damage, or does having no cards stop the whole thing?

You can still choose to draw a card even though your library is empty. The rules state that if an effect offers you the choice to draw, you can take that choice even if there are no cards left in your library, provided no other effect prevents you from drawing. Once you make that choice, you must follow the subsequent instruction to sacrifice a creature. Because that sacrifice was made specifically as a result of the spell's instructions, the reflexive trigger that happens when you sacrifice a creature this way will trigger. The final outcome is that you choose to draw, sacrifice a creature, and deal 3 damage to your opponent.

I'm trying to cast a spell that costs two generic and one red mana. My friend has a card that reduces the cost by two colorless mana. But right then, my creature with zero toughness is going to die from another effect. Does the cost reduction apply to what I pay for the spell first, or does the game handle my dying creature before I can even finish casting?

The cost reduction is applied at the moment you cast the spell. Since your spell costs two generic and one red mana and the reduction is two colorless mana, a rule applies where reductions to generic mana only affect the generic component of a cost. This leaves your new cost as just one red mana. After you have successfully cast the spell and it is on the stack, the game checks for state-based actions before anyone can respond. Because the game performs all state-based actions every time a player would get priority, your creature with zero toughness is moved to the graveyard as a state-based action before any triggered abilities are put on the stack or before your opponent gets priority to react to your spell. So, you pay the reduced cost, the spell goes on the stack, and then the creature dies.

I just played a Saga that lets me pick how many lore counters it starts with. I picked 1 so I could get the first chapter right away. But my opponent's spell just finished, and one of my creatures is sitting there at 0 toughness. Can I use my Saga's ability before that creature dies?

No, the creature will be removed from the battlefield before you can trigger your Saga. Whenever a player would receive priority to act, the game checks for any state-based actions, such as a creature having zero toughness, and performs them all at once. Because these actions must be resolved before any player is granted priority, the creature is moved to the graveyard first. Since you chose 1 lore counter and the first chapter requires exactly 1 lore counter, the ability is eligible to trigger, but it will only happen after the state-based action is finished and you are finally given priority.

My opponent has an enchantment that lets them look at the top card of their deck whenever they draw a card, and if it is a land, it goes straight to the battlefield. They drew a card, and that land entering the battlefield triggered an effect that made them lose all life and also forced them to exile their whole library. They have a card out that says instead of losing the game, they shuffle everything into their library and draw seven cards. Does the enchantment count as one single ability, and do they still lose or do they get the new cards?

The enchantment is a linked ability, which means the static instruction to look at the card and the triggered effect of putting it into play are combined into one single ability. This ability resolves first, causing the land to enter the battlefield. After that, the game checks for state-based actions. Because the land's effect causes both the player to lose all life and their library to become empty, these are multiple state-based actions that would both result in a loss. However, since they have the same result, a single replacement effect replaces all of them. The final outcome is that the player shuffles their library, draws seven cards, and their life becomes 20; they do not lose the game.

My creature was attacking my friend's planeswalker, but then they used a spell that turned the planeswalker into an artifact. Does my creature stop attacking, and can I still block it with something else?

Your creature remains an attacking creature. According to the rules, if a creature is attacking a planeswalker and that planeswalker is removed from combat (for example, by a spell turning it into an artifact), the creature does not leave combat. It continues to be an attacking creature, although it is no longer attacking a planeswalker. Because it remains an attacking creature, it may still be blocked by your opponent's creatures.

I just used a spell to turn my opponent's creature into a different permanent, and at the same time, its toughness dropped to zero. Does it keep the effects it had before? And since two things are happening with its death, does it die twice?

The transformation happens first, where the creature becomes a new object with no memory of its previous existence, though effects from the spell that changed it continue to apply to the new object it becomes. After this change is complete, the game checks for state-based actions. If multiple state-based actions would have the same result at the same time, like the creature dying because of zero toughness and another effect also saying it should go to the graveyard, a single replacement effect will replace all of them. The final outcome is that the creature becomes the new permanent and then is placed in the graveyard exactly once.

My friend lost because of a card that made them leave the game, not just lose. I have a card that says when a player loses, I put all their graveyards into my hand. Does my card still work, and do I get those cards?

Yes, your card still works because the trigger occurs as if they lost the game. Once that ability begins to resolve, however, the rules for zone redirection take over. Because the effect tries to move the cards into a hand that does not belong to the owner, the rules state that if an object would go to a library, graveyard, or hand other than its owner's, it goes to its owner's corresponding zone instead. The final outcome is that your ability triggers, but all the cards from their graveyard go into the departing player's own hand rather than yours.

I have an enchantment that says if I lose the game, I get to bring back all the cards that were exiled this turn. My opponent just used a spell that makes me lose, but they also exiled my whole graveyard earlier. Since those cards are in exile, they are gone from the game, right? So my enchantment won't work?

No, your enchantment will still work. Even though those cards were moved to the exile zone, that zone acts as a holding area for objects within the game, so they are not truly gone or removed from the game entirely. Because those cards are still technically in a valid game zone, your ability can see them and bring them back. Additionally, since you lost the game, your triggered ability will correctly fire according to the rules regarding players losing. The final outcome is that all those exiled cards will return to the battlefield as intended.

I played a card that makes my opponent choose which of my creatures they want to exile. They picked my best creature, but then I realized I could have cast a spell to protect it. Since they already made the choice while I was playing the card, does that mean I can't respond to the spell once it is actually on the stack?

No, you can still respond. Because the rules state that when a spell forces an opponent to make a choice, that opponent makes the choice at the same time you would normally make it while casting the spell, the selection happens before the spell even reaches the stack. However, once the spell has finished casting and is sitting on the stack, players are allowed to cast new spells or activate abilities in response to it. This means your response will resolve first, potentially protecting the creature before the original spell resolves and carries out its effect.

I was playing Celebr-8000 and I rolled two 6s. My friend says that because my card's ability tells me to check if I rolled doubles, it doesn't count as actually rolling doubles for their card that triggers when I roll doubles this turn. What is actually happening?

You are correct and your friend is mistaken. According to the rules, you have rolled doubles if the result of each die is equal to the other, which is true since you rolled two 6s. Even though your card uses that result as an instruction for what to do next, the event of rolling doubles has still occurred in the game. Therefore, when your friend's card checks to see if you have rolled doubles during this turn, it will see that the condition was met and its ability will trigger.

I just cast a spell that moved the top three cards of my library into my graveyard, and I tried to pick the order they went in. My friend says I can't do that, and he also says one card is illegal because it has a red symbol in its text even though the card is blue. Who is right?

If the spell did not specifically say you could choose the order, your friend is right; the general rule that the order of objects in a graveyard cannot be changed takes precedence unless an effect explicitly allows it. Since your spell did not grant permission to choose the order, the cards stay in the same sequence they were in your library. Regarding the card's legality, a commander's color identity is determined by all mana symbols in its cost and rules text. Because that card has a red symbol in its text, it has red in its color identity and cannot be in a mono-blue deck regardless of how the cards are moved.

I'm playing a Brawl game and my commander is a Vehicle. My opponent attacks me with a creature that says damage is redirected to my commander instead of me. But right before they deal damage, someone exiles my commander. Do I take the damage, and do I lose the game because of it?

Since you are playing Brawl, the rule that causes a player to lose the game specifically from receiving 21 combat damage from a single commander does not apply to your match. However, regarding the damage itself, the redirection effect requires the target to be on the battlefield at the moment the damage would be redirected. Because your commander was exiled and is no longer on the battlefield, the redirection effect does nothing. Consequently, you will take the damage directly from the attacking creature, but you will not lose the game due to the commander damage rule.

My friend is playing Commander and has this big legendary creature as his leader. I have an effect that says instead of damage going to a creature, it goes to his commander instead. But right before the damage is actually dealt, he uses another card to exile his commander. He thinks the damage should still hit him or something, but I think the redirection just fails. What happens?

Since your friend is playing a Commander game, his legendary creature is his designated commander. When determining what happens, the rules for redirection take precedence by checking the status of the target; specifically, if the permanent that is supposed to receive the redirected damage is no longer on the battlefield when the damage would be redirected, the effect does nothing. Because the commander was exiled and is no longer on the battlefield, the redirection fails entirely. The final outcome is that the damage will be dealt to the original creature target instead of being redirected to the player or the commander.

I am playing in a four-player game and just declared an attack against Leo. My creature has an ability that triggers when it attacks, but Leo has a card that triggers whenever he is attacked. We are arguing about whether his ability happens before mine because he's the one being hit.

In multiplayer games, the attacking player chooses one of their opponents to be the defending player for that combat phase. Since you are making the attack, you are the attacker and Leo is the defender. When both abilities trigger at the same time, we determine the order based on the players' roles. The rules state that triggered abilities are put on the stack by the active player first (APNAP order), followed by the non-active player. Because it is your turn, your ability is placed on the stack first, and then Leo's ability is placed on top of yours. Since the last ability put on the stack is the first one to resolve, Leo's ability will resolve before yours.

I tried to use an ability that costs two mana to draw a card, but my opponent played a spell right after I did that makes everything cost more. We both passed to see what happens. He says I have to pay the extra mana now even though the ability was already waiting to happen. Is he right?

The opponent is incorrect. When you activate an ability, its cost is set at that moment and placed on the stack. Any spell cast afterward that changes costs cannot reach back to change the cost of something already on the stack. Because the ability's cost was already established before the new spell was played, it remains unchanged. Once both players pass without taking further actions, the ability resolves using its original cost of two mana.

My friend is playing a card that stops me from casting any spells with an even mana value. I have a spell in my hand where I can pick the amount of mana for X. Can I still cast it if I choose an X that makes the total odd?

Yes, you can legally cast that spell. The rules for casting a spell allow you to consider any choices you might make during the proposal of the spell, such as choosing a value for X, to see if the spell meets certain requirements. Because you can choose an X that results in an odd mana value, the spell is not prohibited by your friend's card. Regarding how these rules interact, the priority system takes precedence because you must have priority before you can even begin the process of proposing a spell and checking its eligibility. Once you have priority, you then check the eligibility of the spell based on its qualities, including the choice you make for X, to see if it can be legally cast.

My opponent's creature hit my defender for way more damage than its toughness, and that triggered their ability to make me draw a card. But I have no cards left in my deck, and they have an enchantment out that says instead of drawing a card, I should exile the top two cards of my library. Do I still get to exile those cards?

You do not actually exile any cards because your library is empty, but the action is still processed. Because the damage dealt to your creature was greater than its toughness, excess damage was dealt, which triggers the opponent's ability. Even though you cannot actually draw a card, replacement effects that substitute a card draw with another action are applied regardless of whether a draw is possible. The instruction to exile two cards is applied to the sequence, even if there are no cards available to be exiled.

My friend and I are arguing. I tried to cast a spell that costs one red mana using an artifact that says tap to add a color of a permanent you control, but I only have colorless lands. He says the spell just fails, but I think because I am in the middle of casting it, the spell is already on the stack. What actually happens?

When you cast a spell, you follow a strict sequence: you propose the spell, determine its total cost, activate mana abilities, and then pay the cost. Because your artifact's ability would produce mana of an undefined type since you have no colored permanents, that ability produces no mana instead. Since you do not gain any mana from that ability, when you reach the step where you must pay the total cost, you will be unable to pay the required red mana. Because you cannot fulfill the requirement to pay the full cost, you cannot complete the casting process and the spell is never cast.
