I have this enchantment that says if my creatures die, they get exiled instead of going to the graveyard, and then I can cast them from exile. My opponent just played a spell that makes all my creatures 0/0. Do they still go into exile so I can use my enchantment, or do they just vanish because of the 0 toughness rule?

The creatures will be exiled. Although state-based actions happen automatically whenever certain conditions like zero toughness are met, your enchantment provides a replacement effect that modifies what happens to those creatures. Instead of the creature being put into the graveyard as the state-based action would normally do, the enchantment causes it to be exiled instead. Since the ability to play the cards refers specifically to the cards moved to exile by that replacement effect, the two abilities are linked. The final outcome is that your creatures are exiled and remain available for you to cast.

My opponent has a creature that just took 4 damage, which is more than its toughness. He used an ability to turn it into an artifact so it wouldn't be destroyed. But then I played a spell that turns all artifacts back into creatures. Does his artifact die immediately?

Yes, the permanent will be destroyed immediately. The damage dealt to it stays marked on the object even if it stops being a creature, which is the first thing to consider. Once that object becomes a creature again, the game's automatic state-based actions take precedence in resolving the situation by checking the battlefield. Because the damage remains on the permanent and is greater than its toughness, the game recognizes it as having lethal damage and moves it to the graveyard.

I am trying to mulligan for the first time because my starting hand is bad. My opponent says I have to shuffle and then immediately put a card from my hand onto the bottom of my library, and that they get to cast a spell before I can do anything else. Is that how it works?

Your opponent is incorrect on both counts. First, because this is your first mulligan, the rules state it does not count toward the number of cards you put on the bottom or the number of mulligans you take, so no cards are lost during this attempt. Second, since shuffling is a special action, you receive priority immediately after the shuffle is complete. This means that once the mulligan process determines your hand size, you are the one who gets to act next rather than your opponent. The final outcome is that you keep your full hand and you are the next player to take an action.

I just had my upkeep start and my card said if the die I rolled was a 6, I get a card. The die was a 6, so it triggered, but then my opponent played a card that made me reroll all my dice. Now the die is a 2. Do I still get my card?

No, you will not draw a card. The ability checks its condition twice. First, it checks when your upkeep begins to see if it should trigger, which it does because the die was a 6. However, when you reroll the die, the old result stops being stored and is replaced by the new result. When the ability finally tries to resolve, the rule for abilities with an if clause requires the game to check the condition again. Because the die is now a 2, the condition is no longer met, and the ability is removed from the stack.

I am attacking with two creatures that both have the flanking ability. My friend blocks one of them with a 2/2 creature that does not have flanking. Then, my friend casts a spell that deals 1 damage to that 2/2 creature. Does the creature die from the damage or the flanking thing?

The process happens in two distinct stages. First, during the declare blockers step, the flanking ability triggers because your creature is being blocked by one without flanking, which causes the blocking creature to get -1/-1 until end of turn, turning the 2/2 into a 1/1. Next, when the spell deals 1 damage to the creature, that damage itself does not destroy it. Instead, because the creature now has a toughness of 1 due to the flanking effect and has received 1 damage, state-based actions will move the creature to the graveyard. The final outcome is that the blocking creature is put into the graveyard as a result of state-based actions.
My opponent cast a spell that makes my paired soulbond creature become a blue 1/1 artifact under their control. Does the bond break?

The bond breaks for two different reasons. First, the effect changes control of the creature, which is applied in the second layer of continuous effects; according to soulbond rules, a pair becomes unpaired if another player gains control of one of them. Second, the part of the effect that makes it a noncreature artifact is applied in the fourth layer of continuous effects. Since it is no longer a creature after that layer, the soulbond also breaks because the object stopped being a creature.

I cast an enchantment that attaches to my friend's creature and says I draw a card at the end of the turn. Before it even finished resolving, my friend used a spell to exile their creature. Does my enchantment still work and let me draw that card later?

Because the target was gone, the spell could not resolve properly. If a spell's target is illegal when it tries to resolve, the spell does not resolve and instead goes straight to its owner's graveyard. Because the delayed ability to draw a card is only created during the resolution of the spell as it becomes a permanent on the battlefield, and since the spell failed to resolve due to the lost target, that ability was never actually created in the first place. Therefore, you will not draw a card at the end of the turn.

My opponent has a creature that redirects all damage meant for them to itself. I trigger an ability that destroys that creature, and then my opponent triggers an ability that deals 5 damage to me. Since the destruction is already happening, shouldn't the damage still go to the creature?

The damage will hit you directly. When multiple abilities trigger, they are placed on the stack in a specific order based on when they triggered and who controls them. If the destruction ability resolves first, the creature is removed from the battlefield. When the damage ability subsequently tries to resolve, the game checks to see if the redirection target is still there. Because a redirection effect does nothing if the permanent it targets is no longer on the battlefield when the damage would be redirected, the redirection fails and the damage hits you instead.

My friend is playing Commander and used a card that says when it enters the battlefield, you can sacrifice a creature to deal damage to a player. He sacrificed a creature to hit my commander for the 21st time. He thinks he wins right now, but I say he has to wait for the damage to actually happen. Who is right?

You are right about the timing, and your friend is right that the ability will trigger. Because the sacrifice was made as a direct result of the spell's resolution, it creates a reflexive triggered ability which is placed on the stack after the spell finishes resolving. The player does not win immediately upon the sacrifice; instead, the game waits until the spell has fully resolved and its resulting triggers have been put on the stack before checking state-based actions. The player will only lose once that reflexive trigger actually resolves and the damage is dealt, at which point the game checks for 21 combat damage to a commander and recognizes the loss.

I have a card that lets me cast spells as though they had flash. I also have an ability I can activate to change my creature's type. Can I activate my ability and then immediately start casting my spell with flash, or does the starting to cast part mean I've already committed and can't use any more abilities?

You can do both. First, you can activate your ability because you have priority to take actions like activating abilities. Once that ability resolves, you still have priority to begin casting your spell. The rules for casting allow you to consider any choices—such as whether you are casting it as though it had flash—to determine if the spell is legal to cast during the proposal phase.

My opponent cast a spell that targets one of my creatures to sacrifice it, and it also said when you sacrifice a creature this way, you draw a card. But right before the spell resolved, I used an ability to exile that creature. Do I still draw the card?

No, you do not draw a card. When a spell begins to resolve, the rules require it to check whether its targets are still legal. Because your creature was exiled, it is no longer in the zone it was in when it was targeted, making it an illegal target. Since the target is illegal, the spell does not resolve and the instructions for that target are ignored. Because the sacrifice never occurs, the reflexive triggered ability, which only triggers when a creature is sacrificed this way, is never created. The final outcome is that no creature is sacrificed and you do not draw a card.
I am attacking with a 5/5 and my friend blocks it with a 2/2 and a 1/1. I want to make sure both of their creatures die. How do I do that, and when do they actually go to the graveyard?

To make both creatures die, you need to use the combat damage assignment rules to split your damage. Since your creature is being blocked by more than one creature, the rules allow you to divide its power among those blockers however you choose. You should assign at least 2 damage to the 2/2 and at least 1 damage to the 1/1. After you have finished assigning all the damage from your attacking creature, the game performs state-based actions. These are automatic game actions that happen whenever certain conditions are met, such as a creature receiving lethal damage. At that point, both of your friend's creatures will be moved to their graveyards simultaneously.

I have this thing on the table that says any blue mana I spend to cast a spell makes me draw a card. I just used an ability to get two blue mana, but then my opponent played a spell that is currently resolving. Since his spell is resolving and no one has priority yet, do I still get those two draw triggers when I use my mana later?

Yes, you will still get both draw triggers. The rules state that if an ability creates a delayed triggered ability that triggers when mana is spent, a separate delayed triggered ability is created for each piece of mana produced. Regarding the timing of your opponent's spell, no player has priority while a spell or ability is resolving, meaning nothing else can happen until that spell is finished. Once the spell finishes and players receive priority again, you can then spend your mana, at which point those two separate draw triggers will be put on the stack and resolve.
My friend played a creature that had zero health left after an effect hit it, but then he tried to cast a spell to save it before it went away. Why didn't it work?

The creature was in the battlefield zone. When its toughness reaches zero, a state-based action occurs automatically. Because state-based actions happen whenever their conditions are met and do not use the stack, the creature moves from the battlefield to the graveyard before any player can cast a spell or activate an ability in response.

My opponent attacked me, and when it was time to decide how to block, I tried to play a land so I could get enough mana for a spell. My friend said I couldn't do that because we were already in combat. Am I allowed to play a land then?

Your friend is right. The rules for special actions state that playing a land can only be done during a main phase of your turn when you have priority and the stack is empty. Because the combat phase is its own distinct phase consisting of steps like declaring attackers, declaring blockers, and combat damage, you are no longer in a main phase once combat begins. Therefore, the final outcome is that you cannot play a land during the declare blockers step.

My card says Roll a d6. Whenever the result is a 6, create a treasure. I just rolled a 6, but my friend says I can't get a treasure because there isn't a table telling me what happens for all the numbers. Is he right?

Your friend is incorrect. Because the card does not include a results table, the text of the ability tells you exactly how to use the result of the die roll. This works because the card combines the instruction to roll and the triggered effect into one single paragraph. You first follow the instruction to roll the die, and then you check that result against the specific condition in the text. Since the result was a 6, the condition is met, and the final outcome is that you create a treasure token.

My opponent was attacking my planeswalker with a creature whose power is equal to the number of cards in their hand. Then they played a spell that says they discard their hand and then draw four cards. Does their creature die halfway through the spell because they have no cards left, and if the spell also exiled my planeswalker, does their creature stop being an attacker?

The creature will not die during the resolution of the spell, and it will remain an attacking creature even if the planeswalker is exiled. First, because state-based actions pay no attention to what happens during the resolution of a spell, the creature's power will not be checked while the player is discarding their hand; it will only be checked after the spell finishes resolving and the player has drawn their cards. Second, even though the planeswalker is removed from the battlefield, a creature that is attacking a planeswalker or battle stays in combat even if its target is removed from combat. While it continues to be an attacking creature, it will deal no combat damage if it remains unblocked.

My opponent has that thing that says I can't cast spells with even mana values. I want to cast this spell that has an X in its cost, and I'm trying to use my special land to get green mana by picking a color I control, but all my stuff is colorless. Can I do this?

You can legally begin casting the spell because you are allowed to make choices during the proposal of the spell, such as choosing a value for X that makes the mana value odd, which satisfies your opponent's restriction. However, since you only control colorless permanents, the land's ability to produce mana of a color you control results in an undefined mana type and therefore produces no mana at all. The final outcome is that you can start casting the spell, but you will not have the green mana needed to actually complete it.

My commander has an ability that triggers when it enters the battlefield. I just had it exiled and then put back in my command zone. If I cast it again, will its ability trigger, or does the game think it already triggered once since it is the same card?

The ability will trigger again because the commander is treated as a brand new object once it enters the command zone. Because of this, the game doesn't see it as the same entity that previously entered the battlefield. When you cast this new object and it moves to the battlefield, the rules for zone-change triggers will check the battlefield and see a permanent entering, which then activates its enters-the-battlefield ability. Essentially, the rule that makes objects in the command zone new means the game resets its history, allowing all its entering abilities to fire as if it were appearing for the first time.

I have one creature attacking, so I should draw a card because of my special ability that triggers when a creature attacks alone. But then I used a special action to change something else on the board. My opponent says I don't get to draw the card because they can respond to my action first. Who is right?

Your opponent is right about the timing. Since you only declared one creature as an attacker, that creature is attacking alone. However, because you took a special action, you receive priority afterward, and then your opponent receives priority. This priority rule takes precedence over the immediate resolution of any combat-related effects. The final outcome is that your opponent can respond to your special action before the game handles your ability to draw a card from attacking alone.

My opponent just played a card that makes all creatures non-creatures. I have this thing on the board with fading on it, and it is down to its last counter. Do I still have to sacrifice it when my turn starts even though it isn't a creature anymore?

No, you still have to sacrifice it. While a continuous effect can change an object's type (which is handled in the layer system), changing the type does not remove the object's existing keyword abilities. Since Fading is an ability on the permanent, it remains active even if the permanent is no longer a creature. At the beginning of your upkeep, you will still be required to remove a fade counter, and if you cannot, you must sacrifice the permanent.

My opponent just used a spell that killed my creature. Now there is an ability that says I draw a card when it dies. I have some blue mana left from my turn; can I use that to cast a spell in response to that ability, or does the mana disappear because the creature died?

You can still use that mana. When your creature dies, the game first performs all applicable state-based actions, such as moving the creature from the battlefield to the graveyard, before any player gets a chance to act. After those state-based actions are finished and any triggered abilities are put on the stack, the player receives priority to cast spells. Because mana only empties at the end of each step and phase, it is still available in your pool throughout this entire process. The final outcome is that you can use your remaining blue mana to cast an instant in response to the triggered ability.

My opponent has this weird card that counts as both a creature and a battle. I just hit it with a spell for 10 damage, but its toughness is 4 and its defense is 6. How much excess damage was actually dealt, and does the card stay on the table?

First, we calculate the excess damage for each type. For the creature part, the excess is 6 because 10 minus 4 is 6. For the battle part, the excess is 4 because 10 minus 6 is 4. Since the card has both types, the rules say the excess damage dealt is the greatest of those amounts, which in this case is 6. After this calculation, state-based actions are checked. Because the damage reduced its toughness and defense to zero or less, the permanent is immediately moved to the graveyard.

My creature has infect and its power is equal to the number of cards in my hand. My opponent cast a spell that forced me to discard my hand and then draw five cards. Since my hand was empty during the spell, does my creature die from having zero toughness before the draw happens?

No, your creature survives. State-based actions, such as checking if a creature has zero toughness, only occur after a spell or ability has completely finished resolving. Because the spell finishes by drawing you five cards, your creature's toughness will be back to five by the time the game checks if it should have been destroyed. Regarding any damage dealt, because your creature has infect, the opponent will receive poison counters equal to the amount of damage dealt rather than just losing life.

My friend cast a spell that lets him take a creature from my graveyard and put it in his hand. I have an enchantment that says at the beginning of the next end step, sacrifice that creature. Since he's taking it, does it still get sacrificed at the end of the turn?

No. First, because the rules state that if an object would go to a hand other than its owner's, it goes to its owner's corresponding zone instead, the creature actually goes to your hand, not your friend's hand. Second, regarding the delayed trigger, even though the ability to sacrifice the creature was created when his spell resolved, the rule for delayed triggered abilities says that if an object is no longer in the zone it is expected to be in when the ability resolves, the ability won't affect it. Because the creature is in your hand and not on the battlefield, it cannot be sacrificed. The final outcome is that the creature goes to your hand and nothing happens at the end step.

We are playing two-player Commander. My spell just finished resolving and a creature on the field died because its toughness hit zero. My opponent says they cannot use an ability to change that creature's color because it is already dead, but I think they should get a chance since it is their turn in the rotation. Who is right?

Your opponent is correct. Even though the game rules establish this as a two-player Commander match where priority moves back and forth between you, state-based actions like a creature dying because its toughness reached zero are handled automatically by the game. Special actions, such as choosing a new color for a permanent, are actions a player takes when they have priority that do not use the stack. Because the game processes state-based actions before players receive priority to take special actions, the creature is moved to the graveyard first. Once that automatic process is finished and priority is passed to your opponent, the creature is already gone, meaning they cannot perform a special action on it.

I just used a spell that milled four cards at once, and three of them were creatures. I have a card that says whenever a creature is put into my graveyard, I draw a card. My friend says since they all went in at the same time, I only get to draw one card because it was one single spell. Is he right?

No, your friend is incorrect. Because those cards were put into the graveyard at the same time, you first use the rule that allows an owner to arrange multiple cards entering the same graveyard in any order they choose. Once you have decided that order, the game evaluates the triggered abilities for each card. Since three of those cards are creatures, each one satisfies the condition of your draw ability as it is processed. This results in three separate triggers being placed on the stack, allowing you to draw three cards. The process of arranging the cards happens first, followed by the creation of the individual triggers.

My opponent just hit my creature and me at the same time with a spell that has infect. My creature died, and I have a card in the graveyard that lets me get it back when a creature dies. Do I get poison counters for the hit to me, and can I still get my card back?

Yes, you receive both. The rules for damage dictate that when a source with infect deals damage to a player, that player receives poison counters equal to the damage. Simultaneously, when that same source deals damage to a creature, the creature receives -1/-1 counters equal to the damage dealt. After these damage results are processed and your creature is put into the graveyard from the battlefield, your recover ability triggers. Since the recover ability only functions while the card is in your graveyard, you can then pay the cost to return it to your hand or face the requirement to exile it. The final outcome is that you receive poison counters, your creature receives -1/-1 counters and moves to the graveyard, and you then decide whether to recover the card or exile it.

My opponent has an enchantment that says whenever someone casts a spell, they lose 2 life. He then tried to play a card from his hand that says he can only cast it if he controls a creature, but he doesn't have any creatures out. He thinks I still get the 2 life loss because he 'tried' to cast the spell. Is he right?

No, your opponent is incorrect. The rule regarding restrictions on casting cards from a player's hand takes precedence here. Because the card in his hand explicitly states that he can only cast it if he controls a creature, and he does not meet that condition, he is legally prohibited from initiating the process of casting that spell. Since the spell is never actually cast, the triggered ability on your enchantment, which requires a spell to be cast in order to function, will never see its trigger condition met. The final outcome is that no life is lost and the spell remains in his hand.

My friend is playing a blue and red commander but he just tried to play a green creature during his turn. We're arguing because he says he can just cast it if he has the mana and it's his turn, but I think it's not allowed in his deck at all. What happens?

The creature cannot be played. The rules for Commander decks require that every card included matches the commander's color identity, so a green creature cannot be in a blue and red deck. Although your friend has priority to take actions during his turn, the deck construction rules take precedence by determining which cards are allowed to be in the deck in the first place.

My friend has an enchantment that says whenever a permanent leaves the battlefield, they draw a card. I cast a spell that removes all permanents from the game. He says he doesn't get to draw anything because they weren't destroyed or sent to the graveyard. What should happen?

Your friend does draw the cards. Even though the spell uses the old phrase 'removes from the game,' this is officially treated as exile according to the rules for updating old wording. Because his enchantment triggers when a permanent leaves the battlefield, the game uses a special rule that looks back in time to see what was happening immediately before the event. Since the permanents were on the battlefield right before they were exiled, the trigger condition is met. The rule regarding looking back in time takes precedence for determining if the ability triggers, and the outcome is that your friend draws a card for each permanent that was exiled.

We were setting up my Commander deck and I accidentally put my commander into my sideboard instead of the command zone. My friend then played a spell that affects all cards in the game. Does that spell hit my commander?

No, your commander is not affected. At the start of the game, players put their commander face up into the command zone, which is a valid game zone. Because you placed it in your sideboard instead, it is considered outside the game. Since being outside the game means the card is not in any of the game's zones, and cards outside the game cannot be affected by spells or abilities unless those effects specifically bring them into the game, your commander remains unaffected.

I have an enchantment that says if a creature is destroyed, it gets exiled instead. My opponent cast a spell that destroys my creature and also has a trigger that says whenever a creature is destroyed, draw a card. He wants to draw the card, but I'm saying nothing happens because my creature was exiled. Who's right?

You are correct. Because your enchantment is already on the battlefield, it acts as a replacement effect that must exist before the destruction event occurs. This effect takes precedence by changing the event from being destroyed to being exiled. Since the actual event of being destroyed is replaced, the condition for your opponent's triggered ability is never met. Because the event never happened, the ability is never put on the stack as an object, and no card is drawn.

My opponent's creature died and their ability triggered to let them search for a card. Right when it happened, I wanted to play a land from my hand before they put that ability on the stack. Can I do that?

No, you cannot. Although the ability has triggered, the game follows a process to put all pending triggered abilities on the stack before any player receives priority. Because playing a land is a special action that requires you to have priority and for the stack to be empty, you cannot play it until after the triggered ability has been placed on the stack and it becomes your turn to act.

My friend and I are arguing. He wants to use a card that exiles a creature and gives life based on how many colors that creature's identity has. But then he exiled my double-faced creature, and now he says it's a new object so the color identity might be different because the back side isn't visible anymore. Is he right?

No, your friend is incorrect. Although an exiled object becomes a new object that has just been exiled, the rule establishing color identity at the start of the game takes precedence for determining its colors. The rules state that a card's color identity is established before the game begins and that any effect referring to the color identity of an object uses the identity established for that card as the game began, even as the object changes zones or becomes a new object. Because your double-faced card's color identity includes all colors found on both faces, the final outcome is that the player gains life based on the full color identity of the original card.

I've got ten things on the table and I just cast a spell that has ascend on it. My opponent attacks my creature with something much bigger, so it's doing way more damage than the creature's toughness can handle. Do I get the city's blessing from that extra damage, and what happens to the leftover damage?

You will get the city's blessing because the ascend on your spell triggers when you control ten or more permanents, giving you the city's blessing for the rest of the game. However, the extra damage does not grant the blessing. Excess damage is defined as the amount of damage dealt to a creature that is greater than its toughness. This excess damage is only used if an ability specifically checks for it; it does not count as additional permanents or help you reach the ten-permanent threshold required for ascend.

My friend's commander has been cast twice already, so he owes four extra mana to play it again. But he just played a spell that says 'If you would cast your commander, instead pay {2} and draw a card.' Does he still have to pay those four extra mana on top of the two?

No, he does not have to pay the four extra mana. The rules for playing a commander from the command zone state that a player must pay an additional two mana for each previous time they have cast it. However, since there are no special restrictions on casting a spell that generates a replacement effect, the spell he played is valid and its instructions take precedence. Because the spell uses the word instead, it replaces the entire instruction to cast the commander, including its extra tax, with the new cost of two mana and drawing a card.

So my friend has this weird artifact that lets him tap it to add a color of permanent he controls. He tried to use it, but I told him it wouldn't work because he only has colorless lands out right now. He got annoyed and said he could still do it because it's his turn and I can't stop him. Who is actually right?

Your friend is right about the timing but wrong about the result. Because he has priority during his turn, he is allowed to attempt to activate an ability at any time. However, the rules regarding priority only determine if a player can take an action, while the mana rules determine what happens once they do. Since he controls no colored permanents, the ability is attempting to produce mana of an undefined type. The rules state that if an ability would produce one or more mana of an undefined type, it produces no mana instead. Therefore, the final outcome is that he can perform the activation, but he will receive no mana.

My friend played a card that says when a creature dies, I can search my deck for a land. I just used a spell to destroy his creature, so it went to my graveyard. Now he's saying because his card says 'you may,' the ability doesn't even trigger because he doesn't want me to find a land. Is he right?

No, he is incorrect. First, since the creature was destroyed, it is put into its owner's graveyard because the rules state that any object that is destroyed goes there. Second, even though his card says you may, the rules state that triggered abilities go on the stack regardless of whether the player intends to use the option or not. You make the choice to search for the land when the ability resolves. The final outcome is that your ability triggers and goes on the stack, allowing you to search your deck for a land.

My opponent's creature just entered the battlefield and triggered an ability. I wanted to respond with my own ability that says 'You may sacrifice a creature. If you do, search your library for a land.' But before I could even try, my opponent cast a spell to destroy my creature. Why didn't I get to use my ability?

The outcome is that you do not get to search for a land. This happens because of the rules regarding priority. After the creature's ability triggers and is placed on the stack, the active player—your opponent—receives priority first. Since they cast a spell before passing priority to you, you never had the opportunity to activate your own ability. Because you could not activate it, you were unable to make the choice to sacrifice a creature, meaning the 'if you do' part of your ability never had a chance to trigger.
I just cast a spell that dealt 4 damage to my friend's 4/4 creature. He says the spell itself destroyed the creature, but I thought it was just the damage? What actually happened?

The creature went to the graveyard, but not because your spell destroyed it. The rules state that damage dealt to a creature does not destroy it; instead, the damage is simply applied to the creature. After the spell finishes resolving, the game checks for state-based actions. During this check, the game sees that the creature has taken lethal damage and moves it to the graveyard as a single simultaneous event. Therefore, the damage occurs first as part of the spell resolution, followed by the state-based action that handles the actual removal.

We're playing a four-player Commander game, just a normal Free-for-All. My friend has a card that says if they are about to lose the game, they instead shuffle everything into their library and draw seven. At the same time, one player deals him lethal damage and another player gives him ten poison counters. He thinks his card triggers twice because there were two different reasons he was losing. What happens?

In a standard multiplayer Commander game where players can attack multiple opponents, it is possible for several things to happen at once. In this case, the player is facing two different situations that would result in them losing the game simultaneously: having zero life and having ten poison counters. Because these are multiple state-based actions that would have the same result, a single replacement effect will replace all of them. The player's card acts as that single replacement. Therefore, the effect triggers only once, and the concrete outcome is that the player shuffles their graveyard and hand into their library and draws seven cards exactly one time.

My friends and I are playing with a bunch of extra rules we added, but we're arguing. One person says we can only have one variant style active, and another says my move to pick a player for an effect has to go on the stack like a spell. What actually happens?

Regarding your game setup, your friend is right that while you can add various rule options to a multiplayer game, you can only use one specific variant style at a time. Once that structure is established, we look at how your action works. Picking a player is a special action, which is an action a player takes when they have priority that does not use the stack. You must distinguish these from turn-based or state-based actions, which the game generates automatically. Because the rules for game setup establish the context of your match first, and then the rules for actions are applied, the final outcome is that your choice happens immediately without going on the stack.

I was in the middle of casting a spell because I had an enchantment that let me cast spells as if they had flash, but then my opponent destroyed the enchantment before I finished. Am I allowed to finish casting it, and do I still have to pay the mana symbols exactly like the card says?

Yes, you can finish casting the spell. Once you have begun casting a spell that has flash because certain conditions were met, you may continue to cast that spell as though it had flash even if those conditions stop being met. However, you must still pay the specific mana costs required by the spell. Since mana symbols also represent mana costs, you are still required to provide the exact colors and amounts of mana indicated by those symbols to successfully complete the process. The rule regarding flash continuity allows the casting process to proceed, but you must still satisfy the requirement to pay the mana symbols as defined by the card's cost.

I just played a card that costs nothing and has an effect that happens when it enters the battlefield. My friend says I have to actually do something even if it is free, and he also says my ability that triggers when things enter the field wont work right away. What is happening?

Even though the card costs zero mana, you still have to manually cast it; the game does not automatically put it into play just because there is no cost. Once the card enters the battlefield, its ability will trigger. However, triggered abilities do not happen at the exact moment they are triggered. The rules state that triggered abilities are put on the stack only when players would receive priority. This means the card enters the battlefield first, and then the triggered ability is placed on the stack to resolve after players pass priority.

My friend cast a spell that makes all spells cost two more mana. While his spell was still waiting to resolve, I tried to use Foretell on a card in my hand. Do I have to pay the extra two mana for the Foretell?

No, you do not have to pay the extra mana. A spell that alters costs does not have an effect on the game until it successfully resolves. Because your friend's spell is still waiting to resolve on the stack, its cost-altering effect is not yet active. When you perform the special action of Foretell, you only pay the standard {2} mana required by the Foretell mechanic.
I just played this card that says at the beginning of combat I draw a card, but I didn't actually attack with anything this turn. Do I still get to draw it?

Yes, you do. According to the rules for the combat phase, the very first step is the beginning of combat. Even if you don't declare any attackers—which means the steps for declaring blockers and dealing damage are skipped—the beginning of combat step still occurs. Because the beginning of combat step happens, any ability that triggers at the beginning of that step will automatically trigger as soon as the phase starts. Since your card's trigger is tied to the start of the combat phase itself and not to the act of attacking, you get your card regardless of whether you attack.

I was casting my red creature spell, but my friend has two enchantments out. One makes all spells blue, and the other makes all blue spells green. He tried to use a counterspell that only works on blue spells, but I thought my spell was still red because it started that way. Who is right?

Your friend is right. Even though your spell started as red, the rules state that static abilities from the battlefield apply to spells while they are still on the stack. Because the second enchantment's effect depends on the color established by the first—meaning the second only applies to blue spells—the dependency system requires us to apply the first effect (making the spell blue) before applying the second (turning it green). Consequently, when the counterspell checks if the target is a blue spell, the target is actually green, which makes the target illegal and the counterspell fails.

My opponent has a permanent on the field with a text box that says all our creatures have flying. Then I played a spell that says everything loses flying. But then my friend played another spell on my creature that gives it flying again. We can't agree if it actually has flying or not. What happens?

The creature will have flying. Static abilities are always in effect as long as the source is on the battlefield, meaning the initial ability to fly is a constant truth. However, when multiple continuous effects try to change the same thing, the most recent effect becomes the winner. Because your friend's spell was the last one applied, its effect overrides the previous one that removed flying, resulting in a creature that can fly.

My friend is playing Commander and his commander's ability lets him pull a card from outside the game and put it straight into the exile zone. He tried to bring a blue card, but his commander is only green and white. Is that allowed? Also, if he does get a legal card into exile, and then another spell exiles it again, does the game treat it as a brand new object?

First, we must determine if the card can even enter the game. The player cannot bring the blue card into the game because the rules for bringing cards from outside a Commander game require that the card's color identity matches the color identity of the player's commander. Since the card is blue and the commander is only green and white, the move is illegal. If a legal card had been brought in and then an effect exiled that card while it was already in exile, that card would become a new object because exiling an object that is already in exile creates a brand new object.

My opponent has an enchantment that lets them cast sorceries as if they had flash. While they were in the middle of casting a sorcery, I destroyed the enchantment. They also tried to claim the mana they put in the pool from my creature's ability doesn't count because the creature is gone. What actually happens?

The player can finish casting their spell. Under the rules for casting spells with flash, once a player has begun casting a spell that could be cast as though it had flash, they may continue to cast that spell even if the conditions that allowed it, like the enchantment, stop being met. Regarding the mana, the player's use of that mana is still valid. Because the mana was produced by an ability, the source of that mana is the source of the ability that created it. Once that mana is added to the pool, it remains there regardless of whether the creature that provided it leaves the battlefield. The final outcome is that the player completes the casting of the sorcery using the mana in the pool.

We're playing a four-player game and we realized we never actually decided who sits where or what the turn order was. Now my friend is trying to play a land, but I think it's actually my turn. How do we fix this so he can make his move?

To resolve this, you must first establish whose turn it is. Because seating order is determined by any mutually agreeable method, such as where you were sitting before the game or rolling dice, the players must agree on their positions to define the turn sequence. Once the turn order is settled, the rules for playing a land take precedence regarding the timing of the move. Playing a land is a special action that can only be performed once during each of your turns, specifically during a main phase when the stack is empty and you have priority. The final outcome is that once the players agree on the seating to determine the turn order, the player whose turn it is can play their land provided they are in their main phase and the stack is empty.

We are arguing about this: I have a creature with a +1/+1 counter on it, so it's definitely modified. I want to play a land to trigger my ability that says 'Whenever you play a land, target modified permanent gets an extra counter.' My opponent says I can't because playing a land is just a special action and not a spell, so it doesn't count for the ability.

Your opponent is incorrect. First, you take the special action of playing a land during your main phase while the stack is empty. This action triggers your ability. Next, the ability checks its target to see if it is legal. Because the creature already has a counter on it, it is already considered a modified permanent according to the rule that any permanent with one or more counters on it is modified. Since the special action of playing the land is a valid way to trigger the effect and the creature meets the criteria for being modified, the ability will resolve and you can put another counter on the creature.

I'm in the middle of a game and my opponent has a card that stops anyone from casting spells with even mana values. I have a spell that costs X red mana. Can I cast it? Also, if I use an ability that gives me mana whenever I cast a spell, is the spell I just cast the source of that new mana?

You can cast the spell by choosing a value for X that results in an odd mana value. When you are casting a spell, you can make choices like the value of X during the proposal phase to see if the spell becomes legal to cast. Regarding the mana, the source of any mana produced by an ability is the source of that ability itself. This means the spell you cast is not the source of the extra mana; instead, the specific card or effect providing the mana is the source.

I just cast a spell that says draw three cards and makes my opponent lose life every time I draw, but they have an enchantment out that says I can't draw more than one card each turn. Do they lose three life or just one?

Your opponent loses exactly one life and you draw only one card. Although the spell instructs you to draw three cards, the enchantment acts as a restriction that prevents you from drawing more than one card each turn. Because instructions to draw multiple cards are performed as individual draws, they may be partially carried out; since you cannot draw a second card, the instruction is only partially carried out. Because the ability that triggers when you draw is a reflexive trigger created by the spell, it is checked immediately after being created and triggers based on whether the action occurred during the resolution of the spell. Since you only performed one individual draw, the reflexive trigger occurs only once.

I cast a spell that lets me pick one mode or pay extra to pick two modes. My opponent responded by trying to counter it. Can I wait until their counterspell resolves to decide if I want to pay for the extra modes?

No, you cannot wait. When you cast a spell that has different modes and extra costs like a kicker, you must announce all those choices at the same time you cast it. Even though your opponent acted in response to your spell, which means their spell will resolve before yours does, you have to commit to your specific modes and the kicker cost during the initial announcement. The outcome is that your choices are locked in the moment you cast the spell, regardless of whether the counterspell succeeds.

I was playing a spell that needed a lot of blue mana, and right as I started tapping my islands to pay for it, my opponent tried to cast a counterspell. He said he had to wait until I finished paying everything before he could do anything. Is he right?

Your opponent is correct. When you pay mana to cast a spell, those mana abilities are part of the process of casting that spell. Your opponent does not receive priority to respond to your mana activation; they only receive priority to respond once the spell has been fully cast and placed on the stack. Therefore, they must wait until you have finished paying all costs before they can attempt to cast a counterspell.

We were playing and I cast a spell that exiled my opponent's monster. They have an enchantment that says 'Whenever a creature is exiled, draw a card.' My opponent thought the monster was still technically on the field until the spell finished resolving, so they didn't think they should draw. Who is right?

Your opponent is incorrect. The moment the spell resolves, the creature is put into the exile zone from the battlefield, which fulfills the requirement of being exiled. Because this event has occurred, it meets the trigger condition for the enchantment. Once that condition is met, the enchantment's triggered ability will trigger and be placed on the stack. The final outcome is that the creature is removed from the game and your opponent draws a card.

My friend is playing a green commander, but he just played a blue creature that says "Whenever you tap a creature, draw a card." He tapped a creature and wants to draw, but I am saying he cannot even have that card in his deck. Who is right?

Your friend is incorrect. According to the rules for Commander deck construction, a card can only be included in a deck if every color in its identity is also found in the commander's identity. Since the creature is blue and his commander is only green, that card cannot legally be in his deck. Even though triggered abilities automatically trigger whenever their event occurs, he cannot resolve an ability from a card that should not be in the deck to begin with. The deck construction rule takes precedence because the legality of the cards in the deck must be established for the game to proceed correctly.

My friend has a card that makes his creatures deal double damage, but I used a spell to make his creature have zero power. He says it still deals damage because the doubling effect is active, but I say it does nothing. Who wins?

You are correct. Because the creature's power is zero, the source would deal zero damage. According to the rules, if a source would deal zero damage, it does not deal any damage at all. This means that replacement effects intended to increase or change the damage being dealt have no event to act upon. Since there is no actual damage being dealt, the doubling effect has nothing to replace and cannot function. The final outcome is that the creature deals no damage.
My opponent says I can't cast any spells, so they claim I can't even play a land to trigger my 'whenever you play a land' ability. Is that true?

No, that is not true. Playing a land is a special action that does not use the stack, meaning it can be performed even when you are prohibited from casting spells. Once the land is played via this special action, your ability triggers automatically. Because triggered abilities are not spells or activated abilities, they trigger even when you cannot cast anything. The final outcome is that you play the land and your ability triggers on the stack.

I cast a spell with an escalate cost and I tried to pick two modes but only paid the normal mana cost. My opponent says the second mode doesn't happen, but even if it did, he says my creature would die halfway through the spell because of the discard effect. Am I wrong about both?

You are actually wrong about both parts of that situation. First, because you chose more than one mode when casting the spell, you were required to pay the escalate cost to include that additional mode; if you do not pay it, only the first mode you chose will happen. Second, even if you had paid the cost and both modes occurred, your opponent is wrong about the creature dying mid-spell. While a discard effect might empty your hand during the resolution of the spell, state-based actions like a creature being destroyed for having zero toughness do not check what is happening while a spell is resolving. The game only checks those conditions once the entire spell has finished, meaning your creature would survive the discard and its power would be updated afterward.

We're playing Planechase and my friend rolled the planar die. He has an enchantment that says whenever anyone rolls dice, you lose control of a creature. He chose mine. Then, my opponent cast a spell to destroy that creature right as it was happening. Does my creature's 'when this creature dies' ability still work, and did the roll actually count as rolling dice?

Yes, both things will happen. First, because any ability that triggers whenever a player rolls dice will see the planar die roll, your friend's enchantment will trigger. Second, because abilities that trigger when a creature leaves the battlefield look back in time to determine if they should trigger, your creature's death ability will still work even though it was simultaneously losing control and being destroyed. The final outcome is that your friend's ability triggers due to the roll, you lose control of the creature, and the creature's death ability triggers because the game looks back at its state just before the change occurred.

I just cast a spell that says an opponent gets snow mana and then they pick a creature to sacrifice. My friend says the snow mana is actually colorless, but they also think I should be the one picking the creature because it's my spell. What happens?

Your friend is partially right. While any effect adding snow mana symbols results in colorless mana being added instead, you do not get to pick the creature. When a spell specifies that an opponent makes a choice, that opponent is the one who performs the action. So, your opponent will receive colorless mana and they will be the one to choose which creature is sacrificed.

My friend tried to replace his commander with a different version from his collection because his original was damaged, but I told him he couldn't because the colors didn't match. Then he argued that even if he could use it, the regeneration ability on that card wouldn't stop an opponent's trigger that happens when a creature takes damage. How do we resolve this?

First, you must address the legality of the card; a player cannot bring a card into a Commander game from outside the game if any color in its color identity is not in the color identity of their commander. Second, regarding the ability, your friend is correct that regeneration will not stop those triggers; regeneration is a replacement effect that prevents destruction by removing damage and tapping the permanent instead, but abilities that trigger from damage being dealt still occur. The final outcome is that the card swap is illegal and any damage-triggered abilities will still resolve.

I am playing a card that lets me pick different modes and pay an extra cost to get even more modes. My friend says I have to pick my modes first, then decide if I want to pay the extra cost, and then he can cast a counterspell before I finish choosing. Is he right?

No, he is not right. When you are announcing a spell, the rules allow you to consider all your choices at once, including whether or not you want to pay an additional cost like a kicker to unlock more modes. You do not have to pick one and then decide on the other; you make those decisions as part of the announcement process. Once you have finished making all those choices and paid the necessary mana, the spell is officially cast and placed on the stack. Only after the spell is on the stack does the system of priority allow your opponent to cast an instant in response. The final outcome is that you can decide to pay the extra cost and pick all your modes simultaneously during the announcement, and your opponent can only attempt to counter the spell once it has successfully reached the stack.

I just played this Celebr-8000 card and its ability says whenever I roll two dice, I do something, but then it mentions an extra effect if I roll doubles. I rolled two 5s. My opponent is saying the extra effect doesn't happen because it's not a separate triggered ability. Is he right?

Your opponent is incorrect. Because the ability is written as one continuous instruction where a static part is linked to a triggered part, the entire effect is treated as a single unit that happens when you roll the dice. Since your rolls of 5 and 5 are identical, you have officially rolled doubles. Therefore, both the main effect of the ability and the additional effect for rolling doubles will resolve together as part of that one single trigger.

I just cast a spell that turned my only attacker into a land. My opponent says I can't get my attack alone trigger anymore, and they want to know if I can even take it out of combat. What is the deal?

You will still get your trigger, and you can remove the creature from combat. Because you declared that creature as your only attacker, it met the requirement for attacking alone, which means it is an attacker and no other creatures are attacking. Even though the creature became a land and can no longer attack, you can use a special action to remove it from combat. A special action is something you can do when you have priority that does not use the stack. Because the creature was already considered as attacking alone at the moment of declaration, your trigger will resolve, but the special action ensures the land is no longer in combat.

I have one creature on the board and I declared it as my only attacker. My opponent used a spell that made another creature die, and now they are claiming that because the game checks for things like dead creatures, my creature might not be considered to be attacking alone anymore. Is that right?

Your creature is still attacking alone. When you declare a single creature as an attacker, it is attacking alone because it is the only creature declared as an attacker during that step. Although the game checks for state-based actions like creatures dying from zero toughness before any player gets priority to act, those actions do not change your creature's status unless your creature itself dies. If the opponent's spell causes a different creature to die, the game processes that death during its state-based action check, but your creature remains the only declared attacker and thus remains attacking alone.
My opponent has a card out that says they can't lose, and I have an enchantment that lets me draw cards whenever a player loses. If they hit zero life, do I get my cards?

No, you will not draw the cards. The opponent's card provides a static ability, which is a constant effect that is always true as long as it is on the battlefield. This effect prevents the event of losing from ever happening. Because the loss never actually occurs, your enchantment's triggered ability, which only activates when a player loses, will never be triggered.

I was playing a game where I had a creature that is always an Elf because of its text. My opponent played a card that said all creatures are now Humans. Then, the Elf died, and I have an ability that triggers whenever an Elf dies. My opponent claims nothing happens because the creature was a Human, but I think it should still trigger. Who is right?

You are right, and the ability will trigger. Because the creature's identity as an Elf is a characteristic-defining ability, it defines the object's subtype and overrides any other information, like your opponent's effect making everything a Human. This kind of ability works in all zones to ensure the creature maintains its correct type. Since the creature remains an Elf, when it dies, the event of an Elf dying has actually occurred. Because the event matches the requirements of your triggered ability, the ability will automatically trigger.

I tapped my artifact to make mana from a color I control. Then, in response, my opponent cast a spell that destroyed all my colored permanents. Why didn't I get any mana even though I tapped my artifact first?

Even though you activated your ability first, your opponent cast their spell in response, which puts their spell on top of the stack. This means their destruction spell will resolve before your mana ability does. Once the destruction spell resolves and removes your colored permanents, your artifact's ability finally attempts to resolve. Because there are no colored permanents left to define a color, the ability produces no mana at all.

My commander is a legendary creature that says at the beginning of my upkeep I may draw a card. I want to draw it, but my opponent says I have to put it on the stack first and they might be able to stop me. Since it is my commander, do I get to just do it?

Because you are playing the Commander variant, your legendary creature serves as your commander, but it still follows the standard rules for triggered abilities. Even though the ability says you may draw a card, that trigger must go on the stack when it happens, regardless of whether you intend to use it or not. The choice to actually draw the card is made only when the ability resolves. This means your opponent can respond to the trigger after it hits the stack but before you actually draw the card.

I just cast a spell that exiled three of my opponent's cards face-down, and they were put into separate piles. My opponent has a creature that says whenever a card is exiled, target that card and destroy it. Can my opponent pick one specific face-down card to destroy?

The zone-change trigger occurs first as a result of the cards moving into exile. Once the ability begins to resolve, it looks for the cards in that new zone to find them. However, because the cards were exiled face-down into separate piles, the player must then follow the rules for selecting face-down cards. Since they are not allowed to look at the cards, they must choose a pile first, and then a card is chosen at random from within that pile. The final outcome is that one card from a chosen pile will be destroyed, but the player cannot pick a specific individual card without choosing a pile first.

I just cast two different enchantments that make my creatures deal double damage, and my friend thinks the damage should keep doubling every time it is calculated. If the damage finally stops at 8, how does his creature actually die? Do we have to wait for someone to cast a spell?

The damage will not double infinitely because a replacement effect only gets one opportunity to affect an event, so your two effects will change the 2 damage into 4 and then into 8, but they will not keep looping. Once that 8 damage has been dealt, the game automatically performs its state-based action checks. These are continuous checks that happen throughout the game to see if any creatures have zero toughness or lethal damage. Because his creature's toughness is lower than the 8 damage it received, the game will immediately remove it from the battlefield as a state-based action without needing any spells.

I just cast my spell and rolled a natural 15 on a d20. I have an effect that lets me add 3 to the roll, but my opponent has a trigger that says whenever a die is rolled, they can exile a card from my graveyard unless I pay 2 mana. I want to use my bonus but I don't want to pay their cost. What happens?

The rules for die rolls take precedence in determining the final number, which is 18 after adding your plus three modifier to the natural 15. Separately, the rules for triggered abilities ensure that your opponent's ability goes on the stack immediately because all such abilities go on the stack regardless of whether you intend to satisfy an unless clause. The final outcome is a die roll of 18 and the opponent's ability goes on the stack for you to resolve.

I was playing a card that lets me draw a card whenever my hand is empty. My opponent used a spell that was supposed to take all my cards and put them into their graveyard. Did my ability trigger, and where did my cards actually go?

The rule regarding zone changes applies first to determine where your cards go. Even though the spell tried to move your cards to your opponent's graveyard, those cards actually go to your own graveyard instead. Because your hand became empty as a result of this movement, the state-triggered ability then detects that your hand is empty and places the draw trigger on the stack. It will not trigger repeatedly while the ability is waiting to resolve, even though your hand stays empty. The final outcome is that your cards go to your graveyard and you get exactly one draw trigger on the stack.

My opponent has a planeswalker with 2 loyalty left. I attack with my creature that has first strike and it deals 5 damage. My opponent says I haven't actually dealt any excess damage yet because there is still another combat damage step coming for the rest of my creatures. Is that right?

No, they are incorrect. Because your creature has first strike, it assigns its damage during the first combat damage step, which is a separate part of the combat process before the second step occurs. According to the rules for excess damage, once a permanent is dealt an amount of damage greater than its loyalty, the difference is calculated as excess damage. Since your 5 damage is greater than the 2 loyalty, 3 points of excess damage are dealt immediately during that first combat damage step. The existence of a second combat damage step for your other creatures does not delay this calculation.

I just moved an enchantment from my opponent's creature to mine. This enchantment makes the creature a 5/5 and says it has to attack every turn. My opponent claims that because they have a card out that says players can't attack, the enchantment doesn't work on my creature anymore. What's actually happening?

When you move an enchantment, its ability moves with it and starts modifying your creature instead of the original one, because these attachments modify whatever object they are currently attached to rather than targeting a specific card. Regarding the attacking rule, effects that change game rules, like requiring a creature to attack or preventing attacks entirely, are applied after all other continuous effects. In this case, the enchantment's instruction to attack is a game rule modification. Since your opponent's card also modifies the game rules, both are applied at the end of the effect sequence. However, the global rule that players cannot attack takes precedence over the individual requirement for that creature to attack. The final outcome is that your creature is a 5/5 but does not have to attack.

My friend's commander was exiled by my spell, but then I hit his commander for 5 combat damage with my creature. He says he can just move it back to his command zone even though it is in exile, and that if the total damage from that commander reaches 21 he loses. Is he right?

Yes, your friend is correct. First, we look at where the card is located. Even though the commander is in the exile zone, which is a recognized zone in the game, the rules for Commander games allow a player to move their commander from either the graveyard or exile back into the command zone if it was put there since the last time state-based actions were checked. Second, we check the combat damage rule. In a Commander game, if a single commander has dealt 21 or more combat damage to a player over the course of the game, that player loses. Since both of these are handled during the state-based actions phase, your friend can move the commander back and will lose the game if the cumulative damage reaches 21.

My opponent has a card that is both a creature and a planeswalker. I hit it with two creatures for a total of 5 damage, and right at the same time, an effect gives it three -1/-1 counters. It dies immediately, but I was hoping to trigger an ability that happens when it takes excess damage. Does that still work?

Yes, the ability will trigger. When multiple state-based actions happen at once, such as a permanent leaving the battlefield because of lethal toughness or loyalty, the game looks at the last known information of that permanent from before those actions were performed. Since the permanent was still on the battlefield and had received the damage just before the state-based actions occurred, it is treated as if it were still there for any triggers. To determine how much excess damage was dealt, you must look at both its creature and planeswalker types. You calculate the excess for each type individually—in this case, 2 damage in excess of its 3 toughness and 0 damage in excess of its 5 loyalty—and then use the largest amount, which is 2. So, the ability will trigger based on 2 excess damage.

I just used a spell to add snow mana, and it was supposed to trigger my ability that makes me lose life whenever I add colorless mana. But right then, my opponent's creature died because its toughness hit zero. Do I still lose the life, and does the mana actually count as colorless?

Yes, you will still lose the life, and the process follows a specific order. First, the snow mana is added to your pool as colorless mana because any effect adding snow mana symbols results in colorless mana being added to the pool. This addition causes your ability to trigger. However, before that trigger can even be put on the stack, the game must first perform all applicable state-based actions. Since the creature has zero toughness, it is moved to the graveyard during this step. Only after these state-based actions are finished is your triggered ability placed on the stack.

My friend is playing a red commander and I saw a blue card in his hand when he accidentally dropped them. He says because hands are hidden zones, it does not matter what is in there for the deck legality. Is he right?

He is incorrect. Even though the hand is considered a hidden zone where players are not expected to see card faces, the rules for Commander deck construction are absolute. Because every card in a Commander deck must match the color identity of its commander, seeing an illegal blue card in his hand means his deck is not legal. The requirement for matching color identity takes precedence over the privacy of the hidden zone when a violation is discovered. The outcome is that the player must remove the blue card from their deck to ensure all cards match their commander's red color identity.

I have two cards that both say if a creature deals damage, it deals double instead. If I have a card that says whenever I have no creatures, I deal 1 damage, and I clear my board, do I deal 8 damage? And will it keep dealing 8 damage every turn since I have no creatures?

You will deal 4 damage exactly once. The state trigger occurs first, as soon as you have no creatures on the battlefield, which puts the ability to deal damage on the stack. This trigger will not repeat simply because you still have no creatures; it will only trigger again once the current ability has resolved or left the stack. Once that ability is on the stack and attempts to resolve, the replacement effects take precedence over the original event. The first doubling effect replaces the 1 damage with 2, and then the second effect replaces that 2 with 4. Because replacement effects only get one opportunity to affect an event or any modified events that replace that event, the damage does not continue to double infinitely.

My friend and I are playing Commander and we hit a disagreement. My legendary commander has an ability where instead of it entering the battlefield, it gets exiled and I get a 2/2 token. My friend has an enchantment that says whenever a permanent enters the battlefield, it enters tapped instead. He thinks my commander should enter the battlefield tapped, but I think it just gets exiled. What happens?

You are correct. Because your legendary creature is acting as a commander and its ability contains a self-replacement effect, which means the text specifically replaces part of its own entry onto the battlefield, this must be applied before any other replacement effects. Rules dictate that these self-replacement effects are applied before other replacement effects. Since your commander's ability replaces the event of it entering the battlefield with an event where it is exiled and a token is created, the enchantment that forces permanents to enter tapped never actually sees the commander attempting to enter. The final outcome is that your commander is exiled and you receive a 2/2 creature token.
